en: The Commentary on the Gītā with the Śrī Tātparya-candrikā.
May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians, the preeminent Vedāntācārya, ever abide within my intellect.

May that glorious Lord, the charioteer of Dhanañjaya, grant me an intellect that removes the fatigue of the coming and going on the path of worldly existence— an intellect which the preeminent among ascetics [Vyāsa] directly revealed through his Gītās as the flawless state of being closest to the assembly of the Vedas.
Enough, enough with excessive fear, anxiety, and despondency born of contemplating improper courses;
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow protects us who have come for refuge, proclaiming the sublime Upaniṣad for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Let the virtuous, who lick the essence [of truth], devote themselves to this *Bhagavadgītā-bhāṣya-tātparya-candrikā*, which dispels the darkness of the mind.

Desiring to comment upon the glorious *Gītā*, and for the sake of completing it without obstacle and ensuring its widespread propagation, [the author] performs an auspicious invocation consisting of devotion to the Supreme Teacher. In doing so, by means of composing a summary verse, he reflects upon the Supreme Teacher’s status as the instructor of its meaning and his own state of pleasing his own teacher through following him, beginning with the words "yat-padāmbhoruha... and so forth.

By the word "ya" (which), he indicates the renown resulting from the perfection of all supreme qualities of the Teacher. By the word "ambhoruha" (lotus), because it conveys the sense of being an object of enjoyment, the nature of meditation as devotion is revealed. The word "dhyāna" (meditation) is used with the intention: "I am like Ekalavya to Yāmunācārya, who is my Droṇācārya."

By a single vision, impurities are for the most part destroyed; by continuous recollection rooted in that [vision], their eradication along with their latent impressions (*savāsanonmūlana*) is accomplished—this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "He whose every impurity has been destroyed by meditation. In reality, however, this refers to the state described in such passages as, "If one knows that 'the Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing. "I have attained the state of reality" contains an element of wonder.

Thus, this salutation—performed by means of the triad of speech and the other organs, impelled by the recollection of the benefaction consisting in the removal of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable—is included in the treatise for the purpose of instructing the disciples and for the sake of the attainment of results for the listeners. By this, one is also instructed that worship of the lineage of one's teacher must be performed with the utmost reverence, just as one would for one's own teacher. Accordingly, it is heard in scripture: "And that lineage of teachers is to be known, starting from the Blessed One, thinking 'this is such-and-such a teacher, and that is such-and-such a teacher.'"

Now, by means of describing and contemplating the essential nature, form, qualities, and majesty of the Blessed One—the supreme deity who is his own chosen ideal—he performs, as it were, an unbroken auspicious invocation: "He whose sole object is devotion, which is to be accomplished through one's own duty, knowledge, and dispassion..."

By stating, "Nārāyaṇa is declared in the Gītā-śāstra to be the Supreme Brahman," [the author] demonstrates, in accordance with the summary, the primary subject matter of the treatise to be expounded along with its various modes; and, for the sake of establishing the authority of the scripture, he supports the speaker’s status as the most trustworthy person (*āptatama*) by showing his freedom from error, deception, negligence, and incapacity through his inherent omniscience, supreme compassion, readiness to protect the virtuous, and omnipotence; [and thus establishes him as the source of] the means to the four aims of life, of which liberation (*apavarga*) is the foremost.

Illuminating both the intermediate purpose, which consists of enlightenment (*bodha*), and the supreme purpose, which is the nature of the Lord (*bhagavatsvarūpa*) in all its aspects to be experienced at the stage of liberation (*apavarga*), and thereby harmonizing the commencement of the treatise by demonstrating that the objections regarding the impossibility of beginning the instruction of the scripture—which will be stated—apply to the systems of Śaṅkara and others but not to my own system through the statement of the ultimate identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as conducive to the instruction of the scripture; and [establishing] the consistency of all the statements concerning the distinctions and non-distinctions among the purificatory meditations on the Cause (*kāraṇa-śodhaka-upāsana*).

Proclaiming [the truth], and establishing the systematic arrangement of the subject matter—which sweeps away the quarrels caused by the deceptions of those of little learning and weak intellect through the secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) concerning the injunctions and prohibitions regarding the manifestation, birth, glory, and activities of the one born from the body of qualities (*guṇatanuja*); and indicating the resolution of contradictions established in the second chapter of the *Śārīraka*, since all activities—even of the One who has attained all desires—are performed as mere sport (*līlā*); and [establishing] the specific deity who is the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the world to be known, by means of the principles of the "commonality of cognition across all recensions" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-sāmānya*), the "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), and so forth.

Describing His form as defined by the exclusion of being a third distinct individual—whether as the three-fold source (trimūrti), as a single unity, as equanimity, or as transcendent—and thereby proclaiming His supreme accessibility through the manifestation of the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra) which grants the realization of one's own Self as the supreme human goal; this realization being attained even through the mere pretext of His engagement in all worldly activities from the initial resolve "May I become many" up to His conduct as a charioteer, [the Lord] is endowed with a host of qualities suitable for establishing His attainability, His status as the object of worship, His absolute supremacy, and His extreme accessibility.

Illustrating the Lord’s lordship over the world, omniscience, omnipotence, and universal sovereignty, as well as His supreme redness (paramāruṇikatva), His being the auspicious refuge, His descent for the sake of those who take refuge in Him, His habit of dispelling contradictions, and His pleasing appearance, [the author] connects the ancient account of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa—the supreme subject of the Pañcarātra Veda—with the instruction of the Gītā Upaniṣad, from the words "The Lord of Śrī" up to "He caused [Himself] to descend."

With the second sentence, beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "and" (*ca*), there is an extraction of the known portions for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who desires to know. With the third sentence, beginning with "Even though he knows thus" (*evaṃ jñātvāpi*), however, there is the connection of the question that serves as the introduction to the commencement of the Śāstra.

Here, intending to distinguish and show everything other than the nature of the divine Self as being the referent of the word *nara*, [the author] first extracts and demonstrates that nature—which is the substratum (*ayana*) of that [Self]—as the primary element in both compounds, whether as the external member (*anyapadārtha*) or as the final member (*uttarapadārtha*).

By the words "Lord of Śrī" and so forth: Śrī is mentioned first here for the purpose of making known the specific [nature] of the Lord, for establishing His accessibility, and for the attainment of all auspiciousness. As it is said: "This glorious Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk, leaving His serpent-couch, has come here to the city of Madhurā"; and one should consider such passages as "Artha is Viṣṇu, this is Vāṇī. The qualification "entire" (sakala) is used to exclude the service of holy places and the like, which only remove a few things to be abandoned; here, the absence of anything to be abandoned is established by implication.

Indeed, one who is capable of eliminating every single thing to be abandoned (*heya*) found in another cannot tolerate what is to be abandoned within himself. Alternatively, the meaning is that He is "devoid of the abandonable" because His very nature is opposed to the abandonable; in that case, the word "entire" (*nikhila*) includes all modifications and so forth residing in all insentient things (*acid*), as well as all afflictions and so forth residing in all sentient beings (*cit*). The term "exclusively auspicious" (*kalyāṇaikatāna*) is used to dispel the notion—imagined by those of poor intellect—that there might be even a trace of the inauspicious through some partial distinction. For this very reason, there is no tautology with the phrase "whose sole essential nature is knowledge and bliss."

Alternatively, there is no tautology because this consists of a general statement followed by a specific description; or rather, it is a summary of the detailed exposition of qualities that will be described hereafter, in the sense that he is "constantly devoted to auspiciousness" and thus the very locus of all auspicious virtues.

With the intention that there is no other such entity because the three types—conscious, unconscious, and dependent on others—are equal in their dependence on another and so forth, he says: "other than itself" (*svetara*). By this, even though there is equality in knowledge and experience, the denial of equality in every respect is established. [As it is said: "Eternal, omnipresent, all-pervading," and "All this is indeed the Puruṣa."

He states separately, primarily, the well-known absence of the three kinds of limitation, beginning with the word "ananta" (infinite): "Infinite" means devoid of the three kinds of limitation. Limitation of space is as follows: "It exists in this place, but it does not exist in that place. Limitation of time is: "It exists at this time, but it does not exist at that time. Limitation of substance is: "This is not that," or it may refer to the inferiority of its own nature, such as [the difference between] base metal and gold.

This absence of the three kinds of limitation consists in being all-pervasive across all space and time, and in being the inner controller of all things. Indeed, the absence of limitation by objects refers to the capacity for grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all objects and so forth; it does not, however, mean identity with various mutually contradictory objects, nor the falsity of all objects distinct from itself, because both of these are utterly impossible. We have provided a detailed exposition of this in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*.

Since bliss (*ānanda*) is a specific kind of knowledge (*jñāna*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "knowledge" and "bliss" is justified. If it is argued that, because the word "bliss" is a particularizing term (*viśeṣaśabda*), one should say "knowledge-bliss" (*ānandajñānam*)—just as one says "pot-substance" (*ghaṭadravyam*) and so forth—that is not so; for everything is justified by the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇa*). Alternatively, since the word "bliss" is applied even to insentient things that are experienced as agreeable, the word "knowledge" can appropriately precede it as its qualifier. Or, these two qualifiers may both refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman].

Regarding the term *svābhāvikī* (inherent): although there is equality in the inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*) of the form, attributes, and names with respect to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the qualities (*guṇa*) are mentioned first in order to demonstrate that [the Lord] depends upon the multitude of qualities such as knowledge for the regulation of assuming the body and so forth, and for the sake of making each subsequent [aspect] easier to comprehend. Since the group of six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is the foremost among the entire collection of qualities, they are included by their very name; and other qualities such as good character (*sauśīlya*) and the rest are subsumed by the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*). Although you possess infinite qualities, these six alone are the primary qualities.

They say: "By whom others as well have been placed within the belly of the world, just like you. Regarding the triad of manifestations beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, which are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, the specific sequence of "knowledge, power," and so forth has been established because of the specific manifestation of each member of the triad of pairs—knowledge, power, and the rest—as being oriented toward their respective particular functions in due order.

He directly perceives everything in every way and at all times; he retains everything thus perceived; while retaining it, he masters it; while retaining and mastering it, he becomes unwavering; he brings about what was unaccomplished; and in that regard, being independent of auxiliary causes, he is not overcome by anything, but rather becomes the overcomer of all—such is the intended meaning of the sequence of qualities in the recitation. "Naturalness" (*svābhāvikatva*) means independence from anything else (*ananyādhīnatva*).

For even in the case of liberation and eternity, such qualities as knowledge and the rest are dependent upon the will of the Supreme Self corresponding to them. Here, "limitlessness" (anavadhikatva) means the absence of any superior limit. By these two qualifiers, the "supremacy" and "inherent nature" mentioned in the scripture—namely, "The power of the Supreme is indeed manifold; His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent"—are demonstrated as being conjoined with each respective attribute. This is further illustrated by the words "innumerable" (asaṅkhyeya) and "great ocean" (mahodadhi), as in: "Just as the jewels of the ocean are innumerable, O son..."

And thus, such passages as "Indeed, the qualities of the infinite Great Self are innumerable" have been recalled. By the word "auspicious" (kalyāṇa), it is indicated that the principle of the general rule and its exception establishes that statements denying qualities refer only to qualities that are to be abandoned.

Now, he demonstrates the possession of a distinct physical form as established in the sections concerning the worship of the Cause (*kāraṇopasana*) and in the chapters on the ornaments of Aruṇa (*aruṇabhūṣaṇādhyāya*), and so forth—by the words "conforming to what is intended by oneself" (*svābhimatānurūpa*). Since in the world it is observed that even what is intended may be unsuitable, and even what is unsuitable may be intended, the phrase "conforming to what is intended by oneself" is stated in order to exclude both of those possibilities.

By the term "of a single form" (*ekarūpa*), it is stated that even in states such as the *vyūha* and *vibhava*, there is no abandonment of its essential nature—namely, being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*heya*), bringing about bliss, being the object of worship for those seeking liberation (*umukṣu*), and being the ultimate goal to be attained. Alternatively, it is said that even when transformations such as the *vyūha* occur, the physical form (*vigraha*) residing in the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*) remains established in its original configuration. The statement regarding its "inconceivability" (*acintyatva*) is made with the intention of showing that arguments such as "it is impermanent because it possesses parts" are fallacious due to the sublation of the very basis of the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādha*).

One divine term (*divyaśabda*) refers to the distinctness of its configuration (*saṃsthānavailakṣaṇya*), or simply to its existence within the supreme ether (*paramavyoma*); the other, however, refers to its non-material nature (*aprākṛtatva*). By the word "wonderful" (*adbhuta*), what is intended is the connection with various incarnations (*avatāra*), the state of being experienced as something unprecedented at every moment, and the marvel found in states such as reclining on a banyan leaf or assuming the universal form (*viśvarūpa*). "Eternality" (*nityatva*) means being undelimited by time (*kālāparicchedyatva*).

And thus those who know the secret tradition (rahasyāmnāya) declare: "The eternally unmanifested, naturally perfected [nature] possesses the forms of the senses and the major and minor limbs as its manifestations. And in the Śrīpauṣkara: "O Pauṣkara, for one who has existence within the heart regarding that eternal form and its supreme state, it (the Goddess) shall come into his presence. "Faultlessness" means being free from old age and so forth; or rather, what is intended is that among the successively faultless terms, each preceding one is easier to grasp than the subsequent ones.

The possession of auspicious qualities suitable for being a pure substratum, an object of enjoyment, and so forth, as well as unsurpassed brilliance and other such attributes, has been described [in the preceding verses]. "Unsurpassedness" (niratiśayatva) means the absence of anything superior to itself.

It possesses unsurpassedness, and that [quality] should be understood in relation to each individual attribute. *Aujjvalya* is brilliance. *Sauśurya* is the beauty of the limbs. The scriptural statement "possessing all fragrances" (*sarvagandhaḥ*) refers to agreeable odors; however, the word "sweet fragrance" (*saugandhya*) is used here with the intention that even [ordinary scents like] sandalwood and the like are rendered superfluous by it. *Saukumārya* is softness that maintains the name "flower-smile" despite possessing great strength, as it has been said: "They are both delicate and of great strength. *Lāvaṇya* is the beauty of the entire form as a whole.

As it is said in the *Bhagavat-śāstra*: "Nourishing the universe with a radiance equal to ten million full moons. And they say: "Tejas (luminous energy) itself, when greatly softened by abundant waters, is called *lāvaṇya* (loveliness), which produces delight for the eyes. Youth (*yauvana*) is a specific state of nature to be characterized as succeeding childhood (*kaumāra*), but it is not merely the stage occurring immediately after childhood; for youth is beginningless, and we observe that some among the gods and others are born already in their youth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all the explanations of the analysis of compounds mentioned in the sections on auspicious bases (śubhāśraya) are included.

Having thus established the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its qualities, as well as the physical form (*vigraha*) and its qualities, he now shows the collection of ornaments and the collection of weapons resting upon that form by means of the two words beginning with "svocita" (suitable to itself). Here, the meaning of the word "self" (*sva*) refers to the essential nature characterized by a physical form distinct from what was previously described. In this regard, one should consider such passages as: "His arms are long, well-rounded, and like iron clubs; they are worthy of being adorned by every ornament. Their variety consists in forms such as crowns (*kirīṭa*), necklaces (*hāra*), and so forth.

Even among things of a single class, there is variety due to the differences between individual instances distinguished by specific qualities such as color, shape, and so forth, in the case of substances like jewels, gold, and the like. By the statement "immeasurable" (*aparimita*), which expresses their incalculability, "infinitude" (*anantatva*) is an adjective qualifying the wonders. "Infinite wonder" (*anantāścarya*) means possessing the quality of bringing about a limitless sense of wonder; or alternatively, it refers to those ornaments which possess infinite wonders, such as particular shapes, fragrance, and pleasant touch. The terms "eternal" (*nitya*) and "faultless" (*niravadya*) are as explained previously.

"Immeasurable" (*aparimitatva*) means precisely "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeyatva*), and not the absence of measurements such as shortness or length. Alternatively, "endless" (*ananta*) signifies innumerability, while "immeasurable" (*aparimita*) intends a magnitude corresponding to its etymological analysis (*vigraha*). The "divinity" (*divyatva*) of the ornaments and weapons means their non-material nature (*aprākṛtatva*). In the phrase "conforming to Himself" (*svānurūpa*), the referent of the word "Self" (*sva*) is that which is distinguished by the previously mentioned qualities, form, and ornaments. Regarding "innumerable": the well-known state of having five weapons is due to their predominance; this is the intended meaning. "Of inconceivable power" (*acintyaśakti*): [and so forth].

The sense is that the splitting of the *sāla* trees, the mountains, and the surface of the earth—which would each require great effort to accomplish with tools such as axes, chisels, and spades—was indeed performed by a single great arrow. His state of unsurpassed auspiciousness consists in his bringing about unsurpassed bliss, since he has entered even into the category of ornaments; or else, it means he is complete with all those things renowned in the world as weapons that bring about auspiciousness.

Having previously described Śrī in general terms as that which defines His essential nature, the author now shows her specifically as existing even within His manifestations (*vibhūti*), and by implication, describes Her essential nature and other attributes as well—beginning with the words "svābhimata" (as desired by Himself). "Svarūpa" refers to the divine essential nature of Śrī, characterized by attributes unique to Her. "Rūpa" refers to Her divine form. The word "guṇa," occurring immediately after "rūpa," refers to the unsurpassed brilliance, beauty, and other qualities inherent in that form. The word "vibhava" refers to Her attendants, retinue, and so forth.

The two groups of qualities conducive to accessibility and supremacy are indicated by the terms *aiśvarya* (supremacy) and *śīla* (virtue). Consequently, because the word "beginning" (*ādi*) connects with each [term], it includes knowledge, power, and so forth, as well as compassion, kindness, and so forth. Since it would be inappropriate for supremacy, virtue, and the rest to be considered mere "groups" (*gaṇa*), and since even the quality of "being infinitely unsurpassed" (*anavadhikātiśayatva*)—if taken as a qualifier of the group—would not explicitly convey the excellence of each individual quality, it is appropriate that the compound be understood as having these [qualities] as qualifiers of the [individual] virtues.

The compound *svarūpam, rūpam, tadguṇaḥ, vibhavaḥ, aiśvaryādiguṇagaṇaśca* is a *dvandva*. She whose fivefold nature—beginning with *svarūpa* (essential nature), *rūpa* (form), *tadguṇa* (its qualities), *vibhava* (manifestation), and the multitude of qualities such as *aiśvarya* (sovereignty)—is in accordance with the will of the Blessed Lord, is described by the passage ending with "the multitude of qualities such as being His own beloved. If one were to construe it as "the multitude of qualities such as essential nature, form, its qualities, manifestation, sovereignty, character (*śīla*), and so forth," there would be the undesirable consequence of essential nature and form themselves being included among the qualities. That everything beginning with essential nature is intended by the Supreme Self is evident.

The eternity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists in its existence at all times due to its being changeless. Its permanence (*nityavad-yatva*) is of the same manner as previously established regarding the essential nature of the Supreme Self, or alternatively, it is the absence of occasional traits such as heat induced by His role as a father. Its conformity (*anurūpatva*), however, is—as before—in accordance with the authoritative means of knowledge, consisting solely in the state of being exclusively auspicious; here, passages such as "peaceful and infinite" (*śāntānanta*) are to be kept in mind.

The eternity of form (*rūpa*) refers to its remaining in that very same state even during the stage of descent (*avatāra*), while residing in the singular seat of the Lord who dwells in the supreme abode (*paramapada*). Its conformity (*anurūpatva*) has been established in such passages as: "Just as is the form of this Goddess, with the excellence of her limbs and minor members, so too is the form of Rāma; she is this dark-eyed one for him," and "She indeed fashions for herself a body that conforms to the body of Viṣṇu. The eternity of the qualities of the physical form (*vigraha-guṇa*) means the absence of any diminution whatsoever of its brilliance and other attributes at any time.

Faultlessness (*niravadyatva*) is the absence of being difficult to perceive. Suitability (*anurūpatva*) is of the kind described in such passages as, "Though you possess the youthful state of dense golden luster, you still maintain an innocent state (*mugdha-daśā*). Suitability in terms of wealth (*vibhava*) is—

One should reflect upon these words: "Among gods, animals, and humans, the Blessed Lord Hari is the one who bears male names, while Lakṣmī is the one who bears female names, O Maitreya; there exists nothing beyond these two. Because of the statement regarding her being of "unlimited excellence," her sovereignty—though its scope extends to everything other than that which is designated as the Supreme Lord—is nonetheless accepted by the Lord Himself; thus, there is no fault such as "dual sovereignty" (dvairājya). For, in her capacity as the consort of Viṣṇu, as expressed in the verse, "The wife of Viṣṇu is the mistress of this world," she rules over the entire universe.

Regarding the phrase "the sovereign of all beings" (*īśvarī sarvabhūtānām*), although one cannot intend for her to be the "wife of Īśvara" based on the mention of the correlative "of all beings" (*sarvabhūtānām*) and the feminine suffix, nevertheless, the fact that her nature is such is established by the force of other scriptural passages. Her "faultlessness" (*niravadyatvam*) consists either in having the singular essence of the Lord’s sovereignty or in the absence of any occasion for punishment and the like. For the quality of meting out adverse punishment is a portion belonging only to the beloved of that [Lord], corresponding to His own masculinity.

The constancy of Śūla (the spear) means that even though it is great, there is never any manifestation of self-exaltation when in contact with the lowly. Its faultlessness consists in the absence of any intention to deceive and so forth. Its suitability and its state of being infinitely superior are according to the manner described in such passages as "having similar character and conduct. Thus, by establishing the distinct, eternal nature, qualities, majesty, sovereignty, character, and so forth of Śrī, [it is shown that she is] not merely a power (*śakti*) that is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) like the qualities of knowledge and the rest, nor is she a particular manifestation (*vyūhaviśeṣa*).

The claims that [the Lord] is identical with His own nature (*svarūpaikya*) or anything else have been refuted. As for the doctrine of His being "Power" (*śaktitva*), it intends to convey that He is a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) employed for a specific purpose by virtue of being the Consort (*patnī*). Indeed, in all the scriptures, the word "Power" (*śakti*) is used for the female component even in other dual compounds consisting of both male and female. Furthermore, the doctrines asserting oneness (*ekatva*) have been resolved through the following perspectives: as the locus of a single residuum (*ekaśeṣitva*) relative to the entire universe; as a specific unity (*viśiṣṭaikya*); or in the form of being the single deity (*devatā*) intended for the sacrificial offering of the Self (*ātmahavis*).

For this very reason, it is said: "Due to their pervasive and intense union, they have arisen as if they were a single reality. And it has been stated by the venerable Rāmamiśra in the *Ṣaḍarthasaṃkṣepa*: "The one substratum of both is the state of being the possessor," and so forth. He is the beloved (*vallabha*)—the most dear—of such a Goddess Śrī; or, she whose beloved is Śrī. Nor is there a redundancy of the word *abhimata* (beloved), because its purpose is to manifest an excellence of being beloved by referring respectively to each [member] and to the whole.

Now, he demonstrates the distinction of the eternal attendants (nityaparijana) with the words "by their own volition" (*svasaṅkalpa*). "Own nature" (*svarūpa*) refers to the aspect of duty (*dhamryaṃśa*). "Abiding" (*sthiti*) is remaining without falling away from that state. "Activity" (*pravṛtti*) is functional operation. The fact that the nature and abiding of the eternal ones are subject to the volition of the Supreme Self means that they are established by His will. This [subjection] merely implies the possibility of being withdrawn should there be a lack of desire [on His part]. However, since a lack of desire toward them never occurs at any time, their abiding is perpetual.

And this state of having one's essential nature, existence, and activity conform to the will of the Supreme Self (paramātman) should be understood to apply even to the bound souls (baddha), the liberated (mukta), primordial matter (prakṛti), its evolutes (prākṛta), time (kāla), and so forth; all of this will be elaborated upon later. "Subsidiarity" (śeṣatā) means the state of being a subordinate function (śeṣavṛtti). "The state of being the entirety of the subsidiary" (aśeṣaśeṣatā) refers to the state of possessing whatever form is intended. In this regard, one should look to such passages as: "Various kinds of arrows, assuming forms as long as a bow, followed the descendant of Kakutstha, all of them in human forms."

For since every single service performed by each individual is mutually intended for the sake of all, everyone becomes a performer of all services for him. Alternatively, the terms "entirety" (aśeṣa) and "distinction" (bheda) refer to his essential nature (svarūpa), subsistence (sthiti), and activity (pravṛtti); the state of being a subordinate (śeṣabhāva) with respect to the Supreme Self of all those [three] is what is meant.

In this manner, regarding the state of being a subordinate (śeṣatā) as described, those whose form, nature, or essence consists solely of the love that rests upon Him alone—having abandoned all else—are "those whose sole delight is in the state of being the subordinate without remainder. And they are all eternal. Since the eternity of essential nature is common to all souls, the word "eternal" here excludes the idea of having one's essential nature manifested only at some point, as is the case with liberated souls; rather, the meaning is that they possess qualities such as knowledge that are eternally uncontracted.

For that very reason, they are irreproachable, being entirely devoid of defects such as the conceit of independence regarding afflictions and karma. Their excellence in knowledge consists in its equality with the knowledge of the Supreme Self. Their excellence in action consists in its nature as independent and infinite service. Their excellence in sovereignty consists in their unimpeded power over the regulation of the bodies, senses, and so forth, which they assume by their own will for the sake of serving the Supreme Self.

However, there is no possession of all objects [as their domain], according to the principle: "Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of being non-proximate. Here, the analysis of the compound is: those whose multitude of infinite qualities—such as unsurpassed knowledge, action, and sovereignty—are [present]. And they are immeasurable, innumerable sages (*sūrayaḥ*). Based on the consideration of such passages as, "The sages always see it," and "The wise, praising it, kindle it with longing," he says: "whose pair of feet are incessantly worshipped."

*Vipanyavaḥ*: those whose nature is especially characterized by praise. [The root] *paṇ* is used in the sense of "transaction" and "praise"; *pana* is also used. The prefix *abhi-* conveys the meaning of the word *vi-*. Because they are of a praising nature, there is an expression of their being uninterrupted.

He dispels the limitation consisting in the finite measure of sovereignty and so forth, which would otherwise follow from its being an object of praise—by means of the words "beyond speech and mind. By this, [it is shown that] for whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; for whom it is thought...

Those who claim that such passages as "He does not know; he is unknown to those who know, known to those who do not know," "He, indeed, knows, or perhaps he does not know," and "From which words turn back, along with the mind"—meaning that [Brahman] is unknowable by speech and mind—are refuted. For if that were the case, there would arise a contradiction with statements such as "Seek to know That" and "The Brahman-knower," as well as with the use of the word "That" (*yat*) in the passage "From which words turn back."

If it is argued that [the contradiction] is resolved by establishing [the two statements] as having different scopes, with one being the primary sense and the other the object of a prohibition, you have indeed entered upon our path; however, the distinction is that we establish the scope of the subject matter according to the authority of the scriptures. Some explain [the passage beginning with] "beyond speech and mind" (*vāṅmanasa*) as an attribute of the Supreme Abode (*paramavyoma*), because it is stated as such in the *Śrī Vaikuṇṭha-gadya*.

We, however, [hold otherwise], because in this very sixth chapter, in the verse beginning "Of those who are yogis also," it is designated specifically as an attribute of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the phrase "whose essential nature and character are beyond the reach of speech and mind."
And because it is required for the purpose of refuting wrong views, we declare that the same intention applies here as well.

In the first chapter of the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā, beginning with "appropriate to oneself" (*svocita*), etc., the term "infinite wonder" (*anantāścarya*) is used here as well, just as before. By the word "majesty" (*vibhava*), one includes vehicles, jewels, and so forth. Its infinite dimension (*ananta-parimāṇatva*) is in relation to horizontal, vertical, and other directions, because it is not delimited by *prakṛti* below. The repetition of the word "infinite" (*ananta*) is due to the intention to emphasize the infinity of each individual attribute. Eternality (*nityatva*) means being free from dissolution, unlike the delusions of *prakṛti*. Faultlessness (*niravadyatva*) means being composed of pure *sattva*, thus being devoid of *rajas* and *tamas* and their effects.

"Immutability" (*akṣaratva*) means the absence of creation and dissolution even in part. By the word "supreme" (*parama*), there is an exclusion of the material ether (*prakṛtavyoma*) according to the method indicated by the term "supreme. By this, there is an indication of such scriptural passages as, "In that immutable, supreme ether" (*tadakṣare parame vyoman*). Thus, the connection with the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*) has been stated.

Now, by way of demonstrating the connection with the playful manifestation (*līlāvibhūti*), he shows the connection with the definition of Brahman to be sought through inquiry, as established by the aphorism, "From which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*): "Diverse," etc. This refers to [the world] in the form of sound, touch, and so forth, distinguished as divine, non-divine, and so on.

And here, regarding the manifoldness and variety of objects of enjoyment, the phrase "these" and so forth—in the scripture beginning with "imāni"—indicates all types of effects established by their respective means of valid cognition through the gesture of stretching out the hand; and because the plural number is not restricted, both the manifoldness consisting of the various forms such as gods and others—which serves as the cause for the gradations in knowledge, pleasure, and so forth among the enjoyers—and the variety consisting of the sub-divisions thereof, such as the forms of Brāhmaṇas and others, are shown. Alternatively, the word *vividha* (manifold) itself encompasses the entire manifoldness along with its internal subdivisions.

The term *vicitra* (variegated) refers to the fact that its nature is wondrous and impossible for others [to produce], as in the passage beginning with “the rising of clouds” and ending with “Viṣṇu’s variegated *māyās* manifest. Because there is no gradation in knowledge, bliss, and so forth, and because there is no diversity among the enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) in the Supreme Abode (*paramavyoman*), the class of enjoyers is not mentioned there; furthermore, they have been separately stated as the eternal sages (*nityasūri*) whose sole essence is the state of being the objects of enjoyment for the Supreme. The instruments of enjoyment and the places of enjoyment are also established by implication here. And since such a diverse creation is rooted in the stream of the karma of various beginningless sentient beings, there is no fault of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) or other such defects.

By the word "entire" (*nikhila*), there is the exclusion of [deities] such as the four-faced Brahmā, who serve as the occasional and material causes for only a few creations. By the word "arising" (*udaya*), there is the inclusion of the totality of creation, whether mediated or immediate. Likewise, by the word "manifestation" (*vibhava*), there is the inclusion of the various modes of maintenance performed through Viṣṇu’s incarnations, his role as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), and so forth. Dissolution (*laya*) also takes the form of the periodic (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) types, and so on.

Although it is possible for any one of the [three] beginning with creation to constitute the definition of Brahman, the mention of all three—creation and so forth—is intended to dispel the doubt as to what other function could be performed by the two [stages] not currently under discussion. By designating the three processes of emergence, manifestation, and dissolution pertaining to the world as His *līlā* (sport), His status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is indicated. These processes of arising and so forth in the form of the world are His *līlās*, for His resolve as the cause of the universe is expressed in the words: "May I become many; may I procreate."

Since only that which is distinguished by the subtle *cid-acit* (sentient and insentient matter) is the material cause (*upādāna*), there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding His being changeless (*nirvikāratva*); for, just as a child attaining youth and so forth does not constitute a modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), so too here there is no such modification. Furthermore, by using the term "sport" (*līlā*), [the author] refutes the doubt as to how He, who has attained all desires, could engage in the activity of creating the world, thereby establishing that He alone is also the efficient cause (*nimitta*). By this, those who maintain a distinction between the efficient and material causes are refuted. Nor is it the case that...

In the world, contradiction arises merely from observing a distinction between efficient causes (*nimitta*) and material causes (*upādāna*); however, this does not apply to Brahman as established by the Śruti, because it is distinct from worldly causes. Ultimately, even the Vaiśeṣikas and others accept that in effects such as the conjunction and disjunction of a pot and its maker, or duality and double-separateness, the Lord alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in our position. This should likewise be understood in the case of the intentional production of one's own pleasure and so forth.

Thus, by demonstrating that Nārāyaṇa alone possesses the status of the Supreme Brahman through his association with the characteristics of Brahman, and indicating that general terms such as *Sat*, *Bhūtātman*, and so forth, ultimately terminate in the specific referent named Nārāyaṇa; and making it known that the elaboration here is being performed of the verse from the *Gītārthasaṃgraha*—which echoes the scriptural statement "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman"—namely, "In the Gītā scripture, Nārāyaṇa is declared to be the Supreme Brahman"; [it is shown] that by the aforementioned modes, these three designations belong to him alone.

Citing the word "concordant" (*saṃgatam*), or else establishing the three designations as authoritative regarding the matters already mentioned, and demonstrating that these [scriptural passages]—such as "Thou art the supreme, pure, and highest abode," and "This glorious one is Nārāyaṇa"—have Kṛṣṇa alone as their sole object, he summarizes the distilled meaning of the scriptural texts concerning non-difference, those concerning difference, those serving as reconcilers (*ghaṭaka*), and those concerning the investigation of the cause and meditation (*upāsana*): "The Supreme Brahman is Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa. Thus...

The intention of the three words is that complete co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and complete distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) are both established by virtue of [Nārāyaṇa] being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all.

For this very reason, those who assert that co-referentiality here is based on the sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-bādha*), or on difference-and-non-difference (*bheda-abheda*), and so forth, are refuted. This is evident from the passage beginning with, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna existed," and continuing through, "Therein Brahmā, the four-faced one, was born," and "He who ordains Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed sends forth the Vedas to him."

Intending to refer to such matters as the granting of the body that serves as an instrument (karaṇakalebara) and the teaching of what is beneficial, he says: "Having created the entire world from Brahmā down to the stationary [beings]. Since it is stated that the entire world, from the creation of Brahmā down to the stationary beings, is created by the Supreme Self (paramātman), it is established that the Supreme Self, encased in the sheaths (kañcuka) beginning with *māyā* (the *brāhṛ*), creates each of those things.

Now, in order to state his descent (*avatāra*) by his own will and its purpose, he shows that this purpose is not fulfilled during the state of non-descent, beginning with the words "by himself" (*svena*).

By the phrase "beyond the range" (*agocara*), [the Lord's] being beyond the range is indicated because of His unmanifest nature (*avyaktatva*). As it is said: "O you two, endowed with those characteristics by which Hari possesses an unmanifest form, you indeed possess those same characteristics while bearing manifest forms. Because of the statement beginning with "the gods such as Brahmā," and in accordance with the section of the *Brahma-sūtras* stating, "Even above that [the world of Brahmā], Bādarāyaṇa [maintains eligibility] because of the possibility," it is established that even those belonging to the classes of gods such as Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra possess the qualification for the meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by virtue of their desire and capacity.

Having indicated this, he asks: "In the absence of a purpose for oneself, how would one act? To this, he says: "By [the qualities of] 'unrestrained' (apāra), etc. That is, by an inability to endure the suffering of others that is independent of one's own interest; by a delight in constant association with the dull-witted that is unimpeded by greatness; by a natural disposition that disregards the faults of others; and [by the influence of those such as] Piśāca, Gopāla, and Gopikā.

The meaning is that, even though his own self has been offered, he descends, impelled by a great magnanimity that contemplates how much [of himself] has actually been given. Having reflected upon the form described in the chapter on weapons and ornaments—namely, "O King, that other great form of Hari, which is both universal and multiform, wherein all these powers are established"—he creates, O Lord of Men, forms consisting of all powers, known as gods, animals, and humans, endowed with activity through his own play.

In order to show that even the form of the incarnation (avatāra-vigraha) is a specific portion of the form residing in the non-material supreme abode (*aprākṛta-paramapada-nilaya*), the passage beginning with "his own very form" (*svameva rūpam*) is introduced. It is stated: "This Lord did not undergo gestation, nor did he dwell in a womb"; "His form is not material, consisting of flesh, fat, and bone"; and "The manifestation of this Supreme Self does not consist of an aggregate of elements. Connecting this with what is to be said later, beginning with "Though being unborn" (*ajo 'pi san*), he says: "Without abandoning his own essential nature" (*svasvabhāvamajahadeva*). [And: "Whenever there is a decline of Dharma..."

Contemplating the sense of repetition in such passages as "I manifest myself age after age" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.8) and the meaning of the verse beginning with "Many births of mine have passed" (Gītā 4.5), he says: "Having descended, having descended into those various worlds... [and thus] everyone becomes superior.

This is stated in order to remind us of such passages as, "While being born, the gods worship those forms of descent (avatāra) [of the Lord], not seeing His supreme form," and so forth. By saying that He is "propitiated by various [means] after descending again and again," and by the statement that [the worship] is "in accordance with each person's specific desire," any charge of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) in the bestowing of fruits is avoided. Furthermore, one should here reflect on such verses as, "When He is pleased, what is there in this world that is unobtainable? and so on.

Thus, the general nature of the descent and its purpose have been shown. Here, he demonstrates the specific details relevant to the subject at hand, beginning with the words "the removal of the earth's burden" (*bhūbhārāvatāraṇa*). The removal of the earth's burden is merely a pretext; rather, being the refuge for all is the direct objective, since the destruction of the wicked is ancillary to the great purpose known as the protection of the virtuous. This is why it was said, "under the guise of removing the earth's burden. The phrase "of those like us" means "of those who are not yogis."

He explains the state of being the refuge for all: "The entire... and so forth. In the manner established by such passages as, "That supreme station of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, which neither the gods, nor the sages, nor I, nor Śaṅkara know," it is difficult to grasp even with the purified mind of great yogis; yet, due to its extreme accessibility, it is within reach of ordinary humans—even down to cowherds—by means of the fleshly eye, provided they have set aside all conflicting dualistic distinctions.

The sense is that [the Lord] became an object of grasping. With the intention of showing that the purpose of being the object of both non-crossing and leading across is not merely the state of being worshipful, but also the experience thereof, he says: "parāvareti" (of the high and the low). "Parāḥ" refers to those capable of meditation, such as Brahmā, Rudra, Bhīṣma, Akrūra, and others; "avarāḥ," however, refers to the cowherds and so forth. By the phrase "nikhilajana" (all people), the intended meaning is that there is no distinction even between women and men, as in the expression "stealing the sight and mind of men."
The "divine exploits" refer to acts such as the churning of butter and the dance. Thus, these two qualifiers have been stated as specific modes of protecting the virtuous.

Now, he elaborates upon the manner of destroying the wicked, which is incidental to the protection of the virtuous—beginning with the word "Pūtanā. Since the Blessed Lord Balabhadra is also a partial manifestation of Him, the slaying of Pralamba, Muṣṭika, and others is included as being performed by Him. Furthermore, he shows that the state of being an object of enjoyment is contained within the protection of the virtuous—beginning with the word "anavadhika" (unlimited).

The manifestation of the Beloved’s own form is the sustainer (*dhāraka*); the witnessing of His activities is the nourisher (*poṣaka*); and conversation with Him and so forth constitute the mode of enjoyment (*bhoga*).

This is the intended meaning behind the specification of the distinctions such as being an object of the eyes, the beholding of His activities, and so on. *Dayā* (compassion) is the desire to remove the suffering of others, independent of one's own interest.

*Sauhārda* (friendliness) is the wish for their welfare. *Anurāga* (affection) is love. Thus, the protection of the virtuous and the destruction of the wicked—which serves that purpose—have been described.

Now, the establishment of dharma (*dharmasaṃsthāpana*) is shown by means of manifesting His own adorable nature (*ārādhyasvarūpa*) and by instruction that benefits even those separated by space and time through tradition; this is indicated by the remainder of the passage beginning with "unsurpassed" (*niratiśaya*). All of this will be explained in the verse beginning with "for the protection" (*paritrāṇāya*). For there, after describing the characteristics, existence, and so forth of the virtuous (*sādhu*), it is stated immediately thereafter: "In the granting of the vision, conversation, and so forth, of My own nature and activities..."

"It is not for their protection, nor for the destruction of those opposed to them, but for the establishment of the Vedic dharma—which has declined and consists of my own worship—by revealing the nature of the one to be worshipped; thus, in age after age, I manifest myself in the forms of gods, humans, and others. The sense is this: while the establishment of dharma through instruction can be accomplished even by means of Vyāsa and others, the establishment [of it] by revealing the form of the object of worship must necessarily be performed by me alone. This is shown by the presentation of the two groups of qualities perceivable by the internal and external organs.

The phrase "having made [them] supremely devoted (*paramabhāgavata*) through the acquisition of beauty and good character" means having established them in the supreme dharma consisting of devotion to the Lord.

In this way, the connection between the ancient deeds of the Lord and the instruction on the meaning of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā* has been demonstrated. The phrase "under the pretext of encouraging the sons of Pāṇḍu to battle," however, shows the connection with the narrative of the *Mahābhārata*. Here, by the word "pretext" (*vyāja*), it is meant: "[Arjuna was] agitated by misplaced affection, compassion, and the notion of right and wrong."

In the passage, "The scripture was composed with reference to Pārtha who had sought refuge," the intended meaning of the word *uddiśya* (with reference to) has been explained. By the phrase "the supreme human goal" (*paramapuruṣārtha*) and so forth, the ultimate purpose of the scripture is stated. By this, it is indicated that here—as in the Bhūmavidyā—the mention of the experience of the self is like the mention of worldly sovereignty; it serves to demonstrate that such experiences belong to a lower category of human goals when compared to the experience of the Lord. By the statement "as the means to liberation" (*mokṣasādhanatayā*), through the specification of the relationship between the end and the means, it is shown that the eternally liberated state belongs to the transmigrating self alone.

Those who speak thus are refuted. "Enjoined by the Vedānta" means that which is prescribed by the Vedānta, not that which is produced by the Vedānta; by this, those who maintain that knowledge is not something to be enjoined are discarded.

The sense is that what is being done here is the elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the meaning already declared in the Vedānta. Regarding the phrase "its own object": the meditative passages intended for liberation have as their direct subject matter only the propitiation of the Supreme Person, since they are not directed toward anything else. This is so even in cases such as the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Pratardana-vidyā*, where Rudra, Indra, and others declare themselves to be the objects of worship for those seeking liberation.

The intention is that the Sūtrakāra himself has established that the Supreme Self alone, who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Rudra, Indra, and the others, is the object of worship, in accordance with the aphorism: "But the instruction is by means of the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva. By this, it is indicated that for the Blessed One—who proclaims His own majesty as taught in the Vedānta—there is no fault of "self-glorification" (svaguṇāviṣkriyā), because He is merely describing what is an existing reality (bhūtārtha).

The phrase "its own object" (*svaviṣayam*) demonstrates that the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is invariably connected to the supreme goal in its perfected state; this is stated for the purpose of extracting the primary element to be enjoined. The expression "the yoga of devotion" (*bhaktiyogam*) indicates that it is assisted by knowledge and action, or rather, that it is accomplished through knowledge and action. By this, positions such as their combination (*samuccaya*) are refuted. Although detachment (*vairāgya*) was mentioned separately in the summary verse, it is not mentioned here because it is already included within the two types of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*). Thus, both [knowledge and action] consist of the means and the end.

This constitutes the intended meaning of the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*), namely that the subject matter to be expounded by the treatise is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) as proclaimed in the Vedānta as the means to liberation. By this statement, those who assert that meditation (*upāsana*) is merely a means for attaining lower realms such as Brahmaloka, or that the mere knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences is the means to liberation, are refuted. Furthermore, the sense is that general terms such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "meditation" (*dhyāna*) ultimately culminate in the specific form of devotion. All of this will become clear later on.
Having thus harmonized the scripture, and in order to introduce the prologue to the scripture, he reveals the prior narrative indicated by the words "O son of Pāṇḍu" and so forth;
furthermore, by remaining in the role of charioteer, he dispels the suspicion that he might be deceiving him while performing the duties of a teacher. Regarding the word "therein":

The meaning is that He acted in this manner specifically to introduce *bhakti-yoga* therein; or alternatively, the construction is "when the battle had commenced there. This means when the battle—which served as a pretext for introducing *bhakti-yoga* and was the object of His exhortation—had begun. Furthermore, even during the stage of His incarnation, the Lord’s perfection, sovereignty, and so forth, as well as the fact that His performance of subordinate tasks such as charioteering was rooted in qualities like parental affection (*vātsalya*), were to be demonstrated; thus, the passage beginning with "That Blessed One" (*sa bhagavān*) was spoken.

The summary of His supremacy is presented through four terms—“He is the Blessed One,” “the Supreme Person,” “the Lord of all lords”—by means of which His essential nature, qualities, distinctiveness, and opulence are established.
By the term “Lord of all lords,” His absolute sovereignty and His role as the Father of the universe, as stated in such passages as “Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of all lords,” are made known.

"Being unable to disregard the welfare of the world and being overwhelmed by affection for those who have sought refuge in him"—this constitutes the summary of his accessibility (*saulabhya*). Furthermore, by this, his deceptive nature is also implied. Here, one is reminded of such passages as: "For the benefit of the worlds," "Who is capable of conquering Him whose welfare toward the world is immeasurable? Even though He is incapable of disregarding the welfare of the world, why does He perform lowly tasks such as acting as a charioteer, setting aside His exalted conduct? To this, it is said: "Overwhelmed by affection for those who have sought refuge. [He says: "O Pārtha, you as the warrior and myself as the charioteer"—thus placing the inferior Pārtha in a superior role.

The sense is that he himself, having established himself as superior, engaged in a base task. By the word "Pārtha," even a specific worldly relationship suitable for affection is indicated; for the Lord’s paternal aunt was indeed Pṛthā. And he did not perform this base task in secret out of shame before all the world; therefore, the sense is that this too is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of his affection for those who have taken refuge in him, of his indifference [to worldly concerns], and of the impossibility of his denying the welfare of others.

Alternatively, the sense is that He manifested His dependence on those who take refuge in Him—which is perceptible to all the world—as a means for everyone to attain the goals of human life by taking refuge in Him alone, who is accessible through the scriptures. First, by means of the words of Śāntanu, Naḷa, Sañjaya, and others—such as "O You of character and form"—which describe His unique character, form, conduct, supreme goodness, and His status as the ultimate deity of the scriptures, [He inspired] even those of demonic nature...

Demonstrating the impossibility of understanding [the matter] as it truly is, he introduces the first verse for the purpose of prefacing the *Gītā-upaniṣad* with the words "Thus," beginning with "The Lord of Śrī."

The meaning is: "in the manner previously described. "With his whole self" (sarvātmanā) means not only with his eyes, but also with his mind that does not know what is beneficial here and in the hereafter. Such blindness is the reason for the question, arising from a desire for Suyodhana’s victory. Here, by the initial address "my men" (*māmakāḥ*), which implies a sense of possessiveness (*mamakāra*), and by the method of the reply beginning with "where [is] the Lord of Yoga" (*yatra yogeśvaraḥ*), the intention of the questioner is shown; thus, the words beginning with "Suyodhana" were spoken. [The word] "Saṃjaya" [is used].

[He spoke to] one who had obtained a direct vision of the entire account of the events of the Bhārata war through the grace of Vyāsa, and who declared: "Having attained a state of purity through devotion, I know Janārdana from the scripture. The sense is that [the author] has determined him to be the most authoritative person (*āptatama*) by virtue of his seeing things as they truly are and his speaking of things exactly as he has seen them.
He questioned him regarding the events of the war; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Now begins the second chapter.

Now begins the second chapter, concerning the removal of sorrow. Although there is no interruption in Sañjaya’s speech, the designation "Sañjaya said" is intended to mark the commencement of a new chapter and to dispel any suspicion that this is a quotation from another source.
He explains the nature of the passage beginning with "To him who was thus... by the word "evam" (thus), up to the end of the section ending with "desponding."
It is indicated that this is a restatement of what was said in the preceding chapter. Thus it is said, "when Pārtha was seated.
The word "tathā" (thus) means "in an inappropriate place."

Out of compassion; "immediately following compassion" (*anantaraḥ kṛpāyāḥ*)—the reading *anantaro viṣādaḥ* (sorrow immediately following) is indeed appropriate here. This is because the word *kṛpā* was previously explained as referring to the inability to endure suffering in the phrase "supremely compassionate" (*paramakāruṇika*), and for the sake of consistency with that. *Viṣādaḥ* has the meaning of "one who is despondent. The sense of "seated" (*upaviṣṭam*) is obtained from the substantive noun *tam* (him).

He sat down because of the reference to what was previously stated. Therefore, there is no defect even though the root *ṣad* with the prefix *vi-* does not have the well-known meaning of "sitting down" (*upaveśana*). In this sentence, the sequence of compassion (*kṛpā*), despondency (*viṣāda*), and being filled with tears (*aśrupūrṇatva*) is described. First is despondency;
then [the state of] having eyes filled with tears, which means being overcome by grief for his arms.
"Despondent" (*viṣīdantam*) means having fallen into despondency and sitting down according to the manner previously described in the commentary.
By the word "Madhusūdana," the destruction of the *rajas* and *tamas* that are the roots of grief is indicated.
In the phrase "out of place" (*asthāne*), the meaning of the word "inappropriate" (*viṣama*) is applied figuratively. Here, "dejection" (*kaśmala*) refers to a grief resembling a swoon.

"Because his mind was agitated by grief"—this is implied by the context. The words "Arjuna," "Kaunteya," "thee" (*tvā*), "in thee" (*tvayi*), and "O scorcher of foes" (*parantapa*) are intended to carry a reproachful and sarcastic undertone;
thus it is said, "having reproached him. Furthermore, the word "whence" (*kutaḥ*) rejects the status of a fallacious reason as being a valid reason.

[The compound] contains a reproach (*dhikkāra*). In the word *parantapa*, the term *param* is not the second case singular; rather, it is the addition of the suffix *mum*. Therefore, even when referring to many enemies (*parān*), the form remains the same. The intention is that the root *tap* should not be taken as ending in *ṇic* (causative), because the rule "dviṣat-parayos tāpeḥ" specifies the root as being without the *ṇic* suffix (*niranirdeśāt*). With this in mind, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made as "one who torments others" (*parān tāpayati*).

The meaning of "O scorcher of foes" (*parantapa*) is: "Arise for the purpose of scorching the enemy. One who scorches others is a "scorcher of foes" (*parantapa*). Here, "weakness" (*klaibya*) refers to cowardice; this is explained by the term "languor of heart" (*hṛdayadaurbalya*). Furthermore, since the adjectives found in the preceding verse are also causes for abandoning cowardice, he connects them here as well with the words beginning "this one who is in a difficult situation" (*tam imam viṣamastham*).
From false principles and fallacious reasonings—those whose intellects have departed far from these are the noble ones (*ārya*), the wise;

others than them are the ignoble (*anārya*). In the phrase "not the foremost heaven" (*asvagryam*), since there is no distinction made, the word "heaven" (*svarga*) is indicative of the afterlife in general. Furthermore, because the negative particle (*nañ*) here has the sense of opposition, it denotes the state of being contrary to the causes of heaven indicated by the word *svagrya*.
This is because it would contradict the purpose and the fruit [of the teaching]. It is stated that [the action] is contrary to the next world (*paraloka*).

Since there is no restrictive factor here for the word "petty" (*kṣudra*), it cannot refer to something merely relatively petty; furthermore, considering Arjuna’s extremely great state of mind, what is intended is a pettiness that has reached its ultimate limit.

To demonstrate this, it is said to be "extremely trivial. Alternatively, this may be understood as a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect (*kārye kāraṇopacāra*), or because the abandonment of the cause implies the abandonment of the effect, intended to express the essential meaning resulting from the preceding and following verses.
It was stated that this is "caused by the weakness of the heart"; the meaning is that it is caused by the lack of firmness in the heart.
By the term "O scorcher of foes" (*parantapa*), the contextual meaning is indicated; having supplied the ellipsis, it is said: "Arise for battle."

Now, the objection raised by Arjuna arises from his ignorance of the fact that the commencement of the battle spoken of by the Blessed One is the most beneficial act, insofar as it is the cause—through a traditional succession—of the supreme liberation (*paramaniḥśreyasa*). By stating that such ignorance is rooted in a state of agitation caused by misplaced affection and the like, [the Lord] introduces the reply with the words, "Again... (*punarapi*).
It was stated [previously] that this is "unutterable" because its object is the meaning already expressed.
This is shown in the verse beginning with "How... (*katham...*), for the purpose of demonstrating that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Alternatively, the word "etc. (*ādi*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both what has been included and what has not been included.
The intention of the word "worthy of worship" (*pūjārha*) is that they are to be highly esteemed; this is the sense.
For those who are worthy of worship, the mere cessation of worship with flowers and the like is already an act of rashness; their killing, however, is an extreme rashness.
Furthermore, out of devotion to one's teacher, one must fight against those who oppose him, but not against the teachers themselves.

The thought [behind] "How shall I fight back against my superiors with arrows? is as follows: by the word "I," his belonging to a renowned lineage and so forth is intended. The phrase "I shall fight back with arrows" implies an intention to engage in combat unto death, as shown by the subsequent verse.

Regarding the word *vivṛtam* (explained): it means "I shall kill. Here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of censure (*garhā*), according to the rules "the present tense (*laṭ*) is used with *api* and *jātu* in the sense of censure" and "optionally [the optative] with *katham*. To prevent the misconception that this is a *dvandva* compound in the phrase *arthakāmāṇām*, the meaning of both parts of the compound is stated.

"Excessively attached to enjoyments" (*bhogeṣvatimātrasaktān*) has been stated. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "those for whom there is desire (*kāma*) for objects (*artha*). For a *bahuvrīhi* with a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) first member is indeed not prohibited when the final member begins with *janman* and so forth. "Objects" (*artha*) are those which are desired (*arthayante*), namely enjoyments (*bhoga*). And "desire" (*kāma*) is explained as excessive attachment. Alternatively, they are those who desire objects (*arthaṃ kāmayante*).
Thus, they are intent on wealth and sensual pleasure. If they were free from desire, even the seizing of their enjoyments would be endured;
however, the sense is that this [seizing] is like taking food from those who are hungry. This is stated to indicate an extreme cruelty even greater than killing.
The meaning is established by the words "enjoyments," "blood," and so forth. And the distinction is highlighted by the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase beginning with "by them" (*taiḥ*).
It has been stated that by the phrase "right here," the extreme cruelty intended is shown by the words beginning with "toward them" (*teṣu*).

Since the enjoyments to be achieved through the murder of one's guru serve as a cause for remembering the guru smeared with blood, they themselves become as difficult to digest as if they were of that same nature; thus, there is no happiness even in this world. This is the intended meaning of the word "smeared with blood" (*rudhirapradigdha*).
Thus he says: "having sprinkled with that blood. For a sprinkling (upasecana) is itself being eaten while serving as the cause for the eating of what follows;
here, however, both of these are reversed—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with "And we do not know this," he states the intended meaning preceded by the doubt indicated by the word *ca* (and): "In this way. He suggests that you, fearing the destruction of your kinsmen, might have caused the very destruction of your closest relatives, such as Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and Nakula; this is what is implied by the word *bhavataḥ* (of yours). Following the plural form of the verb *vidmaḥ* ("we know"), he says: "of us."
By the word "us" (*asmān*), the status of all [the enemies] as disciples and so forth is intended, in comparison with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others who were designated as objects to be slain.

Through the first and second halves of the verse, the deliberation and the speaker’s own preferred position are suggested. The phrases "whether" (*yad vā*) and "or if" (*yadi vā*) have the same meaning:
those for whose slaughter life would be undesirable are themselves now seeking to kill us.

The phrase "they remain in accordance with their own nature" (*svahanana-anurūpatvena avasthitāḥ*) is the meaning of the connection (*anvaya*) for the passage beginning with "those very [beings]" (*yān eva*).

By the words "we do not wish to live" (*na jijīviṣāmaḥ*), he expresses a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*) that is characterized by a lack of final certainty and which serves as the cause for his question, saying: "This is how it appears to me."

He clarifies the logical connection (*anvaya*) of the passage beginning with "that which is the highest good" (*yacchreyaḥ*), its resultant meaning, and the perfection of qualities in a disciple required for fitness for instruction, by means of the verse beginning with "that which is great" (*yan mahat*). The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of extracting the specific form to be ascertained. For a disciple is indeed one who is to be instructed;
therefore, he says, "I am your disciple; instruct me. In this context, "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to fortitude (*dhairya*).
Excessive miserliness (*kārpaṇya*) arises either from ignorance regarding specific duties to be performed or from the absence of means to dispel sorrow and so forth.
Some maintain that miserliness here refers to the failure to renounce what ought to be abandoned; others hold it to be an addiction to a wretched way of life that evokes pity.
The statement "he approached the feet of the Blessed One" indicates the result of his reasoning, namely, his status as a disciple, his state of surrender (*prapanna*), and his excellence.
By the word *Hṛṣīkeśa* in this verse, it is suggested that Arjuna was prompted by Hṛṣīkeśa to hear the true meaning;

furthermore, it is indicated that He brings peace to the agitation of the uncontrolled senses, as expressed in the phrase "that which dries up the moisture of the two groups [of enemies]" and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called *hṛṣīka* because they cause delight (*hṛṣanti*). Thus, *hṛṣīkāṇi* refers to the senses.
Having spoken thus—meaning, having made known his own state—"Guḍākā" refers to sleep, according to the rule that "sleep and laziness are *guḍākā*.

He is the lord (*īśa*) of that sleep, hence "Guḍākeśa"; the meaning is one whose nature is awakened, or alternatively, one with matted hair (*piṇḍitakeśa*). By the word "Govinda," there is the quality of being endowed with speech capable of dispelling grief, and [the ability] to obtain the earth designated by the word "go."
And it is intended that [the teaching] is engaged for the purpose of removing the burden.

Thus, by means of this introduction (*upodghāta*), while stating the connection for the commencement of the treatise (*śāstra*) which will be explained at the appropriate occasion, he also explains the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) regarding the subject matter (*artha*) through implication. Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*):
the word "inopportune" (*asthāna*) has as its referent the phrase "presented at an improper time," and its "affection" (*sneha*) is its manifestation.

He has made a separate mention of those two for the sake of their subsequent connection with compassion. By the phrase "fallen from his nature," the meaning of the word *ākula* is expressed; by this, his natural fortitude (*dhīratva*) is indicated, for he himself has stated that [the mind] is "one whose nature is impaired. By this, it is shown that his nature is impaired by the defect of wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*).
It has also been shown that this was stated as the cause for the state of having a mind deluded regarding dharma.

The meaning of the phrase "having a mind deluded regarding dharma" (*dharmasaṃmūḍhacetāḥ*), which serves as an elaboration of the term "by the notion of dharma and adharma" (*dharmādharmadhiyā*), is what was expressed by the words beginning with "of the kṣatriyas. Thus, "dharma" [when wrongly perceived] is itself the "notion of adharma," which constitutes "the notion of dharma and adharma."

It is like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl. In that regard, under the view that [cognition] corresponds to reality (*yathārthakhyāti*), what is intended is the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*).
And this cognition is of a *tāmasa* (dark/ignorant) nature; for it will be stated later: "That which considers non-dharma to be dharma," and so forth.
Here, the analysis of the compound should be understood as "the cognition of dharma and adharma produced by misplaced affection and the like."
This is according to the ancient commentary beginning with "agitated by affection, compassion, dharma, adharma, fear," and so forth.

However, in the reading *dharmādharmābhayākulaṃ*, there is a dvandva compound of the three [terms]. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *prapanna* as used in the context of the passage beginning with "I ask you" is stated to be one who has come for refuge out of a desire to know dharma.
Thus, he states that activity is appropriate when directed toward a worthy recipient, saying "pārthimiddiśya" (having directed toward Pārthi).
Alternatively, the sense is that the introduction of the scripture was made merely for the sake of obtaining a pretext.
To answer the question "by whom? regarding the word "kṛtam" (was done), and to dispel the suspicion that Vyāsa or others might be the authors of this treatise, he says:

"By the Blessed One, the Supreme Person"— by these two words, the author intends to indicate such qualities as being endowed with the marks of fearlessness (*abhayaliṅga*), which are necessary for the authority of the treatise (*śāstraprāmāṇya*).
To exclude other scriptures that have different purposes, it is specified as "inner" (*adhyātma*).
In order to establish that this meaning is based on tradition, he says: "It has been said.

Furthermore, in order to state and analyze the summary verses for each chapter, [he notes] that by means of the summary verse beginning with "asthāna," etc., so much has been summarized by the first chapter, which was not previously specified.

The Great Sage, however, by means of an intermediate connection consisting of a narrative intended to dispel that grief, placed the passage beginning with "He said, 'So be it'" in the second chapter. This too was indicated by those who summarized the fruit of the second chapter as "for the sake of pacifying his delusion. Consequently, [the first chapter dealt with] the agitation caused by misplaced affection and the like.
The meaning of the first chapter is thus established; it is also shown that "that very [subject] with its specific qualities is restated here for the sake of connection.
Now, as for the phrase "of such a kind": how can instruction regarding the supreme reality, welfare, and so forth—which ought to be taught to one desiring liberation—be given to this person?
For he is not a seeker of liberation merely by the statement that he does not desire a kingdom; he does not refuse to desire a kingdom simply because he says he will not kill others.

The doubt is that whether Duryodhana is afraid or otherwise, if he gives even a little, then [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] would become even more desirous of enjoying it than before. The resolution is that, based merely on this current situation and so forth, it is not even possible to determine his lack of desire for liberation (*amumukṣutva*) at this time.
For it is possible that even one who has developed a longing for liberation might subsequently become inclined toward worldly enjoyment and the like;
therefore, terms such as "seeking welfare" (*śreyaskāma*) and "miserliness" (*kārpaṇya*) naturally apply to the state of desiring liberation (*mumukṣutva*).

Furthermore, the Blessed One has now resolved that the removal of the earth's burden is for the sake of the world's welfare. Since there is currently no hero equal to him for this task, he has also intended to accomplish it through this [prince] as his instrument. In that case, if the prince were desirous of sovereignty, the undertaking would have been achieved by him with ease; however, he does not desire sovereignty.

If it were said that "even that which is fruitless must be performed because it is occasional (*naimittika*)," Arjuna would not be satisfied; for he might think that since battle is rooted in a *saṃvalita-adhikāra* (a mandate involving mixed motives)—like the *Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi* sacrifice—how can it be considered "occasional" if there is no desire for victory in the kingdom and so forth? Furthermore, if this great and difficult-to-attain duty is performed by abandoning its ultimate (*sāttvika*) form—then of this [duty]...

By the principle that "there is no loss of effort here," Kṛṣṇa produced such an understanding in Arjuna— thinking that [the merit] would be properly utilized in some birth or another— according to the manner stated as "from Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal.
This was done for Arjuna, who had already long ago witnessed the Lord’s power in its many aspects through the manifestation of the Universal Form and other events.

For one who has realized this, the desire for liberation would be like an attachment to an improper object; thus he says that even begging is better. Therefore, since war must be undertaken, his necessary exhortation should be accomplished in this very manner.
The primary task of the Gītā is the removal of delusion regarding the notion that there is no connection between knowledge and action.

Regarding the phrase "the example of mere departure is useless": laughter in its intense form (*prahāsa*) is intransitive in common usage, being caused by observing the faults of others and so forth, and it is not connected with self-instruction. The meaning is that even as an example for the agent toward Kṛṣṇa, it does not apply.
