*Prahāsa* means derisive laughter (*parihāsa*); that resides solely in Kṛṣṇa. Such was the statement of derisive laughter made toward the daughter of his paternal aunt (*paitṛṣvasrīyā*).

The sense is that [the world] was characterized by qualities such as aesthetic flavor (*sārasatva*); likewise, in order to say that this [present world] has become comparable to a joke, it is stated as if by a joker himself. Now, one might ask:
why is a scripture concerning the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), and so forth, taught with reference to such a person who has not even asked for it?
For the traditional authorities (smṛti) record: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked.
Moreover, this matter—being of a secret, more secret, and most secret nature—is unfit to be taught abruptly.
Furthermore, in passages such as "Therefore, fight" and "Fight," it is clearly perceived that the intent is solely to encourage the contextual battle.

Therefore, it is argued that this scripture does not have the internal self (*adhyātma*) as its primary subject. To this, it is replied: In the interrogative sentence, "That which is the highest good (*yacchreyaḥ*)," the term *yacchreyaḥ* is seen to be unspecified. Nor is there any rule that for Arjuna, only battle was the object of his inquiry as the highest good, given that he was a supreme devotee of the Blessed Lord.
For, when [the king] is present, it is appropriate to desire to know that which culminates in the supreme *niḥśreyasa* (ultimate liberation) by means of the introduction already set forth.

Or, even if his inquiry were restricted solely to the subject of war, nevertheless, the instruction on the supreme benefit is appropriate, as the Lord, being supremely compassionate, took recourse to the general statement, "that which is for your welfare."
It is also clearly stated in various places that even such [injunctions] as "fight" (yudhsva) serve as means to the supreme beatitude (*paramaniḥśreyasa*).
Therefore, this is appropriate: [this work] is an introduction to the science of the self (*adhyātmaśāstra*). || 8 || 9 ||
He refers to him as "him" (*tam*) for the sake of making him an object of ridicule, stating "thus" (*evam*) and so forth.
By the word "of both," that which was indicated has been stated: "of the two who were prepared for battle.
By this, the opportunity for instruction has also been manifested. By the word "failing" (*sīdamānam*),...

The state of being "without exertion" (*nirudyogatva*) is established by the phrase indicating a condition unfit for desisting from battle. By the word "in the midst" (*madhye*), he expresses what is intended: namely, "suddenly" (*akasmāt*). The sense is that here there is no proper cause for desisting from battle, such as unrighteousness (*adharma*) or defeat; rather, if one abandons the onset [of battle] without a cause, there is the fault of cowardice (*parihāsyatva*).

Here, the utter distinctiveness of the speaker, the Supreme Person, is stated as being implied by the mention of his being the Lord of the senses (*aṣīkeśa*) and by the authority of the scripture to be taught; this is shown by the term "Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*).
For although he, by virtue of being the Lord of the senses, restrains everything belonging to Pārtha—the senses and so forth—by mere will, [he remains distinct].

The sense is this: although He is capable of impelling [Arjuna] to descend from the burden of the earth, nevertheless, out of a desire to benefit the world, He sets him in motion by means of teaching the scripture which provides the means for human goals common to both Arjuna and others.
Alternatively, the meaning is that, as Hṛṣīkeśa, He Himself stirred the steadfast Arjuna and, as if smiling, spoke the scripture for the sake of the world's welfare.

Because of the specific relationship [between the speaker and the listener], and because it is appropriate for the statement to be understood as a joke when considering the context of the immediately preceding sentence, it is stated that laughter has a distinct object. Alternatively, since there is no possibility of joking by looking for faults in one who has taken refuge, and because a mere example of laughter would be useless in giving spiritual instruction to a disciple, [laughter is not intended here].

And having intended [this], the word "Pārtha" [is used]. Therefore, by the phrase "as if smiling," there is realized a state of charm (*sarasatva*), ease of comprehension (*sugrahatva*), and the effortless articulation of a vast mass of meanings hidden within the depths of all the Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, the word "this" (*idam*) has as its object the entirety of the Lord's speech that is about to be spoken, even by means of a mere gesture (*iṅgitena*).

And he shows the indication of what is intended to be said by means of the passage beginning with "In jest," and so forth. For even the verse beginning with "Those who are not to be grieved for" (2.11) is not directly the scripture itself, as its purpose is merely to introduce the teaching by appearing in the guise of a joke, in order to draw the attention of the listener toward the subject matter of the instruction.
This is why it was stated [in the previous commentary] that [the scripture begins] starting from the verse "But never at any time... (2.12).

Alternatively, here the verse beginning with "those who are not to be grieved for" (*aśocyān*) is the subject matter of [the statement] "as if laughing" (*prahasanniva*); the portion beginning with "but never indeed I" (*na tvevāham*) is the referent of the word "this" (*idam*). Here, everything up to "do not grieve" (*mā śucaḥ*) is indicated as being within the scope of *bhakti-yoga*, while even for one who practices all means of realization, the surrender (*prapadana*) mentioned in the final verse is connected to the present context.
Because it will be cited as that which turns away those things opposed to devotion.

When it was said, "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for," some might be confused, thinking that while some grieve for those who should not be grieved for, this person [you] has likewise begun to grieve. To remove that misconception, it was stated: "for those who should not be grieved for.
As for the use of the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense in "anvaśocaḥ," it is inappropriate because the grief is of the present day; therefore, it is said: "you speak."
To this he replies: "And because of the discrepancy in the designation of the present tense," namely, "you grieve" (*anuśocasi*).

The use of the verb with the prefix *anu* and the *laṅ* suffix (indicating the past) is intended to express that which has persisted for a long time even within the current day; or else, it is a substitution of the verbal suffix (*lakāra-vyatyaya*) according to the rule "the suffixes, moods, and voices [may be interchanged]" (*suptiṅupagraha-*) while still retaining the sense of the present. Regarding the phrase "and you utter words of wisdom" (*prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase*):

According to the grammatical rule, *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* ("the present tense may optionally be used for what is proximate to the present"), the suffix *laṭ* (present indicative) is employed here to denote the past.

Consequently, there is no contradiction with the expression *tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha* ("he became silent"). In this context, by the word *prajñā*, which denotes superior knowledge, is meant the knowledge of the true nature of the body and the self; [it refers to] conduct performed through such wisdom.

The term *prajñāvādāḥ* (those who speak of wisdom) is used to indicate the condensed meaning of the expression. The word *nimitta* (cause/sign) is employed to suggest that when the distinction between the body and the self is known, there occurs a practice based on conviction regarding the performance of funeral rites—such as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*)—for the sake of one's ancestors, as well as the transgression resulting from their omission;
it is for this indication that the words "they fall" (*patanti*) and so forth were spoken.

He states the conclusion: "The body is the self. Pointing out the intended substantive for the passage beginning with "those whose life has departed," and explaining the word "learned" (*paṇḍita*) as being relevant to the present context, he provides the syntactical connection: "those whose life has departed. Although the words "those whose life has departed" (*gatāsūn*) and "those whose life has not departed" (*agatāsūn*) denote the breathless and the living respectively, nevertheless, regarding that meaning—

Because it is irrelevant to the subject at hand: "How will you go alone upon this path through the forest of darkness—restless, without support, without provisions, and without a guide? And: "If living beings who harbor enmity feel hatred [toward you], then, alas, they are to be pitied by the wise as being overwhelmed by extreme delusion."

Because in such passages as these, the wise alone are seen to perceive sorrow regarding objects that are either "with life" (*saprāṇa*) or "without life" (*niṣprāṇa*); and because it will be explained in detail in the passage beginning with "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for," and in the subsequent sections beginning with "This [Self] is unmanifest" and "But him," that both the eternal Self and the impermanent body are to be regarded as unworthy of grief; therefore, here too—
The intention is that it is logical for [the grief] to have that [the body] as its object. First, bodies are not to be mourned because they are perishable;

likewise, selves are not to be mourned because they are imperishable. Those who possess *paṇḍā*—that is, an intellect capable of such reasoning and refutation—are here called "wise" (*paṇḍita*). He now states the objects of that ignorance, which are brought forth by a grief that contradicts the discourse of wisdom.
Therefore, with the words beginning "deha" (the body), the meaning is that while grief is established [as a fact], wisdom (*prajñā*) is merely a matter of verbal assertion. Having raised the doubts:

"What is the nature of the body? How is the Self distinct from the body and eternal? Why are these two not to be grieved for? Or how is a terrible act such as war a means to attaining the Self?", it was stated [in the preceding verses] that these are objects of ignorance.

He explains the triad according to the sequence established in the intellect with the words "And this," and so forth. The meaning is that this very battle, because it is refined by a particular state of the intellect, brings about the attainment of the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*).

Regarding the phrase "it has become a means" (*upāyabhūtam*), the absence of the *cvī* suffix indicates that this is its very own nature; however, when it is pursued with a desire for some other result, it becomes that [means].

The meaning is that [the Self] is obstructed. By the word *hi* in the phrase "for the Self" (*ātmā hi*), he indicates the well-known authority of such scriptural passages as "It is not born" (*na jāyate*). With the intention that, although the Self possesses birth and death characterized by conjunction with and separation from a body, these do not consist of the production and destruction [of the Self's essence], he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). As for the word *tu* in the phrase "the body, however" (*dehastu*), [it serves to distinguish the two].

This indicates that its distinctness from the self is established by perception and other means of valid cognition. The meaning is that, because it consists of accumulation as a body and because it is insentient, it is by nature subject to transformation, like a jar or similar objects.

Thus, for one who is ignorant of the nature of the means (*upāya*), the end (*upeya*), and that which is to be excluded (*nivartya*), the desire to know has been aroused by the instruction regarding these three. Now,

in order to establish eligibility for the practice of the means toward results pertaining to the next world, the Self (*ātman*)— which must necessarily be known as distinct from the body and is the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as the end— is [discussed] so that, through the desire for its attainment, a desire for the means to it may be generated.

With the intention that [the Lord] teaches right from the beginning, he says: "First. By the word "Listen," it is indicated—so as to exclude the possibility that this verse, like the statement of an opponent, serves merely for refutation—that its purpose is to secure the listener's attention.

With the intention that he states first that portion which is suitable for immediate comprehension regarding the eternality of the selves in their forms as individual souls (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he says: "I. Since the Lord’s grasping of the "I" (the *ahaṃ-graha*) contains within it the quality of being the controller of all, he states the result of that designation: "The Lord of All."

Thus [ends the quote]. The word "tāvat" indicates agreement. Regarding the phrase "ataḥ param," he explains the meaning of the word *ataḥ*, its appropriate connection (*anuṣaṅga*) even to the preceding sentence, and the intended sense of the word *jātu* by means of the passage beginning with "ataḥ.
The phrase "anabhimatapakṣe" refers to the position held by the Advaitins, who maintain that reality is exclusively devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*).

The meaning intended by the term "real" (satya) is held to be its exclusion from the unreal (asat), and not its being a locus of existence (sattā). In this case as well, it would be stated by them that what is intended by "not unreal" (na-asat) is merely the exclusion from the unreal, and not existence itself. The sense is that [the opponent] intends to negate that [existence]. The underlying thought is that since the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is unestablished, its absence (abhāva) is likewise difficult to express; therefore, existence must be admitted.

Even in a statement primarily intended for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in order to exclude an undesirable position, he states the positive concomitance (*samanvaya*) indicated by the word "but" (*tu*), saying "rather, [I am] You and [I am] He.
Although there is a designation of difference in the form "not you" and "not these," he brings them together as the nature of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*);

and by showing the commonality of the form of being subject to rule (*īśitavyatva*), which results from the referents of the words "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "this" (*idam*) in relation to the Lord (*īśvara*).

He states that the statement made regarding a single instance—which is intended as an illustration—is, by its underlying purport (*tātparya*), actually concerned with all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) beginning with Brahmā.

This is shown in the phrase "those headed by you" (*tvammukhāḥ*). He demonstrates the connection of the word *tu* (but/however) and the modification of the case ending in the verb. [The phrase is] "but they are near," as in the passage: "Neither you nor these lords of men... and so forth. Not... [the rest of the sentence].

Having attached the word "tveva" (indeed) [to the previous verse], one might ask: "Since they are illusory (*mithyā*), let the negation alone suffice without this attachment. This is not so, because it would contradict the second half of the verse. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "You were not non-existent; these lords of men were not non-existent. As for the phrase "all of us," it refers to the previously mentioned aggregate of individual souls (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

He distinguishes the portion to be understood [by the phrase] "I and... Here, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* according to the rule: "When *tyad* and the others are used in conjunction with one another, that which is last remains. This should be understood likewise in what follows. Regarding the word "you" (*bhavantaḥ*), it should also be considered in this way.
Due to the infinity of time, even things that are extremely stable, such as mountains and the like, may at some point perish.
The word "syāt" (might be) excludes mere conjecture;

rather, [the meaning is] "we shall indeed exist. Regarding the fact that the description of one's own nature—which is not the primary subject—is intended as an illustration, therein lies the establishment of eternity through the two qualities intended by the designation "I": namely, being the Lord of all and being the Self of all.

And regarding the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), he states the impossibility of its being eternal with the word "just as" (*yathā*). [He is] the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*); the meaning is:

how could He, who is the sovereign over everything existing in the three periods of time, not Himself exist in the three periods of time? And how could He, the controller of all, ever be obstructed by anyone at any time? [He is] the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); His pervasion is unconditioned by space, time, or essential nature.
The etymological definition of the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*): Thus, because it is all-pervasive (*vyāpta*), there is no destruction of this [Self] by that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*);
and since it is the self of all, its existence at all times is established—this is the intended meaning.
Now, one who even entertains doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) as being distinct from the body and perceptible to the senses—how could such a person [know] beyond that?

Could he be free from doubt regarding the Supreme Self, which is distinct [from the individual soul] and entirely beyond the range of perception? It is said: No, for this Arjuna is himself the speaker of such passages as "the eternal, divine Person";
moreover, he has understood the nature of the Supreme Person—the Supreme Brahman—through the words of hundreds of great sages such as Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa.
Having personally witnessed the power of penance and mantras that grant access to the entire world of Indra, possessing unsurpassed devotion to his gurus and deities,

and never wavering from the conduct prescribed for all castes and stages of life, he is nonetheless overwhelmed by the fear of violating dharma; he either wanders in the delusion or harbors doubt that the self and the Lord exist as something entirely distinct from the body, precisely because he lacks knowledge of the specific details of those [higher] modes.

For him, there is indeed grief and so forth. Consequently, he conceives of God and His eternity—established by [attributes] such as being the Lord of all—in a general sense; this is because, through worldly observation, he perceives birth, destruction, and the like, and because he has a superficial understanding of the meaning of scriptural passages such as "After death, there is no consciousness. Thus, he does not know the specific modes of the individual soul (jīva) in their true nature.

There is no fault whatsoever. Regarding the phrase "the Knower of the Field by means of the Self": just as the attributes of the individual soul (jīva) do not belong to it because of its distinction from the Supreme Self (paramātman), so too, by virtue of the distinction from the Field (kṣetra) which will be described later, the impermanence and other qualities inherent in the Field should not be suspected of belonging to the individual soul (jīva) who is its controller; this is the intended meaning.

Then, illustrating by the maxim of "a single grain from a cooking pot" the defects of those compositions— which are like rags made of tattered, old cloth-pieces, stitched together from root to tip by the ill-minded *sauca* weaver, and which reek with the scent of being neither properly joined nor disjoined— he first states the contradiction with the introduction of the treatise and the impossibility of the treatise's commencement.

By the words "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth: the meaning is "in this manner," namely, by the method of stating the commencement of the treatise which is intent upon the instruction of reality (*tattva*).

"From the Blessed One, the Lord of All" means from Him who possesses both [male and female] characteristics, the controller of all, who is indicated by the word "I" (*aham*). If the difference between the individual souls (*jīva*) and the Lord were not ultimately real, [the following would not hold].

There would be a confusion of natures, such as possessing both genders or being subject to suffering. Furthermore, if the mutual distinction between selves were not real, the established order of the bound and the liberated, or of disciple and teacher, would be untenable—this is the sense.
[This was spoken] by the Blessed One himself, and not by some ordinary person on the street. Or else: "You alone know yourself, who you are."

The intention is that by the Lord’s statement "That art thou" (*so'si*), it is understood that He has declared the true nature (*tattva*) of Himself as well as of the individual souls (*jīvas*) who constitute His own body. Regarding the phrase "deluded by ignorance": for one who is wandering about in confusion by himself, even an authoritative person (*āpta*) [cannot provide the truth].

The sense is that it is precisely delusion (*bhrānti*) that must be produced. To the objection—"Why should this instruction not be [delusory], just as [the teachings] of the Asuras and others are [delusory] by way of the descent of Buddhas and so forth?"—it is said: "For the sake of its cessation. The sense is that you yourselves have accepted and provided commentaries on the fact that the *Gītā-upaniṣad* is for the purpose of removing delusion (*moha*).

The plural number is used with the intention of referring to the diversity of bodies, not with the intention of referring to a diversity of selves. [The author] refutes what was stated by Śaṅkara: "In the ultimate sense... This is not so. The passage beginning with "But never indeed do I... is a recitation of a mantra for the purpose of removing delusion, such that we might consider the mention of difference to have another intent; rather, it is this...

The intended meaning is that [the scripture] consists of instruction regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*). Regarding the passage beginning with "I" (*aham*): "I" refers to one's own self as the subject (*pratyaktvena*); "you" refers to another conscious being facing oneself; "these" refers to the many conscious beings turned away from oneself; "all" refers to the many individuals subsumed under a single limiting condition (*upādhi*); and "we" refers to the infinite individuals grouped into a single class by including oneself within it.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "because of this designation": the sense is that here no negation has been made such as "I am not," nor "you are not," nor even "another is not. In response to the objection that, according to the Bhāskara school, since difference is caused by real limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the mention of difference is logically consistent, it is stated there as well in general terms:

He states that the objection is unavoidable with the words "aupādhika" (conditioned). The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to show that even in the examples cited by the opponent, such as the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*), the aspect of difference in that which is conditioned by distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is admitted to be non-real.
This is just as, for instance, of a single face or moon, [multiple reflections appear] through jewels, swords, rivers, oceans, and so forth, even though the limiting adjuncts are real.

Even by means of real limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), difference is not ultimately real. Just as in the case of space and other such entities, which are single and unitary, there is no difference dependent upon limiting adjuncts—such as jars or water-pots—that exists apart from the difference in their conjunctions with those adjuncts, even though the adjuncts themselves are real; so too, for Brahman, who is partless, incapable of being cut or divided, and omnipresent, any difference caused by real limiting adjuncts such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not ultimately real.

Thus it must be accepted. And consequently, the meaning is that at the time of teaching the truth, an instruction contrary to that [truth] is not possible for one who teaches for the sake of welfare. Furthermore, in both cases, contradiction with the Śruti is a defect. With the intention of showing that, in his own position, there is no suspicion of the teaching being intended to delude—unlike the Buddhist scriptures and others—because it is in agreement with the Śruti, he says, "by the Blessed One," or alternatively: the Śruti has been cited precisely to refute the position of Bhāskara; and therefore, by the principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so), [the refutation of other views follows].

The position of Śaṅkara has also been refuted. The word "also" (*api*) serves to conjoin the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the phrase "the distinction between selves taught by the Blessed One," it is indicated that, just as in the case of the Veda, there is independence from other means of valid cognition. For even the eternal Veda is a means of valid cognition precisely because it consists of His command.
In the phrase "the eternal among the eternals," [the word] "pavitrāṇām" (of the purifiers) is used.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as it is said that He is the cause of the purity of the purifiers, if it is stated that He is the cause of the eternity of the eternal, how could there be any possibility of non-eternality?
To dispel this doubt, it is specified as "culminating in non-eternality. Among the purifiers, this [Brahman] is the most preeminent.

The meaning is "like purity. According to Śaṅkara’s interpretation, among eternal things, the Supreme possesses a superior form of eternity; furthermore, the intention is that among living beings (jīvas), only a relative eternity—consisting in existing for a duration longer than [others]—is established. By interpreting [the text] as "like pure," one avoids the delusion of a different meaning that would result in the non-eternity of the living beings.

Rejecting [the opponent's view], he maintains that because of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of eternality, plurality, and sentience, the plurality and sentience of the selves are indeed unconditional (*nirupādhika*); thus, the reading "sa kāmān vidadhāti" (he ordains desires) is incorrect.
For the word "tam" (him), which is the correlative to the word "yaḥ" (who) found in the Śruti, occurs right there in the second half of the verse as "tam ātmastham" (him, situated in the self).

Since the word "tat" (that) is not observed in the first half [of the verse] due to its being in the present tense, and since the reading "cetanaḥ san" (being conscious) is found, let it be so; otherwise, let there be no such word as "sa" (he). This is shown just as in the case of the scriptural statement: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is unswerving on the new moon and full moon days"; from that very [reading], [the view] of those who maintain the non-eternality of the self [is refuted].

Intending to refute others as well—namely, the Buddhists and others who maintain that there is a fundamental distinction based on ignorance and so forth; Śaṅkara and others who maintain that consciousness is subject to arising and passing away;

and the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that the power of consciousness is merely eternal—the identity of the Lord [with Brahman] is established through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the four nominative case-words, and the identity of that [Lord] with Hiraṇyagarbha, Rudra, Indra, and the rest.

Indicating the refutation of the positions of the *pravāheśvara* (the Lord as the stream of time) by demonstrating its indivisibility from distinctions such as time, and pointing toward the expansion of eternal consciousness well-known from other scriptural passages (*śruti*), it follows that even though the word "that" (*yat*) exists in this sentence,
because there is an injunction qualified by all the attributes, those attributes themselves are also objects of the injunction. Likewise, here too, [the Self] is eternal.

The sense is that, beginning from this point, every single part constitutes a predicate because it forms part of the qualified object to be enjoined as understood from the first half [of the verse]. This applies to the view where [the injunction] is not already established (*aprāptatva*). Even in the view where it is already established (*prāptatva*), since it is authoritative, any other opinion would indeed contradict it. As for the passage "That which belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneyaḥ*):

Thus, while indicating that even though there are signs of restatement (anuvāda) in such passages, they must be treated as qualified injunctions (viśiṣṭavidhi) by virtue of the fact that [the matter] has not been previously established,

he states the meaning of the Śruti: "At all times, everywhere, for all conscious beings, there is only one Lord who, propitiated by their respective actions, brings about whatever is required in accordance with those very actions."

Regarding the phrase "of eternal [entities]": again, by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), he states a blow to the very foundation of the undertaking of the treatise, in the form of the impossibility of teaching the doctrine of Śaṅkara. He says: "Through ignorance... Does this Blessed One teach an object known by himself, or one unknown? Even if it is known, is it directly realized, or merely heard?
Thus, considering the alternative— whether that ignorance has ceased in both cases or not,
and even if it has ceased, whether the delusion regarding the diversity that is its effect ceases or not—
he states the refutation for the position that ignorance and its effects cease through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
"Of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣasya)": the sense is that the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) would otherwise possess a vision of what is not the ultimate reality.
"Without distinctions," and so forth: being without distinctions means the absence of difference from those of the same class, those of a different class, or internal differences [within itself];
being immutably fixed (kūṭasthatva) means being established in Māyā, being common to all, or being devoid of modification.

Just as an immutable and unchanging iron mass (kūṭa) serves as the cause of transformation for things associated with it, such as iron filings, so too [is the Self]; for that very reason, its eternity consists in being unconditioned by time.
Its true nature (yāthātmya) is of the kind described. Furthermore, even for people like us, the non-perception of this reality is admitted by others.
Thus, in order to exclude that [duality], there is the statement regarding the direct realization of the true nature (*yāthātmya-sākṣātkāra*). Ignorance is *avidyā*;

its effect is the delusion of difference (*bhedabhrama*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), such things as the instigation to action are included. For the conventional practice of instruction and so forth is rooted in the perception of various kinds of distinctions, such as the distinction between the object to be taught, the words expressing it, the qualified disciple, the teacher, and the purpose.

The point is this: it is your own view that the perception of difference is produced by ignorance alone; therefore, once ignorance and its effects have ceased, how could there be the continued persistence of those very effects? Consequently, a hundred defects—such as contradiction, deviation from established tenets, the futility of composing the scripture, the absence of instruction, and fruitless exertion—along with opposition to the Śruti, would arise.

He raises the objection that even though ignorance (*ajñāna*) has ceased through the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*), the delusion of duality (*bhedabhrama*) may still persist due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and that this [delusion] might not be a cause of bondage. He begins with the word "Now" (*atha*). The phrase "like a burnt cloth, etc. means:
just as a burnt cloth or similar object, although it remains an object of the appearance of a cloth, no longer performs the function of a cloth, so it is here.
The sense is that even though the delusion of difference persists, it does not serve as a cause for *saṃsāra*.

The point is that this [position] is untenable; only an illustration has been stated, but no actual proof, and on the contrary, there is a lack of justification. He states this lack of justification along with an example: "Like a mirage," etc.

The logical consequence here is as follows: if it were certain that the cognition of difference is false because it is sublated by another cognition, then it would not be the cause of an activity corresponding to its own object—just like the cognition of water in a mirage, which persists even after being sublated. And thus, a cognition of difference that persists despite being sublated is like a burnt cloth and so forth; it does not [produce its expected effect].

The meaning is that [the opponent's position] performs its own function; however, because there is no fruit for the persistence of what has been sublated, it results in a contradiction of one's own desired conclusion.

Even on the view that [liberation] occurs through mere hearing, since there is no difference between the object of the direct realization and the object of the hearing—both having the featureless (nirviśeṣa) as their object—the cessation of ignorance is logically established;
therefore, [the author] refutes the nature of the "persistence of what has been sublated" regarding the Lord of All, saying:
"And not... and so forth.
It cannot be said that he was previously ignorant simply because of his status as the Lord (Īśvara), for that would entail the consequence of him being a non-Lord.

If even the Lord were previously ignorant, his acquisition of the scriptures would also be impossible, since there would be no other teacher of the scriptures possessing superior knowledge than him. Or, if such a person did exist—

Whether he be a Lord (Īśvara) or not a Lord, how could he possess perfected knowledge from some source? This would lead to defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is there a succession of Lords in an eternal stream, for that has been refuted. Furthermore, the Lord does not come to understand reality through a scripture composed by himself, because that would entail the defects of the non-eternality of the Vedas and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor did he learn the meaning by merely recollecting the Vedas, which are beginningless; for the prior perception that serves as the cause for such recollection is itself untenable due to the absence of an instructor, and so forth. With these and other such defects in mind, it was stated: "previously ignorant," and so on. [This implies that] if the Lord were previously ignorant or possessed knowledge dependent upon scripture, there would have to exist another instructor for him.

And regarding the persistence of error, he states the contradiction with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*: "He who is omniscient" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*). There is no tautology between the words "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) and "all-knowing" (*sarvavid*), because of the intended meaning that He knows everything both in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and in its specific modes (*prakārataḥ*); or alternatively, "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*) means He attains or reaches everything.

Thus, the impossibility of the reason for instruction has been stated. Now, he says "Furthermore" (kiñca) to show that even the status of being an instructor is untenable. Regarding the phrase "of the present day": not only is the very first instruction created by God untenable, but even the current one is so; for in the lineage of teachers—such as the masters of monasteries (*maṭhapati*) who possess dull intellects—the disciples merely fill their own bellies, and thus there is an absence of [qualified] disciples.

The sense is that [if they were ignorant,] fasting unto death would follow as a consequence. Intending to show the impossibility of the position that they are ignorant teachers, he says: "by their own conviction," and so forth.

The sense is that these [teachers] do not have objects that are unperceived, nor objects that are doubtful, nor objects that are contradictory; nor are they mere repeaters of what others say, nor do they chatter at random like children or madmen.

"Why?"—the meaning is that one must provide an answer to the questioner after considering the following alternatives: for whom? For oneself or for another; in the former case, for one determined to be distinct or for one who is unreal; and even if unreal, for one perceived as such or otherwise. In that regard, if there is a determination of the reality of one's own self as being distinct:

There would follow the faults of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), ignorance, and so forth. If it were certain that [the teaching] is unreal, there would be no instruction, just as there is none from the son of a barren woman and the like.
If it were for oneself, determined to be non-different [from the Self], then instruction would have to occur at all times even without the appearance of Arjuna and others;
yet there is no purpose whatsoever for instruction in that case. But if it were for another who is ultimately real, then [instruction would be necessary] even when there is a difference of bodies.

You accept this. If [you claim that instruction is given] to another who perceives [the object] merely as unreal, then—as in the previous case—there would be the undesirable consequence of instruction being possible even regarding reflections, the son of a barren woman, and so forth, since these are determined to be either indeterminable or non-existent.
Furthermore, if one were to understand another who is merely unreal to be real, then one would simply not be a knower of reality.

Since it remains unestablished that [the Lord] is a teacher of reality—this being the case—he raises an objection regarding the position that [the Lord is known] through the force of subverting cognition as non-different from those things which, though ultimately one, are perceived as different due to delusion:
"Like a reflection. He refutes this with: "No. He explains the lack of logical consistency with: "For not..."
The sense is that by [calling him] "not insane," you would effectively be admitting that even Īśvara and others are indeed insane.
Regarding the phrase "some person": the implication is, "how much more so Īśvara? Regarding the phrase "knowing non-difference":

children and others who do not know difference might well offer such instruction; however, in this case, if the instructor were determined to be other [than the one being instructed], it would entail the undesirable consequence of his being deluded and so forth.

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). Regarding the phrase "something" (*kimapi*): it refers to something either worldly or transcendental, having a visible purpose or an invisible purpose; the sense is, "how much more so for the sake of liberation"? Previously, a further refutation was stated by assuming the nature of the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*); now he says that even that [sublation] is not established according to that [opponent's] own view. This is expressed by the words "bādhitā... (the sublated...).

He establishes [this] by means of the subverting argument (*bādhaka*): for indeed, in the absence of a cause, an effect cannot occur. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the cessation of error would not follow upon the cessation of defects. Regarding the term "beginningless" (*anādi*): this refers to a defect that serves as the cause of the cognition of difference, which has persisted for all this time because it is either beginningless in its own nature or in its stream, and is thus not removable by anything else.
The sense is that if destruction were not to occur even through the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*), then Brahman would be subject to eternal transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Here, some read *ajñānādeḥ*; in that case, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the delusion of difference (*bhedabhrama*) and its object are included. He states the justification for the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*) in the example cited by others, beginning with the words *dvicandra* and *pāramārthika*.

For that which is ultimately real cannot be sublated; the sense is that if it were so, there would follow the absurdity of the collapse of the distinction between sublation and non-sublation. Regarding the phrase "of the cause of the cognition of a double moon":
the cause of a prior cognition is certainly not sublated by a sublating cognition, for otherwise it would follow that even the sense faculties and so forth would be sublated.
Therefore, it is only the superimposed object that is sublated by a cognition apprehending a contradictory property, which has as its object the locus of that superimposition.
In this case, the visual impairment (*timira*) and so forth are not the object of the cognition of two moons or the cognition of the oneness of the moon;

for you [the opponent], however, ignorance, its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth—which are the material cause of all delusions of difference—are objects of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*).

The point is that since the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) has as its object all entities excluding the non-dual Self, even the beginningless cause is indeed subverted. Regarding the word "logical" (*yuktā*): the point is that when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) persists, the persistence of the effect is established. If error (*bhrānti*) persists, how then [can there be liberation]?

Regarding the cessation of wonder, fear, and so forth resulting from that effect, he says: "Even though it persists. By the word *prabala* (powerful), it is indicated that, according to the opponent's position, there is no distinction between the delusion of difference and its sublation. For they both maintain that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the cause of both; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of two truths. And this being the case, which of the two could be the sublater and which the sublated?

Or [is it not]? Nor should it be said that the fact that the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) is rooted in a defect (*doṣa-mūlatva*) is unknown; for at the very first moment, during the time of hearing (*śravaṇa*), there arises the realization of the falsity of everything other than Brahman. Nor does the non-duality (*advaita*) become established merely by the ignorance of the fact that the knowledge whose object is non-duality is rooted in a defect. For instance, in the case of the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the shell is not established merely by the ignorance of the fact that the error is rooted in a defect. This is the meaning.

The establishment of reality [of an object] does not follow from that alone; for even by the cognition of mother-of-pearl—which sublates the cognition of real silver and which itself has its defects unknown—there is no sublation of the actual nature of the silver. If it is argued that the distinction between the sublated and the sublater is determined by priority and posteriority despite the lack of difference in their being rooted in defects, we say no; because once the fact that they are rooted in defects is known, posteriority is of no consequence.

This is because it is understood to be erroneous, like the statement that sublates the [false] perception of a snake in a rope. Otherwise, even by a Mādhyamika statement—known to be rooted in defects—such as "emptiness alone is the reality," there would be the sublation of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) merely on account of its being posterior.

Now, explaining the difference from the illustrative example by means of the fact that the cause also possesses the characteristic of being unreal (*apāramārthikatva*), defined by its being an object of sublation: [The text continues: ...the difference from the illustrative example is explained by the fact that the cause also possesses the characteristic of being unreal, defined by its being an object of sublation.
He concludes that the persistence of what has been sublated is impossible with the words "But here...

(*iha tu*). "In no way whatsoever" means either by beginningless ignorance or by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the cognition of difference, and so forth. He concludes the demonstration of the impossibility of the cause of instruction—which was introduced with the intention of the alternative "whether known or unknown"—by clarifying those alternatives with the words "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
The sense is that for one who knows [the truth] "all the more so," there is at least even a mere illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the sublation of the persistence [of ignorance];

however, for one who does not know, even that does not exist in the case of instruction. The impossibility of the causes of instruction has already been stated; now he states its futility with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). By the passage beginning with "to those appearing like reflections," etc., the position of the individual soul's ignorance (*jīvājñāna*) has already been addressed.

Since this position has already been refuted under the doctrine of Brahman-ignorance (*brāhmājñāna*), the following further criticism is stated: According to them, there is indeed only one Brahman variegated by ignorance and only one individual soul (*jīva*); due to the delusion of that very one, like a dreamer, other souls and so forth appear, just as other men seen in a dream appear to him.

They describe it thus: for that single individual, whose specific bodily state is undetermined and whose time of occurrence is not fixed, the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated—like a dream-world—by the awakening of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
In this regard, the instructor is that very same teacher, such as Vāsudeva or others; or it may be one seen by him. Likewise, the disciple is that very same person, such as Arjuna or others.

Intending the alternative that "he has been seen by him," the author states the refutation regarding the position that "the Guru is that very person" with the words "of the Guru. The phrase "along with its effects" implies [the inclusion of] the relationship of disciple and teacher and so forth; by this, the absence of an instructor, the absence of an inquirer, and the absence of the necessary conditions for instruction are stated. He restates the position that the Guru has seen Him with the words "the Guru."

For a dream is not sublated by the cognition of a person imagined by a dreamer; likewise, since there would be no sublation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) here by the knowledge of the Guru, the teaching for the purpose of its sublation would be purposeless—this is the sense. He refutes this with the words "of the disciple," etc.
The meaning is as follows: first of all, we do not find any evidence for the third alternative here, namely, that Arjuna and others are that very same individual soul (jīva).

Nor does the teacher think, "This disciple of mine, the individual soul (jīva), will become liberated, while I am merely imagined by him like a dreamer. If that were the case, he would not instruct one who has caused his own destruction and is thus a great wrongdoer; for he himself would have ceased to exist simply by the very rule of the dream-nature, and thus would not practice the means to liberation.
If the disciple were to regard the teacher as if seen in a dream, then he would not listen;
for since both the teacher and the excellence of his knowledge would be merely imagined through his own delusion,
why would he himself listen to that specific object of knowledge from him?

The claim that the cessation of one's own delusion occurs through the error of instruction produced by an instructor who is himself imagined [to be authoritative] is laughable; for such cessation is possible even without him, through the mere cessation of one's own perceptual delusion. Furthermore, even though Arjuna was a knower of the Truth, the cessation of his delusion is not seen to have occurred until this very day.
Therefore, the fourth alternative remains: that even the disciple, like the teacher, is seen by yet another who perceives the entire phenomenal world as a dream.

Consequently, just like the knowledge of Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others, the knowledge of Arjuna and the rest would not remove ignorance; thus, the exertion of the disciples and teachers—such as Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna—to achieve liberation by abandoning the three aims of life (trivarga) would be fruitless, and the commencement of the scripture would be untenable.

Now, anticipating the objection based on the principle of "severance" (*apaccheda-naya*) preceded by a mocking tone, he refutes it with the words beginning "Even if [the self] were imagined" (*kalpitatve 'pi*).

Thus, since the teaching would be untenable, and because liberation would never be possible even for that single soul who is the witness of all, there would be no purpose for the scripture; consequently, the commencement of the scripture itself would be untenable—this is the final conclusion.

Thus, since the scripture, its teacher, its listener, and its purpose are all untenable, and since every other philosophical system (*paramata*) has been refuted in general, he concludes with a shift of focus, asking: "What is the use of further minor refutations?
He says, "Enough is done" (*iti kṛtam*). The meaning is "enough" (*alam*); by the phrase "by these improper arguments," he implies that they are useless.
In this regard, hundreds of such refutations as stated in the Śārīrakabhāṣya and other works have been recalled even against the system of Bhāskara and others.

The eternity of the self has been stated for the sake of its being beyond grief. In that regard, he dispels the doubt—namely, how the perception and worldly transaction of birth, death, and so forth can occur if the self is eternal—by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*). He explains the intended meaning of the reference "in this" (*asmin*) by saying "in one" (*ekasmin*).

With the intention that the illustration of the three stages of the body serves as an illustration precisely for the embodied self, he says: "of one abiding in the body. He states what is implied by the nature of the meaning indicated by the sequential mention of "childhood, youth, and old age. He says "having abandoned" in order to exclude childhood and youth, since the abandonment of those two is also a cause for a particular kind of grief, and to clarify the intended sense of the word "just as" (*yathā*).

It has been said: "Of the self," and so forth. For even when the state of childhood ceases, the notion of the stability of the self is the cause for the absence of grief resulting from its destruction; that [notion] is the same here as well—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "attaining another body," he shows the cause of grief called the abandonment of the previous body, which was indicated by the word "immediately" (*antara*) in that context: "from the body."

The meaning of the word *dhīra* (the steadfast) is specified by the context as "the stable Self" and "the wise one. He connects this with what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "those who are not to be grieved for. Thus, by these two verses, that which is to be attained and that which is to be turned away from have been indicated in succession. Now, herein [is presented] that which pertains to Me, which is the fruit resulting from the two subsequent verses concerning the means of attainment.

Having summarized [the preceding], he states the connection with the words "this much" (*etāvat*), ending with "for the cessation of bondage" (*bandhanivṛttaye*). This is the meaning of the phrase "for the sake of immortality" (*amṛtatvāya*).
It is stated here for the purpose of showing that for those whose nature is pure, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is impossible; this is expressed by the word "beginningless" (*anādi*).
The sense is that [beings are subject to transmigration] through the power of karma, and not through the power of an indeterminable ignorance (*ajñāna*) or the like.

It has been stated that "respective actions" (*tattat-karma*) are for the sake of establishing the diversity of bodies, enjoyments, and so forth among souls that are inherently and absolutely identical to one another.

Regarding the phrase "for the cessation of bondage by means of bodies": the meaning is "for the cessation of that bondage which consists of the bodies. Alternatively, another [interpretation] is: "of those performing actions by means of those very same bodies"; in that case, however, the bodies themselves are the causes of bondage.

The intention of the restriction is that [these means] are possible as the instruments for achieving liberation. Regarding the term "scriptural" (śāstrīyam): the sense is that otherwise, by transgressing the bowstring of the Lord, there would surely be punishment. Regarding the phrase "appropriate for a Kṣatriya" (kṣatriyocitam): the sense is that it is not better for you to abandon battle and the like to live on alms.

It was stated [that suffering] is for the sake of not dying. The word "tu" (but/however), which dispels the doubt as to how that which is adverse by nature can be something to be performed, indicates its inevitability (*avarjanīyatva*); this inevitability is the reason why it must be endured. The syntactical connection here is: "this much alone is to be done in this matter.

Now, since the context concerns the *gata-asu* (those whose life-force has departed) and the *agata-asu* (those whose life-force has not yet departed), [the following] is for the purpose of defining them.
When the verse beginning with "nāsataḥ" was intended to be introduced, why is this other matter being stated? To address this, he introduces the topic with the words "ātmanityatve.
First, the fruit of that purpose for which the permanence of the self is described is shown.

[An objection: But surely, grief arises from the fear of falling into the belly of a dog or similar states—which lead to hell and so forth—precisely because of the knowledge of a self distinct from the body.

Regarding the doubt raised after the previous verse: one who desires the fruit does not take account of the hardship involved in the means; furthermore, the fruit is not something to be loathed because it is of the nature of liberation; and this very [discipline] is the means, and no other. Therefore, He says, "Endure.
Or rather, even though the body or the self are not objects of grief, why then are the contacts with the sense-objects [a cause for grief]?

Regarding the point that those which cause suffering are to be respected, he states that they must be endured by the words "merely" (*mātra*). To the question "for what purpose?", he shows the result with the following verse. It is intended to be said in the subsequent [verse] that endurance (*titikṣā*), when preceded by knowledge and being the generator of knowledge, becomes the cause of liberation. Now, [one might ask: "What is the loss of the self (*ātmanāśa*) to you?"

If it is argued that one may also say: "Thus there is grief, or the destruction of the body; having conceptualized [the self] as perishable because of contact with the objects of the senses, the resolution is provided by the three verses beginning with 'But never am I...'"—let it be so, since multiplicity is possible within the method of investigation. In any case, the four verses beginning with "But never am I... [constitute the response].

It has the nature of a summary of everything that is to be said hereafter. Among those, the first [verse], "I am," is an introduction to oneself, because the fruit described as "fit for immortality" is to be attained through devotion directed toward oneself alone. The second verse is not primarily concerned with the impermanence of the body; rather, it is like the verse beginning with "clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*), since it speaks of attaining another body.

This is supplementary to the description of the Self. In the third verse, by the statement "giving cool comfort" (*śītasukhadā*), it is understood that [the earth] is an object even for those seeking liberation who are indifferent to pleasure; this is also indicated by the phrase "it prepares one for immortality.
Therefore, even the happiness of sovereignty obtainable through victory is endurable, and even the suffering in battle and similar circumstances is endurable.

He says, "This meaning [is stated] immediately hereafter," because this matter is stated now all at once due to its exceptional importance, even though it ought to have been explained at the conclusion of the section on the eternity of the self. He explains: "The sense organs, such as the ear, are called *mātrā* because by means of them objects such as sound are measured (*mīyante*). This is said in order to set aside the well-known interpretation offered by Śaṅkara and others.

He states the meaning of the word *mātrā*: “*śabda-etc.*” [The phrase] “*sāśrayāḥ*” (having a substratum) means that the substance (*dravya*) as qualified by its qualities (*guṇa*) is indeed the effect of those *tanmātras*; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase “*tanmātrākāryatvāt*”:
there is no dispute at all regarding the fact that the *tanmātras* are denoted by the word *mātrā*.

The sense is that there are indeed usages such as "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*) and "mere touch" (*sparśamātra*); and since the substance which is the effect of those [qualities] is also a single substance with them, its being within the scope of those words is logically established. Furthermore, because the derivation [of the word *guṇa*] from the root *gam* (to go) is more well-known than the derivation from *bhū* (to be), and because the connection with the object itself is the direct cause of pleasure and so forth.
Having considered this, he states the meaning of the compound while specifying another correlate of touch:

"Their touches are by means of the ear and so forth. He further states that "cold" and "hot" are illustrative examples and provides the meaning of the compound: "having the form of cold, hot, soft, harsh, and so on. Thus, setting aside the relationship of cause and effect...
The sense is that if one were to construe [the verse] as "giving cold and heat" and "giving pleasure and pain," the separate designation would be redundant.
To the question, "Since cold and heat are not applicable in battle, for what purpose is this said? he replies:
"The words 'cold' and 'heat' are for the sake of illustration. The ellipsis to be supplied is "of the falling of weapons and so forth."
However, cold, heat, and so forth should be endured as they arise within the respective duties of one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*).

By using the word "steadfast" (*dhīra*), which is to be mentioned later, and by drawing back what was previously stated in the phrase "the steadfast person there," he says that one should transcend those [pairs of opposites] through fortitude.
Alternatively, right here, by means of the two words *Kaunteya* and *Bhārata*, [he refers to] one born of a Kṣatriya lineage.
It is indicated that your fortitude alone is worthy of one born into a distinguished lineage of Kṣatriyas.

Just as in the performance of austerities, sacrifices, and the like, wind, heat, hunger, thirst, and the slaughter of animals must be endured until the completion of those rites, so too here must the falling of weapons, the slaying of enemies, and so forth be endured. Therefore, the contact with the objects of the senses is unavoidable.
The sense is that since sorrow arising from external causes is difficult to avoid, it is only proper to exercise forbearance toward useless grief.

Here, "forbearance" regarding the portion of pleasure consists in non-arrogance through equanimity; the reason for this is likewise its very nature of coming and going (transience). To avoid redundancy with the word "impermanent," he says "bandhu" (relative); in this context, the word "impermanent" negates continuity in a stream.

The word-break (*padaccheda*) as "eternal" (*nityāḥ*) is weak for suggesting that they must be endured as constant accompaniments; for they are subject to coming and going, and because they are absent in liberation (*mukti*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that there is no eternity even in terms of a continuous flow (*pravāha*).

Why, then, is there forbearance (*kṣamā*)? Is it for the sake of a visible purpose, or for the sake of an invisible (transcendental) purpose, or because it is unavoidable due to being inherent to one's own nature? Not the first, because it is perceived as having the nature of suffering.

Not the second, because it abounds in unrighteousness (*adharma*), such as the killing of gurus and the destruction of families. Not the third, because [one could simply] desist from battle altogether.
The sense is that there is an absence of the falling of weapons and so forth. The word "dhīram" (the steadfast) is used to indicate his fitness for endurance (*titikṣā*).
By [using this term], he dispels the delusion of not knowing the inequality between pleasure and pain, as well as the delusion that the two are equal in measure.
He also answers the doubt as to "for what purpose" [he endures]. [He does so] by describing him as one who regards unavoidable suffering as being like pleasure.

The meaning is as follows: just as one desiring health engages in the hardship of taking medicine and the like because one regards it as happiness since it is a means to happiness; and just as one seeking wealth engages in the hardship of crossing the ocean and so forth; likewise, one who desires the cessation of the threefold suffering and unsurpassed bliss should regard the suffering that is inseparable from its means as being indeed like happiness.

It has been stated— beginning with "as the means to immortality"— in order to exclude the notion that even for one suspected of being a thief or the like, the mere endurance of dualities is a cause of liberation. Furthermore,
the phrase "these" was stated to demonstrate their inevitability and their inclusion within that [endurance].
They cause distress through the torment of thinking [the goal] has not been attained;

yet, because there is a state of being (*sattva*) even amidst the accumulation of the experience of suffering, they do not cause distress—meaning they do not disturb [the mind]. This meaning of "not disturbing" is the one agreed upon by the three schools of thought, as the root *vyath* is read in the sense of "fear" and "agitation. It does not mean "disturbing."

"But they cause pain"; [this is said] because even a soft touch is included under the term "touch. By using the remote demonstrative pronouns *yat* and *tat*, and by the shift in intonation (*viparīta-kāku*) in the phrase "O bull among men," he states the established conclusion: "He alone [is the one].
One such as you is agitated by misplaced affection and the like, for the sake of introducing the meaning of the following verse.
And he concludes for the sake of establishing indifference toward any remedy for the destruction of the self, saying: "Because of the eternity of the selves.

"Only this much" means merely endurance (*titikṣā*), and not grief or the like. "In this regard" refers to those things that come and go—their continuity to be brought to an end by the knowledge of reality—which have an unavoidable presence during the performance of the means to the supreme human goal characterized by immortality.

The meaning is that [one must act] when the sufferings such as the falling of weapons have arrived. The sense is that "it must be done" because, if it were not done, there would be an absence of the fruit consisting of liberation;
furthermore, by abandoning one's own duty (svadharma), there would be sin (pratyavāya), and there would also be the risk of infamy and so forth caused by the lack of fortitude and other virtues.
He introduces the verse beginning with "Not of the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*) as an introduction to the establishment of the subject matter that was previously interrupted, stating: "As for what...

"Inherent" (*svābhāvikam*) means necessarily occurring due to a changing nature (*pariṇāmi-svabhāva*), and not independent of causes. "The cause of non-sorrow" (*śokānimitta*) means opposed to the cause of sorrow; that is to say, it is the cause of the absence of sorrow.
Because previously there was merely a statement of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it was said "in order to establish" (*upapādayituṃ*).

Since this verse also consists merely of a proposition (*pratijñā*) for the purpose of establishing [the point], it was said "he begins" (*ārabhate*). Explaining the specific meaning appropriate to the context of words such as "existent," "non-existent," "entity," and "non-entity," he comments: "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*).

The phrase "of the non-existent and the existent" (asataḥ sataśca) is to be explained as follows: its meaning is specified by the context and other factors as referring to "the body and the self. The result of this indication is stated as "of these two," namely, "of those being perceived.

With regard to the vision of reality (tattvadarśana), the author—intending to indicate the transcendence of the appearance of perception, as suggested by the word "but" (tu)—says: "by those who see reality according to how it is perceived."

By this, Śaṅkara’s statement—that "the word *tat* [is the Brahman], and its state of being so is *tattva*"—is refuted; for it is impossible for that which is eternal and designated by the word *sat* (Being) to undergo destruction. Thus, the word *anta* signifies "ascertainment.
In that regard, the manner in which the word functions is as follows:

In this section concerning the discrimination between the body and the self (*dehātma-viveka*), he states that [the aforementioned interpretation] alone is appropriate in light of the proximity of the phrase "by those who see reality" (*tattvadarśibhiḥ*) and so forth, because [this section] concludes with a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). Now, an objection is raised: It has been stated that "the existence of the body is not found," which contradicts perception and other means of knowledge; furthermore, it is incorrect to say that "the non-existence of the self is not found," as in the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadevedamagra āsīt*).
Because even that [non-existence] is denotable by the word "non-existent" during such a state of universal negation;
furthermore, existence and non-existence with respect to particular states are equally applicable to both the body and the self.

Therefore, he says this in response to the view that this verse should be explained as having the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and so forth as its subject matter, like other commentaries.

Regarding the phrase "of the body" (*dehasya*): by the two terms "insentient object" (*acidvastunaḥ*) and "sentient being" (*cetanasya*), the reason for the nature of existence and non-existence is indicated, as well as the application of the words "existent" and "non-existent" with reference to the sentient and the insentient.
Now, one might object: even so, the challenge regarding the existence and non-existence of the body and the self has not been resolved; to this he replies: "by destruction," etc. (*vināśa*...).
By the word *hi*, the firmness established by the formal argument (*prayoga*) is indicated. He demonstrates that very point with the words “as it has been stated.

In the *Daśaślokī*, through the introduction and conclusion of the Purāṇa, as well as the conclusion of that specific section, and in the middle [of the work]—in the *Śarīrakabhāṣya* [with the statement] “The earth [exists] because of its pot-ness”—there exists the application of the terms *vastu* (real), *avastu* (unreal), *asti* (is), *nāsti* (is not), *satya* (true), and *asatya* (false).

By such statements as these, since the status of being a non-entity is established precisely because [the world] possesses modification, and in accordance with other Śruti and Smṛti texts as well as perception and other means of knowledge, its character as the object of both eternal and non-eternal, and conscious and unconscious entities, is established by way of its being changeless. The words "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) refer to the fitness or unfitness for empirical usage; of these two—

In response to the doubt as to how there can be identity of meaning between the terms "truth" and "untruth" when applied to the domains of the ultimate and the non-ultimate, [the author] cites the words of the Great Sage regarding the fact that the application of terms such as "ultimate" is based solely on the states of destruction and non-destruction: "That which is indestructible... This is because it is precisely through the loss of the prior state—by means of transformation, growth, and so forth, characterized by destruction—that a thing comes to be associated with a different designation.

He shows clearly that the meaning is: "the state of being denotable by the word 'non-entity,' and due to the absence of that, the state of being denotable by the word 'entity. Regarding the phrase "But that which... he states that this is indeed the intended meaning because of the unity of purpose with the two subsequent verses. He says, "In this case also," thereby indicating that even when the word "non-existent" (asat) is applied to conscious entities in certain instances, it is said with reference to specific states such as the non-assumption of names and forms as gods and so forth.

In its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), however, because it is changeless, it is indeed denotable by the word "Being" (*sat*). Regarding the two verses, the reading "upapādanam" [instead of "vyutkramaḥ"] for the "taking up in reverse order" is not correct; rather, it is in consideration of the sequence [of the arguments], as in the phrase "not from the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That very same... A further reason for the matter already proposed must be stated.

The point is that it is not appropriate to abandon the fact that the causality [of Brahman] is understood here by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*) and instead explain it as having another meaning.

He refutes the interpretation imagined by those with false views (*kudṛṣṭi*). "In this context" (*atra*): here, either the refutation of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the demonstration of the proposition that through the knowledge of one all is known, or the presentation of the Sāṃkhya doctrine and so forth, is being carried out.

Furthermore, neither the demonstration of the distinction between the body and the self nor the cessation of grief would be established by the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

Since everything is eternal, the description of even conscious beings as being eternal is the proof of what is not yet established by means of that which is already fully established; this is the intended meaning.
He states the connection with the main subject matter regarding the purpose of what has been said: "The body... etc. That ignorance of which [leads to] delusion—

The intention is that the very teaching of that [truth] must serve for its cessation. Here, the summary verse of the second chapter—"for the sake of pacifying that delusion"—is indicated. Intending to show the lack of contradiction between what precedes and what follows within the doctrine of *satkāryavāda*, he also states the internal consistency of his own argument with the two sentences beginning "sa eva" (that very same...). [He says] "immediately thereafter."

The sense is that there is not even the slightest interval between [the self and the body]. Even for one who does not know the Self and maintains the doctrine that the body is the Self, a desire to cut [wood] is observed; yet that [desire] does not bear fruit [for the ultimate goal], and thus instruction on reality is commenced.
For the Advaitins, jars and the like are unreal because they are merely objects of exclusion (*vyāvartana*); Being (*sat*) alone is the ultimate reality.

Because it persists: the *Śrībhāṣya* explains that "existence" (*sat*) persists everywhere, as in "the jar exists," "the cloth exists," and so forth. It should be noted that the commentary by Śaṅkara on this verse is the source for this [argument].
Furthermore, the intention of Śaṅkara in making this statement is to demonstrate the illusory nature (*mithyātva*) of cold, heat, and other such qualities.

Regarding this, it has been stated that that which is ultimately real (paramārthasat) alone will be explained further on. In the dualist (dvaita) system, however, the word "asat" denotes primordial nature (prakṛti).
Even in the first quarter [of the verse], the word division is simply "abhāva. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that primordial nature exists at all times.

In this view, the statement "non-existence does not exist" is redundant; and if the word "existent" (*sataḥ*) were taken merely to mean "being," there would be a deficiency due to the exclusion of the living being (*jīvat*). Regarding the phrase "in the present context": the position of the logicians (*tārkika*) is that "the non-existent arises" and "what has arisen ceases. In that case, neither of the two parts [of the verse] applies. Rather, the meaning in the view of the proponents of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavādin*) is that the "end of both"—namely, the perception of non-existence and the determination of the negation of both [existence and non-existence]—is observed.

The sense is that although this argument is acceptable to us, it is not relevant to the present context. This meaning of the verse has been introduced in Śaṅkara’s commentary; by the two words "iti" and "upapādyate," the absence of tautology is demonstrated.
He concludes with the word "ataḥ"; by this restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), it is shown that even for other commentators, there is only the appearance of what is unreal.

They turn back. As for what was stated by Yajñasvāmin—that by the word *asat* (the non-existent) impurity, *rajas*, *tamas*, and their effects such as suffering are grasped, while by the word *sat* (the existent) *sattva* and its effects such as happiness are grasped; and that by the words "existence" (*bhāva*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*), prosperity (*bhūti*) and misfortune (*abhūti*), which are synonyms for worldly success (*abhyudaya*) and liberation (*naiḥśreyasa*), are meant; and that the "end is seen of both"—this refers to the two categories.

Perishability is stated [here]. Consequently, this constitutes an elaboration of precisely those two qualities previously mentioned: the nature of suffering, which serves as the cause for enduring the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), and perishability. This has been said: because *rajas*, *tamas*, and so forth are understood through words such as "unreal" (*asat*) due to their connection with the context; and it is with this intention that it was stated that he alone is the subject under discussion.

Regarding the word *nanu* in the verse: by the word *mātrā*, the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and so forth are expressed. Thus, in the *Kapilāsurīyaka*, it is said: "The qualities are the *guṇamātrās*; they are called the characteristics of the qualities (*guṇalakṣaṇa*) and the constituents of the qualities (*guṇāvayava*). Furthermore, the qualities of the *sattva*-type qualities and their respective measures (*mātrā*) are taught therein, such as: "the state of perceiving reality (*tattvadarśanatā*), the nature of the destruction of fear (*bhayanāśasvābhāvatā*), clarity of the senses (*prasannendriyatā*), and pleasant sleep and awakening (*sukhasvapnabodhanatā*)"—these are the *sattvamātrās*. And [they are also found] among the instruments (*upakaraṇeṣu*).
The word *mātrā* is employed [in such expressions] as, "One should wander as a mendicant with few *mātrās*.
However, if the word *mātrā* were taken to mean the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, there would be a redundancy with the words "cold" and "heat."

That too is incorrect; for the word *mātrā* has no primary application (*mukhyaprayoga*) to the *sattva* and other qualities, nor is it well-established elsewhere, and there is no reason to accept an unestablished meaning here. As for the tautology of the words "cold" and "hot," it is resolved by their referring respectively to the general and the particular, and by their being intended as illustrative examples.
In that case, let it be that the terms "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) refer precisely to the pleasure and pain under discussion.
Not so; for if one intends to express that these two alone consist of the nature of prosperity and non-prosperity, it would be illogical to point to their absence as the cause thereof.
Furthermore, the designation of pleasure and pain as the causes of suffering and happiness contradicts both worldly experience and the Veda.
Moreover, the statement regarding the cessation of sovereignty and so forth through pleasure and the like is irrelevant to the subject at hand.

In this manner, the refutation should be inferred even for intervals of a *yojana*. Therefore, because of its consistency with the preceding and following sections of the great treatise (*mahāprakaraṇa*), the meaning is exactly as stated.

Now, with the intention that—because the eternity of the Self, which constitutes the human goal and is the cause for the immediate cessation of sorrow, enters [into the discussion] as a qualification of the object to be attained—the proof of that eternity, though it was the final proposition in the verse beginning with "Not from this" (*nātmataḥ*), is presented first according to the sequence of its presence in the intellect, he says: "But of the Self... (*ātmanas tu...*).

By the word "but" (tu), it is intended to show how the Self differs from the body, given that birth, death, and so forth are witnessed by all the world, and because of the scriptural statement, "Arising from these elements, one perishes after them," which indicates that [the soul] shares the same fate as the body. Even so, there is indeed a distinction.

Without first providing an explanation of the first quarter-verse, the reason for first explaining the second quarter-verse is stated as "atha prāpya" (now, having reached).
