To the objection—"Since [the object] is established by experience, it cannot be denied; therefore, how can there be a negation of its existence?"—the introduction of the verse is made known through the explanation of the word "tu" (but).

The word *tat* in the verse signifies its referent; it clarifies that the referent of *tat* has a neuter gender, expresses the portion of the proposition (*pratijñā*), and therein reveals the distinction between the locus (*āśraya*) and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). [This is shown by the phrase] "that reality of the Self" (*tadātmatattvam*). [The term] "indestructible" (*avināśi*) means that which does not have the nature of perishing.

While explaining the second quarter-verse, which sets forth the portion of the reason (*hetu*), [the author] removes the restriction [on the scope] of the word "all" (*sarva*) that would otherwise result from the requirements of syntactic connection within the sentence.

This, however, indicates—by the force of its own expression—that the externality of the non-sentient (bāhya) is established, while by its opposite, the sentience of the Self (ātman) is realized; from that very fact, it makes known the pervasion of the sentient by the nature of the Self within the non-sentient.
As for the word "by which" (yena): the aggregate of the non-sentient is pervaded, part by part, by the aggregate of the sentient, just as sesame oil [pervades] sesame seeds or fire [pervades] wood.

This is the meaning; or rather, what is intended here is the capacity for all insentient things to enter [into the self]—thus, in either case, there is no contradiction with the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the self.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): the self does not undergo destruction dependent upon weapons and the like, because it is subtler than them due to its pervasiveness of them, just like space (*ākāśa*). Or, by way of contraposition (*vyatireka*): whatever undergoes destruction dependent upon something else is not subtler than that thing.

"Just as a lamp is destroyed by the wind"—manifesting this formal argument (*prayoga*), he explains the second half [of the verse] with the intent of another formal argument, [beginning with the words] "by virtue of being characterized as all-pervasive. The meaning of the term *avināśin* (indestructible) is "that which is not subject to destruction.
Its cause is stated as: "because of its unsurpassed subtlety. And this "unsurpassed subtlety" is in relation to consciousness (*cetanā*).
Regarding the phrase "someone" (*kaścit*), the alternative interpretation that this refers even to Īśvara (God) is contrary to the views of our own school (*svadarśana*).

Since our system maintains that there is no individual soul (*jīva*) or Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from Brahman, to interpret "someone" as referring to an extraneous Īśvara in a context defining [Brahman] would contradict our established tenet (*siddhānta*). This is because the natural inclination of the word "someone" is to denote something other than oneself, and it is precisely the existence of such a [distinct entity] that is being negated.

The intention is that, because [the truth] is understood from the verse, there is no intent to establish the falsity of other entities. In our own position, the inclusion of "God" will be explained later. With the thought that [the opponent's view] contradicts his own system, he says: "some entity distinct from that. This is the designation of the subject (*dharmin*). The meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "it ought not to bring about the destruction of the self."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because it is pervaded by that; therefore, because of its grossness. Thus, "because of its grossness" is the reason itself.
To avoid the charge of being unestablished (*asiddhi*), he says "because it is pervaded by that. He provides an example preceded by a statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*): "the destroyer.

Anticipating the objection that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the mallet and so forth, which are destroyers of jars and the like, he refutes it with the words "in the mallet," etc.

The intended meaning is as follows: First of all, the mere conjunction of a mallet and so forth is not the destroyer of a jar and the like, because it would follow that a jar already placed upon the mallet would also be destroyed. Nor is there any dispute that it is specifically a particular conjunction with a specific part of a particular moving substance that is the destroyer. And likewise, the production of a particular wind is also generally established by perception and thus undisputed. And [this occurs] through the entry of that particular substance into the respective parts of the object.
Destructiveness is admitted in the case of objects being agitated by the impact of extremely hard sounds.

This being so, one must necessarily admit that even here, a specific wind—which exists even in the absence of the previously established causes—acts as the cause of destruction. And that wind is subtler than the jar and other such objects.

However, in cases where destruction occurs merely through impact and the like even in the absence of velocity (*vega*), the specific parts of the substance such as a jar, being struck by the particles of the mallet, penetrate into other regions that are increasingly grosser than their own respective locations and thereby break it;
or else, this occurs due to the escape of internal air rooted in the impact, as in the case of the striking of a bellows filled with air.
"Thus" means: because weapons and the like are not destructive due to the two reasons already stated;
because no other destroyer of the self—which is extremely subtle—is observed; and because even the Lord lacks the intention to destroy it. This is the sense.

He introduces the following verse—"Of bodies..."—as a support for the proposition "not of the non-existent. By the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) and the word "nature" (*svabhāva*), he indicates the absolute nature of the designation "non-existent. To satisfy the requirement for a reason regarding the probandum "having an end," he provides an etymological explanation of the word "body" (*deha*), which serves to establish the subject (*dharmin*).

"Diha means accumulation (upacaya). This means that they have the nature of accumulation and possess parts. The sense is that the word *deha* (body) is used here in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) to denote the subject (*dharmin*), whereas by its etymological derivation (*yoga*), it is intended to indicate the reason (*hetu*). Regarding the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), he explains the meaning of the root and the suffix: "having the nature of destruction.
Here, the term "end" (*anta*) is not intended to mean a final limit determined by investigation or by spatial location and so forth.

The meaning is that the possessive suffix *matup* refers to a state of permanent connection and so forth. He provides the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "accumulation" (*upacaya*).

He states that the perishable nature of the body is established even by scripture (*śruti*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "of the eternal" (*nityasya*). The two scriptural authorities and the two presumptive arguments are indicated by the two phrases "of the eternal" and "of the embodied one" (*śarīriṇaḥ*).

He pacifies the expectation of how and by whom [the body] was spoken of by means of the passage beginning with "action" (*karman*). By the suffix *-in* in the word *śarīriṇaḥ* and by the genitive case, a relationship is understood; the cause designated as "action" is shown because it is relevant to the subject at hand.

This is for the purpose of excluding the bodies of Īśvara and others, since those are not dependent upon action. The term "these" (*ime*) indicates what has been stated as suggested by that reference.
"Consisting of an aggregate of elements": even the fact that they are composed of an aggregate of multiple elements is a reason for their impermanence.

"Perishing at the conclusion of karma" is the result of the etymological definition of the word *śarīra* (body). For it is from *vi-śṛ* (to fall apart) that *śarīra* is derived; indeed, according to certain scriptures, both the birth and the destruction of bodies are explicitly stated.
The point is that even by those who have stated that the body's arising is merely dependent upon karma, its destruction at the conclusion of that karma has necessarily been stated as well.

And thus, by the three words "these," "bodies," and "of embodied beings," the three reasons for the impermanence of the body have been indicated: its nature as a collection of elements, its possession of parts, and its being intended for the experience of the fruits of karma.

He explains the two words "of the undecaying" (*anāśinaḥ*) and "of the immeasurable" (*aprameyasya*) as referring respectively to the probandum—the eternity of the self—and its logical reason, in the passage beginning with "But the self... (*ātmā tu*). This is because eternity is established by the fact that [the self] is incapable of destruction. There is no tautology between the terms "eternal" (*nityasya*) and "undecaying" (*anāśinaḥ*), either because they intend to exclude gross and subtle destruction respectively, or because [the former refers to the self's nature while the latter refers to its state]. Furthermore, the logical reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), since [the existence of the self] is also established for us in our own philosophical system.

Regarding the argument "because of being an object of valid cognition," he says: "For the Self is not [an object of cognition]. The exclusion of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva-paryudāsa*) results in the state of being the cognizer (*pramātṛtva*), by way of excluding the body and so forth, whose very nature consists solely in being objects of cognition; for here the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies something other than that. He says "and likewise" because the distinction between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) will be explained in exactly this manner.

By this, the one who explains "being non-object of knowledge" (*ajñānaviṣayatva*) here is refuted. Furthermore, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) here culminates in "being an object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatva*).

Its absence, moreover, takes the form of the absence of the previously stated reason—namely, "having the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma"—and thus culminates in "being a non-enjoyer" (*abhoktṛtva*).
Therefore, considering that this [absence] is intended to demonstrate the absence of the other two previously stated reasons as well, he states their absences too.
With the words beginning with “na ca,” he states the non-perception of that which would be perceptible if it possessed parts. Regarding the word “sarvatra” (everywhere):

here, the word “all” refers to the entirety of the body’s parts. Therefore, even for the atomic self (*aṇu-ātman*), during the state of conventional usage delimited by this or that specific part—which serves as the cause for pleasure and pain, such as “there is a sensation in my foot” or “there is pleasure in my head”—[it is not perceived].

The perception of being partless has been stated. Alternatively, the meaning is that among the infinite bodies of diverse kinds, such as those of gods and others, the embodied self is not perceived as having parts in any body whatsoever.
The singular number in "I" (aham) indicates the oneness of the Self, the conceiving subject, within a single body.

If the self were composed of parts, then it would occasionally be possible for us to perceive it as "this," because consciousness would necessarily have to be admitted for each of its individual parts.
For if it possessed parts, it would either be of the nature of a collection of parts or of the nature of a whole (avayavin).
In either case, the establishment of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) therein is impossible without a specific quality residing in its constituent parts.

For even in the case of fermenting agents (*kiṇva*) and the like, the power of intoxication—though not established in each individual part—is produced in each one through a particular transformation of cooking (*pākaviśeṣa*), just like a particular taste (*rasaviśeṣa*).

And although a power (*śakti*) cannot be subjected to such questioning, this rule regarding specific qualities is difficult to abandon. The same applies even to the view that cognition (*jñāna*) is a substance.

Just as it is impossible for a collection that is itself devoid of luster to possess luster, so it is in this case: if [the body] were a single entity like a collective whole (*samāja*), then within a single body, mutual quarreling, envy, jealousy, restraint, favor, and so forth would also be perceived [as belonging to that single entity]. Furthermore, since there is no whole distinct from its parts when there is extreme affliction, the status of being the experiencer would belong to the parts alone.
If that were the case, a different part [of the body] would not be able to reconnect with what was experienced by a part of the self delimited by the hand and so forth; thus,

there would be no such reconnection as "I, who touched this with my right hand, touch it again with my left hand," for there is no rule that multiple conscious parts [of a single being] must have simultaneous access to the range of cognition.

Now, establishing the aforementioned point through a different approach, [the author] states "na ca" (and not) regarding the non-apprehension of the fitness [of the body] to consist of a composite of heterogeneous elements. In the case of bodies and so forth, which are composed of the five elements, a distinction in form produced by each respective element is perceived in the skin, blood, flesh, and other parts; however, such [distinction] is not found at all in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Thus it is heard in scripture:

"Consisting entirely of a mass of consciousness," and so forth. Alternatively, "difference in form" (ākārabheda) is intended to mean the difference in the arrangement of hands, feet, and so on. Thus, having combined for ease of comprehension the four reasons established in each of the two verses regarding the permanence of the self and the perishability of the body, [the author proceeds].
He shows this with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). By "having a single form"—the meaning is: because it does not consist of a composite of elements (*abhūtasaṅghātātmakatvāt*).
By "not having the nature of accumulation"—the meaning is: because it is partless (*niravayavatvāt*).
Now, all of this is an invalid reason and is untenable; for instance, regarding that [subject], the state of not being a composite—
Furthermore, the property of having heroic limbs (*vīrāvayavatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) due to its presence in color, taste, and so forth, as well as in the *mahat* and other principles.

Moreover, if "being a cognizer" (*pramātṛtva*) is intended to mean being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma, then it is an inconclusive reason that is not shared by the subject (*asādhāraṇānaikāntya*), because it is excluded from all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). In that case, if even God (*Īśvara*) and others are included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is also the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).

If what is intended is merely the state of being the locus of valid cognition (*pramā*), then if all cognizers (*pramātṛ*) are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fault of the reason being "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇya*), as before. However, if only living beings (*jīva*) are taken as the subject, then because even the eternality of God (*īśvara*) is not firmly accepted [by the opponent], the example would suffer from defects such as the absence of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) due to doubt regarding it.

Furthermore, if "pervasion" means pervading everything, then there is a failure to establish the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because that [pervasion] is absent in individual conscious subjects (*kṣetrajña*) and atoms, and because [the subject] is itself pervaded in relation to God (*īśvara*). If, on the other hand, it means pervading only some things, then there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to [the examples of] scripture, space, and so forth; nor does it prove the impermanence of the body.

Furthermore, [the reason] "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the specific features of the Lord’s divine body, ornaments, weapons, and so forth. Likewise, if "being for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma" constitutes the probans (*taddhetutva*), then it is inconclusive by virtue of the nature of the Lord, the individual soul (*jīva*), and others, as before.
If, on the other hand, [the probans] is "arising for that purpose," then the qualification is redundant (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*); for [the probandum follows] from mere arising alone.

[This is] because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established. Furthermore, being composed of an aggregate (*saṅghātarūpatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just like having parts (*sāvayavatva*). Moreover, if "pervadedness" (*vyāpyatva*) is meant with respect to everything, then there is the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*); for the body and so forth are not pervaded by mountains and the like.
Nor is the reason [otherwise] unestablished, since it is absent in some cases. If, however, it is with respect to some [limited] things, [then...]
In that case, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to the divine and auspicious bodies of individual souls (*jīva*) which are pervaded by God.

If the definition were qualified as "being pervaded by an individual soul," then, as before, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on account of the specific bodies of the eternal liberated ones (*nityasūri*), their actions performed for others (*parakṛtya*), and so forth. By this, the claim that [the probans] consists in "being pervaded by a knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) is also refuted.

If, however, non-pervasiveness is intended [as the reason for the body's destruction], then its establishment as a real entity (*svarūpasiddhi*) would exist in the bodies of yogis and others who possess powers such as *aṇimā*, because those bodies are also capable of emerging from and sinking into stone and other such obstacles.
To this it is replied: first, regarding the two properties of being non-composite and partless, they are [refuted] by the cognition of Arjuna and others.

Since the probandum is the cessation of destruction caused by unmentioned weapons, fire, and so forth—which act as destroyers—there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to [the existence of] the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest. By qualifying [the subject] with "being a substance" (*dravyatva*), there is no inconclusiveness due to color and other qualities which are destructible by fire and the like. Thus, when the destruction established by perception and other means is negated, one might suspect that, like the Great Principle and the rest, destruction occurs solely through the will of God (*īśvara*).

The sense is that even that [agency] is prohibited by scripture itself. Since the status of being a knower (pramātṛtva) culminates in being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva), it results in non-origination by way of negating its objectivity (prameyatva)—which consists in having the experience of the fruits of karma as its purpose;
and since non-origination is pervaded by eternality, there is no origination of the essential nature of the Self.

There is no fault whatsoever, because this is established by the scriptures (*śāstra*). If, however, the mere state of being the substratum of valid cognition (*pramā*) is taken as the reason, then God (*Īśvara*) serves as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*); in that case, there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), but this was already refuted during the commentary on the verse "But not indeed am I" (*na tvevāham*). As for the application of the pervasion (*vyāpaka*), it should be recited with reference to the sacrificial post (*śaraṇa*) and so forth, according to the method previously explained by us.

There too, there is a fault. Furthermore, regarding the proofs for the impermanence of the body, there is no deviation [from the rule] because of the qualification "provided they possess parts and are composites of elements" (*sāvayavatva-bhūta-saṅghātatva*) when being composed of primordial matter (*prākṛtatva*). It is precisely for this purpose that it was stated, "these bodies. Moreover, the state of being for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma is simply the state of having arisen for that purpose; nor is the qualification redundant, since the expansion of knowledge of the liberated self (*muktātman*) is what is to be excluded.

For that [knowledge] is not unarisen, because it previously did not exist. Indeed, something is called "natural" (svābhāvika) merely by virtue of its arising from the cognition of its own nature once an obstacle has been removed, and not by virtue of being unarisen. As for such statements as, "The removal of defects does not produce knowledge in the Self," this refers to the non-arising of the nature of awakening and so forth, but not to the expansion of that [knowledge].
Alternatively, let it be granted that its state of having arisen does not exist by virtue of being in a particular state;
nevertheless, the qualification would serve to exclude that which remains in such a state. Or, let there be independence from qualification;
even so, impermanence is established merely by the fact of having arisen, in the case of those things whose arising is unknown.
In some bodies, the doubt regarding the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) is dispelled by demonstrating that [the destruction] is rooted in karma.

Alternatively, since what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the perishability resulting from the exhaustion of karma, this qualification is meaningful for its propriety. Furthermore, "pervasion" (*vyāpyatva*) is intended with respect to weapons and the like, and the "probandum" (*sādhya*) is the state of being perishable in dependence upon them.

There is no fault whatsoever. [Objection: Is it not the case that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever is pervaded by something X must have its destruction dependent on that X? For this would be over-extended (anaikāntika) by reference to primordial matter (prakṛti), the individual self (puruṣa), time, and so forth, which are pervaded by God (Īśvara) yet do not have their destruction dependent on Him. [Response: No; for what is to be proven (sādhya) is "fitness" (yogyatva), and since that exists in those cases as well. For it is precisely through the embrace of God’s eternal will that...

That [body] is eternal; otherwise, if the Lord were to desire to withdraw even the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, who would be his ruler? If it is argued that there is an inconsistency with bodies and the like—which pervade the individual soul and space and are not subject to destruction dependent on Him—the answer is no, because they too possess the fitness to be destroyed by Him. As for the Lord, He is the agent of their destruction.

The distinction here is that [the opponent] does not treat the soul (*jīva*) and so forth as objects to be acted upon. Consequently, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The body and so forth are susceptible to destruction dependent upon weapons and the like, because they are pervaded by those [weapons]. Whatever is pervaded by something is susceptible to destruction dependent upon that thing. Alternatively, let the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) stand aside.
The probandum (*sādhya*) is "to be destroyed by weapons and the like," and the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is pervaded by weapons and the like.
That which is pervaded by weapons and the like is destructible by weapons and the like, just as, for example, the trunk of a plantain tree and so forth.
Now, space (*ākāśa*) is not pervaded by weapons and the like, because, while being subtle, it does not admit of penetration.

Because it is intended [as such]: as for the subtlety [of the weapon], one might object that the weapon is indeed subtle compared to space because of its small dimension; to this he says, "And of subtlety...
Subtlety consists in not being obstructed by that [space] while simultaneously obstructing it.

Even though two stones may strike one another, neither possesses subtlety; therefore, non-obstruction must also be included [as a defining characteristic]. Since space is unobstructed, it would follow that a weapon would also possess subtlety; thus, what is intended here is its capacity to obstruct. [The term refers to] that which obstructs itself.

There is no deviation [in the reason] because the property of being penetrable by weapons and the like is absent in space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, here the essential point is that whatever is struck possesses non-obstructiveness therein, and from that, subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) follows.
However, in the case of the bodies of yogis and others, the very state of being penetrable by weapons and the like has ceased due to specific transformations (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no absence of destruction dependent upon those [weapons], for their pervasiveness is relative to weapons and the like; thus, there is no deviation [in the rule] by them. Even more so, however, is the destruction of that [body] by the even subtler volitions (*saṅkalpa*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth.
By this, the case of a body sustained by medicinal herbs and other counteracting agents against weapons, missiles, and the like, is also explained.

[This has been] explained; for there, entry is obstructed by medicinal herbs and the like. Therefore, it is established that all eight causes are conquerors of the eight directions. Now, for what purpose is the impermanence of the body, which is already established in the world, being proven here?
For in some bodies, destruction is indeed perceived directly. And even in undestroyed bodies, such as those of Bhīṣma and others—

By parity with that [example], perishability is indeed certain; otherwise, one would not even hurl weapons and the like against enemies, nor would one personally ward off enemies, their enemies, and so forth. Therefore, since the impermanence of the body is universally accepted, and since logic is required only regarding matters of doubt, these four inferences—such as "because it possesses parts" and so on—are useless here.

To this it is replied: first, one purpose of the inferences for the eternity of the self (*ātman*) is to demonstrate the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*): "Whatever is subject to destruction dependent upon weapons and the like is composed of parts, such as the body.
Second, from that very demonstration follows the establishment of the difference between the body and the self by elaborating upon their manifold contradictory properties.
The third [purpose] is the removal of doubt as to whether immortality might possibly be achieved through the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) that ward off weapons and the like.
The fourth is the generation of detachment from one's own body by demonstrating the inevitability of both the destruction of bodies and its causes.

Furthermore, by demonstrating that among all bodies one’s own alone is subject to destruction, [the fifth purpose is the cultivation of detachment] through the performance of actions free from attachment to fruits (*phalābhisandhi*) and so forth.

The sixth [point] is the indication of the possibility of even absolute destruction. The seventh is the state of being beyond grief because of having a perishable nature. The eighth is that one must quickly engage in the means for attaining liberation. In this manner, other points should also be contemplated as appropriate.
Therefore, regarding the words "Therefore, fight, O Bhārata":

The explanation of the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) begins with "of the body" (*dehasya*) and ends with "is not a ground for grief" (*na śokasthānam iti*). Filling out [the meaning] by means of the equipment consisting of the endurance of dualities and the fruit consisting of immortality, as set forth in the two verses beginning with "But the contacts of the senses" (*mātrāsparśās tu*), he says: "By the sacred scripture" (*śastreṇa*).
In this context, the mention of one's own state while grieving for those who have gone to the other world serves to generate honor by exposing the vital point [of the truth].

For it is precisely because it is scriptural that even personal suffering is endured; and it is also intended to demonstrate that even the suffering of sacrificial animals, enemies, and so forth must be borne. Furthermore, it is meant to exclude the notion that war has as its primary aim minor enjoyments such as an undesired kingdom.

It is appropriate that the very result mentioned at the beginning of the treatise [should be the goal]; thus, it was stated, "for the attainment of immortality. Refuting the opponent's view that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*), he explains the meanings of the base and the suffix in the word *yudhyasva* (fight): "undertake the action called battle. This is precisely the meaning, as has been elaborated by us in the *Seśvaramīmāṃsā*.

Now, by the verse beginning with "But it is indestructible" (2.17), that which was stated there is further elaborated upon in the verse beginning with "They do not cut this" (2.23). This is done to strengthen—by means of censuring those who perceive the opposite—the fitness of weapons and the like to kill, and the fitness of the Self to be killed. To dispel the delusion regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "one who [cuts] this," the word "perception" (*pratīti*) has been stated.

Because the word *hantāram* ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the word *enam* takes the second case (*dvitīyā*), since the genitive case used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is prohibited by the rule: *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhāsvalarthatṛnām*. The meaning is that here the suffix merely intends to express the cause of the killing (*hanana-hetu*).

It has been stated [in the phrase] "na kam api" (not anyone) for the purpose of making known that the use of the masculine gender is justified by the intended meaning of the word (*padārtha*), as previously explained in the sense that "no one is capable of acting. Now, regarding the verse: "If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. (Gītā 2.19).

This verse serves as a corroborative reinforcement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) for the passage from the *Kaṭhavallī*. Regarding that passage, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) stated in the commentary on the section "The Self is the agent because the scriptures have purpose" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*) that its purpose is to negate the self's status as either a slayer or one to be slain. And in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), [the author] states: "If he thinks 'I am the slayer'... and so forth.

Having thus restated that it is heard in scripture that the self has no agency in the act of killing, [the opponent] offers this rebuttal: "Since the self is eternal, it cannot be killed. How, then, can this be explained here by the passage beginning with "one who kills this person," etc., which abandons the natural grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth, and instead interprets it by supplying some cause for the killing?
It is said: first of all, there is no contradiction with the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, because they have the same meaning (*aikārthya*).
For here it is stated that no cause whatsoever possesses the quality of being a cause for the destruction of the self (*ātmahanana*);
this being so, it follows that even the self does not possess the quality of being a cause for its own destruction. And thus, in this context—

In the *Śārīraka*, it was stated by accepting that what was expressed in general terms is restricted to a specific [case]. Therein, there is no acceptance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); rather, even though there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "the slayer of the Self," the result is stated.
In that case, another word required for the sense is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) as having an appropriate case ending.

In this context, however, because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the natural connection between the action and the object—which possess mutual expectancy and so forth—is precisely their reciprocal relation. Furthermore, the suitability of the context pertains to the general subject matter. As for the specific conclusion regarding the negation of the Self's agency as a killer, that will occur in the verse beginning with "The Vedas [know] the Indestructible."

Therefore, it is established that even the fact that the word "this" (*ayam*) has a different referent and so forth does not constitute a fault. To dispel the misconception that this constitutes a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*), he says: "by what has been stated. [Regarding the phrase] "because of its eternity":
the sense is that even if something is capable of producing an effect, it does not operate upon that which is unfit for it.

By the statement "having drawn this [word] along," it is understood from the reading of the Bhāṣya that "this person does not kill him. Thus, the word "him" (enam) is stated by being drawn over from the preceding sentence. For this very reason, the sense is that when there is an absence of a cause due to unsuitability, there is an absence of the result, which consists in being the object of that action. This [person] is the cause of killing; this is the Self (ātman).

Thus, in both cases, this word is uttered simultaneously (*tatreṇa*) due to its connection with the verbal root. It is used in the two forms *hanti* (he kills) and *hanyate* (he is killed) because of a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*). The sense is that [the word] conveys the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). How then is there usage such as *manuṣyaṃ hanti* (he kills a human)? This [usage] does not have the mere physical body as its object; for one who strikes a dead body is not called a "killer of his father" (*pitṛhā*).

This is because there is an absence of usage such as "the killer of his mother" (*mātṛhā*) and the like [if the object were not sentient]. Furthermore, it is our established tenet that words such as "human" (*manuṣya*) terminate in the self (*ātman*). In usages such as "he intends to kill me" (*māṃ jaghāṃsati*), the fact that the root *han* (to kill) has the self as its object is perfectly clear. Therefore, only a sentient being capable of being harmed is the object (*karman*) of the verbal root *han*.

This being so, one might suspect that both statements—"it does not kill" and "it is not killed"—would be untenable; anticipating this doubt, he says: "The verbal root *han*... By the phrase "having the self as its object," the doubt is indicated. It is true that the verbal root *han* has the self as its object by its very nature, but [the objection] is not...
In this context, it does not signify the loss of one's essential nature (*svarūpa-pracyuti*); rather, it is intent upon killing (*māraṇa*).
For such is its usage in both worldly and Vedic literature. And killing consists in the disintegration of the body and so forth.
The sense is that it is taught [in grammar] as *mṛṅ* "to abandon life" (*prāṇatyāge*). Thus, the worldly usage is established.

"What is the meaning of the scriptural injunction, 'One should not harm any living beings'? Let its meaning be whatever it may; however, since it is prohibited both generally and specifically, one might suspect that it should not be performed. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "One should not harm. According to the system of other schools, or by the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavāda*) according to his own school, [the text refers to] the act of causing separation from the body as prescribed [in certain contexts].
The sense is that even for [beings] such as the Paśuśatru, there is an absence of the very nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*) because they are most beneficial.

Now, fearing the defect of contradiction with perception and so forth due to the redundancy of the verse from the Kaṭhavallī, "He is not born," which has already been studied here under the single-word qualification "at some time" (*kadācit*), he says: "By those very [arguments] already stated."
By this, the suspicion that [the argument] is a mere assertion is refuted; for it is said, "because of being unchanging due to its permanence.

The meaning is that even the slightest modification has been excluded by virtue of its indestructibility. To explain: destruction (vināśa) is defined as the attainment of another state, which consists in the relinquishing of a prior condition and is fit to receive a different name.
Just as a substance such as a jar or a mountain has the state of potsherds and so forth; and its inclination toward that state is its decay (*apakṣaya*).
That very same substance, now in the state of potsherds and so forth, is its origination (*utpatti*). In this way, transformation (*pariṇāma*), increase (*vṛddhi*), and so on, are to be illustrated.
And he will state this matter in the passage: "For for one who is born, death is certain."
Therefore, by the refutation of perishability, production and so forth are also effectively refuted.

The phrase "all indeed" (sarva eva) is stated for the sake of avoiding tautology; here, the particle *eva* has the same meaning as the word *api*. The sense is that there is no redundancy: not only does the state of being subject to destruction (*hantavyatva*) not exist, but the state of being produced (*janyatva*) and so forth do not exist either.

Regarding the phrase "the attributes of the body" (*dehadharmā*): it has been stated that the body is the object of worldly conventions such as birth and death, as indicated by the expression "when the body is slain.
The reason for this is given as "insentient" (*acetana*). It is said that birth and other such states are attributes of the body and do not belong to the Self (*ātman*).

Thus, for Arjuna—who through perception and other means mistakenly identifies the attributes of the body with the Self—the [Lord] teaches by means of the very mantra of the Upaniṣads: "It is not born."

The meaning is that the mode of existence as it actually is (*yathāvasthitākāra*) is being described through analysis, but there is no denial of birth and death characterized by the conjunction with and separation from a body. The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and). To avoid the redundancy of the words in the verse, he speaks—manifesting the established distinction based on the mention of the "present" and so forth—by saying "therein" (*tatra*). Now, [one might object]: "By the word 'at some time' (*kadācit*), it is indeed [implied] only as being present..."

The experience of birth and death [occurs] there; therefore, the use of the present tense (*vartamāna-nirdeśa*) with respect to that is appropriate. By this, it is meant that all time, excluding the beginning and end of a *kalpa*, is subsumed under the term "at some time" (*kadācit*).

He states the intended meaning of the reference to the prior time by saying "having been" (*bhūtvā*): namely, "at the beginning of a *kalpa*" (*kalpādau*). In that context, the word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) refers to another *kalpa*.

This was stated—"not having been, he will not be"—in order to dispel the misconception that the negative particle (*nañ*) might be construed with each of the two verbs, "having been" (*bhūtvā*) and "will be" (*bhavitā*).

It is the qualified expression "having been, he will not be" that is negated by the subsequent negative. Now, one might ask: why is it said, "he is not this which has been," and so forth? For it could be argued that this is already encompassed by the statement "it is not born" (*na jāyate*), etc. Anticipating this objection, he says:
Regarding the phrase "in some [cases]": this is the intended meaning—specific creations and dissolutions are heard of in relation to specific times and specific bodies.

Yet, these are not merely the conjunction with or separation from a body, because of the statement by Kaṇva, "He emitted living beings upon the earth with water," and because of the determination of oneness prior to creation, which establishes the validity of the proposition that knowledge of one thing [leads to the knowledge of all].

And because of [the Lord's] resolve to become many from being one alone, the birth and destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*) must be understood as merely the manifestation and disappearance of its form; thus, in order to dispel the doubt that the individual souls persist until the final dissolution (*pralaya*), it is stated: "This [soul], having not been," and so forth. And in that regard, the reply is as follows: the "emission" (*visṛṣṭi*) of individual souls means their projection (*vikṣepa*) by means of endowing them with a body.

Prior to creation, there is the determination of oneness because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). Furthermore, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is due to the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman—which has as its body the subtle sentient and insentient reality—into having as its body the gross sentient and insentient reality.
For this very reason, the resolve to become many and so forth is logically established. Thus, [the attributes] "unborn" (*aja*) and "eternal" (*nitya*) [are appropriate].

With the intention that there is no tautology—either by way of summarizing the previously stated meaning as a conclusion, or by intending to express that the Self is not born and so forth within any body at any time through the negation of birth and other states at those respective times—he says:
"Therefore, residing in all bodies. He also explains the word *purāṇa* [as "ancient"] on the basis of the similarity of syllables (*akṣarasāmyāt*).
He provides an etymological explanation according to the logic thus stated: "Even in the past, [it was] new. One might ask: what is this "newness even in the past"?

For that which has not arisen can never possess newness. Even if it has arisen, one would have to say either "it is new even now" or "it will be new later," since newness in the past would not be anything remarkable. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"At all times" (*sarvadā*): either because the word "formerly" (*purā*) indicates the three periods of time,
or because it intends another time conjoined with the word "also" (*api*), which implies an intention included within the function of the particle *jhrvyāṭavṛtti*.

Alternatively, the resolution may be made by intending a contradiction, such as "though ancient, he is new. Furthermore, the word *nava* here refers to the wonder associated with novelty; for the author will later say, "as if a wonder," and so forth—this is the sense. Or else, while the Śākyas might achieve renewal through nourishment and the like, this one [is different].

"Because it is partless and therefore incapable of modification, it was 'new' even previously. With the intention of concluding the matter under discussion—which has been established for Arjuna's benefit—regarding the point he was doubting, [the Lord] says: "Therefore... (ataḥ).

In the verse beginning with "He who [knows] this," which follows the reversal of what was stated previously, the word "eternal" (*nityam*) is a restatement of the ultimate probandum. With the intention that the phrase "indestructible" (*avināśinam*) and so forth constitutes the reason for that, he says:
"Thus. By the word "change" (*vikāra*), transformations other than birth and destruction are intended here.
Or rather, it is simply decay; or else, it is the disjunction of parts suitable for cutting and so forth.

He says "gods, humans," etc., because the act of specifying (*nirdhāraṇa*) requires a plurality of unspecified individuals. Fearing the charge of tautology between the roots *ghātayati* and *hanti*, he states the meaning according to the sequence present in the mind: "How does he cause destruction?"

If [it is argued]: "The negation of being a killer and so forth as attributes of the knower is not tenable; for if the Self is eternal, it is impossible for that very same knower to be killed," then—in order to resolve this doubt and stating the meaning as it results from the context—he connects it with the subject at hand by saying, "these. In this verse, it is not merely the state of being a killer and so forth that is negated; rather, what is negated is that which is occasioned by it.
It is lamentation; the sense here is that the word "how" (katham) is intended precisely to negate the manner in which that [lamentation] could arise.

He introduces the verse beginning with "clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*) preceded by a doubt, saying: "Even though... [and so on]. Now, one might object: even if there were no sorrow regarding the abandonment of bodies such as those of Sārva-bhauma and others, there certainly remains a cause for grief based on the possibility of assuming various bodies—such as those of humans, animals, or stationary beings—in accordance with their respective past actions, or based on the possibility of remaining without having assumed a body at all, as occurs during the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*).

Moreover, novelty alone does not lead to happiness, for even after abandoning a long-reigning king, entering a new prison and such things results in suffering; and likewise, after discarding an old rope, taking up a new one and so forth is of the nature of pain. Furthermore, we do not experience here, immediately following the dissolution of the human body and the like, the acquisition of a new body such as that of an immortal being, in the manner of putting on a fresh garment.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In a righteous war" (*dharmayuddhe*). The word "superiority" (*adhikatve*) is an adjective qualifying "auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇa*). The expression "nine words" refers to what is intended by the term. "Auspicious things" means that it is solely for the cause of joy. The sense is this: previously, grief was felt only toward an object of sorrow; now, however, it is felt toward an object of joy, which is its opposite.

To provide further reinforcement of what was stated previously by distinguishing between the purposes consisting of the correct apprehension [of the object], he introduces the two verses beginning with "nainam" (not him), saying "again. In the half-verse beginning with "nainam," for the sake of clarity,
the incapacity of the instrument and the unsuitability of the object— which were mentioned separately— are presented as mutual opposites (*parasparapratiyogitayā*) within one or the other.

The phrase "the other is the intermediate state" (*itarad antarabhava*) is not mentioned separately in the Bhāṣya. In passages such as "uncuttable" (*acchedya*), the suffix *ya* has the sense of fitness (*arha*).

By this, he shows that even in verses such as "they do not cut him," the fitness of the weapon and so forth for that [act of cutting] is what is being negated. [He explains the phrase] "they are not able" (*na śaknuvanti*) by commenting on the term "gone to heaven" (*svargagata*) as a restatement of the previously mentioned reason.

Regarding the phrase "because the Self is all-pervading": one might raise the objection, "How can the atomic Self be all-pervading? To address this, [the author] says "all principles" (*sarvatattva*). Here, the omnipresence of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not stated in contradiction to numerous scriptural passages and other authorities; rather, by the word "all-pervading," what is meant is its specific capacity for penetration. This is the intention of the author who employs the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
He elaborates upon the manner in which pervasiveness was previously stated to be the reason [for its eternity] with the words "from all.

Therefore, the self is eternal; the meaning is that because of its subtlety, it is incapable of being cut or otherwise destroyed, and thus the self is devoid of destruction. [He explains] "stable," and so forth.

The two words "sthāṇu" (a pillar) and "acala" (immovable) serve to elaborate upon its eternity; alternatively, they signify its incapacity for destruction and its being beyond the reach of any destroyer; or else, they signify its freedom from both natural and adventitious imperfections of transformation—this is the intended meaning.

He explains the verse beginning with "avyakta" (unmanifest), which is intended to resolve all objections by way of removing contradictions regarding perception and reasoning in the previously stated inferences, and to provide a conclusion to the subject at hand. [The commentary begins: "By cutting," etc.
By those means of knowledge through which the body and so forth are cognized as being capable of cutting and so on, that [unmanifest nature] is not [cognized].
It is made known [in this way]: the apprehension of the self occurs only in such forms as "I know," and so forth;

however, according to the scriptures, it occurs in a form qualified by eternality and other attributes. Thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with the previously stated inferences regarding the subject (*dharmin*) as grasped by its own cognition. Furthermore, the meaning of the terms *vyakta* (manifest) and *avyakta* (unmanifest) has been explained in the *Mokṣadharma*.

"The established rule is that whatever is perceived by the senses is *vyakta* (manifest), while that which is not so perceived is to be known as *avyakta* (unmanifest); thus, the sense organ is that which perceives the *liṅga* (the mark).

Now, [one might object]: when it is to be proven that a seed placed in a granary lacks the capacity for sprouting, there is certainly no contradiction with the means of cognizing the property (*dharma*) from the perspective of the individual instance (*vyakti*). Nevertheless, because [the seed] is pervaded by the universal (*jāti*) of "seed-ness" (*bījatva*), which is the domain of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [it follows...]

In general, there is indeed a contradiction. Anticipating the objection that "in this case as well, there would be a contradiction because [the object] is seen to be of the same class," he says: "Therefore, it is of a different class from the cold, etc. The sense is that this is because there is no means of apprehending its similarity and there is a means of apprehending its dissimilarity. He then explains the meaning of the word "inconceivable" (acintya) along with its reasons and its modes.

"All" [in the verse] means that by this, it is stated that the reasons such as "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth—which are accepted by the Buddhists and others as proofs for the non-eternality of the self—and the logical arguments (*tarka*) supporting them, possess a deficiency at their very root because they contradict the portion of perception (*upalabdhi*) and other means of knowledge. Furthermore, the phrase "and therefore" (*ataśca*) means that there is also an absence of any sublation (*bādhaka*) against the previously mentioned proofs. Alternatively, this may be stated as another independent inference (*anumāna*).

For instance: the Self is incapable of modification, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its being subject to modification; "like the nature of God" is the positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*); "like a jar, etc. is the negative example (*vyatireka*). Alternatively, there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a general sense:
whatever is devoid of a means of valid cognition that apprehends a particular form does not possess that form, just as [the color] blue [is not yellow].

Regarding the phrase "having the form of yellow": since the term "unchangeable" (*avikārya*) might give rise to the suspicion of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by the mere absence of occasional change, he explains the meaning of the suffix in order to avoid that [objection], stating "unfit for modification" (*vikārānarha*). The use of the *ktvā* suffix is due to the fact that the act of perceiving (*vedana*) precedes the negation.
But it is not with regard to grief itself. By this, it is stated that self-knowledge is the cause for the absence of grief.
The sense is that for one who knows the Self, there can be no fitness for grief at all.
Thus, it has been stated that when one accepts a self distinct from the body, there is an absence of a cause for grief.
Now, even according to the materialist view (*nāstika-dṛṣṭi*)—the doctrine that the body is the self—it is said that there is no cause for grief.
This is expressed by the three verses beginning with "Furthermore" (*atha ca*). The word "now" (*atha*) serves to introduce an alternative position or to signify a question.

Or; or it has the sense of comparison. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to conjoin the two qualifying attributes. "Always born, always dying" means having constant birth and destruction. He will elaborate upon this meaning in the following verse. For it is not possible for that which is eternal to possess the state of being born or the state of being dead;
nor can the very nature of the acts of birth and death be qualified by eternity.

The compound "nityamṛta" is stated as a summary to dispel the misconception that the word "nitya" (eternal) is a separate qualifier of the self—as in the expression "nityajāta" (eternally born). The term "deham" (body) expresses the result of the force of the qualifiers and so forth. The particle "eva" (indeed) has the sense of the word "ca" (and). He states the result of the restriction [implied by "eva"] with the words "na dehena. Previously, since there was no destruction of the self, the occasion for grief arose.

Thus it has been stated that [the self] does not exist. Now, with the intention that even though the destruction of the self—which is regarded as being of the nature of the body—is unavoidable, you, O mighty-armed one, need not grieve excessively, the word "evam" (thus) is used.
Alternatively, because previously the existence of a self distinct from the body was accepted, there was excessive grief due to the fear of the next world and so forth.

This is appropriate; however, now, like those who seek liberation from the cycle of existence (saṃsāramocaka) and others, the sense is: "O Mahābāhu, since this is merely a matter for joy, how can there be excessive grief? By addressing you as "Mahābāhu," the underlying intention is that for one such as you, a hero, agitation over the death of yourself or another is not fitting. Because the statement requires a reason by virtue of being a formal proposition (pratijñā), [the answer] is found in the following verse.
Or, having extracted the reason indicated by the two qualifiers, he says: "Through transformation," and so forth.

In order to exclude other meanings for the words *dhruva*, *mṛtyu*, *mṛta*, and so forth, [the author] explains the phrase beginning with *jātasya* (*of one who is born*), which supports the present subject, as "of one who has arisen" (*utpannasya*), and so on. The expression "it is perceived" (*upalabhyate*) refers to the establishment through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indicated by the word *hi*. This remains true even if [the verse] is intended to state a reason (*hetu*).

The word "hi" (for) signifies that the respective point is established from the nature of the facts. He raises an objection with the intention of [showing] the contradiction regarding the birth of one who is dead. He explains: even if this matter were based solely on scriptural instruction (*aupadeśika*), it might still be accepted. But here, it is stated as a restatement of what is well-known in the world, namely, "For [one] who is born... And in the world, the arising of that which previously did not exist is observed.

But it never arises for that which has already ceased. Furthermore, if what has perished were to be born again, then because the absolute cessation of suffering would be impossible, the entire science of liberation (*apavarga-śāstra*) would be rendered invalid, and efforts such as overcoming diseases or conquering enemies would be futile; likewise, one would have no reason to grieve over the death of a son or others.
The sense is that, for this reason, this [position] is not logically tenable. He offers a rebuttal: "Of that which already exists" (*sata eva*).

Anticipating the objection—"But both of these have been stated: because there is no dependence on production for that which exists, and because we observe the production of jars and the like only when they were previously non-existent"—he says: "In production... (*utpattīti*).

He demonstrates this with the words: "For [the case of] threads and so forth. The sense is that you yourself also accept this regarding a cloth produced from a single long thread prior to the final conjunction of the threads. And it has been stated by Nārāyaṇācārya:
"The production of a cloth and the like from a single, very long thread is observed. [This is directed at] the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavādin).

Regarding the word "prati," [the author] intends the following dilemma: Is there some entity called a "whole" (avayavin) that is perceived as distinct from the collection of its parts, or is it merely postulated? Having thus set forth the alternative, he states the refutation of the first position with the words "it is non-existent" (asat).
The phrase "merely this much" (etāvat) means nothing more than being endowed with a particular arrangement; this is indicated by the two words "is not perceived by the proponent" (vādinopalabhyate).

He intends [to address] the contradiction between speech and mind. He elaborates on the point already stated with the words "only this much. He refutes the second alternative with the words "kāraka" (agent/causal factor). If we, like the Sāṅkhyas, were to assert that everything is non-accidental (*anāgantuka*), then indeed the fault of the futility of the operation of causal factors and so forth would arise. For we [hold that] substances...
We maintain that all things are non-accidental (anāgantuka) in their essence, while their various states are accidental (āgantuka).

Just as in the case of a jar or similar objects, even in the case of lamps and the like, the attainment of another state is inferred; however, due to reaching a subtle state—as in the case of a jar that has been crushed and shattered—it is no longer perceived. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever; this is the intended meaning.
In this context, a specific practical function such as the fetching of water is intended, since the assumption of a different name has been mentioned separately.

By this, the distinctions of cause, number, dimension, cognition, and configuration—as well as priority, posteriority, being destroyed, not being destroyed, and so forth—are also resolved. [Otherwise,] there would be the conceptualization of a separate substance.

With the intention that the resolution—by means of the mutual obstruction of either the weight of the parts or the whole—to the undesirable consequence of further weights, effects, and so forth, is excessively strained, he says: "No; [it arises] from another substance.
And they say: "If there were another substance in the effect, and yet it is not perceived..."
"The designation 'a jar is two palas' is not tenable. He concludes with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is:
because only that much is perceived, because nothing else is perceived, and because the [theoretical] assumptions can be accounted for in another way.
Now, let it be granted that arising is a particular state of a substance; however, destruction is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*).
And how can that which is opposed to it be called its state? To this he says: "called origination.
The intention is as follows: first of all, we do not perceive any other distinct category of entity (padārtha) called non-existence (abhāva).

Nor is it proper to postulate it on the basis of linguistic usage such as "it does not exist," since [the required explanation] is provided by the very different states already accepted by both parties.

Because that [state] is maintained. Nor does it follow that by abandoning the black state and adopting the red state, there would be the undesirable consequence of the conventional designation "destruction of the jar," for you yourself do not admit that the red state is contradictory to the jar-state, just as the state of shards and so forth is. Nor [is there a problem] for those things that have entered into a single category by virtue of being existent (*bhāvatva*).

It should not be said that contradiction is untenable, for we observe contradiction— characterized by non-coexistence and mutual destruction— in entities such as light and darkness, cold and heat, or fire and grass. Furthermore, because the negation of a negation is accepted as being a positive entity (*bhāva*), otherwise, even a negation, as a member of the same category of categories (*padārtha*), would contradict a positive entity.
It is not possible in any way [for these to coexist]. Thus, destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is the opposing subsequent state;

prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the opposing prior state. Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) are simply the unique, opposing properties residing in a different entity, distinguished by the negation of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) and heteroreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Non-existence through conjunction (*saṃsargābhāva*) is either a specific distinction of place and time, or a specific state produced by that [distinction].

Furthermore, due to the differences among the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) and so forth, there is a variety of linguistic usages such as "it exists" and "it does not exist," just like the conventional designations of "fatherhood" and "sonship.
Now, if destruction is the attainment of a subsequent state such as the state of being a potsherd, then the destruction of the potsherd would be the destruction of the pot.

If it were the case that the destruction of the jar itself were destroyed [upon the jar's breaking], then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the jar reappearing in its state as powder.

Furthermore, if the state of the lump of clay were the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar, then since the prior non-existence would be absent prior to the formation of the lump, there would either be the establishment of the jar or the jar's own essential nature (*svarūpa-abhāva*) [would have existed] even before; to this, he says: "of the substance clay."

The intention is as follows: it is not only the state of being a potsherd (*kapālatva*) that is opposed to the state of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), for states such as being powder (*cūrṇatva*) and so forth are also opposed to it.
Even for one who accepts destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) as being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), a succession of opposing states is unavoidable.

Consequently, since the state of being a potsherd, the state of being powder, and so forth, are indistinguishable in their nature as successive states opposed [to the pot], the conventional usage of "destruction of the pot" is established across all those states. In this way, even regarding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the succession of states opposed [to the effect] can be maintained.
If one does not accept this, then even in the position that non-existence is a distinct entity (*atiriktabhāva*), the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable.

For even in that case, if the substance called "pot" were the cessation of the prior non-existence of the pot, then upon the cessation of the pot, the cessation of the pot's prior non-existence itself would have ceased; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the reappearance of the pot's prior non-existence.
And this being so, since the interruption of the prior non-existence in the interim would be impossible, the pot itself could never exist.

Furthermore, since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) culminates in a positive entity once the causal complex is complete, there would be a re-emergence of that very same individual jar which has already been destroyed.

Likewise, if the antecedent non-existence of destruction were the jar itself, then prior to the production of the jar, at the stage of the lump of clay, there would be the destruction of the jar due to the antecedent non-existence of its destruction. And if that were the case, the jar itself [would not exist].

It could never arise at any time, because it is impossible for it to arise while its own destruction is occurring; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its re-emergence even during the state of the potsherds. And thus, since the destruction of the jar would entail its existence during the state of the lump of clay—given that destruction follows after the existence [of the entity]—the jar would have to be established prior to the lump itself.

And thus, "the prior absence and destruction [respectively] belong only to the two times of the existence of the established entity and its destruction. By the words "the state of being a lump, the state of being a jar," and so forth, he recalls the statement of the venerable Parāśara: "The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, potsherds; from the potsherd, powder and dust; and from that, atoms. For in that context:
It is clear that words such as "non-existent" (*asat*) and so forth are based on the attainment of a different state;

this has also been explained in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*. Now, even so, while it may be appropriate to say, "For that which is born, death is certain," since we observe that things like jars have arisen, it would not be appropriate to say, "Birth is certain for the dead."

But this is not tenable, because one does not observe the re-emergence of a destroyed object such as a jar. Nor is its re-emergence the cause of grief, such that its inevitability would need to be established. To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
The intention is as follows: it is not said that an object undergoes re-emergence in the very same state in which its destruction occurred.

Rather, it is that very same substance characterized by a different state. For indeed, a single substance, having perished in the form of a jar, arises in the form of potsherds. Indeed, the state of being potsherds is the destruction of that substance in its state as a jar, and it is the arising of that very same substance in its state as potsherds. Therefore, it is logically established that there is the arising of what has perished.

The meaning is that this very thing is the attainment of the subsequent state. Here, it is indicated that because the word "attainment" (*prāpti*) is intended to signify the arrival at the first moment, the absence of the term "origination" (*utpatti*) in reference to the subsequent moments is logically consistent.
This being the case, the demonstration that origination itself is to be avoided is equivalent to the demonstration that destruction is to be avoided.

For that very reason, it is also logical that [the scripture] aims at dispelling grief. Alternatively, if you grieve thinking that this insentient substance has been destroyed, then why do you not rejoice, since that very same substance has arisen in its subsequent state? This is the intended meaning.
Because there are different ways of describing a single transformation, it is designated as both "origination" and "destruction.
Thus, it is said that transformation consists of what are called origination and destruction.

In this way, although creation is destruction from the perspective of dissolution, the conventional distinction is maintained with the intention of emphasizing the connection to the purpose of the Puruṣa.
By the phrase "subject to transformation" (*pariṇāmin*), its being of such a nature is stated as the reason for its unavoidability.
The word "iti" indicates that the term "unavoidable" (*aparihārya*) is intended to signify a logical reason (*hetu*).
Thus, the state of being beyond grief has been declared on the grounds of its inevitability.

Now, it is further stated that there is no cause for grief because each respective entity possesses its own fixed nature, and because, in the aforementioned state, one reaches a condition where neither the transformation into the form of happiness nor the form of suffering can be perceived.
Regarding the phrase "beginning with the unmanifest" (*avyaktādīni*): it is stated here that the word *bhūta* refers to the body. Regarding the phrase "human beings, etc. (*manuṣyādīn*):

this is said to dispel the delusion that words such as "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and "manifest" (*vyakta*) refer to specific states of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and to make known that the interpretation offered by Yādavaprakāśa—that they refer to the "existent Brahman" (*sadbrahma*) and so forth—is irrelevant to the present context.
"Unperceived," and so forth. "Having come here from non-perception, he has again gone to non-perception;
he is not yours, nor are you his—why do you grieve in vain? Thus it is said even here: "They abide in their own inherent natures. This is the intended meaning.

Nor is the manifested state, such as humanity and so forth, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of these substances, because that is produced by a specific kind of aggregation and other factors. Nor is the unmanifested prior or subsequent state the nature, because that too is produced by disintegration and other factors. Therefore, the inherent nature is simply the general quality of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

And therefore, just as the unmanifest state and the manifest intermediate state of a transforming substance are not causes for sorrow, so too is its subsequent state. Here, the particle *eva* (only/even) signifies inevitability, or rather, the attainment of one's own nature (*svābhāvaprāpti*); that is, if the very nature [of the substance] is indeed its unmanifest state.
If you maintain that the state of being unmanifest is due to the influence of an obstacle,

even then, since such an obstacle is unavoidable and because— once that adventitious obstacle has occasionally departed— the attainment of humanity and so forth would be obtained without effort, there is no reason whatsoever for lamentation.
If, however, the very nature of things were generally the cause of sorrow, then,

in this world consisting of an infinite succession of individual entities with diverse natures, everyone would at all times be submerged in the very ocean of suffering; thus, there would now be no specific cause for sorrow.
Furthermore, if grief arises from the separation from even a conditioned cause of happiness— such as universal sovereignty—

and you fear the destruction of the causes of happiness, such as your own body, then the protection of the body and so forth must be undertaken. And if you fear public censure caused by the killing of kinsmen and the like, then [you must act] while you are capable.
There would be a great censure resulting from the failure to protect one's kinsmen and others;
furthermore, there would be infamy exceeding even death, caused by cowardice and similar traits.
Moreover, this grief is not as difficult to abandon as the physical pain arising from contact with cold, heat, and so forth.

However, because it is rooted in the conceit that finds delight in what has not been critically examined, it must be abandoned by the cessation of that [conceit]; for this very reason, you—who are seized by the great demon of the delusion that the body is the self—cannot in any way be an object of grief even through an investigation into the secret tenets of the Lokāyata system.
This means: what could possibly be the cause for lamentation?
Thus it has been said: "In that regard, there is no basis for lamentation."

Thus, by not concluding the discourse with mere conformity [to others], he praises his own previously stated doctrine—which is rooted in the delusion of the body as the self and defiled by a series of evils—by stating that those qualified for it are rare in this world and so forth; thus he says, "In this way. This very [doctrine] is indeed Upaniṣadic, distinguished by certain specific words.

The verse beginning with “āścaryavat” [is as follows]: “evam-uktasvabhāvam” is the meaning of the word “enam. He states that the uniqueness (vaijātya) described in the passage beginning with “avyakto'yam” is the cause for its being marvelous. The phrase “svetara-” is stated in order to dispel the misconception that the word “āścaryavat” functions as an adverbial qualifier for the actions such as “paśyati” [he sees].

"Standing as if a marvel" (*āścaryavad-avasthitam*): the sense is that it is precisely appropriate here to state the distinctness of the Self. By this, Śaṅkara’s alternative interpretation, which takes [the subject] as an illustration of the agent, is also refuted.
He uses the word "some" (*kaścit*) for the purpose of specification. Regarding the phrase "among the infinite": even among men who are devoid of knowledge...

It is said "among living beings" (*jantuṣu*) to show that he is not equal to animals. He states the intended meaning of the word "some" (*kaścit*) with the words "by means of the Great [Principle]" (*mahatā*). And as it is said: "When the impurity has been ripened by actions, then knowledge arises.

Here, the word *anvaya* has the same meaning as the word "some" occurring in the preceding and following sentences. The phrase "to another" (*parasmai*) is an expression obtained through the sense of the context.

Having raised the objection that if one were to say, "Even having heard [the scripture], one does not know," there would be defects such as contradiction and the futility of beginning the treatise, it was stated:
"as it truly exists in reality. This means in its entirety endowed with all forms according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and in a manner free from superimposition (*anāropita*).
The intended meaning here concerns merely the rarity of those who know reality.

He explains that the particle *ca* (and) in the sentence beginning with "Even having heard" (*śrutvāpi*) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), and he states those things to be so cumulated by saying: "From the word 'ca'... [The text continues: "First of all, even a seer of the Self as distinct from the body is difficult to find;
how much less one who sees it as it truly is? Even when such persons exist, a speaker is difficult to find; how much less..."

The intended meaning is this: "Though there may be such speakers of all secrets, a listener alone is difficult to find; how much more so one like you, who is a listener exactly as things are, endowed with all the internal and external qualities of a disciple.
First comes hearing; then, through reflection based on that hearing, there arises certainty regarding the Self; and from that, one becomes fit for speaking.

Alternatively, the sequence here is that the perception of a specific detail arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of long-term observation. To dispel the doubt—“If the self transcends the body, why is it not perceived in such a manner?”—the statement regarding its difficulty to know is made.
The underlying sense is: “When a reality cannot be known by anyone at all, why do you alone reproach me?”

Now, just as among beings ranging from the gods down to stationary objects, a disparity is observed within their bodies regarding genus, quality, place, time, and the states of being difficult or easy to pierce,
so too is a disparity seen in the embodied soul, such as happiness, suffering, and the like; and there are also words such as "gods" and so forth [to denote these differences].

[The selves] range from those distinguished as gods and so forth up to the self characterized by divinity and the like. Thus, in order to dispel the doubt that a disparity in characteristics—such as permanence or impermanence—might also be possible, it is said: "the embodied one" (*dehī*). The phrase "even while being slain" (*vadhyamāne 'pi*) is stated by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), as in the expression "while the body is being slain."

Otherwise, the phrase "in the body of everyone" would be redundant, since the fact that [the elements] reside in the body is already established by the mere term "embodied one" (*dehī*). Here, the word "beings" (*bhūta*) extends up to the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). The doubt suggested by the words "all," etc., is the cause for the objection. The phrase "even though they have dissimilar forms" is a restatement; the ellipsis is "due to the distinctions such as gods and so forth, and due to the distinctions in pleasure and so forth occasioned by those. "By the aforementioned nature" means by the previously mentioned qualities such as subtlety and indestructibility. "And eternal" [means...].
However, even though it resides in the Self, there is no discrepancy characterized by permanence or impermanence;
rather, it consists of a gradation of specific states of the attribute of consciousness (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) conditioned by various bodies.
Furthermore, the designation of sentient beings by terms such as "body" and so forth is based solely on the fact that the body is not established as something separate [from the Self].
This is the intention (*bhāva*). In order to indicate the connection with the subject at hand, he states what is excluded by the word "all" (*sarvān*):
namely, that it does not refer merely to Bhīṣma and the others.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for" and ending with "you ought not to grieve," misplaced compassion (*asthānakāruṇya*) is set aside. Then, by the passage beginning with "your own duty" (*svadharma*) and ending with "is superior to death," the confusion regarding dharma and adharma is set aside.

The word *api ca* (and also) is intended to indicate a further reason to be combined [with the previous one] and a distinction from the preceding section. He states the substantive (*viśeṣya*) for the term *svadharma* (one's own duty), which was indicated by the remainder of the sentence, *dhamryād dhi yuddhāt* (for [this is] a duty arising from battle), saying: "this... battle.

*Svadharma* means either "one's own duty" (*svo dharmaḥ*) or "the duty of oneself" (*svasya vā dharmaḥ*). The phrase "to waver" (*vikampitum*) is stated as something established by the force of the context.
