"Prārabdham" (the commenced): this reiterates that which is the cause for the cognition of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and falls within the scope of general prohibitions—namely, "even the killing of a living being.

It recalls that a specific scriptural injunction (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) is more powerful than a prohibitory scripture (*niṣedha-śāstra*), or rather, that there is no application of the prohibition [in this case]. "Like the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, etc.": this refers to something other than righteous war (*dharmayuddha*).

Dispelling the misconception that there is a negation of the true nature of the Kṣatriya as being superior, he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for the purpose of showing that for a Kṣatriya there is nothing more praiseworthy than righteous war (*dharmya-yuddha*). He says, "from what is righteous" (*dharmyāt*). Being righteous (*dharmyatva*) means not deviating from *dharma*. The cause of that is acting in accordance with justice (*nyāyataḥ pravṛttatvam*). And that [justice] applies to those who are unarmed, those who have desisted, those who have sought refuge, and so forth.

Because there is an absence of the employment of weapons and so forth. He states what is about to be explained, which was indicated by the word "for" (hi): "courage," etc. Now, one might object: this very point—that [the sacrifice] is like the Agniṣomīya and other such rites—is not accepted, because even that [sacrifice] is inevitably non-dharma due to its being an act of violence. Nor can "being prohibited" serve as a limiting condition (upādhi), for [the general rule] says, "One should not cause injury."

Because it pervades the probans while being excluded from the probandum by means of a general negation. Nor is "being more specifically enjoined" a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it exists even in cases that are neither enjoined nor prohibited, and thus there is a deviation from the probandum.
Furthermore, a general negation does not have a restricted scope due to conflict with a statement enjoining a particular case.

Because there is no contradiction that would necessitate such a restriction [of the general rule], since the two statements—one concerning the general and one concerning the particular—are intended to convey that [the action] is both a cause of sin and a means for accomplishing a sacrifice. There is no contradiction, for a single act can be both a means for a sacrifice and a cause of its failure.

Nor should it be argued that what causes sin cannot be enjoined; for this is seen in cases such as the consumption of *harītakī* (myrobalan), which is prescribed despite its natural tendency to cause illness.

This is justified because the suffering resulting from violence that is remedied by an expiation entered into for the sake of the sacrifice is slight, whereas the pleasure accomplished by the sacrifice is abundant. And it has been stated by the Sāṅkhyas: "For violence diminishes the faults of the person and will assist the sacrifice," and so forth.
And it says: "The teacher Pañcaśikha [said], 'There may be a slight mixture that is easily avoided and accompanied by reflection.
Therefore, regarding the statement 'like the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice],' which is an illustration of the unproven being used for the unproven, he says:"

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others": the reason (*hetu*) "because it is violence" (*hiṃsātva*) for establishing unrighteousness (*adharma*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, the limiting condition (*upādhi*) does not pervade the subject (*pakṣa*), because the subject consists of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), and precisely for that reason there is no prohibition [of such acts]. This is the intended meaning. He establishes that very nature of non-violence by saying "nihīnatara," etc. For the definition of violence is "an activity that brings about what is harmful."
But here, since it is the opposite of that [injury], it is logical that it is indeed protection; this he makes known through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "Not at all" (*na vā*).

The sense is that this is established by such statements as: "How could one like me, who is constrained, perform sacrifice with animal sacrifices? Let it be granted that in the *āgniṣomīya* and other rites, there is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) on the strength of the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*).
But how is this so here? To this he says: "And here... The sense is that this matter is also established by Śruti and Smṛti.

Now, an objection: through such statements as "Not injuring any living beings except at the sacred sites (tīrthas)," it is understood that the killing of the animal in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others is not truly injury; otherwise, the word "except" [would be meaningless].
Regarding the statement "because its exclusion is untenable," he says: "Therefore. This is the intended meaning:

first of all, mere production of pain is not what constitutes violence (*hiṃsā*) here, because that would lead to the over-extension [of the definition] to cases such as medical treatments involving the application of surgical instruments, which are of the nature of protection. Nor is it merely the separation from life-breaths, because that would apply to things that do not possess that nature.
For we observe the use of the word "himsā" (violence) in contexts such as the seizure of all one's property and the torments of hell;

nor is this a mere figurative usage, because there is no restrictive rule [to justify it], and because the opposite [that it is figurative] would be equally difficult to avoid. Therefore, the truth is simply this: violence is an action that results in harm and produces immediate suffering.

And therefore, the statement "except at [prescribed] sacrificial sites" (*anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*) was spoken from the perspective of common folk who are ignorant of the specific future human goals resulting from animals such as goats. For even in that sentence, the intended meaning is precisely that there is no nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*). And it has been stated by Manu: "Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."

Thus [it is said]. Here too, the term "killing" (*vadha*) is a restatement from the perspective of the common person (*pāmara*), whereas "non-killing" (*avadha*) is the statement of the reality (*tatva*). Although for those who have entered into the ritual (*kratu*), such as the consumption of the remains of the *soma* and so forth, there is no exclusion by means of another definition—as there is for that characterized as killing—[nevertheless...]
Nevertheless, we accept that state [of those actions] solely on the strength of scriptural statements declaring them not to cause sin (*pratyavāya*);

it is not, however, by virtue of their being enjoined merely as auxiliary parts of a sacrifice (*kratvartha*). But then, what is the scope of the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavāda*)?
It is precisely that case where, due to a contradiction with a specific statement (*viśeṣavākya*) that leaves no room for any other interpretation (*niravakāśa*), [the general rule is set aside].
The restriction of a general term that has multiple possible applications is a matter free from dispute.

Furthermore, by way of praising even war involving the killing of living beings, he eradicates the delusion that it is unrighteous (*adharma*). [He says: "by chance" (*yadṛcchayā*). Here, "obtained by chance" refers to its spontaneous occurrence. "Being a means to unsurpassed happiness":
for the word *svarga* (heaven) indeed refers to that which is neither hot nor cold, and which is not mixed with suffering.

Immediately after [the description of] being swallowed [by time], it is said: "That happiness which is brought about by longing is the locus of the word 'heaven' (svarga). Thus, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be the means for unsurpassed happiness.
Its deviation from this state occurs due to the influence of obstacles characterized by the expectation of fruits and so forth.

The suffix *cvi* is not employed here; the intended meaning of the word *aprāvṛta* (uncovered) is "being free from obstacles. Regarding the phrase "of those who are happy" (*sukhinām*), the word "meritorious" (*puṇyavatām*) is the corresponding term. For happiness alone is not the cause for obtaining such a battle;
therefore, the intention here is that by the word "happiness," its means (*sukhasādhana*) is indicated. Alternatively, the word "happy" (*sukhi*) here—
This refers to the relationship characterized by fitness for happiness; the sense is that such fitness consists precisely in the possession of merit.

Thus, it has been stated that because battle is consistent with dharma, it is a means for attaining unsurpassed happiness. Now, he speaks of the transgression incurred by not performing it, beginning with the words "But if...

Since the non-performance of battle is not a cause of sin for Brāhmaṇas and others, the word "thou" (*tvam*) is intended to refer specifically to one who is a Kṣatriya. This is the underlying intention.

"Consisting of one's own duty" (*svadharmabhūtam*): this refers to what was intended by the mention of "this" (*imam*). "Begun" (*ārabdham*): the meaning is that it is begun due to the delusion of regarding even a duty as non-duty because of its fruitlessness. For the mere non-performance of battle is not a cause of sin for a Kṣatriya, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to fight at all times; therefore, it is said:

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been commenced" (*prārabdhasya*) and "the fruit of one's own duty" (*svadharmaphalam*): the word *dharma* here refers to the *fruit*, because otherwise there would be tautology; furthermore, if it were a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), it would fail to result in the undesirable consequence [of the opponent's position]. This is the intended meaning. It is stated "by means of victory" (*vijayena*) so that it may become the subject of future fame.
The meaning of the statement is not merely that you will suffer the loss of unsurpassed human goals, both seen and unseen; rather, you will incur sin, which is the cause of unsurpassed suffering.

Thus, the loss of both seen and unseen fruits, as well as the unseen transgression, have been stated. Now, he describes the seen transgression with the words "and ill-repute. Here, "ill-repute" means a bad reputation. It should be understood that this is not merely [the loss] mentioned in such passages as "not for you alone," nor is it merely the unsurpassed sin pertaining to the next world. "Having fled from what was begun" means...
The sense is that, being utterly terrified, he did not even perform his first duty.
Since the word *avyaya* denotes indestructibility, let its pervasion across all time be stated;
but how is its pervasion across all space stated? It is stated thus: if infamy were not pervasive across all space...
It might be argued that [the term] "indestructible" (*avyaya*) does not apply even to that which pervades all time, because contraction over the course of time makes disintegration possible.
Alternatively, what is intended here by "indestructibility" is precisely the state of being non-deficient in terms of both space and time.
This is stated on the strength of the general reference "beings" (*bhūtāni*) and the force of the connection with the word "also" (*api*).

"Whether capable or incapable," and so forth. He states that the second half of the verse is spoken in response to the doubt that infamy might be desirable: "What follows from that? The particle *ca* serves to dispel that doubt. He provides the reason for Arjuna's high reputation with the words "by his valor," etc., meaning "of one who is esteemed by all."
The meaning is: "of one who is endowed with the elements previously described, both capable and incapable.

Now, is this excess over death something to be abandoned or something to be adopted? It is not the first, because of such sayings as "one who lives sees auspicious things," and so forth. Nor is it the second, because it would contradict the context; to this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": however, [verses] such as "Living, one attains auspicious things" (*jīvan bhadraṇi*) are not to be adopted by you today, for you are the son of a Kṣatriya; they might even lead to hell, since that is established by the *Smṛtis* and other authorities.
Likewise, in the later *Rāmāyaṇa*, there are the words of Raghunātha: "He whose infamy is sung in the world..."
"Anyone who oppresses living beings surely falls [to hell], as long as his name is proclaimed.
The implication is that death in battle leads to heaven precisely for that reason.

Thus, the confusion regarding dharma and adharma has been dispelled. Now, misplaced affection is being cast aside by means of the passage beginning with "out of fear" and so forth, and "out of affection for kinsmen" and so forth. This refers to one who, though being a hero, has desisted from action due to affection and compassion.

The sense is: "May fame belong to me alone. By the reference to "those who" (*yeṣām*), which points to those who are extremely well-known, it is stated that [the reference is] to Karṇa, Duryodhana, and others; by this, he calls to mind the group of enemies who have done him harm. Although Bhīṣma and the others may know the truth as it is, the sense is that Karṇa and the others do not.

The phrase "having become" (*bhūtvā*) is stated in order to eliminate the misconception that it might be connected with a prior future time—as in "Having bathed, I shall sacrifice" (*snātvā hoṣyāmi*)—due to its syntactic unity with the subsequent action "you will go" (*yāsyasi*). To clarify this, he says "prior to this.
He uses the term "highly esteemed" (*bahumata*) with the intention of expressing that he is indeed considered great due to his many virtues. He further describes him as "heroic" and "an enemy."

The sense is this: if you were a hero even before [the enmity], or if you were an enemy devoid of heroism, then indeed the great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*s) would not take you into account. The word "now" (*idānīm*) is used to indicate the persistence of enmity from that moment onward. The result of agility (*lāghava*) is the ease with which one seizes [the weapon]; by the word "agility," it is metaphorically implied.
And here, "the state of being perceived as brave and hostile" means the state of being the object of the conceit of being brave and hostile.
He dispels the doubt raised by the words "due to affection for kinsmen" and so forth with the words "for among the brave," etc.
If either bravery or hostility were not present, then...

He says "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*) with the intention that even through harm, the state of misplaced affection might be strengthened. He describes the manner of censuring their capability, which is the fruit of the matter at hand, with the words beginning "Of us, the brave ones" (*śūraṇām asmākam*).
"And many unspeakable words against the brave"—the meaning is: those harsh, vulgar, and mocking words which are not directed toward the brave, but rather toward those who are fleeing in terror;
with the intention that the word *ahita* here refers to the cause of such unspeakable words, he says: "enemies."

"Regarding the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra": if Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and others were to say anything at all, you might even endure it out of respect for their heroism and status. But how will you endure the many unspeakable insults uttered by those who are "heroes before the city"—those who pride themselves on being heroes yet have committed great offenses? This is the intended meaning. Now, [one might object that] in words denoting qualities...

For the propriety of the suffix *tarap* [denoting comparative degree] applies to words expressing qualities (*guṇa*), not to words denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like; indeed, expressions such as "a potter" (*ghaṭatara*) are not employed.
To this he says: "From that. This means from the doctrine that [the Self] is inexpressible (*avācyavāda*). The result is that [it follows] "from hearing that.
The word *duḥkha* denotes that which is characterized by opposition (*prātikūlya*).

The intention of the speaker, who explains the word *adhikataram* (more) by extracting it as a synonym for *pratikūlataram* (more contrary), is as follows: [he says] "of you" (*tava*), because you are not a mere man of the street, nor are you one devoted to conciliation and the like, such that there would be no cause for grief here. The word *kim* (what/how) refers back to the previous verse, which was intent on the state of being more sorrowful than death.

Thus he said: "In this way," meaning, "you yourself will think so. For even in the context of disparaging the power of the Gāṇḍīva bow and other such things, you will strive to kill even the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), let alone Karṇa and the others. Therefore, although you have now desisted, at that time, driven by even more intense suffering, you will engage in battle; this is my compassion for you.

He introduces the verse beginning with "Whether slain" (*hato vā*) as a completion of the sentence of the preceding verse. The sense is: "In either case, there is gain for you. Although he addresses Arjuna by saying "you shall obtain" (*prāpsyase*), meaning "you shall enjoy," his use of general terms such as "of the hero" (*śūrasya*) and so forth refers to the slaying of Bhīṣma and the others.

This is for the purpose of making known that, because it is a cause of ultimate welfare (*śreyaḥ*), it is not a cause of grief. By the word "ultimate welfare" (*śreyasaḥ*), he includes the attainment of happiness such as heaven and sovereignty according to one's desire.
For human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) does not consist merely in killing; therefore, it is said: "in a righteous war" (*dharmayuddhe*). "Precisely from that" means from that very [war].
The meaning is: "precisely because of the destruction [of the self] established by the treatise as the means to the highest good.
Regarding the phrase "supreme beatitude" (*paramaniḥśreyasa*):
here, the word "heaven" (*svarga*)—due to the context of immortality—refers either to supreme beatitude itself or to its locus.
For example: "Having departed from this world by means of this wise Self, he attained all desires in that heavenly world and became immortal;
those who dwell in the heavenly world partake of immortality"—this was said with reference to Arjuna, who was indifferent toward the celestial heaven.
The sense is that this very meaning is established by the statement [of the Lord]. By the two words "having conquered" and "you shall enjoy," the result is stated.
Regarding the word "without thorns": the sense is that even if a kingdom were achieved while adversaries remain awake, it would not be fit for enjoyment.
To exclude the notion that the result culminates merely in Arjuna’s enjoyment of the kingdom, he says: "not aimed at."

For one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the enjoyment of sovereignty and such things are merely incidental. He states the intended meaning of "perfect enlightenment" (*saṃbuddhi*) with the words "of the son of Kuntī.
It is well known that a *kṣatriya* princess gives birth to a dead child;
indeed, the conduct of a doe's fawn is not to be followed by the offspring of a lioness, nor by one born of a pure field (*śuddhakṣetra*).
The implication is that you must effect the interruption of this most exalted dharma.

The agitation caused by attachment to inferior stations, compassion, and the notions of dharma and adharma has been pacified. Now, he speaks of the manner of practice for one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) who has been established in the nature of reality (dharmatva), saying: "For the seeker of liberation," and so forth.
Indeed, such an understanding is not required by those who desire kingdoms and the like.
The sense is that one should not entertain the doubt, "What is this to me?", on the grounds that it is achievable through battle that is minor, unstable, and mixed with suffering.
He shows that the previously mentioned knowledge of the Self must be maintained during the stage of practice by using the word "thus" (*evam*).

By the phrase "distinct from the body," he means that the consideration of attributes such as what is to be abandoned occurs only when there exists a substratum (the Self) possessing those attributes.

To avoid the confusion of redundancy, it has been stated that gain and loss have wealth and the like as their objects. However, regarding how one may achieve equanimity toward the objects of pleasure and pain—namely, one's own happiness and one's own distress—it is said here: "with an unveiled intellect.

"Modification" refers to states such as joy and sorrow; by stating the absence of these, the lack of despondency and lack of elation included within the seven-fold set beginning with discrimination (*viveka*) are understood. This is indicated by the dative case in the word *yuddhāya* (for the sake of battle).

The cessation of [the view that the scripture] has another purpose is now stated: "Heaven and so forth. What is about to be said, beginning with "Let there never be [attachment] to fruits," is to be kept in mind here.

Regarding the word *tataḥ* ("therefore"), it is more appropriate for it to refer to a specific cause already employed; its meaning as mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and so forth is, however, irrelevant—this is the intention behind the statement: "by means of the cognition of the mere thing to be done" (*kevalakāryabuddhyā*). Furthermore, the word *pāpa* (sin) here does not refer to expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Nor does one who has committed evil "not obtain" [immortality], because there is no logical connection [between the two]. Furthermore, there can be no non-adherence of future [evil] karma.

Moreover, there is no non-adherence of subsequent sins in cases other than knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, in this context, due to the subject matter of immortality and because the fruit is indistinguishable for one seeking liberation, the term refers to all transmigratory actions consisting of both merit and demerit.
And then, with the intention that *saṃsāra*, which is the fruit thereof, is indicated here, he says: "the *saṃsāra* which is of the nature of suffering.
When it was said, "In this way you shall not incur sin," only the absence of being a cause for sin appeared; therefore, he says: "from the bondage of *saṃsāra*.
The word "successively" (*paramparayā*) is to be supplied. The previously stated [verse], "He is fit for immortality," is recalled here.

Now, he introduces the commencement of the subsequent section by way of its primary purpose among the causes for dispelling sorrow mentioned in the preceding section, using the word "thus" (*evam*). By the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*), karma-yoga is first mentioned because it is to be accomplished through the sequential practice of both self-knowledge and karma-yoga; subsequently, however, [self-knowledge] follows as its fruit.
By the verse beginning with "When he renounces desires," the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) will be explained.

[The phrase] "in order to speak" means in order to elaborate upon that which has been introduced as the primary subject. [This is done] to dispel the confusion regarding the mention of two opposing systems called Sāṃkhya and Yoga; for here, by the word "Sāṃkhya," [is meant] "by the yoga of knowledge."

Dispelling the misconception that this refers to the subject matter of the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) to be described for the Sāṃkhyas, he says: "Sāṃkhya. The lexicographers state: "Buddhi, mati, medhā, saṃkhyā, saṃvitti, and upalabdhi [are synonyms]. This is well-known from the Upaniṣads, as in the passage: "The Sāṃkhyas [know] the Person devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). etc.

The term *sāṃkhya* is applicable even to the Self (*ātman*) because of its supreme nature; nor does there follow a discrepancy in meaning in such passages as "by the yoga of knowledge for the *sāṃkhyas*," since that word is used everywhere in reference to the yoga of the intellect (*buddhi*). And even if such a discrepancy were to exist, it is [resolved] everywhere by conforming to the context and other such factors.
It is withdrawn [into the singular] to indicate that the singular number is intended to signify the genus (*jāti*). It is stated as "the reality of the Self" (*ātmatattva*).
By the phrase "for the sake of knowing that," it is shown that the immediate fruit is merely the ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) of that [reality].
Here, "intellect" (*buddhi*) refers to the ascertainment produced by the scripture; whereas "for the sake of knowing that" refers to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) and so forth.

Having delimited the section concerning the designation of the self (*ātman*), he says: "But not indeed... Then, with the passage beginning "but beyond that, its own nature," and so forth, [he discusses] the delusion regarding dharma and adharma. He explains what is intended by the word "here" with the verse beginning "from afar. He states that the expression indicated by the reference "this" is an immediate designation, saying: "being designated."

By this, the distinction between the intellect that has entered into the performance [of action] and the intellect expressed regarding its object is also shown. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Listen to the instruction which generates the intellect whose object is the manner of performance. By this, it is also established that the term *karmayoga* here refers to a specific state of the intellect.

Thus, [the author] rejects another compound with an unexalted meaning for the term *karmabandha*: namely, "bondage by means of karma" (*karmaṇā bandhaḥ*). This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "the third case [is compounded] with a word expressing a quality when that [third-case word] denotes the object produced by it. Since the primary meaning of the word *bandha* (bondage) is impossible here, he states its intended meaning: "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*).
By this, the misconception that there is a loss of connection with the karma being performed is also refuted.

To the objection that, once it has been said "Listen to this," the passage beginning with "Determination" (*vyavasāya*) should have followed immediately, and that the intermediate verse "Not here is the effort" (*nehābhikramaḥ*) is therefore out of place—the author replies: "To be spoken later" (*vakṣyamāṇa*).
At the outset, an incentive (*prarocanā*) is provided by describing the greatness [of the path] in order to generate an intense desire to know.
Such is the sense. By the word "here" (iha), he states the distinction from other types of action:

"the yoga of action. He dispels the suspicion that it refers to the act of stepping forward by stating, "abhikrama means undertaking" (ārambha); the sense is that this term is synonymous with "upakrama" (commencement). [This applies to] the undertaking which takes the form of an action.

To the question "How is there non-destruction?", he says: "Destruction is the destruction of the cultivation that is the means to the fruit. He states the intended meaning [of the verse] with the words "of that which has been begun. Revealing the cause for the apprehension of sin (pratyavāya), he explains the second quarter [of the verse]: "the interruption of what has been begun. The latter half [of the verse] is of the nature of an elaboration on what was stated.

He explains [the phrase] "of this" [as follows]: "from the fear of saṃsāra. The sense is that the fear qualified by greatness is indeed the fear of saṃsāra itself. Even a very small portion [of this knowledge] must necessarily be the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra, even if it has been interrupted due to defects in place, time, and so forth, or through negligence and the failure to perform required duties.

Showing that it is due to "reconnection" (*punassandhāna*), he states that this verse has the aforementioned single purpose and is not redundant with what is to be said in both summary and detailed form, saying: "This is the meaning.
In response to the doubt—"How can there be the consequence of the destruction of what has been performed?"—he shows the exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) of the word "here" (*iha*).

"Indeed, others..."—by this, worldly [rites] are stated as an illustrative example for the cause of apprehension. Regarding the general designation "Vedic," the intended meaning is this: even the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, if their continuity is interrupted, would not yield fruit; moreover, they would lead to transgression (*pratyavāya*). A slight deficiency rooted in impossibility and so forth [is what is meant].

For in that case [of obligatory rites], there is a deficiency; however, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the distinction is that there is no fruitlessness even when there is a deficiency of auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).
And they lead to transgression (*pratyavāya*); the sense is that it is not merely the non-attainment of heaven and so forth, but that one may also incur the loss of Brahminhood and the like.

Thus, under the guise of describing its greatness, the distinctiveness of this action from all other actions has been stated. Now, distinguishing that understanding regarding it— which was promised as being by way of instruction—
from the understandings concerning actions performed for desire, by means of the disparity between their causes and fruits, the Lord instructs as follows:

Regarding the word "kāmya" (desirable), he states what is included by the word "iha" (here): "in all ritual action prescribed by the scriptures. He says "prescribed by the scriptures" so that there may not be a sense of unity even with respect to worldly actions—those neither enjoined nor prohibited—which have distinct results.
This is a statement regarding the inclusive limiting adjunct (*saṃgrāhakopādhi*), intended to exclude the notion that the subject matter is limited solely to the war currently under discussion.

By the word "in all" (*sarvasmin*), there is an inclusion of all varieties of injunctions: the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), and their respective sub-divisions.
In response to the doubt as to how there can be oneness when the intellect is directed toward various actions (*karma*) as its objects:
He qualifies the intellect (*buddhi*) by means of the subject matter implied by the context and the force of the qualification: "by one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣuṇā*).
By the word "resolve" (*avasāya*), he dispels the misconception that it is a mere duty or a task (*kṛtya-avasāya*). He uses the term "certainty" (*niścaya*) in order to avoid tautology.

Demonstrating that the object of resolve (*vyavasāya*) is indicated by the latter member of the compound, he justifies the statement "by one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣuṇā*) with the words "For that... (*sā hi*). He states what is to be excluded by the term "resolute in nature" (*vyavasāyātmikā*) with the word "desiring [fruits]" (*kāmyā*).

Now, one might object: "Without the knowledge of a self that is distinct from the body and extends beyond this world, how could one undertake the great exertion of performing sacrifices and other rites, which are the means for attaining heaven and the like—experiences to be enjoyed in another body? To this, he says:
"For therein... (tatra hi). This means either: "one is qualified by desire," or "that in which qualification occurs by means of desire."
Or: *adhikāra* refers to the domain of desire (*kāmadhikāra*), that is, optional ritual action (*kāmyakarman*) or the qualification for it; or else, it refers to the scripture concerning that.

Furthermore, *adhikāra* is the conceit (*abhimāna*) that "this action is for my sake" because it is a means to achieve what I desire. By the term "self distinct from the body," what is intended is the stability [of the self] such that it is capable of assuming another body.

Otherwise, even if it were determined that [the body] is merely something additional, there would be the danger of the misconception that it perishes simultaneously with the body, leading to the failure to perform those desirable actions intended for the next world.
He clarifies what is intended by the word "merely" (mātra): "not the self. And here, the true nature of the self is [discussed].
What is intended [by "Self"] is its nature as eternal, self-luminous, blissful, possessing the attributes of Bhagavān, and naturally free from sin, and so forth.
Now, an objection: in some cases, for heaven and liberation—which are to be experienced at a time subsequent to the body—mere knowledge of the existence of the Self is required; in other cases...

Regarding the phrase "ascertainment of its true nature" (*tadyāthātmyaniścaya*): why is there this distinction that, while in some cases mere knowledge of the existence of the self (*ātman*) is required for heaven and liberation—the objects of reflection and meditation—in other cases the ascertainment of its true nature is required? To this he says: "Its own nature," etc. (*svarūpa...*): [The text continues: "Its own nature" refers to the specific characteristics of the self, such as being eternal, partless, and so forth. "Ascertainment" means the removal of doubt regarding those characteristics. This is what is meant by "ascertainment of its true nature. It is not merely the knowledge of the self's existence; rather, it is the definitive determination of its specific qualities. Therefore, the distinction between the two is established. Thus, the meaning is that the ascertainment of the self's true nature is required for liberation, whereas mere knowledge of its existence suffices for heaven. This is the point.

This is the intended meaning: regarding the section on desire (*kāma*), is the determination of its true nature required by logical inconsistency or by the authority of the scriptures? Even in the former case, if there were no determination of its true nature, would it be that the very desire for results such as heaven would not exist, or rather, that the performance of the means to achieve them would be impossible?
Not the third [alternative], because for one who has performed the means (*upāya*) without deficiency, the arising of the fruit is independent of anything else;

and since it arises solely for the sake of experience, once that experience is established, there is no dependence on the experience of the true nature of the self (*ātma-yāthātmya*) at the time of experiencing the fruits of heaven and so forth— just as there is none regarding the enjoyments of a universal monarch and the like— at the very moment those fruits are being experienced.
All of this has been stated up to the point ending with "because of possibility" (*saṃbhavāt*). Here, "possibility" refers to the absence of any logical inconsistency.

Nor is it proper to say [the injunction] is based on the authority of scripture (*śāstra*); for does the scripture enjoin something for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) or an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)? Regarding that, the case of its being solely for a visible purpose has already been answered.
Furthermore, it cannot be that [the knowledge of the Self] effects the body which serves as the instrument for sacrifice and so forth, because such a thing has not been observed.

Nor can it enter as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, the Self; for, unlike injunctions such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) found in the sections concerning rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyādhikāra*), there is no injunction stating, "One should know the Self as it truly is."

For it has been established in the *Śārīraka* that knowledge produced by the injunctions of the Vedānta lacks the status of being a subsidiary to ritual action (*karmaśeṣatva*), because it serves as the means for a superior, distinct fruit. Furthermore, even for those who possess the realization of the knowledge of the Self, [the scriptures] indeed set forth fruits such as heaven; for it is said: "Fragile are these boats in the form of sacrifice, which are inferior and consist of eighteen parts."

Regarding those [actions], there are scriptural passages such as, "Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good," and so forth; and immediately following, it is said, "The unwise speak these flowery words," and so on. For the ignorant, there is the ascent to heaven and so forth by way of the path of smoke and the like.

It is proclaimed in the Upaniṣads. Therefore, because there is an absence of an injunction (*vidhi*), even the status of being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) is refuted. All of this has been stated [in the commentary]: "And because of non-contradiction" (*avirodhāt*). This means because there is no contradiction with the scriptures (*śāstra*) and so forth.
The sense is that in the alternative view, there would be a contradiction with other scriptural passages regarding the section on liberation (*mokṣādhikāra*).

But all this is otherwise. For instance: the attainment of one's own nature as it truly exists is indeed the human goal of liberation (*mokṣa-puruṣārtha*). How could that be desired if it were not ascertained? And how could the means for its attainment be practiced without even a desire for it, [which presupposes] knowledge of the true nature of one's own self? Knowledge of the reality of one's own nature...

Furthermore, since [the means] enters into the practice as something enjoined, how could one perform the *puṣpakalpa* (flower-rite) with a fire-pot that has a different locus? And how could there be an experience of the fruit characterized by the manifestation of one's own nature for one who lacks self-certainty? Thus, there is a contradiction with reasoning (*yuktivirodha*). Moreover, the scriptures raise this objection.

Knowledge of the reality of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is the benefactor of liberation in every respect; therefore, in its absence, there would even be a contradiction with the scriptures. Now, one might ask: what is this "oneness" of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by resolve? It cannot be the oneness of the individual instance (*vyakti*), because such a continuum of intellects is possible.

Nor does identity of form follow from the identity of the object (*viṣaya*), because that is untenable due to the distinction between subordinate and primary elements (*aṅga-pradhāna*) within the respective objects. Nor can that [identity] be established on the grounds of having a collective (*samudāya*) as its domain, because that would apply equally even to optional rites (*kāmyakarman*). Therefore, it was stated: "by virtue of having as their object the means to a single fruit. He demonstrates this very point:

Regarding the phrase "from one" and "all": for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), all actions—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—when performed, serve as auxiliaries to the means of liberation either directly or indirectly;
thus, liberation alone is the primary fruit. [The objection: "All [actions] have a single fruit as their means; nevertheless..."
To the question, "How can there be unity in the cognition of those [actions] when the nature of the actions occurring in succession is diverse? he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Because all these actions, by virtue of being means to a single result, are grasped by a single injunction and thus constitute the subject matter of a single scripture, the cognition directed toward them is called "one," since it has as its object the subject matter of a single scripture, even though intermediate distinctions between the actions exist.

This is the meaning. Regarding how those [rites] established by separate injunctions—which possess their own distinct procedures (*itikartavyatā*) established by separate sentences—can constitute the subject matter of a single treatise (*śāstra*), he provides an example for their unity according to the method already stated:
"Just as," etc. For the six sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya*, together with their respective procedures, are [established] by their originative sentences (*utpattivākya*).

The two sentences, which were originally separate and subsequently became two distinct groups through the restatement of those groups, are again enjoined as a unity within the context of the *kāma* (desire) section by virtue of their being means to a single result. Thus, because they fall within the scope of a single scriptural teaching, the cognition of them is also one. "In that manner" is the meaning. [This applies] to those who lack discernment.
Thus he says "the supreme cause" by means of the words beginning with "heaven and sons. "Infinite" because the fruits are manifold;

"many" because of the abundance of fruits. Since the various karmas that are the means to those fruits have distinct purposes according to the infinite variety of fruits such as heaven and so forth, the cognitions regarding them are also diverse for as long as there is a distinction among the fruits—this is the meaning.

Avoiding the charge of tautology by explaining that the terms "infinite" (*ananta*) and "many-branched" (*bahuśākha*) refer respectively to the distinction between primary and secondary forms and the distinction between their various modes, he explains the word "many-branched"— which does not necessarily imply a difference in action— as referring to another point of disparity. He does so with the words "In that case also," demonstrating how even each single [branch] possesses many branches.

Regarding the phrase "from one": for even a single optional rite (*kāmyakarman*), when viewed as delimited by its primary fruit, stands in the place of a single tree; yet, through its various distinct parts delimited by the fruits of non-contradictory subsidiary qualities (*guṇa*), it becomes many-branched. In the scripture on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), however, even the attainment of a full lifespan and so forth [are treated similarly].

It has been stated that [the knowledge of the Self] is included within that single fruit because it serves as a means to liberation through its purposefulness for the performance of spiritual practice (*sādhanānuṣṭhāna*) and so forth.
He concludes with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), intending to establish the stability of the two types of distinction.

This means [the distinction exists] due to the difference between the primary and intermediate fruits. The word "endless" (*anantā*) is used to demonstrate the syntactical connection according to the sequence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
The phrase "having many branches" has been explained by way of inversion.

Now, one might ask: how can there be a single result for obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, which are enjoined as distinct means for achieving different primary and intermediate results?

How much less, then, could there be the status of being the single subject matter of one scripture? And how could there be the performance of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) by one who is free from desire?

If the performance of various optional rites were to occur even in the absence of their respective desired fruits, then it would follow as a logical consequence that a Brāhmaṇa or others might perform the duties of Kṣatriyas and so forth, even in the absence of the specific qualification (*adhikāra*) for them.
The combination of all desired elements is set aside because it contradicts the results and so forth, and it is difficult to carry out.

However, regarding the combination of only a few, he states the purpose of mentioning the unity or plurality of the intellect in order to resolve the doubt as to what the regulating principle (*niyāmaka*) might be for determining which [elements] are to be performed and how many. This is what is meant by the phrase "this has been stated."

The primary and intermediate fruits of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites include the attainment of the state of Prajāpati, the Lakas, and so forth; as well as the destruction of accumulated sins and the avoidance of the sin incurred by failing to perform what is required. Here, both the combined forms of the *nitya* and *naimittika* rites are included under the term "obligatory and occasional" (*nityanaimittaka*).

The word *kāmya* refers exclusively to optional rites performed for specific desires. Now, one might object: "It is improper to say 'having abandoned all those [rites],' because even for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the destruction of previously accumulated sins and so forth is necessarily required. To this it is replied: "Having liberation as the sole fruit.
Since even the destruction of sins and the like are beneficial by way of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are not [to be abandoned].
The sense is that there is a multiplicity of results. [In other cases], they are to be performed as the subject matter of a single scripture;

however, due to differences in application (*viniyoga*), there is a difference in results and a difference in the subject matter of the scriptures. In this case, however, since all [elements] are applied to a single purpose, it is logical that there be unity of result and unity of the scriptural subject matter.

The point is that the principle of "separateness of application" (viniyoga-pṛthaktva) is established even in cases such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is both obligatory and optional. Regarding the phrase "appropriate for the respective castes and stages of life" (sva-varṇāśramocitāni): indeed, certain rites are prescribed for someone with reference to a specific result; yet, even when those very same rites are applied toward a different result, that same person remains the qualified agent (adhikārī).

It must be so; for according to the maxim, "When there is a conflict between what is already established and what is to be assumed, it is proper to accept that which is already established," there is no evidence for assuming a different qualified person (adhikārin). This is the sense: as in the case of the *nitya* and *kāmya* Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices, and as in the case of Vedic study being applied to silent recitation (*japa*) and the like. This was stated in order to demonstrate the possibility of a desireless person performing rites intended for specific desires.

"Having set aside their respective fruits" means by way of being the means to liberation. "Having unified them with the obligatory and occasional rites" means having made them a single scriptural purpose by way of being the means to a single fruit.
"According to one's strength" means that the scripture teaches in accordance with one's capacity.
And Manu has said: "For by performing that [action] even when one is unable [to complete it fully], one attains the supreme goal.

Thus, it has been stated that for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is no fault even if some auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are deficient in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) just as in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. By this, the statement regarding the absence of sin (*pratyavāya*) upon interruption is also not intended to apply exclusively to the interruption of a single instance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* or similar sacrifices.

Furthermore, it has been shown that even when one performs each individual action within the entire collection of rites— which, like the *prayāja* offerings, constitute the single purpose of what is to be performed until liberation— this [text] refers to the non-performance of subsequent rites caused by defects in place and other factors.

Thus, he introduces the following three verses, which censure those qualified for action as a means to liberation, by comparison with the intellect directed toward optional rites (*kāmyakarman*): "Now" (*atha*), etc.
"Those qualified for optional rites" (*kāmyakarmādhikṛtān*).
The meaning of "kāmyeṣu" is those [actions] directed toward desired ends such as heaven, which are characterized by the notion that they are means to one's own self-interest.

With the intention of showing that the term "puṣpitām" (flowering) excludes the fruit and implies that it results in unhappiness, he says "āpātaramaṇīyām" (pleasing at first sight). He says "alpajñāḥ" (those of little knowledge), for it is the state of seeing variously [that is meant].

"Vipaścit" (the wise one): according to the rule *pṛṣodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam*, there is the elision of the syllable *ya* from the word *paśyat*. That [term] signifies "one who possesses great knowledge.

The sense here is that its opposite—being "one who possesses little knowledge"—results from the absence of the discrimination between the permanent and so forth, which is to be accomplished by the Upaniṣads.

In order to dispel the misconception that the phrase beginning with "janmakarma" (birth and action) is a qualification of "gati" (course), and for the sake of supplying what is required by the word "pratītya" (having reached), the expression "vartamānām bhogaiśvaryagatim" (the course toward enjoyment and sovereignty) was placed earlier, even though it violates the [expected] sequence. By this, [the meaning of] the word "vācam" (speech) [is clarified].

It is stated that the intent is focused on the section concerning optional rites (*kāmya-vidhi*). He dispels the misconception that this is a general censure of the Veda by saying, "the declarations of results such as heaven. Here, the word "Veda" refers to the ritual portion (*karma-bhāga*), as in passages such as, "it is sung in the Vedas and in the Upanishads (*vedānta*)."

In that regard as well, the injunctive portion concerns the subject matter of the sections on results, means, and eulogies; alternatively, it concerns the subject matter of human statements and Vedic statements.

The intention is that there is no tautology between the two phrases "speech" (*vācam*) and "proponent of the Veda" (*vedavāda*). Regarding the statement "there is nothing else," he takes the meaning of the preceding and following words as the reason. [This is expressed by] the phrase "apart from its connection."

It was stated with the intention that the negation of the very nature of liberation (*apavarga*) is impossible: "a superior fruit. By the word "proponents" (*vādinaḥ*), there is a manifestation of their habit of speaking in such a manner. This is explained by the present participle ending in *śatṛ* (the suffix *vat*), namely "speaking" (*vadantaḥ*). [The phrase] "whose minds are inclined toward desire" (*kāmapravaṇamanasaḥ*).
"Those whose self is the mind [directed toward] desires" (*kāmeṣv ātmā manaḥ yeṣām te*)—the sense is that this is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound.
"Those for whom heaven is the supreme goal" (*svargaparāyaṇāḥ*): heaven is their "supreme" (*paraḥ*), meaning their ultimate refuge (*parāyaṇam*) or highest attainment;

thus they are "those for whom heaven is supreme" (*svargaparāḥ*). The sense is that they are averse to liberation (*mokṣa*). [They are] those whose selves are desire-driven and for whom heaven is the supreme goal.

Thus, the avoidance of tautology regarding these two words is achieved by taking them as referring respectively to the general and the particular, or to the seen and the unseen, or to the cause and the goal to be accomplished, or alternatively, by taking them as intending the orientation toward desire and the aversion toward anything else. [The text] dispels the delusion of birth and so forth occurring in the midst of the enjoyment of fruits such as heaven.
"Ending with the fruit of heaven and so forth," as it is said: "Having dwelt there as long as their [meritorious] accumulation lasts, they then return again by this very path";
"Having reached the end of that karma which he performs here, from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of karma"; and also: "Even in heaven..."

Scriptural and traditional texts such as "For one who fears falling and is subject to decay, there is no peace" are to be seen here. He demonstrates the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with "birth" in order to show that action, like birth, has as its fruit the remainder of action known as *anuśaya*: "yielding fruits called birth and action."

Regarding the attainment of a superior birth through the remainder of one's karma, the Śruti states: "Frail indeed are these boats in the form of sacrifice, wherein eighteen elements are said to be subordinate; those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good return again and again to old age and death. Furthermore, those here...
Those whose conduct has been pleasant will, it is certain, enter a pleasant womb— either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa,

or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya. But those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is certain, enter a foul womb— either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla.

The passage beginning with "va" and so forth [states this]. Regarding the fact that birth, action, and all else are rooted in the remainder of past karma, there are also Smṛti texts: "Persons belonging to the various castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after death experience the fruit of their own actions; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they are born with distinguished place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence."
They undergo birth; turning away in all directions, those who act contrary [to dharma] perish.

Thus, upon returning from that state, by virtue of the remainder of their karma, they obtain a particular birth, form, caste, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of dharma. This process is like a wheel.

"He dwells in happiness indeed in both worlds," and so forth. Furthermore, this matter should be clearly investigated in the *Vairāgyapāda*. Here, in some manuscripts of the *Kauśika*, the reading is "janmākhyakarmaphalapradām" (bestowing the fruit of karma known as birth). Now, [one might ask: is it not merely the specific nature of ritual acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma?

The seeker of desire (*kāmin*) and the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) are equal [in this regard]; how then is it that the seeker of desire is specifically designated as "abounding in various ritual actions"? To this it is replied: "Because of being devoid of the knowledge of reality.
For even when performing all kinds of action, the man of knowledge acts with an abundance of knowledge.

And because it is the means to a single fruit, it constitutes the subject matter of a single scripture. Furthermore, not all specific ritual acts (kriyāviśeṣa) that are useless for liberation are performed by it; therefore, the sense is that ritual action (karman) is full of exertion and yields only perishable fruits for one who desires liberation (amumukṣu). [This is said] to dispel the delusion of others who think their minds have been stolen away by the words of others.

He states that the two words ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), whose specific qualificands (*viśeṣya*) are not explicitly seen [in the verse], have as their object the qualificands under discussion, by saying "of them" (*teṣām*). By the word "by that" (*tayā*), there is the inclusion of the subject to be explained in the form of a reference back to what has occurred previously.
He states the cause for the captivation of the mind, which is the aforementioned topic, by saying "by that which has sovereignty over its parts as its object" (*bhāgaiśvaryaviṣayayā*).

That which takes up the subject of explanation in the form of a reference back to a preceding verse is here grasped as the relevant topic (*prakṛta*). He states the reason for its removal with the words "by means of the objects of partial sovereignty" (*bhāgaiśvaryaviṣayaiḥ*). This was stated both to avoid the redundancy of meaning with the preceding phrase "of those whose minds are stolen" (*apahṛtacetasām*), and to show that the meaning of that [preceding phrase] serves as the cause for the absence of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by discernment (*vyavasāya*) regarding the relevant topic. Thus, he says "of those whose knowledge is stolen" (*apahṛtajñānānām*).

"Yathoktitaḥ" means in the manner previously described. "Na vidhīyate" means it is not brought about by any cause; from this, the conclusion is stated as "it is not produced. Since the word *samādhi* would lack syntactic connection if intended to mean a specific state of intellect (*buddhiviśeṣa*), he provides its etymological derivation in the sense of being an object of the mind: "It is concentrated (*samādhīyate*) in this," meaning it is deposited (*nidhīyate*) in this, like a treasure (*nidhi*).
He explains the manner stated in the passage beginning with "as has been declared" (*yathoktita*) by means of the verse beginning with "in their minds" (*teṣāṃ manasi*).
The use of the present tense in the word "is enjoined" (*vidhīyate*) is intended to establish that this is an established fact. Regarding the phrase "even at any time" (*kadācid api*), he asks:

for what purpose is there censure of these [people]? He answers: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: because of the contradiction with the intellect characterized by resolute determination (*vyavasāyātmaka-buddhi*).

It is taught that one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) must not form attachments; thus, it is permitted for such a person to perform even optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) while remaining free from attachment.

This is because the mere performance of the action itself does not contradict liberation. What is being stated is that if there is a desire for liberation, one must not entertain a desire for that which binds.

Now, if such acts—as well as those for whom they are intended—are thus censured, then the prescription of such acts by the scripture, which teaches what is most beneficial, would be untenable. Furthermore, the instruction here that what has been prescribed should be abandoned would be a contradiction;
otherwise, there would be either the invalidity of the scriptures prescribing action, or else their validity.

He states that [the author] dispels the doubt—namely, that if that [teaching on rebirth] were authoritative, it would follow that the instruction prohibiting it is unauthoritative—by means of the two subsequent verses, beginning with "In this way, too little... (*evam atyalpa...*).
Those for whom rebirth is the very act of procreation are "those whose procreation is rebirth" (*punarjanmaprasavāni*).

For the assumption of a particular body is like the birthplace [of a tree], because it indicates the necessity of the prior existence of the fruit that is the ripening of karmas—which are like the forest trees of the wilderness of saṃsāra. The taking up of parents is like the mother and father [who provide the physical basis], because they provide the instruction for what is pleasant and beneficial. This is for the purpose of indicating the persistence through all births.

The term "possessing compassion" (*saharuā*) is used because [the Lord] is common to all souls, because He teaches the fourfold aims of human life and the cessation of all that is not an aim along with their means, and because He never ceases [His activity].
This expresses His extreme affection (*vatsalataratva*). These three are the causes for His excellence. Thus, they are engaged in reviving the self.

This is indicated by the three [verses]. For it is not the case that [the sages] are ever engaged merely in [teaching] health and so forth regarding the body and its like; thus, there is the existence of these three in sequence. As for the question "For what purpose do they speak?", it is certainly not for the sake of deception, because they provide instruction on what is beneficial (*hitopadeśitvāt*). Nor is it for the sake of mere enticement that terminates in some other benefit.
Because each individual section culminates merely in its respective specific result,

the Vedas— which consist of the commands of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is supremely compassionate and incapable of having any excellence added to him— teach from beginning to end means for attaining a spark of happiness that is followed by a storm of immeasurable suffering.
It is improper, like an instruction to consume honey mixed with poison; rather, a prohibition alone should be made in that case.

Or perhaps even that [instruction] is not necessary, because perception and other means of knowledge do not occasion such a contingency; for the intention is that a prohibition following one's own [unwarranted] implication is equivalent to washing off mud while still submerged in it. How so?

The sense is that what is contrary to the Vedas should indeed be taught as something to be abandoned, but not that which is enjoined by the Vedas. Regarding the term *traiguṇyam*: since no other meaning is possible here, this is a suffix used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*), according to the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) stating that "for words such as *cāturvarṇya*, the suffix is added in its own primary sense."

Due to the frequent usage of the word "guṇa" (quality), the force of its connection with a specific number, and consideration of what is to be explained hereafter, he points out the specific meaning: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas. For the Vedas indeed have as their subject matter specific fruits such as heaven, specific means, procedures, and specific qualified agents; they do not, however—
Regarding the statement that objects consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are perceived, he says: "Abounding in *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Because of the predominance of these respective qualities, persons are designated by those very terms as a figurative usage (*upacāra*). The definition based on the result mentioned in other commentaries is weak; rather, the point here is that establishing the status of the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*) is what is required. This is the intended meaning.

Thus, there is indeed this separate mention of "those abounding in *tamas*" and so forth, for the purpose of manifesting the diversity of qualified persons regarding the various injunctions and prohibitions concerning individuals in whom the three *guṇas* abound; it serves to demonstrate the greater,
lesser, and least abundance of qualified persons in the *Sāma-veda* and the other [Vedas].
Here, the sequence of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is presented in a non-standard order.
Consequently, they are observed respectively in those who desire worldly success, those who desire success in the hereafter, and those who desire the supreme goal (*apavarga*).
The phrase "of those in whom *sattva* predominates" is intended as an illustration. For this very reason, in the explanatory portion of the text, it says, "If for these... and so forth.
The mention of those "abounding in rajas and tamas" is intended to include all [types of people]. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with their own qualities":

it is just as physicians who provide beneficial instruction, having observed persons of pure, balanced, or mixed constitutions (*prakṛti*) caused by wind, bile, and phlegm, prescribe diets and medicines suited to each respective constitution.
They prescribe wholesome foods and the like, and prohibit unwholesome ones; and in their absence,
just as living beings with minds deluded by false teachings perish through the consumption of unwholesome food, poisons, and so forth,
and just as sons seeking betel leaves and such are [restrained] by their fathers and others from obtaining them—

The sense is that they perish through theft and other such means, just as it happens here [in this world]. Aversion to liberation and the lack of knowledge regarding the means to achieve the fruit one desires are the functions of *tamas*. However, the inclination toward desire and so forth are the functions of *rajas* and *tamas* according to their respective proportions; for people are rendered helpless by the inclination toward desire.
Being powerless to restrain themselves due to the force of their attachment to the fruits of desire, they [act] toward things that should not be acquired, and so forth;

this should be understood as being like those who are bound and so on. "They would be utterly destroyed" means that through the ripening of evil karma, even by resorting to the state of stationary beings (sthāvara) and the like, they become as if insentient.
The meaning is that they would be devoid even of the mere scent of fitness for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
"Therefore" means because the instruction regarding optional rites (*kāmya*) is the most beneficial in the manner described.
By the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "you, however," he indicates a difference between this qualified person and others. What is this difference in qualification?

And how is there a negation of the three *guṇas* for one who is still transmigrating? If that were so, there would be a contradiction with the statement "established in the eternal reality. To this he says: "Now, [he is] abounding in *sattva*. This was said with reference to such statements as "I am your disciple" (*śiṣyas te 'ham*). It is understood from the intended meaning of the address "O Arjuna."

Its distinction lies in the abundance of *sattva*. Since the word *arjuna* is a synonym for "white," and since *sattva* is also designated by the word "white," and because a disparity among qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) must be accounted for, as well as due to the force of such established usage and other factors, this alone is the intended meaning here. Therefore, "make that very [quality] increase."

The meaning is not that you should increase *rajas* and *tamas* by failing to perform prescribed duties and performing prohibited ones, while abandoning the established abundance of *sattva*. To the question— "Since the injunction 'be free from the three qualities' applies equally to all three qualities, how can it be said to increase *sattva*?"— the author replies:

Regarding the phrase "not mutually": it is true that the negation applies equally to all three *guṇas*, yet its scope is restricted to their mixed states; otherwise, the statement to be made later—"steadfast in *sattva* alone"—would be untenable. To the objection that this [negation] appears to be in the form of a benediction, he replies: "Not that. This means one should abandon food and other things that cause an abundance of *rajas* and *tamas*.

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). By this, it is intended either the nature of the fruit itself, or the well-being existing at the time of practicing the means, or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of the endurance of dualities. Regarding the phrase "devoid of the two qualities":
the meaning is that the term "constantly established in *sattva*" contains an implication of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), similar to [the expressions] "subsisting on water" and so forth.
Alternatively, by the word "eternal" (nitya), what is intended here is that it is never overwhelmed by other qualities;
for this very reason, there is "constant increase. The sense is that if it were overwhelmed by other qualities, there would be no eternal increase.
Furthermore, the injunction to "increase the abundance of *sattva*" would not be tenable; for this [quality] is not *rajas*.

One proceeds with the thought, "This is darkness; this I shall increase"; yet from what would one be restrained, and from what, once rajas and tamas are established, would one pacify them? Nor does such a person know sattva and its means, by which he might proceed therein. Therefore, with the intention of asking, "What then should he do, and how? [the author says:]...

He raises an objection: "How so? To that, he explains the two phrases—"free from acquisition and preservation" (*niryogakṣema*) and "possessed of the Self" (*ātmavān*)—in their respective order as providing the basis for both the prohibition and the injunction, beginning with the words "the nature of the Self," etc.
The general prohibition expressed by "free from acquisition and preservation" refers to objects other than those prescribed for one seeking liberation.

This was stated up to the words "of those things external [to oneself]" for the sake of making this known. Regarding the phrase "be possessed of self" (*ātmavān bhava*), having raised the objection that the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is untenable, [the author] says: "intent upon the investigation of the nature of the Self.
This refers to a relationship based on the expectation of attainment through a particular state of one's own intellect, which contains within it heedfulness (*apramattatā*).

This is the condition (*pratyaya*). Or rather, the sense is that one attains the Self only through the very search for its true nature; otherwise, there would be a loss of the Self. Thus, the object for the performance of both prohibition and injunction has been stated. To the question "What follows from this?", he states the two results dependent upon those two [prohibition and injunction] with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
The sense is that you have no direct duty to take the qualities as your object; rather,

because they are devoid of acquisition and preservation (niryogakṣematva), their destruction and manifestation will occur spontaneously and appropriately through the abandonment of non-sattvic food and other such causes.
Now, demonstrating the distinction between those who possess the capacity for perception, he explains the verse beginning with "yāvān arthaḥ" (as much as the purpose). He says, "na ca" (and not).

The sense is that the duties (*dharma*) proclaimed in the Vedas have subjects with restricted capacities according to distinctions such as caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), lineage (*pravara*), and school (*caraṇa*).
The phrase "parikalpita for the sake of all purposes" means it is conceived for the sake of all eligible persons who desire various specific goals.

And this has been stated as established by the meaning of the phrase "in water that has flooded from all sides. "Udapāna" refers to a well, a pond, and so forth. The term "of one who is thirsty" (*pipāsor*) is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) in accordance with the context of the illustrative application (*dāṣṭāntika*).
Now, what is the connection here between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the illustrative application? For [the thirst of] one who is thirsty is not [satisfied] by a well...
In order to dispel the doubt that "one who knows only as much as is necessary [knows] all the Vedas," the sentence is completed by supplying the words:
"only that much is taken up by him," and so forth.
Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "in all [the Vedas]" (*sarveṣu ca*) is intended to indicate the synthesis of both the portions to be adopted and those to be rejected.

[Objection: But surely this [instruction] is inconsistent with the context of the Brāhmaṇa, for it is taught specifically for the Kṣatriya. And what is the distinction here for the Brāhmaṇa, since the knowledge of Brahman is common to all three social classes?
Furthermore, the phrase "one who knows" is inappropriate; for it is precisely one who already knows who proceeds even toward the entitlements regarding desires and so forth.

Furthermore, the word *brāhmaṇa* here does not [refer to the caste]; for when the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied according to the rule *tad adhīte*, and the suffix *aṇ* is added because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group, the form *brāhmaṇa* arises. Here, *brāhma* refers to the Veda, since the context is restricted to the Vedas.
Therefore, the word *brāhmaṇa* here refers exclusively to those who know the Veda; thus, there is no inconsistency in its teaching being intended for Kṣatriyas.
In this context, the word *brāhma* refers to the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*). Śaṅkara’s interpretation, however, is extremely weak;

for the scriptural passage, "Having fully understood both non-mauna and mauna, then one becomes a *brāhmaṇa*," describes a particular state of excellence in the sattva of a yogin. This is also evident from the phrase "of one who knows" (*vijānataḥ*).

The state of possessing distinguished knowledge is being described. And "distinguished" means having as its object the discernment between what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be adopted (*upādeya*). Furthermore, one who possesses such knowledge must be precisely the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). He states what is excluded by the phrase "only that much" with the words "nothing else. Even that which is proclaimed in the Veda is not to be adopted if it is distinct from the means to liberation, because [the seeker] lacks the qualification for it.
The sense is that the dharma of those desiring various fruits—such as gold, the castes, or the stages of life—is not to be adopted by another.

If that were so, then by abandoning everything other than the means to liberation and by transgressing the scriptures concerning obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and prohibited (niṣedha) duties, there would be the fault of acting according to one's own whims (kāmacāra). Anticipating the doubt as to how much [of this] is being stated, he introduces the following verse with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

The sense is that there is no fault of acting according to one's own will (*kāmacāra*), because by relinquishing each respective fruit, only the common essential nature (*svarūpa*) is to be accepted. Regarding the word "in action" (*karmaṇi*), which is a general term, he states the specific instances appropriate to it with the words "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth.
The phrase "by someone" (*kenacit*) and so on is connected to all three categories as well.

Thus, the view of those of false vision—who desire that obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites have as their sole purpose the production of a transcendental merit (*apūrva*)—has been refuted. Regarding the qualification for other ritual acts: the fruit of the obligatory and other rites, as the case may be, consists of the destruction of previously acquired sins, the avoidance of the transgression caused by non-performance, and [the attainment of] rewards such as the *prājāpatya* penance, cattle, sons, and so forth. As for the phrase "as a qualification of the fruit":

just as through originative injunctions (*utpatti-vākya*), rites are produced in their own essential forms, so too [is their connection to specific fruits established] within the context of a particular qualification.
Because it is heard in scripture as being connected with specific fruits such as heaven and the like, heaven and so forth are accepted as the fruit;

likewise, in the context of liberation (mokṣa) as well, since it is heard as being connected with the specific fruit called liberation, that too is the fruit—this is the intended meaning. He states the purport regarding the connection of the word "those" (te) with the subject under discussion:
Regarding the phrase "for the seeker of liberation who is ever-established in *sattva*": this refers to the injunction concerning liberation and its means;

however, it is said that [the scripture] indicates merely the non-existence [of agency], for it is stated that [agency] never exists [in the Self]. By negating fitness for the fruit, the negation of association with that [agency] is also established. This applies both to the eligibility for action in general and to the lack of eligibility for its fruits.

He states two reasons according to the Buddhist method: "of that which possesses a fruit. For one who desires liberation, a longing for a fruit in the form of bondage is not logical; nor is the abandonment of its cause appropriate—this is the sense. Furthermore, the term "of the isolated" (*kevalasya*) does not refer merely to the absence of a fruit, because it has already been stated [that it is] "devoid of fruit" (*phalahitasya*). Moreover...
In that case, the meaning is that [the action] is a purpose (*prayojana*) by its very nature. Regarding this, [the author] says: "consisting of the propitiation of Me.

As for the phrase "of the action and its fruit," although a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) might suggest a tautology, a *dvandva* compound in which both members are primary is more appropriate; furthermore, it is logical here to include the contemplation of non-agency (*akartṛtva*) which will be explained later—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the objection that this negation of being the cause [of action] would contradict the preceding and following statements—"Your right is to action alone" and "Let there be no attachment to inaction"—the author says: "By you.
Here, it is not the actual state of being a cause that is negated; rather, the meaning is that the *contemplation* of being a cause is what is negated.
Is it not the case that the negation of the causality of the fruit is redundant, since it has already been stated [in the verse], "Let there never be [attachment] to fruits"? If, however,
this is a negation of fruits such as the cessation of hunger accomplished by eating and so forth, then, because attachment to the means would also cease,
there would follow the non-existence of even the maintenance of the body and so on, which implies the very abandonment of the performance of the means.

To the objection that there would be an omission [of the result], he says: "Of the result as well. By the phrase "such as the cessation of hunger," the charge of tautology is avoided. One should reflect that "you are not the cause"; the point is that it is not the nature of the cessation of hunger and so forth that is being denied here, but rather the reflection that the Self is not its cause. Now, how can this be so regarding action and its fruit?

Is it being connected [to the argument] that "being itself the cause, it is not the cause"? And in this way, like the Cārvākas and others, one would have to conclude that these two are causeless; consequently, the very practice of the means (upāya) would be abandoned, because effort is inappropriate when something is understood to be causeless. To this, he says: "Both of those..."

"Both" refers to being the cause of action (*karma*) and being the cause of the fruit (*phala*). "In the subsequent [chapter]" means that this indeed is the primary subject matter of the third chapter. For it is said: "The performance of action in the third chapter is taught by means of non-attachment for the sake of protecting the world, having attributed agency to the qualities (*guṇas*) or having entrusted it to the Lord of All. In this way, the objection regarding the lack of a cause has first been refuted.

If it is argued that even so, because the investigation into the self as the cause [of agency] is negated, the consequence of non-performance remains exactly as it was—do not say so. For here, it is not said that there is an illusion regarding performance due to its being a non-performer, which would lead to a contradiction; rather, [it is said] regarding something that has multiple causes, that [the agent] is merely one of them.
