The meaning of the sentence is that the perfection of the yoga of knowledge may occur. However, what is intended later—that the perfection of the yoga of knowledge results precisely from not abandoning the yoga of action—is incorrect;
for the point is that it (the perfection) is produced by that [yoga of action] alone. Thus, regarding both of these...
Intending the syntactical function (*vākyavṛtti*), he states the intended meaning of the verse with the words "without being aimed at" (*anabhisaṃhitā*).

The word "by actions" (*karmabhiḥ*) is to be construed with the phrase "not propitiated" (*anārādhita*). By this, [the author] recalls such passages as: "Those men who have not propitiated Govinda are partakers of suffering."

In the absence of action whose fruit is not intended, there would be an absence of the pleasure of the Supreme Person, which is the means to the highest good; and due to that absence, there would be no cessation of the accumulation of sin; and because of that, there would be no removal of the impurities of the mind consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*;
and consequently, there would be a long persistence of defects such as passion and hatred, while those [defects] remain alive.
There is no pacification of the agitation of the senses, nor the pacification of the agitation toward external objects;

and since there is no abiding in the goal among those who are agitated by external objects, one desiring to practice the steadfastness in knowledge through the renunciation of such actions [ascends] to the seventh floor of the seven-storied gate-tower.
The sense is that it would be laughable to claim that one first desires to act [only after having already acted].
Introducing the intermediate verse while dispelling the doubt regarding the lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), he says: "This very [is the reason].

The meaning is that if one abandons action in the form of worship of the Supreme Person, the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) is indeed difficult to achieve. The first particle *hi* indicates the justification for the meaning of the preceding verse.

The second [verse] is intended to provide a proof for what was stated in the first half of this verse. Furthermore, the diversity of eligible persons (*adhikārin*) mentioned at the beginning of the treatise by the phrase "in this world" (*asmin loke*) is also intended here; this is indicated by the words "some" (*kaścit*) and "all" (*sarvaḥ*). To make this known, it is said: "in this world."

The word *jātu* refers to gross durations such as days and so forth; however, since the word *kṣaṇa*— according to the reading in the *Nānārthasaṃgraha*— "denotes the absence of activity, a division of time, and a short duration"— refers here to the short duration included within that [gross time], there is no tautology.

By the phrase "even at any time," both [the states of waking and dreaming] are included; the meaning is: at all times, with the exception of the state of dissolution (*pralaya*). For even for one who is sleeping, there exists the action known as sleep.
It is precisely for this reason that injunctions and prohibitions occur therein according to the restrictions of place, time, and so forth.

In the phrase "one who does not perform action" (*akarmakṛt*), it is not intended that the agent of non-action is meant; rather, it is said to clarify that he is one who does not perform action—that is, one who does not perform any work. He states what is intended by the word "all": "even though resolved that 'I do nothing at all. And this meaning [is supported by the passage]: "the organs of action..."
This will become clear in the subsequent verse through the qualification "born of *prakṛti*.

From the specific mention of "by means of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*," the particularity [of their nature] is obtained. To the question, "How can there be birth from *prakṛti* for those that are eternally present in *prakṛti*? it is said: "By former... and so forth. And thus they say:
"O Lord of the Earth, these qualities, beginning with *sattva*, are subject to karma.
By this, there is an exclusion of the state of being established in knowledge where the qualities have been attenuated through the application of karma.
By the word "appropriate to oneself," the method that will be described in the third hexad is indicated.

The word *sva* here refers to the quality (*guṇa*). The phrase "all [beings] being helpless" (*avaśaḥ sarvaḥ*) is stated to dispel the misconception that this is a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*). To clarify that they are made helpless by the action [of the quality], it is said "they are made helpless" (*avaśaḥ kāryate*). To exclude the interpretation of the verb *kāryate* as referring to the object of the instigator (*prayojyakarma*), and to manifest its reference to the agent who is instigated (*prayojyakartṛ*), it is said "they are impelled" (*pravartyate*).
He states the purport of the two explained verses with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means:
because the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is difficult to accomplish without the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) due to its dependence upon the *guṇas*;
and because the subjugation of the *guṇas* results from the destruction of sin.

And that [purity] consists in being conducive to the engagement for the sake of liberation; or it is the cessation of the abundance of *rajas* and *tamas*, or the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth, which are their effects. It is this stainlessness (*nirmalatva*) that is intended here.
He states that [the Lord] speaks of the obstacle to non-performance with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means without performing the yoga of action.

With the phrase "remembering in the mind," he states the reason which is established by implication: "whose mind is not destroyed. In the expression "one whose self is deluded" (*vimūḍhātmā*), the word *ātman* refers to the mind.

The object of the mind is delusion, which is turning away from the Self. The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is "those very [objects] from which the senses are intended to be restrained. He describes the manner of improper conduct with the words "having resolved otherwise"; for in the end, it is precisely this state of being otherwise [than what is intended].

There is falsity everywhere. Here too, because his conduct is contrary to the yoga of knowledge as it was intended, it is stated that the conduct of one who merely considers himself to possess knowledge and yoga is false. This is said by way of excluding those who are merely actors in the name of false conduct.

To bring the discussion of the defects to a conclusion, he says: by the words "soul" (*ātman*) and "perverse" (*viparīta*) as well as "destroyed" (*vinaṣṭa*), it is shown that there is hostility toward the means [of liberation].

This very same point was demonstrated in the second chapter, beginning with "one who meditates on sense-objects" (*adhyāyato viṣayān*) and ending with "through the destruction of the intellect, one perishes" (*buddhināśāt praṇaśyati*).
"It has been elaborated" means it was brought to mind by the word "destroyed.

Having set aside the one who desires to ascend the path of the yoga of knowledge at the very outset, [the Lord] praises the practitioner of the yoga of action with the verse beginning "But he... He explains this while connecting it to the present subject matter.

Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): because the complete restraint of the senses and the undertaking of *karmayoga* are mutually contradictory, it was stated—namely, "in scriptural action"—for the sake of establishing their non-contradiction. For the reason that was stated [in the verse beginning] with "Indeed, no one," regarding the difficulty of the path of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), [is now addressed].

This was stated— namely, "in an object of a similar class to that previously practiced"— for the purpose of demonstrating the ease [of practice] by way of its being an auxiliary to the yoga of action itself. If previous practice is accepted as an auxiliary, then it would be impossible to restrain oneself from prohibited actions.

This was stated both to dispel the doubt that the abundance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resides in those very [objects] and to ensure that karma does not result in other fruits; for it is said, "proceeding by means of the vision of the Self," because there is the determination that prohibited acts are contrary to the vision of the Self.
The sense is that even a firm latent impression (*vāsanā*) among those [objects] is set aside.

By the phrase "by the organs of action" (*karmendriyaiḥ*), he demonstrates the ease [of this process], [explaining] that it occurs "by the senses which are naturally inclined toward action. This refers to the context (*prasaṅga*).
Because the term "non-attachment" (*asakta*) requires an initiation into the yoga of action, he states its connection with a portion of the preceding sentence:

"preceded by non-attachment. He thereby shows the manner of qualification and the limit of that distinction, [implying] even compared to one established in knowledge (*jñānistha*), on the grounds that negligence is impossible for the former.

Now, demonstrating that karma-yoga alone is superior on the grounds such as its ease, freedom from negligence, and difficulty of abandonment, he provides the direct answer to the verse beginning with "If [renunciation] is superior to action... He does so even though the word *niyata* (constant) has a minor purpose when taken as an adverbial modifier of the action.

It is indeed appropriate that [the word] functions as a qualifier of the object (*karman*) which stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the abundant purpose (*prabhūtaprayojana*). Consequently, the necessity (*niyatatva*) of the two objects would arise either by their own nature, or by the authority of the scripture, or from both; in that case, the assumption of an intention to express both in a single instance is certainly more cumbersome.
However, in the phrase "for the maintenance of the body" (*śarīrayātrā*), the intention will be explained as referring to the rules regarding the performance of scriptural duties;
therefore, in this context, what is intended is that which is determined by its own nature.
Since the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) has been presented as difficult to achieve, the ease of the steadfastness in action (*karmaniṣṭhā*) [is now shown].
Intending all of this—that it is appropriate to speak immediately after [the previous point]—he says:
"Niyataṃ vyāptam" (It is restricted and pervaded), and so forth. To the question, "By what means, and on what basis, is there pervasion? he replies:
"By that which is conjoined with *prakṛti*. Regarding the word "akarmaṇaḥ" (of non-action), the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of "other than that" (*tadanya*).

And the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī*) indicates that its object is the limit (*avadhi*). Regarding the phrase "even for one established in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhāya api*), how is it that the word "non-action" (*akarma*) here has the state of being established in knowledge as its referent?
For in the verse, "Let there be no attachment of yours to non-action" (*mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi*), it is indeed [that which is meant].

Thus, it has been explained as having the non-existence of action as its object; likewise, here too, since the abandonment of performance might occur, it is appropriate to say that "performance alone is superior"—to this he says: "Renunciation" (*naiṣkarmyam*). Here, at the outset, the relative gradation between *karmayoga* and *jñānayoga* was inquired about; of that very [gradation]...

Furthermore, the answer intended here is that it is improper to define *naiṣkarmya*—which is specified as something to be accomplished by one seeking liberation—as the mere absence of action, which is easily obtained even in deep sleep and other states;
for this would result in the fallacy of the means being indistinguishable from the end, as expressed in the statement: "From the non-commencement of action comes *naiṣkarmya*."

Therefore, the meaning is that here it is *jñānaniṣṭhā* (devotion to knowledge) alone that is designated by the word "action. He states another reason for the superiority of *jñānaniṣṭhā*, which will be explained later, beginning with the words "And while action is being performed," etc.; by the use of the term "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram eva*), he indicates its proximity.

His intended meaning here is shown; he states the underlying purpose for the practice of *karmayoga* even for one capable of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) with the words "from action" (*karmaṇaḥ*) and "from the steadfastness in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhāyāḥ*), where the ablative case denotes that which is the counter-correlative of what has not been previously engaged in.
The sense is that the statement regarding "being greater" (jyāyastva) is improper; he states the introduction to the second half [of the verse] with the words "yadi" (if).

Here, however, the term "akarmaṇaḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as indicated by its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "te" (those). This is what is intended to be made manifest.
It was stated [previously] that this applies to one who is established in knowledge and is inactive.

Now, if even the maintenance of the body were impossible for one who has renounced all actions, then liberation would be obtained effortlessly by such a person— once the means have been acquired— simply through the natural cessation of obstacles.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "As long as...

For the attainment of the fruit does not result merely from entering into the practice of the means (*sādhana*), but rather only from the complete perfection of those means. And that perfection is not obtainable in three or four days, such that we might neglect the body.

Furthermore, since the completion of the means of accomplishment requires a long period of time, the body must necessarily be preserved for that duration; the sense is that because one who has not yet perfected the method remains indifferent [to the goal], there would even be a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if the body were abandoned. Let it be granted, then, that the maintenance of the body is required.

Nevertheless, that [liberation] cannot be brought about for a long duration by one's own will, nor does it cease through mere indifference, because the body has a fixed lifespan determined by the specific karma that initiated it; and they [the authorities] record that for those engaged in ritual action, [results] are strictly determined.

Whether it be marriage, birth, death, or even the voluntary assumption of a body, all such things can easily be accomplished through mere worldly activity alone; to this he replies with the words "acquired by righteous means" (*nyāyārjita*), the intended meaning of which is as follows:
The fruits of karma are of two kinds: determinate and indeterminate.

Those resulting from powerful curses and the like are determinate; others are indeterminate. Their indeterminacy, moreover, depends upon factors such as place and time, but not upon their essential nature.
If that were so, it would follow that actions are fruitless;
consequently, those [karmas] which are indeterminate (*aniyata*) in this regard would fall within the scope of their own respective operations—
namely, those concerning which there exist penances, mantras, medicinal herbs, legal treatises, and so forth.
Otherwise, even those desiring victory and facing obstacles would not accept the fourfold army and so forth; and even the sick would not consume medicine.

If there were no performance of any action by one's own will, there would be an absence of natural agency, and consequently, even the scripture (*śāstra*) would not arise. Therefore, the sense is that by you, who desire to ascend the path of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), the very subjection of the world to karma has been overturned; thus, liberation, which is perfectly accomplished without effort, has been established.
Thus, by the word "only" (*eva*), it is indicated that in the absence of maintaining the body, there is an inherent state of disintegration;

the word "body" (*śarīra*) [is used here]. By the particle "only," it is shown that the rules regarding righteous acquisition and eating what remains after sacrifices are indeed restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*). And such is the maintenance of the body.

Even in the state of bhaktiyoga, which is to be accomplished through jñānayoga, the mention of the scriptural passage on the purification of the heart is intended to show that [the purity] is uninterrupted; furthermore, it is stated that this will be explained later in order to make known that the meaning of the scripture is intended here as well.
He states the reasons previously established: "But those [sins], O Aghamarṣaṇa... and so forth.
Explaining according to the Buddhist method, he sets forth the entire meaning— both the intentional (*ābhiprāyika*) and the literal (*śābda*)—
in summary for the sake of easy comprehension. For this reason,
even for one who is fit for steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*), the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is superior.

Therefore, the intention of the word "you" (*tvam*) is that you should practice the yoga of knowledge alone. To make it known that the verse beginning with "yajñārthāt" establishes the scope for both the injunctions and prohibitions regarding action, he raises an objection: "If that is so... [and] "in the case of the acquisition of material goods, etc. (*dravyārjanādeḥ*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and so forth are included. However, in the phrase "from egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*) etc.," because it mentions passion (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*), the taking up of objects (*ādāna*) and moving about (*viharaṇa*) and so forth are included.
Furthermore, there is the statement that egoism, possessiveness, and the like are specific modifications of the mind (*manovṛtti-viśeṣa*) and consist of the agitation of the senses (*indriya*).

"Of this person" means even of one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*); "by the latent impression of karma" means by that which is ancient, uninterrupted, and augmented by the practice of present activities;
"there will be bondage" means through successive bodily bonds and so forth.
The meaning is that there would be the consequence of the continued persistence of saṃsāra.
Here, based on the Vedic revelation "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu," others have explained that sacrifice is the Lord (Īśvara); and that is not contradictory for us.
Nevertheless,
with the intention that it is appropriate to maintain the same meaning as the word "sacrifice" (yajña) recited at the beginning of the immediately preceding verse, he says:
"by the scriptural term for action such as sacrifice," [referring] to the relationship between the indicator (upalakṣaṇa) and the indicated (upalakṣya).

He shows the general form of inclusion, its purpose and function, and its faultless causality: "from that which has sacrifice as its purpose" (*yajñārthāt*), meaning from that which has sacrifice as its motive (*yajñaprayojanāt*). This is what is demonstrated.
[The phrase] "because it is the remainder" (*śeṣabhūtatvāt*) means that action itself is the bondage, or he whose bondage is by means of actions.

The bondage of action for him consists in its binding nature through the medium of one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not by way of being sinful; for here, the term "bondage of action" refers to actions that are neither enjoined nor prohibited.
This meaning is established by the passage expressing the doubt: "This person will experience bondage through the latent impression of action."
The world consisting of the multitude of transmigrating beings has been shown here as "prior" (prāk);
the meaning is that there is no cause for bondage through action performed for the sake of sacrifice.
This is stated for the purpose of encouraging battle, which serves as a means for obtaining wealth and other such things.

It has been stated that "the acquisition of wealth and so forth" [is required]; however, both [this] and "the renunciation of attachment" (*saṅgatyāga*) are to be enjoined. To make this known, they are formulated as separate sentences.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that the nature of the renunciation of attachment is distinct from the renunciation of agency and its fruits.

Regarding that: if it is argued that even a fool does not engage in any activity without aiming at some purpose, that is true; however, even in the absence of a cognition of it being a means to a purpose, [one engages] by its very nature as a form of worshiping the Blessed One, like the service rendered to a friend.

The occurrence of activity is established by the cognition that [the action] serves a purpose. In the phrase "one who is free from attachment" (*muktasaṅga*), since attachment is intended to mean the cause of bondage, it is stated that he is "free from attachment.
Stating the resolution of the present objection—that [action] yields fruit through the medium of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)—he explains that which is not for that purpose...
By stating that [the knowledge of the Self] is the cause of bondage, he demonstrates the manner in which its object becomes the cause of liberation.

With the word "thus" (*evam*), he refutes the view of the wicked who hold that actions yield results through an *apūrva* (unseen potency) not supported by scripture; rather, [actions yield results] solely through the propitiation of deities as required by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Since the production of the fruit is logically established, there is no need to abandon scriptural statements such as "He, being pleased, pleases him," nor to imagine what is not stated in scripture. By the phrase "propitiated by rituals," the acceptance of the oblation and the resulting pleasure are intended; thus, [the Lord is] the Supreme Person.

The demonstration of the fivefold attributes, beginning with the physical form, consists of: (1) the possession of a specific form established by scriptural texts such as "having the color of the sun," which are invariably concomitant with Him;
(2) the power to be present simultaneously throughout the entire cosmic egg; and (3) the granting of boons, meaning the act of bestowing them.
This is the presentation of the fivefold attributes, starting with the physical form.

By stating "having cut off the latent impressions of karma" (*karmavāsanāmucchidya*), the objection regarding contrary impressions is refuted. He says that [the Lord] confirms the two points previously stated— beginning with "along with sacrifices" (*yajñaiḥ*) and ending with "he lives in vain, O Pārtha" (*moghaṃ pārtha sa jīvati*)— by means of censure, praise, and so forth, [concluding] with "only by the remnant of sacrifice" (*yajñaśiṣṭenaiva*).
By the phrase "the culmination of all means for achieving the goals of human life," the result of the general designation "having created the subjects" is stated here. In this context,
he says "the Lord of the universe" in order to exclude the possibility that the word *prajāpati* refers to Hiraṇyagarbha or others.
The meaning is that [the Lord is the cause] even of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, but not as one who is delimited by the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) and so forth like Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest.
For this very reason it was said: "He is without limiting adjuncts" (nirupādhika). Furthermore, He is [the cause] even by virtue of the very nature of the meaning of the Śruti.

The mention of the qualifiers "the Lord of All" and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that He is the Lord of all beings. The intention is that this entire universe is indeed taught in the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* and other texts as being denotable by the word "Nārāyaṇa" alone.

And the Lord Parāśara, having combined the Lord's status as the Master of the World with his role as the destroyer of all demons and so forth, stated: "In the Kali age, Prajāpati, desiring to effect the deliverance [of the world] through scriptural authority, [worships] Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, the Master who destroys all demons."
And thus, the term *prajāpati* was applied to the Blessed One in his form as a boar in accordance with such scriptural passages as "Prajāpati," etc.; furthermore,
there is the injunction (*niyoga*) of one who is independent toward those who are dependent on their actions.

In this context, regarding the phrase "having created the *prajā*s," the word *prajā* includes all living beings down to the Brahmins who exist within the world, who are subject to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) produced by karma, and who are entitled to perform sacrifices and other rites; therefore,
here the term *Prajāpati* [is used].
In accordance with the word *prajā* occurring at the beginning of the passage, and because it would be improper for that term to undergo such a contraction [of meaning],

the word *prajā*— abandoning its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*)— denotes Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of All, the Controller who is not subject to karma; likewise, the word *prajā* refers without limitation to all the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) who are to be created.

Because the word "pure" (in the verse) denotes the time subsequent to dissolution, it follows that [the passage refers to Brahman]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"; "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; and "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode."
"Verily, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed—neither Brahmā nor Īśāna.
Beginning thus, [it continues]: "Therein Brahmā, the four-faced one, was born; from his mind, the three-eyed, trident-bearing Puruṣa was born."
In such passages as these, since Hiraṇyagarbha and others are understood to be among the progeny,
and Nārāyaṇa is understood to be their progenitor,
the term "having created progeny" is used without restriction to refer to the entire universe.
"Rudra is indeed Nārāyaṇa; he alone is Prajāpati here.
Furthermore: "From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born; the wise one, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, remains speaking them."

Although it is stated that He created all beings along with sacrifices for the sake of their protection, the Supreme Person—who is characterized by having a thousand heads and so forth—is Himself the protector of even the authorized person;
therefore, [it is said]: "Having created beings together with sacrifices... (Gītā 3.10).

Prajāpati, the creator of the universe, has been pointed out; he alone is the creator of the universe in that manner, because of the force of such statements as, "Therefore, having entered you, O Prajāpati, I shall create," and so forth, [it is shown] that he is also the creator of the universe through the mouth of the Prajāpati named Hiraṇyagarbha.

"He who is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"—thus is He heard in scripture as the Self of the universe. Furthermore, the meditation on the gods and so forth mentioned here refers only to those whose nature is that of the Supreme Self, as it is said: "For I [am the enjoyer] of all sacrifices..."
This and so forth is indicated by the two qualifying epithets "the eight-spoked wheel of the universe" and "the Self of the universe.

For this reason as well, he declares that very same one to be the supreme goal; likewise, in the passage "I enter the assembly hall and the abode of Prajāpati," even though he is designated by the word "Prajāpati," he is the supreme attainment.

That it is the Supreme Self alone was established in the sūtra, "And there is no intention toward the effect"; for this reason as well, he describes that very one as the supreme resort (parāyaṇa). Thus, by means of qualifiers such as "the Lord of all," the evidence for that [Supreme Self] has been indicated.

In this way, the scriptural mention of the word *prajāpati*— referring to Śyāma, Ekārūpa, Saptadaśa, Āyātayāman, Ājyadevatā, and Viṣṇu— is also to be considered; for by excluding the perception of a syntactical connection with the word *puraḥ*, it declares its connection with the creation that is beyond the scope of Brahmā and the other [deities].

"Formerly, at the time of creation"— by this he intends the well-known manner in which [the process] is described in the context of cosmogony within the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts. "That Blessed One"—
by the word *bhagavat*, [he indicates] that which is endowed with the fivefold functions such as creation, and from which all things to be abandoned have departed.
The state of being distinguished by qualities that are the opposite of those [of the world] has been shown;
likewise, in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, after describing the dissolution with the words, "In the beginning, this was darkness," it says,
"Then the Blessed One himself appeared," using the term "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*).
Immediately after describing all the forms (*rūpa*), [it says]:
"Because he was first created from that, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa; the person (*puruṣa*) emitted by him is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
Thus, the form of the Prajāpati named Hiraṇyagarbha is described.

It has been stated here that "Nārāyaṇa" was spoken; however, the reference as "Prajāpati said" by means of a third-person designation should be understood as a figurative expression of difference from himself—who is actually the charioteer—as he is designated by the word "Prajāpati. This should be understood in the same way everywhere in what follows.
In cases where the direction [of the breath] is not specified, one should infer it as appropriate.
Since it is observed everywhere that creation is preceded by dissolution, intending to express the same here as well,
he states the purpose of dissolution and the cause of creation, beginning with the word "beginningless" (*anādi*).

The withdrawal [of the world] is for the sake of providing rest to those exhausted by the fatigue of incessantly experiencing pleasure and pain, and for the sake of severing the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that lead to wandering tirelessly on the path of saṃsāra.
Therefore, there is no fault of cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) in this withdrawal, nor in the bestowing of such experiences of pleasure and pain.

The cause is indeed the contact with insentience (*acit*), which is rooted in the beginningless stream of karma and dependent upon the sovereignty of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is itself established by the eternal volition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Therefore, even in that case, there is no question of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) or cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*).

This has been set forth in the Sūtras: "Partiality and cruelty do not [apply to the Lord], because He is dependent on [other factors]; for thus [the scriptures] show," and "But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the soul], so as to avoid rendering the injunctions and prohibitions meaningless, etc.
[Brahma-sūtra 2.1.34–35]. Furthermore, those whose distinctions of name and form were withdrawn into Himself...
The designation "dissolved" (*pralīnāḥ*) and the designation of oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth have been established.

Anticipating the objection that the abandonment of name and form and dissolution into oneself might constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) similar to liberation (*mokṣa*), he says: "all" (*sakala*); [thus they are] unworthy even of the category of the transmigratory world (*saṃsāra*).
What, then, is liberation? This is the sense. Regarding that, he states the reason: "They are like the conscious and the non-conscious.

Even though [the self] is self-luminous, it is "like" that [unconscious state] due to the extreme contraction of knowledge; it is not because of the destruction of knowledge. "Subjects" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha and others.

"Having thoroughly observed" means having looked upon [him] correctly; by this, [it refers to the Lord] whose specific qualities are established by such scriptural passages as, "For Madhusūdana beholds the person being born," and "If you do not look upon him," as well as by Smṛti texts such as, "You are indeed supremely compassionate."

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*): by the term "supremely compassionate" (*paramakāruṇika*), he removes the objection that one who has attained all desires would be incapable of engaging in the activity of the world. By the phrase "with the desire to revive them," he shows that those who are compassionate indeed act solely out of a desire to revive others, without regard for their own interests.

The sense is that there is no fault, because this very activity of His is also His divine play (līlā). With the intention that the mention of "along with sacrifices" (*yajñaiḥ saha*) is for the purpose of establishing the qualification of the means of revival, he says: "by His own worship" (*svārādhanā*); and [he uses] "by sacrifices" (*yajñaiḥ*) to indicate the absence of external rites.

Although a plural designation was previously used, he speaks with the intention that the reference by the singular "by this" (anena) is intended to signify oneness; thus he says, "by this sacrifice" (anena yajñena), referring to "those who perform sacrifices together" (sahayajñāḥ). The readings of Śaṅkara and Yādavaprakāśa, however, are disregarded due to their lack of established authority.

Regarding the word *prasaviṣyadhvam*, even though there are two verbal roots— *ṣūñ* in the sense of "procreation of living beings" and *pūṅ* in the sense of "delivery of the fetus"— there would be understood merely the act of procreation. However, since the fruit of all [rites] such as sacrifices is not merely offspring— as is the case with the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and others— the term refers to a lineage characterized by continuity.

With the intention that prosperity consisting of one’s own excellence is what is intended here, he says: "Increase your own prosperity. By this, the entire range of desirable objects—other than those prohibited and not in conflict with dharma—is meant as being achievable through sacrifice; and even within that, those things which assist liberation and its means are included.

This is said with the intention that there is a greater degree of significance [in this work]. The inclusion of liberation (*mokṣa*) and its conducive means is for the purpose of making known the diversity of inclinations; it is qualified by the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*) in order to include liberation under the term "desired object" (*iṣṭakāma*). It is described as "characterized by the supreme human goal" (*paramapuruṣārthalakṣaṇa*) for the sake of those who have disregarded heaven (*svarga*).

Because of the instruction given to Arjuna— "Do not be concerned with the fruits"— and because of the consistency between what precedes and follows, such as "the highest good," it is appropriate here to state that the purpose is liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, the root *pṛ* (from which *prapūrayitṛ* is derived) is indeed the root *pṛ* meaning "to fill."

Is it not the case that filling (*prapūraṇa*) is indeed taught as the absence of filling? For even here, as in cases such as "departing" (*prasthāna*) or "forgetting" (*prasmaraṇa*), the prefix *pra-* has the sense of non-existence; for this very reason, there is the usage "he milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*).

True; nevertheless, even in the case of "he milks the cow," it is the cow alone that yields the milk, and not a deficiency in the nature of the milk itself; likewise here too, from the sacrifice—which stands in the place of the cow—the desires—which stand in the place of the milk—are obtained; by means of those [desires], there would be its yielding.
The meaning is: "Having taken the fruit from the one who gives the fruit at the proper time, may he give it to you";
by this, it is said that I, propitiated by the sacrifice, grant your desires.

How can there be an increase of the self through sacrifice? And how can sacrifice, which is momentary in nature as an action, be the means for an effect occurring at a later time? Since it has been established by such statements as "There is no other path" that knowledge alone bestows liberation, why is [sacrifice] prescribed as a means for attaining heaven and the like?

Is sacrifice a means to liberation? And they remember [the scriptures]: "A living being is bound by action and liberated by knowledge; therefore, ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action. Likewise: "Neither a practitioner of dharma nor a practitioner of adharma."
And thus; and how is it that various worldly desires, which are outside of liberation, are conducive to it? Anticipating this doubt, he says "How? with the intention of providing a complete answer.

In that regard: "He who cultivates the gods"—the latter part of the first [verse]—the propitiation of the deities is indeed the excellence of the worshipper; from that alone comes the growth of the self.
[The author] recalls the verbal root *yaj*, which is the base of the word *yajña* (sacrifice), in the sense of "worshiping the gods."

By the phrase "as being the means for propitiating the deity," he states "consisting of Me" in order to avoid the inconsistency that sacrifice cannot be a cause of liberation. It has already been stated that action performed as an adoration of the Supreme Self, by existing as an auxiliary to the knowledge that is the means to liberation, brings about liberation.
The phrase "consisting of me" (*madātmakān*) is stated to indicate that this is established by such texts as the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*.

The phrase "become my own self" (*macchīrabhūtān*) is used with the intention that the "nourishing of the gods through sacrifice" means nourishing them by making them possessed of satisfaction. Thus it is said: "they propitiate."
And with that intention, the Brāhmaṇa says: "Therefore, the gods subsist upon what is given from here.
To the question, "How can that which consists of me—which has not been mentioned here—be taken up [as the object]? he says: "For I... [referring to the momentary self].

He explains the second quarter-verse, which serves to resolve the objection regarding the impossibility of the granting of fruits, with the words beginning with "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*) and ending with "may they nourish" (*puṣṇantu*). The word *tat* refers back to the form under discussion. The phrase "propitiated by sacrifice" is stated again for the purpose of establishing the gods' power to bestow fruits.

It has been stated that [the deities] consist of *māyā*. Thus, even though they are momentary, their status as a means for attaining the fruit is established by way of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) consisting of the propitiation of the deity;

furthermore, it is explained that even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), when Indra and the other deities have dissolved, they continue to bestow fruits by way of the cognition of the Supreme Deity. With the intention of resolving the fourth doubt, he says:

Regarding the phrase "svārādhanā" (one's own propitiation): it is stated with the intention that "propitiation by the gods" means the nourishing of those who are propitiating them with what they require.

Regarding the phrase "puṣṇantu" (may they nourish): he says this with the intention of indicating that the latter half of the verse makes known the utility of the very meaning already stated for the sake of liberation. Thus [he says] "evam" (thus).
With the intention that the qualification "supreme" (para) is for the purpose of excluding forms of well-being such as heaven and the like, it was stated:
"called liberation" (mokṣākhyam).

Regarding the statement "May those gods nourish you," the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the failure to fulfill the obligation of nourishment—expressed as "he nourishes the gods"—is stated in the verse beginning with "the desired" (*iṣṭān*). The meaning of "the desired" is: those who are required for the successive propitiation [of the higher deities].
The sense is that those seeking liberation do not desire enjoyments for the sake of filling the belly and so forth.

This was stated with the intention that the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is not restricted [to a specific few]. Regarding the word "all" (*sarvān*), it refers to those who cook for themselves, as this would otherwise contradict the nature of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which occurs when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛbhiprāya*).
It is stated that this is for the purpose of establishing his status as a thief, specifically by way of being intent upon his own gratification. Now, what constitutes "thievery" here?
For he does not steal the enjoyments of the gods either secretly or by force;
nor is there thievery in the enjoyment of what has been given by them and come into his own hands.
For indeed, those who serve kings and others and eat what they have given are not impaled on a stake as thieves.
Such being the case, one might suspect that all those who enjoy the fruits of sacrifices and other rites would, without distinction, incur the status of thieves;
anticipating this objection, he says: "Indeed, theft... [is defined] by the intellect of another, that is, for the sake of another's purpose.

This is for the purpose of excluding that which is imagined as one's own, and that which—though belonging to another—is imagined as one's own purpose through the consent of others; hence the two qualifiers "belonging to another" and so forth. Therefore, [the phrase] "the nourishment of one's own self" refers to that.

"Nourishing one's own self" is the fruit of theft. Its definition is simply "forming the notion of ownership over what belongs to another. "By way of that purpose" refers to the result of [treating] it as belonging to another.
By this, he illuminates the impropriety of nourishing one's own self.
By the word *vastu*, he indicates a lack of intention to express any internal subdivisions of the object to be stolen.
And this being the case, [the verse continues]: "He who [perceives] one as being otherwise..."
By this and other such statements, even the "theft of the Self" (*ātmacaurya*) is characterized;

for that [theft] consists in the conceit of independence— which brings about one's own excellence— with respect to the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is imagined by the Lord solely with the desire to bestow excellence upon Himself.

[Objection: Even so, how can there be "theft" (*coratva*) in this example? [Reply: It is said: for even when the gods are propitiated by worshippers, they grant results solely for the purpose of receiving the sacrificial offering (*havis*); thus, they are indeed thieves. [The author] clarifies the result of the designation of theft with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
The meaning is "due to theft.
By the phrase "not censuring the goals of man," it is also indicated that the non-performance of prescribed duties is a cause for the cessation of one's qualification [for the path].

It will be explained later. By the phrase "it will come to pass," it is indicated that there is an absence of sublation by the non-perception of the unfit, since the transgression (pratyavāya) occurs in another body.
He says, "He explains that very point," in order to avoid the charge of redundancy and to exclude the interpretation that [the passage] has a different meaning.
Therein, the first half [of the verse] is a statement of the manner in which one will "attain the supreme good";
the second half, however, consists of an elaboration on the nature of theft as expressed in the words "given by them" and so forth.

This is a description of the specific forms of the sacrifice, such as the agent who draws it forth and the object to be sacrificed. Regarding the phrase "having Indra and others as its self," etc., the restrictive particle excludes both the notion that the sacrifice is solely for the sake of Indra and others, and the notion that it is for one's own sake.
One should maintain the awareness that even at the stages of procuring the materials and cooking them, the purpose is the propitiation of the Supreme Person.

To make this known, it was stated: "having taken up substances," and so forth. And this [point] is obtained through the contrast with the phrase "those who cook. Since even the propitiation of Indra and other deities is, in reality, of the nature of the propitiation of the Supreme Person, the worship of those respective deities is mentioned here in order to exclude that [lower form of worship].

And it is stated as "as it truly is" (*yathāvasthitam*) in order to establish that [the Self] culminates in the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). Those whose nature (*śīla*) is to eat what is called the nectar (*amṛta*)—the remnant of the sacrifice—are "those who eat the remnants of the sacrifice" (*yajñaśiṣṭāśinaḥ*).
There is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the maintenance of the body, which occurs through the impulse of passion (*rāga*), must be performed solely with the remnants of the sacrifice.
The meaning is that the "virtuous" (santaḥ) are those who subsist by eating only what remains from the sacrifice.

This is what is expressed by the phrase, "they maintain the journey of the body. Alternatively, the word *santaḥ* refers to the "good," as it stands in opposition to the word "sinful" (*pāpa*) found in the second half of the verse.

Just as in the latter half [of the verse], here too, the use of the words *yat* and *tat* to create a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is for the purpose of illuminating the distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). By the word *tu*, once the superiority of the wicked over the virtuous has been indicated,
he says "they" (*te*) in order to illuminate that, by implication, the superiority of the virtuous over even those [wicked ones] is established.
Regarding the term "beginningless" (*anādi*): here it is for the purpose of excluding only the sins committed through the five slaughterhouses, such as the kitchen hearth (*cullyādi*).
In order to substantiate the infinity of sins indicated by the word "all" (*sarva*) and the plural number, it is said: "accumulated over beginningless time. Sins are of two kinds.

[The obstacles are] those that oppose attainment and those that oppose proximity. Among these, it is said—with the intention of restricting the scope of the word "all"—that those opposing attainment are to be removed solely by the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), whereas [those opposing proximity are removed] by "those that oppose the perception of the true nature of the Self. And they record this in the tradition (*smaranti*).

By this, it is also indicated that because they share the specific quality of being contradictory [to liberation], even worldly merits (*puṇya*) are referred to here by the word "sin" (*kilbiṣa*). The term "accumulated" (*upārjita*) is used to indicate the distinction between those [merits] which obstruct both past and future [liberation] and the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of oneself" (*ātmakāraṇāt*): it is stated as "for the sake of one's own self" (*ātmārthatayā*) in order to indicate that the word *kāraṇa* here refers to a motive in the form of a purpose. This is because the censure [of cooking] would be untenable if it were merely for the act of cooking itself; rather, it is censured because it is done for the sake of eating what brings sin. Thus, by the expression "they cook for the sake of themselves," that which is established by implication has been explicitly stated.
"Of sinful nature" means having sin as their inherent character (*svabhāva*).
It is stated with the intention that the word *agha*—by the principle of "predominance of its quality"—refers to those characterized by sin.
"Of sinful nature" means having sin as their inherent character. [This applies] to the word *agha*.

The particle *eva* (only) is used to indicate that [the term] is merely figurative (*aupacārika*) for the sake of the enjoyment of food. He states the relationship that serves as the basis for this figurative usage: "because it results in sin" (*aghapariṇāmitvāt*). This means "because it is a cause of sin" (*aghahetutvāt*). He then states the two undesirable consequences resulting from this:

Regarding the phrase "those who are averse to the vision of the self": for one who cooks [living beings] for his own sake, there is an aversion to the vision of the self because there is no cessation of prior misdeeds;
furthermore, because it serves as the cause for ever-increasing misdeeds, he will again fall into hell.

He states the intended meaning of the scriptural declaration, "He who eats alone becomes solely sinful," with the words "only for hell. The sense is that it does not lead to happiness either in this world or in the next.

He says, "once again," with the intention that there is no tautology because this serves to show respect, as the elaboration of the very same meaning already stated— preceded by the presentation of authoritative evidence— is carried out through the passage beginning with "From food they arise.
Even though, from the perspective of worldly experience, it is impossible to directly demonstrate that [the world] has its root in sacrifice;
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as this is stated by way of an investigation that combines both the perspectives of worldly convention and the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*).

Furthermore, the respective domains of the worldly and scriptural perspectives will be distinguished later. Here, by the word *parjanya* (the rain-god), the rain—which is the effect of *parjanya*—is indicated. In the passage beginning with "from food [comes life]," it is said: "From rain comes food..."
The portion [of the verse], "from that, the creatures," is not explicitly mentioned because it is already established by common worldly experience.
When it is said, "arising from action" (*karmasamudbhavaḥ*), the understanding might arise that it arises from actions consisting of merit and demerit (*puṇyapāpa*);
in order to exclude that, it is stated, "the acquisition of wealth, etc. This is because the primary meaning is possible here.
The sense is that those who claim that the word "sacrifice" (yajña) indicates the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) have been refuted.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), such acts as the cooking of acquired materials are included.
Now, one might object: how can action, which consists of the agent’s activity, have Brahman as its cause?
For it is proper to designate that [action] as being produced by the self (ātman) or produced by the body, senses, and so forth;
nor should the causality of Brahman, which is common to all things, be specified here in particular.

Furthermore, it is logical that the *brahman* originates from the Imperishable (*akṣara*); for whether the word *brahman* refers to the Supreme Self or to the individual soul (*jīva*), both are eternal, and thus there would be no imperishable entity that could serve as their cause. This is because the words *brahman* and *akṣara* refer respectively to the Veda and the Supreme Self.
Śaṅkara’s commentary as well is inconsistent with the status of the *cakravartin* (the Lord of the Wheel).

As for the view of Yādavaprakāśa and others— that the word *brāhma* refers to the *sphoṭa* and so forth, and that syllables (*akṣara*) are its manifestors— that has been refuted precisely by the critique of their respective systems.

Anticipating the objection that the statement, "You are the *sphoṭa* residing in the phonemes," refers merely to the power of the phonemes to manifest their own meanings, he says, "And here. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel that doubt. By the word "here" (*atra*), [it is shown that] the word *brahman* refers directly to the Supreme Person.

Even though [the term] is primary, it is intended that this usage is figurative because, due to the force of context and other factors, its qualities are applied elsewhere than in that [primary sense].
This is because actions such as the acquisition of wealth are to be accomplished by an embodied being; therefore, in that regard—

Since the aspect that constitutes the embodied soul will be explained separately by the word "akṣara," this word "brahman" is intended here to refer to the aspect that constitutes the body. It has been stated that the body is a transformation of primordial matter (prakṛti);
thus, within the body as a transformation of primordial matter, [it exists] as its substance.
First, he states its usage in the context of the primary cause (*prakṛti*) for the purpose of designating it by the word "Brahman":

"Therefore, this... The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: "This [cause], called Pradhāna, is born in the form of an effect, differentiated into name and form, and as the object of experience for consciousness."
Furthermore, the word *brahman* in that context does not have the Supreme Self as its referent,
because the Supreme Self is mentioned separately in the passage: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge— from him this *brahman* [was produced]."

Nor can it have the inner self (pratyagātman) as its object, because a direct relationship with it is impossible according to the statement, "It is neither the form of the Self nor food"; furthermore, the sense is that being "food" would be entirely figurative. This is also because of the mention of the word "womb" (yoni) and because the Supreme Self is mentioned separately from the "mine" (mama).

In the passage, "My womb is the great *brahman*," it is established that the word *brahman* refers to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the meaning of "because" is that the word *brahman* cannot logically denote something produced. Thus, the word *brahman* occurring here refers to the body.
With the intention that the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) is appropriately applied to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) when it has been realized as proximate [to Brahman], he says:
"arising from the imperishable Brahman" (*brāhmākṣarasamudbhavam*). Furthermore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is denoted by the word *akṣara*, as in:
"The perishable is *pradhāna*; the immortal imperishable is *Hara*."
This and more is established. Now, even so, the statement "arising from the syllables of the *brahman*" is incorrect; for one's own body as a whole does not originate from one's own prior intellect.
Furthermore, the nature of a *cakra* (wheel) is not observed here, [extending] from the food and so forth up to the body.
Even if there were a causal relationship, the imperishable soul (akṣara), which is the cause of the body, cannot be produced from food and the like.

Nor is the individual soul (jīva) indicated in that passage by the statement, "From food beings arise," because in that context the word "beings" (bhūta) refers exclusively to the body as a modification of food. To this, he says:
"By means of food, drink, and so forth"— this is the intended meaning: here, it is not merely the body that is indicated as being produced from the *akṣara*,
but rather that which serves as the instrument for action, by virtue of the statement, "Action arises from the *brāhma*."
And the body’s status as a means to that [liberation] belongs only to it when presided over by the inner self (pratyagātman);
and its power of presiding is dependent upon the satisfaction produced by food, breath, and so forth.
This being the case, the body is characterized as a means for the performance of ritual action.
It is entirely logical that [the body] arises from the imperishable (akṣara), because its cause is the presiding of the inner self (pratyagātman).

And its nature as a "wheel" (cakra) is also established, since even for the imperishable, there is a dependence on food, drink, and so forth for the maintenance of the body; for dependence is not necessarily a cause of the wheel-nature only at the time of origination.

Alternatively, action is produced by a body presided over by the individual soul (jīva), and the body presided over by the individual soul is produced from food, according to the scriptural statement: "From food all beings arise. Furthermore, the word "beings" (*bhūta*) here refers to [the elements], as in the phrase "sustaining all beings."
As in such passages, [the term] refers to a body possessed of life.
Therefore, the nature of being a *cakra* (wheel) is appropriate here. He will explain this method and the one immediately following it.
Thus, while this *cakra* is being maintained, for the person who is subject to the authority of the scriptures...

It is stated [in the commentary] beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) in order to extract the specific portion that must be performed. Since a contracted body cannot possibly be all-pervading, and since the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is its substratum, has been specified, the word "all" (*sarva*) is intended to include its various internal subdivisions; with this intention, it was said.

Regarding the phrase "pertaining to all qualified persons": the meaning is that not only is the body of one qualified for *karmayoga* dependent upon sacrifice, but so too is that of one qualified for *jñānayoga*.
As for the expression "established in sacrifice," since it is inappropriate to take this as a locative sense (i.e., "in" sacrifice), he explains: "it means having sacrifice as its root."

Regarding the phrase "set in motion" (*pravartitam*), since there is a requirement for an agent who set it in motion, it is stated with the intention that this must be Prajāpati himself— who, as introduced by the passage beginning with "along with sacrifices" (*saha yajñaiḥ*) and continuing with "sustain the gods" (*devān bhāvayata*), was the one who impelled creatures toward sacrifices—
by saying "by the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣeṇa*). Alternatively, [the *ṣatva* substitution] may be due to the rule concerning the change of *t* to *ṣ*.

The formulation of separate sentences serves to clarify that each of the three— beginning with *aghāyu*— is a distinct defect, and to make known that each preceding one is the cause of each succeeding one.

Here, [the term *agha*] is used either because it is the cause of evil (*agha*), because it is the effect of evil, or simply because it possesses a connection to evil (*agha*) as a unifying factor for both.

The intention is that the word *agha* indicates *āyus* (life-span). Thus, the three modes of fulfillment beginning with "for the very commencement of *agha*" have been stated. Regarding the phrase "for this very reason," the meaning is: precisely because it is *agha-āyus* in the manner described.
He states the intended exclusion for the phrase "only the senses" (*indriyāṇy eva*) by saying "not one who delights in the self" (*nātmārāma*).
In order to establish the intended exclusion regarding [the word] being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the compound and its constituent parts:

"The senses alone" (*indriyāṇy eva*). To the doubt as to how the senses can be a "delight" (*ārāma*), he states the conclusion reached by the passage beginning with "set in motion thus" (*evaṃ pravartitam*) and ending with "one who delights in the senses" (*indriyārāmaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "not remaining from sacrifice" (*ayajñaśiṣṭa*): the word "hence" (*ataḥ*) means because their sole delight is in the enjoyment of poison. The pronoun "he" (*saḥ*) refers to the subject previously explained by the word "that" (*yaḥ*). The word "in vain" (*mogha*) refers to the state of having efforts that yield no fruit.
And because there is a requirement for an effort that must be countered, he says: "even while striving in the yoga of knowledge and so forth."
Thus, since the duty to act through the hands has been stated even for those qualified for the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and so forth,

and because it will be stated later in the passage beginning with "Therefore, unattached" (*tasmādasaktaḥ*), the two verses in that context beginning with "But he who finds delight in the Self" (*yastvātmaratiḥ*) do not concern those qualified for the yoga of knowledge and so forth.
However, with the intention that [liberation] pertains to the state of fruition, he says: "not dependent on means.

By this, the interpretation of others—which holds that this refers to those in the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*) as stated in such passages as "Having granted fearlessness to all beings, one should practice the life of renunciation" (*naiṣkarmyam ācaret*)—is refuted.
This is rejected; for even he who is devoted to the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama*) does not have a cessation of all actions.

Indeed, the undertaking of the duties of different stages of life belongs only to one characterized by caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life, and not to one who is liberated from the names and forms such as caste and stage of life—this is the meaning of the word "liberated" (*mukta*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is used with the intention of excluding those who are established in the means;

thus it is said that [the Lord] is independent of the means of *jñāna-yoga* and *karma-yoga*. To the question, "How then can there be the existence of the goal in the absence of the means? he says: "By Himself" (*svataḥ*).

Thus it is said: for that which is obstructive must be removed, whereas being directed toward the Self is attained spontaneously—this is the sense. Here, the word *rati* (delight) refers to the state of being oriented toward [the Self], since satisfaction (*tṛpti*) and so forth are mentioned separately. "One who delights only in the Self" means in the Self alone.

This is as in the case of "prior and posterior. With the intention that even in the phrase "satisfied with the Self" (ātmatṛptaḥ) a restrictive emphasis (avadhāraṇa) is intended, he says: "by the Self alone" (ātmanaiva). For the words "satisfaction" (tṛpti) and "contentment" (tuṣṭi) are well known as referring to the pleasure arising from a nourisher and an object of enjoyment; having this in mind, [he applies] what is appropriate to each.
He states what is to be excluded: "not by food, drink, and so forth," and "not by gardens, and so forth.
Summarizing the three things to be excluded from the passage beginning with "delighting in the Self" (ātmarati), he states the meaning of the sentence:
"sustenance" (dhāraṇā). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), places of enjoyment and the like are intended; for one who...

The sense is that even for one established in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), the performance of *dhāraṇā* and so forth, as well as [the consumption of] food, drink, and the like, indeed remains to be done by him. Now, one might object: "It is incorrect to say 'for him no duty exists,' because even for the liberated one [it is said], 'he eats, plays... [and so on].

This is because of the scriptural hearing of such effects [as the body]. Furthermore, in this context, the word "effect" does not refer to the body and so forth— as in the expression "not its effect"— because the negation of those is currently irrelevant,
and because their absolute negation would be like that of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice.
Anticipating the objection that this contradicts such sūtras and the scriptural passages concerning their subject matter, he states:
"There is nothing to be done for the sake of seeing the Self. He then clarifies the reason intended by the passage beginning with "He who delights in the Self," stating: "Spontaneously (svata eva)."
By the two terms "from itself alone" and "always," it is made known that there is no dependence on causal factors for the purpose of production and for the purpose of avoiding cessation.

Since there is no purpose (*artha*) for the word "purpose" (*artha*) here, it is stated that "there is nothing to be done. Regarding the phrase "not by what is not done," he says, "no harm whatsoever," with the intention that this is not a prohibition against the object itself, but rather that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform it. Thus, [he distinguishes between] purpose and harm.

[The text addresses] the vision of self and its absence; therein, since the former is already established, it is not something to be proven, and since the latter is already utterly ceased, it is not something to be removed—with this intention, he says:
"Because the vision of self does not depend on a means," and so forth with the words "nor of this... etc.
With the intention of stating that there is no dependence [on others] for the sake of removing obstacles,

he says "by himself alone" (*svata eva*), and so forth. With the intention that the word "exists" (*asti*) refers back to the manner previously specified by the passage beginning with "delighting in the Self" (*ātmarati*), he has said this.

Regarding the phrase "of one who is turned away from all insentient objects": by using the word *sarva* (all) here without restriction, it indicates that the scope refers to the entirety of the objects of enjoyment under discussion, including their internal subdivisions.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "prakṛti" and ending with "asakāryeṣu. Here, the term *pariṇāma* (transformation) [is used].

By the word *bhūta*, it is shown here that the word *bhūta* refers to that which is connected with the activity of coming into being (*bhavana-kriyā*). In the phrase "dependent upon the meaning" (*arthavyapāśrayaḥ*), he clarifies that the word *artha* has the state of being (*bhāva*) as its primary sense; thus, "dependent upon the meaning" means dependent by way of purpose. "Dependent" (*vyapāśrayaḥ*) means acceptance (*svīkaraṇam*).
Or rather, it is intended that the goal (*artha*) itself is what must be relied upon and accepted.
By this, the interpretation of others—that reliance is caused by a purpose—is refuted.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "not of this" is intended as a reason; for he who is liberated is indeed independent of means.
This is stated with the intention of concluding the meaning of the two verses: "For he is indeed liberated."

With the intention that the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) refers back to all the previously stated reasons for the necessity of performing action, he says: "because" (*yasmāt*). Both [the terms] "unattached" (*asaktaḥ*) and "duty" (*kāryam*) [are thus explained].

This was stated with the intention that [the verse] refers to the rampart of the performance of action; namely, "action alone should be performed without attachment. "Action alone" means it should not be performed with a view toward the results of that action, such as heaven and so forth. Regarding the word "constantly" (*satatam*) here:

Even though the qualification for the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) exists, [the Lord] says "until the attainment of the Self" in order to show that the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) alone is to be practiced; for it is stated in the passage beginning with "for one who is unattached" that the yoga of action itself accomplishes the attainment of the Self even without the intervention of the yoga of knowledge.
With this intention, he says: "Unattached... performing action... one attains the Supreme.
The meaning is not that one attains the Supreme by performing some other act subsequent to the performance of action;
rather, when it is said that "performing action one attains the Supreme," he clarifies that the instrumentality of action is established by the very fact of the statement.
"By means of the yoga of action" (karmayogenaiva). Here, [the Self] is indicated as that which is to be attained.

With the intention that the "Supreme" (paraḥ) refers to the individual soul (jīva), who is distinct from the body because this is a section concerning the Self as distinct from the body, he says: "The meaning is that one attains the Self."

The superiority of the yoga of action (karmayoga) is inferred from the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas). By the words "by action alone" (karmaṇaiva), he demonstrates the qualification for the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) as indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed): "the royal sages (rājarṣis)," meaning those who are foremost among the knowers of truth. For kings indeed possess minds that are vast and profound.
Even among them, they are seers of supersensuous objects by virtue of being sages (*ṛṣi*); even among those, they are knowers of the Self;

and even among those, they are the foremost because their senses are naturally restrained and because of their preeminent innate goodness (*sattva*) and other qualities—this is the meaning. As for the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by action alone," [it serves to exclude other means].
Even for one capable in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), there is a focus on not desisting from the yoga of action (*karmayoga*);
for the word "perfect attainment" (*saṃsiddhi*) is intended as an illustration of what is stated by the phrase "he attains the Supreme.
Thus, it is said that they have attained the Self. And this being so—
The restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) in the phrase "by action alone" (*karmaṇaiva*), which implies independence from the previously mentioned yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), is thus justified.

To provide the transition for what follows, he takes up the summary that was stated with the word "thus" (*evam*). By the word "now" (*idānīm*), [he refers to] the verse beginning with "for the sake of the world's welfare" (*lokasaṃgraham*). "The wise man" (*vidvān*)...
"Endowed [with yoga], he should perform [action] constantly and without interruption"—this means "in every way.
If it were said "for the sake of protecting the world," it would be understood that the gathering of people (*lokasaṃgraha*) is not the primary motive;
however, by saying "even though he sees," the necessity of performing action follows from the reasons previously stated.
This sequence of words has been stated to indicate the preeminence of the welfare of the world (*lokasaṃgraha*).

The particle *eva* (only/just) is intended to exclude the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*); with the intention that it should be construed as "you ought to perform action alone," it was said: "you ought to perform action indeed."

Alternatively, the particle *eva* (indeed) is intended to emphasize that the gathering of people (*lokasaṃgraha*) is not required; whereas "action alone" (*karmaiva*) is stated as being relevant to the present context. By the word "you ought" (*arhasi*), the Lord highlights Arjuna’s distinction as one uniquely qualified for the exclusive practice of the yoga of action. Thus, he is called "the best" (*śreṣṭha*).

According to the grammatical rule *praśasyasya śraḥ*, the meaning is "most excellent" (*praśasyatama*). Considering that this quality of being most excellent serves the practitioners by making their performance of duties worthy of emulation, [the Lord] said: "One who knows the whole should not cause those dull-witted ones, who know only a part, to waver."

Having reflected upon what is to be said hereafter, it is stated that he is renowned for his knowledge of the entire scripture and for his practice thereof; [this applies] neither to one who knows only partially but does not practice,
nor to one who knows the whole but does not practice, nor even to one who possesses both qualities.

Since that which is not well-known cannot be followed or practiced, three words are used to exclude such cases. In the verse, "Whatever standard he makes," this must be understood in the sense that the world follows whatever scripture he authorizes as authoritative.
Furthermore, in the preceding statement, "Even considering the welfare of the world,

you ought to act," it was stated only that "you ought to act"; it was not proposed that one ought to accept the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth, such that this [present verse] would be spoken for that purpose.

When the nature of the primary act (*aṅgin*) to be performed has been indicated by the rule "whatever he does," a desire for knowledge arises regarding its specific manner, as that manner is what is required;
therefore, with the intention that it is precisely the description of that [manner] which is appropriate, [the author states]: "Whatever is the means of knowledge... (*yat-pramāṇam*).
Regarding what was stated as "that which is joined with the auxiliaries" (*yadaṅgayuktam*): here, the word *pramāṇa* refers to a limit (*avadhi*);
and the limit of the essential nature of the action to be performed consists precisely of the auxiliaries.
For this very reason, they metaphorically designate the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) by the term *vidhyanta* (the end of the injunction).

"Whatever means of valid cognition [is employed] in accordance with reality"—this is precisely what is intended by Yādavaprakāśa’s commentary as well. Regarding this point, the word "performs" (*kurute*) has been rendered as "practises" (*anutiṣṭhati*) in order to demonstrate the natural sense of the term;
the intention is that otherwise there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a different meaning. [The phrase begins: "Whatever means of valid cognition..."
In order to establish the specific meaning of that which was previously indicated, he states the meaning of the word *tat* (that): "endowed with its members" (*tadaṅgayuktam*).
Now, one might ask: when the member has been indicated by the word *yat* (which), how can there be a reference to that which is qualified by the member by means of the word *tat*?
It is as follows: when it is said that "one who performs what is endowed with a member practices that," the linguistic function (*śabdavṛtti*) is simply that "one practices that member."

Since it is impossible for a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to exist separately from the principal act (*aṅgin*), it is established by implication that [the result] is qualified by those subordinate members.
He clarifies that the benefit and disadvantage resulting from performing or not performing [the act] are intentional.
"Therefore" means: because the performance must conform to worldly custom.

"Until all... means until the attainment of the Self. Now, one might ask: "If he is himself liberated through the yoga of knowledge, what does it matter to him whether the world is gathered or not gathered? To this, He says: "Otherwise. This means: when one who is qualified for the yoga of knowledge, thinking "I am [the knower]," abandons devotion to the yoga of action.
The word "also" (api) in the phrase "even from the yoga of knowledge" indicates the state of falling away from both.

For even I, though entirely indifferent and free from any sense of obligation, perform action solely for the sake of protecting the world out of supreme compassion; how much more so, then, must it be said for you, who are full of concern and subject to the consequences of sin?

By the three verses beginning with "Not by me, O Pārtha," the intention is that through the word "me" (me), the Lord— who is distinguished from other conscious beings subject to karma and who exists as He truly is— is referred to; thus, these are the manifestations of His unique, eternally established, and abundant perfections and attributes.
The qualifying attributes beginning with "of the Lord of All" have been stated. Regarding the phrase "of the Lord of All":
the Śruti and Smṛti are indeed my own commands, and they must be followed by others. For I have no other controller by whose fear of transgression I might act; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "of one whose desires are fulfilled": the sense is that there is no purpose for Me—which previously existed merely as a state of longing—that cannot be accomplished by My mere volition (saṅkalpa), such that action would have to be performed as a means to it. [This applies to] "the omniscient one of true volition."

Furthermore, for me— who have descended into the same class as gods, humans, and animals who are subject to karma— there is no contraction of knowledge or obstruction of will such as they possess; therefore,
the intention is that there is no need to perform action for the sake of removing those [obstructions].

Regarding the phrase "in the three worlds," he supplies an implied qualification by stating "of gods and humans. And it was said by the blessed Parāśara: "O Lord of Men, He creates forms that consist of all powers."
Possessing the activities known as gods, animals, and humans, they move with their own effortless grace.
"For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the Immeasurable One is not born of karma; it is all-pervasive and characterized by an unobstructed nature.
Thus, when there is no longer anything to be done—namely, that various things already attained must be attained—[the state is reached].

He explains by way of emphasizing the intended cause, beginning with the words "Since" (*yataḥ*). He states the purpose established by a consideration of the subsequent verse: "Nevertheless, for the protection of the world" (*athāpi lokarakṣāyai*).
The word "nevertheless" (*athāpi*) conveys the sense of the particle "and" (*ca*). When it is said, "I continue to abide in action,"...
The result is that one never ceases from action to practice the yoga of knowledge; this is what is meant by the statement, "I abide in action alone.
Alternatively, due to the propriety of the context, the particle *eva* (alone) here is to be construed out of its normal position.

To the doubt—"In the absence of any duty or purpose, for what reason then is action performed?"—it is said: "If indeed... (yadi hi). The previous verse, by the mention of "in the three worlds" (*triṣu lokeṣu*), refers to all incarnations; however, this one...
Because of the perception that "he is a human being," [the term] is not common to the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa alone.

Therefore, by means of the words "Lord of All" and so forth, he declares that the reference "I am" has as its object a form common to the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa when combined with the essential nature of the Lord (Īśvara).
"He is the Lord of all, whose resolve is true," as before.
This is stated to avoid the contradiction with his having attained all desires: "created by His own resolve.
Although He is capable of governing everything by His mere resolve alone...

It has been stated that [the Lord] was born as one capable of benefiting the world for the purpose of setting it in motion by means of bestowing knowledge and so forth. Otherwise, if he were to act according to the analogy of a possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśa*),
there would be no subjection to the scriptures for those set in motion, and consequently, the fruit dependent upon the performance of various [prescribed] rites would not exist.

Desire proceeds [spontaneously], because for those things that proceed according to the principle of possession by spirits (bhūtāveśa), there is an absence of subjection to scriptural injunctions; consequently, the fruit would not be dependent upon the performance of those respective acts.
Thus, desire proceeds spontaneously.
According to this and other [passages], he says: "by his own will" (*chandataḥ*). The meaning is: "but not by [the power of] karma.
