By rejecting the state of being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma, [it is implied that] who could possibly overcome one who is intent on benefiting the world? Thus, by the phrase "intent on benefiting the world," [it is shown that no one can defeat him].

He is capable [of assuming] such forms as "one who has assumed at will a vast body according to his desire," and so forth; this is for the purpose of establishing that His commands are to be followed,
and for the purpose of explaining the manner of His well-known power, as indicated by the word *hi*.

It has been said: "Among humans," and so forth. Now, as for this Lord (Īśvara), in what ritual action could he be engaged? For in the ultimate sense, he possesses neither the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas), nor even humanity and the like, which are fit for the performance of general duties (sāmānyadharma).

In response to the doubt— namely, that one who is not subject to the power of karma might perform actions according to his own will even while engaging in various appropriate deeds— the author says, in accordance with the passage beginning, "He highly esteems his own duty as a Kṣatriya, which is appropriate for his lineage."
"Suitable for that family": this is the intended meaning—he says "destruction" (utsāda) here in the sense that they would become ruined.
This is like [the statement] "he is as if non-existent," and so forth.
When non-performance is the cause of destruction, *saṅkara* (intermixture) is its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
Furthermore, there is the performance by Kṣatriyas and others of duties such as Brahmins and so forth— such as abstaining from battle—
and "impairment" (*upahati*) is the subsequent unfitness for ritual action.

Having shown the illustration within his own self, he now makes manifest the intended meaning regarding the subject of the illustration with the words, "In this very way, you too," and "Not by me, O Pārtha. The intention behind the vocative address "Pārtha" is as follows:
He states the forms suitable for being followed by saying "the cultured" (*śiṣṭa*).
The employment of the word *Yudhiṣṭhira* is for the purpose of encouraging him toward battle and for indicating his steadfastness in the kṣatriya duty known as the sacrifice of war (*raṇayajña*).

With the intention of saying, "What need have you for other relatives such as a father? For you are yourself well-known among the foremost of cultured people through your accounts concerning Urvaśī, the daughter of Virāṭa, and others," he says:
In response to the concern that "Arjuna is [about to] desist"— for dharma must be practiced by the learned,
and the yoga of knowledge is the supreme dharma, and therefore following it would lead the world toward liberation alone, resulting in the protection of all the worlds— it was said:
"Those who do not know their own qualification"— the sense is that for those who lack such qualification,
there would be a falling away from both [paths] by entering into that [practice].
He concludes what was stated in the verse beginning with "for the sake of the world's welfare" with the word "therefore."

The manner in which the world possesses or lacks eligibility for the yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge, as well as the manner in which the wise man, setting aside his own eligibility, acts in accordance with the eligibility of others for the sake of social welfare (*lokasaṅgraha*), is stated in the two verses beginning with "Those who are attached" (*saktāḥ*). It is said—"one who knows the Self incompletely"—in order to indicate that the lack of realization refers to the subject at hand. The same applies to what follows: "the wise man among the ignorant" (*vidvān ajñānām*).
This should also be understood regarding the two words [“attached” and “not attached”]. The word *akṛtsnaśaḥ* (not entirely) is intended to exclude the state of being completely ignorant of the Self.

With the intention that what was previously stated—the inevitability of connection with action through its inherent nature—is what is meant by the word *saktāḥ* (attached), he says: "those who have an inevitable connection with action."
The two statements— "the ignorant are attached to action" and "those whose highest aim is worldly action"— refer to persons who are intent upon worldly activity;
for if that were not the case, one would have to abandon even *karmayoga* and perform only worldly actions.

These [duties] should be performed even by the wise; therefore, with the intention that the lack of qualification for the yoga of knowledge and the qualification for the yoga of action are indicated by those two, it was said:
"because of the lack of full knowledge regarding the Self," and so forth.
The same applies hereafter. The phrase "of the ignorant who are attached to action" should also be understood here.
Furthermore, the statement "he should act as they do" does not refer solely to the relationship between the example and the subject of the example; rather, by which...

The intention is that others should perform action having seen his own performance in a certain manner; therefore, a wise person should act in that same manner. For if this were so, the statement "desiring the welfare of the world" would also be consistent. This is what he intends to convey.

He states the meaning of the sentence with the words beginning "in the self" and ending with "should perform. By the two terms "the wise one" and "unattached," that which is established is stated: namely, that they are also fit for the path of knowledge-yoga (jñāna-yoga).
By means of the word "compendium" (saṃgraha), he says "ascertainment of the Dharma" (dharmaniścaya) in order to eliminate misconceptions such as [the mere] pleasing of the world.

The gathering of the world (*loka*) means bringing it together and accepting it; the meaning is the induction of a sense of belonging to the same community (*sayūthyatā*) through a shared intention regarding one’s own practice. Karmic latent impressions (*karmavāsanā*) refers to specific portions of preceding merit and demerit that initiate successive acts of merit and demerit.

Or rather, it is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by specific experiences of propelling each preceding body, which serves as the cause for the memory capable of propelling each subsequent body, just like the impression resulting from the playing of musical instruments and so forth.

"Differentiation of the intellect" (*buddhibheda*) means making the intellect otherwise; and he shows that this refers to the subject at hand by the words "other than the yoga of action," etc. By the word "engaged" (*yukta*), [he refers to one] who acts for the sake of maintaining the world.

The intended meaning is that the application of the previously mentioned state of non-dependence is for the sake of avoiding separation from what one desires; thus it is said, "endowed with intelligence."
The meaning of "joṣayet" (should cause to enjoy) is "should generate delight.
For the verbal root *juṣ* signifies both "delight" and "service. The grammatical construction is: "one should cause those persons attached to action to enjoy all actions."
He states the meaning of the four verses beginning with "From nature" (prakṛteḥ) as follows: "The yoga of action" (karmayogam).
The meaning of the two verses [the first and second] concerns the wise and the ignorant respectively, though presented in reverse order.
In the third verse, however, non-deviation is explained by way of clarifying this very point.
"Required by karma-yoga"— the meaning is that it constitutes the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) of karma-yoga.

Having stated "by the qualities of *prakṛti*," he speaks [the following] in order to exclude those ordinary qualities such as sound and so forth— which, although established through their high degree of common renown and the like, are irrelevant to the present context— thereby specifying the particular [qualities intended].
Regarding the phrase "by means of goodness and so forth," he says "in every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*), which is indicated by the word expressing modality; and he says "conformable to itself" (*svānurūpam*).
As for the term "the agent" (*kartā*), because it is formed with the suffix *tṛc*, there would otherwise be the requirement of a genitive case.

In order to avoid that [misconception], and to eliminate the delusion of speaking of agency and egoity with respect to actions, it is said "in relation to actions. However, if the intention is to express the suffix *-tṛn*, then this is a statement regarding the result. [Thus it is said: "the self deluded by egoism."
Desiring to express the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of the three components of the compound, which have multiple referents, he analyzes it [as follows]: "by means of *ahaṅkāra*.
Here, mere egoity (*ahaṃbhāva*) is not what is being denoted, because that is included within the very nature of the self (*ātman*).

Nor is it the insentient substance called "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra); for since that too produces its effects by mediating through the delusion of the body being the self, it would be more appropriate to designate that very [delusion] as the immediate cause. Nor is it pride (garva).
Because [egoism] is not specified as a cause for such things as being treated with contempt by superior beings, [the author],
intending to show that what is intended here is simply the delusion of identifying the body with the self, says: "Egoism (ahaṅkāra) is [the notion] regarding that which is not the self."

"Self-conceit regarding primordial nature (*prakṛti*). By this, the etymology of the word *ahaṅkāra* is shown through the suffix *cvi*, which denotes the transformation of something into what it was not before. "One whose self-nature is unawakened":
he whose self (*ātman*)—that is, his true nature (*svarūpa*)—is deluded, is one whose self is deluded (*vimūḍhātmā*). [End of] the two directions.
The sense is that, as in the expression "they would be deluded" (*vimuhreyuḥ*), the word *vimūḍha* here stands in grammatical apposition with the object of delusion.
Furthermore, in the phrase "of the division of qualities and actions" (*guṇakarmavibhāgayoḥ*), the genitive case is dependent on the word *jana* (people).

Thinking that the locative case here is used in the sense of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*), it was stated: "in the division of the qualities such as *sattva*, and in the division of their respective functions. Because the word *vibhāga* follows a *dvandva* compound, it is connected with each member. This is because the qualities cannot function directly within the qualities themselves.

When there is the intention to express the sense organs, their objects, and so forth through the action of another, the word ending in the locative case is used by means of a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of two terms. This is stated with the intention that the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is used metaphorically for the effects of the qualities, as in the phrase "in their own qualities" and "in their own effects."
Furthermore, the effects of the qualities will be analyzed. Alternatively, this was stated because the cause is primary and the effect is secondary in relation to it.
In the verse beginning with "the qualities of prakṛti," attachment to prohibited things and the like is not intended to be described, because in that case, immovability would be untenable.
Therefore, it must be stated as attachment to certain means for achieving the goals of human life.

And the human goal under discussion here is the realization of the Self (*ātmadarśana*). In that regard, for someone who has not yet established the qualification (*adhikāra*) for it, attachment to some means toward that end must be enjoined. And the human goal under discussion is [the means] directed toward the realization of the Self.

Thus it has been said. In the phrase "the self deluded by egoism" (*ahaṅkāravimūḍhātmā*), delusion regarding the Self (*ātman*) is indeed the subject under discussion. Therefore, the compound must be analyzed as "those deluded by the qualities" (*guṇaiḥ sammūḍhāḥ*). Furthermore, this applies even though the word *guṇa* is a subordinate member of the compound.

Just as in expressions such as "the teacher's family of Devadatta," the connection with the word *prakṛteḥ* (of nature) is logically established; this is the intention behind the statement, "deluded regarding the Self as it truly exists by the qualities of nature. Furthermore, the phrase "in the activities of the qualities" (*guṇakarmasu*) is stated so as to lead ultimately to the practice of Karma-yoga.
"In actions alone"—the particle *eva* is used to indicate that the purpose is exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). He states what is excluded by that indication: "not that.
He states the reason for its immutability, which is the result of mentioning its connection with qualities and actions.

"Therefore, they" means they are not capable, nor do they possess the necessary power. With the intention of stating that the term "the dull-witted" was used so as to avoid the contingency of disturbing those whose [wrong views] are to be refuted, he describes the process of their wavering: "Those who are dull-witted."

Because of their own dullness— meaning, for those who do not follow the conduct of superior persons, "dullness" here is intended to signify an incapacity for self-determined judgment; or it refers to the smallness characterized by lack of fortitude, which is the cause of being easily swayed, resulting from incomplete knowledge.

"Stupid, small-minded, wicked, unfortunate, and dull-witted"—so say the etymologists (*naighaṇṭukas*). By the words "he should not cause to waver," he shows that this is a supplement to the previously mentioned "rejoicing" (*joṣaṇa*).
Therefore, for one who is qualified for the yoga of knowledge, [the practice] is in the yoga of action.
Anticipating the doubt that this might apply only to one who has not undertaken a lower office, he says:
"even those qualified for the yoga of knowledge. It must be performed even with regard merely to one's own duty, how much more so when it is combined with the welfare of others?

With the intention that [the renunciation] is for one's own sake, he says "Therefore" (ataḥ). He takes up the portion already stated in order to introduce the subsequent verse: "In the primordial nature" (prakṛtau).
However, according to the manner of the verse about to be spoken, the renunciation of all actions is directed toward the Lord of All.

It should be performed; the intention is that by the statement regarding the attribution of agency to the qualities (guṇas) in the interim, the discrimination between the body and the self (*dehātma-viveka*) and so forth are established even by that much. "Having superimposed" means having reflected upon. Relying on this state.
The doctrine of the "leaf-clingers," such as the followers of Kapila and others, has arisen; therefore,
in order to turn them away from their view and to dispel the doubt as to how insentient *guṇas* can possess agency characterized by knowledge, desire to act, and effort, [the following is stated].

And he says: "Regarding the qualities," etc. This refers to what is about to be stated. "This agency" means agency with respect to merit, demerit, and so forth. For inherent agency does not depart even in the state of liberation, because it is not produced by contact with the *guṇas*.

"By means of the discrimination between what has been attained and what has not been attained" means either through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), or by the determination of what is logical and what is illogical. Here, the statement regarding non-agency being subordinate to non-action would be contradictory to what precedes and follows; however, its purpose is for the sake of a specific kind of reflective awareness (*anusandhāna*).
The statement regarding the connection [of the preceding and following sections] is made with the intention of showing the continuity between them.
By this, the meaning of the section beginning with "The agent [is the Self], because of being the subject of the scripture" (Sūtra 3.3.18) is indicated.
Now, with the intention of explaining the meaning of the subsequent section, "parāt tu tacchruteḥ," he introduces the following verse with the words "idānīm" (now).

The statement that "subjugatability" (*niyāmyatā*) is of the same nature as one's own self (*svarūpa*) is because it is that which defines one's essential nature. The three words beginning with "Bhagavatī" express what is intended by the word "in me" (*mayi*).

The term "Bhagavatī" [is used] because it results in [the qualities of] being the controller (*niyantṛtva*), being the object of worship (*upāsyatva*), and being the bestower of fruits (*phalakatva*).

By the three words beginning with "Bhagavatī," the intended meaning is expressed as "in me. "Bhagavatī" refers to her who possesses the entire collection of auspicious qualities necessary for being the controller, the object of worship, the bestower of fruits, and so forth.
The sense is that [the term] also serves to exclude what is to be abandoned (*heya*). Regarding the phrase "Puruṣottama" (Supreme Person):

even when there is no possibility of anything to be abandoned due to His entry for the purpose of governing [the world] and so forth, He possesses a distinction of the nature to be described later in the words, "But the Supreme Person is another."
The meaning is as follows: "And that which is produced by the qualities in Him who has become the Self of all.
The sense is that although the three-fold [nature] is insentient matter (*acit-dravya*), He alone is its ruler because He has become the Self of all.
By this, [it is shown that] "without attachment, for the protection of the world..."
By attributing agency to the qualities (*guṇas*) or by consigning it to the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*),
the state of being the object of the third [case-ending] is stated; thus, it is also indicated in the summary verse of the third chapter that an equal option (*tulyavikalpa*) is not intended.

By the word "in me" (mayi), which is intended here, the statement that [the Lord] is the inner self of all beings is given as the reason for His status as the Lord of all. Furthermore, by this, the passage to be cited later—"The Lord of all beings," and so forth—is made known. The word "all" refers to those things created by Himself.

The meaning is "and those produced by qualities. With the intention that the word "of battle" (*yudhyasya*) is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all scriptural injunctions, it is stated as "battle and so forth. Regarding the word "in the self" (*ātmani*), it is used in the sense of the locative case (*adhyātma* = *ātmani*).

The meaning is "in compound. Here, [the author] reveals that the word *cetas* is the object of knowledge consisting of the contemplation of what is established by hundreds of scriptural texts (*śruti*).
By the phrase "the nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*), he shows the manner in which it is established by hundreds of scriptural texts.

The word *antar* [means] "within. Through the two qualities of being immanent and being the controller—which distinguish [the Self] from kings and the like, as well as from space and the like—the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmatva*) is established.
The phrase *kartāram* means the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartā*) with respect to the activities of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Alternatively, it means "the agent of the act of impelling. This is stated as: "He is the instigator. In order to strengthen the definitive purport (*aidamparya*) of the scriptures already cited, he mentions the support of the corroborative texts of Manu and others: "And the Smṛtis," and so forth. Even in this regard...
He states that this very same point will be explained later in the scripture by means of the sign of repeated practice,

beginning with the words "And of all. Furthermore, in order to reveal the intended meaning of the verse "All [beings] in Me," he shows that both the direct and indirect references to the Lord of Pārtha have the Lord alone as their single object.

Having thus established the nature of the object by employing two statements, [the text] demonstrates that the knowledge of it is the cause for the renunciation of agency; this is shown through the three words: "having renounced," "free from desire," and "free from the sense of 'mine'."

This [verse] elucidates that each subsequent [abandonment] has the preceding one as its cause—a sequence indicated by the order of recitation—namely, the abandonment of agency, the abandonment of fruits, and the abandonment of attachment to ownership (*svakīyatā*).
The phrase "for this reason" (*ataḥ*) means that this matter is established by other Śruti and Smṛti texts. The phrase "performed by Me alone" (*mayaiva kriyamāṇāni*)...
The sense is that it is like a king who, while employing his servants, acts as the protector of all beings;
for just as a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) might have an expectation of a fruit for himself despite acting on behalf of another, this [expectation] is here refuted.

With the intention of stating that it has been said [in the previous verse] "free from desire," he says: "And those... He explains "from that very source" as follows: for attachment to action arises through its fruit, in the form of the thought, "This action is for my sake because it is a means to achieve what I desire."

The sense is that the realization of God’s sovereignty over action constitutes one’s qualification [for renunciation]. Now, if agency has been surrendered to God, how then is the individual soul (jīva) designated as the agent in the command "fight"? And if he is free from desire (nirāśīḥ), how...?
Would one engage even in action that consists of the worship of the Supreme Person? And if one is free from the sense of "mine," how could one perform action while perceiving it as "this is my work"?
Furthermore, if one does not attend to one's own agency, then [one would likewise not attend to] the agency consisting of renunciation.
One should not think [thus]; and consequently, [the claim] that "he is free from fever" would also be untenable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "as the agent by means of his own self.
The meaning is: as the prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) by means of the individual soul (*jīva*) which exists as a subordinate part of himself.

"And by means of his own implements": the sense is that just as this living being is a remnant belonging to another, so too the sacrificial oblation and other items previously intended for him as his own property are, by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so), established as being remnants belonging to another.

"For the sole purpose of His own propitiation. The sense is that for the subordinate (the *śeṣa*), the only purpose is to bestow excellence upon the principal (*śeṣin*). And it has been said in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*:
"That whose very nature consists in being desirable through the desire to bestow excellence upon another..."

"The remainder" (śeṣaḥ) and "the supreme object of service" (paraḥ śeṣīḥ). In the passage beginning with "by his own," the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indicated. Thus it was stated: "the one who is the object of service for all," and so forth. Regarding the word "himself" (*svayam eva*): the sense is that he, being the very object of worship (*ārādhyabhūta*), causes the act of worship to be performed. By the use of the particle "eva" (only), any other instigator is excluded.

Or it is refuted [by the following]: "He causes [them] to act. Although He is the Lord of all and capable of performing everything Himself according to His own will, He [causes them to act] for the sake of establishing that the individual souls (jīvas), who are subordinate to Him, are subject to the scriptures and are the enjoyers of their fruits. These [souls]...

The sense is that the agent causes [the action] to be performed. By means of the words beginning with "prācīna," he demonstrates the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a specific type of fever—the fever of prohibition—regarding the subject under discussion.
Let it be granted that the nature of the Lord is established by scripture; however, as for His being the causer...

To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Lordship (īśvaratva) is the state of being a controller. The sense is that "the state of being the principal (śeṣitva) is the state of being the master (patitva)," meaning that the state of being the principal residing in a conscious being is precisely the state of being the master. Alternatively, [the question may be]: what is the difference between the state of being the principal and lordship as recited in the Śruti and the Bhāṣya?
The doubt is thus dispelled by [the arguments] beginning with "lordship is the state of being a controller."

In the verse beginning with "ye me matam" (those who follow my teaching), because the phrase "my teaching" demonstrates the authoritative conviction (*siddhāntābhimāna*) of the Upaniṣadic Puruṣa, and because the purpose is merely to instruct on the means to liberation, he says [the following] with the intention that this verse is primarily intended to praise that [teaching].

"This very one is direct" means that it is independent of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). It is the essence, the principal element. The lexicographers state: "The word *sāra* is used in the sense of strength and the firm part; as a neuter noun it means 'just' or 'right,' and as a masculine adjective it means 'excellent. And here, its predominance is intended.
Regarding the superiority [of the path] in the means to liberation:

because the word *mānava* here includes those such as Śūdras who are not qualified [for Vedic study], and because it excludes those such as gods who are [already] qualified, in order to avoid both of these [extremes], the word "he" (*yaḥ*)—
by way of restating what is established by valid means of knowledge— is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of the mere possessor of qualification.

This was stated with the intention of referring to "sound" (śabda). Regarding the statement that those humans who are qualified for the scriptures perform [the rites] eternally, such eternal performance must indeed be preceded by a definitive determination; for the performance of one who lacks the certainty of its authoritative validity is not [true] performance.
This was stated with the intention that [the teaching] might sometimes even be broken.

"This alone is the meaning of the scripture," and so forth—this refers to what was said as "this alone"; or else, the construction is: "having determined that 'this is my view, the meaning of the scripture'"; for indeed, the meaning of the scripture is precisely the view of the Teacher.
The term "those who possess faith" refers to a state prior to actual practice; thus he says: "and those who, even though not practicing..."
He says that those in a state even more recent than that are *anasūyā* (the envious), with the words "and those who are faithless.
With the intention of defining envy (*asūyā*) according to the etymology "envy is the manifestation of faults in [others'] virtues," he says "in this.
The word "also" (*api*) is intended to include all three groups together. They.

It has been stated that [the word] "all" [is used]. Now, one might object: "When a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is possible, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not desired. Furthermore, in passages such as "those who have faith," it is improper to supply the verb "they exist" (*bhavanti*), especially since the relative pronoun *yat* occurs in only one place [of the two clauses].
To the objection that "the repetition of what has already been enjoined is untenable," he says: "te 'pi" (those too).
Regarding "eṣām" (of these)—it refers either to the qualified persons (adhikāriṇām) or to the sentences residing in the intellect.
The intended meaning is this: syntactic unity (ekavākyatvam) is not possible here, because of the lack of connection with the word "api" (also/even).

Alternatively, the word "api" (also/even) here may be intended to include other types of qualified persons along with the performers [of ritual action], or it may be intended to indicate the inferiority of those performers. In that regard, although a combination [of knowledge and action] is possible for those who practice the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), it is not required here.

Furthermore, it is improper to disparage those who praise the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). To suggest that practitioners of the yoga of action (*karmayogins*) are inferior to practitioners of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayogins*) is utterly contradictory here; for [the Lord] intends to encourage the constant performance [of action].

Furthermore, the mention of the qualifiers "possessing faith" (*śraddhāvantaḥ*) and "not being envious" (*anasūyantaḥ*) would be purposeless; for those who perform the obligatory rites (*nitya*) could not possibly be lacking in faith or being envious.
However, if these refer to the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], they may be intended to signify their conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Alternatively, the word "api" (even/also) can be interpreted as referring to the inferiority of those in a later stage;

for if there were equal results for both those who perform the rites and those who possess merely faith and freedom from envy, then the scriptures that enjoin the performance of the rites would be rendered purposeless.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Now... Furthermore, the fact that faith (*śraddhā*) and freedom from envy (*anasūyā*) are causes for the removal of sin is [stated in the verse]: "O King of Kings, whether heard, seen, remembered, or even spoken of, or even rejoiced in, Dharma purifies a person."
This is established by the verse beginning with "always" (*sadā*).
With the intention that even by censuring the opposite [of the desired state], the excellence of the stated meaning is expressed,

he says "Bhagavat" (the Blessed One). With the intention that the body is indeed the very thing to be enjoined as the opposite of what was previously mentioned, he uses the three words beginning with "my support" (*madādhāra*).

Furthermore, [the cognition] is dependent upon its own nature, its subsistence, and its activity. Since it is considered to consist of a particular modification of the supreme intellect (*parabuddhi-vṛtti-viśeṣa-rūpa*), how could it be something to be performed or not to be performed? And how could there be performance with respect to an already established reality? To this, he says—by supplying the intended ellipsis: "not by thus reflecting."
"Especially deluded regarding all cognitions"—
this means that due to ignorance of the true nature of the Self as it actually exists, they are confused regarding all cognitions such as "I" and "mine," and regarding the objects to be known.
The meaning is that they are ignorant of the nature and modes of things as they truly exist.
"Destroyed" means rendered unfit for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Is even the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) devoid of the knowledge of what is to be done?

Regarding the statement "it does not exist," he says: "The conscious [being] is the effect. The sense is that because the effect is perceived, it is figuratively asserted that the cause does not exist. He states the conclusion:
"Those with perverted knowledge are deluded in every respect."
In order to provide a transition to the subsequent section and for the sake of ease of comprehension,
he summarizes what was previously stated with the word "thus" (*evam*). He says "of those connected with *prakṛti*" because, for liberated beings, agency does not depend upon the *guṇas*.
With the intention that the immediately following section is devoted to establishing the difficulty and other reasons for the lack of regard for the yoga of knowledge, he says: "Beyond this.
Furthermore, the reason why people do not practice is intended by the words beginning with "similarly" (*sadṛśam*).
In the phrase "even one who possesses knowledge," it is not merely mundane knowledge that is being referred to; for in that case...

Because there is no contradiction with the activity that is favorable to *prakṛti*, and because the word "also" (*api*) would not be applicable [otherwise]; nor is it knowledge culminating in the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*), since in that state there is no possibility of following after *prakṛti*. Therefore, having taken as its object that [state] in which one engages in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*)...

That knowledge which is capable of proceeding is what is intended here; and with the intention that this is the knowledge of the reality of the Self as it truly is, produced by the scripture, he says:
"distinct from primordial matter" (*prakṛtivivikta*). "Of such a kind" (*īdṛśa*).
This is a specification of the essential nature as characterized by being the remainder of another (paraśeṣatva) and so forth, exactly as it exists.
"That very [nature]" serves to exclude the experience of [ordinary] objects. "At all times" means until the attainment of the fruit. "Its own" means its individual or specific [nature].

For passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) are the uncommon causes of activity in the form of volitional engagement (*cetanāpravṛtti*), and these two are mentioned in the immediately preceding verse. Furthermore, their root is precisely the ancient latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, by the word "nature" (*prakṛti*) here, it is the beginningless latent impression—which is worthy of being designated as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*)—that is intended.

It was stated with the intention that [the mind] "desires to speak" (vivakṣita). By the phrase "of ancient latent impressions" (*pracīnavāsanāyāḥ*), he expresses the intended correspondence (*ānurūpya*). By the phrase "in regard to ordinary objects" (*prākṛtaviṣayeṣu*), the meaning is that through the latent impressions of objects such as sound and so forth, one again engages in those very same [objects].
"Why? [The opponent asks: "If he possesses knowledge, let him act in accordance with that knowledge;

why does he act in accordance with his nature (*prakṛti*)?"; this is the meaning. The answer here is: "Beings follow their own nature. Avoiding the suspicion of tautology, [the author] establishes its status as an answer:

He explains: "Inert" (acid). The meaning is that the restriction is that living beings are conjoined with the inert. In this context, it is not appropriate to supply the agent of the punishment as "either me or another," for even one who does not desire [the punishment]...
In accordance with the contextual meaning of these and other passages, it is appropriate that [the world] was indeed created by the Author of the Śāstra.
As for the phrase "what will it do?": the meaning is that nothing at all can be obstructed.

With the intention of stating that the intermediate operation in the capacity of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) to be the cause of activity corresponding to itself is now being described, he says: "in accordance with one's nature" (*prākṛtyanuyāyitve*).

The repetition "of each sense, of each sense" (indriyasyendriyasya) is intended to include all the senses. Thus, there is the inclusion of both the organs of cognition (jñānendriya) and the organs of action (karmendriya). Here, the word *artha* refers to the objects (*viṣaya*), because that which is to be accomplished (the goal) is the object of activity; and thus, speech and the other [functions] are also included here.

The meaning of the word *artha* has been shown. In the phrase "in the case of established [states]," there is an explanation of the meaning of the prefix (*upa-*). Regarding the term "inevitable" (*avarjanīya*): since it is stated that the cause of activity is the desire (*icchā*) resulting from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it follows that this is indeed the latent impression of knowledge (*jñāna-vāsanā*).

By way of being the cause of karma, it is called "karmic impression" (karmavāsanā); this also indicates that there is no other kind of impression. As it is said, "Lust and hatred are established toward each sense-object," just as there is lust for objects such as sound and so forth.
One might raise the doubt as to whether hatred (*dveṣa*) is also spontaneous by nature; to dispel that, he says:
"The experience of that. When the doubt arises as to what follows from that, he states the intended meaning by unifying [the two] with the verse, "One acts in accordance with [one's own nature]."
"Those two, thus"—the meaning is: in the manner described above, which follows the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
By the phrase "with all the senses restrained," it is indicated that they are forcibly constrained for even a moment by closing [the eyes] and so forth. "In their own functions... [and so on].
The meaning is: in the experience of sense objects and in actions such as speaking and grasping.

He then recalls what was previously elaborated upon, from the passage beginning with "From attachment arises [passion]" up to the end, "Through the destruction of the intellect, one perishes," by saying, "And therefore this..."

"One should not come under their sway"—this does not merely signify a prohibition against attachment; rather, by implication, it states that the path of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) is not to be disregarded, and with the intention of declaring that very path as what is to be grasped, he says: "By the yoga of knowledge. However, at the commencement of the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*),...

The sense is that because [the mind] engages with objects of a similar kind long practiced, there is no forceful compulsion by passion and hatred. "Having come, one should not perish" means that one should avoid falling under their power, which is the cause of destruction. As for how destruction occurs upon falling under their power:
He introduces the fourth quarter [of the verse] in response to a doubt with the words, "For those two...
He states that they are difficult to conquer, intending the form that will be described in the verses beginning with, "This is desire, this is anger."
It applies the state of being an obstacle to the subject at hand: "they obstruct the practice of knowledge. The meaning is that they stand like robbers on the path to liberation.

Regarding the word "better" (*śreyān*) in this verse: the terms *svadharma* (one's own duty) and *paradharma* (the duty of another) are not employed here with reference to the [four] social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), because the performance of the duties belonging to other classes, stages of life, and so forth has been long since rejected, making their prohibition impossible. And here...

Because that contingency does not exist; and since it has been stated that "one's own duty, though deficient, is better than the supreme duty well-performed," and because the word *śreyas* denotes being more praiseworthy, it would follow [absurdly] that one's own duty—even when performed by another—would merely be praiseworthy; and this is not the case.
That is appropriate; for a duty belonging to another, whether it be poorly performed or not established in oneself, is censurable as being unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Now, [this concerns] Arjuna, who desired to abandon battle, which is the duty of a Kṣatriya.

If it is argued that the praise of battle as one's own duty (*svadharma*) and the censure of abandoning it as contrary to the duties of a Brahmin and others are being performed, then let it be so; yet, even with this much, while the possibility of the prohibited act (*niṣedhya*) arises, the objection regarding the mere contingency of its being praised has not been resolved. Nor is there [such a thing] here.

Arjuna’s intention was, "Having abandoned my own duty (*svadharma*), I shall perform the duty of another (*paradharma*); in this very case, the notion that it is my own duty (*svadharmatva*) would now perish. If it is argued that while he is deluded by the idea of it being his own duty, the fact that it is actually the duty of another is being made known here—that is not so.

Because it would be impossible for [the statement] "than a well-performed duty of another" to be a mere restatement (anuvāda); such a designation is only appropriate if [the action] is recognized as being the duty of another. And in that case, making known its status as the duty of another would be purposeless, since [the prohibition] concerns only its being unrighteous (adharma).
Because it is that which is to be made known.

Therefore, in this context, the words "one's own duty" (*svadharma*) and "another's duty" (*paradharma*) refer, by virtue of their being praiseworthy and contemptible respectively, to the subject matter at hand: the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) and the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). And thus it would be; now—
The question found in the subsequent verse, "By what [is it done]? (keneti), is likewise appropriate here;

for in this context, the question is "What is the cause of committing sinful acts even against one's will? and that question would be consistent only with the statement regarding the difficulty of the path of knowledge (jñānayoga).

If it is argued that the meaning of the question is "By whom was this abandonment of the duty of a Kṣatriya done even against his will?", we say no; for he was not unwilling [to fight], and because subsequent statements such as "This is desire, this is anger" would otherwise be inconsistent. Indeed, not...
It was stated even at the outset that Arjuna is renouncing the fight not out of desire or anger, but rather out of compassion and so forth;
therefore, the terms *svadharma* (one's own duty) and *paradharma* (the duty of another) refer to duties that are possible for oneself and duties that are possible for another, respectively.
Intending all of this, he says: "Therefore, because it is easily performed.
"Therefore" means by virtue of following the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) described in the two preceding verses.
"Even if deficient" means even if one is lacking in the auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*). How [can there be success] for one who is deficient?

This has been stated in the passage beginning with "śreyastvam" (the state of being the highest good). The phrase "containing non-negligence" (*apramādagarbha*) implies that mere deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) serves as the gateway [to bondage] through the interruption of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The word "su-" (well-) in the term *svaniṣṭhatā* (abiding in oneself) refers to the form of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to that deficiency.

"Even from the excellence of the qualities," etc. Since the word *anuṣṭhita* ends in a suffix denoting a past state (*bhūtārtha*), and since being past consists in having transcended [the present], it is with the intention of indicating that there was first performance and subsequently an interruption that this was stated.
"From that which has been practiced for some time, [but] with negligence"— thus,
if the interruption were not intended to be expressed, then the statement "the yoga of action, though deficient, is better than the yoga of knowledge established in oneself" would be inconsistent.
The sense is that for a rite endowed with its constituent qualities (*saguṇa*) and performed without interruption, there is an invariable concomitance with the fruit.

By explaining the reason stated as "because it is easy to perform," he clarifies the meaning of the term *svadharma* (one's own duty), [showing] that for a rite devoid of its qualities (*viguṇa*), there is no such invariable concomitance with the fruit.

He explains the third quarter of the verse, which is intended to resolve the doubt regarding [the soul's] superiority, with the words "by itself" (*svenaiva*). The meaning is: "by the sense-organ itself, which is active through its association with *prakṛti*"; or rather, the sense is "by its own will alone."
Explaining that what is intended is "in a single birth," he addresses the question of how that which is deficient in qualities can still be a means to the fruit even in another birth, stating:
"by being unhindered by obstacles."
The meaning is that because the nature of *karmayoga* is not completely severed by the presentation of objects of the same class as those previously experienced by the senses;
here, "unagitated" (*avyākula*) means "unimpaired" (*avikala*).

And all of this will be elaborated upon in the passage beginning with, "In this [path], there is no loss of effort. It was stated that [this is so] because there is no certainty regarding the fullness [of results] in the immediately following birth, as such a possibility exists.
The sense is that the fruit is established as occurring either immediately after or in the very next [birth].
If it is argued that the superiority of karma-yoga is stated with reference to its fruit residing in a future birth because it is deficient in qualities, then why is the same not said for jñāna-yoga?
In the word *syāt*, he explains the fourth quarter [of the verse]: "prakṛti...

etc. This is with the intention that even in another birth, the fruit is not possible; for how could there be [a fruit] in another birth for that which has been severed in its own nature and is said to be "bringing fear"?
What is the result? The meaning is that the result of an uninterrupted [action] that is deficient in quality is delayed.
But has it not been stated in the passage beginning with "they act in accordance" that [beings] follow their latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?
And latent impressions impel a conscious being through the medium of desire.
This being so, for one who desires the yoga of knowledge, there would be an experience of sense objects which is contrary to that [knowledge].
He asks, "What is the cause of its activity? with the words, "Then by what?
In this context, the reading found in Yādavaprakāśa’s text—“even though unwilling, he is forcibly constrained as a giver”—is a corrupt reading. Here, the word *atha* has the sense of a question.

Alternatively, [the word] "entirely" (*kārtsnyapara*) refers to the recollection of those designated as possessing knowledge by means of their possession of knowledge. With the intention that the word "this" (*ayam*) [refers to them], it was said:
"This one has set out for the yoga of knowledge."

The meaning of the word *puruṣa* is this: "I do not act even by way of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) without prior desire, because I am conscious. Even those who have no desire act when impelled by wind, water, and so forth;
likewise, in this case as well, [one acts] due to some powerful impeller.
Thinking that [the meaning] must be so, he said "by force" (*balāt*) and so forth.

In order to avoid the contradiction with the question "By whom? regarding the phrase "as if constrained by force," the syntactical connection is stated by means of a change in order: "constrained by the force of wind, water, and so forth."
Just as one acts even when not desiring it, so too does this person act; the meaning of the question is: "By what is that person impelled?"

Then, expanding upon the very meaning already stated in the summary beginning with "of the sense-organ" (*indriyasya*) as an answer to the question, the Blessed One said: "This is desire" (*kāma eṣa*).
[He did so] by showing how the seeds of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the experience of objects give rise to the sprouts of desire, anger, and so forth.

The quality of *rajas* is like the sprinkling of water; in our view, desire (*kāma*) and so forth are attributes of the self (*ātman-dharma*) consisting of specific forms of knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣa-rūpa*), whereas *rajas* is a quality of primordial nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
To the question of how an attribute belonging to one thing can produce an effect in another, it has been stated [in the following].

Regarding the phrase "due to contact with *prakṛti*, which consists of the *guṇas*": the sense is that just as a blister or similar effect occurs on the palm of the hand and so forth due to contact with fire, which is the locus of heat, so too do desire and other such states arise in the self (*ātman*) due to its association with *prakṛti*, which is the locus of the *guṇas*. If that is so, [then it follows] from the association with *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*...
To the question, "Why should even the knowledge of the effects, such as the existence of sentient beings and so forth, not occur simultaneously?", it is said here:
"existing in the form of manifestation and suppression.
The word "of this" (*asya*) refers back to the word "this" (*ayam*) mentioned in the preceding verse.
The objection that there is a consequence of transformation is raised: "How can even the mere commencement of the yoga of knowledge belong to one in whom the quality of *rajas* predominates?
This is refuted by the intention that, through the process of emergence and suppression, there may at some point arise, in the interim, a certain degree of the manifestation of *sattva*.

It has been stated, "of one who has begun [action] for the sake of knowledge. In the word *ārabdha*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in the expression "the Brahmins have eaten" (*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*). By the word *eṣa* ("this"), that which prompts sinful conduct—the subject of the question—is referred to. By that very [prompting], it is said: "one acts in accordance with [one's nature]."

Intending to remind one of the meaning stated in the two verses beginning with "indriyasyendriyasyārthe," the two qualifiers beginning with "prācīna" have been mentioned; [these refer to] the previously mentioned attachment and aversion.

The meaning is that these two, having entered into different states, are designated here by the words "desire" (*kāma*) and "anger" (*krodha*). The explanation of "great-eating" (*mahāśana*) is: "it draws him toward sense-objects.
He for whom there is great eating—that is, enjoyment—is a "great-eater. This one... [ita]

Due to the repetition of the instruction, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, in this context, both sentences have one and the same subject matter, though presented through different aspects. Otherwise, had the question been "What is the instigator of sinful conduct?", the answer would have had to be stated in the form of "This desire and this anger," and so forth.
And immediately thereafter, it should be stated: "one should pierce these enemies here.
And likewise in the six subsequent verses. Thus: *etena*, *kāmarūpeṇa*, *asya eṣaḥ*, *enaṃ*, *yaḥ saḥ kāmarūpam*.

And a universal statement is being made here; it is not a separate designation from "desire" (kāma). Therefore, desire itself is intended here as "anger" (krodha) through a distinction of states; and because it refers to these two distinct states, there is no split in the sentence.

The term *ucitaḥ* (appropriate) [is used]. With the intention that both the two phrases "one who eats much" (*mahāśana*) and "one who has great sin" (*mahāpāpmā*) refer respectively to those two objects according to their predominance and propriety, he says: "This very one... (*eṣa eva*).

"Obstructed movement" is stated as the cause for the transformation known as anger (*krodha*). This was said both to demonstrate the difference between the state of anger and the state of desire (*kāma*) regarding the same single object, such as sound and so forth, and to avoid the logical fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

"Obstructing," and so forth. This explains the state of being a great sinner (*mahāpāpmatā*): it is that which incites one toward violence against others and the like. One who possesses a great sin as its effect is a "great sinner" (*mahāpāpmā*). As it is said: "In a rage, one might even kill one's own gurus."
For this is well known: having presented the previously mentioned cause— known as the quality of *rajas*, described in this verse,

and designated by the term "nature" (*prakṛti*), which is also called "latent impression" (*vāsanā*)— and having characterized it as being distinguished by the state of being the effect of both of those, the pronoun "this" (*enam*) functions as a reference to what has already been mentioned.

With the intention that [the mind] "clings" [to objects], the two words "arising from the quality of rajas" (rajoguṇasamudbhavam) and "innate" (sahajam) have been stated. Regarding the word "here" (iha) in the phrase "here [is] the enemy," it is stated with the intention that the word "here" refers to the domain of the yoga of knowledge sought by one who is characterized by negligence.
"Contrary to the yoga of knowledge."
The manner of enmity is now stated: "By smoke," and so forth. In this context, everything up to the word "yathā" (just as) constitutes a single sentence;

the word "yathā" is understood to be connected to the phrase "ādarśo malena ca" (and a mirror by dirt) because of the presence of the particle "ca" (and). This is indicated for the sake of clarity by the statement "yathā dhūmena" (just as by smoke).

Because in the preceding verse even anger was designated as a particular state of desire, and because in the subsequent [verse] it continues to be referred to by that very term— using "in the form of desire" (*kāmarūpeṇa*) and "the form of desire" (*kāmarūpam*)— here too, by the word "that" (*tat*), [it refers back to that same thing].
Because it is desire itself that is being grasped, the phrase "by that desire" is stated for the sake of clarification.

Although there is a general indication by the word "this," since it is impossible for the insentient to be grasped, and because it is appropriate— given the context— to include all knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), the word "this" [refers to them].

This was stated with the intention that, because of the priority of what is to be explained hereafter and because of the natural sense of the well-known worldly usage of "priority," the term *kṣetrajñāna* (knowledge of the Knower of the Field) refers here to its obscuration— as in such passages as "by which the power of the Knower of the Field is enveloped. This...

Or, regarding the phrase "the multitude of beings" (*jantujātam*): by the word *jantu*, the state of possessing a body is intended, thereby demonstrating their fitness for obscuration. The word *jāta* is used to show that the neuter gender refers to a general category. Their "innateness" (*sahajatva*) consists in being bound by beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

The employment of three examples is intended to demonstrate that even for one who has desisted, there may be a repeated return due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and that it is impossible to turn back by one's own will.

To avoid the charge of redundancy regarding the passage beginning with "Knowledge is covered" (*āvṛtaṃ jñānam*), he says: "He states the manner of the covering. The intention here is that when it is stated, "This is covered by that," even if there is an expectancy as to what is covered, an expectancy as to how it is covered is likewise appropriate.
In this context, the word "knower" (*jñānin*) does not refer to one who possesses perfected knowledge, because for such a person,

there is an absence of knowledge being obscured by desire. Therefore, with the intention that it is more appropriate for the term to refer to all *kṣetrajñas* (embodied souls) whose knowledge is as yet unperfected, [the author says...]

It has been stated that "this living being is a knower" (*jñānin*). Here, the term *jñānin* is used to demonstrate that the possessive suffix (*matup*) refers to an inherent relationship established by scripture, and to illuminate that the veil (*āvaraṇa*) is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus, it is said to be "of the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvabhāva*).
Even for the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), who is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma, there is no obscuration of the knowledge of objects such as sound and so forth;

thus it is said that his knowledge has the Self as its object. Since the term "kāmarūpa" is well-known to mean "having a form assumed according to one's own will," the following was stated in order to dispel that misconception:
"By way of its desired form" means that,
by implication from its nature as desire, it manifests the manner in which knowledge regarding the self is obscured. "By generating delusion toward objects" refers to [desire] as a constant enemy.

The meaning is: "by the beginningless enemy" up to the limit of the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*). Furthermore, according to the position that eternal transmigratory existence (*nityasaṃsāra*) is established, its status as an eternal enemy is proven in the case of certain selves.
The meaning of the word *anala* is the absence of satiety (*alaṃbhāva*) even when [objects] are obtained through yogic powers.
"This pit of craving is bottomless; by whom can it be filled?
Even when great things are thrown into it, it is only further dug up.
In this manner stated, [craving] is the cause of engagement in those improper activities that are difficult to avoid.
The word *duṣpūra* is a synonym for fire, used figuratively with respect to desire; the sense is that, just like fire, there can be neither a division of objects nor a fulfillment [of desire] for it.
Thus the types of obscurations have been described; now, with the intention of teaching that they must subsequently be restrained, he asks "by what?"—meaning:
by what [means] does one overcome the independent self-conceit (ātma-māna) which presides over the self, and [subdue] that which is dependent?

The meaning is "it acts. Here, by the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word "sense-organ" (*indriya*) refers specifically to the external sense-organs. "Intellect" (*buddhi*) here refers to the determination that non-human goals are human goals;
this is intended to exclude cognitions such as those concerning the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) which are not relevant to the present context.
He demonstrates the derivation [of the word *karaṇa*] as an instrument (*vyutpatti*) by stating, "by means of these it presides.

The sense is that it is said [to be the agent] because it deludes by means of these. In order to show the intermediate operation of the senses and so forth, which serve as the instruments for the act of presiding, it is stated that they are "inclined toward objects. [This is further qualified by the phrase] "associated with *prakṛti*."
The sense is that by the word *deha* (body), the inevitability of the senses and so forth, as well as their subjection to the qualities (*guṇas*), are indicated.

The prefix *vi-* refers to the various types of delusion mentioned in such passages as: "That which is the notion of self in what is not-self, and that which is the thought of 'mine' in what is not one's own."

With this intention, he says: "It deludes in various ways. By explaining the manifold nature of delusion through the illusion of enjoyability regarding what is not enjoyable (the self), and the illusion of non-enjoyability regarding objects which are enjoyable, he demonstrates its relevance to the present subject matter.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the self":
Now, since desire has the self as its locus and the senses, mind, and intellect as its instruments,
the restraint of the senses is taught as the means for conquering desire by the verse beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This word "therefore" refers to that which has been under discussion.
Reflecting on the difficulty of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) in the manner previously described, he says, "Because...
and so forth. The reference "you" (*tvam*) is stated with the intention that it pertains to Arjuna’s state at that time, due to his being joined with *prakṛti*.

"You are intent upon the activity of the senses"—by the word "at first," he states what is intended here: "liberation," etc. Here, the restraint of the senses does not mean the absolute cessation of activity, because that is impossible at the outset; and this has already been explained in detail previously for the sake of *karmayoga*.

The restraint of the senses was previously stated in such passages as, “He whose senses... with the mind,” and so forth. Therefore, with the intention that it should be described in the same way here as well, it is said: “conforming to the activity of the senses,” and so on.
From the context, it is established that both *jñāna* and *vijñāna* have the Self as their object.
And in this regard, it is just as in the case of the Brāhmaṇas: "among the Brāhmaṇas, the learned; among the learned, those of perfected intellect."
It was stated with the intention that there is no tautology because [the two terms] have as their objects the essential nature and its distinction [from others].
Regarding the phrase "the essential nature of the Self" and so forth: *vijñāna* means knowledge through discrimination;
the meaning is knowledge by way of exclusion. It refers to the Self as qualified by such attributes as directness (*pratyak*), consciousness (*jñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), and so on.
The essential nature (*svarūpa*). Here, the group of distinguishing attributes consists of atomicity, eternity, being a knower, being an enjoyer, being an agent, and so forth.
Discrimination (*viveka*). Or, it is simply this much: that there exists a self distinct from the body.

The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is what is intended here; qualities such as inwardness (*pratyaktva*) are also intended as distinct [from it], just like atomicity (*aṇutva*) and so forth. Alternatively, all that is the intrinsic nature. "Discrimination" (*viveka*) means the instrument of discrimination, namely the scripture; from that, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) [is established] therein.

With the intention of showing that [the obstacles] are designated as increasingly more contradictory for the sake of establishing their relative degrees of intensity (taratamatva) and so forth, he says: "among those things opposed to knowledge.
Since the word *para* cannot here mean "cause" and so on, it is intended to signify "predominance" (*prādhānya*) alone.
And this was stated with the intention that, by virtue of the context, it refers to opposition to knowledge;
thus, "the paths are primary in their opposition to knowledge.
Furthermore, the primacy of the sense faculties is relative to other opposing factors such as place, time, and so forth, which take the form of generalities.
Or, [the mind is superior] because of its subtlety and difficulty of perception in relation to the body.
He states the reason for the primacy of the senses and the manner of their opposition with the words "yataḥ" (since).
He states the reason for the mind's superiority over the senses with the words "indriyeṣu" (among the senses).
From the preceding sentence, the word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied. This should likewise be understood in the subsequent causal statements.

Self-knowledge [does not arise] even when the external senses have ceased from their objects through the non-proximity of those objects or by forceful restraint, provided that the mind continues to contemplate those various objects.

It would not be so; therefore, even at the time when the sense of touch ceases, because of its opposition [to the others], it is superior to them. He states the reason for the mind being superior to the intellect: "In the mind, when there is another modification," and so on.
Now, one might ask: if the mind is averse to engaging with other objects, how can there be the activity of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) regarding those objects?
For, having apprehended some object with the mind, it is precisely therein that one resolves, "I shall do" or "I shall not do," and so forth.

It is said: here, what is intended is not the cessation of all mental activity (*manas*) nor a mere turning away from other mental modifications (*vṛtti*); rather, it is the cessation of the mind's natural inclination toward other objects, which is otherwise impossible to restrain even by force.
And this was indicated in the preceding sentence: "when the mind is inclined toward objects."

Therefore, even if the mind— due to chance, sleep, laziness, and so forth— is not by its own nature solely intent upon sense objects, it will certainly still possess such a tendency toward them if it engages in the perception of a contrary path through mere stubbornness and the like.
And thus: in the phrase "but of the mind" (*manasastu*), the word "but" (*tu*) is intended to dispel doubt, or rather, to indicate such a distinction [from the preceding].
He states the reason for desire being superior even to the path (*adhvan*) in the words "in all... (*sarveṣu*). This refers to its being the effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And it is described as a synonym for "desire" (icchā) in order to illuminate its status as the cause of a determination (adhyavasāya) corresponding to itself.
As to how desire can arise at the time when the senses, mind, and intellect have ceased their activity, it is stated here: "arising from rajas."
The meaning is that [the mind] arises solely from the mental faculty (manas) which is defiled by the dust stirred up by past karma (*prācīnakarma*).

Now, one might ask: "Even if the turning away of the senses and so forth from other objects is established, what contradiction is there in the continued existence of the desire for those objects? For it is possible for the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and the inclination of the mind (*manaḥ-prāvaṇya*) to be directed toward that very object through the desire for self-realization (*ātmānubhava*). To this, it is said:
"‘That very [desire]’ and so forth. It is true that desire for the self (ātma-icchā) indeed exists;
for that is occasional and rooted in a small degree of sattva. Desire for objects (viṣaya-icchā), however, is rooted in rajas and follows continuously, being brought forth by accumulated past karma."

Therefore, the meaning is that as long as the desire for the Self performs such functions as the perception and determination of the Self, so long will the desire for objects remain powerful and perform only the experience and determination of objects.

Thus, in this context, the statement that desire is the initiator of the preceding [states] should be understood as an indication that the intellect and the mind are also initiators of their respective preceding states.
This is indicated by the two words "arising from rajas" and "having set in motion."

The disparity characterized by the fact that desire arises independently of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth, and thus lacks the nature of an auxiliary cause (*anupakaraṇatva*), has been explained as indicated by the word "but" (*tu*). Dispelling the confusion regarding the word having a different meaning or being a non-sequitur (*ananvaya*), he takes up the fourth quarter [of the verse] as being directed toward the stated meaning, saying: "This is what is said."

Regarding the word *parataḥ*, since it is the meaning of the word *para* occurring in the three preceding sentences, its status as the nominative case is established by means of a suffix that functions for all cases (*sārvavibhaktika*). Furthermore, in the phrase *saḥ* (it),
it indicates the substantive established by the context, namely *buddheḥ* (of the intellect) as well.

The interpretation offered by some—that the ego (ahaṅkāra) is superior because it is the enjoyer, and the intellect (buddhi) is superior because it is the locus—is to be disregarded due to its lack of relevance to the present subject matter and other such reasons.
Now, [it may be objected]: "The objects are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects."

The intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind (manas), and the Great Self (mahān ātmā) is superior to the intellect. The Unmanifest (avyakta) is superior to the Great Self, and the Puruṣa is superior to the Unmanifest. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
For thus, in the Kaṭhavallī, the class of things to be governed is heard;

and this is clearly explained in the section beginning with "Even that which is based on inference, for some" (Brahmasūtra 1.4.1). That same point is recognized again in this verse. It is not [otherwise].

It should not be argued that these two [passages] have different meanings because objects are not mentioned between the senses and the mind, and because the phrases "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great" and "the Person is beyond [the Unmanifest]" are not included therein;
for it is logical that one mentions only a few while the other mentions everything, depending on whether they take the form of a summary or a detailed exposition.
Just as in the sections on creation and elsewhere there is an indication of certain individual and collective principles to be created,
because of the statement "they say," one must necessarily admit that this same meaning is expressed elsewhere; and thus,
for the phrase "He who is beyond the intellect," [the referent is] "the Great Self of the intellect."

Because it has the same meaning as the word "paraḥ" (the other/higher), it is appropriate that it refers specifically to the Self; and this being the case, in the subsequent verse as well— "having thus known [Him] who is beyond the intellect"— the word "ātman" ending in the accusative case is even more appropriately understood as referring to the conscious [Self].
Therefore, how is it explained that "he is desire"?
It is said: although that same triad beginning with the senses is indeed recognized here, nevertheless, that very sequence is not intended to be expressed here in its entirety;
for it was previously stated in this verse: "The senses, the mind, and the intellect."

For here, it is logical to teach the gradation (tāratamya) of these four adversaries—beginning with the senses and ending with desire—which have already been specified; furthermore, there is no violation of the sequence of the senses, mind, and intellect. However, if the intent were to convey the meaning of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad...
Because the objects [of sense] are not specified here, there would be a violation of the sequence by way of mere measure.

Since desire alone is designated as primary both previously and subsequently—given its nature as that which opposes and that which must be conquered—it is therefore desire itself that deserves to be designated here as the foremost of all, in the words: "That which is beyond the intellect, that is He."

Otherwise, the word "he" would have as its substantive the Upanishadic Self, which stands at a distance. If, however, the Self were also intended here as that which is to be controlled, then the Self would likewise have been designated as the locus in the passage, "The senses, mind, and intellect."

And this was not done [in that manner], for in that context, the self (*ātman*) is designated as being subject to delusion (*mohanīya*) by four [passions]. Therefore, only these four were intended to be negated by this [statement]; such being the case, the word "self" (*ātman*) appearing in the subsequent verse must also be explained in accordance with this.
Indeed, this is clearly a restatement of the same point in the words "thus beyond the intellect" (*evaṃ buddheḥ param*).

Furthermore, for the two actions beginning with "awakened" (*buddhā*) which reside in the two feet, their two respective objects are indeed distinct, as is naturally perceived. Therefore, in that context, the word *ātman* ends in the accusative case.

The object of the mind is indicated as that which is to be controlled. However, the word ending in the third case (instrumental) refers to the object of determination (*adhyavasāya*), which serves as the instrument for the control of the mind. Furthermore, the mention of "they say" (*āhuḥ*) does not necessarily imply the intention of the Upanishads; for [the context concerns] the senses.

"In accordance with such passages as, 'If one who is practicing [self-restraint] lets even a single sense-organ leak away, through that his wisdom leaks away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin,' it is appropriate to understand that Manu and others are speaking here. Therefore, by the statement, 'That which is beyond the intellect,
that is He,' it is desire (*kāma*) itself that is being indicated."
Having intended all of this, it was said, beginning with "That is what is being stated" and ending with "the meaning is that it is desire."

Having established that the mind finds its abode in the yoga of action by means of concluding the discussion on the heedlessness of the yoga of knowledge— which began with the verse "One acts in accordance with one's own nature" (3.33)—
the meaning of the entire chapter is now summarized in this verse beginning with "Thus."

Prior to the conquest of desire, the stabilization of the mind is indeed its placement within the yoga of action (*karmayoga*); it is not, however, the state of being completely mastered. This is because it was stated previously that as long as desire exists, there will still be agitation of the mind—this is the intended meaning behind the statement "having established [the mind] in the yoga of action."

The meaning is that it is difficult to approach for those who have not practiced *karmayoga*, whose sins have not been dispelled, and who have not donned the armor of very firm resolve (*sattva*); thus, it cannot be cast off even when its defects are perceived.
Furthermore, by superimposing the status of an enemy upon the insentient Desire (*kāma*), the implication is that it must be destroyed.
The intention is that [the word] "destruction" (*nāśanam*) alone is meant; thus, the gloss for both "abandon" (*prajahi*) and "slay" (*jahi*) is "destroy" (*nāśaya*).
Now, in order to explain the fourth connection (*saṃgati*), he summarizes the subject matter of the third chapter:

"The third chapter," and "with its cause" (*sahetukam*). This means preceded by the causes such as the presence of negligence (*sapramādatva*) and the absence of negligence (*niṣpramādatva*) in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). By this, [it is shown] through non-attachment...

"Having attributed agency to the qualities for the sake of protecting the world, or having entrusted it to the Lord of All, one should perform the duties mentioned in the third chapter. Thus the summary verse (*saṃgraha-śloka*) has also been explained. For one who is incapable, or even if capable yet not well-known, and who is skilled in his own interest, action through yoga (*karmayoga*) alone is to be performed.

The sense is that in the third chapter, the consideration of eligibility was undertaken— showing that for one who is already established [in worldly life], whether incapable or capable, that very same [householder's] duty must be performed for his own sake and for the protection of the world— and the distinction between the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) and the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) was also examined. Now, regarding that which was stated as being the basis for eligibility...

He states, "By the fourth [chapter]," that six topics are discussed here: the authoritative status of Karma-yoga, its nature as being mixed with knowledge, its essential form, its two-fold division, the predominance of the factor of knowledge within it, and the incidental discussion of the Lord’s incarnation. Now, one might object: "Is not the description of one's own nature [in the third chapter] merely incidental, and does this [fourth chapter] not concern the state of action being non-action?"

And: "The divisions [of knowledge] and its majesty are [treated] by the fourth. Now, an objection is raised: since four topics were summarized by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), how is it that six topics are here being enumerated? It is said in response:

"In the statement 'an incidental discussion is the expression of one's own essential nature,' *prasaṅga* refers to the occasioning of [the topic] as being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*). This...

In the phrase "and its divisions," since its divisions cannot be known without its essential nature (*svarūpa*), the essential nature is also intended; or else, by the word "and" (*ca*), that [nature] is included in conjunction [with the divisions]. In the *Saṃgraha* as well, only six topics are intended. "The statement of one's own nature" (*svasvabhāvoktiḥ*) means the statement of one's own nature, such as being an incarnation not subject to karma.
The state of non-action within action is the form of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), because knowledge is internal to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*);
the greatness of knowledge is the predominance of the element of knowledge contained within the yoga of action.
Thus, this [point] has also been explained by the commentary beginning with "by the fourth [verse]" and so forth. [This is] the duty to be performed.

For [this] was already stated in the third chapter; therefore, what is done here by means of a narrative of past events is merely to strengthen that [point]. This is the meaning of the phrase "having strengthened the duty to be performed. Having demonstrated the connection between the direct subjects of the chapters, he states the incidental matter separately with the words "and incidentally" (*prasaṅgāt*). [He refers to it as] "this" (*imam*).
He states the purport of the discourse on the succession of instructions preceded by a formal exposition with the words beginning "Even he who...

and ending with "...should not be so thought. Here, "yoga" refers to *karmayoga* (the yoga of action). In this context, the alternative interpretation [of others] which takes it as referring primarily to *jñānayoga* (the yoga of knowledge) is inconsistent with the subject matter at hand and contradicts what is to be said later, such as "Perform action," and so forth.

And this is the intended meaning: because it was spoken by Vivasvat, the progenitor of Manu and his instructor, and because it was [further] spoken by Arjuna; the word "in the beginning" (*ādau*) would otherwise contradict what is about to be stated later.
Because it was spoken by Vivasvat, the progenitor of Manu and his instructor, and by Arjuna... [the intended meaning is established].
And because the word "in the beginning" (ādau) will be restated later, the resulting meaning is stated as "at the beginning of a Manvantara.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of uplifting the entire world": it means not only for the purpose of inciting Arjuna to battle or for Arjuna alone, but rather for the sake of bestowing liberation upon the entire class of qualified aspirants; this is because the instruction was given at the beginning of a Manvantara.

Its universality across the entire world is indicated; furthermore, its imperishability (*avyayatva*) results from its abiding in the eternally omniscient Lord. Alternatively, its imperishability here is understood by way of its fruit. Moreover, the reference as "this" (*imam*) is intended to indicate that it also possesses the previously mentioned quality of being a means to liberation.
