The passage beginning with "parama" has been stated; the sense is that even previously it was not spoken for the sake of any other fruit. By the words "I have spoken," [it is implied] that at the beginning of a Manvantara, at the commencement of a Mahākalpa, or at the start of the Bhārata, anyone other than myself who could truly know and speak this is difficult to find.

This is the intended meaning. To state the true nature of his own incarnation—which must necessarily be known as a consequence [of the preceding discussion]—and to raise the doubt regarding the apparent contradiction with the time of Manu and others, he said, "I myself," and "I declared it to Vivasvat. For it was not taught by me to Asuras and the like.
The meaning is not merely the purpose of the scriptures beginning with the Buddha; rather, the intention is that [it was taught] to Vivasvat, who is the soul of all the Vedas.

And [it was passed down] from Vivasvat to Manu, and from Manu to Ikṣvāku. Because of the statement, "Whatever Manu said is medicine," it is characterized by speech that serves as medicine for the entire world.

The meaning is that [the tradition] has been obtained through a lineage of instruction descending from one’s father and ancestors— who belong to the ranks of those appointed to clearly maintain established boundaries—
but it has not proceeded from contact with potential deceivers, wicked people, heretics, and the like. All of this...
This is made clear by the phrase "by such a succession of tradition.

The intention is that, because the word *paraṃparā* (succession) includes those who are even more recent than Ikṣvāku, what is intended to be expressed is the uninterrupted continuity of the tradition from the Kṛta-yuga onwards. This is because its destruction is mentioned [elsewhere] at the present time.

Regarding this, it was stated: "The royal sages of old. The royal sages knew [this], for kings possess expansive and profound minds; moreover, by virtue of being sages (*ṛṣi*), they are capable of perceiving objects beyond the reach of the senses.
And they were many—such as Aśvapati, Janaka, Ambarīṣa, and others.
The sense is that all of them, without disagreement, have established themselves in this yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
He states here, as indicated by the word "here" (*iha*), the manner in which time and destiny (*kāladaivya*) act as causes for interruption:
[it occurs] due to the dullness of the intellect of various listeners. In this world, which is filled with diverse types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*),...

The sense is that in this world, throughout the ages such as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, it is observed and heard that intellectual power, capacity for performance, and other qualities have been diminishing over the course of time.
Regarding the word "destroyed" (naṣṭa), what is not intended here is absolute annihilation, since figures such as Vyāsa, Bhīṣma, and Akrūra exist even now.

It was stated with the intention that [the self] exists because it has been said, "it has become as if destroyed. By the expression "this very same one," the result of a definitive indication accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has been stated. By the terms "unswerving in its essential nature" and the two references "ancient" and "now," [its continuity is established].

It is indicated that there is no difference in essence or mode even by a mere difference in time. "You are a devotee" means you possess a mind full of love through the contemplation of the greatness seen in the scriptures; and "you are a friend" refers to the specific quality of accessibility perceived in the incarnations.

The meaning is: "You have become one who is contrary to [my] affection. Furthermore, the two words "bhaya" (fear) and "mā" (me) are also [implied by] the phrases "Instruct me, who has sought refuge in you" and "It was spoken by me to you who had sought refuge.
Regarding the word "prokta" (spoken), he explains the meaning of the verbal root along with its prefix: "at length, together with its ancillaries."

"Parikara" means an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*); it refers to the elaboration or expansion of the word. The sense is that the statement of the limbs here is also detailed. He states what was indicated by the two phrases "I have spoken" and "it was spoken by me today":
"by one other than me. This refers either to the dissolution (*pralaya*) or to the inherent nature of the beginning of a *yuga*.
The meaning is: should the tradition be interrupted, I alone shall be the one to re-establish it;
for it is impossible for anyone other than me—such as Hiraṇyagarbha or others, whose knowledge depends upon the instruments of perception—to know or to speak [this] without my instruction.

The phrase "the secret" (*rahasyam*) and so forth indicates that [the Lord] is the cause for being fit to receive instruction—being endowed with the fullness of qualities such as friendship, devotion, and surrender—and for the fact that He cannot be known or spoken of by anyone other than the Blessed One. This is shown by the word "since" (*yataḥ*); here, the particle *hi* functions as a reason.

Because it is a secret, it should be taught only to a worthy person. The distinction is that because it is the supreme secret, it cannot be known or spoken by anyone other than Me. The reason for its being the supreme secret is stated as: "proclaimed in the Vedānta. The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is mentioned as the noun qualified by the neuter gender.

Because of this, it has been stated with the intention that the words *para* and *avara* refer to the excellence and deficiency of temporal duration, [using the expression] "by means of temporal duration.
[This refers to] the limit of time intended as the cause for being an *avatāra*.

He shows this with the words "our" (*asmad*). "Simultaneously" (*samakālam*) means not far removed in time. The word "you" (*tvam*) is stated as "you yourself" (*tvameva*) in order to highlight that it is intended to express contemporaneity and thus serves to indicate a contradiction. This was stated in response to the objection suggested by the question, "How is this so? (*katham etat*)?

Regarding the phrase "it is impossible," he explains what is intended by the prefix in the expression "I might understand" as follows: "according to the fact. This is due to either (1) the non-existence of another birth, (2) the impossibility of remembering what was experienced in another birth, or (3) the speaker's possession of memories from another birth being unknown to the listener.

This objection regarding contradiction is based on the assumption of a single birth; however, since not all of this is possible within that single lifetime, he raises the question with the word "nanu" (surely). The point is that it can also be explained by means of another birth, for there is no contradiction in a teaching given at one time by someone belonging to a different time.
Regarding the phrase "of the great":

the sense is that this applies not only to the Lord Kṛṣṇa, but to other great beings as well. For accounts of those who remember their past births (jātismara) are heard; and Manu says: "He remembers his former birth."

Regarding the phrase "it is logical": once the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from experience has already been established, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its awakening—due to the influence of specific unseen factors (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) and so forth—resulting in the recollection of what was experienced in another birth;
the sense is that this is just as when, upon drinking breast milk for the first time, one recalls that the milk is the cause for the cessation of thirst.

For others who are great, it is memory (*smṛti*); but for the Lord, direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) whose object is past events is figuratively designated as "memory. The phrase "some [cause]" means either the nature of temporal distance or the absence of a cause and so forth. "He" refers to Arjuna, who is rich in what has been heard and so forth due to his service to elders and other such practices.

Regarding the phrase "to the speaker": the meaning is either "to him who spoke it to me," as in "I have declared it to Vivasvat," or "to the one who spoke it to Vivasvat. Regarding the phrase "this son of Vasudeva": the intention is that [Kṛṣṇa] is one whose divine nature remains concealed by his human activities and birth.
"Lord of all" (sarveśvara) means that he is the Lord even of the Sun and others;

or rather, the sense is that his status as the Lord is manifested even during his descent through superhuman deeds such as lifting Govardhana, as well as by his four-armed form and so forth. [This refers to] the existence of the aforementioned knowledge.

He establishes [the Lord] by means of the effect (*kārya*), that is, by worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), and by means of the cause (*kāraṇa*), that is, by instruction (*upadeśa*). "Since it is thus" means:
having first established His status as the Lord through various authoritative instructions and so forth.
By Arjuna’s own words and by the instruction of the great sages mentioned by himself, the inference of knowledge has been stated.
He establishes [this] through the instruction of his kinsmen as understood from the *Bhārata* narrative, because it is so.
"In this way" means that, preceded by the determination of God's nature through the instructions of many most authoritative persons and so forth,
the inference of knowledge has been stated both by Arjuna’s own words and by the instruction of the multitude of great sages mentioned by himself.

He declares [the author] to be most possessed of knowledge by means of the instruction from his kinsman, which was understood through the story of the *Bhārata*, as indicated by the words "O Yudhiṣṭhira. The meaning is that he has heard it in many ways from many who are most trustworthy, even regarding numerous accounts.
By the phrase "Kṛṣṇa alone," it is meant that he who is renowned as the cause of stability is indeed [the cause] of origination and so forth as well.

The cause is [Kṛṣṇa], and not Brahmā, Rudra, or the like, nor the Pradhāna and so forth; or rather, the meaning is that he is Kṛṣṇa himself, perceived by worldly people as the son of Vasudeva. The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates his well-known status in such Vedic scriptures as, "In the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed."
He shows this with the words, "of the worlds" (*lokānām*). Regarding the word *loka*: "The world (*loka*) refers to the universe (*bhuvana*) and to people (*jana*).

In this context, when one or the other is intended to be expressed, the other is excluded. Here, the words "origination" (*utpatti*) and "dissolution" (*apyaya*) refer to the creator and the destroyer, respectively.
The particle *ca* (and) conjoins unstated qualities—such as being the cause of their maintenance (*sthitihetutva*)—due to the excellence of its conventional usage.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "from which indeed these beings [arise]," His status as the cause of all—which was described as the defining characteristic of Brahman—is stated. For this very reason, Arjuna speaks of Him as "the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in the phrase "for of Kṛṣṇa," the word "hi" (indeed) refers to [the Lord] as "the Lord of the universe."
By this, well-known [scriptural] statements such as these are indicated.

Since the word *kṛte* is common to many meanings, he says "sustained as a remnant of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya śeṣabhṛtam*) in order to suggest that its purpose is directed toward Him. Here, because of the absence of the *cvī* suffix, its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) is indicated.
"All beings are [His] servants," and so forth. The phrase "born for the sake of Kṛṣṇa" means that which has arisen for the purpose of Kṛṣṇa, that which possesses existence [for Him].
This is similar to [the sūtra] "From whom the birth and so forth of this [world proceed]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*).
The word *idam* (this) refers to the diverse collection of sentient and insentient beings established by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
or, it serves to restate the modes such as being created and being dissolved, which were mentioned in the first half [of the verse].
By this, the reason for its subservience to Him is stated, because it possesses origination and so forth dependent upon Him; [as in the question: "In whose womb..."?

As in these and other passages. Now, he replies by way of concession to what was stated by the objector: "He indeed knows. By this emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), it is indicated that there is no dispute on this point.
The reference "this one" (*ayam*)—as before—indicates that the meaning is based on what has been heard [in scripture]. [The phrase refers to] the son of Vasudeva.
"Bhagavān" means "He who knows. The word *bhagavat* refers either to one who possesses names or one who possesses qualities.
By the two terms *vasudevasūnu* (son of Vasudeva) and *pārtha* (son of Pṛthā), there is an indication of his being the son of his maternal uncle and the grandson of his father's sister;
thus, even though he possesses ordinary human relations that conceal his divinity and so forth, as is the case with other men—
The intended meaning is that one knows by virtue of past merit and by virtue of instruction. To the objection that the question would then be without scope, he says:
"Even though he knows. It is not something entirely unknown to him that he asks about.

The sense is that what was already known has been questioned further out of a desire to know specific details. By the phrase "as if not knowing," the manner of inquiry imbued with humility is indicated; it shows a desire to understand those portions not yet understood.

The specific attributes known of the Blessed One are presented by means of the genitive-case words beginning with "nikhila" (entire), in order to generate a doubt as to whether birth and so forth might be illusory. By the phrase "the one who is antagonistic to all that is to be discarded" (*nikhilaheyapratyanīka*), the intended meaning is this: how could He, who removes even the discards such as birth and old age from others, ever personally adopt those very same things?
"Of one whose sole intent is the auspicious" means that for one satisfied by the bliss of his own true nature (*svarūpa*), what is the use of birth? This is the intended meaning.

"Of the Lord of All" implies that if there were some independent controller over him, then birth and so forth might occur; however, the intention is that no such [controller] exists. "Of the Omniscient" implies that if he [were not omniscient], regarding himself...

The intention is that if one does not know what is beneficial and what is harmful, then the undertaking of birth and so forth would occur solely by one's own whim, like the touching of fire and such by children and others. Regarding the phrase "of one whose resolve is true":
even when there is knowledge of what is beneficial and harmful, someone might fall into mud while thinking, "I shall fall upon dry ground."

And it is not the case that "He is not so," for the heart [of the opponent] thinks: "Or rather, his descent is solely for the purpose of protecting the world and so forth"—this would indeed be the supreme reply; yet even that is improper, because protection and such are possible through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone—this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "one who has attained all desires": if there were something to be accomplished...

There would be some purpose [in this], because of the lack of subjection to karma, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*); this is the first [argument] by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The second is: "because he is not subject to the commands of Īśvara and others, who are the cause of birth. Regarding both of these inferences: whatever is devoid of a particular cause does not possess that particular effect, just as is commonly recognized (*saṃpratipanna*).

Alternatively, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) may be understood in a general sense. However, when it is stated as "because of being the Lord of all" and so forth, no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) exists.

Furthermore, the intention to employ a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) is untenable, because there exist positive instances (*sapakṣa*) such as jars and the like which are devoid of the assumption of a body; moreover, the validity of the purely negative inference has been refuted by Sāmānyato Dṛṣṭa and other teachers.
Thus, in the absence of the appropriation of a body and so forth, because of being devoid of contracted knowledge,
because of being free from obstructed volitions, because of being free from the state of having unfulfilled desires,
and because of being devoid of goals to be accomplished or purposes to be served— this is illustrated by the examples of the liberated self, a jar, and so on.

These are the reasons. Alternatively, taking as examples those who are liberated and have attained supreme equality, the reasons are: because of omniscience, because of the possession of true resolve, and because of having attained all desires. Thus, if birth and so forth were to exist, then—

The undesirable consequences intended here are that [the Lord] would be subject to karma, lack sovereignty, lack omniscience, lack true resolve, and have unfulfilled desires— just like the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul).

Furthermore, the reasons for His possessing both sets of characteristics as stated in the verse beginning with "devoid of all defects" (*nikhilaheyapratyanīka*) are His being the Lord of all and so forth.

The mode of birth, which is generally known and serves as a cause for the suspicion of falsity because it contradicts the previously mentioned characteristics, is now described: "of the same genus as gods, humans, and others who are under the sway of karma.
Gods, humans, and so forth are under the sway of karma; [the phrase] "of the same genus as them" means being identical to their birth.
The meaning is "that which is being perceived. Alternatively, the word *janman* here refers to a body (*vigraha*) that is currently being born.

It has been stated [that this occurs] because it is assumed by the Lord (*īśvara*), like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) and so forth. For a magical illusion is indeed the production of various delusions in others by one's own will; therefore, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here based on its resemblance to that [illusion].

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), such things as assuming the role of an actor (śailūṣabhūmikā) are included. Since there is no mode whatsoever to be defined in the case of its being false, he raises an objection regarding the position that it is real: "In the case of its reality. He asks, "How?"—the meaning being: is it by abandoning the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, or otherwise?

"Of what nature? means: is it composed of the three *guṇas*, or is it non-material (*aprākṛta*)? "This" refers to the sense that it is perceived as having the configuration of an aggregate of elements. "Body" refers to the sense that it is apprehended as having the form of an accumulation. And "what is the cause of birth? means: is it mere volition alone?

The meaning is that even for Īśvara, merit and demerit are assumed according to his own will. "When? means: at the time of the ripening of merit and demerit, or at a time such as the decline of dharma? "For what purpose? means:
for the sake of experiencing pleasure and pain, or for the sake of protecting the virtuous and so forth? Such is the underlying intention.

Such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Now, one might object: in the verse beginning with "the inferior" (*avaram*), only a contradiction is raised; how, then, is it understood that there is an underlying intention regarding many questions? To this he says: "By way of a refutation" (*parihāra*). This is the intended meaning:
for a response concerning one subject is not logically appropriate as an answer to a question concerning another.

If that were the case, it would follow that the respondent is ignorant of the questioner’s intention and so forth. Therefore, one must accept that as far as the scope of the reply extends, so far alone does the scope of this question extend. And in this reply, by means of four verses, [the following are addressed]: the reality of birth, the manner of birth, and the true nature of the body.
The causes, times, and purposes of birth are understood as they are to be explained in their proper sequence; therefore, these alone are intended to be the subjects of inquiry. || 4 ||

To these, the Blessed One gave the reply in due order with the words beginning "Many" (*bahūni*). Anticipating the objection that neither the unity nor the plurality of previous births was asked about, nor their knowledge or ignorance, he says: "By this... [He asks: How is the reality of birth stated?
Regarding the point that the knowledge of one's own past births and so forth is understood as being based on scriptural authority because of their multiplicity, he says:

"Many. The intention is this: in response to the question, "How did you, who exist at the present time, speak to one who existed at that time? [the answer is] "Because I spoke [to him] in another birth."

If it were said, "I shall speak now after reflecting upon that," and a direct answer were thus given, [it would be inappropriate]; for it has already been stated with reasons that this question has another purpose. Therefore, regarding the matters that must necessarily be asked about, one should provide answers directed toward those very things which can be explained here.
The qualifiers beginning with "many" (*bahūni*) and so forth are [appropriate] because, if [births] were real, terms such as "many" and "past" would be used naturally.

Furthermore, it was stated that these are "births" (*janmāni*), not "appearances of birth" (*janmapratibhāsāḥ*). Moreover, even the introduction of this matter—which was not previously asked about—would not be tenable unless it were intended as an illustration for the reality [of those births].

Nor can it be said that Arjuna’s birth was merely an appearance; for even the mention of "and yours" (tava ca), which refers to a matter not previously asked about, would not be appropriate except with the intention of providing an example for its reality. Furthermore, Arjuna’s birth was not false, nor was there such a false appearance of it; for if that were the case, [the aforementioned point would be untenable].
Regarding the birth of Kṛṣṇa, how could he have any doubt? || 5 ||
He states that the following verse provides the answer to the three questions beginning with "How" (*atha prakāra*): "The descent... (*avatāra*).

By the two words "unborn" (*aja*) and "undecaying" (*avyaya*), it is said that there are no modifications either in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) or attributes (*dharma*), as in the case of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; or else, the words "unborn" and "undecaying" refer to the cessation of birth and death caused by karma.

By this, it is stated that [the Lord] is the opposite of that which is to be abandoned. Furthermore, by the phrase "the Lord of beings," His non-deviation from being a mine of auspicious qualities is indicated. Alternatively, by the word "unborn" (aja), there is a distinction made from both the insentient field (*kṣetra*) and the sentient knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), who are subject to birth either in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or through the medium of the body.

By taking the word *ātman* in *avyayātmā* to refer to its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the negative particle *nañ* to signify absolute non-existence, there is an exclusion of the liberated soul (*mukta*), who at times possesses the contraction of knowledge and other such qualities. By the word *īśvara*, there is an exclusion of the eternal beings whose knowledge is eternally uncontracted. This same [exclusion] applies here as well in the term *avyayātmā*.

It is as in the preceding and following [passages]. The word "even though existing" (*api san*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. Here, the resolution of the three questions occurs respectively by means of the first half-verse and the third and fourth quarters.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [are meant] omniscience, the possession of true resolve, and the attainment of all desires, which are implied by [the Lord's] sovereignty.
"They are grasped. "Everything"—the meaning is that there is no loss whatsoever of even a fraction of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
"Belonging to the Supreme Lord" (*pārameśvara*) means connected with the Supreme Lord, i.e., brought about by the state of being the Supreme Lord.
He states the purport of the present-tense designation "even while existing" (*api san*) as follows: "without ever abandoning... (*ajahad eva*).

By this, it is indicated that in each of those various incarnations and in each of those respective states, there is merely the voluntary concealment of the very nature of the Supreme Lord (Pārameṣṭheśvara) who exists [eternally]. And so they have said, beginning with "by the six qualities," [concluding]: "You are everywhere indeed possessed of immeasurable and great auspicious qualities."

Thus, in the various incarnations (*avatāras*), the status of being the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratva*) is designated by such statements as: "Even though he is the Great Yogin, he is indeed Kṛṣṇa alone for the worlds," and so forth. Here, the word *prakṛti* does not refer to the material nature consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), as it does in passages such as: "Having taken hold of my own *prakṛti*, I emanate [the world]."
It is called *prakṛti* (primordial nature), because even in his descent (*avatāra*), his body does not consist of the material derived from the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Thus it has been said: "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements;
his form is not material, consisting as it does of flesh, fat, and bone."
Thus [it is said]. With the intention of stating that another *prakṛti* is mentioned here as being applicable to the descent [of the Lord], he says:

"*Prakṛti* means *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature). According to the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭukas*), *prakṛti* refers to the five elements, intrinsic nature, and the root cause. Regarding its etymological analysis (*vigraha*) as well, there is the established derivation: "that which is eternally unmanifest and intrinsic."

Because [the Self] possesses an unconditioned, unique, and specific attribute in accordance with the *ekāyana* scripture, it is designated by the word "own-being" (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the term here refers specifically to the particular nature known as the "internal constitution" (*vigraha*).

Although the state of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddhi*) is already obtained through the word "nature" (*prakṛti*), which is a synonym for "own-being," the explicit mention of "own" (*sva*) is intended to [exclude other possible meanings].

This was stated with the intention of distinguishing [the Lord] from the *prakṛti* consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is common to all living beings (*jīva*). This has also been explained in the commentary on the *Antarāditya* section: "Having resorted to his own very nature, not the nature of those subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*). In this context, the word *prakṛti* [refers to...]
By the phrase "having presided over" (*adhiṣṭhāya*), he demonstrates the independence (*svātantrya*) indicated by the state of being intent upon the body (*vigrahaparatām*).

[This is shown by the words] "in his own form" (*svenaiva rūpeṇa*). Alternatively, the first part of the sentence beginning with "his very own nature" (*svameva svabhāvam*) is intended to convey the summarized meaning. That [portion] ending with "having presided over" constitutes the meaning of the first half-verse.

In this interpretation, the third quarter [of the verse] refers to "by its own form," while the fourth quarter refers to "by its own will. In this construction, the word *prakṛti* denotes the divine body that serves as the material cause for the incarnation.
He [the author] states that the nature of this *prakṛti*, which is the material cause of the incarnational body, is established by numerous scriptural authorities (*bahuśruti*).
Regarding the phrase "the very nature of its own nature":

because of the usage "the cessation of the Brahman-nature," the word *svarūpa* here refers to the body (*vigraha*). By the statement "of solar hue, beyond darkness," its non-material (*aprākṛta*) nature is established.

And its possession of its own unique, unsurpassed radiance is established. Within that context, it should also be understood that [the Lord] resides in a specific location, is served by eternal sages, is the husband of Lakṣmī, and so forth—as in the passage beginning with "kṣayantam. Furthermore, in this context, the word *rajata* refers to the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), and not [to silver].

The world is its domain, because this is equivalent in meaning to the statement "beyond darkness. Furthermore, it is designated by the word *rajas* because its constituent quality (*guṇa*) is *rajas*. Its possession of a physical form (*vigrahavattva*) is established by the expression "dwelling" (*kṣayantaṃ*), which denotes residing in a specific location; for that which is all-pervading cannot reside in a particular place. Likewise, [it is described as] "supreme," "having the color of the sun," and "golden."
The single color is indicated through different aspects due to oppositions dependent on different counter-correlates;

as the teacher Dramiḍācārya has said: "It is 'golden' because of the commonality of form, like the moon's face," or else, for the purpose of excluding its being a modification of gold—thus says the Dramiḍa-bhāṣya.

Regarding the phrase "pure gold with the luster of a peacock's neck," the establishment of its dark-blue color is according to the *Śilpaśāstra*. Alternatively, there is no fault even if there are differences in form in various instances according to one's own preference;
this is like the differences in the forms of the manifestations (*vyūha*) of Vāsudeva, such as the white, red, and other colors, which are designated according to the different ages (*yuga*).

He cites scripture (*śruti*) to show that this very [Self] resides within the heart: "In that" (*tasmin*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). "Consisting of mind" means abundant in, or graspable by, a pure mind. By these two scriptural passages, the specific location of the object of meditation (*upāsana*) is shown; and its [location] is likewise [indicated] in the causal statement (*kāraṇavākya*).

It demonstrates its true nature with the word "all. The term "lightning" (*vidyut*) has been explained elsewhere as "from the color of lightning. This scriptural passage, "one should meditate on the peaceful," has been explained in the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra]: "The form of this very person is like saffron-dyed cloth..."

By stating "clothing" (*vāsaḥ*) and so forth, he also expresses a specific form; thus, in all these scriptural passages, the identity with the statements of the *Puruṣasūkta* previously cited is established by means of descriptions of distinct locations, specific colors, the word "Person" (*puruṣa*), and so on. [This applies] in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

He states that the relationship intended here is characterized by the state of being one’s own and its owner, using the words "ātmīyayā" (by her own). He cites the *Nighaṇṭu* lexicon, which gives "māyā" the meaning "knowledge" (*vayunam*). His intention is that this specific meaning is appropriate in the context of descending by her own will. He confirms the meaning established by the *Nighaṇṭu* through the usage of an authoritative scholar who is the source of that lexicon.

"And thus" [it is said]. Because of the designation "he knows by means of *māyā*," this *māyā* is knowledge as established in the *Nighaṇṭu*; the sense is that the *māyā* well-known to others lacks the capacity to reveal the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*). By this, it is shown that the word *prakṛti* here refers to the *prakṛti* consisting of the three *guṇas*.

The fact that the word *māyā* has the sense of "unreal" (*mithyārtha*) is also employed as stated by Śaṅkara. Regarding the phrase "by his own *māyā*," he says it is not to be understood in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), but rather as "by his own knowledge. He clarifies the summarized meaning of the verse with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

By the phrase "freedom from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, there is a reminder of the qualities such as faultlessness and being a mine of auspicious attributes found in the *dahara-vidyā*, the *Subālopaniṣad*, and other texts, as well as [the statement] "by a mere fraction of his own power," and so on. With the intention that the entire nature of the Lord (*īśvara-svabhāva*) is subsumed under the state of possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*), it was said: "all is the nature of the Lord. His very own...
By the words "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, the statement of Parāśara beginning with "O Lord of Men, He creates forms consisting of all powers,
known as gods, animals, and humans," and ending with "until the Blessed One," has been recalled; this Smṛti [is consistent] with the Śruti concerning His birthlessness (*ajatva*).

Regarding the objection that [the scripture] would be contradicted, he says: "To this he replies. He states: "This [scripture] says... [The opponent argues: "Because it is contradictory to speak of both non-arising and arising, this scripture must have another meaning. To this he replies: "By the others... Because the general prohibition "He is not born" occurs in proximity to the specific injunction "He is born in many ways."
Its scope is restricted; therefore, when the contradiction has been resolved, one should not postulate another intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Nor is this a case of becoming manifold in the form of the world—as in the passage "May I be many"—for the wise fully understand its source (*yoni*).

The intention is that, since the knowledge of the *avatāra-līlā* (the descent and divine play) is most beneficial for those seeking liberation—as established by the immediately preceding statements—it is appropriate to speak of that very knowledge; furthermore, this [present topic] shares the same purpose as that. To reject the doubt that there might be a contradiction between reality and falsity, [the Lord says]: "Presiding over my own nature... (*prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya*).

He states another reason for [the word] *iti* having the sense of "analysis" (*vigraha*) and for the word *māyā* having the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāna*), [in the verse beginning] "many" (*bahūni*). [The relevant words are] "Veda," "I generate" (*sṛjāmi*), and "divine" (*divyam*).
By these words, [the Lord's] being preceded by intelligence, being produced by mere will, and being divine, and so forth, are understood.

However, if words such as *māyā* were taken to mean *avidyā* (ignorance) and the like, all of that would be contradicted. For here, the word *janman* does not denote the appearance of birth, nor is it a synonym for "destroyed"; likewise, the word *vyatīta* does not mean "sublated."

The sense is that one who is possessed by illusion cannot possess all-knowingness; nor can the word "creation" apply to what is false; and that which is produced from the three qualities cannot be divine. || 6 ||

He says, "He states the time of birth," because the answer to the question "When? is being given; for the lack of restriction regarding the *yugas* will be stated later. With the intention that the repetition "whenever...
whenever" refers to the lack of restriction regarding times within the *yugas*, he says, "not at a specific time," just as in the case of a living being (*jīva*).

The meaning is that there is no fixed determination of time— whether in the form of Manvantaras, Mahākalpas, and so forth— produced by the ripening of merit and demerit, or produced by one's own volitional constructs regarding established order; this is for the purpose of indicating the manner of exhaustion [of karma] in terms of both its measure and its essential nature, and for the sake of delimiting a specific portion of dharma and adharma.

And [the phrase] "of that which is declared by the Veda," and so forth, is a qualification. By this, the definition of dharma as "that which is to be done as declared by the Veda" is also stated. Regarding the word *adharma*, it is said "of its opposite" (*tadviparyayasya*), intending that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of contrariety (*viruddha*). And from that, it follows:

The consequence is the opposite of the previously described manner: that which is proclaimed in non-Vedic scriptures, which is devoid of the system of castes, stages of life, and so forth, and for that very reason is not to be performed. Furthermore, it is shown that the decline of dharma and the rise of adharma are mutually inseparable, like the simultaneous sinking and rising of the two ends of a balance scale.
In the phrase "tadā" (then), since it functions as a correlative to "whenever" (*yadā-yadā*), the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) should be understood.

The intended meaning of the word "decline" (*glāni*) is: "I cannot endure even the decline of Dharma, much less its total destruction. Likewise, regarding the rise of Adharma, the intent is: "I cannot endure even its mere emergence, much less its branching out into various sub-branches"; this constitutes the "uprising" (*abhyutthāna*).

The intended meaning of the word "I" is as follows: since no other factor to be depended upon is seen in the statement "I create," it is said that "I alone [create] by my own volition. By this, the dependence of the presiding deity upon time is avoided. Furthermore, the statement "I create myself" does not refer to one's essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Because that [Self] is eternal; and because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth. Nor does it refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), because that would be inconsistent with the context of the passage. Nor does it refer to one's own Self as characterized by the primordial body, because that form is also eternal. Therefore, "the Self" here refers to one's own Self as characterized by the incarnate body (*avatāravigraha*). Thus, [the text says] "the Self."
It is stated with the intention that "it is being pointed out," namely, "in the manner already described. || 7 ||
He states the answer to the question "For what purpose? with the words "Of birth" (*janmanaḥ*).
Here, the word *sādhu* does not refer to the meaning of "conventional usage," because its form is the opposite of the word for "ill-done" (*duṣkṛta*).
Therefore, with the intention that this refers to "well-performed action" (*sukṛti*), he says: "those whose character is dharma according to the definition stated."

By the phrase "with words whose characteristics have been stated," the passage beginning with "of that which is proclaimed in the Veda" and so forth is referred to. Furthermore, there are those who worship other deities through the dharma characterized as previously described, as well as the Vaiṣṇavas, according to the principle of the *hṛdayanyāya* [the method of the heart] regarding the *pradarśana-vidyā*.

They worship the Blessed One solely in the form distinguished by the respective deities; they have no absolute insistence on the manifestation of [specific] incarnations, because all that is required by them is accomplished simply through the appearance of the attire appropriate to those respective deities—with this intention it was said: "the foremost of the Vaiṣṇavas."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is "the foremost among the devotees of the Blessed One. By the two phrases "those whose character conforms to dharma according to the stated definition" and "the leaders of the Vaiṣṇavas," it is indicated that one does not deviate from the duties of one's own varṇa, and so forth.

Thus it is established that they rely upon both the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*prāpya*) exactly as they exist. For "protection" (*trāṇa*) here consists of the attainment of the desired preceded by the removal of the undesired. And for these foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, the undesired is the non-attainment of the Lord; and [protection] occurs precisely through the attainment of Him preceded by taking refuge in Him.

With the intention of describing the removal of that which is undesirable, it is said, starting from "by taking refuge in Me" up to "by the giving of conversation and so forth. For these [servants] do not possess food, drink, betel, or the like, nor do they perform the acts of maintenance and nourishment; rather, it is said with the intention that "I, Kṛṣṇa alone, am all of this."

"Because they are unable to maintain or nourish their own selves without seeing me. And this lack of vision is due to their being in a state where yoga has not yet been perfected. If they could endure for even a short time with their eyes closed before this direct realization, then I too would [be able to see] such a state of theirs.

This was said with the intention that they [the other things] are not like this; thus, "in an instant," and so forth, is stated. Here, one should consider such passages as "for those who do not see you, a moment becomes like an eon. Furthermore, the final stage of the suffering of not seeing [you] is being described.
"May they have all their limbs relaxed.
For the sake of reviving those who are distressed by separation from Him, the forms to be experienced by the devotees are described in sequence as being given through the gift of His own nature,
activities, glances, conversations, and so forth— just like the bliss of liberation and other such states.
The sense is that it is possible to grant [the desired object] merely by one's own resolve, even without an incarnation (*avatāra*).

With the intention of showing that the prefix in the word *paritrāṇāya* indicates the attainment of various desired things preceded by the cessation of various misfortunes, [he mentions] "my name, qualities, and deeds," etc., and "retention," etc.
And it was stated, "His own form and activities," and so forth. Here, "own form" (*svarūpa*) refers to the physical body (*vigraha*).

Thus, the protection of the virtuous from internal fear has been described; now, with the intention of describing their protection from external fear as well, he says: "for the destruction of those who are the opposite of them."
And so on. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of an additional mention (*anvācaya*). This has also been stated in the commentary on the *Antarāditya* section:

"The virtuous are indeed those who are attached [to the Lord]; their protection alone is the primary objective, whereas the destruction of the wicked is merely incidental, since that is accomplished even by mere resolve. Thus ends the offense against the Bhāgavatas.
This is said with the intention that [the wicked] are indeed "timber for evil deeds. It was stated [that this applies] to those who are the opposite of that.

Just as in the saying, "He is affectionate even toward his enemies; you shall be pacified by my arrows in battle and thereby become purified," the destruction of even the wicked is not an absolute annihilation.
However, it is the removal of the knots of the bodies of Rākṣasas and others, who are the causes of perversion;
and upon their removal, even they may become righteous—thus that [destruction] also culminates in the establishment of Dharma. My worship is that which is subordinate to Me.
It is with the intention that "it must indeed be established by me alone" that it was stated, "consisting of my own propitiation.
While the promotion of Dharma can be accomplished through the agency of Vyāsa and others, both by means of practice and by means of instruction,
the production of devotion by revealing the form of the one to be worshipped is the common purpose of all incarnations.

The intention is that even Viṣṇupāla, who was an enemy for three hundred births due to his harsh speech toward hundreds of others, attained liberation after becoming filled with joy upon seeing Kṛṣṇa; thus it is said,
"by the manifestation of the nature of the one to be worshipped," [which occurs] through the excellence of the person's beauty and noble qualities.

One should also contemplate [the verse] beginning with "stealing away the mind through false views. By this, it is stated that the correct establishment of the Dharma is indeed its establishment within one's own limits. The repetition "in age after age" (*yuge yuge*) reveals the intended meaning of the distributive sense. [The phrase] "Kṛta, Tretā, etc. does not, however, mean that it necessarily occurs in every single age.
The meaning is that I manifest, nor is there any restriction regarding a particular age (yuga). || 8 ||

The utility of this incidental introduction, which explains the true nature [of the Lord], for the sake of liberation—the primary subject at hand—is stated by the verse beginning with "Birth and action" (*janma karma*). The word "thus" (*evam*) means in the manner described by the passage beginning with "Though unborn" (*ajo 'pi*).
The word "divine" (*divyam*) has the same meaning as "not material" (*aprākṛtam*), and it is explained by the phrase "unique to Me" (*mama asādhāraṇam*).

The meaning is that the birth mentioned in the statement "May I be many, may I procreate" is excluded; furthermore, this mode—which is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (the Self), like the heat of fire, and which is not observed in other categories of entities—is not sublated by logical reasoning (*tarka*). This is because [birth] is spoken of as being "divine," just like My birth itself, and thus its cause is likewise divine.

The phrase "even merit" is explained as being for the purpose of dispelling the doubt as to whether there is any merit at all. "In reality" (tattvataḥ) means free from doubt and error. When it is said "having abandoned the body," a common understanding might arise that he abandons the body which is the final stage of *prārabdha* karma; to exclude that possibility, it is specified: "having abandoned the present body."

And this [is so]; for by the statement "he who knows does not come to rebirth," the negation of rebirth is established with reference to the state of being a knower. Through the negation of rebirth, it is established that by the phrase "he does not come to rebirth," the cessation of the opposing factor is expressed; and by "he comes to Me," the attainment of the desired goal is expressed.

It is not merely the experience of the bliss of one's own self through the simple cessation of oppositions, but rather [the devotee] becomes a possessor of the knowledge of the secret of the Incarnation; the meaning of the restrictive particle "eva" (only) is that he attains Me alone. Now, an objection is raised: it is improper to say "having abandoned this present body," for liberation occurs only at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma.

This has been determined in the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras]. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding how many births are required to exhaust even *prārabdha* (commenced) karma, for such lack of restriction is observed in the cases of Vyāsa and others. Nor does liberation result from mere knowledge of birth and karma, because that would render futile the teachings on meditation—which require practice over a long period, with uninterrupted devotion, and through difficult disciplines—along with the knowledge that accompanies them. To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "madīya" (belonging to me): through the knowledge of the divine birth and activities [of the Lord], all sins that obstruct spiritual practice (*upāsana*) have been removed; therefore, in this very life, there is the capacity to pacify even those portions of sin that initiate future births and obstruct spiritual practice.

Because all sins have ceased, and because in this very life there is the accomplishment of abundant practice capable of pacifying the portions of sin that initiate future births, there is no taking up of another birth. And they record in the scriptures that those who have perfected their meditative absorption attain liberation right there.

"In birth" [is the meaning]. Thus, because this is mentioned as a cause for the excellence of worship (*upāsanā-pauṣkalpa-hetutayā*), it is a means to liberation through a traditional succession; therefore, the sense is that there is no futility of the scripture concerning worship.
By the manner described above, "having taken refuge in me" refers to the state of intense meditation (*puṣka-dhyāna-avasthā*). [One who is] "solely devoted to me."

This, however, is a statement regarding the attainment of the form of devotion (*bhakti*). "One for whom I alone am the beloved—that is, the object of affection—is *madekapriya*"; as it will be said [later]: "For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge. By this, there is an exclusion of those who are intent upon other human goals (*puruṣārtha*). "One whose mind is fixed on me alone" (*madekacitta*).
The state of meditative concentration (*samādhyavasthā*). He whose mind is fixed on me alone is "one whose mind is centered on me" (*madekacitta*). (9)

He says, "That he said," meaning that this very point—which was stated as a response to the doubt regarding the futility of worship (*upāsanāvaiyarthyam*) and so forth—is expressed by the verse beginning with "one who is free from passion" (*vītarāga*). That same knowledge previously introduced is here referred to as "the austerity of knowledge" (*jñānatapasā*); however, the phrase "those who are absorbed in Me and have taken refuge in Me" refers [to the result] through a traditional succession.
With the intention that this [knowledge] is what is to be accomplished by that, he says "my own" (*madīya*).

Since this verse has already been largely explained in the preceding verse, the phrase "having thus become" (*evaṃ saṃvṛttāḥ*) refers to what was stated in the summary. For instance, the meaning of the phrase "purified by the austerity of knowledge" (*jñānatapasā pūtāḥ*) begins with the words "my own."

The meaning of "those who have taken refuge in me" (*mām upāśritāḥ*) is expressed by the phrase "having taken refuge in me" (*mām āśritya*). The meaning of "free from passion, fear, and anger" (*vītarāgabhayakrodhāḥ*) is intended by the phrase "to whom I alone am dear" (*madekapriyaḥ*);
for attachment to other objects is indeed passion (*rāga*), while the desire to repel those things one dislikes is anger (*krodha*).

Fear is the apprehension of the arrival of the undesirable or the obstruction of the desired in the future. None of this exists for the devotees of Vāsudeva, because, by virtue of Him alone being their sole beloved, there is an absence of attachment toward other objects;

and for that very reason, there is an absence of anger rooted therein, as well as an absence of fear and its opposite, since there is no longer any distinction between the desirable and the undesirable apart from attaining Him.

And this is well known from such passages as "neither anger nor envy," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "with their minds fixed on me alone" (*madekacittaḥ*), it is the meaning of "consisting of me" (*manmayāḥ*). They are "consisting of me" because they abound in me, who am the object of their knowledge;
for here, neither the sense of identity nor the sense of modification is appropriate. This is especially so when the intention is to express my state as the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*).

And because that [Self] is common to all; and regarding the phrase "consisting of Me" (*manmaya*), Śaṅkara’s interpretation—namely, "those who perceive non-difference from the Lord"—is refuted because it contradicts the introduction and other parts of the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtra) and because the word [in question] lacks denotative power. By the statement "he attains Me alone," the meaning of the phrase "they have come to My state" (*madbhāvam āgatāḥ*) is shown, even in the state of liberation.

Because identity (*tādātmya*) is contradicted by the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, the presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) based on them, and the Sūtras; because even here there is the designation of object and agent in the words "He [attains] Me, O Arjuna"; and because it will be stated later, "Having attained My own nature. Regarding the phrase "having attained My state":

The meaning is that they have attained my own nature, characterized by freedom from sin and so forth; or else, as in the passage "He becomes Brahman itself," this designation is used because of extreme similarity.
Furthermore, he states that there is also scriptural authority for the fact that the secret of the incarnations (avatāra) must be known: "And thus... [tathā ca].
He explains the correspondence with the meaning already stated by the passage beginning with "foremost among the wise" and so forth.
Thus, by the etymological definition of the word *dhīra*, that which was previously mentioned— the possession of unbroken knowledge culminating in the attainment of the Blessed One— is expressed.

In the phrase "they fully know" (*parijānanti*), the prefix (*upasarga*) is intended to indicate the previously mentioned manner of existing exactly as it is; thus, it is stated that they know his mode of birth. However, in the reading "only the foremost among the wise" (*dhīmatām agra-sarā eva*), the meaning is that by this specific injunction, the exclusion of all others follows as a logical consequence. || 10 ||

Thus, by way of describing His descent according to His own will— such as among those of the same class as Amuṣya and others— for the purpose of protecting the virtuous and so forth, His accessibility (*saulabhya*) has been stated as being useful for meditation (*upāsanā*). Now, [the text describes] the state of that very [accessibility] when it has reached its ultimate limit.

He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "As they [are]," wherein the account of the *arcāvatāra* (the iconographic incarnation) is also included along with the account of the *kṛṣṇāvatāra*. In this context, the words "as they are" (*ye yathā*) and "to them just so" (*tāṃs tathaiva*) are intended to signify the cessation of the restrictive rules regarding the previously mentioned qualifications, their respective practices, and their modes of performance.
With this intention, he says: "Not only... The phrase "in accordance with his own expectation" means by way of the modes of being a husband, a son, a charioteer, a boar, a man-lion, and so forth.
"Having resolved" means having made it the object of his mental aspiration (*manoratha*). This very point is what is intended here.

He says, "taking refuge," meaning "they take full shelter. This is stated to dispel the doubt that the statement, "I likewise honor them," might be inconsistent with the manner in which they honor Him—namely, that he himself would honor them in that same way. He explains the meaning of "likewise" as: "in the manner of their own resolve," and not otherwise.

The intended meaning is: "in a manner corresponding to their own respective status. Here, the explanation offered by others—that the purpose [of the Lord's action] is to avoid partiality by bestowing fruits according to one's desires—is not entirely consistent with what precedes and follows;
furthermore, there would be a redundancy in meaning with the passage beginning "the fourfold order" (*cāturvarṇyam*). [This applies to] the servants.

The intention is that "serving the one to be served" means having an easily accessible vision [of Him]; thus it was said, "I reveal Myself. The second half of the verse is intended to demonstrate that this stated meaning is also evident in the world; it does not, however, refer to [the Lord's] own [existence] in the manner of the passage beginning with "If indeed I were not to exist," and so forth.

With the intention that [the previous statement] was concerned with the supreme practice of conforming to the world—which is irrelevant here—he clarifies that its purpose is the ease of accessibility beyond the reach of speech and mind, saying: "What need is there for much more?
He uses the word "all" (*sarva*) with the intention that the word "human" (*manuṣya*) includes women and others as well. In this context...
The word *vartman* does not denote a path in the sense of a road, for that would result in an incoherent meaning of the sentence.

Nor does it refer to conduct (*ācāra*), because that too would be irrelevant here and suffer from the aforementioned defect. Precisely for this reason [it is said]: "The wheel has been set in motion by him; by him alone has the boundary of the Brāhmaṇas been established."

Even the adherence to the limits of the scriptures stated in passages such as "the creator of the world" has been set aside. Therefore, with the intention that in this section concerning the teaching on accessibility (*saulabhya*), it is more appropriate to focus solely on the collection of His own unique attributes—such as form, activity, and character—it is said: "Of Me... (*mama*).

"The entire path has my own nature as its essence. For even a word denoting a "path" (*saraṇi*) is used figuratively (*upacārāt*) with reference to one's own nature (*svabhāva*). As in the example: "What is this path that you have become confused about?
[It is] thus with me, who am unfortunate. What was indicated by the term "human beings" (*manuṣyāḥ*) is now being stated.

Regarding the phrase "of the yogins": the meaning is that even those humans with the fleshly eye, though [the Lord] is beyond the reach of speech and mind, experience Him through their external senses— He who appears in forms such as beloved, father, son, friend, brother, servant, and charioteer, as well as in the forms of incarnations (*arcāvatāra*).

By the word "in every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*), he states what is intended: "by those things required for themselves. The meaning is that they follow [the Lord] after having experienced Him, or they exist while experiencing Him. Or, in this context, "manner" (*prakāra*) refers to adornment, processions, festivals, service, and so forth. Here, although [the Lord] is beyond the reach of the speech and mind of yogis, [He is perceived] by means of the senses such as the eyes.
By this statement, it is shown that even in the form of an *arcāvatāra* (an incarnate image), one must contemplate its nature as the Supreme Form (*pararūpa*). As they remember:

"That very [form] which has the nature of Brahman," and the Lord will also say: "With four arms," and so forth. Thus, by way of context, through His acting as a charioteer and other such acts, His extraordinary accessibility (*saulabhya*) is demonstrated.
Even while the Pāṇḍava was looking on, [the teacher] instructed him out of a desire to fulfill his wish for proximity;
yet, even by this much, what solution has been stated for the objections raised by the arguments of inference? To that it is said: "The adversary himself must abandon what is to be abandoned."
The objection as to how [the Lord] could undergo rebirth is refuted precisely because He is not subject to anything that must be abandoned, such as the descent [into a womb].

This absence [of such factors] is due to His being independent of karma, His non-material nature, and the fact that He acts by His own will. Furthermore, the question of how birth and so forth could occur in the absence of merit and demerit, or in the absence of another controller, is also resolved by His own will.

The objection regarding [His] being subject to karma—namely, that He might act for His own benefit, or be devoid of knowledge, or lack power—is refuted by the fact that His incarnations are due to divine sport (*līlā*), which precludes any personal interest, and because He possesses no ignorance. Furthermore, the objection regarding the absence of a purpose has been set aside by the description of purposes such as the protection of the virtuous. As for that which concerns the protection of the virtuous and so forth...

If it is argued that [the Lord] could accomplish [his purpose] by mere resolve alone, why then the descent (avatāra) and so forth? To this, [the Bhāṣya] replies: with respect to the phrase "for the protection of the virtuous," by the commentary beginning with "by my name" and ending with "for their protection through conversation and the like";
and with respect to the phrase "for the establishment of dharma," by the statement "by revealing his own nature as the one to be worshipped."
In the phrase "ye... yathā," this [objection] has been refuted by demonstrating the excellence of His universal accessibility and ease of attainment.

As for what was stated—that "the Lord does not, in reality, possess birth and so forth, because He is not subject to karma, like a liberated soul"—in that case, depending on whether one accepts or does not accept the existence of the Lord, there would be either a contradiction with the evidence that establishes the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādha*) or a lack of a locus for the reason (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Furthermore, what is the meaning of the thesis here: is it that [the Self] is devoid of birth and so forth caused by karma; or is it that it is devoid of birth and so forth not caused by karma; or is it simply that it is devoid of birth and so forth in general? It cannot be the first, because it would entail proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). Nor can it be the second.
Because the reason is unestablished (*aprayojaka*); for the cessation of action does not necessarily bring about the cessation of birth that is not caused by action.

Furthermore, there is sublation (*bādha*) by the very means of knowledge that establishes the nature of the object to be negated, as in the case of inferring the non-heat of fire. Nor is the third [alternative] valid, because the illustrative example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikala*); for even one who is liberated may still assume a body.

This is established by such scriptural passages as, "Eating, playing, and rejoicing. If it is argued that the liberated soul (mukta) is also included within the subject of the proposition, then what is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta)? If one says "a jar" and so forth, we say no; for in that case, the absence of the assumption of a body and the like is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of insentience (acetanatva). By this same logic, [the argument] that "whatever possesses birth and so forth is subject to karma" [is refuted].

The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also refuted. As for the argument that [the world] is not subject to the Lord's injunction—that too has the same meaning as the first [point]; for the scripture that defines merit and demerit is itself of the nature of the Lord’s command.
As for the argument that it is devoid of a cause—that which is devoid of a cause [is not produced].

The claim that "He possesses those [qualities]" is also incorrect; for if the term is used with the intention of referring to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*), because it would entail the existence of an eternal form that is not composed of primordial matter (*aprākṛta*) and is not caused by karma, which contradicts our position. However, if it is used with the intention of referring to the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), then the reasons are established, as the will (*saṃkalpa*) and other such factors can be shown to be its causes.

The objection regarding the intention to express a universal (*sāmānya*) has already been answered for that very reason. In the same way, one should consider the sublation by the evidence grasping the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādhā*) and so forth in cases such as "because of being devoid of contracted cognition" and the like.
Furthermore, in the case of "because it lacks a probandum and a purpose," there is a lack of establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).

Because the purpose—such as the play (*līlā*) of protecting the virtuous (*sādhujana*)—has already been stated, the intention to express the universal [nature of the cause] is even more clearly established for that very reason. In the same way, regarding [the reasons] such as "because of being devoid of contracted knowledge" (*saṃkucitajñānaśūnyatvāt*), one should consider the sublation by the means of apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādha*) and so forth. Regarding the point "because of being devoid of a probandum and a purpose" (*sādhyaprayojanarahitatvāt*):

Furthermore, the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddha*), because it has already been stated that the purpose [of the Lord] consists in the play (*līlā*) of protecting the virtuous and so forth. If it is argued that, nevertheless, present-day happiness did not exist at that time, and thus a state of incompleteness (*apūrṇatva*) would follow from that perspective—
this is not a state of incompleteness, because there is no frustration of what is desired, and because that [happiness] was accomplished at the very moment of the desire.

Even then, if he should so desire, it would be accomplished because of the existence of that capacity; for even that which belongs to a later time is already being contemplated as his own pleasure by the omniscient Lord at an earlier time. The same should be understood regarding the past as well. As for the future, since it too manifests as pleasure, for what purpose would he desire it?
If it is asked [what its purpose is], we say: it is for the sake of arising (*utpatti*). If it is asked what the purpose of that [arising] is—it is that very [arising] itself.

If it is argued that since she does not exist in the prior and posterior moments, those two times would be incomplete—no, because they are complete by virtue of her alone, who is known at all times as being present in those times. [Objection: Is it not the case that for someone there is the state of desiring something, which [occurs] upon the non-attainment of it?

If it is argued that [the inquiry] results in suffering and so forth, we say no; for its occurrence is justified precisely by the fact that the attainment of that [knowledge] is the purpose. For one who lacks the capacity but desires it, suffering arises because that [attainment] is not achieved; however, for one who possesses the capacity, the very desire for it nourishes its nature as happiness. Thus, there is no difficulty whatsoever. By this, [the objection regarding] the absence of a goal to be accomplished and a purpose is refuted.
Even the example cited for the reason is deficient in its probans, because of scriptural passages such as, "He eats, he plays," and so forth.
As for those reasons, such as "because of omniscience" and so forth, which are based on the analogy of having attained supreme equality,

the same defects— such as being devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala)— apply to them as well. Furthermore, these reductio arguments (prasaṅga) are refuted, just like the inferences, due to the absence of pervasion (vyāpti) and other necessary conditions.

Thus, it is established that birth and so forth belong to the Lord as a reality, and the word that establishes this is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the fact that suffering, grief, fear, and the like are occasionally mentioned in relation to his incarnations (*avatāras*),
that is merely a device by which he deceives the world through the power of his state of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and other such qualities.
And by the force of such statements as these, it should be understood that [the world] is merely a mental construction. || 11 ||

Thus, having stated the six topics as being the subject matter of the chapter, that which is relevant and that which is incidental have been explained; now, in order to describe the manner in which the practice of action (karmayoga) under discussion becomes a means to knowledge, six verses proceed by way of its introduction. Among these, four concern the qualified aspirant (adhikārī).

There is a twofold division of objects regarding the nature of karma and its specific sub-divisions. Intending this, he introduces the first verse with the words "Now" (*idānīm*). Since there is no specification of a particular group in the phrase "desiring" (*kāṅkṣantaḥ*), it is stated that "all persons indeed" [are meant]. Those who, by virtue of their desire for liberation...
They too are indeed considered to be initially inclined toward the three aims of human life (*tripuruṣārtha*); such is the intended meaning of the particle *eva*.

Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of actions" (*karmaṇāṃ siddhim*), the word "fruit" (*phalam*) is stated to dispel any doubt concerning the mere establishment of the essential nature of the action. He states what is intended by the word "here" (*iha*): "merely the deities such as Indra. Here—

The meaning is: those who are perceived as deities. The phrase "they worship" (*ārādhayanti*) is stated to clarify the root-meaning of the verbal root *yaja*, which signifies "the worship of deities. By this, acts such as giving (*dāna*) and fire-offerings (*homa*), which constitute the propitiation of various respective deities, are also included. He will clarify this immediately after the words "all actions" (*sarvāṇi karmāṇi*).
He states that the negative formulation (*vyatirekarūpa*) is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), intended for those qualified for the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), by saying "not anyone" (*na tu kaścit*).
By the phrase "the enjoyer of all sacrifices," he indicates what will be stated later in such passages as "For I am indeed [the enjoyer] of all sacrifices."
He raises an objection regarding the meaning and phrasing of the words *hetu* and *para*: "Non-existence in terms of location (*deśataḥ*) is stated.

Passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" are brought to mind by the word "swift" (*kṣipra*). By the phrase "in this very [place]," the non-existence in location—which is the implication of the word "human" (*mānuṣa*)—is indicated.

The sense is that because of the quick attainment of gain even in this very world, there would first be a desire for even inferior fruits. He specifies the success according to what is appropriate for the human world with the words "sons, cattle," and so forth.
He states the conclusion resulting from the section on the fruit of liberation with the word "human," [implying] even though superior fruits exist.

Showing the cause for the desire for trifling fruits and for the lack of revulsion toward the continuous stream of suffering attached thereto, [the author] summarizes the intended meaning of the statement by Kaṇāda and states: "All indeed... The term "worldly people" is mentioned for the purpose of illustrating their inclination toward the three aims of life (*trivarga*).
"Of the undiscriminating" means because of their lack of discrimination. "Desiring quick results" means considering themselves as thinking,
"Better a crow today than a peacock tomorrow," out of disregard for the mass of defects such as meanness, impermanence, and the persistence of suffering.

This is the state of being (*bhāva*). It has been stated by way of a summary of both this-worldly and other-worldly results, which serve as the indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*upalakṣya*), namely:

"sons, cattle, food, heaven, and so forth. By this, it is shown that in the phrase "the accomplishment of actions" (*karmaṇāṃ siddham*), the word "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the general category. All actions [are thus encompassed].

Sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth. (12) Now, one might object: "The accumulation of inexhaustible and infinite sins is common to all; therefore, due to a lack of discrimination, the desire for immediate results is likewise common. Consequently, since no one would be free from the desire for liberation, the scriptures concerning the means to liberation would have no authority. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states two verses.
With the intention of providing a rebuttal to that [objection], he says: "As has been stated.

In the preceding verses, even regarding those minor fruits dependent on other deities, it was shown—by the passage beginning with "the fourfold order of society" (*cāturvarṇyam*)—that the causality belongs to Himself alone, the creator of all. This mention of the fourfold order of society is intended to illustrate His role within the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*).

With the intention of including both the collective and individual creations, the phrase "headed by the fourfold order" was stated. Furthermore, the mention of individual creation is for the purpose of introducing the resolution of the issues of partiality and cruelty; this is expressed by the words "according to the division of qualities and actions."

The term "sattva and so forth" is used with the intention that the subject matter consists of the classifications of *sattva* and the other qualities which are about to be elaborated upon. This refers to the classification of qualities (guṇa) such as "sattva is the highest," as well as the classification of actions (karman) such as "of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas," and the actions beginning with tranquility (*śama*).
Having begun with the statement that [dharma] is to be practiced through tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, it will be stated later:

"Action born of one's own nature is *brāhma*. In this way, it has been elaborated upon in the Purāṇas and other texts concerning the various species such as gods, animals, and humans, as well as in the Vārāha, Pādma, Īśāna, and other Kalpas, as being characterized by the predominance of those respective qualities (*guṇa*).

The manner of unequal creation is to be observed. Since the scriptures and other authorities enjoin that God is to be known as the cause of the entire process beginning with creation, he states "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) here with the intent of indicating protection and the rest as well.
By this, it is stated that the three activities—beginning with individual creation—are also performed by Him as their own agent.

By this, the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then, having created [the elements], I shall enter you and bring forth the creatures" is also explained. This has been stated in the aphorism: "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the scriptural instruction. (Sūtra 2.4.20) || 13 ||

With the intention that it is contradictory for one and the same entity to possess both agency and its absence with respect to a single action, he raises an objection: "How so? He clarifies that agency is primary, whereas non-agency is predicated because of the absence of being a cause of inequality. This is indicated by the word "since" (*yataḥ*).

The word "karma" here does not refer to merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*), because that would be irrelevant to the present context and because there is currently no possibility of doubt regarding subjection to karma. This is because it is more logical for the text to consist of the removal of suspected contradictions, and because an injunction of what is required is stronger than an injunction of what is unnecessary.

With this intention, it was stated that "these actions, such as the manifold creation and so forth, do not smear me. First, he states the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) of the primary incoherence regarding the phrase "do not smear me": "they do not bind me. To the question, "How is the contradiction resolved by this much? he says: "No..."

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because it is denied that [the Lord] is the specific cause regarding the aspect of inequality, as in the phrase "impelled by me. To the question, "What then is the specific cause of the unequal creation? he says:
"Those [karmas]. By virtue of the aforementioned reason, it is appropriate to designate [the Lord] as non-agent.

He concludes with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: by means of the discernment between what has been attained and what has not been attained, and by extracting the specific distinctions established through the observation of gradations in the unequal creation of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which correspond to the relative degrees of merit and demerit.
Just as, among various sprouts, earth, water, and so forth are the common causes, [so too are merit and demerit the causes of the diversity of experience].

The meaning is that just as variety arises from the cause of the variety of its own seeds (*svabīja*), so it is here. Thus, non-agency has been stated due to the absence of any specific motivating purpose.
Now, with the intention of stating non-agency through the lack of desire for the fruits of specific creation, [the author says]:

He explains the passage beginning with "Not mine is action" and so forth. By the words "And because," he intends to indicate that while desire for oneself is prohibited, there is the presence of desire for others; thus, the statement beginning with "created" was made. "Created" refers to the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field).

Thus, by this explanation of karma, it is intended that creation exists for the purpose of establishing the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) in its state as an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). The form suitable for being an experiencer is stated [in the verse]: "having obtained the instruments and the body through creation. The sense is that creation is not for the sake of the knower's obtaining its own instruments and so forth. The word "cause" refers to attachment to results and the like.
By either a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa* compound,

the word "cause" (*hetu*) qualifies its own object— namely, attachment to results and so forth; or alternatively, there is the reading "by causes such as attachment to results," which [qualifies] in accordance with one's own action.

The sense is that [the result] is not merely in accordance with a specific mental volition independent of that [volition]. In the phrase "in the fruit of action" (*karmaphale*), the word "action" (*karman*) refers to the actions of creation and so forth under discussion; however, because the nature of the fruit is such, the intention is that action in the form of merit and demerit has borne fruit. Thus, it is said: "in the fruit of action consisting of the fruits of creation and so forth."

Thus it has been said: "I set in motion [the world] in accordance with various desires rooted in the heart through beginningless, continuous latent impressions (vāsanā), and I bestow fruits corresponding to the merit and demerit caused by those respective desires;
I do not bestow them according to my own will, nor do I grant unequal fruits merely by virtue of my sovereignty."

"I give," [meaning] "I do not afflict others for my own sake"—all this is expressed by the words ending with "there is no longing in me. In this regard, it is said: "Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana proclaimed this meritorious Upaniṣad," thus [it is stated] in the Pañcamaveda.
