He corroborates the meaning stated in the Śārīraka-sūtra with the words "Thus he said.
He also shows the statement of his father, who knew the supreme divinity, with the words "And thus.
For there, after describing the manifestation of Varāha, [he describes] the four worlds, beginning with Bhūr, as before.

The two verses beginning with "samakalpayat" have been stated. Immediately following that, when a brief summary has been made—starting from "And how the Lord created the gods, ṛṣis, ancestors, and dānavas, as well as humans, animals, trees, and so forth, [residing] upon the earth, in the sky, in the water, and in the fire," and ending with "ityādiḥ... vistārāt"—[the detailed account follows].

Furthermore, when Maitreya asked at great length, [the Lord replied] with the following: "These beings, consisting of the fourfold creation beginning with the gods and ending with the stationary, are permeated by their former actions—both virtuous and non-virtuous. Even in dissolution, they are not destroyed, for they remain unreleased from that manifestation. And so forth.

For it is explained that the unequal creation of gods and others is dependent upon their respective karmas. Therefore, by considering the preceding and following context, the term "those to be created" (*sṛjya*) here refers to specific created beings such as gods and humans, while the term "power" (*śakti*) refers to their respective karmas themselves. For he will say later regarding karma as well: [text continues].

In such passages as "The word *śakti* [is used]," and "Ignorance (*avidyā*), known as action (*karman*), is held to be another third power," [the term] refers to the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). Nor does the phrase "merely the instrumental cause" constitute a denial of its being the material cause (*upādāna*), for that would entail a contradiction with the preceding and following contexts of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras. Therefore, it is by virtue of being prompted by specific respective actions...
In this context, the aspect of partiality within the uneven creation described is primarily negated by Him, as in the statement:
"These were slain by Me alone long ago; you be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin. For it is said: "The powers of those to be created are indeed dependent upon the primary cause."
This is also refuted here. [Objection: If this were so, it would follow that the Lord lacks primacy (*aprādhānyam*);

and that too contradicts the Sūtras and other authorities. Furthermore, it contradicts His status as an agent (*kartṛtva*), for according to the rule "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), primacy consists in being the sovereign with respect to the entire circle of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*).

If it is argued that they remember the definition of an agent (*kartṛ*), and therefore this word "Pradhāna" refers to the material cause (*upādāna*)—that is not so; for it would contradict the scriptural texts and other authorities regarding the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause (*nimittopādānaikya*). Furthermore, the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is inappropriate when applied to a material cause. Nor does this entail a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*), because there exists a specific factor that acts as the prompter (*prayojaka*).

Since even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which serves as an instrument, is dependent upon Him, therefore the second verse also expresses that God is required as the common cause and that there is no dependence on any other specific cause. Having intended all of this, he explains the two verses [beginning] with "Of the things to be created" (*sṛjyānām*).
The meaning of the word *sṛjya* (the object to be created) is specified by the context; it is what is expressed by the term *kṣetrajñāna* (the knowledge of the field).

Regarding the word *nimitta* (cause), he says "merely the cause" (*kāraṇamātra*) in order to exclude the sense of being a "cause" mentioned here alongside "material cause" (*upādāna*). [This applies] to the phrase "the potencies of the objects to be created" (*sṛjyaśaktayaḥ*).

The term "of the ancients" (*prācīna*) is stated in order to dispel the misconception that this is a *samānādhikaraṇa* (appositional) compound. For it is remembered in the tradition: "Actions performed with bodies produced in previous kalpas are not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas until they have been experienced. With the intention that the word "entity" (*vastu*) here refers specifically to the objects of creation established by the context and other factors.

This has been stated as the reality of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Thus, by means of these two verses, the fire for the destruction of sin—which is an obstacle to the commencement of the yoga of action as previously described—has been stated.

(14) Having established that yoga of action preceded by such [destruction], He instructs Arjuna by demonstrating its performance by the learned; this is done by the following verse, beginning with "evam" (thus). "Evam" means...

By the statement, "Having known [this], action is performed," it is indicated that knowledge is the cause for performing action. Regarding the word *vyañjanāya*: it is said, "having known [this], one is liberated from sins. Here, because the word *karman* (action) refers to the duties to be performed by one seeking liberation, it is intended to refer back to *karmayoga*, which is the primary subject at hand even though it was mentioned earlier. Therefore, it is described as having the characteristics already stated.

The word "you" (*tvaṃ*) is intended to indicate that you have received the instruction regarding your own true nature. Those who performed the practice mentioned in the passage beginning with "This [knowledge] to Vivasvat... are referred to by the word "by the ancients" (*pūrvaiḥ*).

With this intention, it was said: "by Vivasvat, Manu, and others. To preclude the interpretation of "prior" (*pūrvataram*) as an adverbial modifier of the action, he says: "ancient" (*purātanam*). He states what is intended by that:
"it was spoken by me at that very time. Thus, it is the beginninglessness of the stream (*pravāha-anāditvam*) that is intended here.

Because this [verse] serves as an introduction for the definitive exposition of the nature of *karmayoga*, it was stated: "in the manner that will be explained" (in the verse beginning with) "What is action?
(*kiṃ karma*). Lest there arise the delusion that the words "action" (*karman*) and "inaction" (*akarma*) refer to two distinct things to be known, he says—thereby dispelling that [delusion]:

By the words beginning with "one should see," it will indeed be stated that both action and inaction are portions of the same yoga of action; intending that even in this verse it is said, "I shall declare that action to you," the phrase "of the action to be declared" is used. He speaks [the following] in order to make known its difficulty of comprehension.

To exclude the notion that "this should be practiced by one desiring liberation" implies a mere absence of action (*akarma*), he says: "the knowledge of the true nature of the Self. It has been stated that they are "the wise. Even though it is the subject under discussion, with the intention that— by means of the reference to what precedes and follows in "I shall declare action" and "perform action alone"—

Here, by the word "having known" (*jñātvā*), which functions through non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), the performance of action even while possessing knowledge is included;
for it was stated immediately thereafter: "Therefore, you must perform action alone. The underlying sense is that otherwise, the injunction to perform action would be rendered purposeless. || 16 ||

When it is said, "I shall declare that action to you," it follows immediately that action alone is what should be taught. The word *svarūpa* (essential nature) is intended here. Therefore, the prefix *vi-* here refers to the diversity of duties to be performed; and that diversity consists of the forms of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth.

With the intention of stating what is well-known, he says: "eternal," etc. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), protection, the means for that, engagement [in action], and so forth are included. Having set aside the view that [the term] refers to the state of being established in independent knowledge—which is the essence of the absence of actions mentioned by others—he states what is established through a different interpretation and through proximity: "akarma" (non-action). Here, the meaning is "in this context of the instruction on Karma-yoga.
He demonstrates the sense of the connection with the words "karmaṇi" (in action), using an emphatic restriction to highlight the contradiction that serves as the cause for doubt.

This is for the purpose of avoiding the objection that knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*) are incompatible. Now, this may seem improper, because when one thing is being performed, another is not required for its completion;
because when one thing is being performed, it is difficult to have knowledge of something else; and because when one thing is being kept in mind, another...

Because it is impossible to do so; and with the intention that the exclusion of one [alternative] would follow from the observation of the other in either case, he raises the objection: "What is meant by this?"—referring to this aforementioned impossibility of simultaneous [occurrence], is it due to a difference in the form of the scriptural meaning, or otherwise?
Having in mind this alternative (*vikalpa*), he first refutes it with the words: "It is precisely while being performed.

The sense is that because the action qualified by knowledge is enjoined as a means, there is a mutual connection between them; thus, they do not have distinct purposes. By this, [the view] that they have two distinct purposes independent of one another is [refuted].

The apprehension that they might mutually exclude one another has also been refuted. Regarding the third [alternative] as well, is the difficulty due merely to a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), or rather because of their being contradictory (*viruddha-tattva*)? It is not the first, because walking, speaking, and so forth can be performed simultaneously by a single person. Nor is it the second;

Because there is no contradiction between knowledge and action, just as there is none between going and staying, and because there is no lack of application—following the logic of physical exertion or the recitation of mantras (*japa*) for the purpose of neutralizing poison through a specific form of meditation—the author says:
"For when [action] is being performed... This refers to both: the state of action being qualified by knowledge, and [the state] of knowledge...

And there is the distinction of action (*karmaviśiṣṭatva*). Regarding the term *buddhimān*, [the author] states that, by virtue of the rule— "The suffixes *matup* and others occur when there is a desire to express abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, excellence, association, or existence"— it is intended that "excellent intelligence" (*prakṛṣṭā buddhi*) is what is meant.

The phrase "one who knows the meaning of the entire scripture" is followed immediately by "one who performs all actions"; the sense is that the intellect is described in a manner consistent with that [performance]. When it is stated that one is "intelligent" and a "performer of all actions," this refers respectively to knowledge and practice, for it is precisely the fitness for the fruit dependent upon those two that is expressed here by the synonym "competent."

Intending that what is to be expressed here by the word *yukta* (disciplined) is "fit for liberation," it was stated as "fit for liberation. Since two distinct sentences are established by those two words "he is wise" and "he is disciplined," the phrase "having performed his duty" (*kṛtakṛtya*) must also necessarily be a separate sentence; for there is a distinction between the means and the result, and between the knowledge and its result.

With the intention that the perfection of practice is also a cause for praise because of its preeminence, as if it were the perfection [of knowledge] itself, he states the connection with the word "that" [in the verse]: "He alone is the performer of all actions."
"By perception" means that what is contradicted by perception cannot be established by scripture or by reasoning; this is the sense. Regarding "of that which is being performed":
for an object of cognition that has long since perished and has entered the state of memory cannot [be grasped] because only the cognition itself remains.
And how can there be oneness of knowledge for that which is the effect of knowledge? This is what is intended [by the objection]. How is this tenable?
This is not consistent with reason; at best, it could be understood as a mere meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), as in the case of injunctions regarding ritual perspectives (*dṛṣṭividhāna*).
In that case, however, the statement beginning with "having as its core the contemplation of the true nature of the Self" would be untenable—this is the sense [of the objection].

Because all words [in this context] are unrestricted, there is an inclusion of the acquisition of wealth and so forth. Regarding the phrase "devoid of desire and resolve" (*kāmasaṅkalpavarjitāḥ*), first, the compound cannot be analyzed as "desire itself is resolve" (*kāma eva saṅkalpaḥ*), because that would entail the undesirable consequence of treating them as synonyms. Nor can it be "resolve regarding desires" (*kāmānāṃ saṅkalpaḥ*), since such an analysis is possible within a *dvandva* compound where both constituent meanings are primary and mutually related.
Because a *tatpuruṣa* compound cannot have a single word as its predominant member, the intended meaning is therefore "devoid of desire and resolve";

with this in mind, he says, "devoid of desire. By showing that the word *varjita* (devoid) applies to each [member], he indicates that the *dvandva* compound takes precedence over other types of compounds.

This has been indicated. In the section on action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), with the intention that "desire is indeed the resolve for a fruit," [the author] says, "those who are free from attachment to fruits. Here, "resolve" (*saṅkalpa*) does not mean the resolve to perform the action, because without that [resolve], performance would be impossible. Nor does it mean the resolve for a fruit, since that is already covered by the word "desire" (*kāma*).

Therefore, with the intention that some matter relevant to this section concerning the teaching of the Self as dissociated from *prakṛti* must be stated here, [the author says]: "by *prakṛti*. *Sam* means unification; *kalpa* means erroneous cognition.
The phrase "by *prakṛti*" implies "having transformed into the form of the body. It refers to the unification of the Self with the qualities of that [body].

"Name" (*nāma*) refers to the mental connection with one's own causes regarding specific actions based on the qualities (*guṇa*); or alternatively, it is the mental connection with oneself as being subordinate to the qualities of *prakṛti*—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—as they manifest in forms such as divinity or humanity, and in attributes such as grossness, subtlety, whiteness, blackness, and so forth. By this, the notion of "mine" (*svam*) regarding houses and other objects is also included. In the absence of such desires and volitions:
He states the reason for the intended meaning of the word "wise" (*paṇḍita*): "one who is free from [the notion of] primordial nature" (*prakṛtiviyukta*).

A "wise person" is one who possesses the discriminative knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, such as the self and so forth; for wisdom (*paṇḍā*) is indeed the intellect capable of deliberation (*ūha*) and rejection (*apoha*). Although the word "wise" was mentioned last, it is placed in the position of the subject (*uddeśya*) in the phrase "that wise person."
This is because it is appropriate for there to be an injunction praising knowledge, characterized by its power to turn one away from sin.
The phrase "included within action" (*karmāntargatā*) is stated in order to exclude other independent forms of knowledge that are not under discussion here.
For it is not the case that only the action currently being performed is consumed by the fire of knowledge; otherwise, it would follow that such action is fruitless.
Nor is it the latter [the future], because that is dependent upon the greatness of knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, it is said "ancient" (*prācīna*).

Regarding the phrase "knowers of reality" (*tattvajñāḥ*): they are those who possess certain and unerring knowledge of the true nature of that which is to be attained, the attainer—the Self (*ātman*)—and the means of attainment, which is *karmayoga*. By the word "wise" (*budha*),...
The intended meaning is that they are what is meant to be expressed. He concludes the response to the objection with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 19 ||
In order to dispel the charge of redundancy and to show that the subsequent verse has a different meaning, he says: "He explains this very point.

Regarding the phrase "ever-content" (*nityatṛpta*), the meaning is not "constantly content," because no cause for such contentment has been stated; rather, by explaining the absence of desire through the phrase "having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action," it refers to the abandonment of what is impermanent.

Having intended to explain that [the Self] is devoid of volition (*saṅkalpa*) and that it is appropriate to speak of its eternal self-appropriation (*svīkāra*), it was said: "He is satisfied in his own eternal Self. Regarding the term *nirāśraya* ("without support"), it does not refer merely to a location or other such things that serve as a support.

It is not that [the world] is being rejected, because its abandonment is impossible; rather, it is with this intention that it was said—"unstable," etc.—meaning that the very notion of its being worthy of reliance, which is the object of the worldly people's idea that it should be relied upon, is what is being negated. This is stated because of the desire for an explanation of that [notion]. Thus it was said: "who."

The meaning of the prefix *abhi-* is "facing toward" or "exclusive devotion to that. Since it would follow that even general cognition (*sāmānyato jñāna*) is negated when one says "not at all anything," he provides the appropriate qualifier to exclude that:
"not doing anything whatsoever" (*naiva kiṃcit karma*). This means: "even though engaged in action, he does not do anything whatsoever."
Anticipating the objection that "this is contradictory," he says: "by means of the instruction on action" (*karmāpadeśena*).

The sense is this: *karmayoga* consists merely in directing the senses toward favorable objects, as opposed to their wandering toward contrary objects, which is antagonistic to the practice of knowledge. || 20 ||

By the verse beginning with "yasya," the nature of knowledge has been established; by the verse beginning with "tyaktvā," that very point has been explained. He states that there is no tautology in saying "again" (*punarapi*), because the meaning already stated is difficult to comprehend and must be clarified for the sake of clear understanding; thus, the following three verses further refine that same point.
In order to consolidate for the sake of comprehension those points previously stated scattered across many locations,
and to demonstrate that this very subject matter is worthy of special regard, the same meaning already explained is now set forth again with further analysis;
this is done to dispel the notion that the text is merely intended to prohibit all forms of food, including those that are wholesome and complete in their ritual qualities.
It has been stated that this refers to one who is free from attachment to the fruits [of action]. The phrase "with mind and self controlled" (*yata-cittātmā*) refers to the object to be controlled.

In that context, the distinction between the controller and the object to be controlled is natural. However, for the word *ātman* to mean the essential nature of the mind and so forth would be redundant. Therefore, it is logical that the term refers to the mind (*manas*).

With the intention that this word *citta* denotes the mind (*citta*)—which is a specific state consisting of the functions of intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and discernment (*avyavṛtti*), and which is mentioned alongside them—it is said, "with mind and heart restrained" (*yatacittamanāḥ*). The meaning is: one whose mind is devoid of thoughts directed toward other objects.

The mind itself, through its distinct modifications of determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and reflection (*cintā*), is designated by the terms "intellect" (*buddhi*) and so forth, as well as by the terms "the Great One" (*mahat*) and so on.
Here, the separate mention of the "mind-stuff" (*citta*) is intended to include the states of both the intellect and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

By the phrase "the primal nature and its evolutes" (*prakṛti-prākṛta*), there is a comprehensive inclusion of all things intended by the term "objects," namely the objects of experience, the instruments of experience, and so forth.

"Acquisition of all objects" means "acquisition of everything. According to the *Jayantī*, because of the force of the word "bodily" (*śārīra*), it is established that [the limit] is the body; thus it is said, "as long as one lives. The meaning is that the body, or what pertains to the body, is difficult for the embodied being to abandon. Alternatively:

It is called "bodily" (*śārīra*) because it is devoid of attachment to the fruits of action and other such things that constitute the activity of the intellect. Alternatively, the word *śārīra* is simply a synonym for *śarīra*. In this context, the exclusion of actions performed with material substances or fire—mentioned by others as being incompatible with the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*)—is not tenable. Furthermore, the meaning implied by the word *kilbiṣa* has been stated [as follows]: "the cycle of worldly existence" (*saṃsāra*).
If it were stated simply as "only bodily action" (*śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma*), one might understand this as a prohibition of actions such as sacrifice (*yajña*);

therefore, in order to exclude that [misunderstanding], he states that the word "only" (*kevala*) here has the sense of prohibiting [the necessity of] mediation—namely, by the words "by knowledge" (*jñāna*).
When it is said, "performing bodily action," [it refers to] those things such as the acquisition of wealth for the purpose of maintaining the body, which are necessarily [required].
There would be activity; consequently, there would be unavoidable contacts such as the falling of weapons, cold, heat, softness, and harshness.

In that regard, anger would arise toward those things that obstruct activity, and when activity is frustrated, there would be distress due to the futility of one's efforts, while joy would arise upon success; thus [it is] the yoga of action.

In order to dispel the doubt that [non-attachment] would result in the arousal of all enemies that are contrary to the vision of the Self, non-attachment toward things with visible fruits is stated in the verse beginning with "yadṛcchā" (by chance). In that context,
it is intended to mean the cessation of excessive, intentional activity regarding matters such as the maintenance of the body.
He explains the first quarter-verse: "occurring by chance" (*yadṛcchopanatā*).
When the cessation of all activity is intended, even the activity of swallowing and so forth would have to cease for things that have come of their own accord.
Therefore, what is intended here is the cessation of intention and the like, while [the sense organ] is still actively engaged. By this, when [something] comes of its own accord...

It is also taught that whatever object is acquired for the mere maintenance of the body, one should not then engage with things distinguished by superior sweetness and so forth. By the words "as long as" (*yāvat*) and so on, the previously elaborated passage beginning with "the contacts of the senses, however" (*mātrāsparśās tu*) is recalled. [The phrase] "undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*) and so forth...

Just as one feels no anger toward the sun and other causes of heat because they are performing their own natural functions, and just as umbrellas and the like merely perform the act of warding off the heat, so too must one act here—this is the intended meaning.

By the phrase "battle and so forth," the verse beginning with "having made pleasure and pain equal" is recalled, due to the force of the word "having made. Thus, it is said that "action alone" [is to be performed].

The meaning of the word "api" (even) is stated as: "even though the cause of bondage exists, one is not bound," which serves to exclude contradiction. [The phrase] "without steadfastness in knowledge" means even without the yoga of independent knowledge preceded by the practice of the yoga of action. Regarding the statement "one is not bound," [it implies that] the fruit of steadfastness in knowledge is accomplished through action alone.
He states the intended meaning: "Not [the cycle of] transmigratory existence," etc. (22).

By the words "having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action," "having renounced all possessions," and "with mind and self withdrawn from that [world]," the prior abandonment of attachment through conscious deliberation was described. Now, for one who possesses such discipline, in another state—

By the verse beginning with "of one whose attachment has passed away" (gatasaṅgasya), he describes how even for one engaged in activities such as acquiring materials for sacrifice, there is naturally an absence of attachment; thus, he speaks of the cessation of even infinite opposing actions through the power of *karmayoga*. This is accomplished by means of the previously mentioned intentional abandonment of attachment and so forth.

The mind is established in the knowledge of the Self; therefore, it need not now be further restrained. Consequently, attachment also departs of its own accord along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), through the constant contemplation of the Self as the unsurpassed object of enjoyment. Thus, when attachment has ceased, all possessions do not need to be renounced by one's own effort.

However, he was released by them. Thus, for one who has conquered all that is to be conquered and who proceeds without obstacle through the means as they truly exist, all karma—consisting of merit and demerit performed previously—that constitutes an obstacle to the realization of the Self and its attainment, perishes; this entire point is demonstrated by the words "having the Self as its object."

The word *karman* ends in the nominative case and is connected with the verb *pravīlīyate* ("is dissolved"); however, its status as the object of the verb *ācarataḥ* ("of one who performs") is established by the natural flow of the context. Otherwise, even the phrase *samagraṃ pravīlayataḥ* ("of one who dissolves completely") would remain syntactically expectant. With this in mind, [the commentary] says: "of one who is engaged in the performance of sacrifices and other such acts," and so forth.

It has been stated: by the word "yajñāya" (for sacrifice), the mere filling of one's own belly and so forth is excluded, due to the intended meaning of the prefix and the word "samagra" (complete). Thus, it is said to be "without remainder. The alternative interpretation—that it means "existing together with its fruit"—is to be rejected because its meaning is not well-established and because it merely restates what is already established by the sense of the passage.
It is stated "it is destroyed" (*kṣīyate*) in order to exclude that [meaning], because the verbal root [is used] in the sense of non-attachment and in the occurrence of a cause. ||23||
The verse beginning with "brahmārpaṇam" also establishes that action becomes a means to knowledge through a transformation of its nature;

thus, [the commentator] shows its connection with what preceded it. Regarding the word "prakṛteḥ": it means of all [actions], including the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) types, together with their accessories—that is, as characterized by the ladle (*sruc*), the fuel (*samidh*), the oblation (*havis*), and so forth.

"The word *brāhma* is used in its primary sense only for Puruṣottama. This was explained in detail at the beginning of the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*. Furthermore, when the primary sense is possible, a figurative sense is improper; moreover, the contemplation of everything as having the Supreme Person as its essence is established by the scripture. And he himself will state [this] later:
"I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter (ājya), I am the fire, and I am the oblation"— with this intention,
there is the statement of the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) that [the self] consists of the Supreme Person who has become the Supreme Brahman.
Herein, the contemplation of the unreality (*mithyātva*) of the offering materials, such as the oblation, apart from Brahman, belongs to the Brahman-knowledge.

This is indeed the case, because a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would otherwise be improper. To dispel the misconception that there might be a split in the sentence due to the word *brahmārpaṇam* being treated as separate words, he says: "The oblation (*havis*) is qualified by the term *brahmārpaṇam*. In the compound *brahmārpaṇam*, if it were analyzed as "that in which the offering (*arpaṇa*) is into Brahman," it would be a non-co-referential possessive compound (*vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*). [However, it refers to] the fire of Brahman (*brahmāgni*).
Furthermore, there would be tautology with the word *hutam*. Therefore, this is a *samānādhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound.
Moreover, the word *arpaṇa* here refers to the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) and so forth, by deriving it from the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Even if it were derived from the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so on, the aforementioned fault of tautology and the like would still apply. With this in mind, he says:
"It is called *brahma* because it is nourished by this. The reason "because it has *brahma* as its purpose" (*brāhṛkāryatvāt*) is to be supplied everywhere.
It is *brahma* because it has *brahma* as its purpose, in order to exclude the confusion regarding the injunctions for meditations (*dṛṣṭi*) on the *Ṛgveda* and so forth;
and it is itself become *brahma*, as stated in passages such as "in the fire which has become *brahma*" and so on. By means of *brahma*...

Regarding the word *hutam* here: since there is no mention of a substantive—as in the case of the words *arpaṇa*, *havis*, and *agni*—and since it has been stated that the instrument is "the offering with the mind" (*brāhṇā arpaṇam*), it follows by process of elimination that the third case ending denotes the agent. Thus, it is expressed that "it is offered by the mind as the agent. But surely, in this case, there is a syntactical connection between the preceding and following halves [of the verse]?
It is not seen; nor is the first half a separate sentence, because it is incomplete. Therefore, he says:

"Thus," and so forth, ending with "he composed. Regarding the phrase "consisting of *brāhmaṇas*": the meaning is that, because it has those as its effects or because it has them as its body, it is identical in essence to them, and thus it is worthy of being designated by that term.

By this, he says that the term *brāhmakarmasamādhi* is also explained. He says "he" (*saḥ*). One who has *samādhi*—that is, *anusandhāna* (continuous application)—toward an action consisting of the *brahma*, is so described. Since there is no other possible case-ending here, this is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound. Alternatively, the meaning of the word *samādhi* is "one who composes" (*samādhatte*); [it refers to] that which has the form of the *brahma*.

He brings the action to completion—he connects it. Regarding the statement "one must go by means of that very Brahman," he says "by way of having Brahman as one's essence" (brāhmātmakatayā), indicating that here the true nature of the Self is to be directly realized through the yoga of action; this is expressed by the word "Brahman" in the same way that [the fire] is called "milk-drinker" (brāugdhavir) or "fire-eater" (agnayādi). This results in the state of being the instrument of knowledge.

Speaking thus, he states the meaning of the sentence: "By one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣuṇā*). By the phrase "the means for the perception of the Self," the meaning of "it must be gone to" (*gantavyam*) is shown; by the word "direct realization" (*sākṣātkāra*), and by the passage beginning with "not merely abiding in knowledge" (*na jñānaniṣṭhā*), the meaning of the particle *eva* (only/indeed) is explained.

Following the connection with the meaning already stated, he explains the sense of the section beginning with "Only the divine" (*daivam eva*) and ending with "they offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths" (*prāṇān prāṇeṣu juhvati*), by saying: "In this way, of action" (*evaṃ karmaṇaḥ*). "Divine" (*daiva*) means that which pertains to the gods;
and its being related to the gods consists in its being of the nature of their worship. Thus, it is said to be "of the nature of the worship of the gods."

By the restrictive phrase "only fate" (*daivameva*) and by the expression "others," etc., an alternative view is established. Consequently, the mere connection with the deity (*devasaṃbandhamātra*) is not what is intended to be expressed here as the common factor. Therefore, by the word *arcana* (worship), a distinction from the sacrifices, oblations, and so forth that will be described later is indicated. Even though sacrifice and the like are also forms of worshipping the deity, [they are excluded here].
The word *arcana* is well known in the context of worship consisting of the forms and other attributes of various deities.

Just as in the opening statement, "For yogis through the yoga of action," here too the word *yogi* refers specifically to those established in the yoga of action; this is indicated by the use of the term *karmayoginaḥ*. In this context, there is the vision of divine sacrifice.
To dispel the misconception that [the term] means "is enjoined," he explains it through the synonym *caraṇa*, which is employed in the sense of uninterrupted practice:
"they serve" (*sevante*). According to the lexicographers (*naighaṇḍukāḥ*), "service" (*sevā*) is "existence in the form of devotion" (*bhakti*).
Here, the words "service" (*sevā*) and "meditation" (*upāsanā*) refer to the continuity of favorable activity of the three instruments toward the object of service.

However, they are not solely intent upon meditation alone; rather, the word *bhakti* (devotion) expresses that meditation takes the form of love. Now, since Manu and others have recorded it as an obligatory duty (*nityakarman*)—stating, "The worship of the deities and likewise the placing of fuel"—the sacrifice consisting of the worship of the deities is indeed for everyone.

This is necessarily to be performed by those engaged in the yoga of action (*karmayogin*); as to how it is differentiated, he says: "The meaning is that they establish their firm conviction (*niṣṭhā*) in that very [state].
Now, one might object: in the verse beginning with *brāhmārpaṇam*, a certain variety of *karmayogin* has been mentioned.
In the mantra "Arpaṇam agnau haviḥ," because of the specific mention of Agni, a distinction between sub-categories is perceived.

And therein, by the word "tena" (by that), the agent is also indicated; however, this refers to the common attribute known as the contemplation of the Brāhma-nature inherent in all forms of Karma-yoga. It is precisely in that regard [that the agent is specified].
Because it was stated generally as "by means of the concentration on the action of Brahman," therefore the mention of the "offering" (*arpaṇa*), the "oblation" (*havis*), and so forth,

is for the purpose of indicating the specific factors (*kāraka*) required by the various distinctions of those respective yogic actions. For this very reason, following the context of sacrifice characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti*), [the Lord speaks] with the words beginning, "Others [offer] only to the gods."
The claim that this is a figurative statement regarding sacrifices characterized by worldly activity (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa-yajña*) has been refuted by others.

This is because, in the passage "others [offer] sacrifice in the fire of Brahman," it is impossible for the nature of the sacrifice itself, or the Supreme Self and so forth, to be directly the object to be offered or the means of the oblation; therefore, it must be understood through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the means of sacrifice.
He explains that the word *yajña* ending in the accusative refers to the oblation (*havis*), whereas the one ending in the instrumental refers to the *ṛk*, *sāman*, and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "In this context. Now, an objection is raised: it was already stated previously that "the oblation is offered in the Brahman-fire by means of the Brahman";
here too it is said, "others [offer] in the Brahman-fire. Therefore, the meaning of these two expressions, "yajñaṃ" and "yajñena," must be different.

It must be described [separately]; otherwise, there would be the contingency of tautology, and a specific instruction regarding a matter already common to all forms of karma-yoga would also be untenable. To this, he says: "By the principle that 'the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman.
Here, from the word *yajña* (sacrifice) and the word *juhvati* (they offer), there arises a distinction between the two culminations of sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*).
The sense is that because this is what is intended to be expressed, both its status as a subordinate element and its lack of redundancy are established.

Here, in the Brāhmaṇa passage where [the Brahmin] is imagined as fire, the sacrifices are excluded. Furthermore, because of the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*), the view that all these are to be construed as mental sacrifices (*mānasayajña*) is also untenable here. || 25 ||

Regarding the phrase "the ears and so forth," since restraint (*saṃyama*) is not directly fire and the ears and so forth are not things to be offered as oblations, he states the intended meaning: "The others. Restraint is fire because it reduces the ears and so forth to ashes, characterized by the cessation of their activity. Now, even the regulation of the senses—

To the question, "How is this, which is common to all practitioners of *karmayoga*, stated here as being distinguished? it is said: "They strive for restraint. This applies likewise to what follows. One should grasp the intended meaning of the two words "strive" (*prayatante*) and "here" (*atra*). Similarly, regarding the word "steadfastness" (*niṣṭhā*): because there is a distinction in restraint for each sense organ, [the phrase] is "in the fires of restraint" (*saṃyamāgniṣu*).

The plural number [is used]. Regarding the phrase "sound and so forth," he says—"the prevention of the senses' inclination toward objects such as sound"—in order to dispel the misconception that they [the senses] merely present objects like sound to the [internal organs]. For the restraint of the senses was already stated in the passage beginning with "the ears and so forth"; however, here...

Just as in the passage, "Higher than the senses are the objects, and higher than the objects is the mind," the restraint of the objects and the mind is taught in sequence. The restraint of the object means its removal from one's presence; that is to say, avoiding its proximity. From that alone [comes the restraint] of the senses.
The meaning is that the inclination toward them ceases. What, then, is meant by the "destruction" of the senses?

It is intended as the destruction of their connection [with the mind]. Alternatively, in the phrase "the ears and so forth," the avoidance of proximity to objects was intended; here, however, [it refers to the cessation] even of those [senses] that are already in proximity.

The distinction is that it consists in rendering sense objects ineffective. By the phrase "preventing the inclination toward sense objects," what is intended is the absolute avoidance of prohibited things and the like—since the total cessation of all sense objects is difficult to achieve—as well as the cessation of excessive attachment to those things that are not contrary to dharma. || 26 ||

Since the restraint of the senses and their objects has been stated, and following the sequence "and the mind is superior to the objects," it is the mind itself that must be declared as the object to be restrained; therefore, he makes it known here that by the term *ātmasaṃyama* (self-restraint), the restraint of the mind is intended. [This is seen] in the phrase "in the fire of the yoga of mind-restraint" (*manassaṃyamayogāgnau*). Mind-restraint...
Yoga is [defined] by its being the means for attaining that [state], or it is the restraint of the mind. Yoga is that which is to be attained and so forth;

its being "illuminated by knowledge" means that it is rooted in the contemplation of the nature of the pure Self as distinct from the body. And here, just as the ears and other senses are [the recipients] of sound and other objects, the activities of the senses and the activities of the vital breaths are stated to be the offerings to be poured into the fire.
If it is argued that this would result in the fault of redundancy (paunaruktya) and so forth, he says "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) in order to dispel such doubt.

The functions of the sense organs (*indriya-karma*) consist of seeing, touching, speaking, grasping, and so on; the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa-karma*) consist of inhalation, exhalation, and so on. Alternatively, [the mind] is the cause of the activity of the sense organs, as established in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda* and other texts.

It is a subtle, specific activity. By this, it is distinguished from the prāṇāyāma that will be described later. Here too, as before, the intended meaning of the word "prevention" (nivāraṇa) is the same. Since the ears and other [organs] were mentioned previously, this verse is devoted solely to the restraint of the organs of action (karmendriya). || 27 ||

Because the word *yajña* (sacrifice) is applied to each [term], various distinct forms of dedication to the yoga of action are expressed. For that very reason, the word *apara* (inferior/other) is also connected with each one individually. In this context, those for whom sacrifice consists of material substances are "those whose sacrifice is material" (*dravyayajñāḥ*). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "those whose sacrifices have material substances as their essence."

Because all specific sacrifices accomplished by means of material substances (*dravya*) are included by the force of the word "substance," the worship of deities, giving, sacrifice (*yāga*), and oblation (*homa*) are mentioned separately. Therefore, the intention is that the plural form in the phrase "sacrifices of substance" (*dravyayajñāḥ*) and so forth refers to their respective internal subdivisions. Now, [one might object]:

Since the worship of deities, sacrifice, and so forth have already been mentioned previously, there is no tautology. If that is the case, one might object that it should have been stated specifically as "gifts, sacrifices, and so forth. That too is not correct; for the purpose of indicating an intermediate subsuming category that distinguishes all four—worship, giving, sacrifice, and oblation—from austerity-sacrifices and the rest.

This is stated with the intention of making it known that these are to be accomplished by means of wealth acquired through righteous means (*nyāya*), and because that [righteousness] is applicable to the general term [used here]. Alternatively, while the nature of worship and so forth was previously described as being sacrifice (*yajña*), here the intention is that it refers specifically to the acquisition of the materials for those purposes and so on. Thus, it has been said: "All these are sacrifices of material substance (*dravyayajña*). Or rather, the sacrificial nature of the essence of worship and so forth was mentioned previously; here, however, the intention is that it applies to the acquisition of the materials for those very purposes.

The passage beginning with "In accordance with the rule" (*nyāyataḥ*) and ending with "they strive" (*prayatante*) has been stated. Austerity (*tapas*) consists of the restraint of enjoyments (*bhoga-saṅkoca*); this is the demonstration of its internal subdivisions, beginning with "the *kṛcchra*" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "sacrifices of yoga" (*yoga-yajñāḥ*), "yoga" means union (*saṃyoga*), that is to say, attainment (*prāpti*). And that [attainment] here—
Intending to express that [the practice] consists of visiting sacred fords (*puṇyatīrtha*) and residing there, and so forth, he says "sacred fords" (*puṇyatīrtha*).
Here, the term "sacred place" (*puṇyasthāna*) includes shrines of deities (*devatāsthāna*), hermitages (*āśrama*), specific regions (*janapada-viśeṣa*), and the like.
Now, one might ask: why does the word "yoga" here not refer to the yoga of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-yoga*) or merely to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*)?

To this he replies: "Here" (iha). Since this is a section concerning steadfastness in action (*karma-niṣṭhā*), it is not appropriate for it to concern yogis directly; nor is it fitting for it to concern that [steadfastness] in general, as this is a section concerning its divisions. Among those divisions, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and by the semantic force of the word "yoga," only the attainment of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth should be understood. This has been indicated.

This is because it has been stated by the supreme teachers in the *Saṃgraha*: "The yoga of action consists of the practice of austerity, pilgrimage, charity, sacrifice, and so forth"—this is the sense. Furthermore, since the study of the scriptures (*svādhyāya*) and the knowledge of their meaning are designated as distinct duties and as distinct sacrifices, and because the former [the yoga of action] possesses primacy.

He explains by distinguishing [the types]: "Some are devoted to the practice of recitation (*svādhyāya*). This is because *svādhyāya* is appropriately associated with the study of the texts, because self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is common to all, and because the knowledge of the meaning is useful even for the performance of ritual action (*anuṣṭhāna*). "Others are devoted to the practice of knowing the meaning of those [texts]."

Thus it has been said. Here, the word "other" (*para*) serves to exclude commonality and expresses devotion to that [specific practice]. This is because it is inappropriate for the word *yati* here to refer to a specific stage of life (*āśrama*), and because it is appropriate for it to refer to a specific type of person who is common to all those devoted to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
He provides an etymological explanation by distinguishing between the meanings of the root and the suffix: "those whose nature is to strive.

Intending that the meaning of the word *vrata* here refers to a resolve (*saṅkalpa*) that follows all applications and is common to those established in the yoga of all actions, he says, "those of firm resolve."
In this context, "sharpened" means being unblunted; and that is indeed firmness. || 28 ||

The phrase "devoted to *prāṇāyāma*" is used to indicate the general inclusion of all three groups; however, the separate sentence "they who establish themselves in *prāṇāyāmas*" is formed to make known the internal distinctions among those devoted to *prāṇāyāma*. This is indicated by the words beginning with "*pūraka*."

This is a demonstration of the internal subdivisions of *prāṇāyāma*. He distinguishes the portions that establish those respective subdivisions with the words beginning "the apāna," and so forth. For *pūraka* (inhalation) is indeed the downward entry of the *prāṇa* which is moving upward;
and consequently, the expression "offering into the apāna" is justified through metaphorical usage. Likewise [for the downward-moving breath].

For the upward movement of the breath is indeed *recaka* (exhalation); thus, even the term *apāna* is used figuratively for the breath (*prāṇa*). The retention [of the breath] by preventing its upward and downward movements is *kumbhaka*. The intention behind [the mention of] meditation and so forth is that one should block the courses of both *prāṇa* and *apāna*. "The vital breaths" (*prāṇān*) means the various modifications of the function of *prāṇa*. As for the regulation of food:
He states that [this practice] is prescribed as common to all forms of prāṇāyāma by way of its visible and invisible benefits:
"even among the three [stages], those intent on prāṇāyāma."

Two doubts are being dispelled: first, whether there is a difference in intermediate results among those established in various types of yoga through high and low actions; and second, whether those established in practices such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should abandon sacrifices and the like.

This is resolved by the verse beginning with "All [of these]... (sarve'pi). Because of the expression "in their own desired [ends]," there is an option (vikalpa) due to the lack of distinction in the result.
It has been indicated that, in accordance with the specific capacity and other factors of each case, the "self-evident" (svacchā) [injunction] alone is the restrictor of the particular;
this is for the purpose of demonstrating that the general term *yajña* is not to be restricted.

To this end, the passage beginning with "with sacrifices" (*sahayajñaiḥ*) was stated. [Thus, they become] those whose impurities are destroyed by sacrifice (*yajñakṣapitakalmaṣāḥ*) and those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice (*yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujaḥ*).

By these two [verses], because of the recognition of what was previously stated in passages such as, "The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are freed from all sins," and because in that same context the eating of the remnants of the sacrifice is elaborated upon as being for the sake of maintaining the body, it is mentioned for the purpose of recalling that: "by the nectar of the remnants of the sacrifice."

They are indeed performing the maintenance of the body. It is thus established that even for those devoted to practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma), the performance of sacrifices and other rites must necessarily be carried out by one who maintains the doctrine of their permanence. By the use of the particle "eva" (indeed), it is shown that such activities as the maintenance of the body are not contrary to the realization of the Self; rather, they are conducive to it.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the word “engaged” (*vyāpṛtā*): the sense is that otherwise, activity itself would be impossible. The phrase “one must go by means of the *brāhma* alone” is a concluding statement whose meaning is identical to what was explained previously. Furthermore, the phrase “going to the eternal *brāhma*” has already been explained in the commentary on the *Agnihotra*.

By the half-verse beginning with "Not this" (*nāyam*), it is stated that one who, through the conceit of being established in a particular sub-division of *karmayoga*, abandons the general duties such as the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, is unfit for any human goal. The word "of one who does not sacrifice" (*ayajñasya*) is to be explained [as qualifying the subject]. "This world" (*ayaṃ lokaḥ*).

Regarding this [passage], he shows what is intended by the reference "this" with the words: "not the natural world. To dispel the misconception that there is a negation of the mere nature of the world, he says: "connected with the natural world," because it is more appropriate for the phrase "this world" to refer to the terrestrial world established by direct perception. Why [should it] be otherwise?
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why might this [the performance of sacrifice] not be intended for the attainment of heaven and so forth?", he says: "Because it is the supreme human goal.
The sense is that once it has been established that there is no liberation for one who does not perform sacrifice, its undertaking would indeed be for that purpose.
This refers to the triad of human goals consisting of the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), the heard-from-tradition (*ānuśravika*), and those distinct from liberation. "This world" [is mentioned].

He says, "For that is material" (*sa hi prākṛtaḥ*), in order to reveal the common adjunct that serves as the cause for the [false] instruction and its nature as being contrary to the supreme human goal under discussion. The term "material" (*prākṛta*) is used because it consists of a specific transformation of *prakṛti* and because it is what is to be attained by one who is conjoined with that [matter]. || 31 ||
Having thus taught the internal subdivisions of *karmayoga*, and having stated that even among those various subdivisions,

the obligatory performance of the common *nitya* and *naimittika* rites is required, as well as the transgression incurred by their abandonment, the summary of this very point is now made with the verse beginning with "evam" (thus).

Immediately after the instruction on the various distinctions of the application of manifold types of action, [the Lord] says "Thus are the many kinds of sacrifices," with the intention that this statement must pertain precisely to the subject at hand; for it is said, "Because of such a state. Furthermore, the word *mukha* refers to the means (*upāya*). And the *Nighaṇṭuka*s say: "The word *mukha* [is used] for the mouth, for the primary, and for copper."

Regarding the phrase "of the doors and the means": the meaning is that they are expanded as intermediate subdivisions within the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), which is the means for attaining the Self. He states this with the words "the true nature of the Self. The reference "them" points back to all the forms previously introduced, and "all" includes the collection of every intermediate subdivision without exception.

This is the intended meaning. The phrase "those whose characteristics have been stated" (*uktalakṣaṇān*) means "those whose divisions have been stated" (*uktabhedān*). Alternatively, it may express the meanings of both the words *evam* and *bahuvidha*. [The term] "having the form of cognition" (*jñānākāratva*) is due to their being included within cognition.

[The term] "having the characteristics stated" (*uktalakṣaṇatva*) refers to those mentioned at the beginning as the subject matter of the chapter by the author who says "those whose characteristics have been stated."

It is indicated that the essential nature of *karmayoga* has also been described. By the separate statement, "Know all [these] to be born of action," he declares the primacy of *prāṇāyāma* and so forth, as well as the fact that the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other rites are for the sake of that [practice].
By the words "day after day" (*aharahaḥ*), it is shown that because one becomes unfit for everything else by failing to perform this, it must be practiced until its fruit is attained.
It is also indicated that [this practice] is extremely useful because it removes evil daily and serves as the cause for the elevation of other beings. 32.

The direct connection of this [verse] is with the section beginning with "Superior" (*śreyān*) and extending until the end of the chapter, which establishes that knowledge is the means [to liberation].
Now, it may be asked: since it has been declared that the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material substances (*dravyamaya-yajña*), [how is this so?]

It is appropriate to accept that the primacy belongs to the yoga of knowledge, which is the internal means for the direct realization of the Self. Furthermore, by the statement, "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge," it is understood that the fruit of all this action is included within knowledge; [as is seen in the verse]: "Even if you are among the most sinful..."

Furthermore, such indications as "the worst of all evildoers," "the fire of knowledge consumes all actions," and "one whose actions have been renounced through yoga" are inconsistent with the practice of karma-yoga that follows immediately [in the text]. Even in the verse beginning with "Not by knowledge alone," [it is shown] that [liberation] comes from karma-yoga.

It is understood that [this verse] is intended to emphasize the superior purifying power of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*); furthermore, the statement, "Having attained knowledge, one reaches supreme peace before long," reveals that while the yoga of knowledge is internal and thus swift-acting, the other path is characterized by delayed results. "By which [knowledge], all beings without exception..."

The statement, "Then you shall see Me within yourself and in Me," which describes the nature of knowledge, also confirms that this is the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). For everything is not directly realized merely through the knowledge of the Self as included within the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
Furthermore, in the verse, "The sacrifice of self-study and the sacrifice of knowledge," [knowledge] is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of material objects and the like.
The sacrifice of knowledge has been pointed out; therefore, this section is to be understood as a praise of the yoga of knowledge. To this it is said:

in the passage "Superior is the sacrifice of knowledge to the other two-fold sacrifice," it is not proper to claim that the intention is the yoga of knowledge merely because of the predominance of knowledge; for [the Lord] stated, "Action is indeed superior to inaction."

Because in all such passages, the predominance of action contrary to that [renunciation] is elaborated; and because in the subsequent chapter, it will be stated by the Teacher himself, "Of these two, however, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action," it is impossible to propound a meaning contradictory to that in the middle. Therefore, here—

The term *jñānayajña* (knowledge-sacrifice) refers here to a specific aspect of *karmayoga*. However, in the passage "and those whose sacrifice is study and knowledge" (*svādhyāyajñānayajñāḥ*), it is stated that the term refers to the *jñānayajña* consisting of the repeated practice of the meaning of one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
Since the true nature of the Self (*ātmayāthātmya*) is also the subject matter of *svādhyāya*, there is not a great distance between that [type of *jñānayajña*] and this one.

Therefore, in the concluding verse of the chapter, "tasmādajñānasaṃbhūtam" (therefore, having severed doubt with the sword of knowledge, arise and practice yoga), this is consistent. Furthermore, the phrase "all action" (sarva karma) refers solely to the fact that the portion of knowledge within action is predominant, as in the verse, "even if you are... (api cedasi).

Regarding such passages as "The fire of knowledge burns all actions" and "There is nothing equal to knowledge," there is no absolute restriction to the path of knowledge alone (*jñānayoga*), because their purpose is to praise the aspect of knowledge insofar as it brings about the removal of sin. Furthermore, in the phrase "one who has renounced action through yoga," [the reference is] to action...

What is intended here is merely the attainment of the state of being the instrument of knowledge, free from attachment to the fruits [of action] and so forth. In the verse beginning with "Having gained knowledge, [one attains] supreme peace," the stage of maturation in the form of direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of that portion of knowledge which is included within *karmayoga* is described; [as it continues: "That [knowledge], by itself, through time, in one who is perfected in yoga, [arises] within the self..."

This is because the state of maturation has been clarified immediately in the subsequent [passage], "The man of faith attains knowledge. By this, the statement "by which you will see all beings without exception" is also not contradicted. Having intended all of this, he says: "It has both forms."

"In action" (*karmaṇi*) means "in the application of action" (*karmayoge*); or, in this context, the word "action" (*karman*) refers to that which is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*). "From the portion consisting of material substances" (*dravyamayāt aṃśāt*): the sense is that the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) here refers to the constituent parts of the sacrifice. He states that there is no tautology between the words "all" (*sarva*) and "entire" (*akhila*) because their referents differ here, [explaining it as] "of that which is other than those."

What else is there here to be adopted other than action, and how is that action completed within knowledge? To this he says: "That very [knowledge] itself. By the phrase "by all means," he demonstrates that which is to be adopted other than that [action]. By the phrase "having become the goal to be attained," he indicates that its completion occurs therein [in knowledge].
This is the explanation. He clarifies that the action is completed therein by stating, "that very [action] being practiced.
By this restriction, the relationship between the goal and the means is shown to be based solely on a difference in state.

This is the intended meaning. By this, it is stated that the completion of action occurs within the knowledge residing in one's own heart, with reference to the state of the goal characterized by direct realization (sākṣātkāra). || 33 ||

It is stated in the verse beginning with "tādviddhi" that even knowledge already taught should be heard again and again from those who possess it for the sake of increasing its clarity at every moment during its various stages of maturation; the word "tat" (that) is used here as a reference to something previously perceived.

This is stated to indicate that [the Lord] refers back to the manner described at the beginning of the treatise. From "indestructible" (*avināśī*) up to "taught by me" (*mayopadiṣṭam*), it has been said. The sense is that no knowledge other than what has been taught prior to this is to be heard here. Therefore, regarding the action thus enjoined...

"Being present" refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). "From time to time" refers to the occasion for inquiry that is conducive to ripening. Alternatively, what is intended is the conduciveness to ripening resulting from prostration and so forth by way of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). This is established by injunctions such as, "One should approach the guru alone," and so on.

This is as follows: in order to indicate that a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) of prostration and the other qualities is intended, there is an explanation using a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*):
"by means of prostration, inquiry, service, and so forth. There are scriptural injunctions such as, "From self-study one should proceed to yoga; from yoga one should return to self-study."
The expression "at various times" (*kāle kāle*) indicates repetition (*vīpsā*).

The phrase "in its manifest form" (*viśadākāram*) serves to preclude the charge of redundancy in hearing it again. It does not imply, however, that the Blessed One has now taught knowledge that was previously unclear, or that Arjuna has failed to grasp it.

Even that which was understood unclearly—namely, what has been stated here—is also clarified by the term "conducive to maturation" (*vipākānuguṇa*). It was indeed taught clearly by the Blessed One; and Arjuna is possessed of attentiveness and other such qualities.

Nevertheless, because the door through which the light of the knowledge of reality spreads— the very nature of the internal organ— is blocked by infinite doors of evil earned through beginningless karma, there is currently no great clarity; for indeed, when the eyes have not received eye-salve that subdues bile, [vision] never occurs.
It is like the cognition of the whiteness of a conch shell [produced] by its rays.
When sins have been dispelled through the yoga of action performed as it truly is, there will be a state fit for clear knowledge;
and at that time, for the sake of declaring the portion already known of the reality generally understood through previous instruction—
One must engage in further hearing (śravaṇa) for the sake of knowing parts not yet understood and for the purpose of reawakening what has been forgotten.

This point will become clear through the account of the *Anugītā*. The intention is that this applies to the wise, whether it be "I" or "others. The qualifying term "seers of reality" (*tattvadarśinaḥ*) [is used].
This indicates the cause for [the teacher] being an instructor of this knowledge and so forth;
thus, it is said that [the teacher] is one who has directly realized the nature of the Self. Even by those who perceive reality, it has been stated:
"One should not teach to one who has not resided [as a disciple] for a year, nor to one who is devoid of discipline and other such qualities."

The delay necessitated by injunctions such as "it must be spoken" is not to be disregarded; this is indicated by the phrase "by prostrations and so forth. Beginning with the words, "To him who had approached him properly, that wise one," [the text continues] with, "he spoke that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence."

The sense is that, knowing from scripture that [the teachers] are intent on injunctions, they will instruct [me] correctly because they are seers of reality (*tattvadarśin*). "Prostration" (*praṇipāta*) is falling down very low;
it is intended to include bowing, clasping the feet, and so forth, which constitute the preliminary part of a question. "Inquiry" (*paripraśna*)...

By concealing one's superior intelligence and by not directly stating what ought to be asked, one poses a question concerning a subject related to that [topic]. The sense is that one should not employ fallacious arguments (*kuyukti*) to counter-argue like an opponent (*prativādin*). "Service" (*sevā*), however, means devotion (*bhakti*) or long-term attendance.

With the intention that the "equality" (sāmya), which was previously mentioned as the cause for the synthesis of all [states] within one's own self, has not been discussed here because it will be explained later, he says: "In the contact with prakṛti," and so forth.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then by Me" (*atho mayi*): the meaning is that through My manifestation you shall perceive both yourself and others.

To the question—how can those who are not lords and are subject to karma achieve such realization through the manifestation of the Lord?—He replies: "Because of the similarity to My own nature, [I am] completely pure."

He says "this" [referring to the following], because it was stated that the similarity with the Lord will also be discussed later and thus was not mentioned here. He says "likewise," indicating that there is also scriptural authority for the pure self's equality with the Supreme Self: "Having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless..."
Due to the departure of merit and demerit, he is free from the contact with primordial nature (prakṛti) caused by them, as well as from the afflictions and so forth induced thereby.

By the phrase "of one who is completely released from name-and-form" (nāmarūpanirmuktasya), another passage from that same text, namely "so the knower is liberated from name-and-form," is also called to mind. [This refers to] the state of equality with the Lord (īśvara).
Having dispelled the suspicion that [the cause] might be accidental, he demonstrates the cause established by Śruti and Smṛti by saying "ataḥ" (therefore).

By this, it is also stated that the equality of the individual souls (jīvas) with the Lord (Īśvara), as established by Śruti and other sources, is likewise a cause for their mutual equality. By this, [it is shown that there is equality] among the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) with one another, and with the Lord.

Those who claim that identity (*caikyam*) is what is being taught here have been refuted. Now, one might object: "It appears that what is enjoined here is the perception of all things as being supported within one's own self and within the Lord of All. This is not so; for it is impossible for one's own individual self to be the support of everything. He states that there is also scriptural authority for the equality [of the individual self] with the Supreme Self:

"So be it. Having cast off merit and demerit, he is stainless; because of the departure of merit and demerit, he is free from the contact with *prakṛti* caused by them, as well as from the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth induced thereby.
By the phrase "of one liberated from name and form," it is shown that such a knower is liberated from name and form.

Thus, another passage from that same source is also brought to mind; it is thereby stated that the Śruti refutes the suspicion that the identity with the Lord might be merely occasional. By this, those who claim that the identity of individual souls (kṣetrajñas) with one another and with the Lord is what is being expressed here are answered.

Now, it might be argued that what is enjoined here is the perception of oneself and all other things as being contained within oneself. This is not so; for it is impossible for oneself to be the substratum of everything.

If it is argued that this is possible through a cognition extending up to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), we say no; because the subject matter of the section concerns the absorption of the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, the "seeing of others within oneself" is the contemplation of all things as having an identical form. || 35 ||

Thus, the predominance of the factor of knowledge (*jñānāṃśa*), its quality of being experienced from time to time in accordance with its maturation (*vipāka*), and its defining characteristic have been stated. Now, its greatness—consisting in its capacity to eliminate opposing factors—is described by means of the verse beginning with "apicet" (even if). The word *cet* is a synonym for *yadi* (if).
Moreover, "api ca" (moreover) is used here to indicate that the two [words] have the same referent as when they are joined together;
this is for the sake of clarification. It is expressed by the word "yadyapi" (even though), because of its being the counter-correlative to the term "pāpakṛttama" (the worst evildoer).
The word "ita" (gone/escaped) in the phrase "pāpebhya ita" refers either to a person characterized by sin or to sin itself.
The fifth [case-ending] is used in the words "hatau" (struck) and "saṃtariṣyasi" (you shall cross over), by virtue of their inherent power.

The ocean is metaphorically represented as having the form of evil (*vṛjinam*). He speaks with the intention that its "infinity," expressed by the word "all" (*sarva-*) and so forth, conforms to its nature as an ocean, insofar as it has been active since beginningless time.
"Acquired previously," thus [ends verse] 36.

But how can a single [recitation] have the power to remove sins that have been active since beginningless time? Furthermore, because of such scriptural statements as, "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas," its capacity to remove the very nature of sin is untenable.
Anticipating the objection that [the fire] might simply remain for a while, it is said: "As with the fuel" (*yathaidhāṃsi*).

Furthermore, the analogy of crossing the ocean does not contradict re-entry [into the world]; however, by means of the analogy of reducing wood to ashes, even the possibility of performing an effect again is precluded. [The fires] have been reduced to ashes.

"Kurute" means "perform acts that should not be done. In the word "samiddha," the prefix and the root-meaning indicate the capacity for total burning; thus, it means "completely increased. The plural number in "edhāṃsi" (fuel-wood) is intended to signify that a single [act] serves as the counter-agent to many [faults].

It shows this by the phrase "the collection of fuel for the fire. Because of the statement "all actions," it is understood that [knowledge] causes the cessation even of specific worldly merits that exist in a state of opposition [to liberation].
As for the passage beginning with "what has not been experienced," that is intended for something else; otherwise, the scriptures on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would also be contradicted.
The state of being. || 37 ||

The meaning demonstrated by the worldly analogy is established as having the nature of being supremely pure, just as fire possesses a burning power not seen in other substances. It is equal to the knowledge of the purified self among those subsequent to the knowledge of the Lord mentioned in the phrase "not [mere] purity."

The meaning is that there is nothing else that purifies. Now, an objection is raised: "Even for one who possesses the intention, 'I shall now produce such knowledge,' it does not arise; therefore, because it is the object of human effort, it is not something to be enjoined. This doubt is resolved by the half-verse beginning with "That [knowledge] itself" (*tat svayam*). By the word "that" (*tat*):

He says, "of such a kind," meaning that the state of fruition (*vipākāvasthā*) is being referred to. By the phrase "according to the instruction," it is indicated that [the practice] is based on the treatises (*śāstrīyatva*), is complete (*avikalatva*), and is to be experienced from time to time (*kālekāle vedanīyatva*).
This is because such knowledge possesses an abundance of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and because it removes opposing evils.
With the intention that the cause for [attaining] the Self is expressed by the phrase "perfected through yoga" (*yogasaṃsiddhaḥ*), he says:
"perfection through the yoga of knowledge, action, and form. This means having attained the fitness characterized by the ripening of the *kaṣāyas*.
With the intention that the word "himself" (*svayam*) expresses independence from instruction at that time, he says: [the following].

"By oneself alone" means that although the nature of knowledge is not directly within the scope of one's own effort, its status as something to be practiced (vidheya) is established through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) in the aforementioned form, which serves as its foundation;
this is the intended meaning. Here, the locative case in "in the self" (*ātmani*) denotes the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Now, [the text continues:]

Alternatively, with the intention that [the self] exists even when devoid of those [qualities], it is intended either as having the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or as being "attested by one's own self" (*svātmasākṣika*). || 38 ||
Intending to explain that the two halves of the subsequent verse constitute a detailed exposition of the two halves of the preceding verse in reverse order, he says:

"He states that very point clearly. Possessing faith and so forth is the cause for one's own attainment of knowledge; since it will be stated later, "the ignorant and the faithless," it follows that here too the term "knower" (jña) refers to one who possesses such qualities.

This is stated for the purpose of making it known that "one who possesses faith" (śraddhāvān) is intended; therein, it is said for the purpose of manifesting the tenfold divisions and for the purpose of establishing the arising of faith. From the instruction: "having obtained knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses faith, being in haste," [the author] will indeed explain in the passage concerning "one who lacks faith" that it means "not being in haste."

One who has that very [state] as their intended object because of its supreme worthiness to be attained is "intent upon that" (*tatpara*). Thus it is said: "with the mind fixed exclusively on that alone. Although the word "without delay" (*acireṇa*) occurs in the subsequent sentence, it is required here for the purpose of dispelling the doubt regarding a long duration suggested by the word "in time" (*kālena*).

With the intention that this [phrase] should also be construed with the first half [of the verse], it was stated: "in a short time," "possessing the aforementioned characteristics," and so forth. [Objection: Liberation occurs after the intervention of the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) and at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma; how, then, can it be said to occur "in a short time"?
The meaning is as follows: the word "previously" (*pūrvaṃ*) is used with the phrase "by time" (*kālena*) to exclude a duration of two or three days and so forth;

however, the word "not long" (*acireṇa*) serves to negate any delay such as that required for the practice of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) or the acquisition of another body. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word "peace" (*śānti*) here refers to the means [of liberation], because it has been brought to complete perfection; it does not refer to the state of tranquility (*śama*) which is merely a constituent part of that means.

This is for the sake of clarification. It has been stated that one attains supreme *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, in the final three verses of the second chapter—namely, "He attains peace, not he who desires objects of desire," "He attains tranquility," and "He reaches the *brahma*-nirvāṇa"—the words *śānti* (peace) and *nirvāṇa* refer to the state of the fruit (*phaladaśā*).
The subject matter is the same. Therein, the phrase "he attains peace" found in the middle verse is recognized here as well.
To recall the preceding and following verses, it is stated here: "He attains the state," and the "state of nirvāṇa" is also mentioned. || 39 ||
The very point already stated is established by way of contrast through the verse beginning with "and the ignorant" (*ajñaśca*).

This means one who is devoid of the knowledge obtained through instruction. This is because it is appropriate, according to the sequence previously indicated, that lack of faith arises from a desire for something else; furthermore, it is due to the association with the state of being "unconscious" (*asaṃjñin*). Here, the word "ignorant" (*ajña*) refers to the cessation of the knowledge produced by the scriptures.

This is the intended meaning. Since doubt (*saṃśaya*) has been mentioned separately, the phrase "one who lacks faith" (*aśraddadhānaḥ*) does not primarily aim at the prohibition of trust, but rather the prohibition of longing (*ākāṅkṣā*); for it is precisely intense longing that is meant by the word *tvaramāṇaḥ*.
