Thus, it is said "not hastening" (*atvaramāṇaḥ*). [And] "one whose mind is full of doubt" (*saṃśayātmā*).

"Saṃśaya" means that by which one doubts; it refers to the cause of doubt, meaning a mind that has become the cause of doubt. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is "one whose mind is [fixed] on doubt. Regarding the destruction of the eternal self, characterized by its being devoid of human purpose (puruṣārtha), which is continued in a sequence of prior and posterior states—

The statement "he becomes destroyed" (*vinaṣṭo bhavati*) is made with the intention of expressing the distinction between the meaning of the base and the suffix, in order to demonstrate the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the preceding [rule]. By this, the usage of [the term] in contexts other than that of absolute destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), such as in "destroyed" (*vinaṣṭāḥ*) or "perished" (*pranaṣṭāḥ*), is also indicated. [This applies to] the form *vinaśyati*.
The latter half is the commentary (*vivaraṇa*). By the word "this" (*ayam*) in the phrase "this too" (*ayam api*), there is an indication of the insignificance pointed out by that very term.

As in the passage, "This world does not exist for one who does not sacrifice; how then another, O best of the Kurus?", so here too the word "world" (*loka*) refers to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). This is for the purpose of demonstrating the *kaumutika-nyāya* (the maxim of the lamp).

And it has been stated that "this world" [is meant]. Furthermore, because this is a section concerning liberation (*mokṣa*), the intention is that it is not appropriate for the words "this" and "here" to refer to the terrestrial or celestial realms; with this in mind, he says "dharma and artha. To the question, "How can one whose nature is characterized by doubt regarding the object that serves as the means to liberation fail to achieve other human goals (*puruṣārtha*)?", he replies: "scriptural" (*śāstrīya*).

The intended meaning is this: it is not the case that the scriptures propound action alone—such as that which leads to results occurring within this very body—as is the case with the *Āyurveda* and other such works, such that there would be no dependence on the knowledge of a self distinct from the body.
For, as a rule, the fruits resulting from sacrifices and the like, such as heaven and so forth, are those that occur in a subsequent body.
It is established [in this way]. Therefore, the certainty regarding a self distinct from the body is absolutely necessary.
This is intended as a conclusion concerning the absence of both types of human goals; to clarify that this refers to the phrase "not happiness," he says, "Therefore.

Alternatively, it refers to the doubt extending from the attainment of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), which consists of the experience of infinite happiness, down to hell, which consists of the experience of infinite suffering.

It was stated that it is "not happiness" because it causes mental anguish, with reference to the suffering experienced at that time; or else, what is intended is the absence of that happiness which is rooted in the conceit of being fit for the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*).
The primary subject matter of the chapter is summarized by the verse beginning with *yogasaṃnyasya*.

"By the yoga as taught" means by the yoga of non-attachment (*abuddhiyoga*), which was taught in such passages as, "He who sees inaction in action," and so forth. By this, the exclusion of the yoga consisting of the direct perception of the Self is indicated.

Regarding the phrase "one who has renounced action" (*saṃnyastakarmāṇam*), it is stated "one whose actions have attained the form of knowledge" (*jñānākāratāpannakarmāṇam*) in order to dispel the misconception that this refers to the abandonment of the very nature of action. Here, by means of attaining the form of knowledge— which consists in the relinquishing of agency and so forth—
the sublation of the form of action is figuratively designated by the word "renunciation of action" (*karma-saṃnyāsa*).

The sense is that if [the Self] were intent on abandoning its own nature (*svarūpa*), there would be a contradiction with what precedes and follows. The phrase "by means of the knowledge of the Self as it has been taught" is stated in order to exclude [other means such as] the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and so forth. The term "in the Self" (*ātmani*) is used to indicate that the doubt regarding the Self's being distinct from the body and so on is here being negated. Regarding the term "possessing the Self" (*ātmavantam*): [...]* *I have provided the translation for the portion of the text supplied.*

The word *ātman* refers here to the mind (*manas*), by virtue of the power of the cognition whose object is the relationship [between the self and the mind], and because of the established usage [of the term]. With this intention, he said "the wise one" (*manasvinam*). Here, the sense of the suffix *-mat* is "an excessive degree of relationship";
and that excess is stated for the purpose of indicating an unshakeability by anything whatsoever. [This applies to] the matter taught.
"Whose mind is firmly established"—this is stated in order to indicate that [the mind] consists of the withdrawal of all other supreme purposes.
"That which has become the cause of bondage," and so forth, was said [to this end]. || 41 ||

Having thus established the matter in detail, the point to be performed is concluded for Arjuna by the verse beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This refers to doubt; for doubt arises from ignorance, since the non-apprehension of specific distinctions is the cause of doubt. It is as if a thorn were lodged within the heart.

Alternatively, the phrase "situated within" (hṛtstha) means "internal. The use of the genitive case in the word "of the self" (ātmanaḥ) is intended to indicate that it culminates in a specific relationship characterized by being the subject (viṣayitva).
To highlight this, it is stated as "doubt concerning the self" (ātmaviṣayaṃ saṃśayam). Alternatively, [it may be understood as] "this doubt" (enaṃ saṃśayam).

From this explanation, it is established that [the word] has the self as its object. However, for the sake of connecting the word "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) with the phrase "by the sword of knowledge" (*jñānāsinā*), it is stated as "by the sword of self-knowledge" (*ātmajñānāsinā*). Alternatively, there is a connection with both [words] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāyena*).
By the word "by me" (*mayā*), the teacher’s status as a reliable authority (*āpta*) is indicated through the perfection of his omniscience, compassion, and other qualities.

This is what was intended [by the word "yoga"], because it serves as a conclusion to the instruction on Karma-yoga. The word "yoga" here is used to indicate that it does not refer to other types of yoga; thus it is said, "the Karma-yoga taught by Me. For Arjuna, who was born into the Bharata lineage, rising up for battle—which is his own duty—is itself the rising up for the purpose of Karma-yoga.

In order to reveal the intended meaning of the word "Bhārata," he said, "Arise, O Bhārata! By that very address, it is also indicated that Arjuna was born into a lineage of yogis, thereby making him fit for the means to liberation. || 42 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the illustrious *Gītā-bhāṣya*. 4.

In the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*, this is the fifth chapter. Thus, having distinguished the portions already discussed in order to demonstrate the connection between the fifth chapter and parts of the third and fourth chapters, [the author now addresses] the portion of the fifth chapter not yet mentioned.

And he says "the fourth chapter" in order to demonstrate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Furthermore, the statement that "the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is a cause for knowledge," and so forth, is for the purpose of indicating the primary connection of the fourth chapter. [The phrase] "only in the third" [is used].
The meaning is that it is characterized solely by the instruction on what ought to be done (*kartavyatopadeśa*). He states the purpose of the fifth chapter with the words "Now" (*idānīm*).

Herein, the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*) is as follows: the ease (*saukarya*) and swiftness (*śaighrya*) of Karma-yoga, certain [details], the nature of Brahman-knowledge, and the method—these are taught in the fifth chapter.

Thus, although both ease (*saukarya*) and speed (*śaighrya*) are included here, the mention of speed alone is for the purpose of making it known that while ease was already stated in the third chapter, speed is now being treated in the fifth chapter as being instrumental to [the former]. Therefore, "but speed... [is said].
In that regard, because it was not mentioned there, the phrase "of actions" (karmaṇām) here is connected to both [the preceding and the following].
Now, it might be argued: the renunciation of *karmayoga* has never been stated anywhere;
on the contrary, it has been elaborated upon precisely as something to be adopted; nor has there been any praise for *jñānayoga*.

Since [the Lord] has in some places stated, "He praises both renunciation and yoga," even though both have been praised, one must understand that there is indeed an option between them; for otherwise, there would be no occasion for a further question regarding the superiority of one over the other. To this, he says: "This has been explained."
By the end of the passage beginning with "to be explained," the intended meaning of the statement "renunciation of actions" has been clarified:

the yoga of action (karmayoga) is for the purpose of removing the impurity (kaṣāya); once that is removed, one should abandon the yoga of action and adopt the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga); therefore, it is the yoga of knowledge alone that leads to the vision of the Self.

The sense is that it has been established in the second [chapter] that this is the direct means (*sākṣātsādhana*). The phrase "you praise" (*śaṃsasi*) is used to indicate the connection with the word "again" (*punaḥ*), in order to dispel the misconception that one is praising the re-union of one who had previously renounced. This refers to the third and fourth [chapters].
The statements "the second" and "the third and fourth" were spoken by the author of the Bhāṣya through his own reflection, and are not a mere reproduction of Arjuna’s words.
In this context, if the yoga of action is to be abandoned by one whose impurities have been wiped away, how could it be something to be adopted?
The sense is: if the yoga of knowledge is the means to realization, how can its occurrence be possible without mediation?
With the intention of praising it—since it was stated that action is superior to inaction—he says: "Action is superior to inaction.
This is said because its superiority has been proclaimed. Thus, he praises it.

"You praise [them]"—the word "therein" (*tatra*) means that both are intended as immediate means. In the phrase "of these two" (*etayoḥ*), the singular word *eka* refers to one among those whose connection has been determined. Its neuter gender is used either because it intends to express a general form, or because it functions as an adjective qualifying the word *śreyas*.

The sense is that because the fruit is one and the same—due to its ease and swiftness—the superiority based on those factors is stated here. The grammatical construction is "the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is well-ascertained.
This means it is well-ascertained as being the highest good. Its status as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatvam*), however, [is established].

With the intention that [the other options] are meaningless, he says: "The best" and "well-ascertained. Since the word *śreyas* (the good) is frequently used even for things such as fruits and the like, in order to exclude those meanings and to clarify the meanings of the root and the suffix in accordance with the inquiry regarding gradation, he uses the word *śreṣṭha* (the best).

This has been explained. Here, since there is an option (*vikalpa*) because they achieve the same single result, the statement that one is superior is made on account of its association with qualities such as ease of performance.
Then, demonstrating that the teaching regarding the six gates is restricted to specific types of qualified aspirants—

and thus establishing that both [the paths] are immediate means to the goal— the Lord spoke as follows, thereby confirming that even for one whose impurities have been worn away, this very path is to be practiced because of its ease and swiftness.

Regarding the term *saṃnyāsa*: with the intention that since one who is incapable of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) must depend upon the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), while for one capable of it, [renunciation] is rightly described as the independent means, he says:
"even for one capable of the yoga of knowledge. "[Both] bring about the supreme good."

This is because of this very capacity [of the word], and because of the connection with what will be stated later: "Even by resorting to only one, he rightly obtains the fruit of both. Thus, they have been described as independent. This same point is also indicated by the particle *ca*. [The particle *ca* expresses] conjunction (*anvācaya*), mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*sāmāhāra*).
[The alternatives] are contradicted by the context [establishing] that they are means for achieving separate results.
Therefore, the meaning of "and" (*ca*) here is indeed conjunction (*samuccaya*), which implies separate independence.
If that is so, then both may be adopted optionally according to one's desire; however, as for karma-yoga...
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt as to why [the Buddha] would praise [them]. The particle "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of indicating that specific intention.

The verse [beginning with] "Even though there is no difference between the two in their being means to the highest good, karma-yoga alone is distinguished" should not be understood as referring to one established in the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga) merely because of the term "one who is eternally renounced" (nitya-saṃnyāsī). For, having first asserted that "karma-yoga is distinguished," [the Lord proceeds to explain] the yoga of knowledge...

For it would be inconsistent to speak of liberation for one who is established in [renunciation] alone, and because it would contradict what will be said later: "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga.
Therefore, with the intention that this is a praise of one established in karma-yoga, he says: "He who is a practitioner of karma-yoga..."
This is stated in order to indicate that longing (*kāṅkṣā*) has as its object only external things, and for the purpose of showing that it must be abandoned.

It is said that he is "satisfied by the experience of the Self contained within that" with the intention that longing, when obstructed, becomes a cause of aversion (*dveṣa*). For this very reason, it is said [in the verse] that he "does not hate anything at all," though the words appear in reverse order.

This has been explained. The word "enduring" (*saha*) is used to exclude the mere cessation of the nature of the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). Therefore, it is said "enduring the pairs" (*dvandvasaha*). The sense is that for one possessed of passion and hatred, the endurance of the pairs of opposites is impossible. This is because [the quality of] being a perpetual renunciant (*nityasaṃnyāsitva*) [is required], as indicated by the particle "for" (*hi*).

In order to indicate that [the practice] has another cause, he said, "For that... He stated, "By being established in the application of easy-to-perform action," meaning that here the word *sukha* refers to ease (*saukarya*).
With the intention of explaining what is meant by the statement, “both bring about the supreme good,” he says:
“of jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga. Here, the terms *sāṃkhya* and *yoga* do not refer to the systems of the followers of Kapila and Hiraṇyagarbha, because those two systems are not under discussion.

Because it would be inconsistent with the great context [of the Gītā], and because it would contradict the preceding and following passages such as, "But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action," and "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga," and also because of the Śārīraka-sūtras.

For these two systems have been refuted by the Great Sage himself through such sūtras as, "And because the arrangement [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of a creator], and because of [the nature of] activity. Furthermore:
"O King, many are the persons who investigate Sāṅkhya and Yoga..."
"O scion of the Kuru lineage, these [others] do not accept a single Puruṣa;
however, Vyāsa has declared that unity of the Puruṣa in the Samāsa [Purāṇa].
This is because of the statement regarding their contradictory portions in the Mokṣadharma section.

Therefore, *sāṃkhya* is that which is to be determined by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) through enumeration (*saṃkhyā*), and it consists of such determination; and *yoga* here refers to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
With this intention, the terms "yoga of knowledge" and "yoga of action" are employed. Thus, the ignorant speak of them as distinct.

It is not the distinctness of their own nature (*svarūpa-pṛthaktva*) that is being negated, for that is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*). Nor is this [text] intended to enjoin their combination, as in: "Even one who is properly established in only one [path] obtains the fruit of both," and "That which is attained by the Sāṃkhyas..."

"that state is attained; it is reached even by those [practicing] yoga," and "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga"—since these and other such passages establish that the two are indeed to be practiced separately. Therefore, regarding the unity of the fruit, [it is said]: "Even one who is established in only one..."
Because of such injunctions, he states that the intent here is to negate the distinction created by differences in results:

"They are distinct due to the difference in results. Since this sentence is of the nature of a censure directed at one who asserts separate results, having restated [the opponent's view] with "he who sees," it is indeed enjoined that "he truly sees."
Since the primary sense of the word "fool" (*bāla*) is inapplicable here, he states that it is used figuratively: "those whose knowledge is unperfected.

The figurative application of the term "unripe" (*apakva*)—which literally refers to an effect—to those whose rational knowledge (*yauktika-jñāna*) is unripe is due to their similarity to children. Regarding the phrase "fools, not wise ones," this was stated in order to exclude ignorance that extends even to the performance of non-scriptural practices.

"Those who know only partially"—this refers to the state of being a *paṇḍita* (learned man) according to the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, although the term "children" (*bāla*) has already been used, the statement regarding the absence of that [learning] is not a mere repetition; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the phrase "those who are not learned" (*na paṇḍitāḥ*) also refers to those who possess the delusion of distinctions such as fruits and so forth, and thus they are "children."

Thus, he shows that [the path] is indeed an object of injunction by saying, "the yoga of action" (*karmayoga*). By saying "only the yoga of knowledge" (*jñānayoga*), he means that for no qualified practitioner whatsoever is there a direct vision of the Self [through action alone].
As for those who say, "Only the ignorant speak thus; the wise do not," [he refutes them].
They state this mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*); even for them, this very meaning must be accepted as the result.

To the question, "How can the fruit of both be obtained by one?", he says: "Of both" (*ubhayoḥ*). Here the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*); the word "one" (*eka*) is a synonym for "either one" (*anyatara*); because the fruit is equal for both, [the fruit of] the other...
The meaning is that even in a place other than a temple, that fruit is accomplished.
Having offered criticism of those who assert distinctness on the grounds that [the paths] have different fruits,
he now speaks with the intention of praising those who assert identity on the grounds that they have a single fruit. He explains this very point in the passage beginning with "by the Sāṃkhyas."
To dispel the misconception that [the term] refers exclusively to those established in a specific philosophical system (siddhānta), he says: "by those devoted to knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhaiḥ*).

Here, *sāṃkhya* refers to the scripture concerning the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-śāstra*), and those who know it are the *sāṃkhyas*. Alternatively, *saṃkhyā* means intellect (*buddhi*), which is the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*);
those established in that are the *sāṃkhyas*. Or else, *sāṃkhya* is the Self (*ātman*), and those who know it are also [called] *sāṃkhyas*.

The Sāṅkhyas [hold that] the word "state" (*sthāna*) here refers to the fruit— just as in the expression "he obtains the fruit"— and not to a specific location, because there is no specific location to be reached solely through the yoga of knowledge and so forth.
And that fruit, with the intention that it is the vision of the Self which persists throughout both the preceding and subsequent [sections], is as follows:

Regarding what was stated as the fruit being "the nature of the vision of the Self," here the reading cited by Yādavaprakāśa— *yadeva sāṅkhyāḥ paśyanti*— is disregarded because it is not well-known. As for the term *yaugaiḥ*, it refers to those who abide in that [Self] either through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or due to a specific suffix (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the phrase "by those perfected in the application of action" (*karmayoganiṣṭhaiḥ*), it is stated [in the commentary] that here the words *sāṃkhya* and *yoga* do not refer to the two means [of knowledge and action], because the use of the plural number would be inappropriate; this is the sense.
Having said "one," he speaks [the following] in order to dispel the delusion that there might be a single scriptural doctrine or similar misconceptions.

"Thus, by virtue of having a single fruit": the unity characterized by having a single fruit for two means—which are devoid of the relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) and of mutual conjunction—would lead to an option (*vikalpa*) in practice. And so says the Sūtra: "There is an option because the fruits are not distinct."
Thus it is said: "optional" refers to the statement "he sees. He shows that the statement "not the wise" is a counter-example, [implying] that "only he is wise."

Now, one might raise the objection: "How can the statement that 'the yoga of action is superior' and the statement regarding its optionality be justified? For an option (vikalpa) exists only when things are absolutely equal. To this doubt, the answer is: its superiority is due to its ease and speed.

And because the fruit is absolutely identical, there is no contradiction; furthermore, with the intention that— since [the paths] are restricted to specific types of qualified practitioners— the difficulty and delay of the means do not render them useless, the difference [between the paths] is stated.
Thus he says: "This much is the distinction," so he says. The word *tu* (but) is intended to indicate mutual difference.

By the phrase "due to non-connection" (*ayogataḥ*), it is intended that the very nature of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is not established without the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). Thus he says: "except for the yoga of action. It is possible with hollowed palms (*añjali*).
This is like the expression "to drink the winds" (*pātuṃ vātāḥ*) and so forth. Here, the word *duḥkha* is used in the neuter gender.

Regarding the word *muni*, there is an explanation of the meaning of the base and the suffix as required by the context: "one whose nature is to reflect" (*mananaśīla*). In that regard, because of the force of the section dealing with the contemplation of non-agency (*akartṛtva*), it is stated that this reflection has the Self as its object.
The meaning is: "by oneself alone, without the yoga of knowledge.
This is understood from the consideration of the contrast with the statement, "it is difficult to attain [the goal] through lack of yoga.
It has been stated that one should accomplish the yoga of action easily. The word "not" (na) in the phrase "not for long" (na cireṇa) [is used].

There might be the misconception that realization would not occur even after a long time through the practice of ritual action (*kriyānvaya*); to dispel that, it is said "not for a long time" (*na-cireṇa*). It is not like [the case of] *naka* and so forth. The compound *na-cireṇa* is used here as a single term. In this context, the word *brāhma* refers to the characteristic of the nature of the perfectly pure Self (*pariśuddhātmasvarūpa*).
In order to indicate that the fruit is not separated by the practice of karma-yoga,
it is said that "he attains the Self. Here, "attainment" means direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

By thus stating that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the means for attaining the Self without any intervening steps, it is refuted [by us] that "the renunciation under discussion is denoted by the word *brāhma*," as stated by Śaṅkara. He completes the previously mentioned point by excluding that [view], saying: "endowed with the yoga of knowledge" (*jñānayogayukta*).

Because it is difficult to accomplish, the yoga of knowledge has its fruit delayed; however, because the yoga of action is easy to accomplish, its fruit is not delayed. This verse expresses such a disparity between the two.

The cause for the ease of accomplishment and the swift attainment of results in the yoga of action is stated by the verse beginning with "yogayuktaḥ. The two preceding instances of the word *ātman* refer to the mind (*manas*), because they are mentioned in close conjunction with the phrase "having conquered the senses" (*jitendriya*). This [meaning] is established by the very expression "yogayuktaḥ."

The cause for the purity of the mind is stated by the words "scriptural" and so forth. Here, "purity" refers to the cessation of *rajas* and *tamas*, as well as the cessation of the impurities (*kaṣāya*) such as attachment and aversion rooted therein.
He recalls what was previously established with the words "in a well-practiced action. Of the *pradhāna*...

The sense is that the other's interpretation is weak, because it is more appropriate to speak of the restraint of the mind; for when the mind—which stands as the sovereign over all the senses—is conquered, the external senses are thereby conquered. This is the intended meaning.

It was stated [previously] "from that very [Self]" in order to establish the passage beginning with "of all beings" (*sarvabhūta*). It was stated "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*) regarding the first instance;

here, he shows that the word "being" (*bhūta*) refers solely to the bodies of gods and others, while for the second instance, he shows that it refers to those [bodies] as well as their physical forms (*vigraha*), by saying "of all" (*sarveṣām*).
To the objection that "the identity of different names is indeed contradictory," he replies: "The true nature of the Self.

The intention here is this: it is true that the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not being enjoined, because that would contradict perception, inference, scripture, and internal consistency; rather, what is intended is the state of having a single form (*ekākāratva*).

Just as when it is said, "This very rice grain exists in every house," its belonging to that same species is thereby expressed; likewise, here too, even though the formulation is "This very self exists in every body," [it follows] for those residing in other bodies...
And thus, equality with the Self becomes established.
But is it not the case that even this equality contradicts perception and other means of knowledge?

For the selves are filled with boundless diversity, consisting of gods, animals, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, celibate students, householders, the learned, the ignorant, the capable, the incapable, the wealthy, the poor, the elderly, the young, and so forth.
Otherwise, even scriptural applications extending up to the self, such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," would be undermined; to this he says:
"Of the distinctions among gods and so forth. This is the intended meaning: it is true, [that the distinctions are real].

The inequality among gods and others is indeed established by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). However, that [inequality] is not caused by their essential nature (*svarūpa*), because it is based on the specific transformations of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) conditioned by karma.
Rather, it is with the intention of referring to their pure form (*śuddhākāra*) that equality is stated here.

Since equality (*sāmya*) is intended here, he shows the immediately following statement of equality as its corroborative proof: "Though acting, he is not tainted" (*prakṛtiviyukta... kurvannapi na lipyate*). In this context, it is certainly not meant that one who performs prohibited acts does not become corrupted.
And that being the case, since his effort would be fruitless, it would follow that he would not undertake it at all.

Therefore, in this context, one is not only established in the yoga of knowledge, but even while performing the yoga of action, one is not [obstructed] by anything that contradicts the fruit known as the direct realization of the Self.
The intention is that the meaning is precisely "it is smeared. The phrase "by the conceit of self in what is not-self," and so forth, has been stated;

for the thought is that "I do nothing at all," and so on, is stated immediately thereafter. In the expression "is not smeared" (*na lopyate*), there is a negation of both connection and its latent impressions (*savāsana*).
He says "intended" [to mean] that it is not connected; he concludes by way of the subject at hand with the word "therefore."
Thus, the direct answer to the question asked by Arjuna has been stated. Now,
in order to establish the connection with the subsequent discourse, the intentional words of the Blessed One— who knows his inner disposition— are shown, beginning with the word "Since" (*yataḥ*).
"Yuktaḥ" here means one who is established in yoga; "tattvavit" means one who possesses the knowledge of the reality of the Self contained within that [body].

Thus it is said: "one who knows the reality of the Self in this way. "Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating" refers to the functions of the sense organs of knowledge known as the eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue.
"Going, speaking, releasing, taking"—these are the functions of the organs of action, such as the feet and others. Among these, "releasing" includes the functions of the anus and the genitals.
And it has been said: "The anus and the genitals are two organs whose function is identical, being for the purpose of excretion."
"In the emission of feces and in the emission [of semen] according to desire.
As for "sleeping, breathing, opening the eyes, and closing the eyes," these are the functions of the vital breath known as *vyāna*.
However, "breathing" specifically refers to the function of the particular vital breath designated as *prāṇa*.
By the word "grasping," although primarily referring to the activity of the hands, it also implies by *tantra* (extended application) the activity of the *apāna* [breath]; for it is said:
"He sought to grasp that with his *apāna*; he swallowed it. That which is the grasping of food is indeed the wind (*vāyu*)."

Thus, for the sake of making this distinction known, it has been stated that the ears and so forth are the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), while speech and so forth are the organs of action (*karmendriya*), along with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Here,

the term "organ" (*indriya*) refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) because they are the cause of the activity of all the organs, as seen in such passages as the Dialogue of the Vital Breaths (*Prāṇasaṃvāda*).
The intended meaning is that [the text] indicates the well-known *mukhya-prāṇa* (the chief vital breath) by means of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (indicative function without abandoning the primary sense).
To suggest that the phrase "in regard to the objects of the senses" (*indriyārtheṣu*) likewise functions as an indicator in the same way,
it is stated as "in regard to their own respective objects" (*svaviṣayeṣu*).

[Objection: Surely, since the senses and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are non-agents, the superimposition of agency upon them and the notion of oneself as a non-agent would both be mere errors; for the agency of the Self alone has been established by such [scriptural passages] as "The agent [is the Self], because the scriptures have a purpose" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.33). To this, he replies: "[Of that which has] knowledge as its sole nature."

The claim made here by others—that there is no further connection with the falsity of actions—is improper; for it would follow that even the statement, "the senses operate upon their objects," would not be something to be connected [with the Self].
This is said in order to exclude the senses and other faculties assumed at will by one who is liberated.
And the term "rooted in karma" is used to indicate that even the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are themselves conditioned by adjuncts. "Of such a kind" means having the nature of merit and demerit.
In this context, the phrase "knowledge of reality" refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), because it is intended to denote the ultimate reality.
As in the case of [the phrase] "cause and effect" and so forth, there is no statement here regarding a division between the operations of consciousness and the unconscious.

But surely, even when an action is being performed preceded by an attachment to its fruit, there would still be no fault for the agent if he maintains the realization that "I am doing nothing at all. Furthermore, if agency belongs to oneself alone from the perspective of ultimate reality, what is the purpose of reflecting upon its being merely adventitious?

Even if such an inquiry were conducted, the doubt that the very contact with *prakṛti* might still cause one to sink into the delusion of identifying the body with the self is refuted by the verse beginning with "The Brahmanic" (*brāhmaṇī*). First of all, the term "Brahmanic" (*brāhma*) here does not denote the individual soul (*jīva*), because this is a context concerning the negation of its agency. Nor does it refer to the Supreme [Self].
Because that [agency] was not taken into account in the section demonstrating its conditioned nature (*aupādhikatva*), and because immediately thereafter,
in the verse beginning with "All actions by means of the mind," the intention regarding the body's agency is declared; therefore, of the meaning previously stated—
Since it is logical that the passage is intended to describe the desired fruit,
the word "brahman" here refers to primordial matter (prakṛti) as it has transformed into the form of the sense organs;
for the term "brahman" is indeed used even with respect to the effects of primordial matter.
Therefore, it is said that from this *brahman* name and form, as well as form and food, are born. Having intended all of this, he says: "by the word *brahman*.
He provides an example of the usage of the word *brahman* in its primary sense right from the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Of me..."

Regarding the word "source" (*yoni*): let it be granted that the word *brāhman* has this meaning in the primary sense (*prakṛti*); yet, in response to the doubt as to what relevance this has for the subject at hand, he states the meaning of the sentence as reinforced by the logic of the preceding verse: "Of the senses," and so forth. [Objection: But surely, because of the quality of vastness (*bṛhattva*)—
Furthermore, by the force of the context, let it be stated that [the term] "mūlaprakṛti" refers to Brahman; for in that case, the objection—
that it is impossible to attribute the agency of seeing, hearing, and so forth to the form of *mūlaprakṛti* because it lacks the causality for those functions— is refuted.

The passage ending with "in that which is situated" has been stated. The intention is that even in a figurative usage regarding the cause, the application [of the term] would also encompass the effect due to the identity of the substance.
The plural number in the word "karmāṇi" (actions) is stated to demonstrate that it refers to the various types previously mentioned.

"In the manner stated in 'seeing, hearing,' and so forth"—this refers to the fact that by the statement "he who acts," agency is designated in the Self alone; thus, what was previously mentioned is brought forward to remind one that this [agency] is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). "I do nothing at all"—here, the word "sin" (*pāpa*) refers to the object of the delusion that the body is the Self.

And in passages such as, "What sin is not committed by that thief who steals his own self, who represents himself as one thing when he is otherwise?", the cessation of that [false identification] occurs precisely within the context of contemplating the non-agency (*akartṛtva*) of the Self.

This is stated with the intention that it is appropriate to speak [in this way]. It is said to be "by nature in the form of ego-identification with the self. By the phrase "as the cause of bondage," there is an indication of what is characterized as sin (*pāpa*).
For sin is indeed the extraordinary and unique cause for the attainment of undesirable results.
Furthermore, the word *pāpa* (evil) is employed in reference to many undesirable things, as in the passage: "Neither good deeds nor evil deeds [remain]; all evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn away from here.
Now, one might ask: "How can this be an illustration, given that a lotus leaf is touched by water? To this, he says:
Regarding the word "yathā": this example is not for the purpose of negating contact (*saṃsarga*); rather, it is as follows:

just as the birth, maintenance, and so forth of a lotus leaf all occur in water alone, yet it is not afflicted by the effects of that [water], so too is it with this [Self] regarding its enjoyment, maintenance, and so forth, which are dependent upon *prakṛti*.
The sense is that the delusion regarding the body as the self, which is an effect of that [ignorance], and so forth, would not exist.
To reinforce the meaning thus stated, the fact that this is established by the conduct of the learned is declared in the verse beginning with "With the body.

Here, *buddhi* refers to the determination regarding what is to be done. What is intended is the mere abandonment of the conceit of agency; or else, the meaning is "by those who are devoid of being objects of the notion of 'mine-ness' (*mamatva-buddhi*)."
Then, in the passage beginning with "by the body," the word "alone" (*kevalena*) and so forth is to be supplied.
Alternatively, since the term "body" (*kāya*) includes the group of action-faculties (*karmendriya*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
the phrase "by the senses alone" refers to the cognitive faculties (*jñānendriya*).
For them, there is no "aloneness," meaning they are devoid of activities such as speaking or taking;
and by that, it is also indicated that [for them] there is neither the hearing nor the seeing of the Dharma, and so forth.
This is because self-purification is pointed out here specifically as the fruit, and because activity toward that which is fruitless is impossible.
It has been stated that there is attachment to fruits such as heaven. For purification is required for one who has been defiled by something;
and that defect here is the obstacle to the direct realization of the true nature of the self, even though the self is pure by its very nature, caused by beginningless time.
Intending to speak of karma, he says: "residing in the self."

The verse beginning with "It is logical" (*yukta*) clarifies this point: that it is indeed possible for a single action to be both a cause of bondage and a cause of liberation, depending on specific auxiliary factors such as the presence or absence of attachment to the fruits [of action].

In this context, the word *yukta* (disciplined) denotes a state of concentrated mind (*sāhita-cetastva*). Furthermore, to indicate that this concentration consists specifically in being directed toward the Self preceded by detachment from other fruits, it is stated: "having renounced the fruit of action" (*karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā*) and so forth.
By the statement [of the scripture], the performance of the nature of the action previously mentioned is shown here as being established by implication.
To preclude the notion that the phrase "the steadfast peace" might directly imply liberation (*mokṣa*), he says "firm. This specific qualification is obtained from the context.

It is called *naiṣṭhikī* because it exists in the final state (*niṣṭhā*). By the term "acting according to desire" (*kāmakāraṇa*), independent or arbitrary conduct is not intended, for that has already been ruled out from afar. Therefore, "acting according to desire" (*kāmakāra*) refers to an impulsion whose agent is desire; by this, he means merely the attainment of whatever fruit one desires. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "he is attached to the fruit through the exercise of his own will," the author shows by means of the prefix (*ni-*) that what is intended here is intense bondage, as expressed by the words "he becomes eternally subject to transmigratory existence" (*nityasaṃsārī bhavati*).
Alternatively, such an intention is conveyed by the use of the present tense designation (*vartamānavyapadeśāt*).

He states the summarized meaning of the passage beginning with "I do nothing at all" and ending with "one who is attached to the fruit is bound," in order to provide the transition for the following verse. Therefore...

He states the meaning of the subsequent verse with the word "atha" (now). Since the renunciation of agency was previously described in relation to the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the organs, the connection here is that the renunciation of agency in the body itself—the very locus of those—is now being stated. [The verse begins: "In the body... regarding the renunciation of agency in the body.

In order to demonstrate the activity of this mind that conforms to its becoming an instrument (*karaṇībhāva*), the word "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) was stated. For agency in performing sinful acts does not arise merely from the connection with a body such as that of a god; for that mere connection exists even in one who is not subject to karma.
Therefore, it was stated that [agency] is rooted in past karma. [The senses are] seven primary ones and two secondary ones.

And here [it is argued] that there is no mention of having nine gates; for in the Śruti text, "The city with eleven gates," the number of eleven gates is stated by including both the navel and the aperture of Brahmā. As for the phrase "having deposited in the city," the intention is that the city's connection as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the act of depositing is irrelevant to the present context.

The designation "in the city with nine gates" is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the body and the Self through such attributes as having parts versus being partless, having apertures versus being without apertures, being large versus being minute, being independent versus being dependent, and being the controller versus being the controlled.
The word "itself" (svayam) means that [the Self] is devoid of dependence on the body and other such things.
Alternatively, the meaning is "by its own perfectly pure form.
"Master" (*vaśī*) means one who is not subject to the force of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*), compulsion (*balātkāra*), and so forth;
for [the states of] being the locus of effort and being the cause of bodily movement and the like are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Not at all.

"Acting," and so forth, has been stated. "He dwells in happiness" means that he dwells free from the aforementioned afflictions and the like, even while possessing the conceit of agency (*kartṛtvābhimāna*). The body is like a city; the senses are like the citizens; and the Supreme Self is like a sovereign emperor.
For one who perceives his own self as a servant [to the True Self], there is indeed well-being.

The point is that while under the delusion that the body is the self, one thinks "I am seated in the city" [of the body]; but upon the cessation of that [delusion], the body itself becomes like the city.
Thus, the renunciation of conditioned form within its conditions has been described;
now, with the intention of providing the logical connection that his own natural form—which is to be realized within oneself—is being stated, he says:
"Directly," [referring] to the subject of diverse people.

By the phrase "of the world," it is intended to demonstrate the diversity of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) and so forth. The statement beginning with "there exists" has been made. Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists of the nature of effort (*prayatna*) and the like;
action (*karman*) consists of the movements of the body, the sense organs, and so forth. If this [agency] were inherent to the selves (*ātman*),...
If agency and so forth were [intrinsic], then that would be uniform for all;
however, with the intention that it is not observed to be so, it was stated: "agency unique to gods and others," etc. [Agency] unique to gods and others...
The meaning is that [the connection] is restricted to the state of grasping a physical body (piṇḍa) possessing a genus such as "godhood" and so forth.

"Connection with the fruit" means the experience of the fruit. This is due to the context. The word *prabhu* here refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), in order to demonstrate this; thus it is said, "this one is the lord."
He states what is intended by the word "Lord" regarding the individual soul (*jīva*): "not subject to karma, abiding in its own natural form.

For in this context, through the passage beginning with "all [beings] in Me," the agency of the individual soul is superimposed upon the Supreme Self; therefore, here [the Lord is characterized by] the triad of non-agency and so forth.
Or else, the meaning of the sentence might be that [the self] appropriates [it]; in order to exclude that, he says:
"it does not produce. With the intention that its agency belongs to it alone because no other cause is observed, he states the doubt regarding the fourth quarter: "Who then [is the agent]?"

The word "creates" (*sṛjati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. In order to establish the term *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) in its specific sense relevant to the present context, he first states what is to be expressed: "the primordial matter" (*prakṛti*). Now, one might object: agency and so forth do not belong to the conscious self (*ātman*), nor do they belong to the unconscious latent impression (*vāsanā*), which consists solely of the attributes of consciousness.
Regarding agency and so forth: how can this be consistent if the inherently pure Self does not possess agency by its own nature? If that is so, from where has its latent impression (vāsanā) come?
If it comes from some cause, then if the impression itself were inherent, the aforementioned defect would persist.
But if [the agency] were adventitious (*aupādhika*), how could that [agency] accrue to a self that is not an agent?

If it is due to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); if it is from some other source, then the same applies there as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). It is for the purpose of refuting such objections that the word "but" (*tu*) is used.
Thus it is said: "beginningless time. By the logic of the seed and the sprout, the objection of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth is avoided.
This is stated—"in the form of gods and so forth"—for the purpose of establishing the variety of the causes of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Just as, due to contact with fire, the cognition of "fire-ness" arises in a heated iron ball, [so too does the cognition of a deity arise].
In order to show that it is so here as well, [the author] says: "The word is produced by association.
This means it is produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that is, conditioned by the specific cause known as *vāsanā*.

The two halves of the verse beginning with "He does not take" provide an exposition of the self's lack of agency and so forth, as well as the latent impressions' (vāsanā) possession of agency and so forth. Since there is no possibility of taking on the sins or merits belonging to another, the prohibition [of such taking] is inappropriate.

Therefore, that effect is observed as both suffering and happiness; even in that case, it is impossible to draw to oneself the happiness and suffering residing in another. Thus, with the intention that what is intended to be expressed is merely the removal of that [suffering], he says: "of someone."

Because it is inappropriate for the word "takes" (ādatte) to have the sense of "does" (karoti) and so forth; because the term "all-pervading" (vibhuḥ) does not intend to refer to a particular modification through transformation (*pariṇāma*) and the like, since the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by scripture and other authorities; nor does it refer to sovereignty (*prabhutva*).
Because it is not applicable here,

what is intended is merely the capacity to enter all bodies in accordance with their respective karmas, devoid of restriction to any specific location. For this very reason, regarding adventitious [bodies]...

The status of being a friend or the like, as well as hostility, belongs to the self only in relation to those adventitious bodies; this is established. For this very reason, with the intention that the terms "favorable" and "unfavorable" refer to persons [only through their bodies], he says: "Since this... and so forth.
He raises an objection regarding the arising of the latter half [of the verse] with the words, "of such a nature.
This means that a contrary latent impression (*vāsanā*) is one that is opposed to the absence of latent impressions. To this, the reply is: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance."
Ignorance (avidyā), known as karma, is held to be another, the third power;
by this, O King, the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is enveloped.
One undergoes all the exceedingly continuous torments of saṃsāra;
moreover, because its true nature is concealed by that [avidyā], the power known as the *kṣetrajña* [is obscured].
Recalling the words of the venerable Parāśara, "O King, [ignorance] exists among all beings according to degrees of intensity," he says: "by that which is opposed to knowledge.

Here, the sense is that the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies something other than that (*tad-anya*) or the absence of that (*tad-abhāva*), as it is not suitable for the meaning of mere concealment (*āvaraṇa*).
The meaning of the verse beginning with "svaphala" is that one whose knowledge is contracted by the power of [past] actions (hrajhrsāvaṭa) is subject to experiencing the torments of saṃsāra.
To avoid the implication of its absolute destruction, he uses the term "contraction" (saṃkucita) as a metaphorical designation for "obscuration" (āvaraṇa).

The meaning intended by the word *jantu* (living being) is "conjunction with a body such as that of a god," which is recalled by the authority of scriptural passages such as, "There is no destruction of the knower or of his knowledge. And that [conjunction] is the door through which karma produces delusion.
He states the resolution of the doubt with the words "And therefore.
He explains that the performance of desired and undesired actions, which has been denied in the case of the Self, has another cause, namely:
"from latent impressions" (vāsanā).

Thus, the specific modes of contemplating non-agency as taught in the third chapter have been explained; now, with the intention of purifying the specific knowledge taught in the fourth chapter, he says: "All," etc.
"At its proper time. This means that immediately after explaining the manner of contemplating one's lack of agency (*akartṛtva*), it is now the occasion to explain the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Alternatively, [it refers to] the verse: "Learn that by prostration... (*tadviddhi praṇipātena*).
The phrase "they will instruct" means that the time for the ripening [of the fruit] has been indicated by [the Lord] himself.
"While they are thus engaged" means even for a moment; or else, it means while they are established in the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
[This addresses] the doubt: "If ignorance is veiled, how can it be destroyed by knowledge?"

By the word "but" (*tu*), which serves to exclude [other views], it is indicated that he intends to show a specific quality of knowledge. The passage beginning with "by [knowledge] characterized as previously described" and ending with "by the unsurpassed, stainless [knowledge]" has been stated.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "by the knowledge of the self. This means "having the self as its object."
The sense is that the use of the genitive case in "of the self" (ātmanaḥ) here is questioned as to whether it expresses a general relation or refers specifically to the agent.
He states the manner [of obscuration] referred to by the word "that": "obscuration of knowledge" (jñānāvaraṇam).

This is for the purpose of indicating the extreme profundity of the nature of ignorance, and for the purpose of demonstrating that the light of knowledge—which is unsurpassedly pure—completely fills the belly of the darkness of ignorance; thus begins the passage starting with "anādikāla... (beginningless time).

It has been stated that the meaning of the word "that" (tat) occurring in the second half [of the verse] is "inherent" (svābhāvikam), as this is the natural sense of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). The word "supreme" (param) is an adjective qualifying knowledge;
its meaning he explains as "unlimited" (aparimitam) and "unrestricted" (asaṃkucitam).

The "supremacy" (paratva) of knowledge consists in its having an unlimited object; the intention here is that the cause for this is the absence of contraction. The word "all" is an expression of the object established by the sense of the verb "to illuminate.
The point is that the fact that knowledge has everything as its scope upon the cessation of ignorance is supported by scripture.
He states what is established by the force of the analogy, "like the sun," using the phrase "as it truly exists.

By this, the supply of the substantive "word" (*padam*) to the term "supreme" (*param*), as well as the intended meaning "the supreme reality of the word" (*parama-śabdatattvam*), are both shown; thus, the views expressed by others are refuted.
The contradiction with the opening statement regarding the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) was previously mentioned on the strength of the designation of difference.

Now, he shows that this very same real difference is clearly taught even in the middle [of the text], thereby demonstrating that it is the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*). [This is shown by the words] "of them" (*teṣām*) and "of those whose ignorance has been destroyed" (*vinaṣṭājñānānām*).

The sense is that it is impossible to claim that this plurality is established by error or established by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Having restated the views of Bhāskara and Śaṅkara—who maintain that difference is produced by real and unreal limiting adjuncts respectively—he refutes them with the words "And this is not... [referring to the phrase *na cedam*]. [This refers to] the material cause called ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is of a false nature.

Regarding Śaṅkara, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is that upon the destruction [of ignorance], there is also the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which have been assumed by it and are false. Regarding the other [commentator], the meaning is that upon the destruction of karma and so forth— which are denoted by the word "ignorance" (*ajñāna*)— there is the cessation of the limiting adjuncts, such as the body and the internal organ, which are caused by them.

In the context of refuting the system of Śaṅkara, he demonstrates that the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is established even in the state of purity (*śuddhadaśā*), in order to refute the doctrine that [the self] is mere consciousness (*jñānamātratvavāda*). He says "of them" (*teṣām*);

the genitive case is used because it refers to a relationship (*saṃbandha*), and thus it contains a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*). This is what is meant by the statement "because of the indication of distinction."

Because the Selfs whose limiting adjuncts have perished are taught as having this as their essential nature (dharmatā), it is established that knowledge is invariable concomitant with its own nature; thus, even the doctrine of adventitious consciousness (āgantuka-caitanya) is refuted.
Here, the word "solar" (āditya) refers to the radiance of the sun.

Because the sun’s illuminating power exists solely by means of its radiance; and in the case of knowledge that constitutes one's nature (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), that very same example must apply: just as the moonlight of a gem is not produced but [manifested] through the washing away of its impurities, so too knowledge is not produced in the Self through the removal of defects.

This is also because of such similarities; having this in mind, he states the resulting conclusion: "by means of the example of light. To the question, "What follows for the subject under discussion from that?", he says:

"from that very [example]. The sense is that just as the contraction of light is observed upon the proximity of an obscuring object, and its expansion again upon the removal of that object, so too it is with knowledge.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the knowledge of those [faculties] situated at the beginning is like light.

While light is a specific kind of luminous substance (tejodravya) that is not established as separate from its source, such as a lamp or the sun, knowledge— though a quality (dharma) of the self— is nonetheless a substance (dravya), because it possesses the capacity for contraction and expansion.

And these [arguments] have been elaborated upon in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*. Thus, by establishing that [the soul] possesses a substance equal to light, he states, "From that very [source]," meaning that the previously mentioned state of being veiled and so forth is logically consistent.
The verse beginning with "tadbuddhayaḥ" shows the sequential stages of ascending the staircase to the palace of self-realization through knowledge. Here,
the word "tat" (that) refers either to the innate nature of the Self introduced previously, or to the knowledge of that [Self] mentioned in the preceding verse.

This is said with the intention that [the Self] is being contemplated. It was stated [previously] as "having the conviction regarding the path to such a vision of the Self. Being established in That (tanniṣṭhatva) is the cause for being intent upon That (tatparāyaṇatva), due to the turning away from other objects.
Here, the word *ayana* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), referring to that which is to be attained.

This is for the purpose of excluding [the state of] merely knowing the meaning of a sentence and so forth. It was stated, "by practicing in this manner," because the removal of the impurity that obstructs attainment is the penultimate stage; therefore, the final goal to be attained is what is intended here. To show that the term *apunarāvṛtti* (non-return) is an attribute of the Self—thereby excluding other compounds that would require reference to either the path not mentioned or another [state]—he says: "from which state... and so on, which would otherwise be incorrect.
To the objection that if liberation were also a particular state, it could not be eternal and would thus entail the possibility of returning [to saṃsāra], he says:

"in its own form. The meaning is that this state, consisting in the cessation of all forms conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), cannot be destroyed because no cause for its destruction is possible; even according to the opponent's view, it is of the nature of a final destruction (pradhvaṃsa) and is therefore irreversible.

In response to the inquiry, "What is this direct realization of the Self (ātmasākṣātkāra) like?", [the Lord] clarifies what was previously stated in the verse, "By which you shall see all beings without exception in the Self and likewise in Me," by means of the verse beginning with "vidyāvinaya...
The two words "vidyāvinayasaṃpanne" and "brāhmaṇe" are not... [text truncated].

[The two terms] are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because they are recited together as a group without any further qualification, and because no qualifying term such as "endowed with learning and humility" (*vidyāvinayasampanna*) has been stated as a separate head-word. The difference in form between "cow" (*go*) and "female elephant" (*hastinī*) has been shown; likewise, through the words "dog" (*śva*) and "outcaste" (*śvapaca*), a difference in their respective functions (*vṛtti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) is indicated.
Similarly, by means of the two preceding [terms] as well, a mutual difference is intended. Therefore...
By the term "Brāhmaṇa," he shows that what is intended is merely the heart-region occupied by the genus *brāhmaṇatva* (the state of being a Brāhmaṇa).
He states "a mere Brāhmaṇa" to indicate that the intention is to provide various examples consisting of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types.
"Exceedingly uneven," it is said. Regarding "in themselves":

the meaning is that it is difficult to deny the mutual inequality among bodies. Here, in order to demonstrate that "learning" consists in the capacity for reasoning and refutation (ūhāpoha) which is necessary for equanimity (samarśitva), [the author] shows this.
It has been stated that they are "knowers of the true nature of the Self. Those whose vision and character are equal are called "seers of equality" (*samadarśinaḥ*).

Now, one might object: the disparity of bodies is established by direct perception; since bodies also possess their respective specific qualities, the resulting disparity in knowledge and other attributes is likewise undeniable. Therefore, [how can there be equality] among those who are so extremely dissimilar?
To the objection that a gross universal, like "being a category" (*padārthatva*) and so forth, is ineffective, he says:
"But [the form] is dissimilar. The genitive case in *prakṛteḥ* expresses a general relation;
by this, there is divinity and so forth residing directly in the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and friendship and so forth induced by that.

And it has been stated that this occurs somehow through mere connection with *prakṛti*. It is not the inequality residing in the body that is being negated; rather, that very [inequality] is what is being established here.

Nor is there [any contradiction], for that [inequality] is characterized by being qualified by those respective bodies and by the contraction of knowledge (*jñāna-saṅkoca*) and so forth rooted therein.
Nor is the inequality denied; rather, its being adventitious (*aupādhikatva*) is stated.

Furthermore, being qualified by a body and so forth does not constitute a contradiction, because [the text] intends only the equality of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) as it is in itself. And this is not at all crude.

The sense is that because it is difficult to discern a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of pure selves, and because there is an absence of any other distinct form of differentiation, [the distinction between them is not perceived]. Now, one might object: "Even so, when there is a perception of equality—such as in being worthy of worship—among Brāhmaṇas and others, how is the fault of their food being unfit to be eaten (*abhojyānnatva*) and so forth recorded in the Smṛti? To this, he says:
"But the self," however.

Now, the state of equal vision (*samadarśitva*) is not merely a means for achieving a result that occurs at a later time; rather, it bestows a cessation of afflictions (*kleśanivṛtti*) that is equivalent to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) right now. Thus, the praise of those who possess equal vision is expressed by the verse beginning with "right here" (*ihaiva*). This means: precisely during the stage of practicing the means.

The sense is that since the word *iha* here refers to this world (*loka*), it is more appropriate for it to refer specifically to one's own particular state. "Samsāra is conquered" means they are as good as liberated, because [the context] does not connect with creation and so forth here;
by the etymology "that which is created," the word *sarga* here refers to *saṃsāra*.

The phrase "in the manner stated" is used to exclude the contingency that [all beings], from the *brāhmaṇa* down to the *caṇḍāla*, would possess an identical status regarding touchability and so forth.

This is because it is said: "Indeed, the nature of the Self, being free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) and having knowledge as its sole form, is equal for all *brāhmaṇas*. Here, "being a *brāhmaṇa*" (*brāhmaṇatva*) alone is the predicate; otherwise, [the argument would fail].
"Therefore, those who see with equality are established in Brahman"—since there would otherwise be no logical connection (*anvaya*), the intended sense is that the connection is:
"those who see with equality are established in Brahman, because equality is Brahman"; and thus, with the intention of resolving the aforementioned objection, he says: "The reality... (*vastu*).
To the question, "What follows from that for the subject at hand?", he says: "The abiding in Brahman.
Here, the word *brāhṛ* refers to the pure Self by virtue of its similarity to Brahman. He states the resulting summarized meaning as: "In the Selfs."

In order to indicate that the pleasant and the unpleasant, as well as the joy and agitation dependent upon them, are based on the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and its various states, it was stated: "of one situated in such a body" and "in such a state.
Alternatively, the phrase "in such a state" refers to states characterized by the contraction of knowledge and so forth, produced by the body and other factors.
With the intention that it is difficult to prevent the joy and agitation resulting from the arrival of causes in the form of the pleasant and the unpleasant, he asks:
"How? To this, the answer is: "One of steady intellect.
Although a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) would also suffice, a non-coordinate compound (*vyadhikaraṇa-samāsa*) is used here because of its superior utility.
With the intention of stating that [the self] has been born, he says: "in a stable self.
Regarding the term *asaṃmūḍhaḥ*, the prefix *sam-* here refers to unification (*ekīkāra*);
thus, having combined both such stability of intellect and the state of being undeluded, he says: "that."

It is touched upon [in the following]: by means of the two words "one who knows the Veda" (*brahmavit*) and "abiding in the non-Veda" (*abrahmaṇi*), he clarifies a specific intermediate state established [by them]. By the phrase beginning with "through instruction" (*upadeśena*), having referred back (*anūdya*) to the knowledge produced by instruction by the word "being present" (*san*), a distinguished higher realization (*vijñāna*) is enjoined.

Thus it has been indicated. In order to demonstrate the sequence of stages for unconfused practice for those who desire the maturation of knowledge characterized by equanimity (*samarśitva*), [the author] shows the connection of the words in the verse as a great sentence through the relationship of cause and effect: He shows [this]: "Those who have attained the state of a *yogin* through the purification of their own nature, having become free from the duality of 'I' and 'mine,' and being established in the state of non-duality—[they are] the ones who possess the supreme wealth. This is the meaning: those who have attained the state of a *yogin* through the purification of their own nature—that is, through the removal of the impurities of the mind—having become free from the duality of "I" and "mine," and being established in the state of non-duality, are the ones who possess the supreme wealth. This is the first half-verse. The second half-verse is: "Having abandoned all mental constructions regarding the objects of the senses, they remain in the state of the Self, which is free from the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. This means: having abandoned all mental constructions regarding the objects of the senses, they remain in the state of the Self, which is free from the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. This is the second half-verse. The third half-verse is: "Free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and devoid of the sense of agency, they are liberated while living, having transcended the cycle of birth and death. This means: free from the notions of "I" and "mine," and devoid of the sense of agency, they are liberated while living, having transcended the cycle of birth and death. This is the third half-verse. The fourth half-verse is: "Even when engaged in worldly activities, they are not touched by the fruits of action; like the sky, they remain untainted by the stains of merit and demerit. This means: even when engaged in worldly activities, they are not touched by the fruits of action; like the sky, they remain untainted by the stains of merit and demerit. This is the fourth half-verse. The fifth half-verse is: "Though they may appear to act, they are in truth inactive; though they may appear to speak, they are in truth silent; though they may appear to move, they are in truth motionless. This means: though they may appear to act, they are in truth inactive; though they may appear to speak, they are in truth silent; though they may appear to move, they are in truth motionless. This is the fifth half-verse. The sixth half-verse is: "Having realized the Self as the witness of all, they abide in the state of pure consciousness, free from the veil of ignorance. This means: having realized the Self as the witness of all, they abide in the state of pure consciousness, free from the veil of ignorance. This is the sixth half-verse. The seventh half-verse is: "By the grace of the Guru, they attain the state of liberation, which is the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of eternal bliss. This means: by the grace of the Guru, they attain the state of liberation, which is the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of eternal bliss. This is the seventh half-verse. Thus, the entire sequence of practice, beginning with the maturation of knowledge and culminating in liberation, has been shown.
Regarding the phrase "this has been said": it is for the purpose of ceasing instruction based on the views of outsiders (*bāhyakudṛṣṭi*). The expression "that indeed" (*tattvidām*) has been stated;
furthermore, the word "having become" (*bhūtvā*) is intended to indicate that [the preceding statement] is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Thus, for one who does not experience joy or agitation, it is said that unsurpassed happiness comes to him spontaneously; this is expressed by the verse beginning with "bāhya. To show the distinction from the phrase "he finds happiness" (*sukhaṃ vindati*), the word "attains" (*labhate*) is used in the sense of "he enjoys imperishable happiness" (*sukham akṣayam aśnute*).
The intended meaning is that this is the commencement of inexhaustible happiness. The phrase "leaving aside the habitual practice of nature" is a statement implied by the sense [of the verse].
Furthermore, the "habitual practice of nature" refers to the repeated contemplation of objects of enjoyment, such as worldly sounds and so forth.
The "happiness" mentioned is that which is rooted in the knowledge produced by instruction and other means, as stated in the teaching: "He who finds happiness within the Self."

The phrase "he enjoys imperishable bliss" is stated to show the distinction that this refers to eternal bliss occurring immediately after direct realization; thus, it is described as being "of the nature of direct experience."

In response to the inquiry, "How can one who has relished the touch of women since beginningless time renounce it?", [the author] says, with the intention that the cessation of such attachment is possible through the perception of defects such as the protection of Arjuna, etc., as expressed in the verse beginning with "For those... (ye hi...).

Regarding the phrase "of the ordinary person" (*prākṛtasya*): this clarifies that the state of being conditioned (*aupādhikatva*) is what is intended by the expression "born from contact" (*saṃsparśajāḥ*).
"Born from the contact of object and sense-organ" (*viṣayendriyasaṃsparśajāḥ*): here, "contact" (*sparśa*) refers merely to a connection.
By this, the triviality of the nature of pleasure is expressed.
The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that [worldly enjoyment] is a source of suffering because it is a form of attachment to one's own [limited] objects.
Indeed, there is no worldly enjoyment superior to that of Hiraṇyagarbha and others;
even that, being limited to a hundred years by its own measure, is equal to that of humans and the like.
To demonstrate this, it was stated that they "exist for a short time.

The intended meaning is that although there is a disparity in the duration of their intermediate existence— just as with things like lightning-flashes or bubbles— the fact that they possess a beginning and an end remains unchanged.

Thus, by means of the three qualifiers beginning with "born of contact" (*saṃsparśajā*), [the author] has shown their limited nature, their being mixed with suffering, and their non-reality. To show that for one who is skilled regarding defects already established through direct perception, what need is there for instruction, he says "they are perceived. To show that by the word "wise" (*budha*) what is intended here is the possession of the discriminative knowledge most essential for liberation, [he uses this term].

It has been stated that one who knows things as they truly are does not take delight in those [objects], but rather gradually desists from them; this is the intended meaning. In activities such as crossing the ocean or serving a king, there are defects of acquisition that culminate in the destruction of the body, even for one who has been settled within an inner chamber surrounded by walls and moats.

The defects of guarding (*rakṣaṇa-doṣa*) consist of kings, fire, thieves, mice, and so forth, as well as the hardships involved in warding them off. The defects of decay (*kṣaya-doṣa*) include the lack of peace even in heaven for one who fears falling and whose merit is subject to exhaustion, and so on. Desire is never...

Desire is not appeased by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. When she was not obtained, his longing for that intoxicated woman was directed even toward animals.

As stated in such passages, the defects of enjoyment (*bhogadoṣa*) consist of engagement with unsuitable objects and the like, which serve as causes for increasingly powerful misfortunes driven by passion. Furthermore, because almost all of this is permeated by violence toward others, there are the defects of violence (*hiṃsādoṣa*), which result in continuous streams of suffering in both this world and the next. These five types of defects are as follows.

The meaning is that since [these states] are established through perception and other means of valid cognition, it is proven that they are easily abandoned even by an ordinary person who has practiced them since beginningless time, provided he possesses their cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And it has been stated by the Sāṅkhyas in the section on contentment (*tuṣṭi*): "There are five [types of contentment] arising from the cessation of external objects."
Thus, describing the state that flows spontaneously for one who is unattached to the touch of arms, who finds happiness in the Self,
and who perceives defects in worldly enjoyments, he speaks of the fitness for the direct realization of the Self and for the bliss dependent thereon in one who has become such.
"He is able" means that,
with the intention that desire and anger are difficult to conquer until the fall of the body,
he says "prior to the liberation from the body. This refers to the state of the direct realization of the Self.
The statement "no attachment to desire or anger exists" is intended to inform [the seeker] of the means for preventing such attachment.
By the phrase "right here," the stage of practicing the spiritual discipline (*sādhana*) is indicated.
The expression "he who finds happiness within himself" recalls the reason previously stated.
"By means of the joy of self-experience. Here, "impulse" (*vega*) refers to the extremely rapid activity of the mind, speech, and body.

Among these, impulses born of desire (*kāma*) include the contemplation of unsuitable objects, base flattery, entering the inner apartments of a king, and so forth. [Impulses born of hatred include] the contemplation of means for harming others, harsh speech, physical blows, and so forth.

The impulses born of anger are to be restrained; this is stated in order to exclude the sense of *titikṣā* (endurance) from the word "to endure" (*soḍhum*). "He is able" (*śaknoti*) means that being capable, he exerts effort.
He explains that the word "yukta" here refers to the attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), meaning "fit for self-realization."

The phrase "prior to the casting off of the body" intends that the attainment of the fruit occurs immediately after the body [falls away]; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of that statement being rendered fruitless—this is the intended meaning. With this in mind, it was stated: "He enjoys imperishable happiness at the time following the liberation from the body."

With the intention that even here there is a connection with the happiness that has been mentioned as the result of the aforementioned [practices]—both past and future—one says: "He shall become one whose sole happiness is the experience of the Self."
Thus, having renounced all ordinary objects of enjoyment, instruments of pleasure, and so forth,
