The elaboration of this very equal vision is provided by specifying its various objects in the passage beginning with "abiding in all beings," and so forth.

The term *svātman* (one's own self) is used here to indicate that it is a synonym for "self" (*ātman*), by excluding the sense of the "Self in general" (*ātmasāmānya*) or the "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). Now, one might ask: how is this mutual relationship of container and contained possible? And how can the atomic individual self (*aṇu-svātman*) reside within all beings?

And how can there be a persistence within one's own self, situated in a single location, of all beings who are situated in scattered locations? Therefore, this word "self" (ātman) must refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
To that, he says: "having a form identical to all beings. [Objection: But surely this [contemplation] consists in the recollection of one's own self alone...

To the question, "How can one engaged in yoga perceive the group of selves distinct from oneself as being the counter-correlates of a similarity residing in oneself, and as the substrata of a similarity whose counter-correlate is oneself? he says: "In one... and so forth.

Regarding objects of the same class, by the observation of a single individual instance alone—according to the maxim of the grain in the cooking pot (*sthālīpulāka*)—this portion of the text, consisting of the preceding and following sections, is stated in order to demonstrate that which belongs to that class;
and he provides an illustration with the words "everywhere. The intended meaning is this: "one who perceives equality everywhere."

Thus, the perception of the mutual equality of all selves is stated; that very point is elaborated as "abiding in all beings. For this very reason, the observation of the reality of the Self in external objects, and the abiding of those [objects] within it, would be inconsistent in this context.

Nor is this called meditation on the Supreme Self, because it concerns a specific distinction within the stages of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Nor is the equality of individual souls (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) being asserted here,
since that [equality] is also accompanied by a specific designation such as "me" (*mām*).

This is because it is appropriate to establish [the meaning] within these two verses. If this were to have the Supreme Self as its subject matter, there would be a partial redundancy with the two verses beginning with "He who [knows Me]," and in the restatement of "this Yoga," only equality itself would be expressed.

But there is no relationship of mutual container and contained; for even previously, in the passage beginning with "learning and humility," only equality was stated. Therefore, in this context, what is intended is precisely the mutual equality of living beings.
Thus, by means of the negation of distinctions consisting of specific transformations of the natures of gods, humans, and so forth,
the contemplation of [the self] as being of a single form through its substance of knowledge has been stated. Now,
[the contemplation of it] as the Supreme Self follows from the shaking off of the gradations of merit and demerit that serve as the causes for the distinctions of gods and others.
The "intention toward supreme equality" is expressed by the words "he who [knows] me," etc.
The reason why this verse also has equality as its subject matter has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, having reached the stage of maturation, it is superior to the first stage.

The meaning is that he has reached the state of fruition (*vipākadaśā*). He recalls the similarity between individual selves (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) which is about to be described, saying, "my similarity.
"Has approached" means attained through understanding; he is not liberated at this moment.

The scriptural passage beginning with “the stainless one” (nirañjanaḥ) is cited in order to establish equanimity through the shaking off of merit and demerit; for that [text] states: “Then the wise man, having shaken off merit and demerit, being stainless, attains supreme equanimity.”
The statement "he who sees me" is a restatement (anuvāda), for such a restatement occurs only when its referent has already been established.
To the doubt as to how that establishment comes about, [the reply is]: "First, identity (sāmya) is established by the scriptural passages and other authorities cited;
furthermore, the contemplation (anusandhāna) thereof is enjoined; therefore, the restatement of it is also logically justified."

This is for the purpose of making it known that there is a distinction in the intermediate mode of expression shown by the statement: "He who, seeing my identity [with all], sees Me everywhere in the reality of the Self.
This is because the Supreme Self pervades everything and because all things are established in the Supreme Self.
In this context, comprehension arises spontaneously; however, that [comprehension] is inappropriate here due to the force of the context and other factors.

Therefore, it must be stated that the intended meaning is simply the perception of equality. That too is incorrect, because in the ripening of yoga, which consists of the contemplation of one's own self, there is [the realization of] the Supreme Self and others.
Regarding the doubt that [the object] does not manifest, as previously stated, he says: "Mutually.

This means that by the perception of one, the other is also perceived; that is, by the perception of a single individual instance, another individual instance is also perceived. In such cases as "I am that," there is first of all no negation of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).
Is it being done? No, for I do not resort to non-perception. This very point he demonstrates with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*).
The sense is that the absence of the contemplation of suchness is what is being negated.

With the intention that "it does not perish for me" serves as an illustration, and that similarity is authoritative because it falls within the scope of the omniscient Buddha's cognition, he says, "even for me. This means that even for me, who am the direct perceiver of everything, in the aspect of the contemplation of my own true nature (*svarūpa-anusandhāna*), [it does not perish].
The meaning is that because of that identity, his own essential nature also becomes fully realized.
By the word "he" (saḥ), it is intended to express that he who is in that state is one whose bonds are released;
to make this clear, he says: "Beholding himself as equal to Me because of his equality with Me."

He says "tataḥ" (then) to state the third stage of fruition (*vipāka-daśā*). The previous verse spoke of seeing one's similarity to the Lord by way of being free from the subjection of karma; however, by the phrase "situated in all beings," [the present verse speaks of]...

This is described as follows: because one is free from the shroud of ignorance consisting of karma and form, there is a contemplation of identity by virtue of having an uncontracted nature of knowledge; furthermore, through the power of that latent impression (*saṃskāra*), there occurs a spontaneous flow of such contemplative activity even at the time of emergence from meditation.
By the phrase "whomever you worship, he exists in every way," the distinction of time is established.

Furthermore, it is not the case that existing "in such a manner" is possible only during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). For the contemplation of one's own identity with the Supreme Self, which abides in all beings, is indeed [possible] for oneself as well.
It is the contemplation of the fact that all beings abide in that [Self] as being of one single nature.

And that is not possible for the individual soul (ātman) in its own essential form (*svarūpa*). Rather, it is by way of its *dharma* (nature/attribute) that there is the pervasion of the supreme pure Self, beginning from the words "on the tip of a hair" up to "and that leads to infinity."
This is established by the scripture stating "it is conceived," and also by the Sūtra:
"The entry is like that of a lamp, for so it shows.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the same equality is intended here as well, [the author] says:
It has been stated that [the Self] "rests in oneness" by virtue of its nature as non-contracted cognition;
this means by the abandonment of distinctions arising from the specific association with *prakṛti* conditioned by karma, which take the form of gradations in cognition.
By this statement of oneness (*ekatva*), the purpose of refuting any difference in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been established.

Furthermore, the statement of oneness is also consistent when intended to express that all selves (*sarvātman*) are established as non-distinct from Brahman. The intended meaning of the word "established" (*āsthita*) is "very firmly" (*sudṛḍham*).

And thus, it is indicated that even at the time of emergence from meditation, there is a strength of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which serves as the cause for the continuity of such a stream of reflection.
"He worships me"— the intention is that even the vision of the Self as identical with Me is indeed birth from Me.
The meaning of "in every way" (sarvathā) is that [the yogi] is even engaged in worldly activities.
The meaning of "it abides in me" (mayi vartate) is not that it resides in the Supreme Self (paramātman), because that [residence] is common to all yogis.
Therefore, with the intention that "functioning" here refers to the functioning of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), he says: "He sees Me alone.
To the question, "How can there be a vision of the Supreme Self merely by seeing the individual self (*jīva*? he says: "In his own self.
This means that even though there is an absence of direct realization of one's own self at the time of emergence from meditation, there is a clear and indirect contemplation.
This statement regarding the "fruition" [of the practice] is for the sake of establishing that same state for others as well.

He describes the fourth stage, which brings about an unchanging state even when powerful causes of suffering arise, which constitutes the pinnacle of the maturation of yoga, and which consists in the contemplation of the cessation of the gradations of pleasure and pain conditioned by the varying degrees of karma and knowledge; thus he says, "He describes the pinnacle beyond that," [referring] to the perspective of identifying with oneself (*ātmaupamya*).

This [word *iti*] has no connection with the verb *paśyati*, because that would result in redundancy with the word *samam*. Therefore, its connection is with the phrase "in every case by way of comparison to oneself" (*sarvatrātmaupamyena*). The word *upamā* signifies "equality"; its abstract state is *aupamyam*. [The phrase refers to] all selves by means of what was stated previously.
The meaning is: "by way of similarity such as being distinct from the body.

The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) applies here according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), and it is also connected with the phrase "he sees equally" (*samaṃ paśyati*). This is because all things are extremely dissimilar [in their external appearances].

By dispelling the delusion of similarity based on the association with perceived pleasure and pain, he demonstrates the investigation of similarity through exclusion (*vyatireka*). He states "due to the similarity of non-connection" (*asaṃbandhasāmyāt*) to indicate what is intended here, because investigating non-connection in other cases would be purposeless. He says "in others" (*pareṣu*).

Just as there is no connection for one person with the birth of another’s son and so forth, nor for oneself with the birth of one’s own son and so forth in others, it is implied that this applies equally to the birth of one’s own son and so forth in relation to oneself.
This refers to what is intended by the word "supreme" (*parama*): he is considered one who has reached the pinnacle of yoga.
This is the culmination of yoga with the individual self (jīvātman), because yoga with the supreme self (paramātman) will be described hereafter.

Thus, through the four verses, equality has been stated by way of having the single form of knowledge, being faultless, possessing the same qualities as Brahmā, and not possessing the qualities of others. Here, the statement regarding the reflection on equality is made by means of two verses, while by the third and fourth verses, however—
Some say that these two sections describe the fruits resulting from the contemplation of the equality between the steadfast and the most steadfast.
The method for the practice of yoga and the four types of yogis have been stated.
Now, in order to understand more clearly the previously mentioned means of attaining yoga, Arjuna spoke again.

The passage beginning with "O Lord" (*deva*) and ending with "in experienced [objects]" (*anubhūteṣu*) is intended to demonstrate the impossibility of contemplating equanimity due to the beginningless, habitual, and very firm contrary tendencies (*viparīta-vāsanā*).

"Mutual disparity" means through the distinction between gods, humans, and so forth; that is to say, through the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), and through the distinction between being subject to karma and not being subject to karma. "By way of absolute difference" means that here there is not merely a differentiating attribute, as in the case of a person with a shaved head versus one with matted hair, and so on.
The sense is that, rather, a state of contradictory natures is indeed observed.
In the phrase "for all this time," the accusative case is used according to the rule for expressing continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) between time and distance.
And [the word "samam"] is used in the sense of equality with the Lord (*īśvara*), by virtue of being intransitive.

And the [particle] *ca* has the sense of a conjunction of two types of similarity. According to some readings, there is the text: "by virtue of being free from action (*akarmaka*) and by virtue of similarity with the Lord (*īśvara*). In that case, the first *ca* is for the purpose of including the fact that [the liberated soul], even while possessing similarity with the Lord, has knowledge as its sole form; the second, however, is as before.

Because the disparity between knowledge and human effort is itself the result of the disparity of karma, and because the cessation of those two is already implied by the phrase "by the state of being independent of karma," they are not mentioned separately. [This] was proclaimed by you yourself, who are inherently omniscient.
The sense is that it is possible to investigate and explain this. "I do not see"—the meaning is:
"I, who possess a beginningless pursuit of duality and have an unsubdued mind, do not see.
"Steadfast state" means persistence for a long duration. O Madhusūdana!

The sense is: "Please instruct me in the means for restraining the mind, you who are by nature intent on dispelling powerful adversaries consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*. This is understood by connecting it with the subsequent statement, "For the mind is flickering," where the word "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) is supplied as an ellipsis.

Regarding the particle *hi*: he states that its meaning here is clearly and appropriately "reason" (*hetu*), rather than the sense of qualifying non-conscious matter (*acid-viśeṣaṇa*) as asserted by Yādavaprakāśa. Thus, he says *tathā hi*.

Furthermore, the flickering nature (*cañcalatva*) which serves as the reason must be demonstrated in an instance where it is commonly recognized; therefore, the state of being mobile (*calasvabhāvatva*) is present here.

To demonstrate that the meaning of the word "cañcala" (fickle) is as follows, [the author] states "without ceasing," and so forth. He states the result of this fickleness with the words "by the person. "Pramāthin" means having the nature of agitating; "having agitated" means having thrown into confusion.

The word *balavat* is intended to mean either an adverbial modifier of the action of crushing (*pramathana-kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*), or as referring to the cause, meaning "one who crushes because of his strength. With this intention, it is said: "having crushed by force" (*balāt pramathya*). To show the firmness [of the action] even in the opposite case, he says: "it is firm elsewhere" (*dṛḍham anyatra*). He states what is intended by the reference to "his" (*tasya*).
"By one's own practice" (*svābhyāsena*). "Of a contrary form" (*tadviparītākāra*) means that which has not been practiced before.

"To establish" (*sthāpayitum*) means for the sake of establishing. This is intended to demonstrate that the instability and other qualities shown in the case of the mind (*dārṣṭāntika*) are also intended [to apply] to the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The passage beginning with "pratikūla" has been stated. It was said, "as if by a fan," in order to make known the weakness of the means for restraining the mind, and to show the impossibility of restraining the wind by gentle means. Thus, he says that this statement regarding the difficulty [of the task] is not intended as a rejection, but rather for the purpose of inquiring about the proper means.
"Mind," it is said.

Then, restating what was spoken by Arjuna, the Blessed One spoke in two verses regarding the means sought by him. Therein, he spoke the two words "difficult to restrain" (*durnigraham*) and "fickle" (*calam*), which serve as a restatement of the reason for Arjuna’s initial proposition. [The word *cala*...]
Regarding the phrase "by way of its beingness" (*bhāvatayā*): this means "without doubt," similar to saying "this is true," and it refers primarily to partial acceptance.
He shows the specific distinction intended by the word "but" (*tu*) with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
For in that case, practice performed in a favorable manner would be the cause of inclination; thus, he specifies a particular kind of practice.
And it reveals that fruit [of the practice], beginning with the words "of the Self.

Here, the qualities are eternity, consciousness, bliss, freedom from the subjection of karma, purity, and so forth. The phrase "in some way" is for the purpose of indicating careful attention. Thus, the means of perceiving the mind has been stated.

And then, with the verse beginning "asaṃyata," he establishes the meaning already stated— "I do not see this"— within a specific context. Because this is the section concerning the method of restraining the mind, and because of the force of the co-occurrence of the words "unrestrained" (asaṃyata) and "under control" (vaśya), the word "self" (ātman) here refers to the mind.

He states what was indicated by the wisdom of the mighty-armed one: "even with great strength. The underlying sense is: "That which can be accomplished through skillful means cannot be accomplished through mere prowess. By the phrase "it is my opinion," he intends to express that this is free from doubt; thus he says, "it is indeed difficult to attain."

The phrase "by one whose self is subdued" (*vaśyātmanā*) is explained by demonstrating the logical connection (*anvaya*). That explanation begins with "the former," and so forth. The meaning is that mere action (*karma*), characterized as previously described, is the means for restraining the mind; however, practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) are stated to be its very limbs (*aṅga*).
The meaning is: by one who is striving, practicing yoga.

Thus, having been able to explain the previously mentioned means of yoga (*yogasādhana*) exactly as it is, he now says "Now" (*atha*), because [the disciple] asks with a detailed expansion so that the previously mentioned majesty of yoga (*yogamāhātmya*)— endowed with all its aspects— may be heard. By the term "majesty of yoga," the word "attainment of yoga" (*yogasiddhi*) found in the summary verse is intended.
This has been explained. For greatness (*māhātmya*) is the cause of success (*siddhi*); and here, "success" consists in this:

even for one whose yoga is lax, the attainment of various worlds of merit after a long time, rebirth in a family of yogis fit for yoga, through that means the full perfection of yoga, and from that, liberation (*apavarga*). And this is the success.

[The Lord says: "By a majesty that is not shared by others. [An objection is raised: But surely, in such passages as "In this [path], there is no loss of effort," the majesty of *karmayoga* was described;
here, however, it is the majesty of the yoga consisting of self-realization, which is the fruit of that [karmayoga]. Therefore, how can it be said that [this] has been heard [previously]?
Regarding that, he says: "Internal" (*antargatā*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tac ca*).

For the greatness of *karmayoga* has been stated there [in the previous verse] because it contains within it the knowledge of the Self—which is the sprout of yoga—and because it is the means for accomplishing the full nature of yoga; and therefore, in that which is conditioned by yoga (*yogopādhike*)...

The sense is that when the majesty of the yoga of action—which constitutes a limb [of the whole]—has been declared, the majesty of the yoga which constitutes the principal [whole] is thereby stated as well. Because of the appropriateness of the meaning of the words beginning with "one who lacks effort" (*ayati*), their connection has been shown through a different order [than the literal sequence]. For in that context, it must be expressed that one who has set out [on the path] has deviated from it.

But it is not for one who is merely endowed with faith; therefore, with the intention that [faith] is characterized by its effects, it is said that "he has engaged in yoga. Alternatively, the intended meaning is that the word *upeta* itself here refers to the attainment of yoga brought about by faith.
"Without attaining perfection in yoga" means before the attainment of yogic perfection.
"With a mind unsteady from yoga" means having a mind not conducive to performing complete yoga.
"Whom? means among those who have fallen into the hells of sensual enjoyment or liberation.
To which destination he goes has already been indicated in general terms. This is explained by the passage beginning with "In some cases" (kvacit).

Furthermore, he demonstrates the manner of falling away from both in the illustration, starting with "Just as. Because it serves to explain the state of falling away from both, [the text says] "the bewildered Brahmin."
And because of the mention of "on the path" (*pathi*) as a singular term, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*),
he says "as it truly is" (*yathāvasthitam*), intending that the "unsupported state" (*apratiṣṭhapadam*) refers to the failure of ritual actions that aim at worldly fruits.

The intention is that there was nothing deficient in the performance of the ritual actions, such as the effort involved; however, it became fruitless due to a discrepancy in the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*). Regarding the phrase "the deluded Brāhmaṇa on the path," ignorance is not intended here; for he is being questioned by one who, having set out with knowledge, has turned back.
Therefore, the cessation of the connection with the effects of delusion is indicated here by the word "deluded" (*vimūḍha*); this is the meaning.
Regarding the doubt being pointed out by the words "this doubt of mine," he states another aspect of that doubt which is established by the context:
"Does this [self] simply perish? You ought [to dispel it].
The meaning is that you are qualified because you are endowed with omniscience, compassion, the nature of a dear friend, and so forth.

By the word "Kṛṣṇa" and by the word "you" (tvat), he states what is intended: "by yourself" (svataḥ). The meaning is that you are qualified because you are not dependent on instruments [of knowledge] and are endowed with clear inference and other means of cognition.
He states what is intended by the words "Kṛṣṇa" and "you" with the phrase "by itself" (*svataḥ*).

The implication is that the knowledge of those other than you is dependent on instruments, consists primarily of indistinct inference and the like, occurs sequentially, has only limited objects, and is merely occasional.
By this [it is established that] Hari always knows everything simultaneously through direct perception by His own nature;
having bowed to Him, we shall expound the treatise on the principles of Nyāya.
Thus, however, the statement of the venerable Bhagavantanāmunimiśra has been kept in mind;
for it is intended that [the opponent's view] is not tenable because it contradicts reason.
Now, by way of showing how both types of human goals are attained, he avoids the charge of falling away from both.

[He says] "O Pārtha. By the word "of that" (*tasya*), he refers to the two aforementioned forms. By the word "with faith" (*śraddhayā*), avoiding the interpretation of the words "here" and "there" as referring to the world of mortals and the heavenly world respectively, he states what is intended here.

Regarding the word *prākṛta*: the sense is that just as for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), even merit (*puṇya*) is cast into the category of sin (*pāpa*), so too is heaven and the like; the intention is that this is worthy of being designated by the word "here" (*iha*) and is consistent with the context. As for the word "destruction" (*vināśa*), it refers to [the statement] "no obstacle (*pratyavāya*) exists."

Thus, he says "called *pratyavāya*" (transgression) to show that everything previously mentioned is here subsumed. He says "unsurpassed" (*niratiśaya*) to indicate that the word *kalyāṇa* (auspicious/well-being) culminates in the specific topic at hand. [He uses the form] "goes" (*gacchati*) because it is a reference to an uninterrupted present state.

It has been stated that "even in the three periods of time. Because it is accomplished through infinite merit accumulated over many periods of time, there was an absence of evil deeds even previously; now, there is the engagement in yoga whose nature is unsurpassed auspiciousness; and in the future as well, there will be the attainment of meritorious worlds, the perfection of yoga, liberation, and so forth.

There is an absence of miserable rebirth (*durgati*) throughout the three times. "Miserable rebirth" refers to hell or, more generally, anything undesirable. The particle *hi* indicates either a reason or a well-known fact.
For indeed, in the practice of yoga, no one at any time [experiences such a thing].
The sense is that attainment of an evil rebirth is established by some means of valid cognition.

In order to avoid the distress of falling away from both, he elaborates upon the connection with both [paths] starting with the words "having reached" (*prāpya*), etc., and by the phrase "the supreme goal" (*parāṃ gatim*). This refers to the cause of falling from yoga,
which consists in the attainment of the world of the doers of merit (*puṇyakṛt*), characterized by an excellence over the ordinary human goals.
Even in the absence of the means known as karma, it demonstrates that the majesty of yoga alone serves as the means;

furthermore, having generated dispassion—which is the cause for the termination of experience—it shows that the majesty of yoga alone is the cause for birth in a family fit for the commencement of yoga, as expressed in the words "of whatever class... (yajjātīya).

He says, "of those who have performed exceedingly great merit" (*atipuṇyakṛtām*), explaining that although the state of being a merit-maker (*puṇyakṛttva*) exists in all [beings] to some degree, the application of the term "merit-maker" to certain individuals is based on their possessing an excellence of merit over others, even though they belong to the same class.

It has been stated that they are exceedingly beautiful for the sake of lying down. Indeed, even among things of a single class—such as form, taste, smell, and so forth—even in the world of mortals, a gradation is observed. In this same way, there is a distinction between the divine and the non-divine.
If it is the case that one attains the worlds of merit through previously performed merits;
Regarding the point that one might reach the worlds of the sinful even due to previously committed sins, he says:

"Precisely by the majesty of yoga. The sense is that it is like the employment of wealth acquired for the sake of dharma and artha for the purpose of enjoyment. This [occurrence] is as if from the exhaustion of merit.

It is stated, beginning with "as long as," in order to demonstrate that [the cycle] ceases through the greatness of yoga, because of its inexhaustibility. This occurs by virtue of the arising of discernment (*viveka*), which is produced by the awakening of the *sattva* element rooted in karma whose time of ripening is uneven.

And the arising of dispassion (*vaitṛṣṇya*) due to the intensity of uninterrupted enjoyment and so forth should be understood from the accounts of Saubhari and others. He states that purity (*śucitva*) and prosperity (*śrīmattva*) assist yoga both through the medium of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and through the medium of the seen (*dṛṣṭa*).

Regarding the phrase "of those fit for the commencement of yoga": this means those whose nature is conducive to the commencement of yoga due to their own lineage, even if they have fallen from yoga. Alternatively, it refers to the family of yogis themselves, because a birth even more distinguished than this will be described later.
And because of the force of the qualifying attributes beginning with "of the pure" (*śucīnām*),
it is stated that one has fallen away at the commencement of yoga.

The word "or" (*athavā*) is used for the purpose of an alternative determination (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*); it is intended to show that the mention of an "excellent birth" implies a requirement for an "excellent cause. Thus, it was stated: "if one whose yoga is fully matured should waver."

The phrase "in the lineage of yogins" does not mean birth within the spiritual succession (*santāna*) of some particular yogin, because that alone would lack the quality of being an absolute aid to yoga; rather, it is intended to show that one is born as a son or similar relative specifically to those who are already yogins, so that they may become worthy of receiving instruction.

The expression "let them practice yoga" is an indication in the present tense. Regarding the phrase "of the pure and the prosperous," it was stated merely that they possess a favorable disposition toward the attainment of yoga through another teacher;
however, here, by the use of the word "of the wise," their own fitness to act as teachers is expressed.

Thus he says: "by himself. The greatness [of this] is endowed with the majesty established in such passages as, "Whether a beast, a human, or a bird, those who take refuge in Viṣṇu... Here too, the word *kula* signifies "house," because it has the same meaning as the words *dṛg-geha* (the house of vision) found in the preceding verse. "This twofold kind" refers to both of these.

The sense is that it is appropriate for such a descriptive reference (*anuvāda*) regarding what is common to both [the world and the seeker] to apply to both. By the word "world" (*loka*), he indicates the intention to exclude those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), referring instead to the people whose nature has been shown. [This is expressed by the term] "of the ordinary folk" (*prākṛtānām*).
Regarding the question of how that which is more difficult to obtain might be attained, he states what is intended by the word "such" (*īdṛśa*) with the words "this very... (*etattv iti*).

What follows from this? [The answer is: Because the yoga commenced in a previous body has become slackened, and because the mere birth of a yogi does not by itself constitute a cause for liberation—this is the response given here with the words "therein him" (*tatra tam*). This is because the word *tatra* (therein) shares the same grammatical case-ending as the locative.
In order to dispel the misconception that [the word] "house" (*geha*) refers to a physical dwelling, he states its connection with the meaning of the previously mentioned sentence.
He says that it is called "that" (*tam*) because, in that context, there exists even the notion of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) as the cause regarding one's previous body;
thus, it is stated as such in order to exclude that. He says: "The object of yoga."

Then— the meaning is "due to the connection with the intellect. In response to the doubt as to how this can be established, given that the obscuration of all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is observed in other births, [the answer is] that for those who have performed meritorious deeds, such a loss of latent impressions does not occur.

The example "like one who has awakened from sleep" is stated for the sake of illustration. Regarding the word *saṃsiddhaḥ*, he states what is intended by the prefix (*sam-*): "just as... The meaning of the word *tena* is "by means of the object of yoga. He states the result of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) expressed by the phrase *tenaiva*: [he is perfected] by that alone.
"Indeed, yoga alone is the means of attainment"—this is what he states by the word "indeed" (*hi*). He explains that it is "well-known" (*prasiddham*);
this renown is to be seen in the accounts of the ancient Bharatas, Vidura, Bhīṣma, and others.
Furthermore, by the two words "Pārtha" and "Kurunandana," which indicate the purity of both his lineages and so forth, [the text] refers to Arjuna as well.
The syntactical connection beginning with "of those possessing pure and glorious [qualities]" has been indicated.
He says "one who desires to know" (*jijñāsu*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that, by virtue of the context of the section, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) possess a fragmented nature.

He says "even one who desires to know" (*jijñāsur api*); the suffix *-san* [denoting desire] is used here because of its connection with the word "even" (*api*), which functions through the force of the context.
It has been stated that "the yoga has not proceeded. Although the genitive case in the sense of the object is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*,
nevertheless, here the genitive *yogasya* is used with the intention of expressing a general relationship.
The meaning is that for a yogin who has fallen away from yoga, there is yoga; for one who has begun yoga but has faltered, there is the resumption of that practice;

and for one who is agitated by the winds of yoga while desiring to ascend, there is the means of re-ascension—each being a remedy corresponding to its respective state. This refers to karma-yoga and so forth.

The meaning is that these are the yoga of action (karmayoga) and the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga). Alternatively, it refers to that yoga consisting of the direct realization of the Self, of which karmayoga is the preliminary stage.
Here, the word "Brahman" does not refer to the Supreme Brahman, because it would be logically inconsistent for that [Supreme Brahman] to be something to be transcended.

Furthermore, because the qualification "the Brahman of sound" (*śabdabrahman*) would be inappropriate, it cannot refer to the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor does it refer to the Veda, since the Veda itself cannot be established as something to be transcended.
Nor can it refer to the ritual actions taught by the Veda, or to their fruits, through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In that case as well, there would be the fault of using the word *brāhma* figuratively with respect to the Veda, followed by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for it, and a contraction [of its meaning] from the portion consisting of the Upaniṣads; thus, many defects would follow.
Nor is "word-born knowledge" itself here the "word-Brahman," for that would involve [an unnecessary] conjunction.
For one who desires to know [Brahman], such a transgression would be contradictory; furthermore,
it would entail the violation of scriptural injunctions such as, "From self-study one should proceed to yoga, and from yoga one should return to self-study."

But a person desiring to ascend to yoga is superior to one who possesses only the knowledge born from hearing the sacred word; among the Brāhmaṇas, the learned are superior; among the learned, those whose intellect is firmly established;
among those of firm intellect, the performers of action; and among the performers, those who expound the Veda.

If it is argued thus— [we reply] that too is not [correct], because it would entail the necessity of supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, because it would result in the mention of something irrelevant (*aprastutābhidhāna*), and because there would be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the preceding and following sentences.
Therefore, since the word *brāhma* is used here as well due to its abundance even in the context of the primary subject (*prakṛta*).

And because it is appropriate that [the Self] must transcend [matter]; here, the word *brāhṛ* refers to primordial matter (*prakṛti*). It is designated as "the *brāhṛ* of sound" (*śabda-brāhṛ*) in order to demonstrate its transformations known as the objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment. As it is said: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms..."

Based on scriptural passages such as "having made names," etc., primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which possesses differentiated forms, is indeed denoted by words such as "gods" and so forth. Having all this in mind, [the author] stated "gods, humans," and so on.
He demonstrates the resulting meaning of the phrase "transcending primordial nature" with the words "from the bondage of primordial nature."

By the words "devamanuṣya" and so forth, the passage beginning with "pumān na devo na naraḥ" (the person is neither god nor man) is recalled; and by the phrase "jñānānandaikatānam," the passage beginning with "jñānānandamayastvātmā śeṣo hi paramātmanaḥ" (the Self consists of knowledge and bliss, for it is the remainder of the Supreme Self) is recalled.
Thus, it has been stated that for one who has fallen from yoga, there is an effort extending until he attains perfection once again.

Now, the connection with the supreme human goal, characterized by the attainment of the Self, is described as proceeding from that very state. Regarding the word "prayatnāt" (through effort), the word "tataḥ" (from that) is not to be construed in its literal place [as a separate clause], because there would be no purpose in doing so.
The connection with the cause and human effort under discussion is now stated: "through effort.
The word "from that" (*tataḥ*), because it serves no purpose when construed according to its literal position, refers instead to the cause under discussion:
"since" (*yataḥ*). "Perfection through many births" means becoming fit for right yoga through many successive births.
The meaning is "born. The reason for this is "the state of having one's sins completely purified.

Regarding the phrase "striving through effort" (*yatamānaḥ*), there is no tautology because it refers to one striving by means of efforts such as the restraint of the senses; or else, it means "striving with even greater intensity."
The phrase "even though he had set out" (*calito'pi*) was stated in order to clarify what was previously mentioned and indicated by the word *tu*.
Alternatively, it may be read as "even though he had set out again. This is the explanation of the word *tataḥ*.
Furthermore, the expression "the supreme goal" (*parāṃ gatim*) signifies either yoga itself, or the attainment and so forth resulting from that [yoga].
Such greatness of yoga does not belong to anyone else in practices such as austerity (tapas) and the like;

therefore, with the intention of praising yoga and the yogi by showing that the yogi is superior to those who practice austerity and so forth, he concludes the instruction on the yoga of the individual soul (jīvātman), saying:

Regarding the phrase "it surpasses": the word "exclusive" (*kevala*) and so forth is used to exclude the ascetic practices, knowledge, and actions of even yogins, since these also exist in them. [This refers to] "knowledges other than the knowledge of the Self."

For there exist various forms of knowledge taught in the Yoga-śāstras and in the Upaniṣads, which have as their objects other deities, the moon, the sun, the planets, the vital breaths, the sense organs, and so forth; this is because of the meaning of the word *tapas*. This is stated in order to demonstrate the distinction between the meaning of the word *tapas* and the meaning of the word *karman*.

The mention of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth is intended to show that the gradation of austerity (*tapas*) and other practices, as well as of yoga, is here meant to be understood by way of their respective fruits; thus, the term "human goals" (*puruṣārtha*) is employed.

Thus, having established that the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is superior to [the self], the listener might think his purpose is fulfilled and conclude that there is no further supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Anticipating this, [the author]— just as in the *Bhūmavidyā*— himself presents [the following] which establishes a human goal even more excellent than that.

He himself introduces the subject to demonstrate the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*)—which is the limb (*aṅgin*) of that [yoga]—through the middle hexad; thus he says, "In this way" (*tadevam*). This means: in the manner established by the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarke*). To establish the connection, he states that it is a supplement to the first hexad.

"Being a constituent part of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). This refers to the presentation of the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) therein. "Expounded in the discourse of Prajāpati. This has already been elaborated upon previously.
By this [it is shown that] it pertains solely to the vision of the perfectly pure inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Those such as the Vedāntins of the final age (antimayuga) and others, who speak of [the attainment of] supreme yoga and so forth, are refuted.

"Supreme knowledge" (paravidyā) means the highest knowledge (*parāṃ vidyām*); this is like the passage beginning, "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable is attained. Alternatively, it means the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātmanaḥ*).
This is merely an introduction; the full elaboration will follow immediately after—this is the sense.
Now, why undergo such trouble? Here, the genitive case is possible in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
For instance, among the four yogas mentioned previously, [it refers to] "he who [sees] Me dwelling in all beings..."
"A certain yogi, established in oneness, worships" is what was stated there;
here too, it is that very same person who "full of faith worships Me" who is recognized. Therefore, by way of identifying him, the praise "the most disciplined" (yuktatamaḥ) is bestowed here.
In the phrase *yuktatamaḥ*, the suffix (*pratyaya*) indicates the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Therefore, this is not a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*); regarding this, he says: "abiding in all beings" (*sarvabhūtastham*).
By this, although there was a singular designation (*ekavacana*) as "the yogi" (*yogī*) in the previous verse, here—
By means of the plural number, the scope of the subsequent reference (*anuvāda*) has also been shown. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"In them," etc. This is the intended meaning: for the worshiper of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) will be described in the middle hexad; and its introduction is being made here.

Nor has that [Self] been mentioned previously; furthermore, it has already been established that passages such as "He who sees Me abiding in all beings" have as their object the contemplation of equality.
Therefore, there is no recognition of that [Self] here. Moreover, [the text says]: "By comparison with oneself..."

Thus, in this verse, a yogin superior even to the one previously described— who was characterized by such statements as "abiding in all beings"— has been mentioned. Consequently, by establishing here that the yogin described by the words "abiding in all beings" and so forth is superior to everything, [this verse] relates to the preceding one.

There would be a contradiction. Therefore, since it is impossible for a yogin to be one of those [categories] mentioned here, this genitive case is not used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). This is what was stated: "because he is not included among them.
Now, [one might object]: does this not generally include the yogins previously mentioned as well as those yet to be described?
Could there not be a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of one among those that will be mentioned later?

Not so; for when some [categories] have been understood, it is indeed from among those already understood that something is to be selected, otherwise an elliptical reference (*anuvāda*) would be improper for the purpose of prescribing a specific distinction (*atiśaya*); and that which is to be mentioned later...
The yogi who was previously accepted as the listener, Arjuna,
is also indicated by the phrase "of the one about to be described. Therefore, [this refers to] the yogi about to be described, who is superior to the yogis mentioned previously.

This must indeed be a mere introductory statement (*prastāva*). Consequently, since the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) does not have the sense of "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*), the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) cannot occur [in that sense]. If one construes [the phrase] "of all yogins as well" (*yoginām api sarveṣām*) as a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇya*), then the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Since a high degree of conventional usage is possible here as well, ascetics and others are implicated by the meaning of the word "all. Yet, they are not included by the term "yogin. And when the primary sense is possible, it is not proper to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that [secondary] sense.

The inclusion of those who are even inferior to yogis is entirely appropriate for the purpose of providing an illustration; furthermore, the conjunction of yogis with ascetics and others is absolutely necessary, as it serves to demonstrate their commonality in being inferior.

Intending all of this, he says: "Even for all [beings]. The meaning is that, according to the principle already stated, they cannot be included because they are not contained within those [categories] due to the force of the context. Alternatively, it is because yogins, ascetics, and so forth possess their own respective specific means (*upāya*).

The meaning is that this [path] is endowed with a means superior to all of them; or, the meaning is that it is the most suitable. Having intended all of this, he will later say "the most excellent" (*śreṣṭhatama*).
Why are those who are even inferior to yogis, such as ascetics (*tapasvin*) and others, included here?
In this context, he clarifies that [the example] serves as an illustration: "in comparison with that. He confirms this by means of a worldly example: "in comparison with Meru.
Now, it was stated that there is no distinction in being inferior; if that were so, [what would become of] those such as ascetics?

Furthermore, it would follow that there is absolute equality among all yogins. Yet, even in relation to Mount Meru, there exists a distinction among mustard seeds in terms of their degree of deficiency or excess, consisting of being inferior or more inferior.
To this, he says: "Even though... This does not mean that mutual gradation is now being denied.

However, even among those who possess mutual gradations, when compared to one who is absolutely superior, they are all alike in their mere inferiority; and by that alone, the designation of being "lower" remains applicable—this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "beyond my state of being beloved" [is used].
"I" refers to myself. "Matpriya" means one for whom I am dear—that is, one who is an object of my affection.

"The state of being that" (tat-tvam) means the reality of being such [a devotee], which implies being devoid of devotion to anything else. This is because of the inherent nature of not being held by any other [object].
The sense is that the sustainer is indeed precisely that which is intended as an object of enjoyment.
Here, in relation to the hands, the senses, the body, and so forth, the mind is designated by the term "inner self" (antarātman);
and [the author] shows that desire possesses the state of intensity which is the cause of its swiftness, by means of the words beginning with "atyartham."

By the words "variegated" and so forth, he demonstrates those forms suitable for meditation— which have been indicated by hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts as being worthy of worship, and which will be described in the two subsequent chapters (ṣaṭkas)— and which are intended by the word "me" (mām).

Up to the end of the verse beginning with "āpyāyantaṃ," there is a distinction: those [verses] ending with "vāṅmanasāparicchedyasvarūpabhāvam" are conducive to His transcendence (paratva), while those following them are conducive to His accessibility (saulabhya).

And the mention of both [the easy and the difficult] is because things that are extremely common, such as grass and the like, or things that are extremely rare, such as Mount Meru and the like, are not to be accepted if either one of these two conditions is lacking;
this applies to general terms such as "existent" (*sat*), "knower" (*jñātṛ*), "soul" (*ātman*), and so forth, which occupy the position of causal statements.
Intending to establish the referent of the word *Nārāyaṇa* as that which brings about the presentation of a specific [cause] not established otherwise,
[the author] sets forth the meaning determined by the sūtra "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*),
as propounded by such scriptural passages as "From whence indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*).

He demonstrates the characteristic of the Brahman to be investigated— the majesty consisting of its being the cause of the universe and its manifold forms— in the charioteer Dhananjaya, by means of the verse beginning with "vicitra-".
The connection with the manifestation of divine play (*līlāvibhūti*) has been established by way of [His] causality;

now, in order to remove doubts regarding the presence of defects or the deficiency of qualities that might be suspected in Him on account of His causality, He demonstrates His possession of both sets of characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*), as established by purificatory passages (*śodhakavākya*) and so forth, beginning with the word "untouched" (*aspṛṣṭa*).

If "untouched by all defects" is taken as a qualifier of the qualities (*guṇa*), what is intended is the absence of co-occurrence with defects; if it is taken as a qualifier of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), it refers to the absolute non-existence of defects.
Now, this is presented by way of establishing that [the Lord] is distinguished by a non-material form which is the locus of auspiciousness.

By observing the association with divine ornaments, weapons, queens, attendants, abodes, and so forth, he indicates the possession of eternal glory (*nitya-vibhūti*). Regarding the phrase "as intended by himself":
thus, when the state of absolute supremacy is established through the possession of both types of glory and the possession of both characteristics.

In order to indicate that [Brahman] is also unfit for worship because it cannot be delimited by speech or mind, he speaks of its supreme transcendence with the words "by speech and mind. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists in its lordship (*īśvaratva*) and so forth, or in its blissfulness (*ānandatva*) and so forth. However, its natural radiance (*jyotiḥ*) is that which specifies the particularities of the defined essential nature.

The dharmas. Some maintain that what has been described as "otherness" (*paratva*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa*), while what will be described as "gentleness" (*saumya*) is the intrinsic character (*svabhāva*). He states the causes for the descent [of the teaching] and its gentleness with the words beginning with "apāra... and so forth: "The Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise the Śūdras—each of these [is like] a great ocean."

He demonstrates this established truth through such [epithets] as "the refuge of all the worlds. Regarding the phrase "without being scrutinized": the "particulars" (*viśeṣāḥ*) consist of distinctions of genus, quality, conduct, and so forth. The aforementioned qualities such as compassion are the causes for being such a refuge. By the word "refuge" (*śaraṇya*), the state of being approachable is expressed.
He describes the nature of dispelling that which is opposed to the fruit [of devotion] with the words "remover of the distress of those who bow down.

Although the quality of affection (*vātsalya*) has already been mentioned alongside other qualities as being common to all, it is mentioned again specifically regarding the incarnations (*avatāras*) for the purpose of reflecting upon its particular connection.

He contemplates [the Lord] separately in order to make known His capacity to act, to ensure that those who have committed offenses do not fear, to demonstrate that He is Himself the protector even during states devoid of knowledge and other virtues,
and to remove the supreme aversion that constitutes an obstacle to Him.

Regarding the phrase "the sole ocean of affection for those who have taken refuge," he states the distinction from other incarnations within the *prakṛta* (the manifest world) as being the fruition of the multitude of qualities such as compassion already mentioned,
by saying "akhila... and so forth, beginning with "Though unborn and of imperishable nature."
He recalls what was stated previously. With the intention of explaining that [the Lord] said "me" (mām) while relying on a specific incarnation, he says: "O Vāsudeva."

Intending to attract the minds of the worshippers by means of the two specific qualities of His incarnate form—splendor (*tejas*) and beauty (*kānti*)—which manifest His transcendence (*paratva*) and accessibility (*saulabhya*) precisely during the state of incarnation, he says "anavadhika...
(infinite). Here too, *tejas* refers to brilliance. From that...

Thus, its invincibility is also established. "Lustre" (*kānti*) is loveliness; it is a radiance comparable to moonlight, another synonym for *lāvaṇya*. For this very reason, it is said that [the world] is being nourished. By this—
The passage beginning with "nourishing the universe with his splendor" has been recalled.
Now, in order to state the intended meaning of the word *bhajate*, he first shows the meaning as listed in the Dhātupāṭha:
"the sense is that he worships (*upāste*). [This applies] even for yogis.

By saying "of all," he refers collectively to the two groups previously mentioned; by saying "to all," he refers to those same groups. Regarding the phrase "in my view," he states what is intended by the word "mine" (*me*) with the words beginning with "all.
Here too, the passage beginning with "he who knows everything simultaneously" is to be understood as a corollary.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*, composed by Vedāntācārya, the lion among poets and logicians.
The Eighth Chapter of the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a Commentary on the *Śrīmad-bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*.

To demonstrate the connection [of this chapter], he says, "the seventh. The meaning of the passage beginning with "with the mind attached to Me" (18.57) is that the Supreme Brahman, Vāsudeva, is the object of worship (*upāsya*). It is precisely there that meditation (*upāsana*) is introduced; everything else mentioned here is stated as a supplement to that. This very point is elaborated upon in the verses: "I am all," "Vāsudeva is all," and "the four kinds of devotees... (18.55–56).

The intention is that [the Lord] is established as "Me" and so forth in the subsequent [verses]. By the words "of the Supreme" and so on, there is a rejection of alternative positions such as the conditioned Brahman, the ether, and the like. Because the word *brāh* is used in conjunction with a specific term, there is an exclusion of other deities. By the word *Vāsudeva*, either the specific incarnation or the general [divine source] is intended here. By the words "entire" (*nikhila*) and so forth, there is a description of the attributes suitable for being the object of worship and for being the Supreme Brahman. By the word "entire" (*nikhila*),...

The meaning of the verse beginning with “Earth, water... (*bhūmirāpaḥ*) is established by the inclusion of the states consisting of cause and effect. Since the state of being "higher" mentioned in the statement “There is nothing else higher than Me” is utilized in the passage “Me, who am higher than these,” that very point was illustrated there; here, however, bypassing that, the status of being the substratum as stated in “In Me all [exists]” (*mayi sarvam*) is taken up. The fact of being denotable by the word “all” is the result of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in passages such as “I am the taste” (*raso'ham*). The reason for this is the fact of having everything as one’s body (*sarvaśarīrakatva*), which is established by specific qualities such as being the substratum. Thus, by way of restating [qualities] such as being the Sovereign (*śeṣitva*).

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the specific objects to be attained by the respective qualified persons (*adhikārins*) that will be described hereafter is also based on the relationship of being the body (*śarīratva*). Thus, by way of restating [the Lord's] status as the one to be served (*śeṣitva*), it has been shown that the grammatical coreferentiality with the specific objects to be attained by the respective qualified persons that will be described hereafter is likewise caused by the relationship of being the body and the self (*śarīrātmabhāva*). Since coreferentiality with respect to activity is also intended in passages such as "Know them to proceed from Me alone," everything is established.

The term *niyantṛtvam* (the state of being the controller) [is established]. By the phrase "by all," there is an inclusion of other intended meanings not explicitly mentioned. By the restrictive emphasis "of that very one" (*tasyaiva*), the meaning of the statement "there is nothing else" is expressed. The meaning of the verse beginning with "composed of the three guṇas" along with its half-verse has been stated by the words beginning with "sattva. The fact that the surrender (*prapatti*) expressed in the passage beginning with "unto Me alone" is caused by a specific kind of merit is shown by the words "people who have performed good deeds" (*janāḥ sukṛtinaḥ*).

Because this passage consists of a detailed explanation of the specific modes of concealment previously mentioned, and because it serves as a supplement to the praise of the virtuous (*sukṛtin*), its meaning has not been treated separately here.

The section beginning with "fourfold" (*caturvidhāḥ*) is connected with the phrase "according to the gradation of their merit" (*sukṛtatāratamyena*) and so forth; the construction is that this refers to the "distinction among the worshippers" (*upāsakabheda*).

The meaning of the two verses beginning with "Among them, the man of knowledge" (*teṣāṃ jñānī*) has been stated in the commentary beginning with "the Blessed Lord" (*bhagavantam*). [The verse] "Of many births" (*bahūnāṃ janmanām*)...
With the words "of these three," he states the meaning of the remainder of the chapter, beginning with "thus they go to creation, O scorcher of foes. What is to be known here is as follows:

The form of perfection (*siddhi*) is intended [here]. That which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) is that which is to be practiced (*anuṣṭheya*). By this, the meaning of the summary verse beginning with "one's own true nature" (*svayāthātmya*) has also been elaborated. This, however, is the summary of the eighth chapter: "The eightfold division of the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), the things to be adopted (*upādeya*), and the states of being for those seeking sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the imperishable true nature (*akṣarayāthātmya*), and the feet of the Lord (*bhagavaccaraṇa*) is now stated. Since the subject matter of the chapter consists in the mention of these divisions, it is shown that the exposition of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) was already performed previously. He states the connection [of the current section] by saying "now," as it is an elaboration of what has been introduced.

Out of a desire to know the distinction between that which is to be known—such as the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)—and that which is to be practiced, such as meditation (*upāsanā*), Arjuna said: "What is that?

Since the three types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*) have already been mentioned [in the Gītā], and because of the force of the repetition of the word "who" (*yaḥ*) in passages such as "for the sake of liberation from old age and death," as well as by the very nature of the subject matter, there exists a distinction among these aspirants and a specific determination regarding the objects to be known and adopted for each; this was addressed by Arjuna in the verse beginning with "What is that Brahman? concerning those who seek the reality of the imperishable and the unrighteous.

The term *adhibhūtam* refers to the domain of those who seek mastery over unrighteous things (*adharmaiśvaryārthin*). However, he distinguishes that the verse beginning with *adhiyajñaḥ* is common to all three [goals] by virtue of its inherent meaning, stating:

"Old age and death... The question "How? (*katham*) asks for the manner [of attainment]. The phrase "the state of being *adhiyajña*" is understood from the context. Here, the word *atra* (here) has as its limiting condition the proximity of the Teacher;

he will explain this in the subsequent text: "In this Indra and so forth, who have become my body. On the other hand, the word *asmin* (in this) has as its limiting condition the proximity of one's own direct perception (*svapratyakṣa*).

[The Lord is] the presiding deity; for even Indra and the others are directly perceived by the questioner, Arjuna. This is seen in such passages as, "This Person is established in these two feet," where the words *etad* (this) and *idam* (this) refer to the twenty-two [deities]. Alternatively, the word *atra* (here) refers to the nature of the sacrifice itself. A state of fixed selfhood (*niyatātmatva*) is required for the three; the plural number here is intended to signify the three types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*), with this in mind it was said, "by these [three]. || 2 ||

Regarding the statement "the syllable (akṣara) is the supreme Brahman," [the author] says "it is designated as Brahman" in order to exclude any misconception regarding the identity of the subject and the predicate. The intention is that the word "Brahman" here is used figuratively (upacāra-vṛtti) due to its similarity with the Supreme Self. He demonstrates the etymology and the referent of the word "akṣara" with the words "it does not perish" (na kṣarati), etc. He shows the Vedic usage of the term for the aggregate of individual souls (kṣetrajña-samaṣṭi) with the words "and likewise" (tathā ca). Here, "laya" (dissolution) refers to a specific kind of conjunction. Alternatively, by the word "akṣara" in the Śruti—

The portion of consciousness that has not emerged is designated as a particular state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); thus, there is no contradiction even if [the term] directly refers to dissolution (*pralaya*). Nevertheless, because the intention (*tātparya*) concerns the conscious element which serves as the gateway for the application of the word, that example is cited. Regarding the phrase "the supreme imperishable" (*paramamakṣaram*), he states what is intended by the qualification: "the essential nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) liberated from primordial nature. Primordial nature is the meaning of the word "own-nature" (*svabhāva*); that is to say, it is that which is invariably connected. To the inquiry "What is that?"—
In accordance with the term *adhyātma*, he says "non-self" (*anātman*). The etymological definition of the word *ātman* is that which is connected by dwelling within (*adhi-vasana*);

therefore, its state of being non-self is established from that very fact. "Its impressions and so forth" refers to the impressions of ignorance and karma conditioned by association with that [self]. Regarding the knowability of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and so on:

He shows the scriptural authority (*śruti*) regarding the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*). Starting with, "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? and concluding with, "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'," the intention is that the state of being known through the subtle elements of the fivefold nature—indicated by the word "waters" (*ap*)—is declared for those who know thus: "Those who know this. [Objection: But is it not the case that the present individual self (*jīva*), which is the agent of the means [to liberation], [is the subject]?

What use is there for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) in a description of the nature of the pure Self by means of abandoning its own [empirical] nature? And for what purpose is the description of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and so forth? To this he says: "Both of those. The connection follows the respective order. Since the fifth oblation is intended here, this word *bhūta* refers to the subject matter of birth from a womb; "the state of being a *bhūta*" means the conjunction with a body characterized by humanity and so forth. When the specific emission (*visarga*) is to be known, its state as a human and so on [is required].

And he shows the scriptural authority for its being the cause with the words "in the fifth. He demonstrates that very point with the words "in the fifth. Here, it is stated that [the semen] is "that which brings about the emergence of the state of being" (bhūtabhāvodbhavakara) in order to distinguish it from the emission of feces, urine, and so forth. He demonstrates that same point with the words "born of connection with a woman"; this is established by the force of the qualification "emission" (visarga). Thus, he states the purposefulness of the knowledge of the emission of semen designated as "action" (karma) with the words "and all that. Here...

The neuter gender is used here by way of referring to "action" (karman). "Entirely" means manifold, as it is the cause for the various distinctions between the human and animal species. "With its consequences" means accompanied by the actions that serve as causes and by the results such as dwelling in the womb and so forth. Because the Pañcāgni-vidyā has established that the non-conscious (acit) persists through all states, is difficult to abandon, and produces the sufferings of birth from the womb and so on, it is to be viewed with loathing, as something terrifying, and as something to be shunned.
[The objection that] "it would be established as something to be avoided" is addressed here by the words: "And as for being something to be avoided... (Verse 3).

That which was indicated as something to be known by those seeking sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) should also be applied to the *adhidaivata* (the divine realm). Following the etymological definition of the word "perishable" (*kṣara*) in relation to the *adhibhūta* (the elemental realm), he explains it thus:

the word "sound" (*śabda*) and so forth refers to the ether (*viyat*) and the rest. The etymological derivation "having the nature of perishing" (*kṣaraṇasvabhāva*) is intended to include both—the states such as sound and their possessors—which are both objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*). The meaning is "transient. Regarding the phrase "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇā*), the intention is that the singular number in the expression "the perishable state" (*kṣaro bhāvaḥ*) is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*).

The meaning is that they are "to be attained" because they possess the quality of being attainable. To dispel the misconception that the term *adhidaivata* is a conventional name (*rūḍhi*), he says: "designated by the word *adhidaivata*. Its etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is "that which exists above the deities" (*devatoparivartamāna*). The compound *devatopari* is formed with a genitive of general relation (*sambandhasāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*). He states that the word *daivata* here refers to the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*), whose scope encompasses all other deities, by saying "Indra," etc. Here, "existing above" does not refer merely to spatial location and so forth; rather, it refers to [superiority in] experience (*bhoga*).

With the intention of showing that this is so even by way of excellence, he says the passage beginning with "Indra" and ending with "puruṣa. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that another person is not intended here?

For the contemplation of the nature of one's own self as the *puruṣa* is common even to other qualified aspirants; therefore, what is the distinction here? To this, he replies with the word "ca" (and). The meaning is that the perfectly pure essential nature is not what is to be contemplated here, nor is there to be cultivated here the notion of something impure as being fit for abandonment; rather, the use of the term *puruṣa* here has the state [of being a *puruṣa*] as its primary sense.

"I alone" is the answer to the question "Who? He explains that which was intended as the answer to the question "How? with the words "In sacrifice" (*adhiyajña*). That which is connected to the sacrifice is "in sacrifice. And therein, he states that the connection of the Lord of all is by way of being the object of worship, saying: "existing as the object of worship in the sacrifice. For Indra and others are heard in scripture to be the objects of worship there; how then can it be said "I alone"? To this, the answer is: "here in the body."

By this [statement], he shows what is intended by saying, "here, in Indra and so forth. Since it is stated by the Lord, "I alone am the Adhiyajña here in the body," it is understood that the subject matter concerns His body. And since that body of the Lord—given the context of sacrifice (*yajña*) as the worship of deities according to the root *yaja* (to worship)—refers specifically to Indra and others, it is said, "in Indra and so forth," with this intention. The expression "become my body" recalls what was previously stated in the verse, "whichever form... Thus, the term "body" (*deha*) is used.

The restrictive emphasis "I alone" (*ahameva*) is intended to exclude [the status of] spirits (*bhūta*), the individual souls (*kevala*), Indra, and other such divine beings. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known that [the Self] is not a separate principle (*tattvāntara*), unlike the previously mentioned *brāhma*, *ādhyātmika*, *karma*, *adhibhūta*, and *adhidaiva* aspects. There is also the scriptural statement: "Viṣṇu is all the deities. By this, an answer has also been given to the question "How? (i.e., how is He the object of worship?), because He is the one to be worshipped as qualified by each of those aspects. By the phrase "best among embodied beings" (*dehabhṛtāṃ vara*), it is indicated that He possesses a body, senses, and so forth, which are superior in their *sattva* quality and conducive to spiritual reflection (*ādhyātma-cintā*), as well as His own transcendental nature.

An illustration regarding the possession of bodies such as those of Indra is also intended. He shows that such knowledge of the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*) has entered into the performance [of the rite] itself—it is not merely an auxiliary to it, nor is it restricted solely to those who seek sovereign power—by the words "the great sacrifice. The mention of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites is for the purpose of removing unfitness caused by non-performance, and to indicate the necessity of performing these three. (4)

The verse beginning with "at the time of departure" (*prayāṇakāle*) provides a summary answer to this question; therefore, with the intention that it does not concern the knower alone, he says, "this also. The sense is that [the meaning] arises from its own nature, just like the category of the sacrificial deity (*adhiyajña*), and according to the manner that will be explained. He demonstrates the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with the words "and at the time of death" (*antakāle ca*). Regarding the phrase "he attains my state" (*madbhāvaṃ yāti*), he says "that state which is mine" (*mama yo bhāvaḥ*) in order to dispel the misconception of attaining identity (*tādātmya*), which would contradict the Śruti and other authorities.

Now, one might object: "If there is no distinction in the attainment of the very nature of the Lord, then there would be no difference among those qualified [for liberation]. To this he says, "At that time" (*tadānīm*). What is intended here is the attainment of equality in the specific forms to be meditated upon. And since this equality exists only while the differences that distinguish their essential natures (*svarūpa*) remain, there is no fault whatsoever; this is the sense. Thus the objections have been answered. By the words "there is no doubt in this regard," he demonstrates the well-known motivating factors intended [by the author], such as "just as Ādibharata and others."

By this example as well, the delusion of identity is refuted; for there was no identity between Ādibharata and the deer being remembered, but rather the mere assumption of a deer-body of identical form—this is well known in that very context. The meaning is: "at that time" refers to the moment of separation from the body. || 5 ||
One should not think that this [nature of the final thought] has as its object only the Lord; rather, it is stated here that this is common to all.

This is expressed by the author of the *Prayojakakāra* in the verse beginning with "whatever" (*yaṃyam*). He says "to remember" (*smartum*) and "at the end" (*ante*), meaning at the time of death. By the repetition (*vīpsā*) and by the word "or even" (*vāpi*), he shows that there is no restriction regarding the object to be remembered, nor any disparity between low and high objects. Furthermore, by the repetition "that very one" (*taṃ tam*), he indicates the attainment of each respective object without confusion.

By the use of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), it is intended to express that she is difficult to ward off even by other powerful merits. Here, the word *bhāva* refers to "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*); the reference to the substratum (*dharmin*) is an inseparable implication. If the word *bhāva* were taken here in the sense of "category" (*padārtha*), there would be a discordance with the word *bhāva* used in the present context, as well as a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity in the phrase "it goes to each and every one" (*taṃ-tam evaiti*). In the phrase "it goes to each and every one," this is stated to exclude the mere connection with that common genus in any birth whatsoever. [The phrase] "immediately after death" (*maraṇānantaram*)...

There was no interval between other births in his case regarding his state as a deer in the lineage of Hṛdīka and Bharata. By the phrase "always permeated by that state" (*sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ*), he intends to express the cause for the final recollection; thus he says, "and the final cognition. "Permeated by that state" means "saturated by the cultivation of that state" (*tadbhāvanāvāsita*). Alternatively, "permeated by that state" means "by whom the disposition toward that [state] has been cultivated" (*tasmin bhāvo bhāvito yena*). || 6 ||

Thus, since the fruit depends upon the final causal condition (*antimapratyaya*), and that final causal condition depends upon uninterrupted cultivation (*anavaratabhāvanā*), it is stated by the verse beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*) that you too must perform such cultivation and the action that favors it. By the phrase "at all times," [it is meant] that "he, indeed, living in this manner for as long as he lives..."

With the intention of citing such scriptural passages as "He attains the world of Brahman," the phrase "until departure" (āprayāṇāt) was stated. Furthermore, there is the Sūtra: "Until departure; for even there, it is seen. Since one could also say "until departure" even if the remembrance were performed only once every month or every fortnight, he uses the plural form "day after day" (aharahar) with the intention of excluding such [infrequent] practice.

This means that [the practice] is to be performed during those sattvic times characterized by one-pointedness, as prescribed in such passages as "Applying oneself in the first and last watches of the night" (*pūrvāpararātreṣu yuñjānaḥ*).

Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Where there is one-pointedness, there [it is performed], because there is no distinction. Thus, by the principle that "when a fruitless act occurs in proximity to one with a fruit, the former is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the latter," it is established that this [practice] is a subsidiary to the "striving" (*yudhya*) enjoined here. And that "striving" is mentioned here merely as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), since it is the subject at hand.

And therefore, with the intention of stating that the duties pertaining to one's respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), which are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), must necessarily be performed, he says: "battle and so forth, which effect daily remembrance. The phrase "connected with caste and stage of life" (*varṇāśramānubandhī*) is the defining characteristic that encompasses what is to be illustrated. By the word "enjoined" (*coditam*), it is indicated that the injunctions for tranquility (*śama*) and so forth have as their object that which is distinct from [the aforementioned duties]. By the terms "obligatory" (*nitya*) and "occasional" (*naimittika*), there is the exclusion of actions preceded by a desire for fruits (*phalābhisandhi*). [The phrase] "with mind and intellect fixed therein" (*madhyarpitamanobuddhi*).

The phrase "evam" (thus) shows that this verse is a restatement of what has already been said. "By means" (*upāyena*) means by means of ritual action (*karman*) and so forth. Here, "offering of the mind" (*manasaḥ arpaṇam*) is simply remembrance (*anusmaraṇa*); however, the "offering of the intellect" (*buddheḥ arpaṇam*) is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) to bestow the fruit [of that remembrance].
