This statement regarding the intermediate operation established within the context is found in the words, "and at the time of death, remembering Me alone. Alternatively, here "by means" refers specifically to remembrance supported by ritual action; its result is the mind and intellect offered unto Me.

The meaning of that very [verse] is: "And at the time of death, remembering Me alone. To show that this applies commonly to all three types of qualified aspirants (adhikārin) mentioned previously and subsequently, he says: "Me, in the manner desired. Even though the word *asaṃśayaḥ* is an adjective qualifying Arjuna—as in such passages as, "Hari indeed dwells eternally in all those who are free from doubt; Mādhava does not dwell among those who have doubts due to the force of [false] reasoning"—he states the resulting implication: "There is no doubt in this matter. [This is according to the rule: *amā nonāḥ...* [etc. (Pāṇini 2.2.6).

Because of the statement "in the case of negation," the letter *a* should also be understood here as distinct [from the negative particle]. Passages such as, "He who has the firm conviction, 'Having departed from here, I shall attain that,' for him there is no doubt," should be considered here. || 7 ||

Since meditation was introduced as being remembered by virtue of its being the cause of the final cognition (*antima-pratyaya*), he says "In this way" (*evam*) with the intention that the subsequent section explains the different varieties of that [meditation]. The difference in the goal (*gati-bheda*) which will be mentioned later should also be understood as implied by this. He states the meaning of the three verses beginning with "By practice" (*abhyāsa*) with the word "Therein" (*tatra*).

Since the word *yoga* would be redundant if it meant merely "connection," it is appropriate here to state that it refers to *dhyāna* (meditation). Furthermore, because a *dvandva* compound emphasizes the meaning of both its constituent parts more than a *tatpuruṣa* compound does, it is the one to be accepted; thus he says, "by means of the practice and yoga. The term *nānyagāmin* is not like words such as *naika* and so on.

Its meaning is "not going elsewhere" (*ananyagāmin*). That which has no tendency (*śīla*) to go to another object—that is, to something else—is *nānyagāmi*. By the term "practice and yoga" (*abhyāsayoga*), [he means...]

Since prior reflection has already been mentioned, the phrase "at the time of death" (*antakāle*) is stated to demonstrate that the expression "reflecting upon" (*anucintayan*) refers specifically to the final recollection.

Here, the object of both reflection and meditation is the Person himself; and because he is qualified by the word "Supreme," the intention is that he is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*), which is expressed by the two words "Me" (*mām*).
As for the term "divine" (*divyam*), Śaṅkara’s assertion that it means "situated within the solar orb" is baseless, as it is said: "Having the color of the sun, beyond darkness."

With the intention that [the present statement] is not inconsistent with what is about to be said, he says, "in the manner that will be described. The words "by the two subsequent verses" are to be understood as the ellipsis. To the question, "How can the attainment of the Supreme Person—which is not sought by one desiring sovereign power—be declared as the fruit? he replies: "Because of being the primary cause," and so on. Here, the "attainment of the Supreme Person" refers to the acquisition of sovereignty equal to that of the Supreme Person, characterized by a form suitable for bestowing enjoyments remembered at the time of death; for indeed, that very attainment of equality with Him is what constitutes that attainment.

By the verse beginning with "whichever [object]," he states the meaning of the word *udāra* (exalted). Regarding the word *abhyāsa* (repetition), because of the expression "again and again," it is intended that there may be an occasional interruption by certain [activities] that necessarily occur in the interim. With this in mind, it is said: "at all times, provided they are not opposed to obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) duties. The sense is that this does not refer only to the time of formal yoga practice, since the cultivation practiced at that specific time is already subsumed under the term "yoga. ... The *ālambana* (support); and this is explained here by the word "object of worship" (*upāsya*).

"Go. By the word "yoga," the essential nature of the principal [practice] is expressed here; thus he says, "of yoga. "As described" means having attained the state of being most intensely dear and most clearly perceived. || 8 ||

For a poet is defined as one who perceives what has been traversed; however, here the word "poet" (kavi) refers to omniscience because it pertains to the Lord. With this intention, he says "the All-knowing.

With the intention that the word "ancient" (purāṇa) signifies beginninglessness, he says "the Ancient. To exclude the mere sense that the prefix *anu-* in *anuśāsitāram* means simply "to make known by distinguishing," he says "the Ruler of the universe. Since the Lord already exists, his "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) is for the purpose of commanding.

To exclude the notion that [the Lord] is concerned with only this much, it is stated that He is "the Ruler of the universe. The sense is that for one who is the Lord, His "instruction" (anuśāsana) is indeed His command (ājñāpana). When there is an expectancy for the object of the root *anu-śās*, the word "of all" (*sarvasya*) from the phrase "the Sustainer of all" (*sarvasya dhātāram*) should be drawn back [to connect with it].

Or, with the intention that [the Self] has everything as its object because there is no specific limitation mentioned, it is said "of the universe" (*viśvasya*). One should consider here such passages as: "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart. With the intention that the state of being subtler than the subtle (*aṇor aṇīyāṃsam*), which is necessary for the entry within [all beings], is mentioned here—[an entry] which is mentioned together with "governance" in such texts as "He who has entered within is the ruler of people"—it is said [to be subtler than the subtle].

It was not stated [by us] that [the Lord] is "more subtle. Since the word *dhātṛ* (Creator) is used for the Lord (*ruāṣṭṛ*) in such passages as "The Creator who ordained him in the beginning" and "The Creator fashioned the sun and moon as they were before," and since verbal roots (*dhātu*) contain manifold meanings, it was said that He is the "Creator of all. Furthermore, because it is stated in such texts as "The two worlds are supported by Viṣṇu" and "The abode named Viṣṇu is the support of all," the result is that the status of being the support of all belongs to the Lord of all alone.

Or rather, it is a statement [of fact]. Fearing that some might imagine the impossibility of ascertaining the nature of the Lord, which has been described in the manner stated, through general observations and logical arguments (*tarka*), he says "whose nature is inconceivable" (*acintyarūpam*) with the intention of refuting that; thus he says "whose essential nature is of a different class from everything else. Since the application of letters [to denote Him] does not pertain to His essential nature itself, he speaks of the connection [with letters] by way of a unique physical form established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), saying "transcending the material" (*āprākṛta*). [As it is said: "By whose splendor the sun shines, kindled by that light..."

In passages such as "for whom the sun shines," the possession of unsurpassed radiance is established. The citation here of the scriptural fragment "of solar color, beyond darkness" is intended to indicate other scriptural texts such as "from that [Being], through its greatness, was born the one beyond darkness. By this, the phrase "beyond darkness" intends to refer to the substance of darkness which is the cause of all things. Through the expression "beyond darkness," the following result is established: [the Lord is] unattainable...

The state of being "done" (*kṛtatva*) [is established]; from that very fact, its non-subjectivity (*akarmatva*), eternality (*nityatva*), faultlessness (*niravadyatva*), and so forth, are indicated. And the shadow of this verse is found in the *Māṇḍūkya-śloka*: "One should know the Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest, golden-hued, and reachable by the intellect in deep sleep. By means of the qualities of being beneficial, delightful, and so on, there are designations such as "golden-colored" (*hiraṇyavarṇa*) and "golden-hued" (*rukma-ābha*); whereas through the opposite qualities, such as being difficult to behold for those who are adverse, there is an excess of luminosity (*prakāśātireka*).

The interpretation offered by others—that the word *āditya* intends the light of eternal consciousness and the word *tamas* refers to the object of ignorance—is refuted by the intended meaning (*vivakṣayā*). He demonstrates the syntactical connection of the two verses with the words "him who is thus" (*tamevaṃbhūtam*), and so forth. Regarding the expression "endowed with devotion through the power of yoga" (*bhaktyā yukto yogabaleneti*), since this specific phrasing might lead to the perception of separate meanings—such as the power of conquering the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as mentioned by others—he states "endowed with devotion through the power of yoga" in order to demonstrate that they possess a single, unified meaning, thereby dispelling that [misconception].

This is the cause for the immobility of the mind; and its intermediate operation is intended by the word "yoga-paryāya-yukta" (endowed with the synonym yoga), as he says: "by being possessed of cultivated impressions" (*āruḍha-saṃskāratayā*). By the word "having caused [it] to enter" (*āveśya*), he intends the state of making [the mind] motionless as taught in the sections on yoga, as he says: "having established [it]" (*saṃsthāpya*). Here, the locus for the meditation on the Puruṣa is also the space between the eyebrows, because no other location is mentioned and because that is established by the instructions in other yoga-sections; having reflected on this, it was said.

Regarding the phrase "bhrū-dhvamya" (having closed the eyes): the grammatical connection is "that very divine Person who is thus situated. Because of the restrictive observation in the statement "he goes to that very one," [the commentator] says "he approaches that very one" with the intention that even in the phrase "he [goes to] that Supreme Person," the word "him" is intended to exclude others. He shows that the manner previously introduced in the passage "he who departs goes to my state" is precisely what is intended here by saying "he goes to that state. The point is that this reference is primarily concerned with the state (*bhāva*). In that context, [one should avoid] the delusion of identity and so forth.

The meaning is that he casts [them] aside and becomes equal in sovereignty to Him. The term "equal in sovereignty" is stated to exclude the state of being merely equal to others. By this, it is established that qualities such as omniscience, mentioned in the verses beginning with "the seer," are intended to be meditated upon for the purpose of bestowing sovereignty, and not for the purpose of being attained. It should be understood that the very form specified as to be remembered at the final moment was also previously described as an object of meditation. This applies likewise to what follows. (9–10)

Now, in order to reject the subsequent explanation which serves a weak purpose, he states the meaning of the three verses beginning with "That which is imperishable" (*yadakṣaram*), starting with the word *atha*. Here, the word "recollection" (*smaraṇa*) is inclusive of both meditation (*upāsana*) and the final cognition (*antima-pratyaya*), since both are specific forms of memory. By the phrase "those who know the Veda declare," which indicates that [the Self] is not within the scope of other means of knowledge as stated in the passage "He does not know that Great One who knows not the Veda," there is an indication of the subject matter described in the Vedas, characterized by qualities such as being "neither gross" (*asthūla*). [As it is said: "Neither gross, nor subtle, neither short, nor long... (*asthūlam anaṇv ahrasvam*).

Such scriptural passages as these are intended here. *Brahmacarya* refers to the state of having the vital energy drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) and so forth. This is in accordance with the Śruti: "Now, that which they call sacrifice, that is indeed *brahmacarya*; and that which they call wandering in the forest (*araṇyāyana*), that too is indeed *brahmacarya*. Thus, any practice whatsoever for the sake of attaining Brahman is *brahmacarya*. Furthermore, those very ascetics who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) and who, desiring [Brahman], practice *brahmacarya*, are the agents in this context. By this, both the fruit and the means have been demonstrated.

Since the conventional meaning of the word *pada* is not applicable here, he states the etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "that which is reached" (*padyate*). He explains that by the word *pada* here, the state of being an object of meditation and so forth is intended through the medium of being an object of knowledge, saying "it is reached by the mind. He states the well-known significance intended by the words *yat* and *tat*: "entirely," etc. Since the word *akṣara* here refers to the Supreme Self who is free from defects such as transformation, it is said to be "the nature of the self"; the meaning is "its own unique form. [The phrase] "of the nature of the imperishable" (*akṣarūpa*)...
The meditation on the Supreme Self here is for the purpose of attaining the individual self (jīvātman) whose nature is that of the Imperishable (akṣara).

Regarding the phrase "having restrained all the gates," he says "all [the senses] beginning with the ear" in order to exclude the notion that there are only nine gates and to indicate that they are the objects of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). As to how the sense organs such as touch, which are devoid of connection to specific gates, can be denoted by the word "gates," it is stated here that they are "the gateways to knowledge. With the intention that "restraint" here means the turning away from the outward inclination toward objects such as sound, he says "having withdrawn them from their own functions. And regarding the phrase "having restrained the mind within the heart," the word "indeed" (*hi*) implies... [end of fragment].

Regarding the objection that the state of being an object of meditation (*dhyeyatā*) is untenable, it was stated here: "In Me, who am established in the lotus of the heart, as the Imperishable (*akṣara*). Here, the word *aham* (I) indicates the Person (*puruṣa*) residing therein;

the point is that otherwise, the subsequent statement, "Remembering Me" (*māmanusmaran*), would not be consistent. Intending to show the sublation of the weaker order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) by the stronger order of meaning (*arthakrama*), the passage beginning with "established in the yoga of concentration" (*āsthito yogadhāraṇām*) has been explained immediately after "having restrained the mind in the heart" (*mano hṛdi nirudhya*). This follows the sequence read immediately after the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*).

To exclude other types of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), he says "the concentration called yoga" (*yogākhyāṃ dhāraṇām*). By the rule of the *niṣādasthapati* (the "chief of the Niṣādas"), it is established that among genitive compounds, a coordinate compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) is to be preferred. He states what is intended by the word "concentration": "remaining immovably in Me alone. With the intention that the syllable *praṇava* is designated as "Brahman" because it expresses Brahman, he says "denoting Me. Furthermore, here the mantra is also helpful by way of illuminating the specific meaning of this [state].

With the intention that [the Lord] is to be understood through the word—that is, as what is intended to be expressed—it is said, "recollecting me, who am to be denoted. That the *praṇava* denotes the Blessed One and its status as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*) and so forth are established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other authorities. As it is stated in the *Kaṭhavallī*: "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim, which all austerities declare, and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), that goal I tell you briefly: it is 'Om'. In this passage, the named object is indicated by means of its name. Likewise, the *praṇava*...

"The bow is the self, the arrow is the self, and Brahman is said to be the target; it must be pierced with vigilance, and like the arrow, one should become absorbed in It. Likewise: "Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, through the practice of the friction of meditation, one shall behold Brahman, hidden like fire. And again: "This..."

"By means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures, one should meditate upon the Supreme Puruṣa. Having become united with the light of the sun, just as a snake is freed from its slough, even so is he freed from evil. He is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings, he beholds the Supreme Puruṣa, who dwells in the city and is higher than the high. Likewise, just as the form of fire is not seen when it has entered its source, yet there is no destruction of its subtle mark (liṅga). He...

"Furthermore, one should restrain both of these within the body by means of the *praṇava*. Having made one's own body the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, through the practice of churning with meditation, one may behold the God as if hidden. In this very verse, the reading in the *Yogayājñavalkya* is: "One should behold Viṣṇu situated in the heart. Likewise: "Just as the resonance of a bronze bell subsides into peace, so too should the syllable *Oṃ* be employed for the sake of peace."

"By one desiring peace... that in which sound dissolves is sung as the supreme Brahman. Likewise: "Oṃ Khaṃ is Brahman; Oṃ Khaṃ is the ancient [Brahman]. "The syllable 'Oṃ' is Brahman. Its four feet are the four Vedas. This supreme Brahman, consisting of this syllable, has four feet. Its first measure is the earth, the letter *a*," beginning thus: "The first [measure] is red and yellow, having the *māpad-brahman* as its deity; the second is luminous and black."

The first [mātrā] has Viṣṇu as its deity; the third, which is auspicious and inauspicious, is white and has Rudra as its deity; that which is at the end of this, consisting of one and a half mātrās, is radiant, multicolored, and has Puruṣa as its deity. Here, Puruṣa himself, who is the presiding deity of the half-mātrā, exists in an incarnated state as Viṣṇu, the deity of the second mātrā.

Thus it has been said: "Om is Brahman; Om is all this. Likewise: "All the deities reside in the heart; in the heart the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established. You are in the heart eternally, but he who is beyond the measures (mātrās) is that [Brahman]. His northern direction is the head, and his southern side is the foot. That which is in the north is Oṃkāra; that which is Oṃkāra is Praṇava;

that which is Praṇava is the All-pervading; that which is the All-pervading is Ananta; that which is Ananta is Tāra; that which is Tāra is Sūkṣma; that which is Sūkṣma is Śukla; and that which is Śukla is Vaidyuta."
"That [is] the supreme *brāhma*. Here, by virtue of the context and other factors, the intervening instruction should be understood as in the case of the Pratardana-vidyā.

Furthermore, in the section concerning the departure of the seeker of liberation, the *praṇava* is heard: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays; he is led up with the syllable 'Om'. For the ignorant, there is cessation [of the breath]. Regarding this, there is this verse: "There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. "O Brahmins, always recite 'Om' and meditate upon Keśava. And the Blessed Yājñavalkya said:

The *praṇava* (Oṃ) is traditionally taught as the support for both the deity and the Supreme. Indeed, someone desiring to worship Viṣṇu performs that worship with devotion, just as one might create an image as a manifestive representation using metals, substances, stones, or other materials, and then instill the [divine] presence within it; through faith, devotion, respect, and so forth, the God becomes pleased with him. In the same way, by means of the syllable Oṃ, one worships the Self, and He becomes pleased. Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and having confined the mind within the heart—

Placing his vital breath in the crown of the head and established in yogic concentration, uttering the single-syllabled Brahman "Om" while remembering me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal. He who reaches this primordial syllable by means of the *praṇava*, then through that syllable and the Veda, attains the knowable Brahman. This is the best support; this is the supreme support. Knowing this support, one is fit for becoming Brahman. [He whose] form is unseen...

"The God is the grasper of all states of being and is free from disease; 'Oṃ' is known as His name. When invoked by that [name], He becomes gracious. From the *Dāyamata*: "One should extract the syllable *Oṃ* from the lotus-stalk and join it above. Since the mind, known as the *jīva*, arises from that which is breathless and void, one should place it back there again. With a concentrated mind, one should worship the *Oṃkāra* like the sound of a bell; one will surely behold the stainless, radiant Puruṣa—of this there is no doubt. And the *Yogānuśāsana-sūtra* states: "The Lord (*Īśvara*) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), their results (*vipāka*), or latent dispositions (*āśaya*)."

"The *praṇava* is its designator. Therefore, it is established that the *praṇava* is the designator of the Blessed One, and that by means of it alone one should remember the Blessed One during states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and departure from the body (*utkramaṇa*). "There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends upward to the crown of the head. Going upward by that, one attains immortality... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6).

"Of these, one goes upwards; the others go out in all directions. One among them stands above, which, having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, leads to the supreme goal"—in accordance with such scriptural and traditional texts, this placement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the crown of the head is the means for the departure of the seeker of liberation. The phrase "leaving, he departs" means "having abandoned [the body], he departs. For one who seeks the Self, the Self is the destination.

With the intention that the description of this as the "supreme goal" (paragati) is based solely on the fact that there is no returning from it, he says: "prakṛti... etc. This designation of such a Self by the term "supreme goal" is not only due to the force of the context; rather, he says "yasya sarveṣu... [1.2.13] to show that there is also an actual usage of this term with reference to that very subject within this same chapter. He restates [the previous point] for the sake of connection: "evam... etc. This sequence is not intended to be emphasized between the question and answer at the beginning of the chapter and the preceding part of the previous chapter which leads to it.

This is because [the previous section] was intended to establish [the Lord] as common to both the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*) and the final thought-moment at death (*antima-pratyaya*). Here, however, since it takes the form of instruction on specific objects for the purpose of demonstrating a progressive superiority, the sense is that those seeking the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the imperishable reality (*akṣara-yāthātmya*), and the feet of the Lord (*bhagavat-caraṇa*) are taught in succession. Furthermore, by the use of the term "thus" (*evam*) here, the reasons establishing that this section concerns three distinct classes of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*) have been demonstrated. To explain:

In this regard, some might raise an objection: "Well then, in this context, since it says 'they know that Brahman, the supreme imperishable Brahman,' what contradiction is there in taking the word *brahman* as referring directly to the Veda? Furthermore, because that [Brahman] alone is the self of all, it is appropriate to understand by the term *adhyātma* everything pertaining to it;
and the phrase 'the emission that causes the arising of beings' is rightly taken to mean the creation of the universe, or else the offering of substances intended for the deities."

And here, that sacrifice is characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the perishable state is the *adhibhūta*," based on the etymology "that which exists over beings" (*adhibhavati*), it refers to the multitude of living creatures. "The Person (*puruṣa*) is the *adhidaivata*" refers to a specific state of the Supreme Brahman, or the cosmic aggregate person (*samaṣṭi-puruṣa*) and so forth. "The *adhiyajña* is the deity named Viṣṇu, who presides over the conceit of omniscience," according to the Vedic scripture, "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. The three verses beginning with "And at the time of death" also refer specifically to the final conviction of one who seeks liberation.

This was stated by way of censure. Although the verses consisting of questions and answers in the previous chapter are intended to convey what is to be known and adopted regarding the three types of qualified aspirants introduced therein, the subsequent verses are said to refer to the *jñānin* (the man of realization) because the state of being the primary [qualified aspirant] is extremely difficult to attain. Otherwise, there would be no contradiction with such statements as, "Remembering Me alone, you shall come to Me alone.

For this very reason, although the two verses beginning with "And at the time of departure, how... and "And at the time of death, Me... refer to all three types of qualified aspirants, in their explanation...

The claim that there is a single unified meaning (*ekārthya*) here is also refuted; for even in that case, the focus on three distinct types of qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*) is not perceived. Nor do we see any authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the view that one who seeks sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) must depend upon a final cognition (*antima-pratyaya*) directed toward the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). Thus, in the subsequent verses as well, the same qualified aspirant and the same object of knowledge are repeatedly restated and further clarified in detail. This does not entail the fault of redundancy (*punarukti*), because repetition is a sign (*liṅga*) of the preeminence of the man of knowledge (*jñānin*); as it is said: "He attains the supreme perfection... (*saṃsiddhiṃ vindati paramām*).

The identity of meaning among these expressions—“He has gone,” “He goes to the supreme goal,” and “They call Him the supreme goal”—is well-established and must not be abandoned. Nor is there a supreme perfection distinct from that which is to be reached as the supreme goal. Furthermore, the indirect reference in the phrase “They call Him the supreme goal” would, according to [your view], have to be “the Supreme Person, O Pārtha. [This is supported by such passages as] “the divine Supreme Person,” “He attains that divine Supreme Person,” and “of the Person...”

Furthermore, it is incorrect to assume that these [passages] have different meanings, such as "He is attainable by unswerving devotion, O Pārtha" (Gītā 18.55); for almost all other [commentators] have likewise explained them with one voice.

Here, the method of resolution is as follows: since it is not stated here "I alone am Brahman" in the same manner as "I alone am the sacrifice" (Gītā 8.4), the meaning of the word *brāhṛ* here is like that of *adhyātma* and so forth.

To begin with, the fact that they have different meanings is already perceived. Furthermore, there is no superior conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *akṣara* for the Supreme Self over the word *brahman*, by virtue of which the latter could be explained as the former. This is evident from such passages as: "Those devotees who, ever steadfastly disciplined, worship you..."; "There are two forms of that Brahman: the embodied and the unembodied; these two are the nature of the Perishable and the Imperishable, abiding in all beings. That supreme Brahman is the Imperishable; this entire world is the Perishable. And so forth, where the Imperishable is the supreme.

In the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, the two words *brahma* and *akṣara* have been established as referring to the perfectly pure Self (*pariśuddhātman*). Therefore, when it is asked here, "What is that *brahma*?", the explanation given is "I alone am *brahma*. Consequently, the word *brahma* here refers to the perfectly pure Self, distinct from both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), in accordance with the word *akṣara* as qualified by the word "supreme" (*parama*).

It functions through figurative usage (*pacāra*). Furthermore, this very same [term] will later be described as "the unmanifest is called the Imperishable" (*avyakto 'kṣara ity uktaḥ*). Nor should it be suspected that this verse refers to the Supreme Self; for, just as in passages such as "those who [worship] the unmanifest Imperishable" (*ye cāpy akṣaram avyaktam*) and "but those who [worship] the imperishable, the indefinable" (*ye tv akṣaram anirdeśyam*), here too the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) is understood to refer to an object distinct from the Blessed Lord. Moreover, the word "perfect attainment" (*saṃsiddhi*) is synonymous with the term "supreme goal" (*paramagati*).

It manifests, by its own inherent power (*svarasataḥ*) and through the force of its prefixes, a correct accomplishment characterized by the moment of reaching the cave. For this very reason, words such as *svabhāva* and so forth have been stated to refer to specific objects among those to be known and those to be adopted by the three types of qualified persons (*adhikārin*). Thus, when it is established—through an examination of one's own statements and by referring back to the subject matter of the preceding chapter—that the sentences containing questions and answers concern the three types of qualified persons, it is logical that the subsequent portions of the text also concern all [three] subjects as far as possible. This being the case... [the context continues].

Furthermore, since it is explicitly stated immediately after the three verses that describe the three types of practitioners that those who desire the attainment of the state of Bhagavat attain *kaivalya*, the passage beginning with "practice" (*abhyāsa*) refers, by process of elimination, to those who seek *aiśvarya* (mastery). As for the claim that there is no evidence for those seeking *aiśvarya* requiring a final cognition whose object is the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), that too is not correct; for such [a requirement] is observed in the *Dhruvacarita* of the venerable *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, in passages such as: "Fixing his devotion on the Blessed Lord Hari... and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. Although throughout this section, by means of terms such as "the Brahman-purusa," "the supreme goal," and so forth, only the worship of the Supreme Self and the attainment of Him are understood, nevertheless, it is not appropriate to say that this alone constitutes the subject matter for the qualified aspirant. This is because, in the preceding portion, the entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) into the space between the eyebrows at the time of departure, as well as the meditation on the Supreme Self in that very place, have been enjoined; and immediately thereafter, meditation within the heart and the entry of the vital breath into the crown of the head are likewise enjoined for that same moment.

These two [statements] being mutually contradictory, are they to be established as distinct by way of difference in time, or by way of difference in the qualified aspirant (*adhikārin*)? In this regard, a difference in time is certainly not heard in scripture; on the contrary, identity of time is precisely what is heard. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the difference in the qualified aspirants is established. Furthermore, from such passages as "One hundred and one," it is understood that departure through the cranial vein (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*) is the cause of liberation, whereas departure through other [veins] is the cause of other results. Thus, at the time of death, [between] the middle of the eyebrows and the head...

And since the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is understood as the remainder of the process of departure (*utkramaṇa*), and because the sequence of entering the various channels located in those respective places is perceived, there arises a distinction among those qualified for spiritual attainment (*adhikāribheda*). Furthermore, in the previous chapter, the distinction among those qualified was demonstrated in the commentary through the repetition of the word *yat* in the two verses beginning with "They worship Me in four ways" (*caturvidhā bhajante mām*); and that same principle applies here as well.

[The Lord is] manifest; "he who should meditate upon Him who is subtler than the subtle," "he who departs casting off the body," and "he who remembers Me constantly"—having all this in mind, it was said:
"thus for one who desires sovereignty," and so forth.
Refuting the statement of others that the qualified person is described as "one whose mind is not directed elsewhere," he explains the meaning of the verse beginning with "ananyacetāḥ."

Regarding the word "atha" (then): by the term "nityaśaḥ" (constantly), he intends to express independence from any intervention by other fruits such as self-realization; thus he says, "beginning with exertion. With the intention that otherwise there would be a tautology with the word "satatam" (always) or the difficulty of [the meaning being] restricted, he says, "satatam sarvakālam" (constantly, at all times). By the phrase "ananya-cetas" (with a mind not directed elsewhere), he shows that the remembrance has attained the form of devotion; thus he says, "atyartham" (excessively). Precisely because of this state of having a mind not directed elsewhere, the remembrance is characterized by its uninterruptedness. Ut.

And even when [the word] is used in the vocative, it is employed—as in "O heroes, may you two brothers remember [Me]" (*bhrātarau smarataṃ vīrau*) and so forth. The phrase "of the yogin who is eternally united" is stated to indicate that for such a person, the fruit is immediate, as a restatement of what has been said. Here, by the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), the inner self (*pratyagartha*) of the Lord is intended. With that intention, he says "I alone," in order to exclude the attainment of fruits such as the Imperishable (*akṣara*) which serve as His attributes. He explains this very point by saying "not My state" (*na madbhāvaḥ*).

Because the attainment of the Blessed One is a fruit superior to other fruits, he says "easy to attain" (*suprāpa*) with the intention of excluding any suspicion that excessive effort might be required for its attainment; the meaning is "attained without hardship. This is taught by the rule: *īṣad-duḥ-su-ṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal*. He states "separation from Him" (*tadviyoga*) because the accessibility of the Lord, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in Him, is established through natural inclination (*rāgaprāpta*). This is said to dispel the doubt that what has been stated might be mere hyperbole.

He states that [the teaching] is rooted in Śruti with the words, "Him alone... Here, what is meant by the word *varaṇa* (choosing)? It cannot mean acceptance in the form of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) or being the body (*śarīratva*), because that is eternally established. Nor can it be the opposite of that, for that would be a contradiction in terms. Nor does it mean the granting of attainment, because that would result in redundancy with the phrase "to be obtained by him. Nor is there any other possibility here, as none is conceivable. To this, he says: "for the sake of attaining Him... (*tatprāptaye*).

"Non-meritorious" (*nirguṇa*) refers here to the ripening (*vipāka*) which consists of the constant mindfulness [of the Lord], the perception of His form, the assumption of a similar appearance, and so forth. Its opposites are evil deeds, *rajas*, *tamas*, passion, hatred, delusion, and the like.

"Exceeding dearness to Me" means the state of unsurpassed devotion. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), that which is required for the intermediate stage, up until reaching the proximity of the couch of the Supreme Abode, is included.

All that is intended [by the Lord] is expressed by the words "I alone. The meaning is: "This burden belongs to me alone, who am supremely compassionate. To confirm that the previously stated meaning of passages such as "I am easily attained by him," etc., is firm, he shows that this very same meaning will be explained in detail through the form of scriptural corroboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), stating: "And it will be said... (verse 14).

Prior to this, certain distinctions regarding what is to be known and what is to be adopted for the three types of qualified aspirants have been set forth. Hereafter, he says "ataḥ param" (beyond this), showing the specific distinction between the permanence and impermanence of the fruit—which must necessarily be known as being instrumental to the qualification. In this regard, first, the non-return of the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) is stated.

By the verse beginning with "Having come to Me" (mām upetya), [the author] states that because the infinity of suffering is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible for the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) to be restricted when it is without qualification; therefore, the term "entire" (*nikhila*) is used. Furthermore, regarding birth, its instability as indicated by the word "non-eternal" (*aśāśvata*) is intended here in the form of the instability of the body, enjoyments, and so forth, which are invariably concomitant with birth.

Alternatively, the word "birth" (*janman*) here refers to the body, which possesses birth. As for the phrase "of the great-souled one" (*mahātmanaḥ*), even from mere praise, it is appropriate that greatness (*māhātmya*) constitutes the cause for the perfection [of the teaching] here.

With this intention, he says "yataḥ" (from which). He shows that the "great-mindedness" (*mahāmanastva*) of the wise, which was previously elaborated upon, is being restated here by the words beginning with "yathāvasthita.

Because it is appropriate to designate the attainment of the desired fruit as "perfection," and because of the natural force of the word *parama*, it is said "me, who am the form of supreme perfection" (*paramasaṃsiddhirūpam*).
The meaning is: "who am the form of the supreme human goal" (*paramapuruṣārtharūpam*). "Perfection" (*saṃsiddhi*) means correct or complete accomplishment. || 15 ||

Since a negation cannot apply to that which is not already present, and since it is appropriate to employ as the object of negation that which is proximate to the subject of the negation, the mere fact of rebirth was indicated by way of its negation for those who seek sovereignty as a perishable fruit; therefore, with the intention that only the reason [for this] must be stated even in that case, he says, "attained to sovereignty. By making the Blessed Lord the counter-correlative in the phrase "but having attained Me," and because the prefix *ā-* here intends to include the limit, he says, "in the world of Brahmā. [The context is] the primordial...

With the intention of showing that when even the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) have become like bubbles in the great ocean of the Lord’s Māyā, what need is there to speak of the worlds contained within them, he said "residing within the cosmic eggs" (*brahmāṇḍodaravartin*). By this, the exclusion [of these worlds] from the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*) is established. Furthermore, because the purpose is to demonstrate the impermanence of sovereignty, he said "the abodes of enjoyment and sovereignty" (*bhogaiśvaryālayāḥ*). As for the word *loka*, which is used in conjunction with the word *bhuvana*, it refers to people (*jana*).

Because it is impossible for that world to be an object [of experience] and because there is no returning due to the absence of any further journeying, he says "perishable" (vināśinaḥ) to indicate that by the term "returner" (punarāvarti), only destruction in the sense of a continuous flow is meant; or else, since the term "returner" functions through non-abandoning indication (ajahallakṣaṇā), it refers specifically to the return of the persons who have gone to that world.

The door [to liberation] has been shown. He states the result [of this teaching] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). With the words "Me, the omniscient," etc., he demonstrates the specific reasons for non-return that were indicated by the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "Me. For those who have reached some petty deity—who is not omniscient, whose will is not true, who is composed of a multitude of effects, who is merciless, and who possesses various transformations such as passion and hatred rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*—there would indeed be a return, either by means of another or by that very same [deity]. This is the intended meaning of the qualifying attributes. || 16 ||

He states the summarized meaning of the three verses beginning with *saharotsādi* as "of those [worlds] ending with the world of Brahmā (*brāhmaloka*). He says "created by the volition of the Supreme Person" in order to dispel any suspicion that the stability of the worlds, such as Satyaloka—which are established through the sovereignty of Hiraṇyagarbha and others—is independent. Indeed, it is the sovereignty of the Lord alone that is the cause for the various arrangements, such as the waxing and waning of days and nights. Thus it is said: "Of both Time and Death..."
O Mānava, those people who know that a thousand yugas constitute a single day of Brahmā, and that his night is of equal duration, are the ones who truly understand day and night.

Thus, because the reading there is "ya ityeva" (only "ya"), the syntactical connection follows the respective order. But here, in the verse beginning with "saharohi," the connection of the word "yat" with the word "ahan" (day) is not possible. Consequently, for the word "te," the word "ye" is required; and there too, the syntactical connection is: "those who know thus—those people who know day and night—they alone are the knowers. With the intention that one must accept this as being devoted to establishing the authoritative nature of the determination of time, he says: "those humans and so forth."

The state of being known for day and night, as it is being restated (*anūdyamāna*), must pertain to all subjects according to what is well-known. With the intention that this would indicate that even the Four-faced One (*caturmukha*) is equal to humans and others, the phrase "humans and so forth" was stated. The word "Brahman" (*brāhma*) is used here to dispel the delusion that it refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); the sense is that the division of day and night fixed to the *sahasra-yuga* period is well-known only of him. When a prescription or prohibition is accompanied by a qualification, they extend to the qualification itself.

According to this principle, and because the portion concerning the knowledge of days and nights in the phrase "those people who know the day and night" is merely restated, the intention here is that the knowledge of the period ending with a *sahasra-yuga* is what is actually enjoined; thus it is said, "they know that which ends with a *sahasra-yuga*. That which extends up to the *sahasra-yugas* is "ending with a *sahasra-yuga*" (*sahasra-yuga-paryantam*). Furthermore, based on other authorities, the word *yuga* here refers to the cycle of four ages (*catur-yuga*).

"Let it be so regarding the arrangement of day and night for the Four-faced One (Brahmā); what does that have to do with the subject at hand? To this, the verse beginning with "from the unmanifest" (avyaktāt) is the answer. He states its meaning with the word "therein" (tatra). The intention is as follows:

first of all, the word "manifest" (vyakti) here does not refer to the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, because they arise even before the Four-faced One. Therefore, it refers exclusively to that which is created by the Four-faced One.

It is thus: "manifestations" (*vyaktayaḥ*) are so called because they are manifested. Even there, since there is no dissolution (*pralaya*) of Satyaloka and the other higher realms at every kalpa, one must admit that the scope [of the term] is restricted solely to the objects consisting of bodies, senses, and so forth, existing within the three worlds (*trailokya*). Furthermore, the production of these occurs from the very body of Brahmā. Consequently, even the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) here does not refer to the primordial unmanifest (*mūlāvyakta*); rather, it refers to the body of Brahmā which has that [primordial unmanifest] as its material cause (*upādāna*). And the word "unmanifest" is applied to the body...
The formal argument (*prayoga*) has also been established in the Sūtra: "But it is subtle because of its subtlety.

Thus, [the author] describes this specific cause of creation and dissolution, as well as the non-interruption of the continuum of creation and dissolution due to the non-cessation of that [cause], and the avoidance of the fallacies of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). All [of this] pertains to the meaning already stated.

With the intention of explaining that the verse beginning with "the collection of beings (*bhūtagrāmaḥ*) is pervaded throughout the kalpas, just as in previous kalpas" establishes this very point, he says: "It is that same one. The word *bhūta* here refers to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) as distinguished by consciousness. With the intention that the lack of autonomy—which is the cause of being created and destroyed—is indeed dependent upon karma, he says "subject to karma" (*karmavaśya*). With the intention that the phrase "at the arrival of day" (*aharāgame*) should also be supplied after the word "having become" (*bhūtvā*), he states: "having become [so] at the arrival of day. And this...

The demonstration of the *naimittika* (occasional) dissolution is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark) for the *prākṛta* (primary/natural) dissolution established by the Śrutis and other authorities; by this, the destruction of Satyaloka is established. With the intention that the passage beginning with "the worlds from Bhuvarloka up to Brahmaloka" has been introduced, he says "likewise. Alternatively, the very term "arrival of night" (*rātryāgama*) inherently includes the arrival of the final night of Brahmā. For when the principles (*tattvas*) such as Earth and the rest are dissolved, what need be said of the worlds of Brahmā, the body of Brahmā, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and so forth, which are composed of them?

With this intention, the scriptural passage beginning with "earth" has been cited. For indeed, the merging of the substance of consciousness (cid-dravya) in its state of darkness is heard of in the Supreme Deity alone;

here too, with the intention that such things as "I am the origin and the dissolution of the entire world" are spoken, it was said "in Me alone. Likewise, according to the sequence beginning with "He who ordains Brahman in the beginning," [it returns] again to Brahman.

One should also contemplate the emission [of the universe] and its subsequent dissolution, and so forth. He shows the relevance of such an exposition of creation and dissolution to the present subject with the word "evam" (thus). This alone is to be understood as the intended purport in all sections concerning creation and dissolution. By the phrase "of everything other than Me," he recalls what was previously stated in the verse, "I am the origin and dissolution of the whole. And it is also said in the Mokṣadharma: "Indeed, there is no being, whether stationary or moving, that is eternal in this world."

"Except for that one eternal Person, Vāsudeva. He states the meaning of these two verses with the word "atha" (now). The intention is as follows: It has already been stated that there is no returning for those who have attained the Blessed One. Furthermore, the "Imperishable" (akṣara), which was designated as being beyond the Unmanifest, must necessarily be the individual soul (jīva) itself, because of the recognition [of it] in passages such as, "This other power... different from this... Moreover, the non-returning of those seeking isolation (kaivalya) must be explained by the absence of descent [from higher realms]. Therefore, these two verses refer precisely to that [attainment of the Lord].

Since the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) alone was the subject previously discussed, here too the word-division (*padaccheda*) is simply "from the *avyakta*" (*avyaktāt*). Furthermore, that [unmanifest] connects with both the words *para* ("higher") and *anya* ("other"). In this context, to avoid redundancy, the word *para* refers to its being the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) by way of expressing its superiority. And precisely because the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) is thereby established, the word *anya* refers to a difference in modality (*prakāra-anyatva*). That difference in modality—

With the intention that the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists precisely in the nature of sentience (*cetana*), he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Here, the word *bhāva* denotes any category of entity (*padārtha*) in general. The word-break (*padaccheda*) as "the manifest" (*vyaktaḥ*) is not appropriate; for it has been stated right here [in the text] that "[it is] unmanifest and imperishable" (*avyakto'śakṣaraḥ*), and because the application of the word "manifest" would be untenable if the individual soul (*jīva*) were difficult to grasp. With this intention, he says "by something. Now, one might object: the unmanifest nature of the soul is improper, since its manifestation occurs through perception, inference, and scripture as the case may be; otherwise, [it would be impossible].

Regarding the consequence that [the self] would be like space (*khapuṣpa*), he says: "it is self-cognizable" (*svasaṃvedya*). The meaning is that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establish it only in a general sense. As for its eternity, there is a reminder of the reasons stated in the second chapter: "because it is incapable of arising or perishing. Here, the word *bhūta* refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*); even upon their destruction, the self remains.

Because permanence is obtained without effort through that very statement, he says "the ether and so forth" with the intention that, by the force of the implication of the word "all," both the state of having a cause and the state of having an effect are established therein. For destruction, which has presented itself as a possibility regarding the individual soul (*jīva*), must be negated; and the presentation here occurs by virtue of the soul's entry into perishable objects—just as when sesame seeds are being burned, the oil contained within them is also burned. Consequently, it is stated in various places that [the soul] is like one who remains amidst all perishing beings, its capacity for liberation being obtained through its own power.

Regarding the phrase "even though situated" (*sthito'pi*): since the word "he" (*sa*) in the verse beginning with "of whom [all]" (*yasya sarveṣu*) lacks sufficient purpose there and is required in the subsequent passage, the connection "he is the unmanifest, the imperishable" (*so'vyakto'kṣaraḥ*) has been stated; or else, this is a textual ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). When the question arises as to where the word "stated" (*ukta*) was said, he says: "But those who... (*ye tu*). The fact that the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) in these two contexts is clear from that very place, because of the designation of difference in such passages as "But the Supreme Person is another" (*uttamaḥ puruṣastvanyaḥ*). Therefore, in this chapter as well—

"The syllable *akṣara* is the supreme Brahman. Regarding the two uses of the word *akṣara* in the phrases "the unmanifest *akṣara*" (*avyakto'kṣaraḥ*) and "those who [worship] the *akṣara*," the completely pure individual soul (*jīva*) alone is designated by both terms. Furthermore, in the passage "it is called the unmanifest *akṣara*," both terms are employed because they refer to the intent of the Śrutis that support their respective contexts, or because they are adopted based on the ascension of one's own resolve, as in the case of the statement "they were already slain [beforehand]. When the expectation for an agent arises regarding the phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*), [it refers to] "that which is *akṣara*..."

Having drawn upon the specific agent as was appropriate and relevant in the context of the statement, "The knowers of the Veda say [that he goes]," he says, "the knower of the Veda. By the words "this very one who departs," etc., he shows that the general designation "he goes to the supreme goal" is specified by this [particular individual]. Alternatively, the intention here is that the reference "they call him the supreme goal" serves to re-identify the person previously mentioned in the phrase "he goes to the supreme goal."

In this context, he demonstrates the suitability for the application of the words *akṣara* (the Imperishable) and *paramagati* (the Supreme Goal) with the word *prakṛti*. With the intention that this meaning has been stated as the cause for non-cessation [of transmigratory existence], it is said to be "existing in such a nature" (*svarūpeṇāvasthitam*). Since the mere establishment of the relationship [between the Lord and His abode] was already established by the statement "That is My supreme abode" (*taddhāma paramaṃ mama*), and because there is a rule that an abode (*sthāna*) necessarily depends upon that which resides in it (*sthānin*), the term "abode" (*adhiṣṭheya*)—which is a synonym for *sthāna*—is used in the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*).

He states that what is intended by the word *dhāma* (abode) is "the place of restraint" (*niyamanasthāna*). To the question, "What other [place] is there for restraint, for the exclusion of which the word 'supreme' (*parama*) is used? he replies: "insentient," etc. Here, because of the designation as the "supreme abode," its subject matter is established to be the perfectly pure Self (*pariśuddhātman*). Consequently, he states that even the impure individual soul (*jīva*), being subordinate, is intended as "inferior" (*apara*)—that is, "associated with that" (*tatsaṃsṛṣṭa*). If even the liberated one were dependent upon the Supreme Self, then by whom would he be liberated? By the Independent One.

He says "And that" (*tacceti*) regarding the concern that one might again be cast into the pit of *saṃsāra* by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The intended meaning (*bhāva*) is this: ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like are indeed the cause of *saṃsāra*, but not dependence (*pāratantrya*); and since ignorance and so forth have been destroyed, and since the compassion of the Lord and other such qualities are innate, there is not even a trace of *saṃsāra* for the liberated one. Or rather, it is not only the attainment of the Blessed One that constitutes non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*), but also the attainment of the completely purified individual soul (*jīva*), due to the absence of descent (*avarohaṇa*).

The sense is "yes, so be it. Regarding the phrase "the place of restraint" (*niyamanasthāna*), because of the inclusion of the specific qualification "resorted to," there is a lack of logical consistency; out of dissatisfaction with this, he says "or rather" (*athaiva*). Let the word *dhāma* be a synonym for light (*tejas*); in the context of illumination, the meaning of the sentence is: "That supreme *dhāma* is mine, existing as my subordinate (*maccheṣabhūta*). Although its status as his own subordinate was already stated previously by the passage beginning with "This other [nature]," nevertheless, in that passage it was understood as referring only to the collective consciousness (*samaṣṭicetana*); here, however, its status as his own subordinate is stated even for the liberated one (*mukta*), so there is no tautology. || 20 || 21 ||

In the verse beginning with *puruṣasya*, because the word *tu* indicates a different meaning, and by the force of the phrase *ananyayā bhaktyā*, the word *puruṣa* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) on account of such reasons as "lying in the city" (*puri-śaya*), "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*), "primordial existence" (*pūrva-sadbhāva*), and "giving much" (*purudāna*). Furthermore, because of the frequent usage [of the term] in such passages as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," and because He is qualified by the word "Supreme" (*para*), this verse is intended to teach a result superior to the previously mentioned results; with this intention, he says: "of the knower. [This is] divided.

The words "by the discerning" (*vivecakaiḥ*) are to be supplied as the subject; or the meaning is "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇam*). Since space and the like lack supremacy even though they exist at the beginning and end of space, [the author] shows that the mention of "of whom" (*yasya*) and so forth—made here as if it were a well-known fact—is intended to refer to the supremacy previously mentioned, by saying "from me" (*mattaḥ*). The sense is that there must be identity of meaning between the restatement (*anuvāda*) and the prior statement (*purovāda*). And with the words "by which," he recalls the Śruti passage beginning with "That than which there is nothing higher" and ending with "By that Puruṣa all this is pervaded."
It was stated [previously] that "by another person. To the question, "In what sense is devotion non-sequential? he says: "with mind focused on no other" (ananyacetāḥ). || 22 ||

He states the purport of the section beginning with "But at that time" (*yatra kāle tu*) and ending with "be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna" (*yogayukto bhava arjuna*) by saying "Now" (*atha*). Here, the description of the path of smoke and so forth is for the purpose of its rejection (*heyatva*); however, the instruction on the path of light (*arcirādi*) is solely for the purpose of reflecting upon it—this is the intended meaning. [Objection: But [the goal] is fixed upon the Supreme Person...

If it is asked how it can be said here that [the path] is common to both when the journey via the rays (*arciḥ*) and so forth belongs to this [latter] alone, he says: "Of both. Since it was previously stated that even for one who is established in the Self there is no returning, he says "And that" in order to show that his path as well is indeed via the rays and so forth. [He cites] scripture itself regarding both the commonality and the non-returning.

He shows this with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). The point is that while it is logical to indicate the fruit of the principal (*aṅgin*) even in relation to its constituent parts (*aṅga*), it is not logical to indicate that same fruit for a part that has been mentioned separately as being on the same footing as the principal. By this, the difference between the realization of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) taught in the first six sections and the contemplation of the true nature of the syllables (*akṣara-yāthātmya-anusandhāna*) found here is also demonstrated. To the question of how the passage "those who know thus" (*tadya itthaṃ viduḥ*) can have the inner self as its subject, he replies: "And in the Pañcāgni-vidyā... (*pañcāgnividyāyāṃ ca*).

Since it is stated that "the waters become human in speech," the intermingling with other elements is established. The phrase "consisting of water alone" is said in order to exclude the transformation into the essential nature of the Self. Furthermore, he says "caused by merit and demerit" to demonstrate that even such a connection with a body is merely adventitious (aupādhika).
Because of scriptural statements such as, "Those of pleasant conduct [attain] a pleasant womb... those of foul conduct [attain] a foul womb," this section does not concern inanimate matter alone.

In order to indicate that the destination of both groups mentioned in the two preceding passages—namely, "those who know thus" and "those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity"—is identical, the text employs the single verse beginning with "they [go] to the light," thereby referring back to the distant phrase "those who know thus" and "they [go] to the light. By the word *idam* ("this"), the specific form under discussion is pointed out as being distinct (*vivikte*). Now, [one might object]: "That person who is non-human leads them to the world of Brahman."

The attainment of Brahman by one who has traveled via the path of light (*arcis*) and so forth is heard in scripture; how then can one who meditates on the Self alone attain the path of light that leads to Brahman? To this he says: "By the true nature of the Self. The point is that this person established in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) is not a meditator on the Self alone, but rather one who contemplates his own self as consisting of Brahman. With the intention that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the principle of "as is the meditation, so is the result" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), he says: "And because of the *tatkratu-nyāya*. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a conjunction of these two reasons.

Regarding the fact that the contemplation of the Self as it truly is consists in the contemplation of its nature as being ultimately non-different from the Supreme, he states the proof with the words, "He who [in the Self]... By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), hundreds of scriptural passages such as "the Lord of the universe" are included.

Here, a conflict with the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* and other works might be suspected; however, in this context, in the *Śruti*, *Sūtra*, *Bhāṣya*, and elsewhere, it is stated without distinction that one who contemplates his own self as consisting of the Supreme Self undergoes the journey via the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) and so forth. And regarding that state of being led by Brahman, it is found in the *Śruti* and other texts, as well as here in the passage beginning, "Having departed there..."

Since it is established by the scriptural statement, "The people who know Brahman go to Brahman," it must be accepted that even those who know the five fires attain the Supreme Self as their own Self.

In that attainment, for the knowers [of Brahman], the Supreme Self is the object of enjoyment as qualified by His own attributes; however, for those steadfast in the true nature of the Immutable (akṣara), their own essential nature itself is the object of enjoyment first. Then, through the logic of the honey-cart, the river, and so forth—which is the means for attaining Brahman preceded by the attainment of the status of Vāsava and others—there is ultimately the attainment of Brahman. And such a fixed sequence of stages depends upon prior [preparations].

Because there is no difference between them, and that [distinction] arises from specific past karma—as previously shown in the verse, "In four ways they worship Me"—it is not being said here that the knower of the true nature of the Self is someone other than the seeker; for the very nature and the creative emission (visarga) described as being knowable by the seeker are what are presented here, as illustrated by the example of the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgni-vidyā).

Furthermore, it is only for those seeking *kaivalya* (isolation) that there is exit through the *mūrdhanya-nāḍī* (the central channel at the crown of the head), and non-return has been declared for them. Moreover, the two terms "the true nature of the Self" (*ātma-yāthātmya*) and "the true nature of the Imperishable" (*akṣara-yāthātmya*) do not have different meanings here. There is, however, a slight distinction in their meditation: those who know the true nature of the Imperishable meditate on the Self as having the Supreme Self as its body, whereas the possessors of knowledge (*jñānins*) meditate on the Supreme Self as having their own self as its body. This is precisely the distinction [intended by the text]: "Those who know it thus, and those who... [and so forth].

In the *Bhāṣya* and other works, it is stated that the term "in the forest" (*raṇye*) is intended as a specification of the division [of practitioners]. However, in the *Sāra*, it is said: "For both [types] indeed meditate on Brahman in its entirety through different approaches: some [meditate on] Brahman as having their own self as its body (*svātma-śarīraka*), while others [meditate on] their own self as consisting of Brahman (*brāhmātmaka-svātman*). Therefore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that "the seeker who was introduced in the seventh [chapter], because he is distinct from the knower desiring the attainment of the Supreme Self, is one who contemplates his own self as not consisting of Brahman."

And its placement is at the very tip of the heart, because it is distinct from those knowers who are indifferent to the delay in experiencing their own Self. As for the prohibition regarding the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*), that refers to the meditation on one's own Self devoid of the contemplation of its identity with Brahman.

This too has been clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other works: therefore, He does not lead those who meditate upon the conscious entity—whether mixed with the unconscious or pure—as being Brahman, nor those who do so apart from that [contemplation]; rather, He leads those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman and upon the Self.

By such statements as, "The group of *ativāhika* beings leads those who meditate upon the Brahman-soul as dissociated from *prakṛti*," it is established that they do not return. Furthermore, regarding what is said—that "those devotees who are still under the influence of the *śeṣa* [residual karma] and are desirous of fruits are considered to be subject to falling, and all are of a nature to fall"—even there, the state of being subject to falling is mentioned only because the bliss experienced through the realization of the Self alone is unstable. It does not, however, entail a return to *saṃsāra*; for it is said, "He who has fallen from the world of Indra is indeed fallen."

This is because there is no contradiction in the application of the term "subject to falling" (*cyavanadharmatva*), as seen in passages such as "having come from this world to the world of the gods," where even when one attains a higher state superior to the previous one, the mere loss of the former state justifies the usage; and because the censure is appropriate even if one has fallen from the experience of unsurpassed bliss at that time due to a delay in experiencing limited pleasures. Alternatively, it refers to the characteristic of having experienced a fall—due to a temporary interruption in the experience of the Supreme Self during the state of fruition, despite having experienced it previously during the stage of meditation.

[The verse] "Because you are subject to the law of decay" [is addressed to him]. Furthermore, by the statement "But one who has awakened partakes in liberation," the immediate attainment of liberation is declared for the awakened one;

however, that does not imply that another [who is not awakened] possesses liberation. This is because there is no contradiction, just as in the case of [the verse]: "And having enjoyed vast pleasures, at the end, through my grace, remembering me, you shall attain my world. And just as for a certain seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), in the interim, [there may be] a lapse into the state of Brahmā...

"Service," "he who stands on the path transcends, peaceful and free from disease," and so forth—by such statements, the departure through the path of the gods (*devayāna*) to the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*) for one liberated from attachment to the service of the *brāhmya-kāya* is described. Similarly, here too, there would be an ascent to the supreme void (*paramavyoman*) for one who has fallen from the state of experiencing one's own self. And his journey via the stages beginning with light (*arcirādi*) occurs either after the experience of intermediate fruits, or in the midst of that journey, in the case of one who dies during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).

Since this experience of the intermediate fruit consists merely of a state of rest due to its union with the Moon (*candramas*), there is no contradiction in either case. By this, the view that this [state] can only subsequently become a support for another meditation is also refuted; for, as in the *Madhu-vidyā*, such a status is possible even at the outset. And the scriptures record that the immortal station of yogis who find satisfaction in their own self—the place of the experience of one's own Self—is inferior to the state of liberation: "The yogis who are single-mindedly devoted, who always meditate on Brahman, [attain] the immortal station which brings contentment to their own selves."

"For that is the supreme abode which the wise indeed behold. And for those who abide in the immortal state, there is the designation of "liberated" because of their freedom from old age, death, and so forth, as well as the disappearance of merit and demerit which are the causes of rebirth.

Furthermore, even for those who have cast off the gross body, there exists a fruit intermediate to final liberation (apavarga), which depends upon specific types of contemplation on That (the Self). And that [fruit] is indicated by such terms as "dissolution into primordial nature" (prakṛtilaya) and so on.

The Sāṅkhyas recite: "By means of dharma there is upward movement; by means of adharma there is downward movement. Through knowledge comes liberation, while from its opposite, bondage is held to occur. From dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti); from passionate attachment comes worldly transmigration (saṃsāra). From sovereign power comes non-obstruction."

"Error and its opposite": "Bondage is held to arise from error," and that is threefold: natural (*prākṛtika*), modified (*vaikṛtika*), and ritual (*dākṣiṇika*). Thus, for those who worship *prakṛti* because they lack knowledge of the Self regarding *prakṛti*, there is natural bondage. Regarding this, it is said in the *Purāṇa* concerning those merged in *prakṛti*: "Those who have abandoned all thought remain for a full hundred thousand years. For those who worship only the modifications—the elements, the senses, the ego, and the intellect—there is modified bondage.

Based on human intellect, it is said of them: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten *manvantaras*; those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred years; those who contemplate the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) remain for a thousand years; and those who contemplate the intellect (*buddhi*) remain for ten thousand years, free from feverish distress. Indeed, these are the 'bodiless' (*videha*) ones, whose bondage is that of transformation. Thus, just as it is for those who contemplate the principles beginning with the unmanifest (*avyakta*), so it is also for those who contemplate the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*).

Therefore, excellence [of the fruit] is established as depending upon the specific place and time; for this very reason, in the *Bhūmavidyā*, even one who meditates on the mere inner self (*pratyagātman*) is declared to be an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādin*). However, the distinction is that through the contemplation of the Self within the *Brāhmaṇa* (the Supreme Brahman), there is no return once one rests in the attainment of Brahman. For this same reason, the objection—that if the experience of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) were not the ultimate reality, how could one seeking it be considered a distinct candidate for liberation (*apavarga*), like one seeking sovereign power (*aiśvarya*)—is also refuted, because of the distinction between the external and internal objects of enjoyment.

Furthermore, the distinction between these two states is established by the difference between their fitness for return and non-return. For those who cannot endure delay, this is the final consummation: "Having renounced all duties and all immediate desires, O Lord, I have come to you for refuge—you whose feet transcend the worlds. Even in such passages as, "This mantra will accomplish both liberation (*kaivalya*) and the Blessed One," the term *kaivalya* refers to the bliss of experiencing the Self alone, which is attained by those seeking it.
And because it is situated among the ranks of obstacles, the wise avoid it from the very beginning with great vigilance.

Some, however, desiring to turn away from the experience of Brahman, seek the eternal bliss of self-experience; yet we see neither the authority of the tradition of the Bhāṣyakāra and others, nor any reasoning, in support of that view. For when all karma is exhausted, the manifestation of one's natural form necessarily entails the experience of Brahman; whereas if a residue of karma remains, the consequence would be continued transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Transmigration ceases upon the destruction of all karma that causes old age, death, and so forth, and it is by that much alone that the designation "liberated" is applied. Regarding the experience of Brahman—

If it is argued that there is an absence of experiencing [the fruits] because the karma of bondage has not been destroyed—let it be so; however, there is no restrictive rule that this karma will not perish even later. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, the postulation of an eternal liberation (nitya-kaivalya) devoid of the attainment of the Supreme and so forth is not established without contradicting the Sūtras, Bhāṣyas, Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other authorities.
Therefore, relying on the distinction of states according to the difference in qualified practitioners, they have also established another path leading toward the West.

In that regard, because [theories] such as non-return or the attainment of another state are inconsistent with the dissimilarity [of the two paths], the elixir we have described—which is not contradicted by Śruti and Smṛti—is the infallible remedy.

How is it said that the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) is the great path? To this he says: "In the passage 'At what time... a specific time is introduced. In the *Śārīraka*, liberation is stated even for one who dies during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and so forth; therefore, [it is said] "even in the southern course.
And here, "these two paths, the bright and the dark" is what is being stated immediately following; otherwise, [the sequence] would be "fire, light... and so on.

And it would contradict [the scripture]. The sense is that [the verse] concludes with the word denoting the path: "Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha... By showing the connection with the distant [verse], "At what time departing...", and thereby removing the doubt as to how there can be a return for yogins, he states the sentence-meaning of the verse beginning with "yatra kāle" using the words "yasmin" and so on. Here, "yogins" refers to those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*) and those connected with meritorious deeds (*puṇyakarman*). [The term *yogin* is used] by means of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for those who possess similar forms.

This is because of the grammatical rule *ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). Alternatively, the phrase "those of meritorious deeds" (*puṇyakarmāṇaḥ*) refers to the path. It has been stated that the illustration of the year and so forth is in accordance with such scriptural passages as: "They reach the light; from the light, day; from day, the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, the six months when the sun moves northward; from those months, the year. The clarification of this is found in the *Arcirādi-pāda* (Chāndogya Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 4.3.1–13). In that very section:

"It was compiled by the venerable Varadaguru: 'They say that the rays, the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, the year, the wind, the sun, and the moon, as well as Vaidyuta, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati, are the *ātivāhika*s (conveyors). [The mantra] 'Agni is light' means 'the light whose form is Agni.

By this, the intention is to refer to the ray (*arci*) situated at the first stage of the path of the gods (*devayāna*). For this very reason, Agni and Jyotis are distinct deities and are specific presiding deities of time."
Those who speak thus have been answered. || 23–24 ||

Regarding the phrase "from the world of the ancestors and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the taking hold of the ether and the moon. To the question, "How can the path beginning with smoke and the return of the yogin be spoken of here?

he says: "In this context, the word 'yoga' [is used]. Here, the word *yogin* denotes merely the means (*upāya*); or else, it denotes mere connection (*saṃbandha*). However, by virtue of the efficacy of the path beginning with smoke, [the term applies] to those who perform meritorious deeds.

The meaning is that there is established a specific distinction regarding the connection with form. Now, the scriptural passage beginning with, "Those who here in this world worship sacrifice, merit, and charity—they pass into smoke," is corroborated in this context. || 25 ||

The establishment of the two paths mentioned as being well-known in the Vedas is shown by the verse beginning with "the bright and the dark. Here, the metaphorical application of the terms "bright" (*śukla*) and "dark" (*kṛṣṇa*) to the two courses of travel occurs either because of their connection with the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, or through the intention of expressing purity and impurity, or due to the superimposition of the nature of the traveler upon the destination. In this context, the word "world" (*jagat*), intended to refer to the two classes of people under discussion, signifies both various types of knowers and those of meritorious deeds.
