This is indicated by the phrase: "sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts... (*iṣṭāpūrte dattam*).

The word "various" (*vividha*) is used with the intention of referring to the distinctions among those established in various types of ritual action (*karma-niṣṭha*), as stated in the phrase "they worship. The word "indeed" (*hi*) indicates that this is well-known in the Śruti; thus it was said, "in the Śruti. "Eternality" (*śāśvatatva*) means being without beginning or end in the form of a continuous flow. "Fixedness" (*vyavasthitatva*)... [is explained] by the verse beginning with "These two paths... (*naite sṛtī*). Although even the contemplation of the path, like meditation (*upāsanā*), is for the sake of attaining the Supreme Person, nevertheless, knowledge of the path is for the sake of the traveler's unimpeded progress.

This is established in the world. Here too, such assistance being possible, it does not arise from mere compassion; for it is with the intention that its attainment occurs precisely through His grace that he says, "these two. "Someone" (kaścana) means "anyone at all. "He does not falter" means that the path becomes clear in the manner described by the words, "the door revealed by Him," and so forth. With the intention that the knowledge of the two paths is for the purpose of setting aside the path to be abandoned, he says:

"But rather... Having taught the fruit of the knowledge of the destination (*gati*), and having referred back to that as the reason with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), [the author] says "therefore" with the intention that—since it would be inconsistent to enjoin yoga directly—the word "yoga" here refers only to meditation (*dhyāna*); and that meditation must be of the very nature of contemplating the destination under discussion. ||27||

With the intention that, because of the general indication "having understood this" (*idaṃ viditvā*) and the lack of specific distinction, the meaning of the two chapters—which constitute a single section—is being grasped, he says, "Now" (*atha*). Even the phrase "in the Vedas" (*vedeṣu*) is mentioned as a cause for results, like sacrifices and so forth, and not as their means of exposition; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to restrict its scope to subjects other than the results of sacrifices and the like. Furthermore, the fact that the study of the Vedas bestows results such as the destruction of evil deeds is established by scripture (*śruti*) and other authorities.

Siddham. If [the term "Veda"] were taken as referring specifically to the results of sacrifices and so forth, there would be a restriction even of the subject matter of the two preceding chapters, since that too constitutes the meaning of the Veda. Having this entire point in mind, it is said "through the study of the Veda" (vedābhyāsena). Regarding the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and in giving" (dāne ca), it is intended to demonstrate that it serves to include what has not been mentioned. From here onwards...

Regarding the word *śabda*: in the phrase "the fruit of merit" (*puṇyaphala*), the intention is that the word "merit" (*puṇya*) serves as a qualifier for the fruit, providing a general reference to sacrifices and other such acts in order to demonstrate the excellence of their results. With this in mind, it is said "in meritorious [acts]" (*puṇyeṣu*) with sacrifices and the like as the substantive. Regarding the phrase "the majesty of the Lord proclaimed in two chapters": even though the majesty of the Lord was introduced in the seventh chapter, the sense is that everything else was spoken of as being connected to that. "He attains the supreme station" refers to the practice of yoga.

Since the direct fruit of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is stated separately, there would be redundancy if [the term "fruit"] were intended to refer to that [direct fruit]. Furthermore, if one intends to express the attainment of an additional fruit of merit (*puṇya*), it would result in the fallacy of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

Even if the intent were merely the cessation of *saṃsāra*, the word "fruit of merit" would have to indicate the fruit of demerit (*pāpa*) as well; therefore, the phrase "he transcends all that" is intended to convey the dispassion rooted in the discernment of those [fruits]. For, according to the maxim beginning with "the experience of an extraordinary fruit is the joy of the mind without effort," [this is established].

He says, "This [knowledge] is the cause of freedom from thirst for other fruits," with the intention that there is no other cause. With the intention of demonstrating the gateway in the form of a specific knowledge—which was previously stated to be the cause for attaining the supreme state through the majesty of the Lord—he says, "having become a man of knowledge" (*jñānī*). "Supremacy" (*paratvam*) is due to its transcendence of space, time, yoga, and so forth, as seen in such passages as: "Of the color of the sun, beyond darkness," "In that imperishable, supreme heaven," and "These indeed, O dear one, are the hells compared to the abode of the Supreme Self. This is the first [point].
The meaning is "without beginning. As for the statement by others that "the cause existing at the beginning is Brahman," that is untenable because it contradicts the word "place" (sthāna). || 28 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*.
In the ninth [chapter], one's own majesty in human form and the supremacy of the Great-Souled Ones are proclaimed; therein, yoga in the form of devotion is specifically described.

Thus, while explaining even this summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*), he demonstrates the connection between the eighth and ninth chapters accordingly, beginning with the words "upāsaka" and so forth. "Distinctions" (*viśeṣāḥ*) refers to the various categories of what is to be known and what is to be adopted. Since the majesty of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) and the distinction of those possessing knowledge have already been established previously, [the present section serves] to further clarify their specific power.

The verb *kriyate* (is performed) is used here because [the author] has entered into the worship of the mere measure (*mātramātra*) and its fruits; however, with the intention that the primary subject matter of this chapter is the determination of the essential nature of worship (*upāsanā-svarūpa-niṣkarṣa*), the phrase "having purified" (*viśodhya*) is set apart, and the expression beginning with "of the form of devotion" (*bhakti-rūpasya*) is stated separately. Given that the words *bhajana* and *upāsana* are employed with identical referents both in this very chapter and in other contexts, the intention is that the term "devotion" (*bhakti*) serves as a qualification for the worship established by scripture (*śruti-siddha-upāsana*). With this in mind, it is said: "of the worship in the form of devotion" (*bhakti-rūpasyopāsanasya*).

In this context, it is said that "this is the most secret of secrets" because knowledge has been introduced; because it is concluded with "be intent on Me"; because devotion itself is repeatedly practiced in the middle; because various unprecedented modes—such as being of the nature of direct perception, unsurpassed dearness, praise, and salutation—which enter into the very essence of devotion, are being set forth; because its unsurpassed fruit is presented as something to be attained through its own essential nature; and because it is characterized by praise in passages such as "the royal science."

Furthermore, since this is a discourse by Pārtha, the purport of the chapter is the determination of the nature of devotion (bhakti) through the indicators of intent, such as the introduction and conclusion; the intention is that other matters are mentioned here because they are connected to that [devotion]. As for the phrase "But this [knowledge] of yours," just as the knower of Truth (satyavit) is superior to the knower of the vital breath (prāṇavit), the word "but" (tu) intends to convey that this [devotion] is also superior to both Karma-yoga and Jñāna-yoga.

For those two possess the quality of being secret and more secret, respectively; this, however, is the most secret of all. And this has been stated for the purpose of instilling an extreme eagerness to hear it and to instruct one in the necessity of greater concealment. Just as in the Vedāntic passages that serve to supplement [this teaching], the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is shown here to culminate in the specific sense that will be described; thus, it is called "meditation" (*upāsanā*) in the form of devotion. It is accompanied by the specific knowledge pertaining to meditation.

The distinction between the previously mentioned knowledge and the knowledge presented here is this: the former is indeed the knowledge of specific details regarding the object of meditation and so forth. "Specificity pertaining to meditation" refers to the mode of meditation. He shows the mode of being free from envy (*anasūyutva*), which is relevant to the subject at hand, with the words "having me as its object. Envy (*hrasūyā*) is a particular mental state consisting in the revelation of faults in virtues; the opposite of that is simply the determination of virtues in virtues—this is the intended meaning. By this, [the teacher] distinguishes between disciples who are fit for instruction and those who are not.
Instruction has been given; and they remember the words of the Veda, such as, "Do not give Me to one who is envious," and so forth.
And He will say later, beginning with "This [knowledge] is not for one who lacks austerity," up to "And he who finds fault with Me"—this is the sense. For by means of ritual action and the like...

The removal of sins that obstruct the arising of devotion and so forth; for it is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) that through devotion all sins obstructing the attainment of the Lord are removed—this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "from all that is inauspicious which opposes my attainment. Here, the word "inauspicious" (*aśubha*) is intended to include even those sins denoted by the term "merit" (*puṇya*), which are causes for hell and delusion, and which are synonymous with [attachment to] heaven and the like, as indicated by the phrase "from all. (1)

He demonstrates the superiority of this means over other means by the term *rājavidyā*. If the word *rāja* here were to refer specifically to the Kṣatriya caste, then—according to the maxim that "a specific injunction implies the exclusion of the remainder"—it would follow that Brāhmaṇas and others would lack eligibility. Therefore, disregarding the analysis [of the compound] as "the science (*vidyā*) of kings (*rājñām*)," he says: "the king (*rājā*) of sciences... and "the king of secrets. This was stated with a view toward the result of a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*); however, the actual meaning of the words is "that which has become a king" (*rājabhūtā*).

Regarding the word *vidyā*: it should be understood as included in the group beginning with *rājadanta* (where the order of words is reversed). Because of the same grammatical principle applied to the word *uttama* in the phrase "this is the supreme purifier" (*pavitramidamuttamam*), the word *rāja* here signifies "excellent. Thus, one who would tolerate the difficulty of an unfamiliar meaning says, "the science of kings" (*rājñāṃ vidyā*). To dispel the suspicion that this might be intended to exclude the Brāhmaṇas and others from eligibility, he shows the quality that serves as the basis for its application: "for kings... He states the resulting conclusion: "of those of great mind" (*mahāmanasām*). Or, it may be taken as a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*).

Alternatively, a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is intended here; the sense is that it cannot be known by others. To show that even the term "royal secret" (*rājaguhra*) has a specific purpose, he states "for only those of great mind... [and so forth]. He explains the intended meaning of the word "purifier" (*pavitra*) as qualified by the word "supreme" (*uttama*), in order to exclude those who merely avert a few obstacles or those whose means are contrary [to the goal], stating "attaining Me... Regarding the phrase "direct perception" (*pratyakṣāvagamam*), if it were intended to mean knowledge in the form of direct perception, [the gender] would have been neuter.

Because of the application [of the compound], and because of the possibility of forming a *bahuvrīhi* by making knowledge itself the qualifier of a specific instance of knowledge, he establishes its status as a *bahuvrīhi* derived in the sense of the object (*karman*) through the passage beginning with "it is understood" (*avagamyate*). Now, one might object: this is incorrect, because meditation (*upāsana*) consists of a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-santati*), and because scripture declares that the object of meditation is not perceptible (*apratyakṣa*); furthermore, another perceptible object has no connection with devotion (*bhakti*). To this, he replies: "in the form of devotion" (*bhaktirūpeṇa*). [As it is said: "But by unswerving devotion... (*bhaktyā tvananyayā*).

The passage beginning with "it is possible" (*śakyaḥ*) should be understood here. The phrase "at that very time" (*tadānīm eva*) was stated by virtue of proximity (*āsatti*). With the intention that it is difficult for those things which are themselves results to possess the nature of *dharma*—which consists in being a means to another result—he says, "nevertheless, it is *dharmya*. He explains the word *dharmya* according to the rule of Pāṇini's Sūtra, *dharmapathyarthanyāyādanapete*, by deriving it from *dharma*. He clarifies his intended meaning with the words beginning "for the nature of *dharma*... (*dharmatvaṃ hi...*) and so forth.

The intention is that the word *dharma* is derived from the verbal root *dhṛ*, which signifies "sustenance" (*dhṛti*) as a synonym for "joy" (*prīti*), with the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) intended. And it has been stated by the learned: "When one speaks of that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*) as something to be embraced under the term 'Dharma,' it is for the purpose of elucidating the definition of the referent denoted by the word *dharma*," and so forth.

Since there is no further delimiter for the "highest good" (*śreyaḥ*) here, [it refers to] liberation (*mukti*), isolation (*kaivalya*), nirvāṇa, the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), and the deathless (*amṛta*). Thus ends the section on the suffix *ṭyu*.

And because of the textual reading, the words "unsurpassed" (*niratiśaya*) and so forth were stated. "For this very reason" means: because it is of the nature of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) both in its essential form (*svarūpataḥ*) and in terms of what is to be accomplished (*sādhyataḥ*).

"Easy to perform" (*kartum susukham*) means easy to carry out (*karaṇe susukham*). To dispel the misconception that the word *susukham* functions as the object of the action denoted by the suffix *-tumun*, he says "easy to undertake" (*susukhopādānam*).

He explains the intended meaning of the prefix (*upa-sarga*) and the word *sukha* here by saying "exceedingly," etc.; for it is exceedingly favorable both in its essential form and in its objective content, and thus it is to be practiced with ease (*sukhena anuṣṭheya*).

The meaning is "which. For all other karma is indeed destroyed by its fruit; but this [karma], though easy to perform, is not exhausted even by its fruit. With the intention that the word "avyaya" (imperishable) is used in the sense of excellence—since even the fruit in the form of liberation is not sufficient for it—he says "akṣayam" (indestructible). || 2 ||

Demonstrating that liberation is not accomplished in the absence of the practice of knowledge based on faith in the manner described, and stating the reason why— despite its nature as a fruit consisting of unsurpassed bliss— it is not practiced by anyone, he supplements the passage beginning with "There is no other path for going" with the verse starting with "Those who lack faith. He explains that the word "of this" (asya) refers back to everything previously mentioned by saying "consisting of unsurpassed," etc., and that "of dharma" (dharmasya) expresses a general relationship.

To demonstrate the logical connection resulting from the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) whose referent has not yet been specified, he says: "having reached the stage suitable for [becoming] material causes" (*upādānayogyadaśāṃ prāpya*). Alternatively, the intention is that the prohibition of faith occurs when its occasion arises, as indicated by the word "for" (*hi*). To show that the cessation of the cause extends to the cessation of the performance of the effect, he says: "devoid of the basis consisting of trust" (*viśvāsapūrvakatvādhārahīnāḥ*). The phrase "in the form of death" (*mṛtyurūpa*) means "in the nature of an obstacle. Or rather, they possess the nature of death precisely because they contain death within them. Regarding the phrase "they turn back" (*nivartante*): [The commentary continues: ...because they are devoid of the substratum which is trust. The term "obstacle" (*bādhaka*) refers to the essential nature [of death]. Or else, they have the nature of death simply because they are pregnant with death. Regarding the statement "they turn back": [The commentary continues: ...it is said that they cease to exist, meaning they do not arise again. The sense is that they do not manifest once more. By this, it is shown that the cessation of the cause results in the cessation of the effect. Furthermore, the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) is used here to indicate the state of being an obstacle, just as one speaks of "the death of a thief" (*caurasya mṛtyuḥ*) to mean his destruction. Therefore, the meaning is that those who lack the basis of trust, having reached the stage of being fit for material causes, perish; and having perished, they do not arise again. Thus, the cessation of the cause implies the cessation of the effect. This is the intended meaning. [The commentary concludes: ...Therefore, the cessation of the cause implies the cessation of the effect. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the cessation of the cause. Now begins the section on the cessation of the effect. To explain this, he says: "And because of the absence of the cause, there is the non-arising of the effect" (*kāraṇābhāvācca kāryānutpattiḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a cumulative conjunction. The meaning is that the non-arising of the effect follows from the absence of the cause. The word "effect" (*kārya*) refers to the body, etc., which are the objects of experience. The phrase "non-arising" (*anutpatti*) means the absence of production. The sense is that the body, etc., do not arise again. By this, it is shown that the cessation of the effect follows from the cessation of the cause. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the cessation of the effect. Now begins the section on the cessation of the fruit. To explain this, he says: "And because of the absence of the effect, there is the non-arising of the fruit" (*kāryābhāvācca phalānutpattiḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a cumulative conjunction. The meaning is that the non-arising of the fruit follows from the absence of the effect. The word "fruit" (*phala*) refers to the experience of pleasure and pain. The phrase "non-arising" (*anutpatti*) means the absence of production. The sense is that pleasure and pain do not arise again. By this, it is shown that the cessation of the fruit follows from the cessation of the effect. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the cessation of the fruit. Now begins the section on the cessation of the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). To explain this, he says: "And because of the absence of the fruit, there is the non-arising of transmigratory existence" (*phalābhāvācca saṃsārānutpattiḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a cumulative conjunction. The meaning is that the non-arising of transmigratory existence follows from the absence of the fruit. The word "transmigratory existence" (*saṃsāra*) refers to the cycle of birth and death. The phrase "non-arising" (*anutpatti*) means the absence of production. The sense is that the cycle of birth and death does not arise again. By this, it is shown that the cessation of transmigratory existence follows from the cessation of the fruit. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the cessation of transmigratory existence. Now begins the section on the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*). To explain this, he says: "And because of the absence of transmigratory existence, there is the attainment of liberation" (*saṃsārābhāvācca mokṣaprāptiḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a cumulative conjunction. The meaning is that the attainment of liberation follows from the absence of transmigratory existence. The word "liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to the state of absolute freedom. The phrase "attainment" (*prāpti*) means reaching. The sense is that one reaches the state of absolute freedom. By this, it is shown that the attainment of liberation follows from the cessation of transmigratory existence. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the attainment of liberation. Now begins the section on the summary of the entire treatise. To explain this, he says: "Thus, through the cessation of the cause, the cessation of the effect, and so forth, the cessation of transmigratory existence is established, and from that, liberation is attained" (*iti kāraṇanivṛttyā kāryanivṛttyādikrameṇa saṃsāranivṛttiḥ siddhyati, tasmācca mokṣaprāptiḥ*). The word "thus" (*iti*) indicates the conclusion of the sequence. The phrase "cessation of the cause, cessation of the effect, and so forth" (*kāraṇanivṛttyā kāryanivṛttyādikrama*) refers to the aforementioned order. The word "established" (*siddhyati*) means proven. The sense is that the cessation of transmigratory existence is proven by this sequence. The word "from that" (*tasmāt*) refers to the cessation of transmigratory existence. The phrase "liberation is attained" (*mokṣaprāptiḥ*) means reaching the state of absolute freedom. The sense is that one reaches the state of absolute freedom. By this, the entire purpose of the treatise is summarized. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter of the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*. [End of excerpt]

Because there is a desire to express a turning back (*pratinivṛtti*) which requires a limit (*avadhi*), and because no such limit is specified here; because it is impossible to conceive of the Supreme Person as a limit since He is mentioned separately in the phrase "without reaching Me" (*māmaprāpya*); and because the locative case in the word *saṃsāravartmani* naturally requires a substratum (*ādheya*), and since prefixes have multiple meanings, it is said that they "move intensely. Thus, they diligently serve this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of unsurpassed human goals both in its essential nature and in its results.

Thus, with the intention that the power of evil karma is most wondrous, he says, "This is a great wonder. The sense of the address "O scorcher of foes" (parantapa) is that even the internal enemies which cause lack of faith must be overcome by you. || 3 ||

Thus, the greatness of that which brings about the primary subject matter of the chapter has been stated; now, with the intention of further stabilizing that very point by way of the greatness of what is to be attained (*prāpya*), he says: "Listen first. With the intention that the designation "all this" refers to every object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is said: "consisting of the conscious and the unconscious. Since the phrase "by the one of unmanifest form" would be irrelevant here if it referred to a physical body (*vigraha*), this figurative usage refers to his essential nature (*svarūpa*).

To demonstrate this, it was stated "by one whose own nature is unmanifest. In order to exclude a pervasion consisting of mere proximity—like that of ether or the heart—he says "by me" to indicate the mode of pervasion established by many means of knowledge, which is intended here. He shows the purpose and the cause of the pervasion in the manner described with the words "there exists. Here, "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) is established by the immediately following text; for this very reason, "governing" (*niyamana*) is also established by implication, since sustaining is dependent upon governing.

It is heard [in scripture]. However, its status as a subordinate (śeṣitva) has been stated previously, and its being the embodied one (śarīritva) is established by implication. Furthermore, the Scripture shows that [the Lord] is all-pervasive because His essential nature is not manifested, using the word "just as" (yathā). The example of the earth is intended to indicate all insentient things mentioned in that context. With the intention of showing that by virtue of the pervasiveness in the manner described, the notion of the world's independent existence (pṛthaksiddhatā) is refuted by the phrase "resting in Me," he says "therefore" (tataḥ). — Śrī Viśvarūpa.

In other [scriptural] passages, everything is said to be dependent upon a formal body (*vigraha*); however, here, because the state of being established in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is intended, the phrase "in Me as the Inner Controller" (*mayyantaryāmiṇi*) is used to avoid redundancy.

By the words "therein," he states that these two—sustenance (*dhāraṇa*) and control (*niyamana*)—are taught together with pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Staying and controlling" means staying and causing activity.

With the intention that sustenance and the status of being the Remainder (*śeṣitva*) are established there by implication from the statement regarding the relationship of body and embodied, he says "and the status of being the Remainder. "By Me this is pervaded... [and so forth].

Having stated "all," the statement "and I am not established in them" would be contradictory and opposed to such scriptural passages as "He who dwells in the earth... To this, he says: "But I... The mode of abiding introduced here as "all beings are established in Me" is what is being negated; for it is heard in scripture [at Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1] that when asked, "In what, O Blessed One, is He established?", the answer is, "In His own glory. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "resting in Me": the sense is that nothing [rests in Me] by way of its own nature, nor through volition, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth. He explains this further with the words "resting in Me. Regarding the word "pervaded" (*vyāpta*), he says: "not as in the case of jars and the like. For a material object supports another material object through a conjunction that prevents it from falling; such is not the case here—this is the sense. With the intention that what contradicts common worldly experience is impossible, he raises an objection: "How so? He then provides the answer, having in mind the possibility [of support] as between a body and its possessor: "I am the support of all beings, yet I do not rest upon anything. Nor is there anyone who sustains Me, nor is there any sign of My support. (Gītā 9.4–5) Just as the body is supported by the embodied self, so too am I the support of all beings. Yet, because I am without a material cause (*upādāna*) and am devoid of any other substratum, I do not rest upon anything. Furthermore, there is no one who sustains Me, nor is there any sign of My support, for I am without a material cause and am devoid of any other substratum. Thus, even though I am the support of all beings, I do not rest upon anything. This is the meaning. As it has been said: "The Lord is the support of all beings, yet He does not rest upon anything. There is no one who sustains Him, nor is there any sign of His support. (Vedāntasāra 12) The word "sign" (*liṅga*) refers to a mark or evidence. Since I am without a material cause, there is no mark of My support, just as there is no mark of support for space (*ākāśa*). Therefore, although I am the support of all beings, I do not rest upon anything. This is the meaning. As it has been said: "Space is the support of all beings, yet it does not rest upon anything. There is no one who sustains it, nor is there any sign of its support. (Vedāntasāra 13) Thus, although I am the support of all beings, I do not rest upon anything. This is the meaning. As it has been said: "I am the support of all beings, yet I do not rest upon anything. There is no one who sustains Me, nor is there any sign of My support. As it has been said: "The Lord is the support of all beings, yet He does not rest upon anything. There is no one who sustains Him, nor is there any sign of His support. (Vedānt

Regarding the phrase "by my resolve" (*matsaṅkalpena*): the intended meaning is that there is no contradiction because it is prescribed that [the Lord] sustains [the world] by His own will, whereas sustaining [it] through dependence on another is prohibited. By the word "divine" (*aiśvara*), it is implied that this is not common to others; and by the word "behold" (*paśya*), its wonderfulness is indicated—with this intention, he says "elsewhere. Regarding "yoga"—whether it refers to the nature of that which is being joined (*yujyamāna*) and so forth—since it was said "behold my yoga," the very nature of yoga must be explained immediately thereafter; thus, he shows the expectation for it by asking "what is this? In the verse "the sustainer of beings, yet not dwelling in beings," the meaning is appropriate [to the context].

The word "body" (*deha*) alone is the substantive. Alternatively, just as in the expression "the creator of beings" (*bhūtabhāvanaḥ*), the natural force of the grammatical construction in "my self" (*mama ātmā*) establishes the meaning of the word "self.

Thus he says: "My resolve is composed of mind" (*mama manomayaḥ saṅkalpaḥ*). By this, the view stated by Śaṅkara—that the designation "my self" is made by superimposing the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the aggregate of the body and so forth, in accordance with worldly understanding—is refuted. For resolve itself is well-known elsewhere as an effect of the mind, and thus it is designated by a term that denotes the mind.

He is designated here by the word "ātman. Alternatively, the word "ātman" here refers specifically to the mind (manas) in the form of volition (saṅkalpa), as in such passages as "by the mind alone [is] the creation of the world. However, the term "consisting of mind" (manomaya) is used to make known that he is the knower of its object. || 4-5 ||

Now, the ninth [chapter] concerns one's own greatness and the transcendence of great souls within the human state; in this ninth [chapter], the specific yoga is proclaimed as being in the form of devotion.

Thus, while explaining even this summary verse (*saṃgraha-śloka*), he demonstrates the connection between the eighth and ninth chapters accordingly with the words beginning "Upāsake" (In the worshipper). "Distinctions" (*viśeṣāḥ*) refers to the differences regarding what is to be known and what is to be adopted. Since the majesty of the Supreme Person and the distinction of the knowers have already been established previously, here only the purification of their power is performed by way of being included within the meditation (*upāsanā*) and its fruits; for the primary subject matter of the chapter is the determination of the nature of meditation—this is the intention behind the term "purification" (*viśodhana*).

The word "ye" (which) has been separated [from the compound] and stated separately as "of the nature of devotion" (*bhaktirūpasya*) and so forth. Because the words *bhajana* and *upāsana* are used with identical referents both in this very chapter and in other contexts, it is said "of meditation in the form of devotion" (*bhaktirūpasyopāsanasya*), with the intention that here the term "devotion" serves as a qualification for that very meditation which is established by scripture (*śruti*).

In this context, it is said: "But this is a most profound mystery of yours," because knowledge has been introduced; and because [the Lord] concludes with "Be of mind intent on Me"; and because throughout the middle [of the discourse], devotion alone is repeatedly practiced; and because various unprecedented modes that enter into the very nature of devotion—such as its being of the nature of direct perception, its being unsurpassedly dear, its being praised, and its being the form of sacrifice and salutation—are set forth; and because its unsurpassed fruit is presented as something to be attained through its own essential nature, by means of the passage beginning with "This is the royal science... and so forth.

Furthermore, because we observe explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the form of praise, the purport of this chapter is the definitive determination of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) through the indicators of intent (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introduction and conclusion; the intention is that other matters are mentioned here only as being connected to that [devotion]. This, however, is for you...

Thus [it is said]. Here, just as the knower of Truth (satyavit) is superior to the knower of the vital breath (prāṇavit), by the word "but" (tu), it is intended to show that this [knowledge] is also superior to both Karma-yoga and Jñāna-yoga. For those two possess the quality of being secret and more secret respectively, whereas this is the most secret of all. And this has been stated for the purpose of establishing an excellence in the desire to hear and for the purpose of instructing on the necessity of greater concealment. Just as in the Vedāntic passages which are to be supplemented, here too—in order to demonstrate that the word "knowledge" (jñāna) culminates in the specific sense about to be described—it is called "meditation" (upāsanā) characterized by devotion (bhakti). [It is] accompanied by the specific knowledge pertaining to meditation...

The distinction between the previously mentioned knowledge and the knowledge presented here is that the former is a specific cognition regarding the object of meditation and so forth. "Specificity pertaining to meditation" refers to the mode of meditation. He shows the manner of being free from envy (*anasūyutva*), which is relevant to the present context, with the words "having me as its object. Envy (*asūyā*) is a particular mental state consisting in the revelation of faults in virtues; the opposite of this is simply the determination of virtues as virtues—this is the intended meaning. By this, [the teacher] distinguishes between disciples who are fit for instruction and those who are not.
Instruction has been given. And they remember the words of the Vidyā: "Do not give Me to one who is envious," and so forth.

Furthermore, He will say: "This [knowledge] is not for one devoid of austerity," beginning with that, up to "and he who is envious of Me"—this is the sense. For by means of ritual action (*karman*) and the like, there is the removal of sins that are obstacles to the arising of devotion; whereas by means of devotion, all sins that are obstacles to attaining the Blessed Lord are removed—this is established by valid authority (*pramāṇa*).

According to my intention, it has been stated [in the previous verse] that [the Lord is free] from all that is inauspicious (*aśubha*), which is opposed to the attainment of Me. Here, by the word *aśubha*, what is intended by the phrase "from all" is also the sin denoted by the term *puṇya* (merit), which is a cause of delusion and is synonymous with [attachment to] heaven and other such states. || 1 ||

He demonstrates the superiority of this means over other means by the phrase "the royal science" (*rājavidyā*). If the word *rāja* here were to refer specifically to the Kṣatriya caste, then by the maxim "a specific injunction implies the exclusion of the rest," it would follow that Brāhmaṇas and others would lack qualification [for this practice]. Therefore, disregarding the analysis of the compound as "the science of kings" (*rājñāṃ vidyā*), he says: "the king of sciences... the king of secrets. This was stated with an eye toward the result of a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*); however, the actual meaning of the words is "that which has become a king" (*rājabhūtā*).

Regarding the word *vidyā*: it should be understood as included in the group beginning with *rājadanta* (where the subordinate member precedes). Because of the same grammatical principle applied to the word *uttama* in the phrase "this is the supreme purifier" (*pavitramidamuttamam*), the word *rāja* here signifies "the best. Thus, one who endures the difficulty of an unfamiliar meaning says, "the science of kings" (*rājñām vidyā*). To dispel the suspicion that this refers to a prohibition of eligibility for Brāhmaṇas and others, he shows the quality that serves as the basis for its usage: "for kings... He states the conclusion: "of those of great mind" (*mahāmanasām*). Or, it may be taken as a non-abandoning secondary indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*).

Alternatively, a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is intended here; the sense is that it cannot be understood by others. He shows that even the term "royal secret" (*rājaguhyam*) has a purposeful, metaphorical meaning in the words "for [it belongs] only to those of great mind. To exclude those who merely avert obstacles to the means or those who avert only a few, he states the intended meaning of the word "purifier" (*pavitra*) as qualified by the word "supreme" (*uttama*): "attaining me. Regarding the phrase "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣāvagamam*), if it were intended to mean knowledge in the form of direct perception, its neuter gender would be justified.

Because of the application [of the compound], and because of the possibility of forming a *bahuvrīhi* by making knowledge itself the qualifier of a specific instance of knowledge, he establishes its status as a *bahuvrīhi* derived in the sense of the object (*karman*) through the phrase beginning with "it is understood" (*avagamyate*). Now, one might object: this is incorrect, because meditation (*upāsanā*) consists of a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*), and because scripture declares that the object of meditation is not perceptible (*apratyakṣa*), whereas no other perceptible object can be connected with devotion (*bhakti*). To this he replies: "in the form of devotion" (*bhaktirūpeṇa*). Passages such as "But by exclusive devotion He can be known" (*bhaktyā tvananyayā śakyaḥ*) should be considered here. The phrase "at that very time" (*tadānīm eva*) was stated on account of proximity (*āsatti*). For those which are themselves the fruit...

With the intention that the nature of being *dharma*—consisting in being a means to another result—is difficult to find, he says: "nevertheless, it is *dharmya*. [The suffix -ya is applied] in the sense of "not deviating from *dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, or *nyāya*."

Thus, following the Sūtra, he provides the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *dharmya* as "that which pertains to *dharma*" (*dharmāṇām idam*). He clarifies his intended meaning with the words "For the nature of *dharma*... and so forth. The point is that the word *dharma* is derived from the verbal root *dhṛ*, which is synonymous with *prīti* (joy), with the intention of expressing the instrumental sense (*karaṇavivakṣayā*). And it has been stated by the learned: "The statement 'it is *dharma*' regarding that which is to be undertaken is made with the desire to define the referent denoted by the term *dharma*," and so on. Since there is no limiting factor for "the good" (*śreyas*) here, [the result] is liberation (*mukti*), as expressed by the synonyms *kaivalya*, *nirvāṇa*, *śreyas*, *niḥśreyasa*, and *amṛta*. This is according to the *Naidhuṇṭuka*.

And because it is stated in the text, "In the unsurpassed [state]," and so forth; for this very reason, [it is said] "because it is of the nature of a human goal both by its own essence (*svarūpataḥ*) and by its being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyataḥ*). The phrase "easy to perform" (*kartum susukham*) means "easy to carry out" (*karaṇe susukham*). To dispel the misconception that the word *susukham* functions as the object of the action denoted by the suffix *-tumun*, he says "easy to undertake" (*susukhopādānam*).

He explains what is intended here by the prefix (*upa-sarga*) and the word *sukha*: namely, "exceedingly" (*atyarthe*), because it is exceedingly favorable both by its own essence and by its object; thus, it is to be practiced with ease (*sukhena*).

This is the meaning of "yam" (which). For all other karma is indeed destroyed by its fruit; but this [karma], although easy to perform, is not exhausted even by its fruit. With the intention that the word "avyaya" (imperishable) is used to express its excellence—since even the fruit in the form of liberation is not sufficient for it—he says "akṣayam" (indestructible). || 2 ||

Demonstrating that liberation is not accomplished in the absence of the practice of knowledge based on faith in the manner previously described, and stating the reason why the fruit—which is by its very nature unsurpassed bliss—is not practiced by all, the verse beginning with "Those who lack faith" (*aśraddadhānāḥ*) elaborates upon such passages as "There is no other path for going" (*nānyaḥ panthā ayanāya*). He explains that the word "this" (*asya*) refers back to everything mentioned previously, using the phrase "in the unsurpassed," etc.; and the word "of dharma" (*dharmasya*) expresses a general relationship.

To demonstrate the logical connection resulting from the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which has "non-objects" as its referent, he says, "having reached a state suitable for [becoming] material cause" (*upādānayogyadaśāṃ prāpya*). Alternatively, the intention is that the prohibition of faith applies when there is an occasion for its occurrence; thus, he says, "devoid of the sequence beginning with trust" (*viśvāsapūrvakakramarahitāḥ*), in order to show that the cessation of the cause extends to the cessation of the performance of the effect. "In the form of death" (*mṛtyurūpa*) means having the nature of an obstacle. Or rather, they possess the nature of death precisely because they contain death within them. Regarding the phrase "they turn back" (*nivartante*):

Because there is a desire to express a turning back (*pratinivṛtti*), which requires a limit (*avadhi*), and because no such limit is specified here; because it is impossible to conceive of the Supreme Person as a limit since He is mentioned separately in the phrase "without reaching Me" (*mām aprāpya*); and because the locative case in the word *saṃsāravartmasu* naturally implies a substratum (*ādheya*), and because prefixes have multiple meanings, it is said that they "move intensely" (*nitarāṃ vartante*). Thus, they diligently pursue this cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of unsurpassed human goals both in its essential nature and in its results.

With the intention that the power of evil karma is most wondrous, he says, "This is a great wonder. The meaning of the vocative "O scorcher of foes" (*parantapa*) is that even the internal enemies which cause lack of faith must be overcome by you. || 3 ||

Thus, the greatness of that which brings about the primary subject matter of the chapter has been stated; now, with the intention of further stabilizing that very same subject by means of the greatness of what is to be attained (*prāpya*), he says, "Listen first. With the intention that the designation "all this" refers to the entirety of things established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [he says] "this conscious and unconscious..."

It has been stated [that the Lord is] "of the nature of consciousness. Since the expression "whose form is unmanifest" (*avyaktamūrti*) would be irrelevant here if it referred to a physical body, it is said "by one whose essential nature is unmanifested" (*aprakāśitasvarūpeṇa*) in order to show that this usage is figurative with respect to His true nature. To exclude the notion of pervasion as mere proximity—as in the case of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth—it is said "by Me" (*mayā*), intending the mode of pervasion established by many means of knowledge; thus he says "to the Inner Ruler" (*antaryāmiṇe*). He shows the purpose and the cause of the pervasion in the manner described by saying "there exists" (*asti*).

In this context, sustaining (*dhāraṇa*) is established by the immediately preceding text; for this very reason, controlling (*niyamana*) is also established by implication. For it is heard in scripture that sustaining is dependent upon command. Furthermore, being the "residual" (*śeṣitva*) has been stated previously and is established by implication through [the Lord's] being the embodied one (*śarīritva*). And because His nature is not manifest, He shows in scripture that He is all-pervading, as in the passage beginning with "Just as... (*yathā*). The example of the earth is intended to indicate all insentient things mentioned in that particular section. This is the manner already described.

With the intention that by the phrase "residing in Me" (matsthānī) the independent existence of the world apart from Me is refuted on account of My pervasiveness, he says "from That" (tataḥ). In [descriptions such as] the Śrī-Viśvarūpa, everything is said to be dependent upon a formal body (vigraha); however, here, because the state of being established in the essential nature (svarūpa-niṣṭhatā) is intended to avoid redundancy, [the Lord is referred to] as "Me," the inner controller (antaryāmin).

This has been stated. He says "in that very [place]" to show that these two—sustenance (*dhāraṇa*) and control (*niyamana*)—are studied together with pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Sustenance and control" means the maintenance and the activity [of the Lord]. With the intention that "sustenance" and "being the subordinate" (*śeṣitva*) are established there by implication from the statement regarding the body and the embodied one, he says "and being the subordinate."

Having stated, "By Me all this is pervaded," the statement, "And I am not situated within them," would otherwise be contradictory and opposed to such scriptural texts as, "He who dwells in the earth... To address this, He says, "But I [am not]. What is negated here is the mode of abiding introduced by the words, "All beings abide in Me"; for it is heard in scripture [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1], "In what, O Venerable One, is He established?"—"In His own glory. [The phrase] "abiding in Me" means that nothing whatsoever—neither by its own nature, nor by volition, nor by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), etc.—is so situated. He explains what was said: "In Me..."

"Established"—this is the meaning. Regarding the word "pervaded" (*vyāptam*), he says: "not as in the case of jars and the like. For a material object supports another material object through a conjunction that prevents its falling;

the point is that it is not so in this case. With the intention that what contradicts common worldly experience cannot possibly occur, he asks: "How? Anticipating the possibility [of support] as in the case of a body and its possessor, he says: "by my will. For it is prescribed that the supporting power is dependent on His own will, and not through independence.

The intention is that there is no contradiction because what is being negated is the state of being a sustainer (*dhārakatva*). By the word "divine" (*aiśvara*), it is implied that this is not common to others; and by the word "behold" (*paśya*), its wondrous nature is indicated—with this in mind, he says "elsewhere. Regarding "behold my yoga," whether yoga refers to the essential nature of that which is joined (*yujyamāna*) and so forth, since the very nature of yoga must be explained immediately after saying "behold my yoga," he shows the expectation for that by asking "What is this? In the phrase "the sustainer of beings, yet not dwelling in beings," due to the propriety of the meaning—

The word "body" (*deha*) alone is the substantive. Alternatively, just as in the expression "the creator of beings" (*bhūtabhāvanaḥ*), he states the meaning of the word "self" (*ātman*) as established by the natural force of a non-co-referential designation: "my self" (*mama ātmā*). By this, [he shows that] one superimposes the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) upon the aggregate of the body and so forth, in accordance with common worldly understanding.

Śaṅkara’s statement that there is the designation “my self” has been refuted. It is *saṅkalpa* (volition) itself, well-known elsewhere as the function of the mind (*manas*), that is designated here by the word “self” (*ātman*) which refers to the mind. Alternatively, the word “self” here refers precisely to the mind in the form of volition, based on such passages as “by the mind alone [is] the creation of the world. The term “consisting of mind” (*manomaya*), however, is used to indicate that the mind is its essence.
Śrī: Now begins the tenth chapter.

To state the connection (*saṅgati*) for the tenth chapter, or rather to summarize the meaning of the ninth chapter—or the meaning of the three chapters beginning with the seventh—the author states: "Bhaktiyoga. While explaining the summary verse—*The infinite nature of His auspicious qualities and His absolute sovereignty; this extensive [teaching] is declared in the tenth chapter for the sake of the arising and growth of devotion*—the author states the connection with the words "Now" (*idānīm*). In the preceding section, the essential nature of *bhaktiyoga*, along with its ancillaries, was described.

The phrase "now" (*idānīm*) is intended to demonstrate that while in the preceding section there was a concise statement regarding one's own auspicious qualities and so forth—being primarily devoted to the detailed exposition (*prapañcana*) of the nature of *bhaktiyoga* along with its ancillaries—here, however, there is the detailed exposition of those very qualities; thus, the present occasion has arrived and there is no tautology. This is what is meant by the word "extensively" (*vistīrṇa*). In the former [section], there was a concise description of one's own auspicious qualities and so forth, as the primary aim was the detailed exposition of the essential nature of *bhaktiyoga* together with its equipment (*saparikara*); here, however, it is the detailed exposition of that [nature]. This is the appropriate occasion.

The two words "now" (*idānīm*) and "expounds" (*prapañcayate*) are intended to show that the repetition regarding attainment is what is meant by the word "extensively. By stating Arjuna’s fitness for hearing the matter about to be spoken and the fact that this matter is a means to his supreme welfare and so forth, [the Lord] speaks with conciliation and a request for attention.

With the verse beginning "If [you wish] even more," intending to show that the reason for his affection is stated by the Lord himself through his own declaration even without being asked, he reveals the object of such affection with the words "having heard my majesty. For those who possess great arms, the mention of another's excellence usually provokes envy;
however, in this world crowded with Śiśupāla and others, such affection has arisen in you by the power of destiny—thus, O mighty-armed one, [I speak] to you who are being pleased.

This is the state of being *an-anya* (non-other). Alternatively, the sense is that just as you achieved victory over external enemies through the strength of your arms, so too have you conquered internal enemies through the power of love for Me.

This is because, according to the context and the nature of the matter, [the verse] refers to the destruction of what is harmful and the arising and growth of devotion to Me; for it will be stated later: "He is liberated from all sins and becomes united with unshakable Yoga. Regarding the restatement of what has already been said:

Because there is no further purpose [to be served], the phrase "once again" (*bhūya eva*) is intended to mean the detailed elaboration (*prapañcana*) of the meaning of the most secret [teaching] already commenced; with this intention, it is said that [the teaching] concerns precisely the detailed expansion of the majesty of the *mantra*. By this very [statement], the reason for the supremacy of the speech is also shown. With the intention that the command "listen again" is given to Arjuna while he is already listening for the sake of a specific hearing, [the Lord] says, "with your mind attentive" (*tad-avahita-manāḥ*). Previously, [he spoke] to one who was free from malice (*anasūyave*) for the cessation of faults...

That was merely described as "dense"; now, for you who take delight in what is being said, it is described as "extremely dense" due to its perfection of qualities; therefore, the sense is that you must remain exceedingly attentive. ||1||

The extreme rarity of this knowledge about to be declared is stated in the verse beginning with "They do not know Me," in order to show that it is even more worthy of reverence. By the two terms "the hosts of gods" and "the great seers," it is intended to indicate the spheres where there might otherwise be a possibility of those who deny [this knowledge],
namely those who perceive objects beyond the senses and possess superior knowledge.

The phrase "nor even" (*nā api*) negates here the knowledge of His manifestation (*prabhava*), but not manifestation itself; for a qualified negation involves greater complexity (*gaurava*), and since there is no arising dependent on karma, it is improper to negate the knowledge of that [manifestation]. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, the phrase "He who knows Me" refers specifically to the knowledge of His manifestation, and not to the knowledge of His birth;

for this very reason, the subject matter of the secret of the Incarnation (*avatāra-rahasya*) is also not connected here. By the word "elaborated" (*prapañcita*), it is precisely the knowledge of His manifestation that is expressed, and not the knowledge of His birth.

Because of the very statement "the unborn" (*aja*), the subject matter of the secret of the incarnations (*avatāra-rahasya*) is also not applicable here. That has already been explained at length previously; however, something else is elaborated upon here. Therefore, since even the divine sages (*devarṣis*) cannot know it, and since it is the "origin" (*prabhava*)—meaning the pre-eminent existence (*prakarṣeṇa sattā*)—residing in the Lord, it must indeed be "power" (*prabhāva*); with this intention, it is called "power. Having analyzed this power, he says: "My name," etc. The reason for its being concerned with birth is not applicable here.

By the phrase "with this intention" (*ityabhiprāyeṇa*), the causal nature of the word *hi* is demonstrated. Regarding the term *sarvaśaḥ*, it is not intended to signify the totality of gods and others, since that is already established even by the non-restrictive plural number; therefore, he clarifies what is intended by that [term] with the words "of their own nature," and so forth. To the doubt as to how this ignorance of power constitutes a cause, he elucidates the manner in which it serves as a cause, which is his intended meaning, with the words "of those... (*teṣām*).

"O gods... [The text] states that [the fruits of action] correspond to merit in order to avoid the charge of partiality and cruelty, and to establish their limited nature. With the intention of such scriptural passages as: "Who truly knows? Who here has declared it? Whence was it born, and whence is this diverse creation? The gods are later than this creation; then who knows from whence it first came into being? He from whom this creation arose, whether he made it or did not make it—he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he surely knows, or perhaps even he does not know," [the author] says "from that. "That which the gods... [and so forth].
"The sages do not know it, nor do I, nor does Śaṅkara; they do not know that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord"—such Smṛti passages are also to be considered.

Revealing the utility of what is about to be stated regarding the fact that [the Self] cannot be known even by the gods and others, he states the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "He who knows Me," namely:

"This very [Self]... Although the phrase "he who knows" conveys the sense of a restatement (*anuvāda*), the intention is that the purpose lies in prescribing the means (*upāya*) by way of restating the result (*phala*). Thus, [the text speaks of] the means.

"Ma" has been stated. First, he explains the etymology of the word *aja* (unborn) in order to demonstrate what is excluded by it: "It is called *aja* because it is not born. He states the exclusion from that which is appropriate [to be so excluded] as the result of the power of the qualification: "by this [word]. By both [the terms] "from a changing substance" and "from that which is associated with it," the fitness for exclusion is demonstrated. [The question arises: how can the eternal individual soul (*jīva*), which is described by such passages as "unborn, eternal, and everlasting," be [unborn]?

Regarding the point that [the term] "unborn" (aja) serves to exclude [others] merely by virtue of association, he says: "of the transmigrating conscious being" (*saṃsāricetanasya*). Since even the Lord (*īśvara*) possesses an association with various forms of insentient matter (*acit*) by virtue of having all things as his body, the phrase "produced by karma" (*karmakṛta*) is stated in order to exclude him. Furthermore, since even the liberated soul (*mukta*) possesses the beginninglessness of its own nature (*svarūpa*), he asks how it could be something to be excluded; to this he replies: "for the liberated self, being unborn, has a beginning. Here, by the qualification "being unborn," what is intended is beginninglessness in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa-anāditva*). It is not the beginninglessness of the nature itself.

The sense is that there would be tautology if one intended to speak of [the nature] during the state of liberation. In the state of liberation, there is no contact with non-conscious matter (*acit*); if one intended to speak of the prior contact, there would be a distinction from the bound soul (*baddha*) alone. Therefore, he says "of that" (*tasya*) to explain how the exclusion from its own nature at that time is stated. The intention is that *yogyatā* (capacity) consists both in having an active nature when auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) are present, and in possessing the absence of the effect due to the absence of those auxiliary factors. [It is] devoid of limitation by specific times.

And he says "without fault" (*niravadyam*) because this meaning is established by the scriptural passage enjoining freedom from fault. He states "thus" (*evam*) for the sake of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Since knowledge difficult to attain even for gods and great sages arises by the power of fortune in some mortals of dull intellect, its use here as a term of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is appropriate. Furthermore, in the second half of the verse, there is no proper syntactical connection between the words "unconfused" (*asaṃmūḍha*) and "mortal" (*martya*) with the indication of the fruit, [as in]: "The man who, unconfused, thus knows Me... (*yo mām evam asaṃmūḍho jānāti puruṣaḥ*).

And since the notion "it is mine" has not arisen, there is no possibility of delusion such that its negation would be required. With the intention that the shadow of what will be stated immediately hereafter—namely, "He who knows Me in truth is joined with unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt"—is appropriate here, it was said, "he who knows among mortals is undeluded. To explain the meaning of the word *asaṃmūḍha*, he clarifies the intended sense of the prefix by saying, "others... [and so forth].

Because it will be stated immediately thereafter: "He who knows this glory and yoga of Mine in truth is united with unshakable yoga; there is no doubt about this," it is intended here as well that the liberation from sins conducive to that [knowledge] alone is meant; thus it was said, "by those opposed to the arising of devotion to Me. Furthermore, whether the Supreme Lord of the World is realized or not realized, there is no occasion for delusion such that its negation would be necessary. And how can the Supreme Person alone be the Great Lord of the World while Brahmā, Rudra, Sanaka, and others remain living? Or...

In response to the doubt that there might be a distinction [of the Lord] from the class of eternal Sūris even though He is characterized as both bound and liberated, he clarifies the manner in which delusion arises and its nature by saying, "This has been stated. Since in the world one observes various species among the respective presiding deities, there is room for doubt here as well, despite the general understanding [of His nature].

Just as with the presiding deities of humans, gods, and so forth, the sovereignty of the presiding deities of the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) and others is also dependent upon the will of the Lord, whose scope regarding space and time is limited and rooted in specific karma.

By virtue of its logical connection (*arthayogitayā*), the Lord alone possesses sovereignty that is devoid of any upper limit. The intended meaning is that because the word "Maheśvara" (the Great Lord) is used here to denote sovereignty that extends to all objects, the exclusion of even the eternal beings (*nityas*) is established as a matter of course. To the question, "How is superiority established over those of the same class? it is stated: "by some particular action."

To the question, "How can there be a commonality (*sājātya*) between the Lord of the Egg (*aṇḍādhipati*) and those transmigrating beings whose nature, existence, and activity are dependent upon Him? he says: "Of him also... There are three types of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*): contemplation of action (*karma-bhāvanā*), contemplation of the Veda (*brahma-bhāvanā*), and contemplation of both (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*). Regarding the practice of these three contemplations and so forth for them as well, [the authorities] Bhagavān Parāśara and Śaunaka...

This has been elaborated by the *Dīpikās*. For instance, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha and others, it is said: "All those [beings] beginning with the gods are impure, for they have their origin in karma. And: "From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all living beings situated within the world are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) produced by karma;

therefore, they do not assist those engaged in meditation (*dhyāna*). That these [deities] are not to be worshipped by the enlightened (*pratibuddha*) and that they are dependent upon the Blessed Lord is very clearly stated in the fifth Veda (the Atharvaveda): "The enlightened do not serve the Brāhmaṇa, the blue-throated one (Śiva), nor any other deities who are remembered [as such]."

"Because their fruit is limited, these two are remembered as the best of the wise—[namely] grace and wrath; following the paths shown by them, they are the agents of creation and dissolution," and so forth. The word "ca" (and) serves to combine [Hiraṇyagarbha] with the state of being an effect and other such qualities, along with his connection to the three states (*bhāva*). By referring to the class of Brahmā’s sons, beginning with Sanaka, Sanatkumāra, and Rudra, he says, "as well as others. [The phrase] "aṇimādi" [refers to the supernatural powers].

The powers of *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, and *vaśitva*—as well as the mention of the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) being uncreated (*akṛtrima*) in some instances—indicate that [these powers] were established from birth. Otherwise, there would be contradiction with such passages as: "Mahādeva, the Great Soul, having offered himself into the Mahāmegha [sacrifice], became the God of gods. With the intention that the word "world" (*loka*)—derived from the etymology "that which is perceived" (*lokya*)—encompasses everything, he says "the effect" (*kārya*).

The phrase beginning with "entire" (*nikhila*) is an explanation of what is intended by the word "great" (*maha*); and "by having the nature of exclusive governance" explains the word "Lord" (*īśvara*).

Explaining what is intended by the statement "for the sake of the arising and increase of devotion," and [establishing] the connection of the forthcoming section with what has been said and its resulting fruit, he says, "Thus. To avoid the redundancy of the two words *buddhi* and *jñāna*, he explains them as referring respectively to cause and effect— either through the use of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the usage "he knows because of his intelligence" (*buddhimattvāt jānāti*), or through the etymological derivation "that by which one perceives" (*buddhyate anayā*).

"Buddhi" is the capacity of the mind for discernment (*nirūpaṇa*). With the intention that what is intended here is the knowledge (*jñāna*) which serves as the cause for non-delusion (*asaṃmoha*), he says: "Knowledge is a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding the specific distinctions between conscious and unconscious entities. The explanation of the two words *buddhi* and *jñāna* as referring respectively to "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) and "liberating cognition" (*mokṣadhī*) is disregarded, as it would entail the undesirable consequence of restricting the scope of these two terms. Delusion (*saṃmoha*) is the notion of similarity among dissimilar things; he illustrates this with the word "previous" (*pūrva*).

The meaning is: "from what was previously grasped," that is, from what was experienced as residing in [the state of] *āpatti* (affliction) and so forth. And this is an illustration of the attainment of the path of recollection (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The word "forbearance" (*kṣamā*) is not used merely because of the absence of the modification called anger in states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the like; rather, its application is intended to mean its use when the causes of anger are present but [anger itself] is absent. With this in mind, he says: "by the modification of the mind. The meaning is: even though there exists abuse, beating, and so forth—which are the causes of anger—[there is no anger]. But how can there be the cessation of an effect when its cause is present? If that were the case...

Its status as a cause would indeed be lost. It is replied: there is no rule that an effect must necessarily exist when a cause is present; rather, [the objection arises] from the consequence that [the cause] would be unimpeded, constant, and universal, because a cause that is eternal and all-pervading would always be present. If it is asked, "In that case, what is so wonderful about forbearance? [the answer is:

just as a collection of conditions for a boil is suppressed by gems, mantras, and the like, so too is the collection of conditions for anger suppressed by the powerful obstacle known as discernment (*viveka*).

The sense is that [the truth] is difficult to restrain because of its obstruction. Although the perception of the reality of things as they truly are is also required, nevertheless, there is no fault on the part of the speaker regarding mere speech according to what was seen, because error may come about by chance; with this intention, it is stated merely as "concerning what was seen. Since truth is rejected by such statements as "Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings, even if it is a cause of harm to others," [truth] is defined as being of the nature of benefit to living beings.

It is thus specified. With the intention that the word *bhāva* (state/feeling) possesses a well-known excellence when applied to a mental modification (*manovṛtti*), and following the principle of "the foremost being the standard" (*agrayaprāyanaya*), he states that the word *satya* (truth) is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) by saying "conducive to that. Although each of the two words *śama* (tranquility) and *dama* (self-restraint) has the capacity to denote the restraint of both [internal and external senses], since the repetition must be avoided, a distinction of objects must be stated; therefore, in accordance with the order of restraint, it is said that *dama* and *śama* have the external and internal organs as their respective objects. This is because restraint [is required] from scriptural injunctions...

Because they are prohibited, it was stated that [the senses] are directed toward objects that are harmful (*anartha*). "In the same way" means precisely toward those harmful objects. While the mere quality of being favorable and the mere quality of being unfavorable constitute the definitions of pleasure and pain respectively, nevertheless, the word "experience" (*anubhava*) is used in order to establish that they are modifications of the mind (*manovṛtti*). Since [pleasure and pain] are listed in the middle of the sequence beginning with "existence, non-existence, fear, and fearlessness," even in the case of "existence and non-existence," their status as having mutually contradictory objects must not be abandoned. And therefore—

Between the words *bhava* and *abhāva*, there is merely a difference in suffixes, but no difference in meaning; furthermore, in this context, the word division should be taken as *a-bhāva*. It must also be stated that both of these are of the nature of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).

Moreover, it is appropriate that pleasure and pain—the two topics at hand—are the causes of those [modifications]; thus, the alternative explanation by others, such as "existence (*bhava*) means intention," and so forth, is weak. This, therefore...

Intending to encompass all this, he says "anukūla" (favorable). By the word *bhavana*, exaltation (*uddharṣa*) is intended here, because it is the opposite of depression (*avasāda*). For the author of the Sūtras stated in the context of *sahokti*: "The attainment of that [equanimity] comes from discernment, detachment, practice, virtuous action, and being neither depressed nor exalted. To avoid the redundancy of using both the words "pleasure" (*sukha*) and "pain" (*duḥkha*), he shows that the words "fear" (*bhaya*) and "fearlessness" (*abhaya*) refer to specific aspects of those two by stating "āgami... [and so on].

"No. Even according to the definition that "fear is the apprehension of future harm," it is that very same specific cognition which constitutes suffering (*duḥkhatva*) because of its disagreeable nature.

For in our system (*darśana*), there is no other quality (*guṇa*) called "suffering. In the phrase "not being a cause of another's suffering," the word "suffering" is intended to mean that which is harmful (*ahita*); for in medical treatment and the like, causing pain that is beneficial in form does not constitute violence (*hiṃsā*). This has already been explained at length previously, in connection with the prohibition of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).

The recollection of an enemy who has become the object of violence arises; therefore, with the intention that the equality toward enemies and friends—which is elaborated in another section—is what is intended here due to the absence of hatred and the like, he says, "in oneself" (*ātmani*). The statement of the venerable Parāśara, "one whose mind is equal toward one's own side and the opposing side," is recalled here by those respective words. Regarding "in matters of gain and loss" (*arthānarthayoḥ*): it should be understood as [equality] toward one's own benefit and the benefit of others, and toward one's own harm and the harm of others, and so forth.

Because "contentment" (*tuṣṭi*) is recited alongside "equanimity" (*samatā*), the word "all" (*sarva*) is used for the purpose of including even the prosperity of enemies; for contentment alone is naturally attained by the self everywhere, whereas enmity and the like depend upon limiting conditions such as the perception of adversity—this is the intended meaning behind the statement that [compassion] has contentment as its essential nature. Furthermore, this is the mental cultivation known as "sympathetic joy" (*muditā*) among the four beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This is stated in order to exclude the asceticism (*tapas*) of those whose afflictions are rooted in external scriptures and the like.

Regarding the term *śāstrīya* (prescribed by scripture): it is stated as "bodily affliction" (*kāyakleśa*) to indicate that there is no status of austerity (*tapas*) when a scripturally prescribed restriction of enjoyment—though resulting from illness and the like—is devoid of the nature of suffering. Regarding "giving" (*dāna*), the phrase "of one's own objects of enjoyment" (*svakīya-bhogyānām*) is used to exclude the giving of things belonging to others, as well as even one's own things that are of a nature to be abandoned. The meaning of "bestowing upon another" (*parasmai pratipādanam*) is the production of another's ownership (*parasvatvāpādanam*). Since the mere state of being known (*prathātvamātra*) is common to both [types of giving], therefore—

The distinction is made by means of "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) and "being devoid of qualities" (*nairguṇya*). This and what follows are as explained previously. With the manner of a lion's glance (*siṃhāvalokitaka*), he says: "and likewise austerity and charity. The meaning is that these are specific modifications of the mental faculty (*manovṛtti-viśeṣa*). Intending to show that they are indicative marks (*upalakṣaṇa*) rather than merely those already mentioned, he says: "such as these. *Bhāva* refers even to intention (*abhiprāya*).

In this context, due to the usage of the word "bhāva," it is the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) that is the object [of the term]. Regarding the fact that all factors—such as the agent, the instrument, and so forth—are dependent on Him for their activity, He says "the causes of engagement and withdrawal" (*pravṛttinivṛttihetavaḥ*) to establish this by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument. In the phrase "from Me alone" (*matta eva*), the status of being a cause understood through the ablative case is stated to be by way of an operation (*vyāpāramukhena*), in order to exclude what others have asserted, such as mere proximity (*sannidhimātra*). The intention of the particle "alone" (*eva*) is that I am the single cause even of those various things that are mutually contradictory.

Even among those great beings renowned as the causes of creation and maintenance, who stand in a relationship of cause and effect, one should not entertain the suspicion of independence; rather, even though they are produced by the volition of others, their root must be understood to lie in my own volition—it is with this intention that he says "of all" (*sarvasya*), providing the Great Sages (*maharṣayaḥ*) as an illustration.

The phrase "of whom these creatures in the world [are born]" is intended to express this very point, namely, "of the entire collection of beings," and so forth. [The mention of] "creation and maintenance" refers to the Great Sages.

And this should be applied sequentially among humans. Here, for the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*), the qualification "immediately preceding" (*anantarātīta*) is intended, as was previously [stated] for the case of Manu. Regarding "Bhṛgu and the others," the fact that they are the foremost will be stated in the words, "Among the great sages, I am Bhṛgu. The word "seven" is used to remind one of such passages as, "These seven are declared in the Purāṇas to be Brāhmaṇas. With the intention that they are the founders of the lineages (*gotra*) of those to be chosen in the selection of a Ṛṣi-ancestry, he says:

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of perpetually setting in motion creation": the word *nitya* (perpetual) is used to exclude occasional (*naimittika*) creation and the like. Regarding the phrase "born from the mind of Brahmā": this refers to such passages as, "In the beginning, he created seven sons from his mind," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "Indeed, during a day of Brahmā, fourteen Manus preside in succession, and there is only one Manu in a single *manvantara*; how then can there be four? To this, he replies: "And those who belong to the Sāvarṇikas. This refers to the days of Brahmā.
Rudrasāvarṇi, Dharmasāvarṇi, and Dakṣasāvarṇi—these four were born as mind-born sons of Dakṣa’s daughter; they were of my own nature.

Only this much is to be enjoined here; the word *yat* (that which) is used to indicate that everything else is merely restated (*anūdyate*) as already established by the Purāṇas and other sources. Regarding the phrase *santānamaya* (consisting of lineage): according to the reading "the world (*jana*) is said to be the people (*loka*)," the "world" here refers to the lineage. The meaning is: those who are born into the world, i.e., those born from one's sons, grandsons, and so forth. The demonstrative pronoun *imāḥ* (these) includes even the eternal creation that persists through different times; it does not exclude it, for [this is] the Lord’s [creation].

With the intention that [the knowledge] there too is immediate (*aparokṣya*), he says: "moment by moment until the dissolution. The terms "producers" (*utpādakāḥ*) and "protectors" (*pālakāḥ*) refer respectively to the great seers (*maharṣis*) and the Manus. However, in the reading with feminine endings, such as "producers" (*utpādikāḥ*), the connection is to be made with the respective subjects as appropriate. "My state" (*mama yo bhāvaḥ*)...

"Those whose state (*bhāva*) is that very [state]"—this is a statement resulting from grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "state," or it is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*). He shows that this designation is made with respect to the similarity of intention, as in the expression "the state of a servant is indeed the state of the king," by saying "they abide in my view. By this, he excludes both the similarity of intention arising from mere independence (as in the case of a servant or similar) and mere following after [his will] intentionally, by saying "those who follow my resolve."

"Both this majesty (vibhūti) and yoga"—this is a restatement of the previously mentioned subject matter according to the sequence of the intellect. This same meaning has been stated in due order in the summary verse beginning with "Your own auspiciousness" (*svakalyāṇa*). Following that, the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence are explained by [the author] starting with "Majesty is sovereignty" (*vibhūtir aiśvaryam*). "Majesty" refers to the state in which the origin, maintenance, and activity of everything are always dependent upon Him.
