Because they are defined by that [dependence], there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between them and that [Lord]. This applies to both origin and maintenance as well.

Because it is dependent upon volition (*saṅkalpa*), it is the object of regulation. Here, "activity" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the operation for the sake of one's own effect, since [terms such as] "motion" (*spanda*) are not universal. Lexicographers state: "Vibhūti means manifestation (*bhūti*) or sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Furthermore, the word *vibhu* has been used previously in the sense of a controller. Therefore, in this context, "vibhavana" denotes precisely regulation, because that meaning is natural to its etymological derivation (*bhāvārtha*) and because there is no contradiction. This is similar to how the word *vibhūti* occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other entities.

The nature of that which is to be restrained will be explained later. By the etymological derivation from the root *yuj*, "yoga" here is said to possess both genders (masculine and neuter). The phrase "without beginning" (*aprakampena*) is stated in order to show that one must abandon the superimposition of non-independence, suffering, ignorance, and so forth upon the Lord—who is in fact independent—and likewise the superimposition of independence established by Himself upon the non-Lord, who is actually dependent on the Lord. Based on the consideration of what precedes and follows, he states through the word "devotion" (*bhakti*) that the term "yoga," when associated with a practitioner, refers specifically to a particular kind of yoga.

Regarding the phrase "by yoga": with the intention that even for an object established by scripture, extreme clarity occurs only when there is direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), he clarifies the underlying meaning of the statement "there is no doubt here" with the words "my own manifestations."
With the intention of elaborating upon the meaning already stated by way of demonstrating its removal [of obstacles], he says: "Vibhūtijñāna...

(Vibhūti-jñāna). With the intention that this very knowledge transforms into the form of devotion (*bhakti*), there is the statement regarding its being the "fruition" (*vipāka*) of the knowledge of the manifestations (*vibhūti*). With the intention that the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the entire range of effects, beginning with Brahmā, without restriction, the words "variegated" (*vicitra*) and so forth were spoken. Here, the word "origin" (*prabhava*) signifies the action of arising and so on.

He says "the cause of origination" (*utpattikāraṇam*) in order to exclude the sense of being subordinate (*traparatva*). Herein is also implicitly included the possession of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa-yoga*), which will be explained later in the manner of creation. With the intention that even the capacity for the activity of the *brahmā* and others is dependent upon me—thus meaning "everything [proceeds] from me"—he says "all."

"From Me alone" (matta eva). With the words "Thus this," etc., he shows that [the passage] has the nature of a restatement of the previously mentioned manifestations and so forth. By the two terms "inherent" (svābhāvika) and "unrestrained" (niraṅkuśa), there is a statement of the lack of limitation regarding cause and effect as established by Śruti, in order to exclude [the notion of] a modern-day Īśvara. Regarding the word "Me" (mām), which is intended in the sense of the speaker’s incarnation being easily accessible, he explains the meaning of the word "yoga"—which is extremely useful for the devotion (bhajana) expressed in the phrase "they worship Me"—with the words beginning with "of good character" (sauśīlya), etc. Because of his good character...

The word *salya* is used for the purpose of demonstrating the class of divine qualities of the Self; *saundarya* [is used] for the class of qualities of the most attractive, divine, and auspicious form. With the intention that by the word *budha* (wise) those previously mentioned great souls possessing the specific knowledge under discussion are intended, the term *jñāninaḥ* (the knowers) is stated. The grammatical construction is: "having understood, they are endowed with devotion" (*matvā bhāvamanvitāḥ*). Since the purport is that such knowledge is a means to devotion (*bhakti*), by the word *mām* (me), the qualities to be contemplated during the state of worship are indicated here.
He states the meaning of the group as "bhāva is a particular state of mental activity," and clarifies that very distinction with the words "those who long for me."

With the intention that the detailed exposition of the state of non-possession [of other qualities] is to be performed immediately hereafter, he shows the expectation for that by asking, "How? With the intention that the demonstration of the specific forms established through the particular sequence of the ripening of devotion is carried out by the four qualifiers beginning with "maccittāḥ," he has stated "mayi niviṣṭamanasaḥ" and so forth. To demonstrate the intended meaning of "madgataprāṇāḥ," he first provides a synonym, saying "madgatajīvitāḥ."

Thus [it is said]. To the question, "How is it that the life residing in the devotee is [said to be] 'residing in Him'? he replies with the words "without me" (*mayā vinā*). Since the two terms "awakening" (*bodhana*) and "speaking" (*kathana*) would be redundant if they referred to the same object, a distinction in their scope must be stated. In this regard, with the intention that by the word "awakening" (*bodhayantaḥ*) the making known of an unknown matter is understood, and by "speaking" (*kathayantaḥ*) the description of what has already occurred is understood as existing within oneself, he says "by their respective [means]" (*svaiḥ svaiḥ*), and so forth. The term "divine" (*divyāni*) signifies superhuman nature (*atimānuṣatva*).

What is intended here is the state of being a marvelous performance (*adbhutattva*). Its very quality of being an object of enjoyment is expressed by the word "delightful" (*ramaṇīyāni*). Since both [the terms] "they are satisfied" (*tuṣyanti*) and "they rejoice" (*ramanti*) refer to the storyteller and do not have significantly different meanings, they would serve little purpose [if used together]. Therefore, it is appropriate that one refers to the storyteller and the other implies the audience as the subject of the narration. Furthermore, in the world, the practice of storytelling is observed to be for the sake of pleasing others in order to achieve some other personal goal of one's own; thus, "satisfaction" (*toṣa*)...

The word *ca* (and) serves to exclude longing for anything else; therefore, the phrase "they are satisfied" (*tuṣyanti*) refers to those who speak with no other motive. By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that "they rejoice" (*ramanti*) is rooted in hearing [the teaching]. Furthermore, regarding the two phrases "they are satisfied" and "they rejoice," their shared agency—as stated in "with their minds fixed on Me" (*maccittāḥ*) and so forth—is not to be discarded, since speaking and hearing can occur at different moments within the same person. Having all this in mind, he says: "those who speak... and so on, ending with "...they rejoice."

It has been stated that knowledge of the Lord’s qualities and manifestations (*vibhūti*) is the cause for the arising and increase of devotion (*bhakti*). It is now said that for one whose devotion has increased in such a manner, this [knowledge] becomes the cause of a specific state consisting of the most vivid direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), which precedes the attainment of the Lord, with the Lord’s grace acting as the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*). This refers to those "who desire constant union (*satatayoga*) with Me. For a yoga consisting of constant meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is not possible; by the word "constant" (*satata*), a daily [practice] is intended.

Furthermore, this [state] is not natural, nor has a continuous connection (*sātatyayoga*) in the form of attainment occurred at present; therefore, the sense is that it is appropriate to take it as having the meaning of an aspiration (*āśaṃsā*).

Regarding the phrase "that very same": the meaning is that it is included within the scope of the aspiration itself. Since the state of being characterized by love (*prītirūpatva*) in devotion is established precisely through the aspiration for continuous connection, the purpose of connecting "preceded by love" (*prītipūrvakam*) with "devotion" (*bhajana*) is weak; however, when connected with "I give" (*dadāmi*), it serves to describe the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of devotion.

With the intention that there is a great purpose in manifesting the multitude of the Blessed One’s qualities, such as His supreme magnanimity, the syntactical connection "I give [it] with affection" was stated.
Regarding the phrase "they come unto Me," those who are deluded by failing to grasp the words and their meanings have explained it as the attainment of identity [with the Lord].

With the intention of stating that the removal of the obstacles to the arising of the aforementioned application of the intellect belongs to those very [beings] themselves, he says, "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). Here, by the word *anukampā* (compassion), what is intended is not mere innate pity, but rather a specific grace (*prasāda*)—as will be stated in the phrase "for my grace"—which is the cause for the attainment of the desired after the cessation of the undesired.

For if it were taken to mean mere innate compassion, the word *artha* (purpose/benefit) would be redundant; and if it were taken to mean something else, there would be no further purpose. As for its being an object of a mental modification (*manovṛtti*), however...

The sense is that this is extremely useful for the yoga of the intellect (*buddhi-yoga*). To the question, "What kind of unprecedented state is this of the all-pervading Lord?", it is said here: "as the object" (*viṣayatayā*). For knowledge, which is likened to a lamp, its "luminosity" is its shining forth on all sides; and that must be a shining forth of a specific mode [of being]. With the intention that from such a clear experience comes the cessation of ignorance and the cessation of inclination toward the material qualities (*guṇa*) such as sound, he says: "my auspicious qualities..."

"And manifesting the multitudes" (*gaṇāṃścāviṣkurvan*): because they are designated as being of the nature of causes (*hetu*), a different meaning must be expressed here for the words "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) and "darkness" (*tamas*). Furthermore, the word "ignorance" refers to action (*karman*) by virtue of its opposition to knowledge; as it has been said: "Ignorance is another [power] known as action. And "darkness," which is produced by action and acts as an obstacle to the light consisting of the direct intuition of the Lord, is by the very nature of things simply the inclination toward other objects. [This is] the unsurpassed object of enjoyment...

It is logical that the knowledge of the Blessed One causes the cessation of inclination toward other objects of enjoyment, according to the maxim beginning with "When the lotus has bloomed" (*sthite 'ravinde*).

Having this in mind, it was stated that [knowledge] is opposed to ignorance (*jñānavirodhī*), and so forth. By the word *tamas* (darkness), the view that it is characterized by the function of *tamas* (the quality of inertia) is also refuted by this.

Although devotion (*bhajana*) is preceded by the cessation of inclination toward sense objects, nevertheless, that subtle inclination which persists due to the residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is said here to be destroyed by devotion.
Thus, there is no mutual dependence.

He demonstrates the contextual connection between the preceding and following portions of Arjuna’s speech—beginning with *paraṃ brahma* and ending with *amṛtam*—by the word *evam*. The phrase *sakaletara-*, etc., is stated by way of reflecting on the passage beginning with *yo mām ajam*. He states what was expressed by the words *tuṣyanti ca ramanti ca*: "it generates unsurpassed bliss for those who hear it."

Although the word "in detail" (*vistara*) was used by both the questioner and the respondent in the phrases "my own yoga in detail" and "of me [the teaching] in detail," it is stated that "desirous of hearing its expansion" (*tadvistāraṃ śrotukāmaḥ*) in order to show that the intended meaning of the word "detail" here refers to the expansion of the subject matter (*arthaprapañca*), as indicated by the word "detail" itself, since the matter to be explained consists of such an expansion.

Desiring to hear the detailed exposition, Arjuna demonstrates his understanding of the meaning stated in brief and his lack of malice—based on his conviction in its truth—through the verses beginning with "The supreme Brahman" (*paraṃ brahma*). Here, because the word *bhavān* (you) ends in the nominative case, it cannot be syntactically connected with the subsequent verb *āhuḥ* (they say). Furthermore, since the words "the supreme Brahman" and so forth appear first, they are perceived as the subject (*uddeśya*), while *bhavān* is perceived as the predicate (*vidheya*). And for a subject, its prior establishment is required.

Thus he says: "For you are that whom the Vedas declare. He cites the scriptural passages (śrutis) in their respective order for all three [cases]. Among them, the passage beginning with "From which, verily... (*yato vā*) is the statement defining the Brahman to be meditated upon (*upāsya-brāhma*). The statement "the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*) is employed as a corollary (*purovāda*) to demonstrate that the Brahman to be meditated upon is indeed the supreme goal to be attained, and to establish the qualification of the word "supreme" (*para*). In both instances, the passage "He who [knows this]... (*sa yo ha*) is extremely clear.

The statement "he becomes Brahman indeed" has been explained in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*. Furthermore, when there is identity of mode (*prakāraikye*), the usage of the term for the essence (*tattvavyavahāraḥ*) is primary (*mukhya eva*), as in the expression "this is that cow. The designation "Brahman" due to similarity with the end of Brahman means that it is almost primary (*mukhyaprāya*). The example "this is that cow" also concerns a designation based on similarity (*sādhamryamūla*). Alternatively, some hold that even in the phrase "he becomes Brahman indeed," the particle *eva* may have the sense of the word *iva*, because of the existence of the *Nighaṇṭu* lexicon which states: "the words *iva*, *vat*, *vai*, and *eva* [are synonyms]."

Furthermore, because there exist ritual injunctions such as, "One who is contending should sacrifice a dwarf (vāmana) dedicated to Viṣṇu; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds," it is clear that here one does not become Viṣṇu merely by means of the animal sacrifice. Nor does one who is contending possess the qualification for liberation. Moreover, the result indicated is not merely "he becomes Viṣṇu," but rather "he conquers these worlds," which refers to a worldly fruit.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that by being endowed with qualities such as prowess, one becomes like Viṣṇu and conquers these worlds. Thus, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "he indeed becomes Brahman" is based on the reason of similarity (*sādharmya*). [This is supported by the scriptural statement: "He attains supreme equality. Having introduced the subject matter for the purpose of demonstrating this scripture, he clarifies it with the words beginning with "tathā" (so). Because of the usage of grammatical coordination, and because there is no mention of coordination with other distinct entities, [it refers to] the Lord's [identity] with those respective scriptures...

He demonstrates that the intended meaning is connected through the manifestation of the mode of supremacy already established, by means of the passage beginning with "the supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*) and "then that which is beyond this" (*atha yadataḥ*). Furthermore, because of the unity of context with the *Puruṣasūkta*, whose purport is established by such designations, everything desired is proven: by the sentence "having attained the supreme light," the fact that it is to be reached by the liberated and so forth is established, as is the specific usage of the term "supreme light."

By the passage beginning with "That which is the light of lights," its supremacy is established by implication through its being the object of worship for the gods and its status as the light of all lights. To demonstrate the purifying power that is unique to the Lord and qualified by the word "supreme" (parama), the author uses the term "the supreme purifier" (paramaṃ pāvanam) here, in order to exclude the possibility of it being a mere name (*saṃjñā*). In the phrase "that which causes destruction," the two instances of the word *kalmaṣa* have lost their case-endings; however, based on the parallel reading in passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Reality," they are understood to be separate words ending in the nominative case. It is exactly so.

It is studied with its case-endings in another Vedic text, beginning with "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," and so forth. By this, the one who is not averse to the Lord—who asserts that [the compound] is a genitive (pañcamī) tatpuruṣa—is refuted, as it contradicts all Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtra, and reasoning. In the statement "for thus the Śrutis declare," the entire passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]" is to be understood as following; the intermediate phrases are subordinate sentences intended to clarify those respective meanings.

Thus, he states that the meaning established by the Śruti is also established by the words of the great sages—who appear in the form of Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa—and by the words of the Omniscient One, which, like the Śruti, require no other authority.

With the words "the Person" (puruṣam), [the text] includes half a verse. By the word "all" (sarva), the quality of being uncontradicted is intended. The phrase "knowers of the true nature of the higher and lower principles" is an expression intended by the word "sages" (ṛṣi);

by this, it is stated that they possess authoritative knowledge. With the intention of excluding other specific [deities] such as Brahmā and Rudra, the word "you" (tvām) is used; or rather, it means "you who have descended. "Eternal" (śāśvatam) means permanent. "Divine" (divyam) means residing in the supreme heaven. "The Person" (puruṣam) refers to the one who dwells in the city (puri), beyond the highest.

This has been established in passages such as, "He beholds the Person who lies within. The reversal of the order in the expression "the eternal, divine Person" (śāśvataṃ divyaṃ puruṣam) is intended to indicate that the eternality of the Person residing in heaven is here meant in His specific form characterized by the immortal three-quartered manifestation proclaimed in the *Puruṣasūkta*.

The term *ādideva* means "the primordial God"—that is, the cause of the universe whose activity consists of the world as a form of sport (*līlā*). And they [the authorities] remember this: "Like a playing child," and "As a child with toys. This has also been aphorized: "But like the world, it is mere sport. By this, it is stated that even Brahmā and others who have entered into the class of gods are instruments for the sport of the Supreme Person and are His effects. "Nārāyaṇā..."

By the process [of manifestation] described in such passages as, "From Nārāyaṇa is born Brahmā, from Nārāyaṇa is born Rudra," and "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa—neither Brahmā nor Īśāna," and "We two were produced from your body," His state of being changeless (nirvikāratva) is expressed. The term "vibhu" means all-pervading like space and eternal; or, according to the process [of manifestation], it refers to Him who is pervasive; or, it means the Ruler. By this, the pervasiveness and governance appropriate for the status of being the Cause, as established in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and other texts, are recalled. By these words, [it is shown that] He is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa.

Thus it was indicated. Although the word "all" (*sarva*) provides a general summary, Nārada and others are mentioned separately because of the intention to express their authoritative status (*āptatva*). By the term "divine sage" (*devarṣi*), their preeminence in *sattva* (purity) is also revealed by way of their class. Among them, he [Nārada] is the most excellent, as it is said: "And among the divine sages, Nārada. Asita and Devala were his father. And the venerable Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara. "All the sages speak of you," and so forth.

The phrase *saṃvādayati yeceti* (and he corroborates this with those who... is explained as follows: the connection is that those who know the Vedas (*vedavidaḥ*), meaning those who know the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) of the Vedas, and those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavidaḥ*), meaning those who know the meaning of the Vedānta, declare Kṛṣṇa to be the Great Soul (*mahātman*) and the eternal Dharma. By the word *mahātman*, all-pervading supreme sovereignty and so forth are intended; or else, it signifies the state of being the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as in the passage: "He indeed is this great, unborn Self" (*sa vā eṣa mahānaja ātmā*). For sacrifices, gifts, and the like are limited by space, time, and other such factors.

[Other dharmas] yield fruits [that are themselves] impermanent, whereas this [dharma] yields an eternal and unsurpassed fruit and is itself eternal; thus, the word *sanātana* (eternal) is an epithet of dharma. Here, the word *pavitra* (purifying) refers to the destruction of sin; the word *puṇya* (meritorious) refers to the means for attaining specific desired fruits; and the word *maṅgala* (auspicious) refers to an auspicious entity that becomes the cause of great prosperity by its mere presence. The expression "the three worlds are the lotus-eyed one" (*trailokyaṃ puṇḍarīkākṣa*) is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based either on the relationship of cause and effect or on the relationship of body and embodied. "The three worlds" (*trailokya*) refers to the bound, the liberated, and the eternal beings.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, by way of illustration, the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth are mentioned. By the term *puṇḍarīkākṣa* (Lotus-eyed), the possession of a distinct form as established in the *Antarāditya-vidyā* is shown. Regarding the statement, "As a lotus is like the buttocks of a monkey, so are his eyes," among the six meanings uttered in the Draviḍa commentary, those three meanings which were adopted by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are as follows: Thus, indeed: [text continues]

This has been shown in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*: "His eyes are as pure and long as the petals of a white lotus that has blossomed by the rays of the sun upon a beautiful lotus stalk emerging from deep waters.
And this has been elaborated upon by Varadaguru in the *Tattvasāra*: "By the word 'Nārāyaṇa,' [the text] establishes that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme reality."

This indicates the *anuvākas*. Beginning with "The glorious one whose abode is the ocean of milk," and continuing with "For *Hī* and *Lakṣmī* are your two wives," "In the shoreless waters," and "Him who is within the ocean," and so forth, [the text] has been recalled. By the phrase "having come after leaving," what is intended is merely his descent [into the world]; for even during the state of the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, his form, reclining upon the serpent-couch in the ocean of milk, remained right there. Directly...

[The word "iti"] does not mean figurative (*aupacārika*), but rather that it is designated by another name; such is the meaning. The word "tathā" (so) is used to indicate a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratva*). Since the division of the passage to be explained is understood from the statement "the celestial sage Nārada likewise," it is shown that we shall also apply the citation of the aforementioned sentence according to that same division.

In that regard, the phrase "entirely" (*kṛtsnam*) and so forth refers to Nārāyaṇa alone, because he is the locus of all things, or because he possesses excellence in every respect. The portion beginning with "that merit" (*tatpuṇyam*) and so forth belongs to Brāhma.

[The passage] may have Nārāyaṇa as its subject matter according to the literal force of the words, or it may be a praise of the place [Vaikuṇṭha] resting upon Him according to the specific context. "By yourself" means that you alone are self-knowing and the teacher even of Brahmā and the others. In passages such as "Earth, water," etc., His status as the Lord of all, His being the cause of all, and His being the body of all have been stated.

He says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) for the purpose of establishing consistency; the sense is that this has been stated by the great sages through authoritative traditions (*āmnāya*) and by you as well. He states the intended meaning of "I consider [this] truth" (*ṛtaṃ manye*) to be that it does not intend praise or the like; for the intention [of such statements] is that one praises others by attributing those qualities to them. By the word "me" (*mām*), he intends such passages as "I am your disciple; teach me, who have taken refuge in you. Here, the root *vad* refers to instructing while repeating what has been taught by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

When used in this sense, it takes two objects. Thus, the restatement of what has been taught is for the purpose of requesting a specific instruction. By the two qualifiers "not shared by others" (*ananyasādhāraṇa*) and "limitless and unsurpassed" (*anavadhikātiśaya*), the absence of any equal or superior is intended; by "inherent" (*svabhāvika*), independence from anything else is meant. Therefore, the connection is not with "they do not know. [As stated: "Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor—in their entirety, and devoid of all qualities subject to abandonment—these are the meanings denoted by the word *Bhagavat*."

In accordance with this statement of the Blessed Parāśara, he demonstrates the meaning of the word "Bhagavat" as that which is unknowable by gods and others, beginning with the words "supreme knowledge" (niratiśaya-jñāna). Here, the word "manifestation" (vyakti) does not refer to a physical body or the like, as it might in such passages as "of what nature is this manifestation of the Bhagavat? and so forth.

[The opponent's view is] remote because it is not relevant, and because it was not asked about immediately [after the previous statement]. Therefore, since [the Lord] intends to speak immediately after saying, "You ought to tell me in its entirety," one must accept the meaning: "Others do not even know the manner of your teaching, let alone its manifestation like perception and other means of knowledge. With this intention, he says, "the manner of manifestation" (*vyañjanaprakāram*), just as in the phrase, "the manifestation of the syllable and the non-syllable. For the expression "those of limited knowledge" (*parimitajñānāḥ*) is a statement intended to convey the purport of the words.

The capacity of the gods and others to describe the majesty of the Blessed One has been rejected; now, with the verse beginning "He Himself," [the Lord] speaks of His own capacity to declare His own majesty. Here, the designation "Puruṣottama" is used; as for the remainder, it refers to the qualities conducive to that designation. To distinguish this, the address "O Puruṣottama" was already employed previously. In this context, regarding the Self, the intention is based on such scriptural and traditional texts as: "You alone know Yourself, who You are."

The word *tvām* (you) is the substitute for *mām* (me). By the phrase *svayameva* (by oneself alone), the statement of the result is expressed as "by one's own knowledge alone. The meaning is that [it occurs] by the self (*ātmanā*) without being assisted by others. The sense is that it is not like other [beings], for whom it is said, "From me comes memory and knowledge" (*mattaḥ smṛtirjñānam*). Alternatively, the word *jñānena* (by knowledge) is an explanation of *ātmanā*; for the term *ātman* is listed in the sense of "living being" (*jīva*), as well as in "effort," "the sun," "fire," and "intellect" (*matau*).

In order to exclude the sense of "meditation" (*cintā*) and other meanings for the word *bhāvana*, he says "the producer" (*utpādayitṛ*). To dispel the suspicion of tautology between the two terms *bhūteśa* ("Lord of beings") and *jagatpati* ("Lord of the world"), he states his nature as the controller (*niyantṛ*) rather than the owner (*svāmin*). Although the word *pati* is etymologically derived in the sense of "protection," it has a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of "one who is the superior" (*śeṣitva*). [As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords, Him, the supreme Deity of deities; the Lord of lords..."

"May we know the Supreme God, the Lord of the world, the one to be praised, who exists beyond the highest. To make it known that these four meanings established by the Śruti are expounded by the four phrases beginning with "the creator of beings" (*bhūtabhāvana*), the term "the supreme deity even among deities" (*daivatānām api paramadaivata*) is explained by means of the words found in the Śruti. Since the word *deva* denotes a specific class and thus lacks a correlative (it is not a relative term), the second occurrence of the word *deva* is used figuratively to refer to a particular excellence; thus, he shows the basis for this figurative usage as following from both the primary and secondary senses, by saying "as follows."

The mention of beasts, birds, and reptiles is for the purpose of showing that mutual distinctness is of no consequence, and to demonstrate absolute difference. Just as a worm is to the gods and others, so too are even the gods to the Supreme Self. As they say: "When [the Self] is seen, all worms are regarded as gods. The analysis of the compound is *saundarya-sauśīlya* (beauty and good character).
This is an illustration of both [external] qualities and the qualities of the self.

He states that the word *ātman* is for the purpose of excluding [the Lord's] being a mere manifestation (*vibhūti*) of another, by saying "as something unique to You" (*tvadasādhāraṇye*). Since it is impossible to connect [the word] with the verb "you ought to speak" (*vaktum arhasi*) while treating *vibhūtayaḥ* as a nominative plural, one must supply the relative pronoun *yāḥ* (which ones), so that it becomes "those which are manifestations. Alternatively, since they are indeed divine, they must necessarily be spoken of; therefore, the phrase "you ought to speak of them" implies a repetition of the sentence. By the indication of fitness in the word "you ought" (*arhasi*), the request for that [speaking] is intended.

Since it is impossible for even the Lord to speak it in its entirety and for Arjuna to hear it, what is requested here is merely its manifestation through words and grace. With the intention that this was already stated previously in the verse, "For Your manifestation, O Blessed One," he says, "The meaning is: You Yourself must reveal [it]. Because there is no restriction on the plural number and because of the mention of "in its entirety" (*aśeṣeṇa*), infinity is intended here, as in: "There is no end to Your expansion."

With the intention that [this is known] from such subsequent passages as "and so forth," it is said "by infinite [powers]. It has been stated that the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *vi-* and ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) signifies "restraining" (*niyamana*). Furthermore, with the intention that no other meaning is appropriate here—due to the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which is to be restrained—it is said "by those specific restraints.

The word *viśeṣa* is used to indicate an excess of curiosity regarding the vast range of objects to be restrained. Since the instrumental case here cannot have the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or the like, it is used in the sense of "having become thus" (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).

With the intention that the sense of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is intended, the word "proper" (*yukta*) was stated. Here, if the word *vibhūti* were taken to mean "those to be governed," then the aśvattha tree and the others would not be the cause of pervading the world; nor would there be a pervasion of that which is qualified by them, or of [the world] together with them, or of anything other than them. Furthermore, those to be governed could not serve as characteristics (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*) for the act of pervasion, because that would be purposeless. However, since specific modes of governance follow from scripture, [the term] serves to exclude the pervasion of space and so forth.

With the intention of explaining how that [omnipresence] arises from being the controller, he says, "pervading as the ruler. For such scriptural passages as "He has entered within, the ruler of people" are heard. By the phrase "pervading, You abide," the scripture, "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading," is recalled.

He states that the word "yogi" refers to a specific type of yogi, both because of the particular context and by the force of the passage beginning with "always contemplating you," etc.; thus he says, "being established in the yoga of devotion. By the word "san" (being), even the status of one who has already perfected yoga is excluded. Here, the reading of others is "yogin" [without the suffix -san].

It is not [the word] *nārṣaḥ*. Because of the lack of syntactic competency (*asāmarthyāt*), the qualification "always" (*sadā*) is established as [meaning] "through devotion" (*bhaktyā*). Since there is an incapacity for reflection prior to knowledge, and because the phrase "how might I know? functions as a cause for reflection—given the grammatical rule that the suffix *śatṛ* is used in the senses of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*) for an action—it is stated that he has "proceeded to reflect.

Because the specific substratum (*dharmī*) denoted by "you" (*tvām*) is already established, the words "perfectly," etc., are spoken to indicate a desire to know the specific modes (*prakāra-viśeṣa*).

With the intention that a question is for the purpose of making known a specific point not previously understood, it was stated, "as previously mentioned," and so forth. The locative case in the word *bhāveṣu* is intended to express the locus, or it serves as a reference back to the subject at hand by way of its being the controller (*niyantṛtvena*).
He is called Janārdana because he causes those who are hostile to go to hell (naraka), or because his desired object is entreated by those who are favorable.

To indicate the cause for the desire to hear the details, and to clarify the specific meaning intended by the word "Yoga," he speaks the result implied by the word "furthermore" (*bhūyas*): "I [am] the All... Here, because it is mentioned alongside "insatiability" (*atṛpti*), the word "immortality" (*amṛta*) refers to its nature as an object of enjoyment in terms of its majesty. To establish that it is the most excellent object of enjoyment, he says: "which is being spoken by You"—that which has issued from the moon of Your mouth.
The meaning is "that"; he explains what is intended by the word "hi" with the words "mameti."
To Arjuna, who was thus questioning him out of insatiability, the Lord, being exceedingly pleased, demonstrated his fitness by way of describing his noble lineage and other qualities.

Then, because it would be impossible to describe or hear each of His manifestations (vibhūtis) in detail, He said, "Hanta," intending to speak of the manifestations as summarized under certain specific attributes.

The sense is that [Arjuna] is full of such qualities as freedom from envy, being pleased [with the Lord], and lack of satiety. This refers to the primacy of being the sovereign (śeṣitva) in relation to qualities and so forth.

Because there would be no pervasion (vyāpti) of all the examples to be mentioned if every intention to speak were included, and because the qualities are to be designated according to their predominance, he states the specific meaning that serves as the summary by means of the word "predominance" (*prādhānya*). He confirms that this alone is what is intended to be spoken by correlating it with what follows: "of the priests" (*purodhasām*). Regarding the questioner who asks, "Tell it in detail," he says "the world" (*jagati*) to state the summarized meaning. How then can it be said, "I shall tell it according to its predominance"?

Regarding the doubt [that there might be an end], it is said: "There is no end to my expansion. The word "of the manifestations" (*vibhūtīnām*) is the ellipsis to be supplied; for it will be stated later: "The expansion of my manifestation has been told by me. He shows that what is intended by the word "there is not" (*nāsti*) is impossibility—namely, the impossibility of speaking in detail. He states that this is not due to a deficiency in the capacity of either the speaker or the listener, saying: "Because of their infinity. Thus it is said: "There is no end. The term "manifestation" (*vibhūti*) is used with respect to the categories of reality to be described hereafter.

He states the reason for this: "The word *vibhūti* means that which is to be governed. The word *vibhūti*, whose object is that which is to be governed by another, is intended here in the sense of "that which is to be manifested" (*vibhavana-karma*).

The point is that elsewhere—in such passages as "Brahmā, Dakṣa, and others are Time," "Viṣṇu, Manu, and others are Time," and "Rudra, Kālāntaka, and others [are Time]"—the word *vibhūti* is seen used for those things to be governed, as in the phrase "the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of Janārdana. He asks: "Why so? and provides the answer:

"Of all"—the sense is that the aforementioned state of dependence (*tādadhīnya*) is referred to by the word *etat* (this). Furthermore, he shows that the immediately following verse also has that same meaning by saying "likewise" (*tathā*). Now, an objection: in the previous commentary on this verse, it was stated, "the possession of a multitude of auspicious qualities such as amiability, affection, and beauty"; yet here, what is indicated by the word "possession" (*yoga*) is said to be sovereignty and so forth. How is this consistent? It is thus: in both cases, both [sets of qualities] are included by the word "etc. (*ādi*), and therefore they have the same meaning. For this very reason...

Indeed, in the passage "this majesty (vibhūti) and yoga," [the term *yoga*] refers to "the yoga consisting of a multitude of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of what is to be abandoned. However, in the passage "by which majesties," because it is natural for the word *vibhūti* to have the same meaning as the word *vibhūti* found in the preceding question, it is stated to have a restrictive sense. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the question and its answer.

With the intention of stating that the two points asked about—namely, "in detail my yoga and majesty"—are being explained in detail through the pair of answers summarized by the verse beginning with "I am the Self," he says "therein. By this, the two grounds for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) found in the previously mentioned and those yet to be mentioned are stated as appropriate. "Abiding as the Self" demonstrates the actual logical connection of the result; for although the word *ātman* has many meanings...

Because the word *śabda* (sound) is most commonly associated with its substratum, it requires that substratum, which is the body; therefore, with the intention that the word *bhūta*, though not included within the compound, should be extracted by the intellect and connected [to the preceding], he said, "of all beings who have become my body. To the question of how the Lord can be the Self in relation to the elements and individual souls—which are His bodies—he shows the definition of the Self: "For the Self... Thus, the triad is one.

Some say that [the sūtra] provides a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). In that case, following the direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and other means of knowledge, one should consider the threefold nature—beginning with birth—to be the definition of Brahman, and the utility of all three must be understood as serving to exclude even the slightest possibility of doubt. Others, however, maintain that there are three definitions. Regarding this, the distinction is as follows:
"That substance which can be entirely controlled and sustained for its own sake by a conscious being," and so forth.

The definition of the body as stated in the *Bhāṣya* must also be considered. Furthermore, other definitions of the body have been refuted in detail in various places. Our conclusion, which is the intended meaning of the *Bhāṣya*, is that the body is a substance that serves as an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) with respect to that which is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). Here, by the term "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*), only the body is meant.

He says "tathā" (so too) in order to dispel doubts regarding the explanation, to indicate that the word "āśaya" (intention/abode) has the heart as its object, and to establish that being the substratum, the controller, and so forth, are the defining characteristics of the Self. Immediately after the statement "I am the abode of all," the text begins with "These two persons...

and concludes with "The perishable consists of all beings"; from this declaration, it is determined that the word "all beings" refers to the individual soul (kṣetrajña) as qualified by the non-sentient (acid).

The same applies here as well. Likewise, in this very context, after stating, "There is another, the Supreme Person, who is called the Supreme Self," it is said: "The imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. Here, beginning with the words "sustains" and "Lord," [the text] establishes His nature as the substratum and the controller.

It is clear; furthermore, the establishment of lordship is well-known through the conventional usage of the word *īśvara*. Indeed, the term *īśvara* is not applied to those such as Garuḍa who merely restrain snakes and the like. By the inclusion of these two verses, it is shown that the words *īśvara* and *ahaṃ* (I) have a single referent here. For in this context, the word "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*) refers exclusively to the individual soul (*jīva*), because of the statement, "mounted on the machine by Māyā. By the word "causing to wander," the status of being a controller and so forth is established. And by the mention of abiding in the heart, the capacity for supporting all things—as stated in passages such as "all this is strung upon me"—is indicated. Thus, the entire aggregate consisting of the conscious and the unconscious...

He shows the Śruti stating that [Brahman] is the body-substance of all beings through the non-exclusion of the word "all beings" in the passage beginning, "He who... in all beings. He cites the sentence beginning, "He who... in the self," to elaborate on how [Brahman] is the embodied one with respect to the conscious element (cidaṃśa). He explains the second half of the verse by connecting it with the first half—since abiding as the Self serves the purposes of being both the material cause and the efficient cause—stating, "Thus... Thus, because it abides as the Self, the word "I" refers to one's own immutable nature as the material cause.

This is the establishment [of the sequence]. Since it is improper for there to be a beginning, middle, or end merely from the perspective of space or time, he speaks of their "arising" as a figurative expression for that.

Beginning with “Of the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu” and ending with “And that which is the seed of all beings, O Arjuna, that am I,” [the Lord] introduces this section on grammatical coordination by connecting it with the verse “I am the Self,” saying: “Thus, by the Blessed One... By this, [he explains] the verse beginning with “I am the Self.”

The alternative view—that all four quarters are the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*)—is thus refuted. [The phrase] "specific manifestations" is used because they are mentioned as being primary; this is how it was introduced.

[Objection: But surely words such as "body" (*śarīra*), which denote the body, do not terminate in the Self; likewise here too, it is more logical to accept *lakṣaṇā* (indication) rather than postulating a primary denotative power (*śakti*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*). To this, [the author] says: "The Blessed One," etc. The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies a reason. The meaning is that words denoting inseparably related attributes (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) have a primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) even with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*) through those very [attributes]; since they are established even in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth by way of their functional form, there is no burden of postulating a separate denotative power. This is what is meant by the phrase "they terminate in" (*paryavasyanti*). Words denoting the body [terminate] naturally in that...

He shows that [the terms] terminate in the Self (*ātman*) by means of the condition of non-separable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*), using the word "as" (*yathā*). However, words such as "body" (*śarīra*) do not terminate in the substratum (*dharmin*), because they are "extractive" (*niṣkarṣaka*) words—just like words such as "quality" (*guṇa*). With this intention in mind, it was stated: "Words such as 'god,' 'human,' 'bird,' and 'tree'...

He dispels the suspicion of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and other causes by saying: "by the Lord's being the Self of each of those. For [a statement] that contradicts both the introduction and the conclusion...

The meaning [of the word] must be accepted as being in the middle; the sense is that it is not proper to accept either through delusion or in reality that the Brahmin consists entirely of things to be abandoned. Regarding the phrase "because of the statement of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*): the sense is that the body does not exist without the self. When it is said, "there is no smoke without fire," or "there are no qualities without a possessor of qualities," it follows that either fire and so forth alone are the ultimate reality while smoke and so forth are illusory, or else [fire and so forth] are of the nature of [the smoke].

Or rather, such a cognition does not arise; it is the same in this case as well. [Objection: But when it is said, "There are no others in the house without Yajñadatta," or "There is no serpent and so forth without the rope," one perceives the existence of that one alone and the non-existence of everything else besides it; why should it not be the same here? To this he replies: "And because of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). Since the commencement (*upakrama*) is incompatible with the time of the contradiction, there is no arising of the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) due to its opposition to the commencement. Thus, regarding the commencement...

The sense is that this is established by the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddha* (established by the context). By the phrase "by way of being governed," even the disparity between the pervasion of smoke and fire is demonstrated.

Thus, with this much of the text, the view of the wicked who claim that the statement, "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings," expresses the identity of the individual souls (*jīvas*) residing in all bodies with the nature of Brahman, has been uprooted.

"Of the Ādityas," that is, of the offspring of the Ādityas. According to such statements as "the one who is not the youngest, though born of the youngest," it is said that he is the twelfth and the most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*).

Here, as well as in the subsequent [verses], the word *utkṛṣṭa* is used for the purpose of specifying a particular distinction within a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). And he [is the most excellent] "of the household priests..."

The word "primary" (*mukhya*) is placed everywhere in the required locations as a synonym for what is about to be stated. Here, among the categories being extracted, the primacy of some is perceptible, while that of others is based on scripture (*āgamika*). In some cases there is immediate grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and in others it is mediated by the individual soul (*jīva*).

If the word *jyotis* (light) were taken to refer only to the stars, it would be impossible to specify the sun—which is external to them and lacks that connection—therefore, it is stated generally as "of those that illuminate. Since the sun is like a firefly compared to the supreme light that is the cause of the universe, the term "in the world" (*jagati*) is specified to exclude that [supreme light]. By the suffix *-mat* in the word *aṃśumān*, what is intended is its possession of an excellence of illumination suitable for specification; otherwise, there would be redundancy. Because the word *ravi* applies commonly to all twelve Ādityas, the singular number is used to denote the collective whole.

The phrase "the group of Ādityas" is stated as an illustration for the term *prāya* (a class). The Maruts are forty-nine sons of Diti, who consist of seven groups of seven. He says "this is not [to be taken literally]" with the intention that if the Moon were also a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), then its selection would have to be from that specific category. To the question, "What then is the meaning here?", he replies, "the lord of the lunar mansions. This is introduced by the word "primarily" (*pradhānyataḥ*).

This is the intended meaning. Now, an objection may be raised: among all the preceding and following instances where the sense is that of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is improper for any one of them here to have as its sole purport a mere relationship; for by the word *nakṣatra*, only the light shining at night is to be understood according to the "umbrella-bearer" logic (*chatrinyāya*), as per the Vedic text: "The stars are indeed the lights of those who perform good deeds. Alternatively, the lunar orb itself may be considered a *nakṣatra* because it is a place of enjoyment for the inhabitants of heaven, as stated: "He who sacrifices here does not perish in that world; that is the *nakṣatra*-ness of the *nakṣatras*. The *nakṣatras* are indeed the dwellings of the gods. To this, he replies:

"Among beings, I am consciousness," and so forth. Since a primary sense is possible, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate. Furthermore, the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) does not apply here in every instance; for there is an absence of selection in such passages as: "Among beings, I am consciousness"; "I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna"; "I am the discourse of those who discourse"; "I alone am inexhaustible time"; "I am the origin of those yet to be"; "I am gambling among those who cheat, and splendor among the splendid"; "I am victory, I am resolve," and so on. Therefore, in this context, [the moon] belongs to the class of stars.

The sense is that, because of the absence of a specific [relation], the general relation denoted by the genitive case comes to rest upon a particular [relation] established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For *gīti* (chanting) is the meaning of the word *sāman*; the statement "I am the Sāmaveda" is shown to be intended to dispel the doubt as to how that [Sāmaveda] is distinguished among the Vedas. He shows this by saying "the Ṛg and the Yajus. The excellence of the Sāmaveda is due to its having chanting as its primary element and its possession of many branches (*śākhā*), whereas the others lack these qualities and are thus inferior for that reason alone; it is not, however, because of any difference in their degree of authority (*prāmāṇya*). "In the beginning, indeed, there were only the Ṛk and the Sāman."
That very thing was named *Ṛk* and that was named *Sāman*. That *Ṛk* and *Sāman* spoke together: "Let us two become a couple for the sake of procreation. The *Sāman* said, "No;
my greatness is indeed greater than this," because of the predominance of the *Sāman* as the *Sāmaveda*, which consists of song (*gīti*).

[The Rigveda] has primacy; they say the Vaiśya caste was born from the Ṛgveda, they say the Yajurveda is the source of the Kṣatriya, and the Sāmaveda is the progenitor of the Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, by "gods" (devāḥ), those dwelling in heaven are intended, as it would be inappropriate [to include them] in the enumeration beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. The word *vāsava* is explained by the word *indra* for the purpose of highlighting his preeminence; for the root *idi* means "supreme sovereignty. "Higher than the senses are the objects... [and so on].

Regarding the question of how there can be a selection [of the mind] in the statement "Among the senses, I am the mind" (*indriyāṇāṃ manaścāsmi*), since the mind is mentioned separately from the senses in passages such as "The mind is superior to the objects" (*arthebhyaśca paraṃ manaḥ*), he says: "Of the eleven senses, that which is the most excellent is the mental sense (*manaindriya*). The intention is this: since the mind is designated as a sense in passages such as "The senses are ten and one," how can there be a separate designation for it? This is justified by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), whereby the selection is logically consistent. For there is no element among the elements that is designated as "consciousness."

With this intention, he says, "This too... (iyamapi). The word "genitive" (ṣaṣṭhī) is to be supplied. Just as in the passage beginning, "The splendor of the splendid... the essence of the essential," the portion consisting of the qualifying attribute within the qualified object is intended to be expressed; with this intention, the term "of sentient beings" (cetanāvatām) was stated. Now, one might object: elsewhere, something called "consciousness" (cetanā-saṃjña) is mentioned as the sixth among the elements, as in: "The great elements are space, wind, fire, water, and earth; the sixth, however, is the element of consciousness, the Self."

"The seventh is called [the element], and the eighth should be known as the mind (manas)," and likewise, "The sixth, however, the element of consciousness (cetanā-dhātu), is taught as the mind. And here, since the mind serves as the substratum for consciousness, there is no contradiction in not mentioning consciousness separately from it. Therefore, it is appropriate that in the phrase "I am the consciousness among the elements," the sense is one of selection (nirdhāraṇa). Not so. For the status of being a great element (mahābhūta) does not follow merely from being mentioned as the sixth among the elements; for it is possible to include them in a numerical sequence in other ways as well. And in this context, [they are mentioned] as the seventh and the eighth.

Because the two [entities] thus specified are not admitted to be primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and because the word "consciousness" (*cetanā*) has an unfamiliar meaning, it is appropriate to accept its well-known meaning;
therefore, the genitive case here is correctly used solely with the intention of expressing a mere relationship.

In the phrase "of the Rudras," the mention of Śaṅkara by name among the Rudras is intended to highlight his preeminence. Because there is no great distance between the classes of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, the term "Yakṣa-Rākṣasas" is used; however, this does not imply that the Lord of Wealth (Vitteśa) has even a scent of being a Rākṣasa. Alternatively, as in the expression "among the stars, I am the moon," what is intended here is merely his inclusion within both classes. Furthermore, by the name "Vitteśa," the preeminence of Dhanada’s unique sovereignty is highlighted. Since Himālaya will be mentioned later as the foremost among all mountains in general, the word "śikhara" in the phrase "Meru of the peaks" [is used to specify].
A specific mountain is intended [by the word *parvata*]; with the intention that this word is capable of indicating that distinction, it is said: "of mountains adorned with peaks.

The sense is that the suffix (*pratyaya*) is intended for praise. Because of its possession of specific peaks composed of excellent jewels, gold, and so forth, Meru possesses a preeminence [over other mountains].

By the designation "Bṛhaspati" (Lord of the Great), the excellence of being the "Lord of the Vast" is established; he is the Lord of Speech (*girām patiḥ*). By the word "senānī" (General), there is here the inclusion of a commander of an army subject to [human] karma; Skanda’s excellence is characterized by his being the General of the Divine Army (*devasenānī*). By the word "saraḥ" (lake), since it intends to refer merely to a stationary reservoir of water distinct from a flowing stream, the ocean is included; for rivers will be mentioned separately later on.

Since [the Lord] will later speak of "the divine sages" (*devarṣīṇām*) and "the sages" (*munīnām*), and because he qualifies them here with the word "great" (*mahat*), he intends to refer to a specific class of sages known as the *maharṣis*; with this in mind, he says "of Marīci and the others. By the word "speeches" (*girām*), he does not intend mere sound, for that term is not applied to the roar of the ocean and the like. For this very reason, it does not mean a mere syllable either, since he will later state separately, "Among syllables, I am the letter 'A'."

For that very reason, even the expression "the one syllable" (*ekamakṣaram*) refers to something other than the letter *a*. With the intention of showing that in passages such as "The Brahman is the single-syllabled *oṃ*," the word *akṣara* is employed as qualified by the word "single" (*eka*) even when referring to the *praṇava*, he says: "of those denoting meaning. Among those denoting meaning, the *praṇava* has preeminence because it denotes the most exalted of all meanings and so forth. Just as leaves are held together by a pin, all speech is held together (*saṃtṛṇṇatva*) by the *praṇava*.

And because of the Śruti: the excellence of the *japayajña* (recitation-sacrifice) over other sacrifices is established elsewhere: "The *japayajña* is ten times superior to the *vidhiyajña* (prescribed ritual sacrifice). Furthermore: "What [use] would he have for animal sacrifices involving slaughter? How could one like me be fit to sacrifice with animal sacrifices that are violent? What need has that Great-Souled One for sacrifices consisting of violence, by whom Keśava has been worshipped both at his falling asleep and his awakening"? By the force of such statements, there is permission for violent sacrifices for those who are otherwise unfit for non-violent sacrifices. Even in that case, [the engagement occurs] through scriptural injunction (*vidhi*).

Because there is no intention to cause harm, because scripture speaks of benefit, and because it results in the gratification of the deity, there is no sin. However, for those seeking rewards, that fruit is short-lived and mixed with suffering. But sacrifices consisting of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), which depend on qualified practitioners, lead to liberation due to their being exceedingly pleasing to the Blessed One.

For this very reason, Hiraṇyakaśipu, Uparicara, and others performed sacrifices with flour-made animals. Thus, regarding other sacrifices, there is great difficulty involving the application of violence and so forth, the determination of specific qualifications, and the establishment of the scope of the subject matter through the word "and so on" (*ādi*). However, in the case of the *japa-yajña* (recitation sacrifice), because there is no such application [of violence], because the meaning is understood without dependence [on external objects], and because one is suddenly established in *samādhi* by means of *sabīja-yoga* (meditation with seed), the *japa-yajña* is most excellent among all other sacrifices, as it is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*).

"A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection even through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter. Whether he performs other [rites] or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, because it is a cause of success even for widowers and others, and since specific mountains have been mentioned previously while trees will be mentioned later, the phrase "of all mountains" is used to exclude both of those categories and to accord with the well-known status of Himavat as the king of mountains.

Now, it might be argued that the phrase "of all trees" is inappropriate because the *aśvattha* is inferior in comparison to the *pārijāta* and other such trees; to this it is replied that it is "worshipful.

The sense is that even the *pārijāta* and others do not possess the same status of being worshipful as the *aśvattha*. The gods who perceive mantras are the celestial sages (*devarṣis*), and among the celestial sages, [there is] Nārada.

The manifold excellence [of this work] has been elaborated upon in many places within the Mahābhārata itself. Citraratha is the king of the Gandharvas. Regarding the phrase "of the Siddhas" and so forth: the Siddhas are those who, by virtue of specific merits accumulated in previous lives, have possessed from birth the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. There is a scriptural tradition stating, "The first knower is the Siddha," referring to Kapila; and they say, "There they beheld Kapila, the eternal Vāsudeva.
This [work] is also like that of Paraśurāma and others.

The term "born from nectar" (*amṛtodbhava*) indicates excellence by virtue of its origin. Here, "nectar" (*amṛta*) refers either to water or, in the state of being churned, to the nectar of immortality itself. By the word "lordly elephant" (*gajendra*), the elephants of the quarters (*diggaja*) are intended. Among them, the primary one is Airāvata, the mount of Śacīpati, the lord of the world-protectors. The quality of being "born from nectar" should be understood as applying to Airāvata as well, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). Alternatively, it may be seen as arising from the *Rathantara* Sāman chant. By the very word "lord of men" (*narādhipa*), the excellence characterized by being a sustainer is established.

The phrase "of weapons" refers to those that are recent, for even the thunderbolt (*vajra*) produced from the bones of Dadhīci is inferior when compared to the *sudarśana* discus and other such [divine weapons]. "Of cows" means of those that yield milk.

The term "divine Surabhi" indicates that the word *kāmadhuk* ("wish-fulfilling") is used here in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), referring specifically to a particular individual cow. By the word "procreation," the unique quality of Kandarpa as the cause of generation is established.
The excellence has been stated; the meaning is that it is dependent upon me. Alternatively, the word *prajana* is used for the purpose of excluding *kandarpa*, which does not lead to progeny.

Regarding the question of how there can be a separate designation for the two synonymous words *sarpa* and *nāga*, he says: "Serpents (*sarpāḥ*) have one head; *nāgas* have many heads. By the word *yādasa*, Varuṇa [is indicated].
To include him as well, he says, "the aquatic creatures dwelling in the water. Alternatively, it may be intended as referring to all water-dwellers in general;

Varuṇa’s connection with them is by virtue of being their lord, since there is no commonality of species between him and them—hence the term "grāha" (crocodile). Arthamā is the king of the ancestors (*pitṛs*). "Of those who restrain" means of those who exercise restraint; thus he says, "of those to be punished."

The excellence of Prahlāda is shown by the passage beginning with, "He who was always the standard of comparison for all virtuous men. Since the eternal principle of Time (*kālatattva*) will be described later as "I alone am imperishable Time," and since Yama has already been mentioned previously, a specific person distinct from those two is intended here by the word "Time" (*kāla*). Furthermore, it is not logical for insentient Time to be a reckoner;

if the term *kalayatām* were meant merely in the sense of "knowers," then the selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of Time from among them would be inappropriate. Therefore, he shows the specific meaning appropriate to that context.

Regarding the word *anartha* (misfortune): the sense is that there is indeed no misfortune other than death. By the term *mṛgendra* (lord of beasts) itself, the lion's excellence is established. Among birds, the excellence of Vainateya (Garuḍa) is established by his superior speed, his being composed of the Vedas, and so forth.

If, by the word "pavatām" (of those that blow), the unique action of blowing were intended, then the act of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) would not be logically possible; therefore, to justify it, the phrase "of those whose nature is to move" (*gamanasvabhāvānām*) is stated. This means "those whose habit is to move through space. For even the stars and other celestial bodies, impelled by the wind (*pavana*), revolve through space. Here, the movement associated with purification—as in the case of the "Soma-purifier" (*somapavana*) and similar terms—is not intended. Since the Rāma intended here is the slayer of Rāvaṇa, who was himself the conqueror of Paraśurāma (who declared, "I am the foremost among weapon-bearers"), the author states the excellence characterized by his "infallible weapons" (*amoghaśastratva*) as being appropriate for him.

Regarding the statement "the status of being a wielder of weapons (*śastrabhṛttva*) is the manifestation (*vibhūti*) here," [the author] asks: why could Rāma himself not be the manifestation, as in the preceding and following cases? To this he replies: "because of the absence of any other referent (*arthāntarābhāvāt*).
The meaning is that neither a specific insentient object nor another sentient being denoted by the word "wielder of weapons" is possible here. Among other possible referents—

He says, "And Āditya, etc.," because there might be a break in the style (*rītibhaṅga*) if one were to specify the unique attributes (*svāsādhāraṇadharma*) of each. The meaning is that since the quality of being a wielder of weapons and so forth is common to all others as attributes belonging to the Blessed Lord as the subject (*dharmī*), there is but a single style; the distinction between selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and non-selection is merely a difference in phrasing and is not a fault. In this context, by the word "Āditya," the Sun intended is the one described as "the radiant Sun among luminaries" (*jyotiṣāṃ raviraṃśumān*); [as for the others], "Among the Ādityas, I am... [and so on].

Viṣṇu is said to be the Sun (Āditya), who is equal to Rāma. Makara is the king of fish. As for the Gaṅgā (Jāhnavī), her excellence is proclaimed by those who know the three worlds through her origin from the foot of Viṣṇu, her being borne upon the head of the Omniscient One (Śiva), and her flowing throughout the three worlds.

If the word *sarga* were intended to mean "mere creation" (*sṛṣṭimātra*), it would be incompatible with the connection [to the phrase] "the beginning, the end, and so forth"; therefore, he states that here the word *sarga* has the sense of "object" (*karman*), saying: "they are called *sargas* because they are created (*sṛjyante*). It is not appropriate for the words "beginning," "middle," and "end" to mean specific parts [of a whole], as their meaning would not be distinctive. Nor do they mean specific points of time, since time will be mentioned later and there would thus be no purpose for its separate designation here. Furthermore, they do not refer to the actions of arising and so forth.

The sense of being the material cause (*mātrārthatā*) is not intended, because that would result in redundancy with what will be stated later: "And [I am] the origin of those who are to come. Nor is it the case that the Lord's status as the sole cause and so forth is being asserted here, for that would be redundant given the sequence already stated: "I am the beginning, the middle, and the end. Furthermore, this is not a general conclusion regarding Him, since there are further statements made subsequently. Therefore, it is more appropriate to understand this through *lakṣaṇā* (indication) as referring to the causes of birth and so forth as established in common worldly experience. Even in that context, since the material cause has already been declared in the words, "I am the seed of all beings," only the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is intended here.

By the unqualified expression "of all creations" (*sargāṇām*), it is intended that the entire class of instrumental causes relative to all objects of creation existing in all places and times is under His control. This is summarized by the three statements beginning with "always" (*sarvadā*). "The science of the self" (*adhyātmavidyā*) is the knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

It is superior to other sciences both in terms of its subject matter and its fruit. By the phrase "of those who speak," it is not intended merely that they do not dispute with one another; [rather, it means they proclaim this truth].

In this context, because the specific type of discourse called *vāda* (debate) is not being recalled, and because the term "science" (*vidyā*)—in the phrase "among the sciences, the science of the inner self"—is applicable as the subject matter of the discussion concerning its purpose; furthermore, it is not intended here that the specific discourse called *vāda* is meant [as the referent], for when it is possible to indicate excellence in relation to others, it is improper to abandon that [general sense]. Therefore, the form common to all three types of discourse is what is intended here by the term "of those who debate" (*pravadatām*).

Regarding this, he says: "for those engaged in cavil, wrangling, and so forth. By the phrase "engaged for the sake of determining the truth," he demonstrates the superiority of debate (*vāda*) over the discussion of one seeking victory (*vijigīṣukathā*), which yields only meager results, by showing that debate culminates in the fruit of liberation (*apavarga*).

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad it is heard: "A is Brahman. Likewise, the fact that [the letter *a*] is the source (*prakṛti*) of all phonemes is elaborated by the very scripture which states: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech; this same [speech], when manifested through the contact consonants (*sparśa*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*), becomes manifold and takes on various forms.

Thus, he declares it to be the source of all letters. To establish the plurality required for the selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), he shows the meaning of the suffix: "sāmāsika" means a collection of compounds. [This refers to the compound] whose referent is other than the preceding or following members.

He states that the *dvandva* compound possesses superiority over the *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, and *bahuvrīhi* compounds by saying "sa hi ubhayeti. With the word "ākṣaya" (inexhaustible), he intends to convey that although there is an infinite limitation consisting of various transformations established by Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources—such as "the *kalās*, *muhūrtas*, and *kāṣṭhās*," which are the causes of the world's destruction—it is nonetheless, in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), without beginning or end; with this intention, he says "kalā. It is beginningless (*anādi*).

"O twice-born one, no end to this Time (Kāla) exists," and "I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, set forth; I have neither end, nor beginning, nor middle"—by such passages, this presiding over Time is made manifest. With the intention that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is spoken of here—since he is conventionally designated by the word *dhātṛ* (Creator) and qualified as being "facing in all directions" (*viśvatomukha*)—the author says "of all. By the word *dhātṛ* itself, [it refers to] the characteristic of being the creator of everything contained within the cosmic egg.

To demonstrate that His excellence is established, it is said that "He has created everything. By this, other interpretations—such as [the view] that He is merely the distributor of the fruits of karma—are refuted.

To indicate that the term "on all sides" (*viśvataḥ*) here intends only the four cardinal directions, it is stated that He is "four-faced. Furthermore, by this, His role in promulgating the four Vedas and so forth is also implied.

Regarding *karmānurūpadaṇḍa* (punishment according to one's karma): since the two persons named Yama and Kāla, who are authorized over the limitation of time, have already been mentioned, the term "all-destroying Death" (*sarvahara*) is used here to indicate that a specific person authorized over the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), who carries out the commands of Yama, is meant by "Death. To clarify this, it is stated as "the destroyer of all vital breaths. The claim made by some that the Lord who withdraws everything at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) is the "Death" referred to here is weak, because it has been stated [elsewhere] that he is "the end of beings" (*bhūtānām anta*). Furthermore, because it is recited in conjunction with "origination" (*udbhava*), the word "Death" (*mṛtyu*) here refers to death itself.
Some say "para" [means "other"]. The word *udbhava* (emergence) primarily denotes the action of arising (*utpatti-kriyā*), since its locus of emergence and so forth are specified separately here;

with the intention that it is appropriate to take it as denoting an action, it is stated as "the activity called emergence. Qualities such as *kīrti* (fame) and so forth are not intended here as specific attributes, because they have emerged even in men and thus lack the connection with the specific feminine suffix. Furthermore, the word *nārī* is not used here in the feminine gender.

It refers to the mere category of objects, as there is no primary contradiction [in this sense]. Therefore, it is specifically a woman who is being identified. In that context, with the intention of referring to Śrī alone, it is said: "I am Śrī and I am Kīrti. These are indeed the unique powers (śaktis) of the Blessed Lord; however, elsewhere, those respective terms are used due to specific presiding deities (abhimāna).

The preeminence of the *Bṛhat-sāman* among the *Sāmans* is established by the Śruti itself: "In the beginning, this was both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*. It was indeed Speech and Mind; Speech was the *Rathantara* and Mind was the *Bṛhat*. As the *Bṛhat* was being created first, it looked down upon the *Rathantara*; then the *Rathantara* conceived a fetus. The preeminence of the *Gāyatrī* among the meters (*Chandas*) due to its status as their mother is elaborated upon in the Śrutis and in the *Chandoviciti*. For example:

The *Bahvṛca-Upaniṣad* states: "The Gāyatrī is indeed the foremost among the meters. Among the months, Mārgaśīrṣa possesses preeminence because it is the time for the impregnation of the seed of the year, and because among the presiding deities of the months—Keśava and the others—it is the month of the first, Keśava, and because it is the time for commencing the classes of religious observances (*vrata*). By the very term *Kusumākara* (the Flower-Maker), the preeminence of spring as the cause of happiness for all living beings is made manifest. This is also established by such scriptural injunctions as: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in spring," and "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, and likewise a Kṣatriya in summer," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *chalayatām*, it is stated that they are "deceiving" (*chalaṃ kurvatām*) with the intention that the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *tat karoti*.

With the intention that the designation "deception" (*chalatva*) applies here because victory and defeat are merely superimposed through the movement of the dice and so forth, it is stated that this is "characterized by dice" (*akṣādilakṣaṇam*). Furthermore, because there is no expression such as "I am the gambling of those who gamble" (as there is in the expression "the splendor of the splendid ones"), and because the term *chalayatām* denotes merely the act of employing deception, [it is understood as such].

With the intention of expressing that gambling is superior to other grounds for deception—such as buying, selling, debt, inheritance, fraudulent agreements, and so forth—the phrase "in places of deception" (*chalāspadeṣu*) was used;

the meaning is "in places of fraud. By the word "dice and so forth" (*akṣādi*), there is an inclusion of the entire category of gambling, both with animate and inanimate objects. Alternatively, the expression "characterized by dice and so forth" (*akṣādilakṣaṇam*) was stated in order to include only those involving inanimate objects. And its superiority consists in being accomplished without effort and without conflict with *dharma*.

Because it is impossible to issue an order for the seizure of all one's wealth merely by agreement; and because the two preceding words, *tejasvin* and *sattva*, are already occupied by the qualities of brilliance (*tejas*) and courage (*sattva*), it would be inappropriate for the words *jaya* (victory) and *vyavasāya* (perseverance) to be construed with them. Therefore, with the intention that the appropriate words *jetṛ* (conquerors) and *vyavasāyin* (persevering ones) are implied by the sense through the influence of the preceding and following words, he stated: "of the conquerors" and "of the persevering ones. Thus, in this context, a distinction between the substance (*dravya*) and the perseverance (*vyavasāya*) as forms of *sattva* has been expressed.

Regarding the statement "Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva," here too—as in the case of Rāma—he speaks thus because he is a direct incarnation. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "the state of being Vasudeva’s son is the manifestation (*vibhūti*) here," it is indicated that the reason for this was already stated previously in the context of Rāma, precisely because there is no other possible meaning. Now, one might ask: what kind of manifestation is this "state of being Vasudeva’s son"? For the mere fact of being a son does not constitute a distinction, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
