Nor is it by virtue of being the son of a specific father named Vasudeva; for even that [status] is common to many...

Because it is impossible to single him out on the basis of being common to others, nor can he be identified merely by the conventional usage of the word "Vāsudeva," since that alone is not sufficient to establish his superiority;
furthermore, being the son of Vasudeva is not what needs to be taught here, as that is already well-known to Arjuna. Therefore, it is not appropriate for him to be presented as a direct incarnation.

For this very reason, it was not said, "Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am [such-and-such]. To this, it is replied: Here, the word "Vasudeva" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to the period beginning from his descent with four arms in the house of Vasudeva.
The form consisting of superhuman qualities, body, prowess, and so forth, is recognized as possessing a preeminent excellence known even to cowherds.

And that [excellence] is mentioned in reference to Arjuna for the purpose of providing an illustration. Here, the intended meaning is that there is a preeminence—due to factors such as extreme proximity—to the direct name "we" (asmacchabda) over all other pronouns. This is because Yudhiṣṭhira’s excellence is supreme in righteousness (*dharma*), Bhīmasena’s in strength (*bala*), and [Arjuna’s] in beauty and other such qualities.

The doubt that [the sons] of Mādrī might be Arjuna is thereby removed. There is no occasion here for indirectness (*pārokṣya*), because everything here is spoken by the All-Seeing One as something directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). For "seership" (*ṛṣitva*) consists in seeing supersensuous objects due to a particular kind of vision; and that has been explained for the most part already. Therefore, with the intention that the meaning intended by the phrase "of the sages" (*munīnām*) is distinct from that [ordinary seership], based on the etymological power of the word and in accordance with the Vedic text, "Only by knowing this does one become a sage," he says: "Sages are those who, through reflection (*manana*), perceive the true nature of the Self. And such a person—

The excellence of the Blessed Vyāsa is established by his own words, such as: "Having investigated all the scriptures again and again, this one thing alone is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon always," and: "I consider you today to be the most excellent even compared to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, though he was distinguished by his asceticism, because of your realization of the knowledge of the secret."
This [Kalkī] is also counted as one who has descended from the divine realm, as it is said: "The Lord Kalkī, the knower of the Vedas, whose bed is the netherworld (Pātāla).

Here, by the term "poets" (*kavayaḥ*), the status of being a mere author (*nibandhṛtva*) is not intended; for if that were the case, Vālmīki and others would surpass all others. Therefore, with the intention of defining a poet as "one who sees beyond" (*krāntadarśī*), he says: "Poets are the wise ones" (*vipaścitaḥ*). As for Uśanas, his distinction among the wise is as follows:

This is well known from such passages as: "Because of his proficiency in political ethics (*nīti*) and other qualities, there is no man whom he does not lead, except for Bhārgava; the accomplishment of the remaining tasks, however, rests with those who possess intelligence. *Note:* The term *śeṣasaṃpratipatti* refers to the successful management or execution of the remaining duties or objectives. The text asserts that while the sage (Bhārgava) is peerless in leading others through his wisdom, the final execution of specific tasks depends on the intellect of others. The phrase "except for Bhārgava" (*anyatra bhārgāvāt*) indicates that even this great sage is an exception to the general rule of universal influence. The mention of *nītinipuṇatva* (proficiency in political ethics) highlights the specific domain of the sage's expertise. The concluding statement emphasizes that the ultimate realization of goals is contingent upon the presence of intelligent individuals.

"Transgression of rules" is a statement regarding the fitness for punishment; for even a minor transgression is a cause for hell due to its gravity. One should say, "I am policy (*nīti*) among those who possess policy," but by the phrase "of those desiring victory," he explains what kind of distinction this is: that policy is the means of victory for those seeking conquest. What is intended here is a specific function of the intellect. Since silence, which consists of the restraint of speech and is well-known in the world, lacks secrecy, it is not the [intended] determination.

[The word *mauna*] has been explained; however, if the term *mauna* were to refer to subjects such as self-knowledge (*ātmavidyā*) and the like, there would be an abandonment of its conventional meaning. Nor is *mauna* a secret attribute (such that it could be used like the expression "the essence of those who possess essence"), to which he replies: "I am the *mauna* among the secrets (*guhya*) related to the secret ones. It is universally accepted that secrets are to be concealed and that *mauna*—even more so than whispering into the ear—is a means for such concealment. Therefore, in this context, the genitive case denotes a mere relationship, specifically the relationship between the object to be concealed and the concealer.

It rests upon a specific excellence of form. Since mere consciousness was previously stated in the passage, "I am the consciousness of beings," what is intended here in the phrase "knowledge among the knowers" is a specific knowledge characterized by an excellence conducive to the goals of human life; that is "knowledge," while anything other than that is said to be "ignorance."

The phrase "the seed of all beings" does not refer merely to *pradhāna* (primordial matter), because *pradhāna* is not directly the seed of all beings. Nor does it refer to a seed characterized by rice and the like, because such a seed lacks connection with the mobile beings included within the term "all beings. Therefore, with the intention that what is intended here is simply the material cause (*upādāna-dravya*) in its causal state in relation to each respective effect-state, without distinction, he says "in every state. By this, [he excludes] the creation of primordial nature (*prākṛta*) and occasional causes (*naimittika*).

Since [the Lord] has been described in passages such as "I am the beginning," etc., His causality is also demonstrated here by virtue of His having the respective substances—which serve as the cause of eternal creation—as His body (*śarīra*). Furthermore, he states what is intended by the phrase "and that which... as follows: "both perceived and unperceived. "Unperceived" means cognizable through inference and other such means.

This is the meaning. In the passage beginning with "That does not exist," he shows the specific positive concomitance (anvaya) that results from the statement of negative concomitance (svavyatireka), using the word "all.

He states the purpose intended by the Blessed One in mentioning the inseparable connection between the opening and the conclusion with the words "by this. Furthermore, we have already explained at length that in certain instances there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) even with things distinct from the substance, because the substance which serves as their substratum is the body of the Blessed One.

The phrase "there is no end" (nānto'sti) serves as a reminder of the very impossibility of describing [the Lord] exhaustively that was stated previously. If the word *divya* were intended to mean "residing in a particular location," it would contradict the earlier detailed description (*prapañcana*) of those who are non-divine (*adivya*) and reside in indefinite locations; therefore, it is said, "of the auspicious ones" (*kalyāṇīnām*). This begins with the statement, "the auspicious manifestations of Myself" (*vibhūtīrātmanaśśubhāḥ*). The term *uddeśataḥ* means "by way of enumeration" or "in part"; the meaning is that they are brought forth by way of their principal forms through the extraction of their manifestations (*vibhūti*). That...
According to the intention of some, it is "in brief" by means of certain limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Having begun with the words "by way of prominence," he concludes with the verse beginning "Whatever... with the intention of summarizing those principal manifestations (*vibhūti*) that were not explicitly mentioned but must necessarily be stated. Having kept in mind the contextual meaning of the word *vibhūti*, it is said [in the commentary] that [the Lord] is "endowed with the objects to be ruled. Here, the word *sattva* refers to living beings (*jantu*). The word *jāta* is used to indicate the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). He avoids the redundancy between the two words *vibhūtimat* and *śrīmat*.

Regarding the term *kāntimat* (possessing splendor): with the intention of avoiding redundancy by means of the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), where one wishes to specify a particular object to be restrained, he says, "or [a place] abundant in wealth and grain. Since the reading *urjitam* (prosperous) would otherwise be redundant if intended merely in its general sense of excellence and so forth, he explains the specific meaning as follows:

Regarding the word "kalyāṇa": the term *ūrja* refers to the quality of being armored (*sannāha-śīlatva*) due to its lack of dejection. The phrase "possessing majesty" (*vibhūtimat*) and so forth serves to demonstrate those who possess strength (*bala*) and other such qualities. Since it might be understood from the statement "born from a portion of my splendor" (*mama tejoṃśasaṃbhava*) that he is derived from a mere physical portion of the substance of splendor residing in a body, the term *tejas* used here is intended for the purpose of the present context in order to preclude that interpretation.

He states the meaning of the word *tejas* (splendor) as "the capacity to overcome others. What is this so-called "overcoming" (*abhibhava*) here? And how can there be the existence of parts within that? To this he says: "mine" (*mama*). By the phrase "of inconceivable power," the intention of the word "mine" is explained for the purpose of extracting those parts that are suitable for thought. Through this, the establishment of qualities such as being beyond all sensory range, imperishability, and the effecting of the impossible is achieved. This is illustrated by the fierce wind that desires to shake the mountains, [which likewise overcomes] the grass.
The sense is that [the sound] arises from a mere fraction of its momentum, just as in that case; thus, it is "born from a portion of fire" (*tejoṃśasaṃbhava*).

In this way, what was introduced with the words "predominantly" (*prādhānyataḥ*) is concluded. Then, with the verse beginning "Or rather" (*atha vā*), he states a summary of all manifestations, both primary and secondary. Regarding the word "being spoken" (*ucyamānena*): the sense is that the word *etad* (this) refers to the absence of an end to the description. [This is said because of] the lack of knowledge regarding the conclusion of the manifestations.

With the intention that the purpose of form (*rūpa*) would not otherwise be established, he asks, "What is the purpose? With the intention that by the word "this" (*idam*) the variety apprehended by the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indicated, it is stated to be "consisting of consciousness and the rest. By the words beginning with "the effect" (*kārya*), there is an exposition of what is intended by the term "entirety" (*kṛtsna*). "Gross" and "subtle" are to be connected respectively to the states of effect and cause. By the words beginning with "its own nature" (*svarūpa*), the purpose of the manifestation is stated; [it refers to] the nature among impermanent things.

Existence (*sadbhāva*) means origination; however, in the case of eternal things, it is the exclusion of non-existence. For even the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of eternal entities is established by the eternal will of the Lord. This has already been explained in detail previously. Here, [the term "existence"] is used to exclude the notion of partial incarnations (*aṃśa*) such as those that descend from a portion of the essential nature, and because of the context concerning His governance, it refers to my own majesty (*mahiman*).

Thus it has been said. Here, by the word *mahi* (great), the very power of restraint (*niyamanasāmarthya*) under discussion is intended. This is synonymous with the phrase "born from a portion of fire" (*tejoṃśasaṃbhava*). With the intention that the word *eka* here refers to being extremely minute, it is stated as "by a ten-thousandth part of a ten-thousandth" (*ayutāyutāṃśena*). In this context, *stambhana* means restraining from one's own will, or rather, presiding over [the subject] in the form of bringing them under one's own control. Regarding the phrase "by a single portion," he corroborates his own stated meaning as follows: *yatho*...

"What is meant by 'possessing universal power' (*viśvaśakti*)? It means that the universe itself is the power; the sense is that the universe serves as the specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) appropriate for its effects. Since the term 'born from a portion of light' (*tejoṃśasaṃbhava*) is stated immediately thereafter, it is logical that the word 'portion' (*aṃśa*) in the phrase 'by one portion' (*ekāṃśena*) should also refer to that same [universe]; this is the intended meaning."
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

In order to introduce the chapter on the meditation on the Cosmic Form (*viśvarūpa-dhyāya*), he summarizes the subject matter of the chapter on manifestations (*vibhūti-adhyāya*) with the words "Thus" (*evam*). By stating the purpose—that it is for the perfection of the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) and for its increase—it is indicated that Arjuna’s desire to see [the Lord] immediately follows from the growth of his devotion. The phrase "distinct from all others" (*sakaletara-vilakṣaṇe*) means either by way of being distinct from everything else, or by way of having a nature distinct from everything else. By this, His state of being infinitely superior is established.

It is liberated; for it is recognized here through the reverse order of what was previously stated—that it is unique, essential, and characterized by limitless excellence. Since the relationship between cause and effect can be established as desired between the two phrases "distinguished from everything else" and "unique to the Lord," and since their purpose is to convey the absence of any superior [state], they are not redundant. This subsequent chapter is rooted in the desire to see [the Lord], which is the fruit of the increase in devotion dependent upon the certainty regarding the meaning of the scriptures heard.

He introduces Arjuna’s words concerning the form of the Lord with the phrase "him, this very one" (*tam etam*). "Him" refers to the one who transcends all; "this very one" refers to the one described in the manner previously stated. By the expression "from the presence of the Blessed One," his status as a reliable authority (*āptatva*), which serves as the basis for certainty, is indicated. The underlying intention is that if one hears from another teacher, even if a desire to see [the Lord] arises, a formal request for a vision would not be appropriate.
With the intent of explaining the meaning of the verse beginning with "Thus indeed is He" (*evam etad*), he says: "having ascertained 'it is exactly so'."

Now, one might object: having accepted what was previously stated with the words, "It is even as you have said," the subsequent statement, "I wish to see Your form, O Lord," appears to be a desire to see a different kind of form. If that is so, how can it be said that he "desired to directly perceive the Blessed One in such a state"? To this, [the answer is: the meaning established by the passage ending with, "Pervading all this, I stand with but one part, supporting the world," is not here [concerned] with a particular physical body.
The sense is that [the Self] is recognized through direct perception by means of its bondage.

Here, in order to pray for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), he demonstrates his gratitude, faith, and devotion through these subsequent verses beginning with "for my grace" (*madanugrahāya*). Among those, with the first verse—due to the natural force of words such as *adhyātma* and because of the separate mention of the seventh case-meaning in "the origin and dissolution" (*bhavāpyayau*) and so forth—he says, "delusion regarding the self and the body," with the intention of restating the hearing of the means for perceiving the reality of the Self and the result thereof. [This is] because delusion has departed...

With the intention that by the word "me" (mama) the essential nature qualified by delusion (*moha*) is intended—since it was previously designated as such—the phrase ending with "of my delusion" (*mohatasya*) was stated.

By the words "for my grace" (*madanugrahāya*), he expresses the intended meaning that there is nothing else for him to attain that has not yet been attained; thus he says, "for the sole purpose of my grace. [This concludes] the encouragement to battle.

By this, even the slightest suspicion has been dispelled. The word *guhya*, as qualified by the word *parama*, is explained by the word *rahasya* in order to eliminate the notion of mere secrecy implied by the statement, "And I am the silence among secrets" (*maunaṃ caivāsmi guhyānām*). The qualification *parama* (supreme) is indicated by the repetition of the word *parama* in the reading, because [this yoga] is the ultimate remainder of the most secret yoga of devotion. With the intention that speech is "pertaining to the self" (*adhyātma*) because it dwells within the self as its expounder—

It was stated that [the teaching] must be spoken regarding the self (*ātman*). Having extracted the portion primarily concerning the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the introductory context and from the meaning of the verse introducing the middle hexad, he speaks of it using the term *adhyātma* (inward self) in the words "But never indeed I... (*na tvevāham...*). In accordance with the expression "designated as *adhyātma*," and because the word "this" (*ayam*) is intended as a direct reference, it is explained as being "concerning my own self. By the prefix *vi-* in the word *vigata*, it is shown that what is intended is a complete destruction, including the latent impressions (*savāsana*).
The word "all" [is used]. "Cast far away" means that because even the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been rejected, the sprout of rebirth is destroyed.

In order to set aside the interpretation that the passage beginning with "For [I am] the origin and dissolution of beings" (bhavāpyayau hi) serves as a reason for the subject at hand, and to indicate its distinct meaning, he says, "And likewise" (tathā ca). Regarding the phrase "from the seventh up to the tenth," the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra) indicates the statement found therein by citing the text as he has memorized it. He states "of those other than you" (tvadvyatiriktānām), which is suggested by the non-restriction of the plural number and expressed in the passage beginning with "I [am the source] of the whole" (ahaṃ kṛtsnasya).

Since these words are spoken by Arjuna, whose delusion regarding his human nature has ceased, the intention is that by the word "from you" (tvattaḥ), the Supreme Self's nature as the means for both origin and dissolution is intended.

Thus it has been said; for since the word *apyaya* cannot be construed with the ablative case, there would arise the notion of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) through the compound *bhavāpyaya*.

To exclude that [misconception], it is said: "origination and dissolution. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of a general cause common to both instrumental and material causes; thus, the connection is with *apya-ya* (dissolution). The intention is that the connection with *tvattaḥ* (from You) in the phrase *śrutau* (in the Veda) serves little purpose. The word *vistaraśaḥ* means "in detail. By the address "O Lotus-petal-eyed One" (*kamalapatrākṣa*), it is indicated that even in this incarnation, the possession of a non-material form characterized by lotus-like eyes—as established in such teachings as the *Antarāditya-vidyā*—is clearly perceived.

For it is heard there that the imperishable majesty of Puṇḍarīkākṣa alone consists in His being the Lord of all the worlds, their desires, and so forth. In the phrase "His majesty," the word "His" (tava) is to be understood as an elliptical addition (*anuṣaṅga*). By the word "imperishable" (*avyaya*), what is intended here is His boundlessness in terms of time, object, number, and excellence; with this intention, the passage from "eternal" (*nityam*) up to "immeasurable" (*aparimitam*) is stated. [The passage continues: "Earth, water..."
The status of being the Residue (śeṣitva) and so forth has been elaborated previously through such passages as "There is nothing else higher than Me," "All is in Me," and "The wisdom of the Buddha.

The word *hi* (for/indeed) is intended to indicate the desire to see what is about to be stated. The sense is that this meaning is consistent with the context, since it lacks compatibility with [other interpretations] such as being a logical reason (*hetu*) or a well-known fact (*prasiddhi*).

With the intention that by the term "O Supreme Lord" (parameśvara), qualities such as being the supreme authority—which serve as the cause for faith in the meaning of the statement—are intended, he says, "O Supreme Lord. To manifest this, and to exclude the view that [the scripture] is merely for one's own personal confirmation while establishing it as the Veda (śruti), he says, "it is determined thus: 'This is so. For base men (kāpuruṣa) are those who perceive faults in those who have taken refuge [in the Lord]; therefore, here, in himself who desires to see [the Lord], there is unsurpassed manliness in the form of disregard for faults.

With the intention that [the Lord] is intended by the term *Puruṣottama*, it is said, "an ocean of affection for those who have taken refuge. Alternatively, the etymological derivation *pūrayati sanoti* ("He fills and bestows") is intended here; or else, what will be stated later—namely, "having entered, He sustains"—is made known. Thus, both His transcendence (*paratva*) and accessibility (*saulabhya*) have been declared through these two designations. Even though there is the reference "those" (*te*), the use of the word *aiśvaram* (divine) is intended to manifest the nature of His lordship (*īśvaratva*).

However, that which was stated as "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) is explained by the passage beginning with "of all," according to the method previously elaborated. The intended meaning is that the referent of the word "Lord" (īśvara) is indeed characterized by such attributes. The persistence of the nature [of the Lord] in qualities such as being the ruler consists in His possessing qualities, states, and activities corresponding to each of those [attributes].

[He exists] as the manifestor. Alternatively, regarding his existence as the ruler (*praśāsitṛ*), they—being powerless—accepted his function within Keśava according to their respective capacities, because by the maxim of "the letter *ṭa*," he removes erroneous determination through the mere sight of himself and serves as the cause for correct activity. His existence as the protector (*pālayitṛ*) is by way of stimulating the quality of goodness (*sattva*) and so forth. His existence as the creator (*sraṣṭṛ*) is due to the production from his own limbs of Brahmā, Rudra, and others, as well as the four castes and so on. Saṃ... [The text continues].

His abiding in the state of being the *hartṛ* (the destroyer) is established by the devouring and so forth that will be described later. His abiding in the state of being the *bhartṛ* (the sustainer) will be made clear by such passages as "therein, all is situated in one" (*tatraikastham*). His abiding in the state of being a mine of auspicious qualities means that, by virtue of possessing an incarnate form (*avatāra-vigraha*), he is incapable of assuming the semblance of ignorance and other such defects. Furthermore, because it will be stated in passages such as "the Lord of Brahmā" (*brāhmaṇam īśam*) that even those like Brahmā and Rudra, who might be suspected of being superior, abide within a single part of Him, He is the Supreme (*paratara*).

Abiding in you is logical. The phrase "being of a different genus from all others" is either a summary of everything previously stated, or its resultant conclusion, or a statement intended to convey the specific designations of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). In the interpretation where the passage is taken as referring to His essential nature (*svarūpa*)—in accordance with the request for a vision of the meaning as it appears at first sight in the words "Behold my sovereign yoga" (*paśya me yogamaiśvaram*)—the term "sovereign" (*aiśvaram*) alone is figurative, while everything else is primary. However, by way of the connection to His essential nature, the desire to see His form (*vigraha*) is implied. This is the sense of the word "form" (*rūpa*).

Or [it may mean] "intent upon all the unique aspects such as the essential nature (svarūpa) and form (rūpa). "Form" (rūpa) means "mode" (prakāra). Since the word "to see" (draṣṭum) is used even for a cognition that has a form similar to the act of seeing, the phrase "to perceive directly" (sākṣātkartum) is stated in order to exclude that [cognition] and to restrict [the meaning] solely to visual cognition (cākṣuṣajñāna).

By the words "of everything" (sarvasya) and so forth, the aspect heard [in scripture] is expressed by the pronoun "that" (tat). Here too, priority belongs to the sense of "essential nature"; whereas if it refers to "form," [priority belongs to the latter].

And regarding the sense of "merely the manner," it should be understood as before. "Yoga" means the conjunction with auspicious qualities such as knowledge and so forth. Here, even the power of sovereign lordship (*aiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇimā* is included among the qualities; however, the intention is that its mere role as a facilitator of yoga is not intended here because it does not constitute an internal factor for the specific form desired to be seen. The form that will be shown is what is intended here. Nor is some other matter, such as the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*), being presented to Arjuna. Yoga...

With the intention that sound is also recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*), he says, "Behold. By the word "Lord" (*prabhu*), he shows the possession of specific qualities with the intended meaning: "If you think so, then nothing is difficult for you. This is expressed by the passage beginning with "other than you," and so forth. Alternatively, this is a statement intended to convey the meaning of the term *yogeśvara*. Just as in expressions such as "Lord of Horses" (*aśvapati*) or "Lord of Wealth" (*dhanapati*), the term *yogeśvara* refers either to the abundance of qualities or to the mastery over even those qualities; such is the sense. Regarding the word "you" (*tvām*): it is inappropriate to assign another meaning to the word "self" (*ātman*); furthermore, he will later say "me" (*mām*).

[This is] the state of being. [The word] "indestructible" (*avyaya*) is used here as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) to dispel the doubt that the term is purposeless, to remove the contradiction regarding the demonstration of its nature as the non-perishing phenomenal world (*kṣaraprapañca*), and specifically to show that it has as its object the matter required by one who desires to see [the Lord]. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "you, the All" (*tvāṃ sakalam*). The meaning is: you whose form is distinguished by all qualities, manifestations, and physical bodies.

Showing the specific state resulting from the manner of Arjuna’s question and so forth—which serves as the reason for the Lord’s manifestation of His own self—he explains the consistency of the Lord’s words beginning with "Behold" (paśya) by saying "Thus. Having reflected upon the manner that is about to be described, he says "resting on all," (*sarvāśrayāṇi*). Because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it takes the neuter gender.

The solar orbs and so forth are infinite substrates (*adhikaraṇa*). Alternatively, the word "substrate" (*āśraya*) may, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or due to a difference in intended meaning, refer to that which is supported (*āśrita*). By the phrase "by the hundreds and thousands," it is shown that He possesses infinite non-material forms (*aprākṛta-vigraha*), which encompass all the distinctions made by those who propound the doctrines of the Supreme (*para*), the Manifested Array (*vyūha*), and the Expansive Power (*vibhava*). That form which resides in a single solar orb is identical to the countless forms residing in the solar orbs throughout the infinite Brahmā-eggs (*brāhmāṇḍa*). This is likewise true for other forms such as the Śrī Viśvarūpa. This very point is also intended by the Vedic scripture: "In every form, He is the corresponding form" (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpaḥ*).

Some say: the statement "look" is made with the intention, "I shall act in such a way that you will see. By the word "of various kinds," he explains "of diverse types," intending here the infinity of specific varieties for each [form], such as ornaments, weapons, emblems, and the number of arms. Regarding the phrase "not material" (*aprākṛtāni*), the intention is that by the word "divine" (*divya*), qualities such as existing in heaven are not intended; for it will be stated later that they pervade even the earth and other elements, and it is necessary to state their distinction from ordinary matter.
Furthermore, among the four [forms] beginning with Vāsudeva, there are white, red, yellow, and... according to the differences of the *yugas*.

Due to the transformation of His dark form (*kṛṣṇarūpa*) and because He assumes various colors in accordance with the meditations of those seeking specific fruits in other incarnations, there is a state of having manifold colors. With the intention that by the word "form" (*ākṛti*) a specific configuration common to gods, humans, animals, and so forth is intended, he says "of various forms" (*nānākārāṇi*). Although there is the occasion for His own infinite forms—as in the passage "by the hundreds and thousands"—here, for the sake of relevance to the present topic, the phrase "all gathered in one" (*ihaikastham*) refers to a single form alone.

Intending to specifically demonstrate this, he says, "In me alone... With the intention that the primary deities—the thirty-three—are first indicated by the words "Behold the suns," etc., there is the presentation of specific numbers such as "twelve" and so forth. He says "for the purpose of illustration" in order to exclude the notion that these are merely objects of perception according to what will be described later. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "not perceived by Arjuna and others."
The phrase "not seen before" is an elliptical expression that also includes "not heard before," or rather, they are collectively subsumed under the mere quality of being uncomprehended;

with this intention, he says, "not seen before in any of the scriptures. By this, it is indicated that even regarding supersensuous objects which are known in a general way through scripture, there exist many specific details that can be grasped only through direct perception.

With the intention that by the very use of the singular ending in "in this body" (*iha dehe*), one [entity] is intended to be expressed as the subject to be demonstrated, he says: "in this, my, single body. Since the oneness of the body is already stated by the singular number and by the specific indication of what is about to be shown, the word "situated in one" (*ekastha*) intends his abiding in a particular part of that [body]. As for what has been said by some—that [the body] is a constituent part of the one whole [Lord]—that is because the world is composed of *prakṛti*, whereas the Lord’s form (*vigraha*) is not.

And because its non-ordinary nature has been established, it is refuted; with this intention, he said, "even there, [it is] situated in one place, situated in a single part. Alternatively, since the entire [body] is stated to be situated in one place, its abiding in a single part thereof is implied as a result. Furthermore, by the phrase "whatever else you wish to see," the victory of the Pāṇḍavas over the Dhārtarāṣṭras and so forth is also included. There too, by the force of the conjunction (*samuccaya*), he states that it rests upon a single part of the body, saying "that too. (7)

However, in the phrase "but you will not be able [to defeat] me," he draws out and demonstrates the reason for that inability—which was indicated by the word *tu*—as stated in the preceding verse, beginning with "I am... By this...

He states what is intended by the word "vetti" (he knows) as "niyata" (fixed). It is said "by the *prākṛta*" because it is the opposite of the divine (*divya*). Regarding the phrase "tathābhūtam" (of such a nature), the sense is that by the word "mām" (me), the state of being distinguished by [the qualities of] form and so forth is intended here. He states what is intended by the word "dravya" (substance) as "mad-asādhāraṇam" (uncommon to me). And he states the meaning of the word "yoga," which is supported by the term "Īśvara" (Lord) as the result of the context and other factors, as "ananta" (infinite). Lordship (*īśvaratvam*) is the power of governing; its consequence...

And "union" (yoga) refers precisely to the union with the powers and attributes appropriate to that [state]. Because his vision is divine, he perceives the qualities such as knowledge; the sense is that he will later say, "I see [the Lord] characterized by such specific attributes as infinite power."

By the phrase "Hari, the great master of yoga," he states their previously assumed forms which conceal [their true nature], namely, that they are stationed as charioteers for Pārtha and are the sons of his maternal uncle.

By this, there is also an indication of affection (*vātsalya*) and other qualities which serve as the cause for the manifestation of their divine form. Because of the qualification "great" (*mahat*), there is a sense of wonder. Furthermore, since the word "great" qualifies the "master of yoga," it is intended here that it more appropriately qualifies "yoga"; thus he says, "of the masters of the most wonderful yogas. This applies to others as well.

By the word "Lord" (Īśvara), what is intended is the state of Yoga being dependent upon Him. The phrase "Hari is the Great Lord of Yoga" demonstrates the meaning of the general and specific statements intended by those two words: namely, that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman. Because of their close proximity in the sequence—"Behold my sovereign Yoga" and "the supreme sovereign form"—these two possess a single unified meaning. When it is said, "We shall show you the sovereign form," it does not mean the form of some other person distinct from Himself.

The term "svāsādhāraṇam" (its own unique) was stated to exclude the possibility that it might be understood as mere intellect (*dhī*). Here too, the word *rūpa* should be understood as referring either to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) together with its suffixes, or to the physical body (*vigraha*) which manifests that nature, or simply to the general form common to both the essential nature and the rest. To show that by the word "Pārtha" there is intended the relationship that causes affection and serves to demonstrate his essential nature, he says: "the son of Pṛthā, the paternal aunt. He explains what was called "the form of supreme sovereignty" by the words: "that [form] is manifold... (*tad vividham*).

The state of being the refuge of the entire world exists both by virtue of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and through its embodied form (*vigraha*). Alternatively, this is a demonstration of the introduction [to the verse] beginning with "aneka" (many); for it is precisely from that [verse] that it is understood that "it is such. This meaning is established by the words "standing here in one place" (*ihaikastham*) and so forth. By the word "praśāsitṛ" (ruler), the status of being a presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) is intended. The multiplicity in the faces, ornaments, and weapons should also be understood as arising from the diversity of their respective classes (*jāti*). For when there is a connection with many faces belonging to various different classes, [the result is manifold].

In the meditations on the Śrī Viśvarūpa, it is recited in the scriptures of the Blessed One that otherwise the description of having "many eyes" would be purposeless, since that is already established by the multiplicity of faces alone. "Anekādbhūtadarśanam" means that whose vision is manifold and wonderful; the sense is that it is perceived as possessing an infinite and unsurpassed degree of marvel. "Divyatva" means being non-material (aprākṛta). "Sarvāścaryamayam" means being the locus of all wondrous principles. For this very reason—

By the phrase "the vision of many wonders," there is no tautology; one should understand it as: "The form of this Great Soul is this most wonderful universe," and so forth. To exclude the notion that the word *deva* here refers merely to a specific class [of beings] or the like—without regard for its actual nature—and to demonstrate that its referent is characterized by a physical body (*vigraha*), the term "shining forth" (*dyotamāna*) is used. He describes the manner of its infinity and the cause thereof with the words beginning "entirely" (*nikhila*). This refers to its being the substratum of the entire world.

Because it is explicitly stated [in the text], the fact that [the Lord] is the substratum of the three times is also established as a result. Both of these results—namely, the unfitness for delimitation by space and time—are present here as far as possible, either through the medium of the body (*vigraha*) or independently thereof. As for infinity (*anantya*), which consists in the absence of delimitation by objects, it resides in the essential nature (*svarūpa*). However, because the word *ananta* occurs among the group of qualifiers of the body, it refers to the body as well. This is seen in the passage, "Having seen the wonderful one," where [the Lord is described as] "wonderful, with infinite length and breadth."

He will state that the word *yugram* refers specifically to the object of form (*rūpa*). Therefore, others maintain that the intended meaning is merely to demonstrate extreme breadth and so forth. In this way, the subsequent restatement—“in its infinite length and breadth”—which is yet to be spoken, is also rendered consistent. [This applies] even to this body (*vigraha*) which pervades the universe.

It is logical that there is no obstruction anywhere due to a particular power (*śakti-viśeṣa*). Even for yogins endowed with the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), a specific supernatural accomplishment (*siddhi*) is described as "emerging from and sinking into the earth. Therefore, its status as the substratum of the entire universe, beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which will be explained later, is not untenable. For this very reason, one should not suspect that the quality of being the substratum of all is stated here merely in the form of a metaphorical ornament (*ābhūṣaṇa-rūpeṇa*); rather, in that context, the phrase "in the body of the God of gods" functions as a qualification of the body.

This is because [the scripture] states that [the Lord] possesses infinite length and breadth. Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of the form resting on the leaf of the banyan tree, all things are contained within even the smallest space by means of a power that accomplishes the impossible, or by way of a subtle form; for such is not stated there, and the opposite is stated instead. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as it is heard in the text. And this has been established by the word "inconceivable" (acintya) in the *Ārambhabhāṣya* itself. With the intention that what was already described by the term "having many mouths" is here further specified by the word "facing all directions," he says: "whose faces are situated in all directions. Because it refers directly to the embodied form, [the text speaks of] the universe...

The claim made by others—that in this context, as in passages such as "That eye, indeed, is facing in all directions," the [Deity] is not everywhere endowed with a face—is incorrect; the point is that faces are absent in the hands, feet, and so forth. Furthermore, disregarding the order of the text, the section beginning with "the Deity" (*devam*) has been explained first, following the sequence of perception from the indistinct to the distinct. This is done with the intention that the perception of the specific forms inherent in the [Deity] must precede the perception of its being qualified by separately established substances, and that such a demonstration is appropriate.

Although the ether (*āmbara*) and the other elements were mentioned previously, they are shown again later by the words "suitable for themselves" (*svocita*) and so forth. Here too, the mention occurs by transgressing the order of recitation and bypassing the ether in order to demonstrate the gradation of internal and external status. In this context, the phrase "he showed" (*darśayāmāsa*) is to be construed with what precedes it.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter. 16.

The manner of the division into triads for the third group of six has already been explained by us in detail. Having demonstrated that division into triads therein, [the author] sequentially restates the meaning of the three triads—which are intended for the purification of the principles—in order to introduce the sixteenth [chapter] as being connected with them, stating: "by means of the three preceding chapters. The reading is *guṇasaṅgatadviparyayahetukatvam*; even in the absence of the suffix *kap*, this remains a bahuvrīhi compound.

Thus, at the end of the previous chapter, the *Śārīraka* was introduced with the words "the most secret *Śārīraka*. Furthermore, by the two terms *anadha* and *bhārata*, its qualified recipient has been indicated; for it will be said: "Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, you are born to a divine fortune. Since the determination of the meaning stated therein depends upon the *Śārīraka*, it must first be explained that a person is subject to the *Śārīraka*.

And this will be stated at the end of the chapter: "Therefore, the Śāstra is your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; having understood what is prescribed in the rules of the Śāstra, you should perform the action here. It is for that very purpose—that is, to discern the specific qualifications of the practitioner indicated at the end of the previous chapter—that the division between the divine (*daiva*) and the demonic (*āsura*) is declared at the beginning of this chapter. With that intention, it has been summarized: "The sixteenth [chapter] is spoken for the sake of stabilizing the knowledge of the practice of reality, preceded by the declaration of the division between the divine and the demonic."

Intending all of this, he says "immediately following. This refers to the entirety of the subject matter already stated; it is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the discernment of practice (*anuṣṭhāna-viveka*) which is yet to be stated. Alternatively, there is no intention to mention that [discernment] because it consists in the purification of a portion of what has already been stated. Furthermore, the practice mentioned in the summary verse (*saṃgraha-śloka*) is also included by the qualification "of the entire [subject matter]. He states the final result—namely, the description of the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—in order to express the necessity of the scripture (*śāstra-avaśyatām vaktum*).

In the statement regarding being under the control of Śārṅga, what purpose does the mention of the division between gods and asuras serve? To this, [the author] replies: "By being under the control of Śārṅga and by its opposite. For the command of the Blessed Lord is Śārṅga; the gods, who follow it, are favored by Him, and therefore one should act accordingly. The asuras, who transgress His command, are suppressed by Him, and therefore one should not act accordingly—this is the intended meaning. The word *sarga* (creation/emanation), which will be mentioned later, is employed here to indicate their natural enmity.

The distinction here is based on the qualities (guṇas) and actions that will be described later in the passage beginning with, "By which one [experiences] dream, fear, and grief," and so forth. Since fear is indeed of the nature of *tamas*, the intention is to show that it does not occur for one of a *sāttvika* disposition belonging to the divine creation; thus, for the purpose of defining fear, the text teaches its opposite by stating, "the desirable and the undesirable. The words "separation" (*viyoga*) and "union" (*saṃyoga*) are to be construed respectively with the "undesirable" and the "desirable. This is a statement of the essential nature [of fear], and it is not included as part of the formal definition of fear.

For that [suffering] is indeed suffering born from the perception of the causes of future suffering. Here, "purity of being" (sattva-saṃśuddhi) refers to the purification of the "being" (sattva), which is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) serving as the locus of the self; its thorough purification is the cessation of all defects.

In that regard, intending to express the cessation of all defects such as lustful desire (*kāma-rāga*), envy (*asūyā*), and deception (*vañcanā*) through the removal of *rajas* and *tamas* which have become the root [of those defects], he says: "the state of being untouched by *rajas* and *tamas*. Here, the term "knowledge-yoga" (*jñāna-yoga*) does not serve to exclude karma-yoga and the others, since they too are to be adopted as being characterized by *sattva*. Therefore, what is intended here is the scriptural discernment of the pure nature of the Self common to action, knowledge, and devotion; thus he says: "separated from material nature" (*prakṛti-viyukta*). In this context, knowledge itself is "yoga" because it is the means.

Alternatively, *jñānayoga* is the reflection (*cintana*) accomplished through knowledge produced by the scriptures. The passage beginning with "acquired by just means" (*nyāyārjita*) is a demonstration of the scriptural form of giving (*dāna*), since performing otherwise will be described as being *rājasa* or *tāmasa*. This should be understood according to one's capacity. *Dama* is self-restraint; it is the turning away from improper paths, which has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its object, as established by common experience and scripture. He says "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) because he will later describe the restraint of the external senses with the word "tranquility" (*śānti*).

By this, the interpretation of some who explain the meaning of these two words in reverse order is refuted. Since "they sacrifice with sacrifices of name, out of hypocrisy, and contrary to injunctions" (Gītā 16.17) will be spoken of later as the demonic sacrifices (*āsura-yajña*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) here refers to the inclusion of the Sāttvika sacrifice intended in this context of the path to liberation.

Fearing that one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*) might refrain from practicing even those portions of the Veda that concern the realm of deities excluded [from the primary path] and which enjoin rituals for the sake of small fruits—on the grounds of the maxim of the "well" (*udapāna-nyāya*)—the author states "along with its manifestations" (*savibhūteḥ*) to show that such exclusion is already established by the context of the practice of the Veda by the three higher castes (*trairvārṇika*).

The intention is that for one who recites [the Upaniṣads] after reflecting in the sequence beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas declare," being impelled by the injunction to practice the Upaniṣads, the entire procedure for practicing the Upaniṣads consists of the practice of the Praṇava, the eight-syllabled, the six-syllabled, the two-six (twelve-syllabled), and the single-syllabled [forms]. By this, passages such as "Abandon other words" are also shown to have another purpose [namely, the exclusion of other speech], because the purport [of the scripture] lies in the fact that the Praṇava alone is to be adopted during the state of meditation, as in: "Meditate on the Self as 'Om' alone."

Although *svādhyāya* means that which is studied by oneself—that is, one's own recension (*sva-śākhā*)—nevertheless, because of the principle that "it is not taught for the sake of one person alone," and because the meaning common to all recensions must be investigated, and because the injunction for silent recitation (*japa*) applies without distinction to all, it is stated in general terms as "devoted to the study of the Veda. Having defined austerity (*tapas*) as the contraction of enjoyment beginning with the head, he cites its specific varieties, starting with "the *kuśīla* [vow]," etc.: "By eating once a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for..."

"One should not be devoid of fasting by means of fasting or giving"—for the sake of such enjoined propitiation of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), the fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is here called "fasting on the twelfth day. Alternatively, among the lunar-day observances (*tithi-vrata*) and the observances of two lunar days, fasting on the twelfth day indeed exists as well. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the austerities (*tapas*) to be described later, which are produced by the three instruments (*karaṇa*). He says "for the purpose of producing devotion to the action that pleases the Blessed One" in order to exclude those austerities whose fruits are characterized as *rājasa* or *tāmasa*. One who is purified by austerity has the qualification for worship and other rites.

Since the triad of instruments (the three qualities) is uniform within itself even in others, he says "in others" (*pareṣu*) in order to exclude that [uniformity]. The intention is that its cessation must be stated in the context of the occurrence of crookedness (*kauṭilya*). The phrase "avoiding injury to others" (*parapīḍāvarjanam*) is an elliptical expression for avoiding injury to oneself as well. Alternatively, the sense is that even the self-injury of fools is intended as injury to others. Just as one becomes a speaker of truth by speaking only what has been seen, nevertheless, because of the rule "truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings," it is spoken as being beneficial to living beings.

The phrase "avoiding injury to others" (parapīḍāphala) is to be understood as before. Since it is impossible to abandon sleep, eating, the great sacrifices, the staff, the water-pot, and so forth—which are obtained through one's nature or prescribed by the scriptures—he restricts [the meaning] to a specific case by saying "that which is opposed to one's own welfare. Since the word *dama* (self-restraint) has already expressed the restraint of the mind—as in such passages as "peaceful and self-restrained"—he says "of the senses" with the intention that here *śānti* (tranquility) refers to the state of the external senses.

Just as in the case of non-anger (*akrodha*) and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), [the author] defines non-malicious speech (*apaiśuna*) by way of its opposite, namely "speaking for the harm of others. Although the fact that its object is living beings is established by the mere word "compassion" (*dayā*), the repetition of the term and the use of the plural number are intended to include all objects such as enemies, friends, and so forth. As stated by Gautama: "Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of laziness, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of possessiveness. And elsewhere: "Compassion toward all beings is the flower," and so on.

Regarding this, he says: "In all beings... [The verse continues: "When this entire world is afflicted by the threefold suffering, then toward those beings who are objects of pity, one should feel compassion. Thus Prahlāda spoke concerning the purification of the heart known as compassion (*karuṇā*). The meaning of "intolerance of suffering" is the desire to dispel it. From the verbal root *lup* in its *yaṅluk* form, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, the word ending in *p* is *lolup*; however, when the suffix *ac* is applied, it becomes *lolupa*. This indicates the state of being non-greedy, expressed as *aloluptvam* or *alolupatvam*.

Regarding the verbal root *lūñ* in the sense of "cutting," the form *lolū* is derived with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅ-luk*). In that context, taking the Vedic shortening prescribed by the rule "tve ca," he states that there is also a reading "alolutvam. With the intention of showing that what is prohibited here is fickleness in the form of a desire for the unworthy, he says "in objects" (*viṣayeṣu*). Since the primary meaning of "gentleness" (*mārdava*) is not applicable here, he says "absence of hardness" (*akāṭhinyam*) in order to demonstrate its figurative sense, which suggests qualities such as a pleasant countenance and so forth.

For a solidified substance is unfit for the penetration of others; likewise, here, by the expression "of a rigid nature," he indicates—through the intention of contrasting it with that [solidity]—the resulting softness [of the heart] toward virtuous people. Since being disregarded and so forth are conducive to yoga, shame rooted in those [feelings] is inappropriate for those established in *sattva*; therefore, he mentions a specific kind of shame appropriate to the occasion: "in the doing of what should not be done."

Regarding the word *vrīḍā* (shame): the meaning is that great men, whose lineage, learning, and conduct are renowned, feel shame even for others who perform improper acts, let alone for themselves. To avoid the redundancy between "lack of greed" (*alolupatva*) and "lack of fickleness" (*acapalatva*), he says: "in the presence of desirable objects. By this, it is also shown that there is no addiction to games, jesting, hunting, gambling, and so forth. The word *tejas* (splendor) refers to something other than the elements (*bhūta*); it is used either for the capacity to overcome others or for independence from others.

Therefore, what is intended is a state of being unassailable by falsehoods that is invariably concomitant with it. And this is achieved through the absence of meanness, which provides an opening for the wicked; with this intention, he says, "by the wicked. He shows the distinction between non-anger and forbearance (*kṣamā*) by stating, "even when experiencing pain caused by another. Indifference (*audāsīnya*) is merely the absence of agitation toward those who have committed no offense; it is not, however, forbearance. For it is said that anger may arise even toward those who are innocent: "Brahmins, courtesans, physicians, dogs, and cocks..."

The intention [of the verse] is: "I do not know the reason why they become angry at the mere sight [of me]. Regarding the phrase "toward others" (*pareṣu*), the meaning is "in relation to the experience of suffering by others. Since fear and fickleness have been mentioned separately, he says "even in great calamity" with the intention that *sāttvikī dhṛti* (steadfastness born of sattva) here refers to the non-lapsing maintenance of the resolve to practice one's duty (*śāstrīyānuṣṭhāna-saṃkalpa*) even when a great crisis has arisen.

The meaning is that when a great calamity has arrived, the Blessed Lord Hari should be remembered; for by abandoning even the primary duties that are easy to perform, every other duty would indeed be accomplished. And he will speak of sattvic fortitude (dhṛti): "That fortitude by which, through yoga, one maintains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses without deviation—that, O Pārtha, is sattvic fortitude."

"By yoga" means by that which is unfailing, having as its purpose the worship of the Blessed One who is the means to liberation, and thus independent of any other purpose. For the body, speech, and mind—whose *sattva* has been impaired by contact with impure persons, the use of impure substances, and so forth—are rendered fit for various ritual actions (*karman*) through purification (*śārīraiḥ*). He says "by [the purifications] of the arms" (*bāhya*) to indicate that in the absence of such [purification], there would be no efficacy. He says "by [the purifications] of the self" (*ātmika*) to exclude the fitness for action consisting in the proficiency of the instruments (organs) and so forth, which is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) has already been mentioned, he says "not obstructing others" (*pareṣvanuparodhaḥ*) in order to show its specific distinction from that. For when the weak are brought under the control of the powerful, they are restrained from acting according to their own will; this is "obstruction. He says "not obstructing" (*anuparodha*) to mean the non-performance of such an act. However, for oneself, the restraint of one's own independent activity is indeed austerity (*tapas*); therefore, he specifies "of others. "Pride" (*māna*) and "conceit" (*garva*) are synonyms, but here it is intended to be prohibited in general. Nevertheless, [pride] that is proportionate to one's lineage, heroism, learning, and so forth— (Aligned with the provided text and Sanskrit conventions)

He might also carry away that which exists; however, since it would otherwise not be appropriate for falsehood to be mentioned here according to the nature of the Asuras—which will be described later—the prohibition of pride is stated with its prefix (*sa-upasarga*) by saying, "Pride in the wrong place. When it is said "the divine endowment" (*daivīṃ saṃpadam*), the prosperity of the gods might be understood; and that [prosperity] does not follow from falsehood.

Therefore, in order to introduce the intended meaning, he first states the etymology as "pertaining to the gods" (*daivī*), because of the distinction [made in the Gītā]: "One should know *sattva* to be the divine quality (*devaguṇa*), while the other two qualities are demonic (*āsura*)," and because it follows the Lord’s injunction that "from *sattva*, knowledge is born," and because it is an object of affection and the cause of the supreme human goal. He says "And that... [referring to the verse], for it has been said: "But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature (*daivīṃ prakṛtiṃ*), worship Me with undistracted minds, knowing Me as the imperishable source of beings."

Regarding the phrase *jātasya*, since the root *jan* (to be born) is normally intransitive, it becomes transitive through the influence of a prefix (*upasarga*), just as in the case of *pari* and other such prefixes; therefore, he explains the application of the second case (*dvitīyā*) for the object by saying *tām abhimukhīkṛtya* ("having directed her toward [him]"). Alternatively, the second case occurs due to its connection with a *karmapravacanīya* particle according to the rule *abhirabhāge*. Thus, *abhimukhīkṛtya* means "having made her the target," just as in the expression *yathā daivī*.

It comes about; that is to say, it happens to one who has been born in such a manner. What is intended here is the realization of the inevitable occurrence of such prosperity for those endowed with these very qualities. And so it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Indeed, if Madhusūdana should behold a person at the moment of birth, he should be known as sāttvika; he is truly one who contemplates the goal of liberation. This is what is meant by the phrase "to one who has been born for the purpose of accomplishing that [prosperity]. (2–3)

In the passage beginning with "deceit (dambha) and pride (darpa)," the word *bhavantī* is supplied as an ellipsis. "For the sake of proclaiming one's own righteousness" means not out of a sense of following the Lord’s command, but rather for the purpose of making such a claim. "Causing a lack of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done" implies that it is the cause for transgressing the scriptures (*śruti*). Regarding the specific nature of pride (*darpa*), which is synonymous with the arrogance denoted by the term *atimāna*, he states: "caused by the experience of sense objects. By this, he excludes the joy arising from causes such as the sight of the venerable Teacher (*ācārya-bhagavat*).

The phrase "this is not the way" (*asthā*) clarifies that which was previously stated as being "inconsistent with one's own knowledge and lineage" (*svavidābhijānānanuguṇa*). The mention of "knowledge and lineage" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for strength, wealth, and so forth. What is intended here is the transgression of the following rule: "One should conduct oneself in this world by maintaining conformity in age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage, as well as in dress, speech, and behavior. With the intention that verbal harshness and physical violence are not excessive faults when directed toward the wicked, he says: "A nature that causes distress to the virtuous."

The meaning is that for this very reason, from the exclusion of the virtuous (*sādhu*), there must also necessarily follow the exclusion of the Śārūyas. Ignorance—consisting of sleep at the improper time and so forth, as well as regarding inappropriate objects—is common to both the Āsuric beings and others; and there is no fault [in this]. He distinguishes them by the term "parāvara" (the high and the low). Based on such ignorance, there arises in other scriptures the conceptualization of a reversal of the high and low principles (*tattva*) and the adoption of conduct contrary to the Vedas. The demonstration here of the absence of the few qualities previously mentioned is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, the word "ca" (and) serves to include all that has not been explicitly stated.

He says that those whose nature is to transgress the command of the Blessed Lord manifest an *āsurī* (demoniac) disposition. Regarding them it is said: "Whether as a Brāhmaṇa or as a Kṣatriya, he sees this [Self] being born, [obstructed] by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*)"; and in the words of Prajāpati, concerning the devotion to the three aims of life rooted in the identification of the body with the Self and so forth, it is stated: "This is indeed the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Asuras.

Here, the word *saṃpat* is to be understood either with reference to those who take pleasure in violating the command of the Blessed Lord, or with the intent of reproach, or simply in the sense that they "attain" [such a state]. ||4||

In order to generate faith regarding the divine nature and agitation regarding the demonic nature, that which was stated previously in the passage beginning with "Those established in goodness go upward" (Gītā 14.18) is here recalled in brief by the half-verse beginning with "The divine endowment... Liberation is defined as the cessation of ultimate misfortune in order to express that it culminates in the attainment of the desired; thus he states the primary meaning of the word [liberation] as "from bondage," or alternatively, as being mediated by the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*). "Bondage" (*nibandha*) means fixed or constant bondage. In this context, he recalls the phrase "they go downward" by the term "downward course" (*adhogati*). ||4||

In this context, the statement "do not grieve" is not intended to prohibit grief for that which is inherently ungrievable as initiated at the beginning of the Śārīraka [section], because that has already been refuted in many ways; furthermore, the possibility of its removal is established by the words, "you have been born endowed with divine nature."

Therefore, when it is stated that the Asuric nature leads to bondage, even though one’s own self does not transgress the limits of Śārṅgapañcama (the divine standard), the author says "having heard this," in order to dispel the grief of Bībhatsu—who, having heard of the two kinds of prosperity, suspects his own Asuric nature on the mere basis of the fact that he possesses a hidden egoism (as described by the rule "firm and with hidden egoism") which is a quality of the *dhīrodātta* hero, and who thus witnesses this within himself. By making known that this [hidden egoism] is actually his own natural disposition (*svaprakṛti*), he removes his sorrow.

With the intention that "you yourself are bringing grief here at an improper time," he says, "Do not grieve. With the intention that "for those of divine nature who are preeminent in dharma, sons of an asura-like character are not possible," he uses the vocative "O Pāṇḍava" and says, "of the foremost among the righteous. (5)

Anticipating the doubt—“What is the cause of the division between the divine (*daiva*) and the demonic (*āsura*) among all selves that are equal in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth?”—the author refutes it by restating the distinction with its specific characteristics. Furthermore, in order to make known that [the demonic conduct] must be utterly avoided, he introduces the intended subject matter regarding the account of the demons (*asuras*) with the verse beginning, “Two types of creation of beings (*bhūtasarga*). The phrase “in this world” is not for the purpose of excluding other worlds, since the division between gods and demons is established everywhere. Nor...

It would be appropriate to point out merely the ground of meaninglessness; therefore, with the intention that what is intended here is the indication of the performance of prescribed and prohibited acts according to the forms established by worldly perception, he says, "of the agents of action. Alternatively, the qualification "in this" is used with the intent of referring to the world of action (*karma-loka*). Since the root *sṛj* has many meanings—as in the verse, "creation (*sarga*), nature (*svabhāva*), liberation (*nirmokṣa*), certainty (*niścaya*), chapter (*adhyāya*), and emission (*sṛṣṭi*)"—he first states that the root here refers to the activity of the agent due to the force of the context, saying, "creation means origination."

In response to the doubt as to how there can be a distinction between the divine (*daivata*) and the demonic (*āsura*) within the very nature of their origin, the author says "prācīna... (beginning with the word *prācīna*), intending to synthesize what is meant by the term *sarga* (creation) in the context of this division between the divine and the demonic expressed by the phrase "in this world" (*asmin loke*). The meaning is that the mention of "divinity" and "demonism" at the time of origin is intended to signify the attainment of the respective states of divine and demonic endowment (*saṃpad*). Furthermore, disregarding the meanings of the word *sarga* as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) or "that which is being created" (*sṛjyamāna*) because they are not well-known in this context, it is explained as referring to the well-known sense of "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*).

When it is said, "The divine creation has been declared in detail," one might understand this as a description of the origin of the gods and so forth, similar to the narration of genealogies and dynastic histories; yet that was not what was done. Although individuals established in the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of action, and the yoga of devotion were indicated by such statements as "If one renounces desires" and "Others [perform] sacrifice as the divine alone"—nevertheless, the primary intent there too lies precisely in the detailed exposition of their respective duties.

Therefore, with the intention that the detailed description of the divine creation (daivasarga) here is given by way of its effects, [the Lord] spoke the words beginning with "for the sake of performing [right] conduct. With the intention that this is a summary of what was previously explained in detail in the passage beginning with "Fearlessness, purity of being," [He] mentioned "karmayoga" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the demoniacal creation (āsuraṃ sargam)," he says "of the demons (asurāṇām)" because, according to what will be stated later, the intended meaning is exactly thus. If one were to say, "Hear from me the demoniacal creation," there would be the perception of a genitive case in the sense of an agent (kartari-ṣaṣṭhī) due to its connection with the act of creating; therefore, [he uses the word "creation" (sarga) instead]. Furthermore—

With the intention that it is appropriate to indicate the highest degree of authority required for the command "Listen" (śṛṇu), he says, "from me. Just as that which is to be accepted cannot be accepted if it is unknown, so too that which is to be rejected cannot be rejected if it is unknown; therefore, with the intention that you should be attentive in this matter, he said, "Listen. ||6||

In this context, the terms "engagement" (*pravṛtti*) and "withdrawal" (*nivṛtti*) do not refer to worldly matters, because engagement on a wrong path and withdrawal from the right path for the sake of attaining or avoiding desired and undesired worldly results are already established as belonging specifically to the *asuras*. Nor do they refer merely to what is prescribed and prohibited, nor to objects obtained through passion or aversion, because that would result in the redundancy of stating, "neither purity nor conduct."

Therefore, he states with the words "the means for worldly prosperity," etc., that the intention here is the absence of discrimination between those dharmas that incite activity, those that cause transformation, and those that bring about cessation, which are required by one seeking liberation. These two types of dharma are recorded in traditional scripture (smṛti): "Prajāpati proclaimed the dharma characterized by engagement; the sage Nārāyaṇa proclaimed the dharma characterized by withdrawal."

In the phrase "they do not know," as in the expression "untruth is not spoken among them" or "truth does not exist among them," the mere absence of truth is not intended; rather, he says "they do not know" with the intention that, despite being instructed a hundred times, they fail to understand due to the abundance of darkness (ignorance).

The phrase "fitness for [performing] duties" (kṛtyayogyatā), mentioned previously, is explained here by the words "fitness for Vedic rites. External purity is not present due to a lack of practice in bathing and so forth, and because of the non-performance of obligatory duties; internal purity, however, is absent due to the lack of spiritual qualities (ātmaguṇa). With the intention of negating both the effect and the cause in their respective order—expressed as "neither purity nor conduct"—the author says "that" (tat). Now, one might object: regarding the duties of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana), other fruits are heard in scripture, such as "for householders, the Prājāpatya [world]."

To the question, "How then can it be said to be the cause of purity?", he says: "As has been stated... By stating the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumad-bhāva*) is here rendered firm. This [principle] should also be understood to apply to the abandonment of other obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "according to one's knowledge" and so on: because of a delight in deception, there is speech that does not correspond to one's actual knowledge; because of the nature of violence (*hiṃsā*), there is an absence of speech that is beneficial in form. ||7||

Thus, it is not merely that truth is not spoken; rather, there is the speaking of its opposite. To explain this immediately following, he says "Moreover" (*kiṃca*). Here, the word *asatya* (unreal) does not refer to falsity (*mithyātva*), because that has already been refuted by [the arguments of] worldly perception, contradiction with one's own words, and so forth, being far too crude [for such a context]. Furthermore, it is impossible to deceive the Asuras—who possess deep-seated attachment based on the assumption of the ultimate, stable, and divine nature of things—by means of the elaborate and fallacious arguments regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*).

The interpretation that "just as we are mostly false (unreal), so is the entire world," is also weak; for the word *jagat* (the world) does not refer exclusively to sentient beings alone, and because the negations here are intended to exclude the previously mentioned [falsehood] rather than negate it, and because—like the phrase "without foundation, without a Lord"—they intend to negate what is established by the Śruti, given that the Asuras are by nature hostile to the Śruti. Therefore, this word is intended to negate that which is established by the Śruti as being "unreal" (*anṛta*).

And that Truth is Brahman alone; this is well-known from such passages as, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is defined as Brahman by virtue of being the controller of both the conscious and the unconscious: "The name of this very Brahman is 'Truth' (Satya). These, indeed, are its three syllables: *sat*, *ti*, and *yam*. That which is *sat* is immortal. Day after day, he who knows this goes to the heavenly world."

Thus, [the author] states the intended meaning with the word "satya" (truth), namely that those who follow the doctrines of Kapila, Guru, Kumārila, Jina, Sugata, Cārvāka, and others, assert that the world is non-Vedic in nature (*abrāhma*).

Furthermore, regarding the word "apratiṣṭha" (unfounded), since it is impossible to negate a foundation established by direct perception due to its contradiction with all the world and so forth, he states with the word "tathā" (likewise) the intended meaning as the negation of everything that stands as a foundation in the scriptures. He elucidates this very point through a specific example with the words "by the infinite Brahman. By this, [he explains] the term "pratiṣṭhā" (foundation).
The interpretation [of the Lord] as being solely for the sake of merit and demerit has been refuted. The meaning is that He "supports all the worlds" both by His essential nature and by His activity.

For when it is stated in the scripture that [the earth] is supported by the primordial tortoise, Śeṣa, the directional elephants (diṅnāgas), and so forth, the rationalists (haitukas) indeed prattle thus: "He is merely the supporter of the earth..."

Some maintain that if there were another [being] distinct from Him, he would be different from Him; others likewise desire this. The Jainas [assert] constant falling due to [the soul's] heaviness (*gurutva*). Furthermore, the word "non-lord" (*anīśvara*) here does not intend to negate worldly lords such as images or kings, because they do not negate those [worldly lords]. As they state: "The Cārvākas say it is established by worldly usage.

Nor does it have the purpose of merely negating Brahmā, since that would be redundant with the words beginning with "untruthful" (*asatya*). Therefore, he states "by one whose resolve is true" (*satyasaṃkalpena*) and so forth, indicating that the intent here is the negation of a non-worldly controller (*alaukika-niyantṛ*) according to the etymological derivation.

The sense is that those who imagine the activity of the world to proceed from something non-conscious by nature—like a magnet and so forth; or from the doctrine of the Jainas and others that "this entire world consists of living and non-living beings and is without a Lord"; or from the teaching of a conceited "Lord," as in "who else could exist other than this one known as the Supreme Lord who is established within me?"; or from the force of a continuous succession of Lords limited by space and time—they are indeed *āsuras* (demonic). This is the intended meaning.

Others as well are seen to be lords who act as instigators, and they are so heard in scripture; how then is there the Lord's governance of all? To this he says: "I am all. Even the activity of other governors, in the form of their governance, is dependent solely upon the Lord. And thus it has been stated in the Sūtras, beginning with "The agent [is the Self] because the scripture has that purpose," and concluding with "But [the agency is] from the Supreme, for that is heard."

Thus, it has been stated that they do not accept the dependence of the world’s origin, maintenance, and activity upon the Supreme Brahman. Regarding this, since the independence from Brahman for the world's origin was previously asserted, he says, "And they speak thus," in order to demonstrate that very point through other means. The passage beginning with "not from one another" (*aparaspara*) does not form a single syntactical unit with what precedes it, because there is no connection with the phrase "what else? (*kimanyat*), and because it would result in an overly strained interpretation. "This alone is sufficient to establish their demonic nature."

The supposition that "what else is being said? is beset by the necessity of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, the phrase "they say thus" is not spoken with the intention of implying such ellipsis, since that is already established by the very words "this view. Therefore, with the intention that the statement beginning with "arisen from mutual union" is intended as an elaboration of the point that [the world] has desire as its cause, he says: "woman... The alternative explanation—that it means "devoid of the relation of cause and effect due to the continuity of activity"—is extremely weak; for it abandons the most well-known meaning and results in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the phrase "having desire as its cause. With this in mind, he says: "not being thus."

What else is observed? Although the birth of sweat-born beings and stationary plants is seen even without the union of a woman and a man, nevertheless, the creation of gods and so forth is not observed to have God alone as its cause. As for that which is seen to be non-womb-born, we accept it on the strength of observation to be just like that which is womb-born.
