Therefore, since the accomplishment of an effect is possible from the mere collection of specific causal conditions established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), what is the use of postulating a creator in the form of God, whether accepted on the basis of scripture or otherwise? This is the sense.

The phrase "nothing whatsoever is perceived" (*kiṃcid api nopalabhyate*) serves to clarify the disregard for the alternative reading *akiñcitkāmahetukam*—due to its lack of established authority and other reasons—and it reveals that the reading *kim anyat* is intended as a negation. This is why [the author] says "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is: "by the power of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatireka*). The phrase "caused by desire" (*kāmahetuka*) is an indication of perceived causes; it is mentioned specifically because of the predominance of desire. Just as even the scriptures of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), though composed by those very persons [who claim to be seers], are so [unreliable], likewise it is said that people—out of hatred for the sharp medicinal herbs and the like—do not speak of the history of the city of the world, even though it is a well-established fact occurring in every aeon (*kalpa*), created by the Architect God (*Īśvara-śilpin*).

"This view" means a perverted view. He uses the word "having taken hold of" (*avaṣṭabhya*) to exclude the sense of "attacking" or "assailing. He says "not seeing" (*adṛṣṭvā*) because the meaning of the verbal root *√naś* here is intended as "disappearance," since there is no destruction of this eternal self. [The self] is specified as being distinct from the body, because the inner self, which is self-luminous, is eternally perceived as the substratum for the superimposition of the body.

With the intention of avoiding the charge of tautology—that "having little intelligence" is stated here as the cause for the loss of the self—he says, "like a pot," and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that, like domestic animals or wild beasts, there is a natural non-perception of the distinct self due to the power of karma; whereas "those of little intelligence" refers to the inability to overcome that [non-perception]. Thus, the perverted view regarding the supreme and the individual self has been described; now, by the words "then they produce fierce arrows," etc., its fruit is stated.

Regarding the phrase "of fierce deeds," he says "they are the destroyers of all" in order to exclude the understanding that they merely possess fierce vows and the like. "Inauspicious" means they bring about harm even to those with whom they associate. They "prevail for the destruction of the world" because they transgress the boundaries of dharma established by the Lord for the sustenance of the world—boundaries taught in such passages as, "Beget offspring by this [rite]; let this be the fulfiller of your desires," and "Nourishing one another, you shall attain the supreme good."

And others who follow them, being dull-witted, through their imitation of his conduct, teaching, and so forth, become the cause of the destruction of the entire world—devoid of the growth consisting of worldly prosperity and liberation—and lead to ruin in the form of affliction by the threefold suffering; such is the meaning. ||9||

For desire (kāma) is said to be the cause of the world; therefore, it alone is intended by them as that which is to be resorted to. It is stated in the verse beginning with "kāma" that hypocrisy, pride, and so forth, up to impure vows, constitute the means (itikartavyatā) for resorting to that [desire]. The reason for its being difficult to satisfy is that its objects are difficult to attain; or rather, since the attainment of objects is the fulfillment of desire, its difficulty in being satisfied consists precisely in the fact that its objects are difficult to attain. "Resorting to" means intending it as one's purpose.

With that intention, he says, "desiring to accomplish that. He explains that by the word *moha* (delusion), what is intended here is the blindness resulting from the failure to distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, which serves as the cause for engaging in contrary activity.

Regarding the phrase "through ignorance": those who grasp at what is non-existent and acquire it—that is, women—are here called "those who grasp at the unreal. For those intent upon dharma acquire things through righteous means, whereas those whose minds are inclined toward desire acquire the implements for that purpose through theft and other such means; thus the author says, "having acquired possessions through unjust means. Here, the word *parigraha* refers to the objects of acquisition (*parigrāhya*). The statement, "They strive to amass wealth by unjust means for the sake of enjoying their desires," is merely an elaboration of this same point. Therefore, the interpretation "those who are attached to the inauspicious" is also weak in this context.

The phrase "having taken up" avoids redundancy because it refers either to the immediate undertaking of the practice or to the conceit of ownership. With the intention that the vows prescribed by heretical scriptures (*pāṣaṇḍāgama*) are themselves impure—since they cause a person to become unfit for sight, touch, and so forth—he says: "engaged in vows not ordained by the Śāsana."

Even for those who are devoid of the true intent of the Dharma (dharmābhisaṃdhi) and are dominated by darkness (tāmasa), there occurs a connection with falsehood in their vows that are outside the Vedas—vows by which they have been brought under control through deceptive means such as snake-charms, stone-crushing spells, the paralyzing of the sun, or the speaking of idols. Alternatively, "falsehood" (anṛta) refers here to a resolve rooted in pride of valor and the like that is contrary to the Śāstra; even regarding vows prescribed in the Śāstra, for those who do not understand the intention of propitiating the Blessed Lord, there is the state of being employed in a way that is un-Śāstric due to acting contrary to the Śāstra.
Deceit and pride have already been explained. Here, intoxication (mada) refers to that arrogance which, rooted in wealth, noble birth, learning, and so forth, initiates improper conduct. (10)

Thus, the successive mental fluctuations and so forth of those who have set out [on the path] are described by the words "immeasurable anxiety" (*cintāmaparimeyām*) and so on. To indicate that these involve futile exertion directed toward unattainable objects, he says "today or tomorrow" (*adya śvo vā*). Regarding the phrase "immeasurable" (*aparimeyām*), he states "unbounded" (*ataparicchedyām*) to show that its infinite branches are intended because its objects are innumerable. As for the expression "until the end of dissolution" (*pralayāntām*), the mention of the limit being the fall of the body is weak [in its precision].

The intention [of the author] is as follows: the claim that one wishes to accomplish in a short time what can only be accomplished over an infinite period of time serves a purpose, namely, to demonstrate an extreme degree of delusion. Furthermore, the word *pralaya* (dissolution) is most appropriately used in its well-known sense; for since thinking persons do not persist until the final dissolution (*pralaya*), it is illogical to say that thought itself ends with the dissolution. With this in mind, he says: "having as its object that which is to be accomplished within the time limit of a *prakṛta-pralaya*. The sense is that among the innumerable objects of thought, even a single one is difficult to accomplish.

Those for whom the enjoyment of sensual pleasures (*kāmopabhoga*) alone is the supreme among their desired objectives are called "those for whom the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is supreme" (*kāmopabhogaparamāḥ*). He expresses this by saying, "the enjoyment of sensual pleasures alone. He states that the word "only" (*eva*) is intended to exclude heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), as indicated by the phrase "nothing more than this. Regarding the expression "having reached certainty" (*saṃjātaniścayāḥ*), the sense is that the suffix *-kta* in the word *niścita* functions in the sense of the agent (*kartari kta*), just as in the expression "Brāhmaṇas who have eaten" (*abhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*).

Cintā concerns the object to be accomplished, whereas āśā concerns the fruit. Because the objects of hope are innumerable, those hopes themselves are likewise manifold, being hundreds of times [more numerous]. Regarding the phrase "devoted to desire and anger" (kāma-krodha-parāyaṇāḥ), since anger cannot be the object of one's pride as something to be ultimately attained, the intended meaning is merely the one-pointedness of desire and anger; thus he says, "having desire and anger as their sole resort" (kāma-krodha-eka-niṣṭhāḥ). Here, the word *ayana* refers to a support or basis; for desire, when carried along, [is the vehicle].

There is no tautology here, because the intent is to recall what was previously elaborated upon—that [the mind] transforms into the nature of anger. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the enjoyment of desires": it means for the purpose of experiencing sense objects. The underlying thought is: "Alas! That which ought to have been performed as a means of worshipping the Supreme Person—purified by being a means to the highest liberation—has instead been directed toward the sake of a mere semblance of pleasure that brings misfortune, is utterly trivial, and is momentary. Regarding the word "unjustly" (*anyāyena*): the enjoyment of desires is not accomplished through wealth acquired by righteous means, such as through sacrifices; rather, the intention is to express that they accomplish it through striving (in unjust ways). Thus, the accusative case in "accumulations of wealth" (*arthasañcayān*) is syntactically connected with the second [verb]. ||11||

Thus, by such statements as "Liberation, characterized by great bliss, consists in the manifestation of the splendor of one's own innate light," it has been stated that the enjoyment of desire is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha), and for its sake, the pursuit of wealth as a human goal is undertaken. Now, in order to illuminate the examination of what has been obtained and not obtained, and what has been done and not done, for one who is engaged therein—remaining like a yogin established in the perception of distinction—the words beginning with "This today" are used. By this, the infinity of the objects of reflection mentioned previously is also illustrated.

The words "son," "field," and so forth are used to indicate that the scope [of the agency] is distinct from the wealth that will be mentioned later. To exclude the kind of supervision over what is done and not done by those of a *sāttvika* nature who are dependent on God and others, he says, "by my power alone" (*matsāmarthyenaiva*), suggesting that even such a reflection, when permeated by egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), is of the nature of an error. He explains the intended meaning of the particle "alone" (*eva*) by saying, "not by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. The same intention applies to passages such as "I alone," which are devoted to explaining the word "I" (*aham*) as drawn out by the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
"This exists, and this also exists"—in such reflection, there is the communication of the reality of the abundance of objects. ||13||

Thus, the intention regarding the attainment of the desired has been stated; now, that regarding the cessation of the undesired is expressed in the words "asau mayā" (He by me). Here, by the phrase "mayā" and so forth, he expresses the identity of the self with the qualities associated with the slaying of the enemy, such as being powerful (*balavat*). A hero (*śūra*) is one who, like a tiger or similar creature, treats the enemy force as straw and is habituated to entering [the fray] without fear, since in the list "the hero, the coward, the wise man, the dullard," the hero is mentioned in contrast to the coward. A valiant one (*vīra*) is one who is free from afflictions such as exhaustion during the exertion of battle.

Regarding the question, "What is the reason for relying on one's own power while disregarding the examples of the activities of infinite wise men? he says, "By those of dull intellect. The intention is this: those who are greedy for wealth and the like, being deceived by authors whose intentions are concealed, engage in acts such as giving gifts and performing sacrifices; thus, they become wretched, abandoning even goals that are already established. [He says] "by the weak," because a powerful person cannot be deceived, as it is said: "One who is not to be won over by subversion..."

The intended meaning is according to the maxim: "People are arrogant because of their own strength. Regarding the phrase "by what is merely imagined": the sense is not that it is established by the means of valid cognition consisting of perception, positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as asserted in the Lokāyata system, but rather that it is something purely hypothetical. ||13||

Thus, the delusion that the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired depend solely upon one's own power has been described. Therefore, he says, "I am independent," indicating that even the state of being [the cause] regarding one's own power and so forth is intended here as a falsehood, expressed by the word "Lord" (Īśvara). Furthermore, he says, "and of others," indicating that the conceit of being the controller of everything other than oneself is also intended as a falsehood.

The meaning is that when it is said, "The circle of the earth is upon your shoulders, for you are the controller of all," the arising of affection and so forth toward such [beings] occurs precisely because of the description of Him as being of such a nature. Because of the consistency between what precedes and what follows, the word *bhogī* (the enjoyer) refers to the capacity for enjoyment (*bhoga-sāmarthya*). To the objection, "If that is so, then am I not likewise of such a nature simply by the very nature of my own dharma?"—he states the intended meaning of the word "I" (*aham*) with the words "by Himself alone" (*svata eva*). "Siddhaḥ" means endowed with excellence in knowledge and other qualities; or, it means one whose desires are already fulfilled (*siddha-samīhita*). "Sukhī" means happy.

The meaning is that he is one who possesses the happiness resulting from the birth of sons and so forth. Alternatively, the apparent tautology between the words "bhogī" (enjoyer) and "sukhī" (happy) may be avoided by considering them as expressing cause and effect respectively. That these qualities, beginning with lordship and ending with noble lineage, are rooted in residual karma from previous lives has already been established through the Śruti and Smṛti. ||14||

"In this world" (*asmilloke*): the intended meaning is that there is no other world; or rather, the designation "in this world" is made with the intention of negating the possibility of such a being at all times, as implied by the word *asti*. The sense is: "even when searching throughout the entire world. By its own inherent power, a counterpart to me is denied even in each of these very forms individually. While it would have sufficed to say merely "who is like me?", the use of the word *anya* (other) is for the purpose of highlighting that the very fact of being "other" is the reason for the lack of similarity.

Alternatively, one should understand [the thought] as: "There is no one equal to me; I alone am equal to myself," similar to the expression "like Rāma and Rāvaṇa. The thought "I shall sacrifice" and "I shall give" is merely a pretension resting on hypocrisy (*dambha*). This is because it is subsequently qualified by the phrase "hypocritically, not according to the injunctions. The thought "I shall rejoice" is not intended with a desire for heaven and the like, but rather through obtaining titles such as "Great One" (*mahat*) based on being a sacrificer and so forth.

Even in the realization expressed by "I shall sacrifice" and so forth, he demonstrates the destruction of the ego inherent in the context [of worldly activity] with the words "independent of the grace of the Lord. The phrase "thus deluded by ignorance" alone would have been sufficient; however, the word "they think" is stated for the sake of clarity. ||15||

For those who have generally cast their burdens upon the Lord are resolute; he states their opposite by saying "everything by themselves. "Having done so" means "having thought so. The mind itself is the *cita* (the thinking), as it consists of the function (*vṛtti*) in the form of thought; its plurality is spoken of due to the diversity of its activities, which he demonstrates with the words "I should act thus," and so forth. "Vibhrāntāḥ" means distracted or scattered.

The two are *bhrānti* (delusion) and *viparīta-jñāna* (perverted knowledge), while *moha* is ignorance (*ajñāna*). Alternatively, according to the maxim, "An action intended in one way is performed by fate in another," he states that thoughts themselves take the form of delusion with the words "in this manner. "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; it only increases further, like a fire fed with clarified butter."

The meaning that "it increases even further" is illuminated by the prefix; thus he says, "attached intensely. Regarding the statement, "This has been done, this is to be done, and this other is half-done—thus, one who is joined with such efforts is brought under the control of Kṛtānta (Death)," he says, "having died in the midst [of their work]. With the intention that for those attached to impure sensual enjoyments, the fruit is of exactly that same nature, there is the qualification of hell as being impure. And its impurity consists in its being composed of pus, blood, fat, and so forth. ||16||

Regarding the phrase "conceited by themselves" (*ātmasaṃbhāvitāḥ*), he explains that it contains a restrictive sense—similar to the expression "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣaḥ*)—by virtue of being devoid of any expectation of being honored by others, saying: "honored by themselves alone. To manifest the fault consisting of self-praise and the like, he says: "themselves by themselves. For even those who are truly virtuous feel ashamed when they are honored by others. The reason for their silence is that they "are full of pride" (*paripūrṇamananyamānāḥ*). The meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is "doing nothing at all"; the intended sense is that they do not perform even the slightest act, such as saluting their teachers.

To explain that one disregards imperceptible deficiencies due to the intoxication of perceived prosperity such as wealth, he raises an objection with the word "How? Since [the verse] states, "The pride of learning, the pride of wealth, and thirdly, the pride of noble birth," and because these are taught as being conjoined, and because wealth is not mentioned here [in this context], he says, "And by the conceit of learning and noble birth," implying that the cause of pride associated with that [wealth] is actually based on learning and noble birth.

Sacrifices connected with names are "name-sacrifices" (*nāmayajña*). Here, the connection is intended to mean "by way of the relationship between cause and effect," for the purpose of excluding the intention for results such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; thus he says, "having names as their purpose. Since the word "name" (*nāman*) is also used in reference to fame and other things, and since the intention for those [other things] is established by the passage beginning with "out of hypocrisy" (*dambhena*), and because of the excellence of its conventional usage as a designation (*saṃjñā*) and its suitability for the sense of mockery, it is stated that they have "names alone as their purpose"—meaning they possess only the title of "sacrifice. For this very reason, it is said: "It is merely the name of a sacrifice."

But has not the interpretation, "However, in reality this is not a sacrifice," also been shown to be weak? For that meaning is already established by the statement regarding its being "not preceded by injunction" (*avidhipūrvakatva*). The phrase "by means of hypocrisy as a motive" (*dambhena hetunā*) is a statement of a specific intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) as the cause. The phrase "for the sake of proclaiming oneself as a sacrificer" (*yaṣṭṛtvakhyāpanāya*), however, is an elaboration of that [hypocrisy] in terms of its object and its purpose. An "injunction" (*vidhi*) here is an enjoining statement (*vidhāyaka-vākya*). As it has been said: "The abandonment of the context is being 'not preceded by injunction'"; thus he says, "not according to the scriptural command" (*ayathācodanam*). (17)

In order to avoid the charge of redundancy and so forth, he states that the immediately following verse concerns the opposite qualities of the procedure for *sāttvika* sacrifice, saying: "If, however, they sacrifice with these [qualities]... He then explains, in sequence, the order of the procedure for the hypocritical sacrifice (*dāmbhika-yajña*) with the verses beginning with "independent of others" (*ananyāpekṣa*). [He shows that] the Blessed Lord alone is everything.

Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the rejection of the notion that one is merely the agent; it is for the avoidance of this that it is stated in the Smṛti: "If, relying on egoism, one performs acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, one obtains their fruit, but that leads to rebirth. Although mere possession of power is not in itself a fault, the phrase "by the power of the Blessed One" implies the opposite: the consideration that one's own strength is sufficient.

Arrogance, rooted in both of these, is the cause of universal contempt; it rivals the worship of those worthy of worship and consists of the desire for the attainment of what is favored by the Lord and the gods, and the avoidance of what is unfavored—namely, desire and anger, which are the opposites of this [devotion]. "Dependent" (saṃśritāḥ) means properly relying [on them], that is, regarding them as the causes of their own independence. Here, the phrase "in the bodies of others" (paradeheṣu) intends to include priests, thieves, and so forth who are either favorable or unfavorable to the sacrifice. The locative case establishes their state of being situated [therein].

And that impelling [activity] is for the purpose of setting [the world] in motion, as has been previously explained at length through scripture and other means; he recalls this by saying "the impeller of all," which is contrary to their understanding. The sense is that the very act of promoting their welfare is the cause of their malice. Regarding the term "Puruṣottama" (Supreme Person): the sense is that He, of whose mere knowledge of His distinct nature one becomes fulfilled, is indeed a source of great benefit, yet He has become an object of hatred and malice for them.

The description of qualities such as the instigation [of all beings] is intended to clarify the specific nature of envy (*asūyā*), which consists in the manifestation of faults within virtues. For in the section concerning the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama-prakaraṇa*), it was stated for the purpose of instigating [the recollection of] the Smṛtis and so forth: "And I am seated in the heart of every being"; that very point is what is being recalled here by the words "in my own body and in the bodies of others. This is the underlying intention.

By the phrase "kuyuktibhiḥ" (by fallacious arguments), he indicates the sequence of connection between the two [terms] "pradviṣantaḥ" (hating) and "abhyasūyakāḥ" (envious) as cause and effect in reverse order, or rather, he completes the sentence by drawing in the word "yajante" (they sacrifice). Regarding the fallacious arguments: [the objection] that if [beings] are dependent on the Lord, how can there be subjection to karma; and if fruits are rooted in karma, what is the use of the Lord? and so forth. Bṛhaspati also characterized envy under the guise of the definition of non-envy: "One does not destroy the virtues of the virtuous, nor does one praise even those with meager virtues."

"She does not take delight in the faults of others; she is proclaimed to be 'free from envy' (anasūyā). By means of the characteristic of intolerance, he explains hatred with the words, "not tolerating me. And this state of intolerance should be understood as extending even to the transgression of His commands. Furthermore, this is the cause for the fall of one's own kinsmen into the impure hell, as it is said: "The ancestors of him who hates Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the God who is the best among the wise, sink into hell for eternal years."

Thus, one should also reflect here on such passages as: "Those who hate the Great-Souled One and do not remember Keśava—there is no access for them to holy pilgrimage sites, even for those who merely associate with them. He states that the phrase "by sacrifices consisting of mere names" is illustrative, meaning "all [rituals] such as the *yāga* and so forth. (28)

With the two verses beginning with "To them, I... and so forth, it is stated that even for sacrifices and other rites preceded by such hatred and the like, I alone am the bestower of the appropriate adverse results. With the intention that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of avoiding the charge of partiality and cruelty, he says: "Those who hate Me in this way. Here, by means of the four qualifying attributes, it is intended that only the four types of evildoers mentioned in the verse beginning with "The evildoers do not [attain Me]" are meant; thus, this is their explanation. For instance:

The term "lowest of men" (*narādhama*) refers to that very same group. As for the phrase "having resorted to a demonic nature" (*āsuraṃ bhāvamāśritāḥ*), its meaning has already been explained previously as being synonymous with "those who hate. In this way, the words *kṣudra* (mean) and *āsurāḥ* (demonic) should also be understood as having meanings equivalent to the words "deluded" (*mūḍha*) and so forth, as appropriate. Furthermore, their absolute non-distinction [from the preceding] is due to their unity within the demonic host. Because one moves (*saṃsaraṇāt*) in a single form without interruption through the revolutions of the wheel of birth and so forth, it is called *saṃsāra*; it is a continuum (*saṃtāna*). Here, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in "the person transmigrates (*saṃsarati*) in this."

Regarding the term *saṃsāra* and the statement concerning its multiplicity, he says [it is due to] the infinity of the revolution of the wheel, beginning with the words "birth and old age. He says "even there" (*tatrāpi*) because the word *saṃsāra* is distinguished by its commonality with both existent and non-existent births. To exclude the specific kind of *sāttvika* birth mentioned in such passages as "This birth is indeed more difficult to obtain than that," he states that it is "among the *āsuri* [births] alone," meaning among those hostile to me.

Such an adverse birth is to be understood as occurring even among the four types of wombs, beginning with the gods. Following such scriptural passages as, "It is He alone who makes one perform evil action, whom He wishes to lead downward," [the author] states "tattat" (this or that) to provide the means for what was said [in the previous verse], "I hurl [them]. Even the granting of a cruel intellect and so forth, which serves as the cause for engaging in sinful activity, does not entail partiality or cruelty on the part of the Lord, because it is itself the result of prior hatred and other [afflictions]. ||19||

The succession of ever-increasing degradation is described by the verse beginning with "āsurīm. By the word "mūḍhāḥ," he states the result [of that degradation]: "those whose knowledge is contrary to mine. Alternatively, false knowledge itself is here [defined as] "untruth" (anṛta) and "delusion" (moha); and this, in accordance with the sense of the sentence, is specified as having its own [objects] as its domain.

Since even for those superior beings, the attainment of the supreme *brahma* is to be accomplished through perfection over many births, it would be inappropriate to either encourage or prohibit them from engaging in that [birth] among the *tāmasa* ones; therefore, the attainment of knowledge born of *śārīra* [birth], which constitutes the first stage of such attainment, is here rejected for those *āsura* beings who are not yet fit for *śārīra* [birth]. To clarify the nature of that knowledge born of *śārīra*, he says: "The Blessed One exists.

Since the state of being inferior depends upon a superior limit, and since the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is capable of providing that complete limit, he says "therefore—from that birth"—intending that the word "therefore" is not appropriately used here as a logical reason. ||20||

With the intention that what must necessarily be avoided will be stated in brief, he connects the subsequent passage with the words "of this" (*asya*). With the intention that the very non-attainment of the Self as it truly exists is itself the destruction of the Self, and that this [destruction] is of the nature of an *asura*, he says: "of the destruction of the Self which consists in the nature of an *asura*. With the intention that by the cutting off of the root, the entire nature of an *asura* is indeed cut off, he says: "the root cause. [This refers to] hell, which takes the form of the nature of an *asura*.

The sense is: what else could be more than this [other] hell? Or rather, the intention may be that this instruction is rooted in that very [hell] for the purpose of abandoning the nature of an asura; or, it may be intended to convey the same meaning as the immediately following phrase, "through the doors of darkness. Regarding the phrase "the destruction of the self," the sense is according to the sequence beginning with, "He becomes as if non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6). A door is indeed the cause of entry; with the intention that here the status of being merely a cause for attainment is intended, he states the sequence of resorting to a figurative usage: "the path is the cause"—this is the meaning.

"Door" means destruction; the sense is that one perishes at the very moment of entering. With the intention that the statement of the faults of what is to be abandoned serves as an aid to the injunction for abandonment, he says "therefore. Hell, such as Raurava and others, is a cause for the exhaustion of sin; however, with the intention that its nature is such that it is extremely terrible because it is a cause for the accumulation of sin, he says "one should abandon it from afar. ||21||

The abandonment of that which is to be abandoned was enjoined by means of describing its defects; now, with this verse beginning with "by these," the continuous flow of the fruits of that very abandonment is being described. The phrase "by the causes of knowledge contrary to Me" is a statement of the fruit of *tamas*; or, the word *tamas* here indicates [the entire range] up to that point, because one is liberated from the gates of *tamas*, one is liberated even from *tamas*. With the intention that the pursuit of the highest good (*śreyas*) is preceded by the knowledge of reality, he says: "having obtained knowledge concerning Me."

By the phrase "he practices what is beneficial" (*śreya ācarati*), the cessation of the previously mentioned hostility toward the Lord and so forth is intended. "Beneficial" (*śreyaḥ*) means that which is praiseworthy; and with the intention that this [beneficial practice] consists of acting in accordance with the Lord’s will—which is the essence of all the Śārīraka [Upanishads]—he says, "in accordance with my will" (*mad-anukūlye*). Therefore, the meaning is: "precisely because of practicing what is beneficial.

Then, referring to the passage beginning with "without having reached Me," he says, "Me alone as the supreme goal" (*mām eva parāṃ gatim*), indicating that the Supreme Person is the ultimate ground of attainment designated here by the term "supreme goal."

It has been stated that three qualities are the primary and most significant among those belonging to the nature of the asuras; immediately after those, the cause for avoiding what is least significant is now stated, saying: "disregard for the *śruti*. The word *śruti* first occurs in the Vedas alone because they instruct all persons in every condition regarding their welfare; with the intention that [the term] subsequently applies to other things by association, he says: "*Śruti* means the Vedas."

He states that "injunction" (*vidhi*) means "instruction" (*anuśāsana*), because here it is not the voluntary action—which is the opposite of the Vedic injunction—that is intended by the word "Veda," but rather its operation, which is what is meant by the term "injunction. He states the conclusion: "My instruction, known as the Veda. Alternatively, he intends the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "injunction" with "the Veda" itself. By the phrase "my instruction," he recalls such statements as: "The Śruti and Smṛti are my very command."

By this, those who otherwise describe the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are also refuted. For the optative suffixes indicate the intention of the Commander (the Lord), either by implication or by direct denotation. With the intention that here "acting according to one's own will" (*kāmakāra*) is the opposite of being commanded, and does not refer to optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*) and the like found in scriptural injunctions, he says: "by a path conforming to his own will. By the statement beginning with "Then, by what impelled is this [man]? it is meant that he is impelled by desire. As for the verse: "Those smṛtis which are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there are... [and so on].
"All these are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as having darkness as their ultimate end. Reflecting on such passages, he said: "Not even any [merit] pertaining to the next world..."

"Siddhim" means the attainment of the means (*upāya-siddhi*) which serves as the cause for happiness in the hereafter (*āmuṣmika*). "Not happiness" means not the happiness of heaven (*svarga*) and so forth. Alternatively, "siddhim" refers to the fruit of heaven and the like, while "sukham" refers to the happiness of this world (*aihika*). For this very reason, the word "something" (*kiñcit*) is used. Even in this world, happiness arises only from the supreme grace of the Puruṣa produced by the performance of *śrāvaṇa* and other rites. Therefore it is said: "Those men who have not propitiated Viṣṇu are partakers of misery."
He says, "Whence [could there be] the supreme goal? in order to demonstrate *kaimutya* (a fortiori), by associating it with other forms of happiness. ||23||

With the intention that everything stated in this chapter is for this purpose, it is taught [in the verse] beginning with "Therefore, O Śārṅgī. Here, with reference to the non-connection between the words "to be done" (kārya) and "not to be done" (akārya) based on whether they are produced or not produced, he says: "In the determination of what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted. This is because the efficacy of performance depends upon reality and unreality.

With the intention that these [terms] are for the purpose of illustration, the word "common to the acceptable and so forth" (*upādeyādisādhāraṇa*) is used. Here, "acceptance" (*upādāna*) means mental assent according to the scripture. It is incorrect to say "only according to the scripture," because that would contradict such statements as "The Śruti, the Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous. Therefore, he says "according to the Dharmaśāstra. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he indicates "having understood for the sake of non-destruction" and so on; thus he says "whatever [is prescribed]. For all scriptures, whether directly or indirectly, enjoin all actions solely as a means of propitiating the Supreme Person.

Regarding that, concerning the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and its attainment: by the phrase "named Puruṣottama," he causes one to remember the supreme reality previously described in the statement, "I alone am to be known by all the Vedas. And [by the words] "and that which serves as the means for attaining that": the sense is that the very nature of all [actions] performed by abandoning attachment to fruits is indeed to serve as the means for attaining the Supreme Brahman. Here, by the expression "making [them] understand," the meaning of the word *nidhāna* (depository/establishment) is explained as being of the nature of an injunction.

With the intention that one should not perform actions contrary to one's nature, it was said, "you ought to act. For this reason as well, he states "to undertake" in order to show the commonality of the determination regarding the true nature of performance. The mention of "you" in the middle follows the word "you ought," intended to highlight the excellence of fitness in one who is born with a divine disposition (*daivī saṃpat*).

This is what is meant: O best of beings, you must not fall away from the supreme dharma—which consists of exclusive devotion to the Lord in the form of *karmayoga* and *bhaktiyoga* according to one's qualification—by pursuing the semblance of the Vedic scriptures, which are essentially deceptive and intended to delude, though they appear as the essence of the eternal Veda known as the *Śruti*, through your skill in adopting the excellence of false asceticism. On the contrary, that very dharma alone is to be constantly adopted. The word "here" (*iha*) is used to indicate the sphere of eligibility for action, or rather, to signify that one remains subject to the power of *karman*.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Tātparya-candrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-bhagavad-gītā-bhāṣya*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.

In order to introduce the seventeenth [chapter] because of the faults mentioned [in the previous ones], he takes up what was stated with the words "devāsura" (among gods and asuras). He states the connection by showing that the subject under discussion is being elaborated through a different perspective, with the words "now" (idānīm); the meaning is: immediately after stating that the determination of what is to be avoided and what is to be accepted has the scripture alone as its source. He explains the summary verse: "The entire demonic [nature] is characterized by its opposition to the scriptures; the scriptural [nature] is distinct from it by virtue of its qualities; thus the characteristic of that which is established by scripture is declared in three ways in the seventeenth [chapter]."

By the words "of that which is not prescribed by the scriptures," etc., the subject matter continuing through the chapters consists of the general and specific classification of scriptural matters. The phrase "stated in the seventeenth [chapter]" is to be connected with each of the three sentences of the summary verse. Alternatively, there is a connection through the final summary: "all this has been stated in the seventeenth. Following the statement "having known what is declared in the Śārṅgavidhi," how is the question "those who abandon the Śārṅgavidhi" to be understood?

Regarding the phrase "saṅgacchata" (you should come together), he says "tatra" (in that regard): [this refers to] one who does not know that what is not enjoined by the Śruti is fruitless. This is the intention: for discerning people, the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) arises spontaneously regarding either a purpose itself or the means to that purpose. Therefore, the desire to know the distinctions among the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth culminates in the specific fruits rooted therein. Furthermore, when there is knowledge of fruitlessness, there can be no desire to know specific fruits. Consequently, in the world...

Even established practices such as agriculture, medicine, and the like, which are objects of activity for discerning people, are seen to be fruitful. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the Veda would be rootless. Furthermore, how many dharmas established by worldly custom (*ācāra*) are there? Nor could these have any result whatsoever; for otherwise, it would follow that discerning people would not engage in them. Nor is it possible for there to be an absence of fruit when an action is performed preceded by faith, provided there is no deficiency in its constituent parts.

Furthermore, for discerning people, there is no way to proceed with those actions that are devoid of visible purpose—actions performed by countless individuals at great expense, loss, and effort—unless they culminate in an unseen result (*adṛṣ�ṭa*). Therefore, if it is argued that this [action] differs in some respect from what is prescribed in the *śāstra*, then that difference would consist merely in a gradation of fruits induced by the distinctions among the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest. Thus: "Since he acts according to his own will, having abandoned the injunction of the *śāstra*..."

The previously stated [verse], "He does not attain perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal," was likely intended to mean the absence of preeminent happiness; or else, the qualification "by one's own will" (*kāmakārataḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding those devoid of faith. Thus, Arjuna’s intention is that since this [action] is merely imagined based on false instruction, numerous scriptures, one's own conjecture, or the conduct of the elderly, it is logical that its fruitlessness is averted here through the application of intent toward dharma, faith, and so forth.

To ensure that the qualified person is not subject to doubt regarding the result, he explains the qualification of the agent as an adverbial qualification of the action: "in sacrifice and so forth, conjoined with faith. Here, "sacrifice" (yāga) is intended to include giving (dāna) and other such acts; or rather, it includes them because there is no difference in their being worship of the gods. In this context, by the word *kṛṣṇa*, [the author] intends that the root *kṛṣ* signifies "earth" (*bhū*) and the suffix *ṇa* signifies "accomplishment" (*nirvṛtti*), thus encompassing everything required.

He intends [the word] *nirukti* (etymological derivation) as that which is conducive to success (*siddhi*). By the word "but" (*tu*), the exclusion of both scriptural finality (*śāstrīyaniṣṭhā*) and acting according to one's own will (*kāmakāra*) is intended. Intending the repetition here of either the transformed interrogative *kiṃ* or the word *āho*, he says: "What is *sattva*? In order to exclude meanings such as destruction and so forth, and for the sake of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *sattva* and the others, he reveals the essential nature (*svarūpa*) through synonyms in order to introduce the etymological derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇa-vyutpatti*): "Finality (*niṣṭhā*) means stability (*sthiti*). The question "But what is their finality? is precisely the same matter [as the previous one] which is addressed by the words "sattva" and so forth.
With the intention of specifying [them], he states the result: "of these..."

Although the question "How many kinds of faith are there? could have been asked at any time, [the author], by saying "Thus questioned," etc., removes the suspicion that this statement might be inconsistent with what was previously said, and explains the purpose of stating the threefold nature of faith. The meaning is: "He was questioned in a manner contrary to what had been previously taught.

The phrase "having placed [the matter] in his heart" means: in order to gradually introduce the direct answer. This is intended to make known that the question was characterized by extreme disregard [for the previous teaching].

The sense is that there is either an immediate or a direct statement of the answer. "Threefoldness by way of the qualities" (guṇatastraividhyam) means the state of being connected with a distinction in results caused by a distinction in the qualities; this is the intended meaning. For here, since the Sāttvika nature has been introduced through the connection with faith (śraddhā), he says, "he explains that very [point]," with the intention of subsequently demonstrating the division of the aforementioned faith into Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa types. That is to say, the meaning is that those specific results are dependent upon specific types of faith. The *sattva* and other [qualities] of a person...

With the intention that those [qualities] being accumulated produce faith toward an object corresponding to themselves, he says, "abounding in the quality of *sattva*. Among all things dependent on the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), the designation is made by means of a particular one due to its predominance. In that context, by stating that a person possesses *sāttvika* faith, the reason for their *sāttvika* nature is established as a matter of course; this is because faith itself has been specified by its very nature. With the intention that the specific character of faith is what he wishes to make known, he says, "Hear that [faith]."

"Unmixed with suffering" (*duḥkhāsaṃbhinna*) means that the fruits of service consist of attaining proximity (*sāyujya*) and so forth to the one to be propitiated; it is with this intention that the state of being unmixed with suffering and so on is mentioned. This should be understood for the following two [verses] as well. The word "other" (*anya*) is used to indicate the absolute dissimilarity of the *tāmasa* beings to these [others]. The "multitudes of beings" (*bhūtagaṇāḥ*) refers to the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Rudra and others.

Thus, by implication, the prohibition of the question has been established; now, with the intention of stating it explicitly, he says "even this. To remind one of what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "He does not attain perfection," it is said that "there is not even a fragment of happiness. By the words "but rather [it is] only misfortune," there is a reminder of the previously mentioned falling into hell. The word "terrible" (ghora) is intended to make known the excessive effort required for its result, in the desire to restate the possession of faith mentioned in the interrogative sentence.

With this intention, he says, "even that which is exceedingly terrible. Now, one might ask: since the question regarding sacrifice was "they worship, endowed with faith," how does the subsequent answer, "they suffer through austerity," cohere? To this he replies: "this is for the sake of illustration. Showing the comprehensive form [of the category], he states the conclusion: "that which is not ordained by the scriptures" (*aśāstravihitam*). This refers to what is taught in non-Vedic Āgamas; and even that which is Vedic, if performed by those lacking qualification (*anadhikārin*) without regard for the rules concerning place, time, materials, and ritual action, is "not ordained by the scriptures."

By the phrase "intended by the terrible synonym, the word 'ghora'," he means "involving great exertion. By the expression "sacrifices and so forth," it is indicated that even though sacrifices were mentioned in the question, they are not included here for the sake of illustration; for this very reason, the subject matter of the question and the answer is identical. Regarding those acts not enjoined by the scriptures, another enjoiner is stated: [those] joined with hypocrisy and egoism.

By these and other such statements, it is shown that the strength [mentioned here] is *asāttvika* (non-essential) because it is joined with desire and passion (*kāmarāga*). For it was previously stated: "And I am the strength of the strong, which is free from desire and passion. The mention of the emaciation of the aggregate of elements residing in the body is intended to show that there is not only hell in the next world, but even in this world there is the emaciation of the body. [This is supported by the scriptures: "The Inner Ruler is immortal," and "The Supreme is not characterized by both [attributes] even from the standpoint of its location."

For, by the words beginning with "sarvatra hi," [it is shown that] emaciation is impossible for the Supreme Self either in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) or in its attributes (*dharma*); and even if such emaciation were possible, it would follow [absurdly] that it could also occur through fasting and other practices enjoined by the scriptures. Furthermore, emaciation in the form of the contraction of knowledge, happiness, and so forth is well-established in Śruti, Smṛti, and common worldly experience for embodied beings who are individual knowers (*kṣetrajña*). By the phrase "situated within the body" (*antaśśarīrastham*), the state of being an individual knower delimited by the body is indicated. Thus, by the intention to refer here to the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is a qualifying part of the Supreme Self who has all bodies as His abode, according to the method previously stated in the passage "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi*)—the word "Me" (*mām*) is used here.

He says, "Instruction" means that the individual soul (jīva) is a part of My own self. This figurative expression is intended to indicate the abundance of faults [in those who harm such beings], on the grounds that harming a living being who has become My body is equivalent to harming Me. Because of the transgression of the scripture, tamasicity is [implied]; because of the combination of both [tamasic and rajasic factors], rajasicity is suspected. In that regard, first, there is the state of being preceded by faith.

It is employed as a means for attaining results; that [employment] occurs only in relation to scriptural matters. Even there, since it is not invariably so, the threefold nature of scriptural faith is mentioned with this intention. By this, according to the principle of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), the threefold nature caused by differences in results regarding non-scriptural matters is refuted. Here, it is stated that from the distinction of faith, the determination of the distinctions of those established in *sattva* and the other *guṇas* follows. By the term "of embodied beings" (*dehinām*), it is indicated that the qualified person (*adhikārī*) conforms to their respective bodies.

With the intention that diversity is what is intended to be expressed, he says "of all. This means "even of the Brahmins and others. Regarding "of embodied beings" (dehinām), it refers to those whose bodies are characterized by an abundance of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth.

The sense is that it is "conformable" (*anurūpa*). Regarding the doubt—namely, how there can be a difference in faith restricted to specific individuals when the scriptures are common [to all] and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth that inspire them are likewise common—the author says "And that... (*sā ca*) with the intention that this is another statement arising from its own nature (*svabhāvajā*). To express the non-commonality of the cause for the sake of the non-commonality of the effect, he states: "Nature is one's own non-common state. What is this state, and what is the cause of its non-commonality?

Regarding the phrase "wherein he says 'the eastern,'" the meaning is that the causal relationship between *ruci* (inclination) and *śraddhā* (faith) is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To the question, "What is this *śraddhā* which is distinct from *ruci* and is its effect?

he replies, "For *śraddhā*... Lexicographers (*naighaṇṭukas*) indeed list the word *śraddhā* even for a conviction that extends to urgency, as in the definition: "*śraddhā* [occurs] in the senses of trust (*viśvāsa*) and longing (*kāṅkṣā*)."

Now, an objection: since it is heard in scripture that "desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intellect, and fear—all this is indeed the mind," how can there be an assertion of their inherence in the inner self (pratyagātman)—which is designated here by the words "self" and "embodied being"—when faith and the rest are attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) that defile the self, and when, because they are produced by the qualities (guṇas), the possibility of them being attributed to the qualities also exists? To this, he says: "By latent impressions" (vāsanā). For the self, whose very nature is pure, [is affected] by the root of karma...

The meaning is that these are specific transformations of knowledge (dharma-bhūta-jñāna) conditioned by association with primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the qualities (guṇas). He explains that they are born from association with the qualities through the process indicated by the word "dehi" (embodied one), in order to assign the designations "sāttvika" and so forth to the various types of faith, and to dispel the doubt as to how the attributeless Self can have a connection with latent impressions (vāsanā) rooted in *sattva* and the other qualities. Thus he says: "Of those... (teṣām).

The sense is that just as the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) occurs in earthy substances and the like due to their connection with specific fires such as medicinal herbs, so it is here. With the intention that it is improper to reject those things established by scripture as causes of their respective effects merely because they are unperceived, he says, "to be defined by their effects. To the question of how supersensuous (*atīndriya*) factors that have been experienced can be the cause of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he says, "endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth. In relation to the root cause, faith is designated as being of the nature of *sattva* and the rest.

He says "there is no difference" and then "and therefore. To the question, "Since faith has already been introduced as being threefold—consisting of the *sāttvika* type and so on—why is it said again, 'Listen'?", he replies:
"That faith, whose nature... Since its general form and its threefold division are already known, the word "listen" is used with the intention of referring to its specific, previously unknown modes.

In this context, "according to *sattva*" does not refer to the quality (*guṇa*) of *sattva*; for if the faith of every person were dependent upon that [quality], there would be no possibility of distinguishing between *rājasa* and *tāmasa* faith. If it is argued that *sattva* is required everywhere as a concomitant factor (*sahakārin*), we say no; for *rajas* and *tamas* are likewise such factors. Indeed, the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) initiate all effects only by existing in a state of mutual dependence, like wind, bile, and phlegm. Therefore, what is indicated here is that [the quality] which serves as the common cause for all forms of faith.

He states that *sattva* is indeed the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) supported by the three qualities, saying: "Sattva is the internal organ. He explains the correspondence [between them] by saying: "The internal organ is endowed with such-and-such qualities. This means it is endowed with *sattva* and the other qualities which stimulate the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that produce a liking for particular objects. Previously, it was stated that for embodied beings, that [liking] is born of their own nature (*svabhāvajā*); here, however, its being caused by the internal organ is stated. These two are not optional alternatives, because once [the causal relationship] is established, such an option is impossible. Nor is there an alternative based on a difference between persons.

Because of the statement "of all," nor is there a conjunction [of the means], since they are perceived as being independent; to this he says, "the word *sattva*. The sense is that it is not improper to designate any one among those factors included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in various instances. Regarding the term *śraddhāmaya*, since the suffix *-mayaṭ* would be purposeless if it were taken in its own primary sense (*svārthika*), and even if it were taken in the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), it would be irrelevant to the context; therefore, with the intention of expressing the connection with the result of faith, he states that it has the sense of "modification": "the transformation of faith. Thus, [he describes] the fruit produced by faith in general.

The state of being related has been stated; therein, by the passage beginning with "whatever faith he has," the specific fruit for one possessing a specific faith is declared—thus he says, "the person who. To highlight the distinction from other types of faith, the words "yat" and "tat" are explained as referring to the manner [of faith] through the phrase "of whatever kind. Just as in the expression "ghee is life," this is a conventional metaphor (āropa) intended to express an excellence in the relationship between cause and effect; thus he says, "he is a transformation of such faith."

By this, the suspicion of tautology regarding the statement "that very same [is he]"—on the grounds that there is no difference in the predicate—is also dispelled. Since the person (puruṣa) is eternal, and since the expansion of his inherent attribute, knowledge, is regulated by means of the senses, while the body and so forth are merely specific transformations of non-sentient matter (acit), one might ask: with reference to what is the mention of "faith" and "transformation" made? To this, he says: "by virtuous action" (puṇyakarma). The intention is that the question arises here because of a desire to understand the distinction between the results.

With the intention of showing the subsequent classification of faith (*śraddhā*) into *sāttvika* and so forth for one whose faith has been introduced, he says, "He explains that very [point]. This means that the specific differences in the fruits are dependent upon the specific differences in faith. The *sattva* and other qualities of a person...
[End of Chapter 17]. Now begins the eighteenth chapter. 18.

In the final triad of chapters, which primarily concern the purification of one’s duties, [the author] says "by what has preceded," intending to show that this [chapter] occurs subsequent to it, and to indicate the unity of the section by way of the division between gods and asuras in the sixteenth and seventeenth chapters, which is devoted to distinguishing what is to be abandoned from what is to be adopted.

The general characteristic of Vedic action is its connection with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). Regarding the distinction therein between the means for liberation (*mokṣa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), which is indicated by the use of the terms "that" (*tat*) and "good" (*sat*), the intention of one who analyzes it is as follows: this division is obtained through the power of the qualifiers and so forth. Because it is remote, the designation is "that" (*tat*). It is "good" (*sat*) because it is real. Thus, the distinction is established.

However, in the knowledge of that [Self], the word *sat* (real) is used with the intention of expressing the nature of the true path. As for the division [of the qualities] into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* according to the sequence, it is merely an imagination conceived by someone. Having thus explained these matters, he says "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*) with the intention of establishing the connection that the purification of the essential nature of the portion that serves as the means to liberation is performed in the subsequent chapter. [The verse continues: "The notion of agency in the Lord, the acceptance of *sattva*, and the absence of fear..."

Regarding the summary verse which states, "The transformation of one's own karma is said to be the essential meaning of the scripture," it should be understood that the non-mention of the identity and nature of renunciation (tyāga) and relinquishment (saṃnyāsa), as well as the presentation of the notion of agency in the Lord as a subordinate element, is intended to show that the quality of *sattva* is to be adopted here through the function of the underlying purport (*tātparya-vṛtti*). With this intention, he says: "by describing the effects of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*."

With the intention that the word "essence" (*sārārtha*) here refers to the primary duty mentioned at the beginning of the summary—namely, "having as its sole object devotion which cannot be accomplished without self-knowledge, detachment, and one's own duty"—he says, "the essence is the yoga of devotion. This is because, although there is no difference in the nature of the means such as sacrifice and charity which lead to heaven and other goals, [devotion is superior].

With the intention that Arjuna now asks in order to clarify that specific nature of yoga by which it serves as a means to liberation, the author connects the present question with the preceding context by saying "tatra tāvad" (first, in that regard). The explanation of the increase of *sattva* and its means is for the purpose of [understanding] action as a means to liberation characterized by renunciation (*tyāga*) and so forth. Since the word *saṃnyāsa* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of a particular stage of life (*āśrama*) and so on, yet also possesses the power (*śakti*) to denote mere renunciation, there arises a doubt regarding their distinctness or identity. Furthermore, due to the conflicting views of various disputants and other factors, there is a lack of certainty regarding the specific nature of these two.

He states the reason for the specific desire to know the truth regarding renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*) in the verse beginning with "For renunciation and relinquishment... Since the essential nature of action is common to both [worldly results] such as heaven and [spiritual goals] such as liberation, it is only through its association with specific qualifiers designated as "renunciation" and so forth that it becomes a means to liberation. Therefore, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, the designation of it being a means to that [liberation] applies specifically to the qualifiers. He explains that what is intended here by the word "truth" (*tattva*) is the reality (*yāthātmya*), which serves to eliminate doubt and misconception.

When it is said, "I wish to know distinctness," this implies a desire to know the specific nature of that which has already been ascertained as distinct; yet that is not tenable, because there was no cause for the ascertainment of distinctness in the preceding [case], whereas in the subsequent case...

Since oneness alone will be explained [later], this question is therefore untenable and its answer would be inconsistent; thus, he says: "This is the intended meaning. What is intended to be expressed is precisely this: "I wish to know the truth. The mention of "separateness," however, is merely for the purpose of introducing one of the two alternatives of doubt. Or, with the intention that the sentence means "If there is separateness, I wish to know that," he asks: "What? ||1||

If the question is raised out of a desire to know the nature of their distinctness and unity, then he says "Now" (*atha*) to explain how the presentation of various opinions—beginning with "In which part [are] the optional rites" (*kāmyānām*)—is relevant therein. This is the intended meaning: here, a definitive conclusion is to be established through reasoning (*nyāya*); and reasoning applies only to that which is doubtful; furthermore, doubt here arises from the conflicting assertions of various disputants. Thus, the presentation of these conflicting views serves to clarify the subject matter of the reasoning.

By this, it is also indicated that a further question is raised in this chapter to resolve the conflicting views regarding the two terms *saṃnyāsa* and *tyāga*, even though their meanings have already been stated. With the intention that the rejection of their distinctness is established by implication through the answer given by accepting their identity, he says: "the very same essential nature. Since his own view will be stated as "hear my certain conclusion," he uses the two words "the wise" (*kavayaḥ*) and "the discerning" (*vicakṣaṇāḥ*) not to indicate excellence of meaning or respect for the speakers, but rather with the intention that they refer merely to those possessing the knowledge necessary to resolve the conflict; thus he says: "some."

Because of the qualification "renunciation of optional (kāmya) actions," it is understood that other [types of] actions are not to be abandoned; and because of the subsequent qualification "renunciation of the fruits of all actions," it is intended here that there is no renunciation of the very nature of the optional action itself. With this in mind, he says: "renunciation of its own nature. The intention of those who speak of the renunciation of the nature of the optional action is as follows: one does not perform an optional action simply because, like obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) duties, there would be sin (pratyavāya) from non-performance, nor out of fear of becoming unfit for other rites.

Nor can [action] be for the sake of attaining the three aims of human life (*trivarga*), because that is antagonistic to liberation (*apavarga*). Nor is that very same action itself the direct means to liberation, for that would entail the futility of practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*). Nor can it be accepted as a subsidiary part of knowledge (*vidyā*) through the principle of separate application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*), since there is no contradiction even if the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth refer only to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties. For this very reason, the section of the *Brahma-sūtra* stating, "And there is dependence on all [duties], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse," is explained by the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) as referring to the dependence [of knowledge] upon the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).

Therefore, those desirous of liberation should not perform optional rites (*kāmya-kriyā*), which are the causes of hells designated as "heaven" and so forth. For those who say that there is the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, this is the underlying intention: since the fruit is opposed [to liberation], its abandonment is required; therefore, let only the fruit be abandoned. Nor does this entail the consequence of performing actions fruitlessly, for they are to be performed just like the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.

For those who maintain that the renunciation of all karmic fruits consists solely in seeking the pleasure of the Blessed One, this is the underlying intention: it is feared that because they conflict with [the attainment of] fruits, the optional (kāmya) rites might not be abandoned. Therefore, let only the fruit be renounced. Nor does this entail the consequence of performing [rites] fruitlessly; for their performance is justified precisely as being for the sake of the pleasure of the Blessed One alone, just like the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. And in this way, it is not the case that there is no injunction.

For it is heard in such passages as, "He who, without knowing this Imperishable (akṣara), offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years—all that becomes for him as if it were finite," that it is only through the knowledge of the Supreme Person designated by the word "Imperishable" that those very same ritual acts become means for attaining both eternal and non-eternal fruits. Therefore, there is no abandonment of the essential nature of even optional (kāmya) rites, just as there is none for the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) ones.

Since it is impossible for the dispute to concern different subjects, and because the words "renunciation" (tyāga) and "relinquishment" (saṃnyāsa) must necessarily have the same meaning, the resolution of the doubt regarding their distinct meanings is obtained by implication; thus he says, "In that case. By this, those who—while accepting that the words "renunciation" and "relinquishment" have distinct meanings—assert that one refers to the abandonment of the nature of optional (kāmya) acts, while the other refers to the disregard for the fruits of obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) acts, are refuted. For here, it is not said that there is a renunciation of the fruits of actions other than the optional ones.

And because there is no restriction [of scope], the phrase "all actions" (sarvakarma) includes all three types of action. This is what was stated: "of all actions—obligatory, occasional, and optional. Furthermore, even for obligatory acts, a connection with results is understood from such passages as, "The Prājāpatya [penance] is for householders," and so forth. Here, in order to refute the view that the words *tyāga* (renunciation) and *saṃnyāsa* (relinquishment) intend to establish a difference in meaning, he clearly states two reasons for their synonymy with the word "tathā" (thus).

With the intention that, when there is a doubt regarding two meanings, a determination of only one of them is not logically tenable, it was said, "by the word *tyāga* alone," and "because their mutual synonymy is observed. This is the intended meaning: for in the verse, "But the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of obligatory action is not appropriate," the very renunciation that was prohibited is subsequently referred to by the word *tyāga* in the phrase "its abandonment through delusion," and is censured as being of the nature of *tamas*.

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of mutual connection [of meanings] from sentences such as "The old ox" (*jaradgava*). Thus, when it is said, "It happens for non-renunciants after death," the very same meaning is strengthened by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) as "but not for renunciants under any circumstances. Nor is the negation of one thing the contrast (*vyatireka*) of another injunction. Therefore, these two words have the same meaning even when they are used in a negative context. "It is accepted"—the remainder is that this was accepted by the Blessed One, the respondent. ||2||

By the verse beginning with *kāmyānām*, the contradiction [between the two views] is shown by way of the presence or absence of conflict regarding the results. Then, by the verse beginning with *tyājyaṃ doṣavat*, the dispute is demonstrated through the presence or absence of inherent defects in its essential nature, by means of such factors as the production of demerit (*pratyavāya*). Even ritual violence (*vaidhahiṃsā*) is accepted as a defect by the followers of Kapila because it is prohibited; as stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa: "The scriptural (heavenly) [means], like the perceptible, is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess."

And it has been said by the teacher Pañcaśikha: "There may be a confusion of one's own fruits that is easy to avoid and not accompanied by remorse. Therefore, their view is that "Vedic violence will bring about fault for the person and will assist the sacrifice. Thus, by the word "some" (eke), [the author] refers to them in general.

He states that the proponent [of the opposing view] is indicated as being "faulty" (doṣavat) either by the force of the logical connection (*hetvanvaya*) and so forth, or by the power of the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) called "fault"; specifically, he says this refers to the followers of Kapila and the Vedists (*vaidika*). By this, the doctrine of those who advocate the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the nature of all actions is also shown to be outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*). Regarding the phrase "possessing faults such as passion" (*rāgādidoṣavat*): since it is agreed upon by all established philosophical systems (*siddhāntin*) that faults such as passion are the causes of bondage, that is used as the illustration; or else, action itself is what possesses faults such as passion.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is a "bondage. In this interpretation, the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes violence and other such acts. Although the word "karma" here refers to action in general—encompassing all actions such as sacrifice and the like—it specifically refers to those actions enjoined by the Śruti in another context, namely the view that "the actions of sacrifice, gift, and austerity are not to be renounced. This is because there is no specific indication [to limit it otherwise] therein, and because if it were restricted to optional (kāmya) actions, it would result in redundancy; thus, the sense is that it applies to all [actions].

Since there would otherwise follow the consequence that the scripture enjoining [all actions] as things to be abandoned would lack authority, [the Lord] specifies [the subject] as "one who desires liberation. Here, the word "others" refers to those who follow their own [personal] opinions. With the intention of stating his own view—that sacrificial, charitable, and ascetic action is not to be abandoned but must indeed be performed—he says "the wise. This means those who know the truth regarding the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. ||3||

With the intention that the word "tattra" (therein) indicates the state of doubt regarding the subject matter of the inquiry—by way of restating the point of disagreement in the present context—he says, "thus, there being disagreement among disputants. By the phrase "from me, having ascertained," he says, "hear from me the certainty regarding the object of renunciation," in order to dispel the suspicion that this might be another [unauthorized] view. [The word] "mattaḥ" (from me).

The meaning is "free from defects such as delusion. The passage beginning with "For renunciation... does not concern the threefold division of renunciation (sāttvika, etc. that will be described later; rather, it concerns a sub-division of the sāttvika type of renunciation. This is because the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "proclaimed" (*saṃprakīrtitaḥ*) points toward what was previously stated, and because the particle *hi* indicates the listener's agreement and so forth. With this intention, he says: "Renunciation [consists] in [the attitude] even while actions are being performed," and so on.

In the verse beginning with "mayi sarvāṇi," the Lord teaches that one who is intent on renunciation must reject the notion of performing actions as being fruitless and must dispel the doubt raised by the Sāṅkhya school; He then distinguishes the nature of these three [types of renunciation] with the words "born of action" and so forth, and "as the means to My own fruit" and so forth. The underlying sense is this: the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) should reflect that the Lord engages him solely for His own purpose, as a means to achieve His own pleasure.

The contemplation of the Lord as the agent [of all actions] arises from the fact that one's own agency is dependent upon Him, requires His permission, and so forth. However, the renunciation of agency consists in the contemplation of one’s own self as being impelled by another in the case of actions performed by many agents; this will be clarified in the subsequent sūtra. ||4||

Thus, it is stated by the passage beginning with "yajña-dāna" that the restatement of the three kinds of renunciation is intended to exclude the renunciation of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*). Some maintain that ritual acts such as sacrifice should be performed prior to the arising of the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) and the like, but must be abandoned thereafter; to refute that view, he says, "never at any time. With the intention of the Śruti text, "He indeed, living thus for as long as life lasts," he says, "but until departure from the body. Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Until death, for that is also seen [in scripture]."

The phrase "day after day" (*aharahar*) is an indicator of the prescribed time for performance. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of ritual action for one who is established in knowledge? It cannot be for the sake of providing indirect assistance (*ārādupakāritva*), since the positions of combined practice (*samuccaya*) and the like are not accepted here. Nor can it be for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), because that is established solely through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with its ancillaries.

Nor is it for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*) consisting of the recollection of that [Self], because that too must be accomplished through proficiency in mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; nor do we perceive any other purpose sought by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) that could be accomplished by ritual action (*karman*). With the intention that even a dull-witted person does not engage in activity without aiming at a purpose, there is the demonstration of the expectation [of a purpose] by asking "Why? The word "etc. (*prabhṛti*) is used with the intention of including [other factors] not explicitly mentioned. The phrase "connected with caste and stage of life" (*varṇāśramasaṃbandhī*) refers to this.

The sense is that the position which holds that there is an abandonment of the essential nature even of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites is here being refuted. With the intention of indicating that sacrifices and the like provide indirect assistance (*sannipatyopakāra*), he uses the word *manīṣin* (wise) here to refer to the nature of the knowledge of what is to be performed; thus he says, "of those whose nature is reflection" (*mananaśīlānām*). This is a statement of the result derived from the etymology: "those who rule over the mind are wise ones" (*manasa īṣiṇo manīṣiṇaḥ*). He says, "reflection is meditation" (*mananam upāsanam*), in order to exclude the kind of logical reflection (*yauktika-manana*) that occurs subsequent to hearing (*śravaṇa*).

The phrase "for the wise" clarifies the manner of assistance established by the co-occurrence [of the terms] with "purifying. By the words "for those seeking liberation," etc., [the author] explains this. Having begun with, "One should meditate upon the syllable Om until the end of life," the meditation is concluded with the statement, "But he who, by means of this very syllable Om consisting of three measures, meditates upon the Supreme Person"—thus it is determined that the worship must be practiced as long as one lives. Therefore, its subsidiary [practice] must also be performed throughout one's entire life.
