The meaning is that this [conduct] is described by such passages as, "He, indeed, conducting himself thus for as long as life lasts," and so forth. The word *prājña* (wise) is used because, unlike meditative worship (*upāsana*), it does not cease upon the completion of the subsequent rite. ||5||

Thus, by the statement regarding their purifying nature, the position that what is defective must be abandoned is refuted. The meaning already stated in the verse beginning with "Hear my definitive conclusion" (niścayaṃ śṛṇu) is further strengthened by the concluding verse beginning with "Even these" (etānyapi), for the purpose of establishing their faultlessness; hence there is no tautology. He connects the preceding and following sections as having the relationship of reason and thesis with the word "yasmāt" (because). He explains that the word "api" (even) is used to indicate that these [sacrifices] share the same security and outcome as the meditation (upāsana), which was suggested by the word "manīṣin" (the wise one), stating: "Even these, like the meditation."

He says, "consisting of My worship," in order to establish that actions are purifying and so forth by means of their being pleasing to the Supreme Self. He avoids redundancy by stating "renunciation of the fruit" through the word *saṅga* (attachment), whereas here he speaks of "possessiveness toward action. The word "certainly" (*niścitam*) implies: "In this matter, you should not entertain doubt again.

The word "supreme" (*uttamam*) implies that even among those who are not omniscient, all other doctrines—such as the renunciation of one's own nature—which contradict this, are inferior and therefore unworthy of respect. ||6||

Now, with the words "of that which is obligatory" (*niyatasya*) and so forth, the inferiority of other views and the superiority of his own view are elaborated. He explains that by the word "obligatory" (*niyata*), what is intended is that which is difficult to abandon because it is enjoined by one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). With the intention that the word *saṃnyāsa* accompanied by the particle *tu* here is a restatement of the nature of abandonment as taught in the verse "that which is to be abandoned is like something defective," and that this very [abandonment] is censured in the second half of the verse as "its abandonment through delusion," he says: "the renunciation of that."

Since it has been established that [the performance of rites] must necessarily be carried out because they lead to purification, the objection that renunciation is therefore untenable is addressed by the Teacher with the intent of reminding us of the previously explained inconsistencies regarding both visible and invisible results; with this in mind, he elaborates on the untenability [of the objection] in the words, "Even for the maintenance of the body... He says, "Even by mere eating and so forth, the worldly maintenance of the body could be accomplished," and to this he replies, "For the maintenance of the body... He says, "[The body is] nourished by enjoyments consisting of the five elements," and to this he replies, "For [the body] consists of food (annamaya)..."

The statement regarding nourishment (*āpyāyana*) is made because it is impossible for that which is an effect of the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*) to be a modification of food. With the intention that the term "vision" (*darśana*) is qualified by the scriptural passage—"Upon the attainment of memory, there is the loosening of all knots," and "The knot of the heart is rent asunder"—which conveys the same meaning, it is described as being of the nature of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. Because it is the most vivid [of all cognitions], the word "realization" (*sākṣātkāra*) should be understood here as a synonym for vision. He concludes the refutation of the doubt that knowledge might be beneficial even when performed only once with the words "Therefore... (tasmāt).

The meaning of the phrase "it is not tenable" is: how could there be an effect in the absence of a cause? With the intention of restating that it possesses the rule of being non-abandonable according to the method described, he says, "thus, for those who produce knowledge. With the intention that this is a refutation of the view restated as "that which has defects should be abandoned," he says, "bondage, delusion, and so forth. He explains the word *tāmasa* by means of the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "originating from that" (*tatra-bhavaḥ*), [rendering it] as "having its root in *tamas*.
Even though it expresses a mere relationship, the specific result is realized in the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

He explains that darkness (tamas) is the root [of the ego], mediated by the intellect (buddhi), because it is rooted in the tamasic intellect, stating: "Darkness has as its cause ignorance, which is its effect. Now, one might ask: since the fact that it is rooted in darkness should have been shown simply by its being co-uttered with the "I-notion" (aham-moha), what is the purpose of stating that it is rooted in ignorance, which is the effect of darkness? It is for that very same purpose; for there is no point in merely reiterating what has already been stated using different words. However, it is appropriate to provide further understanding, provided it is not contradictory.

Now, in the verse "Negligence and delusion arise from Tamas, as well as ignorance itself," it was explained that because the word *moha* (delusion) refers to a distinct form of erroneous cognition (*viparītajñāna*), it denotes the state of ignorance (*ajñāna*). However, here [it is said]: "Ignorance, moreover, is the opposite of knowledge."

How is it said that "perverted knowledge" (viparītajñāna) is thus? It is either for the purpose of demonstrating that even the absence of knowledge serves as a cause for engagement by means of perverted knowledge, or with the intention of expressing another purpose for the word *moha* found in the verse, or to make known that the word *ajñāna* (ignorance) found in the verse has *moha* as its object. He clarifies that the intellect characterized by *tamas* is the cause for the renunciation of action by means of what is to be stated later, beginning with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*).

With the intention that those who know reality do not abandon [action], he concludes the result of the description of the *tāmasa* [type of renunciation] with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the obligatory, occasional, etc.," there is the inclusion of even those optional acts (*kāmya*) performed without desire for fruit, which will be mentioned later. By the phrase "in the case of perverted knowledge" (*viparītajñāne*), he demonstrates the distinction from the *rājasa* renunciation, which is rooted in false knowledge; for it will be stated later that *rājasa* intellect is "incorrect" (*ayathāvat*).

Thus, although there is no absence of the essential nature of the qualities that define its own character—since it is designated by the term "nature" due to its being an internal factor—nevertheless, by way of the reversal of those qualities that specify the defined nature, [the Lord], recollecting the *rājasa* intellect which is about to be described, explains the renunciation of the *rājasa* type with the words beginning "Even though...

(*yadyapi*). Because of the restrictive particle in "it is only suffering" (*duḥkham ity eva*) and because of the statement "out of fear of bodily affliction," it follows that the delusion regarding its being unrighteous (*adharma*) does not exist here. "There is suffering in the acquisition of objects."

In accordance with this [scriptural] teaching, he says: "consisting of suffering," and "causing dejection of the mind. The point is that non-dejection (*anavasāda*) is indeed counted among the seven means for the perfection of discrimination (*viveka*). With the intention that, when there is a conflict between an internal and an external factor, the abandonment of the external is appropriate, he says: "only the practice of knowledge. The scriptural restatements (*anuvāda-vākya*), such as "Having abandoned even those prescribed actions, O best of the twice-born, one should be diligent in self-knowledge, in tranquility, and in the study of the Vedas," are the source for this. Regarding the statement "having performed a renunciation of the passionate type" (*rājasa-tyāga*), he explains what is intended by that restatement: "not according to reality" (*ayathāvasthita*).

The term "fruit of renunciation" (*tyāgaphala*) here is intended to mean the fruit of renunciation that will be described [later], because this is a section concerning those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and because there is no possibility of attaining fruits such as heaven—which are achieved through ritual action—once action has been renounced; with this intention, he says, "consisting in the arising of knowledge. He dispels the apprehension of mental despondency caused by the fact that [action] is essentially suffering by saying, "for not... The meaning is that the Blessed Lord, propitiated by rituals in the manner previously stated in the passage beginning with "Indeed, by the desire for fruits," brings about precisely the non-despondency of the mind. ||8||

Now, having extracted what was already recalled by the words "For renunciation... and so forth, he confirms that very [renunciation] as the primary subject of the treatise because it is rooted in knowledge as it truly is—the activity of pure being—by means of the verse beginning with "The duty... He explains its meaning as "constant" (nitya), since the word "niyata" here also qualifies the action, following from the introductory statement: "But the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate."

In fact, the state of being an effect (kāryatva) belongs only to the purpose; for it is precisely because of its subservience to that purpose that the means is considered an effect. Therefore, how can that which is fruitless be something to be performed? To this he replies: "It is to be performed as a form of my worship. He states what is intended by this: "it has itself as its purpose. Even the renunciation of agency is to be understood through this underlying intention. For this very reason, in the verse beginning with "the infinite" (Ananta), the word "renouncer" (tyāgī) is explained as one who renounces attachment, the fruit, and agency. ||9||

For one who possesses the renunciation of the "thorns" rooted in *sattva* and so forth, the characteristic consisting in the absence of modification—well-known from such statements as "the *sāttvika* state prevails" and "he sits like one indifferent"—is described by the verse beginning with "he does not hate. By this, it is also established that the renunciation characterized above is rooted in *sattva*. Therein, he explains [the sequence] in a different order according to the propriety of the causal and effectual sequence, starting with "one who is permeated by *sattva*" and so on. Lexicographers state: "The intellect (*dhī*) is that which possesses the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*)."

And there is a scriptural passage: "May wisdom and intelligence enter me together for the attainment of what has been and what is to be. Regarding this, he states the result—namely, knowledge of reality as it truly is—as consisting in non-deviation and non-confusion with respect to the matters taught by the Teacher. Here, with the intention that the mention of the word *kuśala* (skillful), which is a synonym for the auspicious (*śubha*), is a restatement of the cause of attachment that is being prohibited [by the term *akuśala*], he provides the reasoning regarding its undesirable fruit. He explains how renunciation is the cause of that which was called "renouncing" by means of the words beginning with "in all... (*sarvasmin*).

The intention is as follows: just as in the case of another person’s action performed by someone else, there is an absence of aversion and so forth due to the certainty that there is no obstacle or other impediment because of the lack of any connection to oneself, so it is here as well. It is stated that "of those being performed" because, during the state of non-performance, there is no possibility of the occurrence of joy or aversion. Now, it may be argued: while it is reasonable to say that one does not become attached to what is wholesome (*kuśala*)—since even when performing optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) for the sake of heaven and the like, one remains free from attachment and thus does not incur a connection with their results—it is, however, contradictory to say that one does not hate wholesome action.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of attachment to the fruits [of action]. For hell and the like would not be desired by anyone. Thus, regarding the lack of aversion even toward causes of visible transgression, the resolution is stated here by way of their being objects of negligence (*prāmādika*). Now, one might ask: "Could there not be freedom from stain even through intentional sinful acts for a particular qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*)? To this he says: "Not for one who has not desisted" (*nāvirataḥ*). Having connected the meaning of this verse with the present context as a supporting reason, he concludes the subject under discussion (*paramaprakṛta*) with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 10 ||

He says, "Then he said," with the intention that the verse beginning with "of the fixed" (*niyatasya*) explains the reasoning previously set forth, and that by means of the illustration of the renunciation of results, the aforementioned threefold *sāttvika* renunciation is concluded by the verse beginning with "not indeed" (*na hi*). Here, in the phrase "until death" (*ā dehamṛte*), there is no reference to all living beings in general, as that would be irrelevant; therefore, he says, "by one whose body is still sustained," with the aim of explaining the meaning of the word "part" (*avayava*) as the reason why the abandonment of the essential nature of action is impossible. [The word] "possible" (*śakyam*)...

The neuter gender and singular number [of the word *tyāga*] are due to its focus on the act of abandoning, or else because of the intention to express it as a general form. He explains the impossibility caused by the state of being an embodied being with the words "of those things necessary for the maintenance of the body. To the question, "Let the acquisition of wealth and so forth related to that be worldly matters; what need is there for scriptural ones? he replies with the words "and for the sake of that. This is based on the natural force (*svārasya*) of the Śruti.

With the intention of removing the doubt that [the Self] might abandon its own nature (*svarūpa*), he says "yas tu" and so forth. To satisfy the expectancy of the word "is designated" (*abhidhīyate*)—namely, by what means?—he cites the scriptural passage beginning with "by renunciation, some" (*tyāgenaika*). He confirms that this serves to demonstrate the conclusion of the subject under discussion by stating "of three kinds" (*trividha*). ||11||

For even the establishment of Vedic rites as means to achieve results is determined solely by the very same process used for worldly actions. And worldly actions bear fruit according to their own inherent capacity even in the absence of a desire for a result. With this intention—that it is the same regarding Vedic rites—the author raises the objection with the words "nanu" (but...).

Now, one might object: "Since the Agnihotra and other rites, as well as the Great Sacrifices (mahāyajña) and so forth, have distinct applications—such as being limbs of the stages of life (āśrama) versus having heaven and the like as their purpose—there may be no contradiction in performing them for the sake of heaven and so on. But what contradiction is there in performing them for the sake of the stage of life? To this, he says: "Even of the obligatory and occasional rites... By the example of sowing seeds and so forth, it is stated that they are "unskillful," thereby indicating that even those performed through negligence (prāmādika) are binding. For a seed that falls upon the ground through negligence does not fail to bear fruit.

Therefore, with the intention that this collection of actions is like sowing the seeds of a poisonous tree for one who desires the taste of mangoes, he states the abandonment of its own nature by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*). This threefold division [of results] is undesirable for those who do not seek liberation (*amumukṣu*), because even heaven and the like are undesirable from the perspective of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). With this intention, there is the mention of hell, heaven, and so forth. The term "after death" (*pretya*) is intended to demonstrate that the fruits such as rain, which are accomplished through rites like the *Kārīrī*, exist only during the state of being alive.

Otherwise, there would be an obstacle even for those who have renounced [the world] while still in that very body; with this intention, he says, "at a time subsequent to the performance of the action. Here too, the non-connection with results that have not yet perished should be understood as referring to actions performed through negligence (*prāmādika*), according to the manner previously stated. This response is stated merely by way of a proposition (*pratijñāmātreṇa*) to the objection raised, and not by means of any formal reasoning; regarding this, he says, "this has been stated," meaning that the distinctness of application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*) is to be grasped through the distinctness of the injunctive statements (*viniyojaka-vākya*).

Through the principle of separate application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*), it is established that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices have various fruits such as the destruction of sin. [The objection] is answered: the remaining point is the challenge regarding their having contradictory fruits. Now, an objection is raised: since the restrictive statement, "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path," enjoins knowledge alone as the means to liberation and thereby excludes ritual action (*karman*), how can there be a mention of its application within the context of liberation? To this, he says: "And the application to liberation... and so forth.

Just as in cases such as "he wishes to kill with a sword" (*asinā jighāṃsati*) or "he wishes to go by horse" (*aśvena jigamiṣati*), where the connection [of the instrument] occurs because of the very nature of the meaning, here too there is a connection of the desired meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as an instrument. Therefore, because it is a means through a mediated succession by way of the arising of knowledge (*vedana*), its application is to liberation (*mokṣa*). However, the sense is that when there is an intention to express an immediate means, there is a prohibition by such statements as "There is no other path" (*nānyaḥ panthāḥ*).

With the intention of beginning to answer the intended question in another way, he restates the portion already mentioned for the sake of coherence, using the form of a conclusion: "Therefore, that [is so]. This means that because the abandonment of one's essential nature and so forth belongs to the quality of darkness (tamas). Thus, regarding that which is regulated by caste, stage of life, and so on—

The meaning is: "in the manner of that which is difficult to abandon. In this very verse, because the opposite of the absence of renunciation—namely, its presence—is stated by the word *saṃnyāsa* in the line, "It exists after death for those who do not renounce, but never for those who have renounced," the doubt regarding the distinctness of renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*) is also dispelled; thus he says, "And that itself is renunciation. (12)

To the question, "What is the connection between the statement beginning with 'the undesirable' and 'the desirable' and the subsequent mention of the five causes? he says: "Now" (*idānīm*). This means that the direct object of the inquiry having been answered. By both the terms "Bhagavat" and "Puruṣottama," he makes known, in the manner previously stated, that [the Lord] is the inner controller of all and is free from any defects inherent in or caused by that [world].

By the words "He explains the manner," it is shown that right here there is a purification of the nature of the contemplation of non-agency—which has been introduced from the third chapter onwards—along with its cause and its actual state. Since three types of renunciation have been introduced, the connection is that this is the purification of the manner of the final one. To the question, "Since all three kinds of renunciation were introduced as being characterized by *sattva*, why is there an exposition of only the manner of renouncing agency? he says: "For that very reason. Here, the word "iti" signifies the sense of a reason.

Even though the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and others are the agents [of the sacrifice], the patron (yajamāna) and others are seen to possess a sense of ownership (mamatā) regarding the ritual act and its fruit. Why, then, should this not be the case for him [the yogin] as well? To the question—how can the cessation of the notion of ownership regarding the act and its fruit follow merely from the renunciation of agency—the author says: "For the Supreme Person... The particle *hi* indicates that this is established by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [As it is said: "O Hari, You sport with beings who move downward and upward, constrained by the threads of karma, just as one plays with toys, or as a child plays with other children."

He states with the words "by his own," etc., what is well known from such passages as, "Indeed, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, this entire universe, moving and unmoving, exists. For the Supreme Person is heard in scripture to be the presiding lord over the instruments [of perception]. Therefore, even during the state when the instruments belong to the individual soul (jīva), the status of the Supreme Person as the primary beneficiary (śeṣitva) does not cease—just as a king remains the primary beneficiary of the ornaments on elephants and horses; with this intention, he says, "and by his own instruments, bodies, and vital breaths."

He states that even the granting of seen and unseen fruits [of karma] is his *līlā* (divine play) because there is no contraction [of his will], by saying "for the purpose of his own *līlā*. The sense is that this has been investigated in such passages as "Like the world, his *līlā* alone is the motive. However, in the reading "for the purpose of *līlā* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes compassion and the protection of devotees who are its root cause.

Now, since scriptural action is enjoined solely as a means of propitiating the Supreme Person, it is logical that it belongs to Him from its inception until the attainment of its fruit. However, worldly action is not taught in such a manner, nor is it perceived as such; for its fruits, such as the cessation of hunger, are observed to pertain exclusively to the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, if worldly fruits belong to the *jīva*, [how can they be considered subordinate to the Supreme?]

It might be argued that since even the action which is the means to that [attainment] must have that [attainment] as its purpose, it is impossible to establish—through such statements as "for the sake of the perfection of all actions"—the renunciation of attachment to all objects of sense. To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). In the phrase "of the Supreme Person alone" (*paramapuruṣasyaiva*), the genitive case rests upon a specific relationship known as that between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). The sense is that just as the rearing of five birds and the like, as well as their resulting happiness and so forth, are subsidiary to a sovereign emperor, so it is here as well.

In the phrase "in Sāṃkhya, in the Kṛtānta," the Sāṃkhya system is intended; for in that system, God is not admitted, and since an agent distinct from the instruments is not admitted, it would be impossible to state the distinction between agent and instrument as in the verse, "The agent and the various kinds of instruments. Furthermore, if that system were contrary to the Veda, it would be inappropriate to cite it for the purpose of teaching the principles (tattva). Even if it were not contrary, one must necessarily accept its being rooted in the Veda, and thus it ultimately rests upon the Veda itself.

And because it is universally accepted that, for the sake of semantic propriety (*arthaucitya*), one should set aside conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and rely upon etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*), the portion of the Vedas itself which is engaged in determining reality as it truly is, is intended by the term *sāṃkhyakānta*. With this intention, he provides the etymological derivation: "Saṃkhyā means intellect (*buddhi*). In accordance with the context, he qualifies that intellect as "as it truly is" (*yathāvasthitā*).

As for what was stated here by Śaṅkara—"Sāṃkhya is that [system] in which categories (padārtha) are enumerated; it is Vedānta, for it is the 'end' (anta) of what has been done (kṛta), namely action (karman)"—that is incorrect, because the connection with action is established even within the Vedāntas. Furthermore, since the conventional meaning must necessarily be set aside, it is more appropriate to adopt the most fitting etymological derivation.

The word *anta* is listed by lexicographers (*naiṣaṇṭuka*) as meaning "certainty" (*niścaya*). With the intention that this very [word] is qualified by the word *kṛta* because it has been intentionally brought about (*buddhipūrva-saṃpādita*), it is stated that "it is concluded" (*anusaṃhite nirṇaye*) [in the verse]. Alternatively, the word *nirṇaya* here refers to the object determined (*niṇīta-vastu*), since the word *kṛtānta*—which is a synonym for *siddhānta* (established conclusion)—is conventionally used to denote the specific doctrine accepted by each [school]. For this very reason, it is specified as "concluded" (*anusaṃhita*). Indeed, it is not the case that certainty itself is what must be concluded.

Alternatively, it is specified that the determination (nirṇaya) of the ancients was adopted by others; for the word "determination" [itself] does not [mean finality]. In that case, its connection is with the phrase "proclaimed at that time. By the word "accomplishment" (siddhi), the state of reaching the final result and so forth is not intended here; rather, with the intention that this is because the very nature of action has just been described in the words, "Whatever action one undertakes, these five are its causes," he says: "origination" (utpatti).

Since the expression "my causes" (*madīyāni kāraṇāni*) is impossible because there is no sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) regarding that which is designated here by the word *daiva*, it would lack logical connection; therefore, he provides the appropriate connection: "Receive [them] from me. The intention is that this is for the purpose of instructing the concentration of the mind upon the five causes to be described hereafter, according to their respective natures as discerned.

With the intention that this treatise would be contradictory for those who do not accept a twenty-sixth principle and yet maintain that the twenty-fifth principle is merely the locus for the superimposition of agency, [the author] establishes that the text refers to its etymological meaning, stating: "For the Vedic...
The term *śarīrendriyaprāṇajīvātmopakaraṇam* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. An "accessory" (*upakaraṇa*) is an apparatus employed for the sake of a desired effect. ||23||

Intending to show that there is no tautology in the two verses by virtue of the explanation already stated, and also considering that [the opponent's] view is contradictory, he says: "He said this. The meaning is: *tat* refers to what is established by scripture (*śruti*), and *idam* refers to what is intended to be expressed. It is *nyāyya*, meaning not departing from logic (*nyāya*); for according to the grammatical rule, "the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of 'path of dharma' and 'not departing from logic,'" the word *nyāya* here—because other meanings would be inappropriate and in accordance with its etymology—refers specifically to the Śārūka (the treatise on logic). With this intention, he says: "established by the Śārūka."

Thus: when there is a worldly intention (*laukikavivakṣā*) together with what is established by scripture (*śāstrāsiddha*), one must say "or something else than that. With the intention that [the rule] is prescribed when [the object] is specified, and the opposite word applies when it is prohibited, and that the worldly [usage] is obtained by implication (*kaimutya*), he says "or when prohibited. The statement "in every ritual act" (*sarvasmin karmaṇi*) is a statement of the resulting conclusion.

Just as in the case of physical, mental, and verbal actions, there is a fixed determination of the body and so forth based on their predominance, these five causes are not like that; rather, all five are required for every action. With this intention, the statement "not being physical" (*aśārīratva*) and so forth is made. Indeed, the classification into physical and so forth is based solely on predominance among all those things consisting of the five causes. Although these [five] have been employed by the Supreme Self through His own will in the creation of the world and other such acts, the mention of other causes is intended to show this.

Vasiṣṭha said to Karālā, "They call the field (kṣetra) the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna)"; following that, he says, "the body is the substratum. And the Śruti establishes the term "substratum" for the body in the passage: "This body is mortal, seized by death; it is the substratum of this immortal, bodiless Self," deriving it from the sense of "that upon which something is presided over" (adhiṣṭhīyate). Since the instruments and so forth, though presiding over by the individual soul (jīva), are mentioned separately, he says "consisting of the aggregation of the great elements" in order to exclude them.

Because the Universal Creator is mentioned separately here by the word *daiva* (fate), and because the word *kartṛ* (agent) is intended here to indicate the maxim that "the fruit of action accrues to the performer," it is stated that the agent is the individual self (*jīvātman*). Now, one might object: agency indeed consists in being endowed with the exertion toward an action preceded by knowledge and the desire to act; since pure consciousness alone cannot constitute the self's status as a knower, its agency—which is rooted in that—would likewise be impossible. To this, he says: "This individual self possesses both the capacity for knowing and for acting."

The non-inclusion of such sūtras as "jño'ta eva" (BrSū 2.3.18) is because the Śruti and other authorities are likewise drawn from that very source. With the intention that the word "karaṇa" here refers only to the organs of action—since the causes for the production of action have been set forth—he says "vāk" (speech).

Although the organs of perception (*jñānendriya*) are indirectly causes for action by way of producing knowledge of their respective objects, nevertheless, because action is performed through the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) alone when mere things are perceived, and because there is no intervention by another activity [other than that], it is said to be "with mind" (*samanaska*). Furthermore, since the mind is common to the operations of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) as well as the organs of perception, it is designated as an organ of action. [The body...]

Because it is stated right here [in the scripture] that [the organs consist of] speech, mind, and so forth, there is a claim that the mind (*manas*) is a *karmendriya* (organ of action) in view of its functions such as volition (*saṃkalpa*). The Sāṃkhyas have also stated this very thing:

"The sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin; they call the organs of action (*karmendriya*) speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Here, the mind is of both kinds; it is an organ because of its commonality with the others, being characterized by volition. Thus, when the causes of action are being enumerated, it is mentioned separately.

To specify that [activity] which is appropriate for it, he says, "a distinct activity in the accomplishment of the action. For the functional activities—such as speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and the volition of bliss—in each of the organs like speech and the rest, are indeed mutually distinct.

Indeed, bodily action rooted in effort alone is designated by the term "volitional movement" (*ceṣṭā*). By the word "fivefold wind," it is expressed through sound (*śabdena*) that [the breath] is produced.

Only that much is intended to be expressed here. Since another cause for this [maintenance] is to be indicated, and because speech and the other organs have been presented by means of words such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*), and because it is heard in the dialogues of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and elsewhere that the maintenance and activity of both the instruments and the body depend upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the author says "by that which expresses its activity," intending that a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the vital breath is appropriate here through a word denoting activity, which is the cause of the vital breath's functioning. The phrase "by the word 'activity' (*ceṣṭā*)" connects with what precedes.

By means of the recollection of the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth, he explains the appropriateness of defining the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the manifold nature of its functions in the verse beginning with "body and senses" (*śarīrendriya*). To avoid the redundancy of the two terms *pṛthak* (separate) and *vividha* (various), he says: "of that which sustains the body and senses, and which is divided into [the states of] *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so on. Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is established in relation to the substratum, the agent, the instrument, and their respective operations, as well as through the distinction of objects consisting of the groups of body and senses; this refers to the specific functions such as exhalation, closing the eyes, and opening the eyes, which are determined by the various modifications of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* etc.).

The sense is that there is a diversity [of functions] through their activities. Here, the word *pañcātman* refers to having five modes of functioning (*pañcavṛttitva*); thus says the Sūtra: "The mind is designated as having five functions. And the mention of having five functions indicates the other pentad of functions consisting of Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya. Regarding the phrase "and the divine, which is my fifth," he says that in this context, the word "here" (*atrety*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of singling out the primary factor called the "divine. This is the action (*karma*).

Regarding the phrase "the causal aggregate" (*hetukalāpa*): since it is impossible for the Supreme Self to be enumerated as the fifth according to the sequence of the reading of the meaning of the *Śruti* and so forth—and because speech functions sequentially, even if one were to enumerate them as far as possible, there would be no purpose in using the ordinal designation "the fifth"—as is seen, for example, in the *Kaṭhavallī*.

Beginning with the statement, "The objects are superior to the senses," and continuing with, "The Unmanifest is superior to the Great (Intellect), and the Puruṣa is superior to the Unmanifest; there is nothing superior to the Puruṣa—that is the supreme goal," the Supreme Person is indicated as the primary cause of all activity, beginning with the senses, and as the ultimate limit to be mastered.
With the intention that it is the same here as well, [the author] says: "The Supreme Self, the Inner Controller.
Now, in passages such as "Fate is past action" and "Fate is destiny, the allotted lot," [fate] is used as a synonym for fortune in the form of prior karma.

They read the word *daiva* (destiny/divine). And its status as a cause is logical. Therefore, how can it be said here that this refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? It is as follows: for it is not possible for actions that have already perished to function as causes in their own essential form (*svarūpa*). Consequently, one must state that the causality belongs solely to the will of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), which takes the form of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by those actions. Hence, it is better to represent that very [will] by the word *daiva*. Furthermore, the word *daiva* is indeed used in common worldly usage as a synonym for *daivata* (deity).

This is well-known in the two Vedas; for example: "Truth, truth, again truth—raising my arm, I declare: there is nothing higher than the Vedic scriptures, and no deity higher than Keśava. No other meaning is possible here. Likewise, in the Śrīmad Rāmāyaṇa: "Having bypassed one's own mother, father, and guru, how can a deity that is not under one's own control be propitiated through various means?"
Likewise, in the Sabhā Parva: "Listen to the supreme divinity, which is difficult to be known even by me; it is Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa of universal form and great splendor."

Thus, in the Yogaśāstra composed by Yājñavalkya, the very same meaning previously stated as "the seer (ārṣa), the meter (chandas), the deity (daivata), and likewise the Brāhmaṇa of the mantras" is further indicated by the passage beginning with "the seer, the meter, and the deity," and so forth. In that very work, for the purpose of deluding the Daityas, Prajāpati replies to the question, "What is called the adhidaiva? [as found] in the Chāndogya.

The term "day" is designated as the "adhidaivata" (the divine sphere) for the person who abides in the deity named Āditya; its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "day" with respect to the divine, and its secret name is "I" (*aham*) with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. Others have also explained the word "deity" (*daiva*) here as referring to Āditya and others who favor the eyes and other senses. We, however, declare that the "deity" here is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who favors even Āditya and the rest.

Such is the distinction. And it is employed in the *Stotra* [of Lakṣmī], as well as in the opinions of those who know the supreme truth regarding the renowned deities: "In the matter of Dharma, his own tradition (*samaya*) is the authority, as are the Vedas; and his chosen deity is the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Therefore, the word *daiva* here is a synonym for *devatā* (deity). And since it refers here to the cause that impels all things, and because there is no specific [other] deity [intended], it is appropriate that it refers to the Supreme Deity; thus, the Supreme Self, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), is the one who controls the actions [of all].
It has been stated that [the Self] is the primary cause for the accomplishment of action.

Just as He is the Self of all, yet no one else is His [Self], He is therefore the *paramātman* (Supreme Self). Just as the individual soul (*jīva*) is the primary cause for the activity of the body and so forth, so too is He the primary cause for its [the Supreme Self’s] activity; it is with this intention that the term "inner ruler" (*antaryāmin*) is used. He establishes that this is merely intended to be expressed by means of the preceding and following passages, beginning with the words "For it has been said," and so on. Now, an objection: "An agent is defined as one who is independent (*svatantra*); and here, the 'knower of the field' (*kṣetrajña*) is referred to as the agent."

Thus it has been pointed out. Therefore, one must accept that [the agent] is both the instigator of other causal factors (*kāraka*) and is not itself instigated by other causal factors. Consequently, even destiny (*daiva*)—like the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth—must be stated here to be subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) in relation to that [agent]; to this he says: "And dependent upon the Supreme Self. For, in the case of a person who possesses arisen knowledge, desire, and effort...

The meaning is that while [the soul] possesses the status of being an instigator of other causal factors and so forth, the arising of knowledge and the like depends solely upon the Supreme Self, as established by scripture; thus, it has been settled in the *Śārīraka* that the soul’s agency dependent on another and its independence are not contradictory. Not understanding this intention, and thinking that the Supreme Self acts as a prompter like wind or water, he objects with the words "But if this were so. If the Supreme Self prompts [the soul] in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, then there would be nothing for the soul to perform.

For indeed, there is no injunction for one who is being carried away by a stronger force. If one then restrains him, even so it is not an injunction; for there is no injunction for the movement of one who is weak and restrained by a stronger force. If one then restrains him, even so it is not an injunction; for there is no injunction for the movement of one who is weak and restrained by a stronger force.
Thus, wherever the Supreme Self impels, since cessation is impossible, a prohibition is fruitless. But where He does not impel, there indeed activity itself is impossible.

The sense is that there is no requirement for a prohibition [against such activity] on your part. Here, this is the pinnacle of the objection raised by all schools of thought other than the Cārvāka; however, in their case, since even engagement [with the world] is impossible, there is no requirement for a prohibition—this is the sense. This is the ultimate point of the challenge faced by all systems except the Cārvāka: "How can it be possible to say that one is 'worthy of punishment or reward' when one is impelled by previously accumulated unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) prescribed for punishment and reward?"

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa, the seer of the Pañcama-veda-Upaniṣad, himself resolved this objection—just as the objection regarding the soul’s lack of dependence despite its being a knower and an agent—namely, the objection that even if the soul were dependent [on God], injunctions and prohibitions would become purposeless. He states this with the words "this too" (*idam api*). The meaning of the Sūtra is that for the very reasons that injunctions and prohibitions would otherwise be purposeless, the Supreme Self impels the conscious being toward subsequent actions only after taking into account the effort made by that conscious being. In that case, since all activities are dependent on the Supreme Self, how...

Is it being said that [the Lord] depends on the effort performed [by the individual soul]? In response to the doubt that, if the objection regarding futility were refuted merely by establishing its non-futility, there would be no distinction from the point to be proven (sādhya), he states the intended meaning of the Sūtra with the words "this is what is meant."

This is the intended meaning: that which consists in the Lord’s bestowing upon the soul the power of activity fashioned by His own volition—like a mechanical device; and His abiding as the universal substratum through His essential nature and volition, in accordance with all prior activities—likewise like the ground; and also the granting of the power to preside over instruments, bodies, and so forth; and the presentation of external objects as the support for activity—all of this is conducive to the soul’s status as an agent.

And since this [indifference] is common to all engagement and withdrawal, there is no room for objection therein. Indeed, it is precisely this indifference of the Blessed Lord that is said to be common to all engagement and withdrawal. Thus, when a person who has acquired power acts, the Lord’s role as the permissive authorizer (*anumantṛ*) for the sake of accomplishing the task is not a denial of the individual soul’s agency; rather, it supports it. Therefore, even on this account, the futility of injunctions and prohibitions does not follow.

Nor is the mere association with another agent called the Supreme Self (paramātman) within a single action the cause of the individual soul’s (jīva) being unenjoinable; for we observe in the world that injunctions, prohibitions, and their fruits apply even to those actions which cannot be performed by each individual alone but are carried out by many, since independence and other such qualities are established by the fact that one who possesses the power of action cannot be restrained by others when there is a desire to act.

Thus, even in such passages as, "Everyone is caused to act helplessly by the qualities born of material nature," the soul's agency is well-established because activity proceeds preceded by knowledge and desire, and because specific desires are rooted in the particularities of one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For this very reason, here in the context of the five reasons, the soul is defined solely as an agent through the application of the designation "agent."

As for the unequal distribution [of results] regarding the body, organs, power, knowledge, and desire; the failure to prevent those who act toward what is harmful; the acquiescence [in such acts]; and the resulting demerit (*pratyavāya*)—all of these are due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the inequality of beginningless prior karma (*pūrvakarman*), and thus do not entail partiality (*vaiṣamya*) or cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) on the part of the Lord. Even though the inequality of activity is rooted in the inequality of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), that very *adṛṣṭa* is initiated by Him through the mediation of the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*); and since that [scriptural process] is likewise [dependent on karma], there is room for the application of injunctions and prohibitions.

For it is not the case that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which was previously the cause for sacrifices and so forth, independently—by its own intellect and through its capacity for cessation—reduces one to a state unfit for instruction and then impels them toward sin; for that [unseen merit] is likewise [subject to cessation]. Otherwise, since the engagement in what is beneficial or harmful would have the unseen as its sole root, one would not require the scripture; thus, for the proponent who argues in this way, there is a contradiction with their own words, because the same consequence would apply even to the previously acquired unseen merit.

Now, if you think that since the scripture lacks a perceptible basis, it would follow that the scripture is purposeless, and since the opponents admit that the scripture is meaningful, it is therefore impossible for it to lack a perceptible basis—this too is not so, because the same consequence would apply even to worldly injunctions and prohibitions. For in those cases as well:

If the diversity of activity, engagement, and so forth is rooted in the diversity of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), what is the purpose of an injunction such as "Bring the cow"? Or do you maintain that even this injunction, brought forward by its own causal complex, occupies the midst of the causal complex for activity or cessation? If so, you should likewise perceive that the Vedic injunction is the same. If you then say, "In that case, let us abandon even worldly injunctions," then alas! Since mutual social interaction, linguistic convention, and so forth would become impossible, the Lokāyata materialism itself would collapse; therefore, remain silent.

Thus, although all actions generally have their roots in unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) that cause inequality, if one were to teach that very unseen factor as a specific cognition of the Lord (*īśvara-buddhi-viśeṣa*), there would be no room for objection; for such a Lord is understood through the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is this a fault. As stated by the teacher Vādīhaṃsāmbuvāha: "When inequality exists among actions, what could an agent do that is not unequal?
Or, out of magnanimity, what could a granter of boons give if they desired an evil state?"
Therefore, this is the essence of the common rebuttal for all those who do not adhere to the Cārvāka system:

because of the necessary connection with a sequence of causes—whether seen or unseen—that are desired by each respective [system], the production of various unseen results (adṛṣṭa) and so forth is logically established in their respective ways for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life.

"Because of [the Lord's] own will, the person acts; since that [will] is for his sake, the injunction here has scope. Here, by the words ending with "being dependent on another," it is stated that the soul's agency is dependent on another due to its dependence on common assistance such as the provision of the instruments and the body. By the words beginning with "for the accomplishment of action," however, the soul's independence regarding specific activity is shown. Even in that case, the other's slight contribution is stated by the words beginning with "residing within him. This means: "him who has exerted effort. (24, 25)

If this were so—that even though there are five causes, the self alone is the agent—then the contemplation of non-agency would be nothing but an illusion. Furthermore, agency must be difficult to relinquish for the sake of preserving injunctions, prohibitions, and the like. Nor can it be argued that independence from auxiliary factors (sahakārins) is what is prohibited; for since such independence does not even arise as a possibility, its prohibition is impossible.

Furthermore, there arises the doubt that no one ever thinks "I am doing" while being independent of the body, senses, staff, wheel, and so forth. To address this, the verse beginning with *miti* explains that the contemplation of non-agency (*akartṛtvānusaṃdhāna*) consists in the removal of the delusion of natural agency—which is independent of any other controller—and the removal of the conceit of being independent in action for those who possess the delusion of identifying with the body and such, when that action actually depends on many factors. In this context, the phrase "with the permission of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmānumatipūrvaka*) includes the apprehension of the primary cause, the Pradhāna, which sustains everything. The term "the Self" (*ātmānam*) refers to...

The meaning is "one's own self. For this very reason, the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) here does not, as before, denote the substratum (*dharmin*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply the phrase "the cause for the commencement of the action. With this intention, he says: "only the self alone as the agent. Here, the word "but" (*tu*) serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

It has been explained. Or, even if it serves to remove doubt, the particle *eva* (only) has as its referent the individual (*vyakti*) denoted by the word *kevala* alone. If it is objected: "In this context, by the word *kevala*, there would be a mere restatement of the soul's natural agency (*kartṛtva*)," we say no; for when the performance of action through the cooperation of the four factors is under discussion, it would be inappropriate (*asvārasya*) to exclude that [agency] in a censure of one ignorant of it. Furthermore, that [agency] is required [in the context]. Regarding this, what has been stated by others—that because the Self is immutable by nature, [there is no agency] in the act of presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—[is incorrect].

"Because conjunction is impossible for that which is immutable; for conjunction belongs to that which is subject to modification, or agency would belong to that which has conjoined; but since there is no conjunction of the immutable Self with anything else, acting in combination is not possible"—this is incorrect, because the Self is devoid of modifications such as the arising of its own nature and so forth.

For, through such scriptural passages as, "As fire is in wood, and as oil is in sesame, so also the Puruṣa resides within Pradhāna—pervasive, conscious by nature, and self-knowing," the doctrine is established that [the Self] exists in conjunction with another substance as the substratum for knowledge, desire to act, and so forth, and that its agency arises from acting in cooperation with auxiliary factors.

Otherwise, even here, there would be the undesirable consequence of breaking the enumeration of the agent as one of the causes, since it is stated: "These five are its causes. The phrase "that person of evil intellect" is a restatement of what was already said; intending to avoid redundancy, he explains this by saying "one of perverted intellect. "One of unformed intellect" means one whose intellect has not been perfected through the scriptures of spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*); thus he says "unperfected."

"Whoever sees [the self] does not see it; he who does not see it, he truly sees"—because of this contradiction, even though vision exists, it is censured as being equivalent to non-existence due to its incorrect nature; with this intention, he says "not as it actually is. Since seeing things as they actually are is possible regarding external objects, he restricts [the censure] to the subject at hand by saying "the agent. One's own nature—that is, one's essential character—should not function toward things other than those to be attained through the scriptures.

The intention is that one should proceed by casting the bondage of karma—whether it arises from one's own nature or is encountered in unavoidable circumstances, as well as in relation to one's own body and its substrates—upon each according to its respective share. ||26||

When there arises the inquiry, "If such a state of affairs follows from the presence of evil-mindedness, who then is the one possessed of good-mindedness?", the purpose of contemplating this kind of non-agency is stated by the verse beginning with "yasya" (of whom). Here, the word *bhāva* means intention (*abhiprāya*), because it does not connect with any other meaning. And that [intention] is specified, both by the context and by its grammatical co-occurrence, as a particular mental modification (*manovṛtti*) whose object is agency.

Regarding the term *ahaṃkṛtaḥ*, although it has the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), since a particular modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*) cannot itself be the object of the conceit "I," what is intended here is merely its being rooted in that [conceit]. Thus he says: "produced by the conceit 'I'" (*ahaṃbhimānakṛta*). Here, either the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) is used as a metonym for the conceit "I," or else, in the expression *ahaṃkṛtaḥ*, the suffix *-kta* denotes the agent—as in the phrase "the Brāhmaṇas who have eaten. "Produced by the conceit 'I'" is the statement of the resulting meaning. Now, since the Self is the referent of the "I," how can there be the abandonment of the conceit "I"? To this he replies: "I do [this]."

This must be applied with a restrictive sense (*sāvadhāraṇam*), for otherwise there would be a contradiction with the state of being a direct knower (*sākṣātkartṛtva*). Thus, since the abandonment of agency is explicitly stated, the abandonment of attachment to the fruit is established by implication through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

He says "in this [state]" to indicate that the statement "whose intellect is not smeared" is being restated. To exclude the killing of others—which is prohibited by such injunctions as "not one who has not desisted from evil conduct"—he draws upon what is established at the beginning of the scripture and says, "even having killed in battle. The meaning is that he does not kill, because he is distinct from other killers who are fit for connection with the results of action due to possessing the defilement (adṛṣṭa) born of the conceit of killing; otherwise, there would be a contradiction in saying "even having killed, he does not kill."

As for what has been stated by others here—namely, "Because the Self lacks the status of being an agent of killing, it is said that it is not connected with its effect, the fruit of demerit"—that is incorrect, because of the inconsistency of the qualification [in the verse], "He whose state is not characterized by egoism" (BhG 18.17). For according to their own view, even another person who is ignorant lacks agency; and furthermore, they must admit that the taint of the fruit of action is illusory even in his case.

With the intention of stating that the question beginning with "How [could he kill] Bhīṣma? is answered by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument through the general statement "these worlds," the author says "not only" (*na kevalam*). Here, since a suitable alternative interpretation is possible, the explanation of the phrase "he does not kill" (*na hanti*) as "he is not bound" (*na nibadhyate*) is not appropriate.

Therefore, he says "tataḥ" (therefore), intending that since the two statements—"he whose state is not characterized by egoism" and "whose intellect is not tainted"—stand in the relation of cause and effect, their result is also described as being in the relation of cause and effect: "he does not slay, nor is he bound. By the phrase "is not bound," the intended meaning is the non-connection with results that are opposed to liberation, which is achievable through action; thus he says, "he does not experience that result."

By this, the alternative interpretation—namely, that "at the time of the action there is no ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), while at the time subsequent to the action there is the retrospective cognition (pratisaṃdhāna) 'it was done by me,' which constitutes the taint (lepa); thus, through both [negations], there is a prohibition of adverse consequences (pratyavāya) both in this world and the next, expressed as 'he does not kill' and 'he is not bound'"—is refuted. ||17||

Thus, the renunciation of the *sāttvika* type has been clarified. Now, for that purpose, the worthiness of *sattva*—which was previously and subsequently introduced in various ways through such passages as "ever established in *sattva*" (*nityasattvastha*)—must be clarified in its entirety. To the question of how the description of the methods of impelling to action (*karmacodanā-prakāra*) fits in the middle of this discussion, he says: "All this" (*sarvam*). The meaning is that the statement regarding the methods of impelling to action is intended to elaborate upon the threefold division of qualities (*guṇa*) in knowledge and other factors associated with that [action]. This refers to the subject matter of actions that ought to be performed, and so forth.

The meaning is that although the words *jñāna* (knowledge), *jñeya* (the object of knowledge), and *jñātṛ* (the knower) have general referents, they are intended here as specific [categories] because they serve the purpose of the threefold injunction of action (*karmacodanā*). By this, the interpretation that the word *jñāna* here refers to the scripture (*śāstra*) is refuted. To the question, "How can *jñāna* and the others, which are distinct in nature from an injunction (*codanā*) consisting of an impelling statement, be said to be varieties of injunction? he says: "connected with the knower, the known, and the act of knowing. The meaning is that by virtue of being merely adjuncts to an injunction, *jñāna* and the others possess a mode of being expressed by the word "injunction" (*vidhā-śabda-ukta-prakāratva*).

Thus, regarding the threefold collection of karma (*karmasaṃgraha*), there is a threefold nature by way of its essential form accompanied by two causes. To dispel the suspicion that another threefold classification of unmentioned objects might be stated, he says "therein" (*tatra*) to analyze one of the three. [He uses] the word "collection" (*saṃgraha*) in the sense of the object (*karman*).

He states the etymological derivation: "collecting" (*saṃgraha*). It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the collection itself is the action," or "the collection of the action. Here, by the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*), what is taught in such passages as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*)—namely, the performance of the ritual act—is intended. However, with the intention that the action itself functions as the instrument in relation to the result, he says: "the substance and so forth which have become the means" (*sādhanabhūtaṃ dravyādikaṃ*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of genus (*jāti*) and other categories is meant. Now, one might object: here, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is that very thing which is called the instrument.

If it is argued that it is logical that the triad beginning with knowledge (jñāna) alone is explained by the terms instrument, object, and agent, and that for this very reason the subsequent restatement—"knowledge, action, and the agent"—is coherent—this is not so. The reason is that there is no natural force (svārasya) in the words [of the original passage], and because there is no purpose in restating what has just been mentioned using different terms; rather, the meaning is that the intermediate subdivision already stated is useful for clear discernment (viveka).

He dispels the doubt that, because of its association with the agent and the instrument, the word "object" (*karman*) might also refer to a specific *kāraka* (case-role) by stating, "the object is [the sacrifice] and so forth. The sense is that the very nature of action (*kriyā*) is indeed analyzed as being threefold according to its subordinate aspects (*guṇataḥ*). He states, "the agent is the performer," meaning that while he was previously designated as being in the state of the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), he is now again designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being a subordinate element of the action in his state as a performer (*anuṣṭhātṛ*). ||18||

The very categories already mentioned as "knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower" are here restated as "knowledge, action, and the agent. Since the states of being a knower and an agent are merely different conditions [of the same entity], the knower is not mentioned separately here, as he is already established by the mention of knowledge; furthermore, the word "object" (*jñeya*) refers specifically to the sphere of action. As for the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is not treated separately because it is included within the scope of action.

Since there is no evidence for the intention to refer to the Sāṃkhya doctrine by the term "enumeration of qualities" (guṇasaṃkhyāna), and because such an enumeration would be irrelevant to the present context, and furthermore, since an enumeration of the nature of the qualities themselves would not include cognition and so forth, it is said to be an "enumeration of the effects of the qualities. Listen accordingly—this means "exercise the attention required for listening correctly. He states the intended manner of that "correctly" as "distinguished according to their qualities" (guṇataḥ). ||19||

The description of sattvic knowledge and so forth is intended to demonstrate that agency is dependent upon the *guṇas*. With the words beginning with "brāhmaṇe" (in the Brāhmaṇa), he describes the external diversity intended by the word "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*), as it is conceived by those who do not know the Self. Here, because the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the cognition occurring during the state of performing actions connected to the injunctions for the rites under discussion, the "beings" are specified as those who possess eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikārin*). In this context, the word "state" (*bhāva*) is a synonym for "category" (*padārtha*). The word "one" (*ekam*) is spoken with the intention of expressing unity of genus.

Because the plurality of selves has already been established, because the claim made by others—that the Advaita view is knowledge characterized by *sattva*—is baseless, because "diverse states" (*nānābhāvāḥ*) is stated immediately thereafter as a reference to plurality, because the detailed exposition of the contemplation of equality is recognized here [as that very point], and because of the word "agent" (*kartā*).

With the intention that [the term "Self"] is appropriately restricted to the inner Self (pratyagātman) and thus cannot refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman), he says, "called the Self. By the words "white and long," etc., there is an indication of such scriptural passages as, "The milk of cows of many colors is of one color," and so forth. Here, since the word "all beings" (sarvabhūta) includes the generic classes such as Brahminhood and the like, the meaning is that the word "divided" (vibhakta) refers to the further subdivisions of qualities and so on. To the question of in what form there is oneness, he says, "in the form of knowledge" (jñānākāravat).

He states the reason for the contingency of the expenditure that is being negated with the words, "even in those things whose nature is expenditure. He says, "and [that which is] unfit for attachment to results and so forth," because the previously mentioned absence of modification in the form of attachment to results and so forth is also subsumed by the word "expenditure" (vyaya), which is intended to mean "unchangeability. Here, "attachment" (saṅga) means connection; the meaning is "experience. Even if it refers to desire, "enjoyment" (bhoga) is established as its purpose. It is stated "at the time of eligibility for ritual action" because [the Self] has knowledge as its fruit, which is connected to the injunctions for ritual action.
The meaning is: "at the stage of deliberation, thinking 'this must be done by me'"; the meaning of "by which knowledge he sees" is that he makes it an object of cognition. ||20||

To avoid the charge of redundancy regarding words such as "separateness" (pṛthaktva) and so forth, he says: "by way of the separateness of forms such as the Brāhmaṇa and others. The phrase "in all beings" is a qualified reference (viśiṣṭānuvāda), while "the entities therein" is intended to extract the substantive (viśeṣya); with this in mind, he says: "even the entities called 'Self'. And by the word "separately," the meaning is "of various kinds" or "distinguished by separateness. This is intended to refer to the distinctions of genus, the distinctions of the substantive, and the distinctions of qualities and so forth.

There is no tautology among the terms *pṛthaktva*, *nānā*, and *pṛthagvidha*. The statement regarding their fitness for connection with results and so forth is intended to express their distinction from what was previously mentioned. The expression "he knows knowledge" (*jñānaṃ vetti*) is a metaphorical attribution of agency. ||21||

The word "kārya" (action/task) here does not refer to that which is merely a vessel for origination; rather, its cause is the propitiation of those whose powers were previously described as limited. With this intention, he says: "in a single task to be performed, such as the propitiation of hosts of spirits and the like, it yields very little fruit. Since even the mere performance of the nature of the action lacks fitness for association [with great results], and because there is a desire to speak of the fruit even in that case, he says: "like an action possessing complete fruit. This means: "like an action that serves as the cause for complete fruit."

Since it is impossible to negate merely the cause of knowledge or attachment which have already come into being as effects, he says "in reality" (vastutaḥ) to indicate that the cause of attachment for a discerning person is what is here prohibited. This remains true even if the reading is "causeless" (ahetukam).

This very meaning should be understood as intended to distinguish [this practice] from that which is based on mere reasoning (*haituka*). The phrase "just as before" means "like the worship of a king. Since the meagerness of the fruit is already established by the statement that it is "attached to a single effect and lacks a cause," the intention here is that the word "meager" (*alpa*) intends an inherent meagerness of its own nature—like the light of a firefly—and thus there is no tautology. Furthermore, it is stated that the fruit is "extremely meager" because it concerns the propitiation of beings such as ghosts (*preta*), and it is "meager" because it is limited in scope.

The previously stated phrase, "from sattva knowledge is born," is intended to show that rajasic and tāmasic forms of knowledge are actually ignorance (ajñāna). For it has been said: "This is declared to be knowledge; that which is otherwise than this is ignorance."

"By the Lord of the qualified [agent]" means by means of the contemplation of the nature of the qualified agent as characterized by non-distinction, distinction, and so forth, with respect to the ritual action (*karman*). This is a statement of the agent's dependence (*aṃśatva*) as a qualifier within the qualified ritual action.

Although the word "attachment" (*saṅga*), when analyzed, has a specific scope in teaching the abandonment of attachment to results and agency, nevertheless—in the phrase "free from attachment" (*saṅgarahita*)—because there is no restrictive factor and because it is required [by the context], it refers to a general object beyond the explicit mention of the desire for results. Thus he says: "free from attachment to agency and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*) is included. The quality of the agent mentioned in such passages as "one who is free from attachment and devoid of egoism" is here applied by way of that [agent] as a qualification of the action.

To the question, "How can an action performed out of attachment to fame and aversion to ill-repute be said to be done without attachment or aversion? he says: "Out of attachment to fame and aversion to ill-repute. By this, the repetition of the word *saṅga* (attachment) is avoided. Alternatively, it is stated that it was "not done" either because the negative particle *a-* is intended to be non-compounded, or because it is intended as a statement of the resulting implication. With the intention that this is for the purpose of negating what was previously stated in such passages as "and that penance which is done with hypocrisy," he says: "without hypocrisy. The phrase "only as a duty" is a reminder of the *sāttvika* renunciation. ||23||

By the phrase "desiring objects of desire" (*kāmepsu*), the opposite of what was stated by "not desiring results" (*aphalaprepsu*) is clarified; that is to say, "desiring results" (*phalaprepsu*). Here, the compound is formed with a genitive of general relation (*sambandhasāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*). Since alternatives and the like are impossible here, it is stated that the word *vā* has the sense of *ca* ("and"). Because it is dominated by *rajas*, which is characterized by activity, there is great exertion due to the mixing of useless effort; and in all such cases, the conceit of being oneself the cause is what is intended by the word "with egoism" (*sāhaṃkāra*).
With the intention that for this very reason [this path] involves great exertion and yet possesses its own purpose, he says: "This action involving much exertion was performed by me alone. (24)

Because the word *kṣaya* (destruction) intends to express the fault of the immediate expenditure of wealth, and because of the power of the prefix (*upa-*), the word *anubandha* (consequence) refers to the suffering that follows as a result of that; thus he says, "when an action has been performed. With the intention that violence may concern either oneself or another, there is the general statement therein: "affliction of living beings. He explains that human effort, which is the counterpart to destiny, consists in the convergence of the collection of visible causal factors related to the person, by saying: "the capacity of the self to complete an action."

Since the direct perception of future consequences and so forth is impossible, he says "is not reflected upon" (avimṛśyate) to mean that there is no investigation through reasoning or scripture. Because ignorance regarding the consequences and so forth has been mentioned separately, he says "regarding the Supreme Person" (paramapuruṣe) to indicate that the meaning of the word *moha* here is delusion which is the opposite of the knowledge of non-agency already under discussion. ||25||

By the phrase "one who does not speak of 'I'," attachment in the form of the conceit of agency is prohibited separately; therefore, he explains that in the expression "free from attachment" (*mukta-saṅga*), the word *saṅga* has a restricted scope, namely, "one who is devoid of attachment to the fruit. For that very reason, attachment in the form of identifying the action as one's own is also prohibited. [The opposite is] "one whose habit is to speak of 'I'."

One who speaks with "I" is a speaker of "I"; one other than that is a non-speaker of "I. With the intention that speech is preceded by the mind, he says [the agent is] "devoid of the conceit of agency. Since agency is being analyzed, he says "having commenced" to indicate the fortitude (dhṛti) required for it. Because the enthusiasm consisting of effort is already established by the word "agent" itself, and because it is common to agents characterized by passion (rājasa) and so forth, he expresses a specific distinction by saying "having an exerted mind."

Since the phrase "free from attachment" (*muktasaṅga*) has already stated the cessation of attachment to results such as heaven, the expression "unperturbed by success or failure" (*siddhyasiddhyornirvikāra*) indicates that its scope concerns visible results. Alternatively, being unperturbed is the fruit of being free from attachment. ||26||

By the phrase "desiring the fruit of action," the seeking of fruits such as heaven mentioned in the revealed scriptures (*ānuśravika*) is expressed; by "passionate" (*rāgī*), the author intends to express attachment to incidental fruits of this world (*aihika*); and by "seeking fame" (*yaśorthī*), he indicates the desire for renown. Since being free from unworthy recipients, wasteful expenditure, and so forth, constitutes a merit, the term is qualified by "in accordance with the requirements of the ritual. By the word "non-violent" (*ahiṃsātmaka*), the author intends to express a nature contrary to what has been stated in such passages as, "One may indeed obstruct oneself, one's wife, or one's sons, but never a servant or a laborer"; thus he says, "without having tormented others."

The statement "performing action with them for the sake of employing the agency" is a summary of the result; likewise, [the phrase] "devoid of the purity required for action" is also [a summary]. The sense is that the accomplishment of fitness for action does not arise merely through physical cleanliness, such as being fit for seeing, touching, and so forth.

Since [the status of] being a common person (*prākṛta*) and so forth is established by the absence of attentiveness and other factors, he states "in the scriptural" (*śāstrīye*) to indicate that by the word "unfit" (*ayukta*), what is intended is unworthiness. He states "situated in contrary duties" (*vikarmastha*) to indicate that here a degree of unworthiness greater than that indicated by the term "impure" (*aśuci*)—namely, the unfitness of the *rājasa* nature—is intended. For his unworthiness is indeed excessive in this way, as in: "Having touched Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Lokāyatikas, Nāstikas, twice-born men situated in contrary duties, or Śūdras, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. … Thus.

He explains that by the word *prākṛta* (ordinary/vulgar) is intended the absence of those specific qualities conducive to the performance of *sāttvika* actions arising from the study of the scriptures and the instruction on their meaning; thus he says, "one who has not acquired knowledge. Furthermore, he explains that here the meaning of the word *stabdha* (stiff/stolid) is a nature characterized by stillness, which is the opposite of initiating prompt and necessary salutations and the like even toward venerable persons; thus he says, "one whose habit is non-undertaking. And *śaṭhatvam* (roguishness) is the state of performing unpleasant acts in a concealed manner.

And because of the context, he states that this occurs "by way of the tamasic actions taught in the scriptures," namely, "having a taste for rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). To avoid redundancy, he further describes his deceitfulness by way of worldly actions such as trickery and deception, saying "intent on guile. "Tomorrow..."

According to the maxim, "One should do today what must be done tomorrow," one ought to be prompt regarding scriptural duties. The opposite of that is indolence (*ālasya*). Since the failure to begin [an action] has already been expressed by the word "stolid" (*stabdha*), the term "in those [duties] already begun" is used here. Regarding the word *viṣādī*, since the verbal root itself signifies despondency (*avasāda*), the prefix indicates its intensity, and the suffix expresses habitual disposition; thus he says, "one whose nature is excessive despondency. And this despondency was defined by the author of the *Vākya* as: "Despondency is the dejection of the mind, its lack of luster, born from the unfavorable conditions of place and time, and from the recollection of objects of grief and the like."

Because the state of karma that has begun but is not quickly completed—characterized by slow activity and so forth—is indicated by the word *alasa* (lazy), the term *dīrghasūtra* (long-threaded) specifies this through its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) and its association with words such as *śaṭha* (deceitful). One who performs rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is characterized by a habit of deliberating for a long time regarding the misfortunes to befall others. The verbal root is *sūtra* in the sense of "threading" (*sūtraṇe*). "Threading" means "deliberation"; the suffix denotes habituality (*tācchīlya*). Because of long deliberation, one is called *dīrghasūtrī*.

The sense is that the metaphorical designation "long-threaded" (dīrghasūtrī) is based on his similarity to one who makes long threads for the purpose of catching birds and the like that have committed no offense; however, [another] interpretation of the term is weak. ||28||

The threefold nature of knowledge has been stated; now, the threefold nature of the wise will be explained. To dispel the suspicion of redundancy due to synonymous repetition, he restates the previously mentioned subject as having a specific scope: "knowledge regarding the duties to be performed.
