With the intention of establishing the logical connection—that what is relevant to the present context is being introduced next—he says: "Now."

Regarding the doubt as to why the threefold nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), which was previously mentioned, is stated here again: [the author] says, "consisting of the ascertainment of all principles (*tattva*) and all human goals (*puruṣārtha*)," thereby stating that the meaning of the word *buddhi* here is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) produced by the scriptures and so forth—which occurs prior to that [determination] and serves as its cause—and is distinct from the contemplation of what is to be accomplished during the state of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-daśā*). By this, the view expressed by others—that "knowledge is a function (*vṛtti*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), whereas the intellect is the possessor of the function (*vṛttimat*)"—is refuted.

He clarifies that very point: "Intellect (buddhi) is knowledge in the form of a certainty preceded by discrimination. "Preceded by discrimination" means preceded by an inquiry that culminates in the rejection of alternative positions. He states the common characteristic of the threefold fortitude (dhṛti) useful for the three types of practice under discussion with the words "of that which has been undertaken. This too is simply a particular state of the nature of intellect, consisting of firmness in one's resolve and so forth.

Since the objects to be described are distinguished by their qualities and the words themselves possess unmixed natures, there is no tautology due to the connection [of the terms]. He states that the threefold distinction is expressed through the word "pṛthaktva" (separateness) in the phrase, "the threefold difference being declared as separateness. Likewise, because of the connection with the hearing of the word "aśeṣeṇa" (in its entirety), which refers to the completeness of effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, there is no tautology; this is shown in the instruction, "listen accordingly. The meaning of "listen" is to listen attentively, free from doubt and error.

The intention behind the vocative address is that, just as one conquers human and divine wealth during the conquest of the quarters, one must likewise conquer the wealth of tranquility (*śama*) and the other virtues. ||29||

In order to avoid the suspicion of redundancy with the terms *kārya* (what ought to be done) and *akārya* (what ought not to be done), he states—following the passage beginning with "thus," etc.—that the words *pravṛtti* (engagement) and *nivṛtti* (withdrawal) refer primarily to action (*karma*), by means of the phrase "serving as the means to prosperity," and so forth. This is because the rajasic and tamasic forms of intellect are qualified by the attributes "speaking what is untrue," and so on.

Here, the expression "as it truly is" (*yathāvasthitatva*) is used to indicate that the cessation [of those actions] is intended in its actual sense. By the words beginning with "of all castes" (*sarvavarṇānām*), he explains that the terms "what is to be done" (*kārya*) and "what is not to be done" (*akārya*) refer here to the visible and invisible operations consisting of the primary rites and their constituent procedures (*itikartavyatā*) under discussion. In that context, the qualification "in specific places, times, and conditions" is added so that this may be understood by those of subtle intellect. For it is recorded in tradition: "The body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and action..."

"Having examined [the case] with his intellect, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe penances," and so on, including "the place, the time, as well as himself," etc. Here, even the possible and the impossible are included by the very words "what ought to be done" (kārya) and "what ought not to be done" (akārya). Since the knowledge of the nature of fear and fearlessness is common to all, what is intended here is the knowledge of the causes thereof; and that, being specific to the context at hand, he states: "Transgression of the scriptures is a ground for fear. Fear is that from which one fears.

For those who know the truth, fear and fearlessness indeed stem from the Lord, the ruler of all; for without His impulsion, nothing can be obstructed or unobstructed by anyone. Therefore, the point is that compliance with and transgression of His command are themselves the causes of fear and fearlessness. Since the knowledge of the existence of bondage and liberation is common to all [schools], the term "reality" (*yāthātmya*) is specified [to qualify it]. By the word "reality," the doctrine that bondage is illusory and the view that liberation is a state like that of a stone are both excluded.
"He knows" is a metaphorical attribution of agency; the meaning is that he makes [the object] his own domain by his own free will. ||30||

Because the word *dharma* applies commonly to both the *pravṛtti* (active) and *nivṛtti* (restraining) types of duty through its etymological derivation as "that which effects steadfastness" (*dhṛti-sādhana*), and because both [types] would otherwise follow [as the meaning], it was stated that there are two kinds as previously mentioned. ||31||

By the phrase "consisting of *tamas*," the fact that it is rooted in *tamas* is established. By the phrase "obscured by *tamas*," he intends to express that its expansion is currently restrained by *tamas*, as he says: "being obscured by *tamas*. By the phrase "having all objects for its aim," he indicates the inclusion of everything—both what has been stated and what has not, whether in the form of established or yet-to-be-proved entities—as in the verse beginning with "whether an object exists or does not exist. By this, it is shown that the doctrine of those outside the Vedic fold (*bāhya*) and of those with wicked views (*kuddṛṣṭi*) is *tāmasa*. And it was said by Manu: "Those *smṛtis* which are outside the Vedas, and whatever [views] are based on wicked perspectives..."

"All those [actions] are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as having darkness as their ultimate end. Herein lies this distinction between the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* intellects: in the *rājasa*, there is incomplete perception and perception otherwise, according to the explanation that "one does not know things as they truly are"; whereas in the *tāmasa*, one considers everything to be the opposite, because of the statement that "one perceives all objects [perversely]."

Some others, however, say that "viśeṣa" (distinction) consists of the difference in the mode (*prakāra-anyathātva*) and the difference in the object of the mode (*prakārya-anyathātva*). Although in both cases it is a non-attribute (*atad-dharma*) that is superimposed upon the substratum (*dharmin*), nevertheless, when there is a reversal of the attributes that define its own nature, it is *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness); as, for example, the error of silver in mother-of-pearl. But when there is a reversal of the specific attributes that define its established form, it is *rājasa* (of the nature of passion); as, for example, the error of a yellow conch. ||32||

The yoga intended here is that which, though maintained by kings through the discourse on the three aims of life (*trivarga*), serves as a means to liberation (*apavarga*); and he states that this is indeed the yoga of exclusive devotion (*ananya-upāsana*) which was previously enjoined. Thus, [he says] "yoga."

The worship of the Blessed One is the means for liberation. Here, attachment to any other fruit constitutes deviation. He states that the restraint of yoga is by its very nature and by its result a form of great bliss; thus it is said that those who have set out with yoga as their goal are the means for its accomplishment. Mental activity is indeed a direct instrument, as is vital breath activity, because of their mutual embrace according to the principle: "Where the mind is, there is the breath; where the breath is, there is the mind."

As it is said: "Furthermore, having reached the path of the wind, the mind wanders like the wind. Likewise, through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), there is the conquest of the afflictions, sins, and so forth that are antagonistic to yoga. As for the non-activity of the external senses, it occurs either in the form of practicing the limbs of yoga at the time of rising, as expressed in such passages as: "One should practice self-study (*svādhyāya*) and sit in yoga; from yoga one should contemplate self-study. Through the perfection of self-study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed," or in the form of being restrained during the practice of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*). ||33||

In this context, the word *prasaṅga* does not mean "incidental," as that would be irrelevant. To show that steadfastness (*dhṛti*) has its own sphere of operation and to follow the method of the subject matter at hand, the words "dharma" and so forth are used to indicate the respective means [to those ends]. Furthermore, lest the word "fruit" (*phala*)—which is a general term—be restricted to the fruit of sattvic renunciation, namely liberation (*apavarga*), he says, "even here [in the phrase] 'one who desires fruit'. Explaining the intended figurative usage, he states the resulting meaning both verbally and substantially with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). ||34||

With the intention that the word "dream" (*svapna*) here also implies deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says "sleep" (*nidrā*). To exclude madness and other states brought about by fate, he shows that intoxication (*mada*) here has its root in evil deeds, saying "produced by the experience of sense-objects. Anticipating the doubt—how can a person maintain dreams and the like which are not under one's own control—he says, as before, that the definition of the cause applies here as well: "dream and intoxication are the objects [of the definition]. Thus, because dream and intoxication are the locus of the conceit of being a good person, they are explained separately from fear and the rest.

"Durmēdhāḥ" means one of dull intellect; the sense is "due to being dull-witted. With the intention of indicating that the very act of holding [the object] here implies that it must be relinquished, he says, "he does not let go, he holds fast. Nor should it be argued that steadfastness is contradictory for one who is afraid; for, by not looking toward what is to come, the dull-witted person remains intent on following the causes of that fear. An object that gives rise to fear is one characterized by intense opposition due to the impurity of false pride; that which gives rise to grief consists of the binding and killing rooted in anger and so forth; while that which gives rise to despondency consists of the useless expenditure of wealth and the like. ||35||

In order to establish the logical connection with the subsequent text, he clarifies what is indicated by the word "pūrvoktāḥ" (previously mentioned). The term "bharatarṣabha" (O bull among the Bharatas) is used here to indicate that [the recipient] is capable of attaining the most excellent happiness born of the *sattva* quality. The phrase "idānīm" (now) means that this is the occasion for the inquiry regarding the specific results (*sādhyabheda*) corresponding to the specific means (*sādhanabheda*) already described.

Because it lacks adventitious sweetness, the happiness of *sattva* depends upon practice (*abhyāsa*). Even in the world, there exists a low-grade pleasure that is acquired through habit; having taken that as a starting point, [the text] speaks of "supreme" [happiness] by way of gradual progression. "Delight" (*rati*) means extreme attachment. Since there is no word here to restrict the scope of the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*), it is stated to have a universal application. ||36||

With the intention of stating immediately the causal factors for [the fact that this happiness] depends on practice and is the cause for the end of suffering, he says, "He qualifies that very [happiness]" (*tadeva viśinaṣṭi*). Regarding the phrase "that which... (*yattad*): the relative pronoun *yat* followed by the demonstrative *tat* is used as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in order to highlight its well-known status from the Vedas and other sources. The expression "that happiness" (*tatsukham*) is an extension (*atideśa*) of the term "pleasure" (*prīti*). By the phrase "as if an object," he indicates that only a superficial aversion is intended; thus he says, "as if suffering" (*duḥkhamiva*). By this, it is shown that even those who are dull-witted regard it as something to be abandoned.

For there is no such thing as pleasure that does not transform like poison or like nectar; therefore, he speaks of it figuratively as "the manifestation of the nature of the isolated Self through the power of practice. Since merely stating that the intellect belongs to the Self would be fruitless, he says "having the Self as its object. With the intention that clarity (*prasāda*) is indeed the cessation of the turbidity consisting in the intellect's contact with unsuitable objects, he says "the state of having all other objects withdrawn."

Because it brings about the cessation of old age, death, and so forth, and because it cannot be abandoned due to its being the supreme object of experience, it is comparable to nectar (*amṛta*). Since the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Self—which is the sole essence of one's own nature when that nature has manifested as it truly is—is already included within this [state], it is not mentioned separately here. ||37||

The meaning is: "of objects," that is, of the respective sense-objects such as food and so forth. The phrase "when [the causes] of pleasure, such as hunger and the like, have ceased" is a statement of the cause of the opposition to the perceived pleasure of the *rājasa* type. As stated by Parāśara in the *Bhāgavata*: "Fire produces the state of being a source of pleasure through cold, water through thirst, and food through hunger; and the opposite is produced by their contraries. Likewise: "Pleasure is the subsiding of hunger and thirst, as well as the subsiding of cold and so forth."

"...for that too is indeed suffering, due to the foolishness of the intellect. Furthermore, by the phrase "like poison in its transformation," the fact that [sensual pleasure] results in suffering is indicated; this is for the purpose of excluding the mere state of being indifferent once the cause for perceiving it as pleasure has ceased. For pleasures such as those derived from adultery—which consist of momentary, inferior joys abounding in fear and other such factors—lead to extremely terrible and unsurpassed suffering occurring in the immediate future; thus, he describes their future toxicity by stating they are the cause of hell and other such states. (38)

"Anabudhyata" (he did not perceive) indicates that the consequence (*vipāka*) is non-comprehension. Since the word "mohana" (deluding) does not connect with the sense of a state (*bhāva*) here, he states its instrumental meaning as "the cause of delusion. Because the pleasure produced by sleep and the like lacks the quality of being a cause for erroneous cognition, it is stated here that "delusion" (*moha*) is the non-manifestation of an object as it truly exists. With the intention of explaining that it is well-known in the world that the ripening of *rājasa* pleasure causes delusion, whereas *tāmasa* pleasure causes it even at the time of its occurrence, he clarifies this by saying, "For sleep and the like... [nidrādayo hi...].

The meaning is that "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*) implies not being dependent upon reasoning or scriptural authority. To the objection that one observes merely the absence of activity in the case of a lazy person, rather than the absence of knowledge, he says: "Laziness is the dullness of the functioning of the senses. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the senses... For the gradation of the effect corresponds to the gradation of the functioning of the instruments (the senses). And the dullness of knowledge consists in its having a limited object-scope. The sense is that this [limited scope] is inherently characterized by the absence of the manifestation of other objects.

He states that negligence (*pramāda*) has the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is required [for its existence], by saying "consisting of non-attention to what is to be done. Thus, it is shown that both delusion (*moha*) and negligence are permeated by ignorance; as for how they are caused by it, he says "and therefore" (*tataśca*). For the dullness of cognition (*jñāna*) culminates, in due order, in absolute ignorance.

The state [of sleep] is a cause of happiness because it is a cause for the cessation of fatigue and so forth, and because of anger toward those who interrupt it, as is well known in the world. Furthermore, it serves to withdraw the operations of the senses by means of the cessation of bodily agitation and the like; and it serves to remove the exertion involved in the mental fabrication of one-pointedness of intellect through the removal of inattention. By this mention of the appearance of happiness, it is implied that sleeping at improper times and the like are not to be practiced. And they remember: "One who sleeps for two watches (six hours) is fit for the increase of *brahma*," and so forth. And the experts in Āyurveda say:

"And because of the excessive attachment [to it] at the wrong time, sleep when indulged in at such times would destroy both happiness and longevity like another night of universal destruction (kālarātri). With the words "Therefore" (ataḥ), he concludes the section on the classification according to qualities by means of the purpose which culminates in practical application. ||39||

The section on the effects of the *guṇas* is concluded by the verse beginning with "na tad asti" (18.46), by way of stating that the three *guṇas*—which have been described as consisting of all various experiences of fixed place, time, and fruit—are impossible to abandon entirely prior to liberation, which is characterized by attaining the Lord who consists of pure *sattva* transcending the natural *guṇas*. However, the section on the three *guṇas* itself is not concluded here, because immediately thereafter [in 18.47], it is stated: "by the *guṇas* arising from one's own nature."

The phrase "among the gods in heaven" (*divi deveṣu*) is an elliptical indication for those who hold authority over the highest regions of existence. Similarly, the phrase "on earth," and so forth, is intended to describe those who possess the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, such as humans and others. Following the passage beginning with "the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha," he states "among the Brahmins and others" to clarify the intended meaning of the plural number. The word "living beings" (*prāṇin*) is used to dispel the misconception that, due to the context of the *guṇas*, the word "space" (*kha*) might refer to a specific quality.

Even when they are determined as a collective form, the word "born" (jāta) is used with the intention that even there, no being exists apart from the qualities (guṇas). Alternatively, the word "born" may be taken separately to indicate that [the self] has been associated with the qualities from birth throughout the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).

Thus, the subjection of all transmigrating beings to the three *guṇas* has been stated. Now, the actions and other duties, which are distinguished by the scriptures according to the qualification of those entitled [to them]—who possess bodies characterized by varying degrees of those respective *guṇas*—are being analyzed. To show the connection with the supreme subject at hand, he demonstrates what was introduced at the beginning of the chapter with the words "by renunciation," and so forth. The meaning is that [renunciation] is not different from the meaning of the word *saṃnyāsa*; for even in the Śruti, both "by renunciation" (*tyāgena*) and "from the application of renunciation" (*saṃnyāsayogāt*) refer to the same subject matter.

"Of one who has become thus" means one who is endowed with the threefold renunciation. "Together with his livelihood" implies that agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth—which will be described later—are specific modes of subsistence; this is the sense. Here, the compound "Brāhmaṇa-Kṣatriya-Vaiśyas" is used because, being twice-born, they possess the qualification for the Vedas. The increase of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest in accordance with past actions has already been explained in detail. Therefore, it is shown here that action caused by those [qualities] is "nature" (*svabhāva*), insofar as it is the unique characteristic of persons in whom those respective qualities predominate.

By this, even the suspicion that the qualities (*guṇas*)—such as *sattva* and the rest—are subject to their own inherent nature rather than being adventitious (*aupādhika*), as suggested by the statement, "O Lord of the Earth, the qualities are under the control of karma," is refuted. The method of the differentiation of the qualities is elaborated upon in the *Brahma-purāṇa* and other texts; its summary is as follows: "Darkness (*tamas*) is in the *śūdra*, passion (*rajas*) in the *kṣatriya*, and the highest goodness (*sattva*) in the *brāhmaṇa*. Stating this meaning, he explains the subject at hand: "The quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*) is aroused by the suppression of passion and darkness.
This refers to the word "highest" (*uttama*) [in the verse], as in "passion in the *kṣatriya*" and so forth.

He states the positive concomitance (anvaya) as well with the words "of the Kṣatriya," and so forth. The term "neither deficient nor excessive" is used for the purpose of distinguishing [the Vaiśya] from the Śūdra. Since even the qualities (guṇas) that transcend the senses have their classification dependent upon the scripture, and because it is impossible for the qualities to be the agents in the classification of duties, the phrase "together with the qualities" was stated. Because they are classified by the scripture in relation to the qualities, [they are called] "qualities."

Since the differentiation of essential natures does not depend upon scripture, he says "they have been explained" with the intention that what is intended is their distinct cognition. He explains the explanation by way of differentiation with the words "the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. With the intention that the word "action" (karman) itself includes the livelihood (vṛtti) as well—either because the livelihood exists for the sake of that action or because it is implied by it—he says "and the livelihoods. The meaning is "means of subsistence."

The re-explanation of virtues such as *śama* (tranquility) and *dama* (self-restraint), though already explained previously, is for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding any internal distinctions that might arise from their prescription in connection with specific castes (*varṇa*), and to demonstrate that they are to be accomplished through human effort in the form of self-restraint and so forth, thereby establishing their status as "actions" (*karman*) as stated in the phrase "the action of a Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, it should be understood that the cultivation of these qualities applies to purity (*śauca*) and other such duties as well. One who possesses faith (*mati*) is an *āstika*; the state of being such is *āstikya*. And that [faith] is not [based on mere] authority...

In what cases would this lead to error? It does not constitute such an excellence regarding objects established by perception and other means of knowledge. Even regarding scriptural matters, there is the possibility of it being a "wrong view" (kudṛṣṭi) in instances such as doubt. Therefore, it was stated [in the previous verse] that "the entire Vedic meaning" [is the object]. The statement that the ascertainment of truth is "preeminent" is intended to indicate the distinction between this and the "knowledge" (vijñāna) and so forth mentioned alongside it. He explains this with the words "by anyone," etc. The phrase "of the entire Vedic [meaning]" was stated in order to exclude the collection of Vedic meanings as accepted by those of wrong views and the like; [this is done] by summarizing them according to their primary importance.

[The author] clarifies this with the words beginning "The Blessed Lord... and so forth. Since the qualifiers have already been explained previously, they are not [further] engaged here... [omitted]. Following the sequence of the meanings already stated—namely, that [the Lord] is "to be known through all the Vedas and Vedāntas"—this is the sequence for extracting the scattered statements. He concludes the meaning of the verse with the words "That is this... The term *brāhma* refers to the ritual action (*karman*) of a Brāhmaṇa; with the intention that the word *brāhma* here refers to the Brāhmaṇa caste (*jāti*), he says "of the Brāhmaṇa. (42)

With the intention that the word *śūra* (hero) is used as the antonym of *bhīru* (coward)—as in the expressions “a hero,” “a coward,” “a sage,” or “an idiot”—he says: “the capacity for entering without fear. This [capacity] is a combination of mental and physical [factors]. He says: “not being overcome by others,” because if one who has entered were to be defeated by enemies, even the entry itself would be a fault; therefore, *tejas* (splendor) is mentioned here to avoid that. The distinction between *dākṣya* (dexterity) and *dhṛti* (fortitude) is shown to be this: [fortitude is] the non-abandonment of what has been undertaken even when obstacles arise. It is distinct from mere physical capacity for action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*).

Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in battle," he states that it indicates the cause for the attainment of the fruit [of the Lord's grace], namely: "even when there is certainty of one's own death. With the intention that by the term "Lordly nature" (*īśvarabhāva*) what is intended is the power to restrain the wicked and to favor the virtuous, he says: "in those other than himself. The phrase "in persons who have attained their fruit" refers to the domain delimited by his own kingdom and so forth.

Following both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he shows that agriculture (*kṛṣi*) consists of cultivation (*karṣaṇa*) for the purpose of producing crops, both in terms of its result and its essential nature. This same principle should be understood in the explanation of trade (*vāṇijya*) as well. With the intention that "that work in which cattle are to be protected is *gokṣya*," he says "cattle-rearing" (*paśupālana*). Alternatively, *rakṣyam* may signify the abstract state of being protected; thus, it means "the act of protecting. Or, there is the reading *gaurakṣyam*. One who protects cattle is a *gorakṣu*; his work is *gaurakṣyam*, namely, cattle-rearing.

Just as the work of a merchant (*vaṇij*) is called *vāṇijya*, so too the work of a *viś* is *vaiśya*; the suffix *vyañ* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *vyañ* is added after words expressing qualities, such as *brāhmaṇa*, etc., in the sense of their work.

According to another scripture, he states that service is connected to the three preceding classes: "Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa has six duties; the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya have three duties each. As for the Śūdra, [it is said]: 'One who finds delight in his wife, is pure, maintains his dependents, and is devoted to the performance of Śrāddha rites—by means of the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*), he shall perform the five sacrifices...'"

"He should not neglect [them]," and so forth—thus various duties (dharma) are enjoined. To the question, "How then is there such a limited enumeration of those actions here?", he says: "This very... He provides examples of those to be demonstrated, saying: "For sacrifices and so forth... He states another reason for their being illustrative examples, saying: "Peaceful dispositions (śama) and so forth also... As to how peaceful dispositions and the like—which are common to all three castes seeking liberation—are stated here as belonging to the Brāhmaṇa alone, he says: "But for the Brāhmaṇa..."

Regarding the phrase "arising from one's own nature" (*svabhāvaprabhava*), because it follows what was stated previously, the intention here is that the word "born of nature" (*svabhāvaja*) is used with the desire to express its innate character; thus he says, "Since the predominance of *sattva* is natural, tranquility, self-control, and so forth are the means for attaining happiness. The connection is: "That is their function," which has not been explicitly stated. In order to illustrate the functions already mentioned, he analyzes the fourfold division of those functions and distinguishes them, beginning with the words "the function of a Brāhmaṇa," and so on.

The duty and livelihood of a Śūdra are recorded by Yājñavalkya: "The service of the twice-born is the [duty] of a Śūdra; living by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "Service to Brāhmaṇas alone is declared to be the most distinguished duty of a Śūdra. With this in mind, [the author] says: "But the duty and livelihood of a Śūdra consist solely in the service of the three preceding castes."

Is this not already stated? For it has been said, beginning with "delight in one's wife," and the Lord Himself has declared: "For by taking refuge in Me, O Pārtha, even women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras attain the supreme goal. Furthermore, initiation for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One is prescribed, beginning with "One should initiate a Brahmin in spring," continuing through "and a Śūdra in winter, and a woman in the rainy season, according to the ritual of the Pañcarātra."

Likewise, it is clearly stated that even for Śūdras and others who have undergone initiation (*dīkṣā*), the worship of the Lord and so forth is permitted: "He [the Lord] is to be worshipped and served by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have received the marks [of initiation] and are constantly engaged in their own duties, according to the Sāttvata rule which was sung by Saṃkarṣaṇa. Similarly, introducing the characteristics of the ages (*yugadharma*), it is said: "In former times there was an age called Kṛta, wherein the eternal Dharma existed; in that time, O best of men, nothing remained to be done."

In the Kṛta Yuga, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were characterized by their respective marks; they were always devoted to their own duties. United with a single Veda, they performed rituals according to a single mantra and procedure. Though their specific duties varied, they followed one Dharma through the single Veda and remained devoted to that one Dharma. Through action conjoined with the four stages of life (āśramas) and adapted to the time, and because they were not attached to the fruits of their actions, they attained the supreme goal. Furthermore, for those yogins who were devoted to the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), whose minds were absorbed in the fire-sacrifice within the heart, there was but one qualification.
The qualification for the single Heart-Space (*hṛdayākāśa*) belongs to those yogins who have been liberated from the mixed scriptures and whose souls are devoted to the *Hṛdaya* sacrifice.

For Brahmins who follow the Vedas and have been liberated from the mixed scriptures, the qualification is for the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) together with the mantra, and not otherwise. For the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas, as well as for those who have truly surrendered, the qualification is for the sequence of the fourfold manifestation without mantra. However, for the discerning, there is qualification for the powerful wheel of mantras (*mantracakra*) that is accompanied by ritual action.

For those who have completely cast off the sense of "mine," whose souls are devoted to their own duties, and who are perfectly devoted to the Supreme Lord through action, speech, and mind—only for these four is there indeed eligibility when [the office] is chosen.

Thus, the specific rule regarding eligibility has been established. And in the seventh chapter, concerning the injunction for vows (*vratavidhāna*), it is said: "In the case of Śūdras, however, gifts and worship are always [permitted], as well as the performance of vows; but uncooked food is prescribed, or else [food] obtained through the grace of a Brāhmaṇa. One attains excellence through one's own duty, and likewise through worship. Therefore, one should always perform propitiation according to one's own eligibility. A Brāhmaṇa is authorized in all matters of worship, such as that of Vāsudeva and others, just as..."

Likewise, the Kṣatriyas and others do not [perform it]; therefore, one should practice what is declared in the scriptures. "O Maudgala, one should pass these days with devotion through eating only at night; however, at the beginning and end of the vow, the drinking of *paripīḍa* is indeed prescribed for him. Thus, the sequence for specific vows is established; for those concluding with *vauṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, or *vaṣaṭ*, the prescribed counter-measure is performed with a salutation (*namaskāra*).

Likewise, in the *Nāradīya* [Purāṇa], in the *Śrīmadaṣṭākṣarakalpa*, it is stated: "Neither the vowel *praṇava* (Om), nor the limbs (*aṅga*), nor other such methods are required; for women and those of the Śūdra caste, the mere recitation of the mantra is prescribed. Similarly, observances such as the *ekādaśī-vrata* and others are taught in the Purāṇas and other texts as being common to all. Likewise, many other rules regarding what is to be avoided and what is not are recounted in the *Dharmaśāstras* and other works. For example: "By drinking the milk of a brown cow (*kapilā*) and by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman... [and so forth].

"For a Śūdra, no expiation is prescribed by means of Vedic syllables. However, the twice-born may be purified by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that has merely touched the lips once. For them, the same rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies, with the additional requirement of shaving the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails every day, and so forth.

Therefore, passages such as, "Recitation [of mantras], austerity, pilgrimage to sacred sites, renunciation, the practice of mantras, and the propitiation of deities—these six lead to the downfall of women and Śūdras," should be understood as referring to matters that conflict with the service of the three higher castes, which is otherwise enjoined. Furthermore, because of statements such as, "Śūdras who are devotees of the Lord are remembered as Bhāgavatas, equal to Brahmins," and because texts like the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* declare the equality of the four castes in their status as Bhāgavatas, it is even possible for a Śūdra to cease the service of the three higher castes by virtue of his exclusive service to the Lord. Thus, what indeed remains to be done by a Śūdra?

And it has been stated that "service consists precisely in the attendance upon the three [higher] castes"?—to this we reply: although all prohibitions have as their object those things distinct from what is enjoined, and although specific duties are indeed prescribed even for Śūdras who possess particular refinements, qualities, and distinctions, nevertheless, all of these must be performed by those Śūdras appointed to them with the sole intention of service, provided they do not conflict with the primary duties defined by the exclusion of the three castes. For this very reason it is said here that "the work consists of service"; otherwise, one would have to say simply "service."

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to accept more than what is necessary for the purpose at hand. Those who know the secret traditions (rahasyāmnāya) declare: "The Brāhmaṇa has the function of knowing, making known, and directing; the Kṣatriya has the function of protecting through knowledge; the Vaiśya has the function of cultivating the seeds of knowledge; and the Śūdra has the function of serving as the basis for knowledge. At the end of the Kṛta Yuga and the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras become divided. Once they are divided, their vision is no longer as it was, nor are their palates as they were."

The flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and forest trees did not provide [sustenance] as before. Seeing this, envy arose among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. The Śūdra, the first-born caste, said, "I will no longer rise up for you"; the Vaiśya, the second-born caste, said, "I will no longer cultivate your seeds"; the Kṣatriya, the third-born caste, said, "I will no longer protect you. To them, the Brāhmaṇa said, "You have all settled down; I will not speak to you. In this context, *paryutthāna* means service (*paricaryā*).

Thus, the objection that praise such as "the Śūdra is a devotee of the Blessed One" might lead to the conclusion that he should cease from serving the three higher castes is also refuted, because the injunction for rising to greet [a superior] applies specifically to a Śūdra who is exclusively devoted to the Blessed One. Indeed, it is precisely because these statements are intended as praise for devotion to the Blessed One that there is the following negative censure: "Among all castes, those people are Śūdras who are not devoted to Janārdana. What, then, is the basis for this praise and censure? It is the internal manifestation of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest.

In relation to which [the state of being a Brahmin] alone is proclaimed as "Brahmin-hood" and so forth in the Śrutis and other texts, such as: "Having fully realized both non-mauna and mauna, one then becomes a Brāhmaṇa"; and "The seer of reality, the wise man who knows Vāsudeva as the pervader (Viṣṇu), attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa; even a Caṇḍāla established in right conduct—the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa," and so on. As for those properties, however, which are dependent upon the gradations of qualities such as the body and the *sattva*, they [are different].

Thus they remain established. For this very reason, even Vidura—who was well-versed in the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa*—declared his own lack of authority regarding that discourse, saying: "I am born from a *śūdra* womb; therefore, I do not venture to say anything more than this. However, in the case of a *śūdra* or similar person who possesses an abundance of qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and who is endowed with the nature of a *rājarṣi*, there is a prohibition against considering their commonality of birth, based on the expectation of a specific distinction such as the cessation of contempt and the like. As they record in the traditional texts (*smṛti*): "Even a *śūdra*, when endowed with these [qualities]..."

"One deserves honor in old age. For this very reason, [it is said]: "That devotion which is eightfold—even if it exists in a barbarian (mleccha), it should be given to him, received from him, and he should be worshipped just as I am. This and other such statements have been fully established even by means of the *anuloma* method. Furthermore, the statement regarding equality refers to equality in terms of the fruit of supreme excellence and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction with the principle that Śūdras are not eligible for [Vedic] study (*apaśūdra-naya*) and similar rules. As the Teachers have stated: "By virtue of being a Bhāgavata, a Śūdra..."

"Even for a Brāhmaṇa, there is a 'karṣa' [of land] due to his own [status], yet there is again an inequality because of the 'karṣa' [of the Śūdra]; thus everything is consistent. Therefore, it is well said that there is identity between the livelihood and the duty of the Śūdra."

Regarding the question of what purpose there is in the *Mokṣa-śāstra* for the classification of the duties of the various castes (*varṇa-dharma*), he says: "In their respective duties" (*sve sve karmaṇi*). Here, that the word *saṃsiddhi* has as its object the attainment of the supreme state (*paramapada*) is established by the context; for he will later say, "the eternal, immutable state. Alternatively, the word *siddhi* refers to what he will later call "the perfection of renunciation" (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*).

This is the subject matter. The mention of the "supreme goal" (*paramaprāpya*) here is intended to indicate that this is the ultimate end of that [practice]. Now, one might ask: how can even a Śūdra, who is devoted solely to his own duties (*svakarma*), attain the supreme state? For it has been established in the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtra) under the section concerning the Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*) that he lacks qualification for the knowledge (*vidyā*) which is the means to liberation. True; however, there is no contradiction, because what is intended is the attainment of the supreme state through a gradual succession by way of an intermediate qualification. This applies to those like Vidura and others who, being "rememberers of their births" (*jātismara*), reconnect with the supreme knowledge commenced in a previous life.

It should be understood that by performing one's own duties, one avoids the transgression caused by their non-performance and thereby attains direct fitness for perfection (*saṃsiddhi*). As the venerable Śaunaka has said: "Even Dharma, Vyādha, and others, though born into despised castes due to their previous habits, attained perfection, just like the female ascetic (Śramaṇī). Now, an objection may be raised: how can the various duties of the specific castes and stages of life—which consist of propitiating Indra and other deities capable of bestowing only limited fruits—be the cause for attaining the supreme state? To this, the answer is: "One who is devoted to his own duty... [The full verse continues: "He attains perfection. This means that even those whose duties yield limited results lead to the supreme goal when performed with the understanding that they are merely steps toward the ultimate end. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is stated: "Even those who perform actions for the sake of worldly enjoyment, if they do so without attachment, having abandoned the desire for rewards, reach the supreme goal through the very same path. Therefore, all duties prescribed for the four castes and four stages of life are indeed causes for attaining the supreme state. For this reason, the Lord says: "Better is one's own duty, though imperfectly performed, than the duty of another well-performed. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is fraught with danger. By this, he shows that one should not abandon one's own duty out of fear of imperfection and take up the duty of another. One should rather strive to perfect one's own duty through practice. As it is said: "Through practice one becomes proficient in one's own duty; through proficiency one attains perfection. It is also said: "Even a man of low birth, if he performs his own duty, attains the highest state; but one who abandons his own duty and follows another is lost. Therefore, one should never abandon one's own duty. As it is said: "Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit, than the duty of another well-performed. Death in one's own duty is preferable; the duty of another is dangerous. This is the meaning. Thus, because it is a reference back to what was previously stated, the word "tat" (that) refers to the manner [of the preceding]; hence he says, "Listen likewise.

It is stated by the verse beginning with "From which proceeds activity" (*yataḥ pravṛttiḥ*) that the Supreme Self—who is the cause of all and the inner controller of all—is recorded in the scriptures by words denoting Indra and others who are His own created bodies; therefore, since they are for the sake of propitiating Him, it is logical that the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) are the means for attaining perfection. Furthermore, the word "activity" (*pravṛtti*) here refers to mere exertion.

To exclude [the notion of] "otherness," he says "in the production and so forth. The sense is that the word *pravṛtti* (activity), here conjoined with the word *bhūta* (being) which denotes both sentient and insentient things, encompasses all types of operation because there is no specific qualification [to the contrary]. That form by which all this is pervaded (*tata*) is stated as being suitable for [serving as] every kind of cause. It is "pervaded" (*tata*) by way of being the controller—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the doubt as to how that which was indicated in the third person as "it" (*tam*) can be explained as "me" (*mām*), [the answer is that] it is because of the attainment of the restatement "from whom" (*yataḥ*).

For this purpose, he causes one to remember the prior statement, "from Me alone. The statements regarding being the cause, being superior to all, being all-pervasive, being the controller of all, and so forth, are to be applied according to their respective possibilities.

Thus, the fact that the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) must not be abandoned in their essential form, as well as the manner in which they serve as means for attaining the Supreme, has been shown. Now, it is reaffirmed—by the words beginning with "Better is one's own duty" (śreyān svadharmaḥ)—that even those who are qualified for the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga), and whose duties are included within the yoga of action (karmayoga) through their connection with the primary duties mentioned in such passages as "Others offer sacrifice as the divine" (daivam evāpare yajñam), and through their connection with specific observances (niyama), must likewise not abandon these very duties.

In this context, the term *svadharma* does not refer to duties restricted to specific castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), for if that were the case, it would follow that the term *paradharma* would include the duties of other castes and so forth. That, however, is not tenable; since such [other-caste] duties are prohibited and thus constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*), it would be improper to speak of *svadharma* as being superior to them by virtue of its excellence. For indeed, it could never be said that merit (*puṇya*) is superior to sin (*pāpa*).

If it is argued that this is a prohibition of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), which is a duty of a Brāhmaṇa as stated in the verse, "It is better to eat alms," we say no; for if that [renunciation] has already been attained, a prohibition is illogical, and if it has not been attained, the answer has already been given—that it would simply result in sin. Furthermore, in times of distress, the immediately following mode of life is difficult to abandon. Therefore, in this context, the terms *svadharma* (one's own duty) and *paradharma* (the duty of another) refer to these two stages of life.

As before, the objects of *karmayoga* and *jñānayoga* have been explained. From the words "in this way" (*evam*) up to "one's own duty" (*svadharmaḥ*), there is a single sentence; otherwise, there would be the consequence of a lack of connection with the subsequent text. He says "by one's own" (*svenaiva*) in order to exclude the intention that the word "own" (*sva*) refers to caste (*jāti*). He explains what was stated—that it is fit to be undertaken by one's own nature—by saying "by one's own nature" (*prakṛti*). He states that the word "deficient in qualities" (*viguṇa*) has the sense of being something to be abandoned, even if it is deficient in qualities, by saying "even though deficient. This is because, due to the absence of any other alternative, it is of a secondary or inferior kind.

The meaning is that even [the former] is not approved. Here, "another" (*para*) refers to one distinct from the one fit for *karmayoga* who was designated by the word "self" (*sva*); and with the intention that he is fit for *jñānayoga*, he says, "the senses being the master" (*indriyajyeṣṭhe*). To the question, "How can there be proper performance for one who is prone to negligence? he says, "sometimes" (*kadācit*).

To dispel the doubt that "determined by nature" (*svabhāvaniyatam*) implies a restriction based on caste (*jāti*), he says, "that very same" (*tadeva*). The sense is that just as for creatures born from the viṣa-tree, the nimba-tree, the tintriṇī-plant, and so forth, their food is determined by their own nature. The word *kilbiṣa* (sin) is used here to indicate the state of being most undesirable, and by the word *saṃsāra* (transmigration), it is shown to culminate in its fruit.

This has been explained. Alternatively, he says "jñānayoge" with the intention of either negating what is possible for one established in the yoga of knowledge, or with the view that a specific negation is intended to permit the remainder.

It is said that [the author] recalls what was stated in the third chapter in order to dispel the suspicion that [this passage] has a different meaning, with the intention of expressing an excess of reverence, and to avoid the charge of redundancy. "By virtue of being innate" means because it is determined by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). To the question, "How then is there an absence of the need for renunciation? he says, "It is easy. It is not appropriate to intend by the word *doṣa* (fault) "sin" (*pāpa*), because that is impossible in the case of what is enjoined. And thus, the statement "one should not abandon it" would be inappropriate, since the sinful portion must be abandoned by everyone.

Therefore, it is said here that "being flawed" consists in consisting merely of bodily suffering and the like; with the intention that those who are indolent might develop the notion of its abandonability even on account of that much, he says, "even though it is painful.

By this, an alternative interpretation—that the statement "even though it is flawed" is a restatement (anuvāda) made while following the system of the Sāṃkhya—is refuted. [An objection: How can one desiring liberation have the notion of abandonability toward what is declared in scripture to be the highest good, simply because of an inability to endure minor sufferings? Since there is thus no occasion for such a prohibition, it would not be logical. To this he replies: "even though he is fit for the yoga of knowledge. Even— *Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence ("Even"), indicating the source may be incomplete.*

The word "anyasya" (of another) is for the purpose of indicating by way of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so") that one might engage in [worldly activity] without considering one's own specific qualification (*svādhikāra*), even when seeing an effortless means [to happiness]; therefore, it is restricted [by the scripture].

A restriction has been stated [in the previous verse] regarding the inequality characterized by being with suffering or without suffering, as well as regarding non-negligence and so forth; now, it is said in this half-verse beginning with "sarvārambhā hi" that even being with suffering is common to both. By the phrase "undertakings of action and undertakings of knowledge," he indicates that the word "all" (*sarva*) here refers to the totality of things pertaining to the subject matter of the present scripture. Suffering...

Since both [action and knowledge] are equal [in their difficulty], what is the point of restricting oneself to only one? And how is it that the former (action) is the cause for the latter (knowledge)? To this he says: "To such an extent" (*iyān*). The meaning is this: in the undertaking of actions, there is merely physical exhaustion; however, in the undertaking of knowledge, even though it is very near [to the goal], the effort required to restrain the senses and the mind through the search for the inner object—which is like searching for a clod of earth at the elbow—is of the nature of suffering.

Although it has already been stated that "his intellect is free from all fear," the phrase "free from longing" (*vigata-spṛhaḥ*) is used again because it is appropriate that it refers to the renunciation of agency—which is recited alongside the renunciation consisting in the cessation of attachment to results—and because it intends to express the pinnacle of renunciation, which consists in the cessation of attachment to the mental association of agency even with respect to one's own self in activities such as eating. Thus he says: "free from longing for the agency of the Self. Furthermore, the statement "he attains [it] through renunciation" does not refer to the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) and so forth, because that would not connect with the subject under discussion, namely, "one should not abandon action."

With the intention that [this chapter] is appropriately concerned with the renunciation mentioned at the beginning of the discourse, he says: "Thus, by means of the determination of its non-difference from renunciation. Here, the term *naiṣkarmyasiddhi* does not refer to liberation (*mokṣa*), because attainment is enjoined again later through the words "having attained perfection" (*siddhiṃ prāpta*); nor does it refer merely to the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), because of the qualification "supreme" (*paramām*); and since the intended meaning can be conveyed by the word *naiṣkarmya* alone, he says with the intention that what is intended here is the commencement of the attainment of the fruit of steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*).

Regarding the phrase "the supreme culmination of meditation" (*paramāṃ dhyānaniṣṭhām*): he explains that this is established either by the force of the compound or by the power of the qualification "supreme," as being established for one who is "free from action" (*naiṣkarmya*). He clarifies that it is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) as well. He states that the purpose of what has been said accords with the subsequent text by saying "the attainment of the yoga of meditation to be described hereafter," and so forth. He elucidates the etymology of *naiṣkarmya*—as one whose actions have departed (*nirgata-karma*), thus "niṣkarmā," and the state thereof (*bhāva*)—by describing it as "consisting in the cessation of the activities of all the senses."

He states that the phrase "having attained perfection" (*siddhim prāptaḥ*) is a restatement of what has been said, by providing a detailed explanation of the means and the reason [for its attainment] in the words "until departure" (*āprayāṇāt*). Since this refers to the attainment of Brahman for one who has already attained perfection, the term "perfection through meditation" (*dhyānasiddhim*) is used to indicate that the subject matter is distinct from that [attainment]. Following the subsequent text of the word "how" (*yathā*), he explains that it concerns the manner in which the goal is reached through human effort, saying "in whatever manner one exists. "Listen to me" (*me nibodha*) means "understand with certainty from me. [This leads to] the supreme fruit.

Generally, [the practice] culminates there; therefore, with the intention that this very state is called "completion" (niṣṭhā) because it is the ground where the means reach their ultimate limit, he says: "that very Brahman is specified.
By the word "knowledge" (jñāna), he indicates its rest in the meditation (dhyāna) which is about to be mentioned immediately hereafter, as in the phrase "consisting of meditation" (dhyānātmaka).

Here, the word *buddhi* refers to the cognitive faculty directed toward the object intended by the aforementioned word *brāhmī*; its purity (*śuddhi*) consists in being free from defects such as incomplete apprehension of the object, doubt, and error—this he expresses by the phrase "with respect to the reality of the Self as it truly exists. By the word *dhṛti*, he refers back to the previously mentioned *sāttvikī* fortitude of the kind already described, using the expression "by turning away from sense objects. In this context, the action of restraining the mind through *dhṛti* is stated; furthermore, for one who has already renounced sense objects, passion and hatred [are absent].

The phrase "having cast aside" (*vyudasya*) is used to indicate that even the temporary casting aside of attachment and aversion toward sense-objects is intended; furthermore, he says "caused by those" (*tannimittāḥ*) to avoid redundancy with the statement "having fully resorted to dispassion" (*vairāgyaṃ samupāśritaḥ*). By this, the result of the non-proximity of objects is demonstrated. Alternatively, the sense is that even subtle attachment toward remote objects must be restrained. "Secluded" (*vivikta*) means being devoid [of distractions]; he qualifies this for the sake of the present context as "in a place secluded from all things that are contrary to yoga. "Eating light" (*laghvāśī*).

By this, he states that the previously mentioned passage beginning with "not for one who eats too much" is being recalled, saying: "free from overeating and fasting. To avoid redundancy with the phrase "having restrained speech, body, and mind" (via the passage beginning with "having restrained the self by fortitude"), he says: "one whose functions of body, speech, and mind have been directed toward meditation.

Directing the function of the body consists in adopting a steady posture and so forth; of speech, the avoidance of anything other than the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om) and the like; and of the mind, the taking of a virtuous object as its support.

He states that those [qualities] mentioned are supplementary to the yoga of meditation with the words, "being thus. He explains what is intended by the word "constantly" with the phrase, "day after day until death. Because he speaks of the removal of passion and hatred (*rāga-dveṣa*) as referring to passion and hatred directed toward sense objects, the expression "having fully resorted to dispassion" (*vairāgyaṃ samupāśritaḥ*) refers to the domain of pride (*ābhimānika*). In that context, "proper resorting" means the correct stabilization of the tranquility already previously established; with this intention, he says "increasing his state of detachment" (*virāgatāṃ vardhayan*). The same should be understood regarding the liberation from egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth.

The term "force of latent impressions" (*vāsanā-bala*) is specified because the forces of the body, mind, vital breath, and so forth do not constitute obstacles to yoga. Here, "arrogance" (*darpa*) refers to the assertion of self-importance caused by the power of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Even arrogance arising from being a yogi or from tranquility (*śāntatva*) must be abandoned, for it is remembered in the Smṛti: "The arrogant one transgresses dharma."

Because the cessation of the activities of mind, speech, and body has already been mentioned, he says "whose sole happiness is the experience of the Self" to indicate that the word *śānta* (peaceful) here refers to a specific cause of tranquility. The cessation of sensory activity and the subsiding of anger and other passions result from being free from desire for external pleasures; and that [freedom] arises from the attainment of abundant internal bliss—this is the sense.

He states that among all those mentioned, the practice of meditation (*dhyānayoga*) is the primary factor by saying, "thus becoming, performing the practice of meditation. Here, *yoga* is meditation itself, or rather, union through meditation.

By reflecting on the meaning of the intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*), he states that the word *brāhma* here refers to the pure Self (*śuddhātman*) in the verse beginning with "sarvabandhe. Thus, by the verse "brāhmabhūtaḥ," it is stated that the experience of the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is to be accomplished through *karmayoga* and other means, serves as the basis for the qualification for supreme devotion (*parabhakti*). With that intention, the manifestation of the state of being solely subservient to the Supreme is also mentioned. Here, the state of being *brāhma*—known as *brāhmatva*—is that which is to be accomplished through yoga.

It is with this intention that there is the statement regarding the manifestation of uninterrupted knowledge. Since it has already been stated that the nature of being a subordinate (śeṣatva) is an essential concomitant of one's true being, he says, "But from this [state], another... He says, "with a tranquil self," because this refers to the cessation of the unfitness for supreme devotion previously mentioned in such passages as, "Madhusūdana finds no footing in a mind defiled by passion and the like. He says, "removing affliction... [to indicate] the removal of the suffering caused by the *kleśas*.

"By [the afflictions] and so forth, he is of a stainless nature. By the word "and so forth," the latent impressions (*āśaya*) of fruition are included, because those two also consist of impurity. The afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and fruition: the five afflictions are ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), and the rest; karma consists of merit and demerit; fruition (*vipāka*) consists of birth, lifespan, and experience; and latent impressions (*āśaya*) are the formative tendencies (*saṃskāra*). As it is said: "Established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering."

What was previously stated—that "he does not grieve"—is here referred to. Likewise, what was stated—that "having obtained which, he considers no other gain to be superior to that"—is here recalled as "he does not desire. Here, the variant reading *na hṛṣyati* (he does not rejoice) has not been accepted because it is not well-known. In this regard, first of all, a complete lack of thirst for external things arises through the bliss of self-realization; however, since the Supreme Self is heard in scripture to possess a bliss even greater than that of the individual self (*pratyagātman*), the desire to experience That remains firm—this is the intention behind [the statement] "other than Me..."

What is the meaning of the word *sama* (equal)? It is intended to mean that which is the cause for the non-arising of sorrow and longing; thus, with this intention, it is called "equal" (*sama*) in the sense of being unworthy of regard.

The meaning is that it is equal in its lack of regard (*anādara*). By the phrase "the entire [world]" (*nikhilam*), he reveals the fruit of the discrimination between the higher and lower reality, which is accomplished through disregard for others. By the term "the collection of things" (*vastujātam*), [he refers to] the body and so forth.

It is indicated that only those things ending with a pillar—such as beans, mustard seeds, and so forth, when compared to Mount Meru—are fit to be disregarded as insignificant internal differences. By the phrase "like grass," the intention is that one who desires to ascend a mountain of jewels would have no attachment to a heap of straw. Here, by the word "Me" (*mama*), he indicates that the forms intended are those previously elaborated for the purpose of generating and increasing supreme devotion, as well as those to be meditated upon during the stage of worship as described in other scriptures, through the words beginning with "I am the Lord of all."

Regarding the term "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*): the sense is that for one who is already the Lord of all that is to be ruled—the bound soul—what need is there for other objects to be ruled? [He is] the one whose play consists in the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe.

Thus [it is said]: "The meaning is that the Śruti says, 'But the Cause is to be meditated upon' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). Alternatively, the meaning is: while He—who is the great benefactor through the granting of the instruments and bodies, and who is the cause of the four classes of beings—remains established as the very agent of creation and dissolution, what other refuge could there be? "In whom all scent of everything to be abandoned has been dispelled": the meaning is that when He is perceived as He truly is, there is no cause for contempt or aversion toward Him, as there might be toward other things. "In the limitless," and so forth.

The meaning is this: even the excellence of each individual quality is enough to attract the mind; how much more so when they are thus combined? Furthermore, since that which is supreme and easily accessible is precisely what should be taken as a refuge, there is here a collection of qualities suitable for accessibility. The phrase "an ocean of the nectar of loveliness" (*lāvaṇyāmṛtasāgara*) is an indication of the qualities of the physical form of the auspicious refuge. Regarding the word "Śrīmatī": *Śrī* is indeed that which is to be resorted to by all; yet she herself eternally resorts to him—this is the underlying thought. The word *śrī* is etymologically explained as that which is resorted to (*śrīyate*) and that which resorts to (*śrayate*). The suffix *matup* denotes eternal connection.

And there is Śruti: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," and so forth. It is also remembered in Smṛti: "This Mother of the World, the Śrī of Viṣṇu, is eternal and inseparable. By this, it is made known that everything—such as being the object of worship and the goal to be attained—belongs to Him who is accompanied by His Consort. Those who know the Rahasyamnāya also declare this very same meaning: "His power is eternally present. The epithet "lotus-eyed" is an illustration of the beauty of His limbs. As it is said: "Just as a lotus is like the seat of a monkey, so are His eyes; 'He whose name is Ut' (the Risen One) is He."

"He has risen above all evils; indeed, he who knows thus rises above all evils"—thus, for the sake of meditation by one desiring liberation from all sins, even the state of having lotus-eyes is taught. Furthermore, in such passages as "I am purified by your gentle glance," the purifying power of His look is declared; this is the intended meaning. Regarding enjoyment, origination, and so forth, all of this is on one side, while lordship is on the other;
and with the intention that He is not a lord of everything alone, [the author] says "His own Mistress. (54)

He states the fruit of that [inquiry] with the words "tatphalam āha" (he states its fruit). The ellipsis to be supplied is "both immediate and mediate. With reference to the attribute called "Supreme Lord" (sarveśvara), which was indicated by the nature of being the cause of all things mentioned in the preceding text, he explains the meaning of the word "yaḥ" (who) as "svarūpataḥ" (by way of essential nature). The connection with those attributes that define the essential nature—which are to be contemplated in all meditations and are established by the purificatory statements consisting of injunctions and prohibitions—is indicated by the term "svabhāvataḥ" (by way of inherent nature). For in the absence of the attributes that define it, the entity would be devoid of inherent nature (niḥsvabhāva) due to its essential nature being unestablished.

"Some maintain that the word *svarūpa* refers to the property (*dharma*) that defines the essential nature, whereas the word *svabhāva* refers to ease of attainment (*saulabhya*). For the word *yāvat* is appropriately used to refer to a form that is capable of being considered as either superior or inferior.

With this intention, he says: "as far as [He is] by qualities and by manifestations, and who I am. Here, the word *guṇa* (quality) refers to the entire range of attributes, including those that define His specific nature, His knowledge, His powers, and so forth. The reversal in the order of explanation for the two phrases "as far as" (*yāvān*) and "who" (*yaḥ*) is intended to demonstrate the sequence in which they are grasped by the intellect. Since the term "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is not required in the context of "as far as" and "who," whereas it is required in the context of "he fully knows" (*abhijānāti*) in order to exclude doubt and other such errors, the phrase is construed as "he fully knows [Him] in reality."

The statement "having known Me in truth" (*māṃ tattvato jñātvā*) is made even though the previous statement was "He knows Me in truth" (*māṃ tattvato 'bhijānāti*); this is for the purpose of indicating an excellence of intensity, since even that which serves as a means is extremely difficult to attain due to its being most delicious (to the taste). Furthermore, by the very phrase "having known Me in truth," the subsequent mention of the cause—the perfection of the means—is established as a restatement intended to establish immediate sequence; for the immediate succession of the entry is explicitly stated by the words "immediately thereafter" (*tadanantaram*).

In passages such as "But by unswerving devotion... (18.55), since devotion itself was previously stated to be the cause even for entry, the syntactical connection shown there is simply "he enters Me through devotion. The form "praveṣṭum" (to enter) was used previously to indicate its identity with what was said before, while "praviśati" (he enters) is used here to establish the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). Knowledge as it truly is also belongs to one whose devotion has reached its ultimate limit. And the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is avoided by the distinction between the stages of devotion.

He states, with the words beginning "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), that such a state alone is the direct means to liberation. By using the word "vision" (*darśana*) to refer back to [the term] "knows in reality," he indicates that the phrase "knows in reality" has the sense of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). With the word "here" (*atra*), he refutes the view of the wicked who hold that even through supreme devotion (*parabhakti*), the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone is the goal, and that this alone is the direct means to liberation. The particle "eva" (alone) serves to exclude mere vision.

Although the word "devotion" (bhakti) is separated [from the verb] here, while the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is not, nevertheless, it is more appropriate to refer back to the separated term; otherwise, there would be the consequence of redundancy with the phrase "having known in truth" (tattvato jñātvā) and so forth. Since there is no purpose in merely restating the devotion that produces vision, the meaning is that that very [devotion] in its subsequent state is what is being referred to. He states the reason already mentioned: "But by devotion through exclusive [devotion]" (bhaktyā tvananyayā). This is the intention: according to the principle of the opening statement (upakrama-nyāya), the earlier [term] is stronger; and between the explicit and the implicit, the other should be understood in accordance with the explicit. ||55||

To dispel the doubt that "in the preceding [chapter] the steadfastness in knowledge was taught, whereas hereafter the steadfastness in action is being taught," he states the connection by reiterating the specific stages of development within steadfastness in action itself even in the previous section, saying "thus. Here, "development" (vipāka) refers to the process culminating in supreme devotion, supreme knowledge, and ultimate devotion, as described in the two preceding verses.

Since it was previously stated that "all actions" (*sarvakarmāṇi*) refers to prescribed duties (*vihitakarman*), [the author] now refutes the view of Śaṅkara and others—who maintain that this is a mere suggestion intended to praise non-duality with the Lord by implying the performance of even prohibited acts—by saying, "Now, even of those actions performed for desire" (*kāmyānām api karmaṇām*). The intention is that the word "all" (*sarva*) here is meant to include all scriptural duties not explicitly mentioned. He explains this very point with the words "not only... (*na kevalam...*) and so forth.
With the intent that the very goal mentioned in the previous verse is here indicated by the term *pada* along with its qualification, he explains it as "that which is reached" (*padyate*). (56)

He says, "Because of this very [reason]," to state that the fact of being the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) is the reason for the instruction on the subsequent method. To ensure the word "mind" (*cetas*) is not redundant, he explains the manner in which the mind is intended to effect the renunciation of action toward the Blessed One: "by realizing one's own belonging to Me and My being subject to control. Here, he establishes the intended meaning of the word "mind" through the mention of its preceding qualifications, stating: "with a mind directed toward the Self" (*adhyātmacetasā*).

The meaning is: "by means of a cognition whose object is the Self as qualified by being the remainder of another, and so forth. By the word "all" (sarva), not only completeness in its own nature (*svarūpa-kārtsnya*) but also completeness in its adjuncts (*anubandhi-kārtsnya*) is intended in the manner previously stated; thus he says, "having agents and worthy of worship. He states that by the term "yoga of the intellect" (*buddhi-yoga*), everything—the non-agency, contemplation, and so forth—that is unique to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is made known through recognition; thus he says, "this very yoga of the intellect."

In the verse beginning with "With the mind fixed on Me (mañcittaḥ) [cross over all difficulties]," the word *mañcitta* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what was already mentioned in the previous verse; furthermore, since that [previous] passage is intent upon enjoining action characterized by a particular state of intellect, and since in the subsequent passages as well there is a clear encouragement toward one's own duty known as battle, the author here also expresses that same intention: "Thus, with the mind fixed on Me, performing all actions. The underlying sense is that if merely being "fixed on Me" were the thing enjoined, then the subsequent rejection of the notion that one should desist from battle would not be coherent.

Because the word *durga* (fortress) is most commonly known to refer to fortresses consisting of mountains, forests, water, and so forth, and because it is possible for a Kṣatriya like Arjuna—who is desirous of battle—to require the crossing of such [physical] obstacles, [the author] has specified the term as "pertaining to worldly existence" (*sāṃsārikāṇi*) in order to dispel even the suspicion that it might refer to those [physical ones]. By the phrase "by my grace" (*matprasādāt*), he intends to indicate the exclusion of the postulation of an unseen force (*apūrva*) and the like—which would contradict the rules of etymology, the Vedas, and the Smṛtis—and to show that He requires nothing more than the removal of obstacles in His own bestowing of the fruit. With this intention, he says: "By my grace alone."

Thus, having established that actions—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—which are termed *karmayoga* through their connection with specific mental dispositions, discipline, and so forth, have as their ultimate fruit the attainment of the Supreme Lord through a gradual succession, it is concluded that *karmayoga* alone must be performed by you in every way. Then, with the half-verse beginning "But if," He speaks of the transgression incurred by failing to perform it.

He describes a specific form of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) which serves as the cause for disregarding beneficial words: "on account of the thought, 'I alone know everything regarding what ought and ought not to be done. Regarding the phrase "you will not listen," the intention is that even when it is being heard, there is an intent to avoid the fruit of hearing it. With the intention that by the word "you will perish" (*vinaṅkṣyasi*), he wishes to express the continuation of the self-destruction—which has persisted since beginningless time—even in the future, he says: "you will become destroyed. The sense is that this is a reference back to what was previously stated: "through the destruction of wisdom, one perishes."

In order to set aside the possibility that [the teaching] originated from another authoritative person due to causes such as not having heard it, and to avoid the implication that the statement "you shall perish" is merely like a curse, he expresses his intention regarding the establishment of the truth of what he has taught by declaring himself to be the most authoritative: "For there is no one... For other speakers whom I have encountered speak only of limited subjects; I, however, am the knower of all kinds of benefit and harm for every qualified person.
The meaning is that even those scriptures spoken by others and those meters not mentioned here are authoritative solely because they take the form of my command. ||58||
